article.title: SEC Fines 4 Companies $7M for Downplaying Breaches Tied to Massive SolarWinds Hack
article.description: The agency said Unisys, Avaya Holdings, Check Point Software Technologies and Mimecast provided misleading disclosures about the incidents, leaving investors in the dark about their "true scope."
article.text: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has levied civil penalties totaling nearly $7 million against four companies it alleges misled investors about their cybersecurity risks and downplayed intrusions into their systems by the same hackers behind the SolarWinds attack. In an order Tuesday, the SEC said Unisys Corp., Avaya Holdings Corp., Check Point Software Technologies and Mimecast all filed public disclosures that "minimized" cybersecurity incidents likely related to SolarWinds. The order follows the regulator's yearslong investigation into public companies affected by the SolarWinds breach in 2020, which ranks among the most devastating cyberattacks ever, compromising thousands of SolarWinds customers, including major companies and government agencies. The attack, known as Sunburst, is widely believed to have been carried out by hackers affiliated with the Russian intelligence service. Investigators say they pulled it off by covertly inserting malicious code into SolarWinds' flagship Orion software, which spread to the company's customers through a routine software update. The SEC began issuing sweep letters to potential SolarWinds hack victims back in 2021, and is currently suing the company and its security chief Tim Brown for civil fraud. "As today's enforcement actions reflect, while public companies may become targets of cyberattacks, it is incumbent upon them to not further victimize their shareholders or other members of the investing public by providing misleading disclosures about the cybersecurity incidents they have encountered," Sanjay Wadhwa, acting director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement, said in a statement Tuesday. "Here, the SEC's orders find that these companies provided misleading disclosures about the incidents at issue, leaving investors in the dark about the true scope of the incidents." Unisys, Avaya and Check Point all learned in 2020 and Mimecast learned in January 2021 that their systems had been accessed by a threat actor "likely behind the SolarWinds Orion hack," the SEC said. All four companies went about disclosing the incidents in different ways, though they all kept investors in the dark about the scope of the intrusions, the SEC alleges. The regulator said all four cooperated with the SEC's investigation and took voluntary steps to improve their cybersecurity controls. Unisys, which agreed to pay a $4 million civil penalty, described its cybersecurity risks from two SolarWinds-related intrusions as hypothetical, "despite knowing that it had experienced two SolarWinds-related intrusions involving exfiltration of gigabytes of data." "Downplaying the extent of a material cybersecurity breach is a bad strategy," Jorge Tenreiro, acting chief of the SEC's Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit, said in a statement. "In two of these cases, the relevant cybersecurity risk factors were framed hypothetically or generically when the companies knew the warned of risks had already materialized. The federal securities laws prohibit half-truths, and there is no exception for statements in risk-factor disclosures." Unisys referred Law.com to an 8-k it filed Tuesday announcing that it had resolved the matter, and declined to comment further. The SEC also said Avaya knew the hacker had accessed at least 145 files in its cloud-based file-sharing environment but stated only that it had accessed a "limited number of [the] company's email messages." Avaya will pay a $1 million penalty under the SEC's order. Check Point, which will pay $995,000, described its risks from intrusions in "generic terms," and Mimecast, which was fined $990,000, failed to reveal the specifics of the exfiltrated code or the number of encrypted credentials that were accessed by the threat actor. In an email, an Avaya spokesperson said the company is pleased to have resolved the matter and highlighted its cooperation with the SEC. "Avaya continues to focus on strengthening its cybersecurity program, both in designing and providing our products and services to our valued customers, as well as in our internal operations," the spokesperson added. Check Point, an Israeli company, noted in an email that the company disclosed last year that it was in settlement discussions with the SEC after cooperating with its investigation into whether it should have reported its 2020 intrusion in its annual report in 2021. "As mentioned in the SEC's order, Check Point investigated the SolarWinds incident and did not find evidence that any customer data, code, or other sensitive information was accessed," a spokesperson told Law.com. "Nevertheless, Check Point decided that cooperating and settling the dispute with the SEC was in its best interest and allows the company to maintain its focus on helping its customers defend against cyberattacks throughout the world." A spokesperson for London-based Mimecast told Law.com that it made "extensive" disclosures after learning of an intrusion in January 2021, "and engaged with our customers and partners proactively and transparently, even those who were not affected." The spokesperson said the company "believed that we complied with our disclosure obligations based on the regulatory requirements at that time," but "as we responded to the incident, Mimecast took the opportunity to enhance our resilience." The spokesperson noted that while Mimecast is no longer publicly traded, "we have cooperated fully and extensively with the SEC. We resolved this matter to put it behind us and continue to maintain our strong focus on serving our customers." The SEC enforcement actions come as companies grapple with new SEC rules demanding prompt disclosure of material cyberattacks and annual reports about cyber risks and vulnerabilities. The rules, which took effect in mid-December, are intended to help investors better understand how companies are managing and responding to cybersecurity risks by requiring companies to describe "material" cybersecurity incidents within four business days of making that determination. But companies say the SEC has given them little direction about the level of detail the SEC expects, and early filings have been mostly cursory. article.title: 'Risk Management Is a Team Sport': What GCs Should Learn From Uber Cybersecurity Verdict
article.description: "The CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is," said Donna Gallaher, a data privacy risk adviser.
article.text: The October conviction of former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for concealing a 2016 data breach from government regulators sent ripples of anxiety through the C-suite over the prospect of more executives being held personally liable after a hack. At a recent panel on what the verdict means for corporate security and legal teams, the consensus was that Sullivan's prosecution was unusual, and his actions egregious. But while companies shouldn't panic, general counsel and security chiefs should band together to tackle cybersecurity incidents with transparency and open communication. "Cyber and privacy is a companywide concern, and that includes the board of directors, all the way down the line," said Cari Robinson, a cybersecurity expert and former Revlon general counsel. "Teamwork is critical. If I don't have a collaborative, transparent and open relationship with my CIO, my CISO, I'm not going to be able to give advice to the company or ultimately to the board of directors." The panel, hosted by the woman-led market network Fourth Floor and moderated by founder Breen Sullivan, also included virtual chief security officer and data privacy risk adviser Donna Gallaher and ClearOPS founder Caroline McCaffery. Robinson, who also headed cybersecurity investigations as an assistant general counsel at IBM, said general counsel should have an "open and collaborative" relationship with security chiefs so that they can fully understand the incident and how to best advise the CEO on what the company's response should be. Sullivan's conviction may have shaken the cybersecurity community, but Robinson said the government is unlikely to turn its sights on executives who act in good faith. Where Sullivan and Uber went wrong, she said, was in confining their handling of the breach to just a handful of top executives, including then-CEO Travis Kalanick, while keeping the general counsel and Uber's legal department in the dark. "It was an easy situation for the government to make an example of," Robinson said. Gallaher said she was struck by the apparent communication gap between Sullivan and Uber's general counsel at the time, Salle Yoo. Rather than keep Yoo in the loop, Sullivan decided, after consulting with another Uber in-house lawyer, that the hack was not disclosable. That lawyer, Craig Clark, also kept the breach from the general counsel and was given immunity for testifying against Sullivan. "Risk management is a team sport," Gallaher said. "And as much as the attorney is playing chess while the CISOs are playing checkers when it comes to navigating the legal processes and how to maneuver the legal system, the CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is." She said general counsel should cultivate a strong relationship with their company's security chief as a hedge against risk. "Some people might be looking at the Uber case as a general counsel and seeing the CISO got a criminal conviction and thinking, 'That kind of sucks for him.' Well, it's going to suck for you if you end up having to have to do battle with the CISO, who has more technical expertise than you do," Gallaher said. "So just get ahead of that now. Make that person your friend." Legal and security chiefs may speak different languages, but should work together to understand the facts of an incident, Robinson said. "If you told me, 'There's an intrusion in the system and we're in trouble because they have access to all of our stuff,' I'd have to ask you a million questions about what happened, how did it happen, can it be stopped, et cetera. So if you're not having those discussions, then you're not going to be able to make a good decision for the company." Uber was criticized back in 2016 for a lax culture around security that led to two similar data breaches within two years. As cyberattacks grow in sophistication and frequency, Robinson said executives will need to speak up when they spot issues, or walk away from a toxic company culture. "If you find yourself as a CISO or general counsel in an environment that is so toxic that you raise an issue and you're just told to go away and be quiet, and if you don't feel like you can change that culture by opening up the lines of communication, you know what? Free legal advice: Leave," she said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. article.title: Bill Would Unleash Hackers to Hunt for Federal Contractors' Cybersecurity Flaws
article.description: Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems.
article.text: Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems. Vulnerability disclosure policies have been a requirement for federal agencies, along with smartphone, laptop and other device manufacturers and suppliers, since 2020. A bill working its way through Congress, the Federal Cybersecurity Vulnerability Reduction Act,, will expand the VDP requirement to all private companies that contract with the government. The lawmaker behind the bill, Rep. Nancy Mace, R-South Carolina, said in a statement that the measure would help shore up the government's digital infrastructure by ensuring a "proactive approach to cybersecurity" and "enabling contractors to identify and address software vulnerabilities promptly." Contractors would have to follow guidelines for setting up VDPs established earlier this year by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. "This legislation, aligned with internationally recognized standards, empowers contractors to stay ahead of malicious actors, preventing potential exploits and protecting sensitive information," said Mace, chair of the House Oversight and Accountability Committee's cybersecurity, information technology and government innovation subcommittee. The bill is supported by HackerOne, a cyberattack-resistance platform and marketplace that matches hackers with companies and facilitates bug bounty payments for ethical hackers. Unlike bug bounties, a more mature cybersecurity program that pays hackers who find vulnerabilities and gives them express permission to do their testing, VDPs mostly provide hackers an avenue for reporting security weaknesses. HackerOne chief legal officer Ilona Cohen said hackers, who take great pride in being able to spot security flaws, are already looking for them in corporate systems. "This work is already being done. People are already looking at these systems. The question is, do you want to create an avenue by which they can report it to you, or would you rather have them tweet it? Personally, I'd rather the former," she said. Cohen, a former legal adviser to President Barack Obama and general counsel of the Office of Management and Budget during the Obama administration, said VDPs are one of most effective ways to fix security flaws and head off cyberattacks. Back in 2015, Cohen's office helped oversee the response to one of the largest data breaches in government history, where hackers posed as posed as an employee of a contractor used by government agencies to perform background checks. "That resulted in a billion records being compromised and 20 million personnel records being compromised. The way the hackers entered the system was through contractors to the agencies," she said. "So if you want to protect these sites, you really have to shore up cybersecurity through all entry points." The Department of Defense already has already embraced the policy, partnering with HackerOne on a pilot program that encouraged hackers to detect software vulnerabilities in its defense industrial base. Cohen said the Defense Department and the participating contractors "were surprised at the number of vulnerabilities identified in their systems and found it quite useful to be able to mitigate and respond to those. Expanding that will be very important to national security." Mace's bill, assigned to the House Armed Services Committee and House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, comes at a time of accelerating cyberattacks targeting a broader swath of companies. "The threat landscape is definitely evolving and it is becoming more sophisticated. They have professionalized ransomware attacks and it can be hugely disruptive to companies," Cohen said. "So the best solution is to prevent it from happening in the first place." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. article.title: US Judge Disinclined to Overturn Former Uber Security Chief's Conviction in Data Breach Case
article.description: "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in 2016
article.text: A federal judge said Wednesday that he's inclined to uphold a jury verdict finding former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan guilty of trying to cover up a 2016 data breach, a conviction that rocked the cybersecurity community in October. Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Dawson said Sullivan orchestrated the cover-up and hid it from both his employers and the Federal Trade Commission, which was investigating Uber's data security practices in the wake of a different data breach in 2014. Sullivan met with Federal Trade Commission regulators investigating Uber's security practices in 2016, assuring them that Uber had addressed the security vulnerabilities that led up to the 2014 breach, such as reusing passwords and storing data access keys on a public GitHub page. Just 10 days later, hackers breached Uber's AWS servers a second time in a similar fashion. Dawson said that knowing the second hack would "play very badly" with regulators, Sullivan bought the two hackers off with a payment of $100,000 and funneled it through Uber's bug-bounty program. "Sullivan knew exactly what he had done. He covered up a data breach, he covered up a crime and he obstructed the FTC's effort to safeguard user data," Dawson told the jury, describing Sullivan's actions as "comprehensive and calculated." Sullivan also signed off on a letter proposing that the FTC close its two-year investigation and enter into a settlement agreement. "Joe was supportive of proceeding with the recommendation to settle," former in-house attorney Sabrina Ross testified at the trial. Sullivan was fired in 2017, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at trial. In 2020 the ex-security chief was charged with one count of obstructing the FTC's investigation and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. His prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach. Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts specializing in cybersecurity and incident response, said it is rare for the government to charge someone with taking affirmative steps to conceal a felony, but prosecutors could feel emboldened by Sullivan's conviction. "The fact that it was used here—and used successfully—should make any in-house counsel for any company perk their ears up," Baker told ALM. "There's a very interesting legal precedent that will create ripples from a compliance perspective." At a hearing Wednesday on Sullivan's motion for acquittal or a new trial, his attorney John Cline argued that the government failed to show Sullivan had a duty to disclose the breach, and that prosecutors made only a general contention that Uber's in-house counsel relied on Sullivan and his team to keep them updated on any significant security developments that would require disclosure. U.S. District Judge William Orrick, who presided over the nearly monthlong jury trial in September, was unconvinced. "I think there was more than sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction," he said. Dawson said there was much more to Sullivan's obstructive actions than mere omission. "There's misrepresentation, there's concealment, there's hush money, there's a variety of obstructive acts and the Ninth Circuit has recognized the variety with which obstruction can be accomplished," he said. "I would urge the court not to get caught up in just the omission slice. There was a more comprehensive strategy rather than sitting in a corner and staying silent." Cline said he plans to appeal the conviction and will likely rely on the Ninth Circuit's recent ruling in United States v. Kirst to support the argument that Sullivan did not make affirmative misrepresentations to the FTC, and that simply failing to inform authorities of the breach is not enough to support a conviction. "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," he told Orrick. The judge replied, "well-flexed," and took the arguments under submission. "There's misrepresentation, there's concealment, there's hush money, there's a variety of obstructive acts and the Ninth Circuit has recognized the variety with which obstruction can be accomplished," he said. "I would urge the court not to get caught up in just the omission slice. There was a more comprehensive strategy rather than sitting in a corner and staying silent."

Cline said he plans to appeal the conviction and will likely rely on the Ninth Circuit's recent ruling in United States v. Kirst to support the argument that Sullivan did not make affirmative misrepresentations to the FTC, and that simply failing to inform authorities of the breach is not enough to support a conviction.

"We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," he told Orrick.

The judge replied, "well-flexed," and took the arguments under submission.

article.title: Ex-Uber Security Chief Appeals Conviction That Shook Cybersecurity World
article.description: "Joe Sullivan used tools and strategies that all CISOs utilize to protect the data of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers, and was prosecuted for doing his job," Sullivan's appeals attorney said
article.text: Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan is appealing his conviction for covering up a 2016 data breach and obstructing a regulator's investigation into Uber's security practices. Sullivan was sentenced in May to three years of probation following a nearly monthlong jury trial in 2022. He faced up to eight years in prison for obstructing the Federal Trade Commission's ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices and misprision of a felony, a rare charge that involves taking active steps to conceal a crime. His indictment in 2020—considered the first time prosecutors had sought to hold a tech executive criminally liable in a data breach—sent shockwaves through the field of cybersecurity, raising anxiety among chief information security officers that responses to breaches at their own companies could land them in prison. At Sullivan's sentencing, U.S. District Judge William Orrick said the unique nature of the case, as well as Sullivan's strong character, weighed heavily in his decision not to sentence Sullivan to prison time. "I hope everyone in the CISO community takes this as a lesson, and not leniency," Orrick said. Uber hired Sullivan, a widely respected fixture in the security world, to help strengthen its data security after a similar data breach in 2014. Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Sullivan said he knew the breach would be embarrassing for Uber if it were made public. Just days before, he'd given a lengthy deposition to the Federal Trade Commission on Uber's progress in tightening security as part of the regulator's continuing investigation into the 2014 incident. So he chose to deal with the situation quietly, paying the two hackers $100,000 in Bitcoin through Uber's white hat bug bounty program while continuing to help Uber's in-house legal team negotiate a settlement that would bring the regulatory agency's investigation to a close. Along with in-house attorney Craig Clark, who got immunity in exchange for his testimony, Sullivan pursued an aggressive legal theory that they believed would settle the matter without having to report the breach to the FTC. Sullivan is being represented by Orrick partner Aravind Swaminathan, who in a statement to Law.com said Sullivan "used tools and strategies that all CISOs utilize to protect the data of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers, and was prosecuted for doing his job." Sullivan's appeal, filed late Tuesday in the Ninth Circuit, says prosecutors built their case on "innuendo," asking the jury to view Uber's bug bounty program "not as an effective way to protect users, but as hush money. It faulted Mr. Sullivan for not directing Uber's legal department to notify the FTC (a job for Uber's CEO, if anyone), and for not editing submissions to the FTC that Mr. Sullivan had not drafted, signed, and in some instances even read. The government theorized, without proof, that Mr. Sullivan was motivated by a need to protect his own reputation as a cybersecurity professional." Swaminathan said Sullivan's conviction sets a dangerous precedent for other security chiefs who fear they may be targeted for prosecution based on their handling of data breaches. "The misprision conviction—a charge rarely brought by federal prosecutors—criminalized the Uber security team's use of their world-class and leading Bug Bounty program to protect the personal information of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers," he said. Swaminathan also described the obstruction charge as "profoundly flawed," saying: "Despite the fact that Mr. Sullivan was not responsible at Uber for the FTC's investigation, including the drafting or signing any of the submissions to the FTC, the government singled him out among over 30 of his co-employees who all had information that Mr. Sullivan is alleged to have hidden from the FTC." He added that Sullivan "sets a dangerous precedent for CISOs and CIOs, who now fear criminal liability anytime there is any investigation by any government authority that touches the information technology or security of their company." The case had divided the cybersecurity community—with critics saying he acted selfishly to protect his own reputation and avoid more regulatory scrutiny but supporters calling the government's case overreach. "Joe is being punished for something that actually happens all the time and for which we don't have good legal guidance," former Facebook security chief Alex Stamos said during a webinar in March, two months before Sullivan's sentencing. Since the sentencing, Sullivan has gone on a speaking tour about what other security chiefs can glean from his case, as cyberattacks continue to grow in frequency and sophistication. "I've had a lot of opportunities to talk with security leaders about my case," he told an audience of security professionals at DEF-CON in August. "They often reach out to me when they're getting nervous because they have a bunch of lawyers showing up to their meetings or they're getting together in closed rooms. "So I've a lot of chances to talk with security leaders to talk about what my case might mean for them and how they can set up their organizations and relationship with the government to be better so that what happened to me doesn't happen to them," Sullivan said He said one thing that worries him about his case is that requests for money from an outside security researcher are often viewed as extortion, especially with the ubiquity of ransomware. "This is an issue that comes up on a daily basis, especially with new programs and especially with new researchers. We also want to create an ecosystem where companies feel comfortable engaging with those researchers," Sullivan said. "One of my biggest disappointments from the case is I think I set that backward because of how this case was perceived and how those researchers' slash hackers were perceived." Sullivan said he heard stories of companies rolling back bug bounty programs and "their lawyers getting very anxious about them" in the year since his conviction. Meanwhile, he said security professionals fear their companies may not honor the responsible disclosure commitments that assure security researchers that they won't be referred for prosecution. "I think we really need to look at cases like this from the perspective of the researcher, and I feel like it's hurt things a lot, from everything I've heard," Sullivan said. "We need to get more proactive in communication about the realities and expectations between the public, researchers and companies. We need to get better at having consistent, shorter policies. I still don't know what the guidance for people is for this unauthorized access question … where do you draw these lines. It's not as clear as it should be." article.title: California High Court Holds AI Vendors Liable for Biased Job Screening
article.description: California's highest court has handed down a landmark ruling with major implications for the AI industry: making vendors that use algorithms to perform other employment-related tasks for other companies directly liable for discrimination.
article.text: California's highest court has handed down a landmark ruling with major implications for the AI industry: making vendors that use algorithms to target job ads, screen out applicants or perform other employment-related tasks for other companies directly liable for discrimination under state law. "The major impact of this is with outsourcing, and that's what a lot of companies are doing for a lot of their employment-related functions," said attorney Randy Erlewine of the San Francisco law firm Phillips, Erlewine, Given & Carlin. "Everyone is being hired these days online, and you've got these major third-party platforms that may have discriminatory biases or metrics, and the employer may not know it is discriminatory." Erlewine represented Kristina Raines in a class action lawsuit against U.S. Healthworks Medical Group, a company that contracts with employers to perform medical screenings of job candidates. Raines's job offer was revoked after she refused to answer a health history survey riddled with questions she considered intrusive about venereal diseases, menstrual cycles, pregnancy and mental illness. Raines settled with her prospective employer, Front Porch Communities and Services, but also went after U.S. Healthworks. After a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, the Ninth Circuit asked the high court to weigh in on whether California's Fair Housing and Employment Act permits a "business entity acting as an agent of an employer to be held directly liable for employment discrimination." The court on Aug. 21 ruled unanimously that it does. "[W]e recognize as a necessary minimum that, consistent with the FEHA's language and purpose, a business-entity agent can bear direct FEHA liability only when it carries out FEHA-regulated activities on behalf of an employer," Justice Martin Jenkins wrote for the court. Amanda Herron, an attorney in San Diego with Gordon Rees Scully Manusukhani, said the ruling has the potential to impact a variety of industries, from recruiting and background checks to HR and consulting. "Previously, the job applicant who claimed they were discriminated against, their only recourse was to sue the prospective employer directly. Now the California Supreme Court is saying that prospective employers were always on the hook, but now their agents can also be sued," she said. "We can't say for sure what the impact is going to be yet, but it seems like it will double the amount of defendants who can be named in these FEHA suits." Herron said the ruling is a departure from the court's prior decisions where it declined to hold individuals acting on behalf of their employers liable for discrimination under FEHA. But in this case, the court reasoned, business entities with five or more employees are "more likely than an employee agent to have comparable bargaining power to the employer." Companies like U.S. Healthworks operate on national scale. U.S. Healthworks performed 200,000 medical screenings last year, just in California. "These third parties have the expertise to make that portion of the employment related function either cost effective or more expedited. And from a public policy standpoint, they should be the primary ones to bear the cost," Erlewine said. "The employer should be happy for this. If the employer is innocent and in good faith outsourced to a party that was responsible for violating discrimination statutes, that third party is going to be liable." Employers are still on the hook for discrimination, though companies can negotiate "the question of indemnification regarding any potential FEHA liability that might arise." Companies will likely have to re-negotiate their vendor contracts to spread around liability, said Matthew Roberts, an employment law counsel with the California Chamber of Commerce. "What the employer might be able to do here is say, 'If you end up doing something that violates FEHA, we want an indemnity provision here where if we get sued you're paying for it all,'" he said. The ruling also will have a nationwide impact, as business agents need only to work with California companies, not employ California workers themselves, for the law to apply to them. "This is going to be one more impediment when it comes to doing business in California," said Niloy Ray, a shareholder at the labor and employment law firm Littler Mendelson. Ray said the cost of litigating the potential flood of new employment discrimination cases will also rise along with the pool of defendants. "As it stands, it creates joint and several liability, and that's a massive outcome," he said. "Whether or not you have indemnity provisions or other financial arrangements in terms of who ultimately bears the cost, the cost of litigation for all of those entities has just increased. Now you have multiple entities and each has their own insurance company, and it becomes more complicated to figure out who will be ultimately responsible for those costs." The ruling comes as state legislators and policymakers grapple with what role government should play in regulating the use of automated tools that use algorithms to make decisions about employment, health care and insurance eligibility. One proposed law that would have prohibited developers from using tools that results in algorithmic discrimination, was scuttled in the State Assembly this year. The California's Civil Rights Council is also working on regulations addressing the use of AI and machine learning algorithms in employment decisions. The council's proposed regulations have gone through two revisions this year, and is still be hashed out. "Some of that extreme breadth has been scaled back, but not to the point where we're back to just the end user being liable," Ray said. The Raines decision, Ray said, bolsters the idea that both AI vendors and the companies with which they contract will share liability for discrimination. "Think of this liability as a wall that's being built. Many of the bricks are already in place because of the proposed revisions, and this just adds more bricks to the wall." article.title: Supercomputers Soon Will Crack Encryption. Is Your Company Ready?
article.description: Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet.
article.text: Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet. The Cloud Security Alliance's countdown to "Y2Q" clock will hit zero in 2030, the same year the U.S. Department of Homeland Security predicts that a quantum breakthrough will occur, posing a new threat to the means by which companies secure their customer data, business transactions and confidential communications. The upshot is catastrophic, and affects all data in transit. Everything from internal company emails and Slack messages to health and bank records are at stake, said Rebecca Krauthamer, founder and chief product officer at quantum cybersecurity software firm QuSecure. "Any time you're communicating with somebody else, 99% of the time that's vulnerable," she said. "Any time data is traveling over the internet is when it's at risk." ChatGPT, like any other application, is also at risk of attack. "ChatGPT, that's an application where you're sending and receiving data, so anything you put in ChatGPT is this kind of data that is quantum vulnerable as well." she said, adding that at a recent talk the CIA's chief technology officer likened the potential for breaches to a "potential quantum WikiLeaks." Krauthamer said the timeline for quantum computing is accelerating, citing IBM's ambitious plan for scaling quantum systems. The company says it expects to unveil a 4,158 qubit processor by 2025. Krauthamer said it takes about 4,000 qubits of computing power to break the equivalent of today's encryption. The United States, China, and other foreign governments are also pumping billions of dollars into quantum development. While it remains to be seen when quantum computers will come online, stewards of sensitive data should start preparing for a post-quantum world now, rather than wait for that day to come. Researchers have known about the looming quantum threat since the 1990s, when mathematician Peter Shor demonstrated that quantum computers could do the complex math required to break a widely used encryption method called RSA, named after inventors Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman. RSA is an asymmetric cryptography algorithm, explained technologist Donna Dodson, former director of the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence. "You have a public key and a private key, and they're mathematically related keys. One is used to lock the door, and the other to unlock the door. Public key cryptography is designed to authenticate who I am and who I claim to be. It's used to create a digital signature which says this message comes from me and nobody else and hasn't been altered since I signed it digitally." Quantum computers will enable digital miscreants to factor large numbers much easier than with classic computers, enabling them to access public and private keys and intercept data traveling between points. "This has been a known problem from a long time, but we've moved from theory more to practice," Dodson said. "A lot of public key infrastructure is based on RSA. That all falls and goes away and it ends up being a really big deal." Krauthamer said the most vulnerable data tends to have a longer shelf life, such as legal and financial records. "The people that have to get ahead of it are in heavily regulated industries," she said, such as health care, finance and insurance—fields where personal information needs to be protected for a number of years. Otherwise, she said, "you have both a confidentially and an integrity problem." For example, she said, "Let's say you use the RSA algorithm, which is a popular algorithm to sign something. But if the RSA algorithm breaks and somebody else can figure out my private key from my published public key they can reverse the math using a quantum computer. Then they can sign as 'Donna Dodson' all day long. They can put a document out there and say 'Donna Dodson signed this in 2023,' and it's now 2030 and I can't prove that I didn't." One type of attack called "harvest now, decrypt later," involves bad actors collecting encrypted data they can sit on and wait to decrypt at their leisure. Paul Fuegner, head of marketing at QuSecure, said there are a variety of criminal and nefarious actors interested in stealing and decrypting that data, including foreign nation states. "Nation states may want to get into state secrets or the secrets of other organizations or companies. It could be for defense purposes or ideological reasons, or they may be looking to make a power play to change the dynamics globally." Another bad actor, of course, is thieves. "From your personal data—like your PIN number to get into your bank account to the nuclear codes, it spans that spectrum" of data that can be exposed, he said. Recognizing the prospect of attack from foreign adversaries, the White House put out memos in recent years mandating that government agencies upgrade their systems. Last December, Congress passed the Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act, which requires the government to take inventory of its cryptographic systems and update the most at risk. "After 11 federal agencies were hacked by agents of Russia and China in 2020, we must do all we can to strengthen and protect our nation's systems and keep our data secure," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-South Carolina, said in a statement following its passage out of the House of Representatives. Dodson said that in concert with the global cryptographic community, the National Institute of Standards and Technology has identified replacement algorithms for key management and digital signature. NIST is still working on standards for these algorithms, which it plans to release in 2024. "There's more work to be done," she said. "These new cryptographic algorithms have to be secure against the threat of quantum computers, but we're going to live in a world where there are quantum and classical computers together. These algorithms have to be secure against quantum and classical computers. People forget that second part of the equation." But it's not all doom and gloom, Dodson said. "The sliver lining in my mind here is the opportunity to create a more resilient cryptographic platform that allows for new algorithms and new key management capabilities to come into play." This kind of resiliency can be costly, she said, but it's still cheaper than a catastrophic breach, as "advances can come from math and information theory that could cost your crypto infrastructure." In an era when companies in highly regulated industries are demanding more elaborate security measures, Krauthamer said organizations shouldn't wait to start migrating to post-quantum cryptography. "With this level of breach that can and will happen, you can't afford to take a wait-and-see approach if you are managing sensitive data," she said. "It's almost hard to process this scale of what this kind of breach could look like. But it's important to realize it's a solved problem, we just have to get ahead of it. You just need some software to fix this." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. The Cloud Security Alliance's countdown to "Y2Q" clock will hit zero in 2030, the same year the U.S. Department of Homeland Security predicts that a quantum breakthrough will occur, posing a new threat to the means by which companies secure their customer data, business transactions and confidential communications.

The upshot is catastrophic, and affects all data in transit. Everything from internal company emails and Slack messages to health and bank records are at stake, said Rebecca Krauthamer, founder and chief product officer at quantum cybersecurity software firm QuSecure. "Any time you're communicating with somebody else, 99% of the time that's vulnerable," she said. "Any time data is traveling over the internet is when it's at risk."

ChatGPT, like any other application, is also at risk of attack. "ChatGPT, that's an application where you're sending and receiving data, so anything you put in ChatGPT is this kind of data that is quantum vulnerable as well." she said, adding that at a recent talk the CIA's chief technology officer likened the potential for breaches to a "potential quantum WikiLeaks."

article.title: International Regulators' Unease With AI Data-Scraping Creates Gulf With US
article.description: International privacy regulators are calling on social media giants to protect their users' publicly available information from web-scraping, a common business practice in the U.S., but one that in other jurisdictions could constitute a data breach.
article.text: International privacy regulators are calling on social media giants to protect their users' publicly available information from web-scraping, a common business practice in the United States, but one that in other jurisdictions could constitute a reportable data breach. "Social media companies have obligations under U.K. data protection law to protect the information people post on their platforms," said Stephen Bonner, head Britain's top privacy watchdog, the Information Commissioner's Office. "We are seeing increased reports of mass data-scraping from social media and remind organisations that such incidents may require reporting to the ICO as a personal data breach." ICO was joined by 11 other data protection authorities from China, Australia, Switzerland, Norway, Jersey, New Zealand, Colombia, Argentina, Mexico and Morocco in a statement that Bonner said should help provide "certainty, and consistency across borders, in how data protection applies to information people post online." It's also a warning that companies must have a lawful reason for collecting personal data, even when it is publicly available. Social media platforms and website operators that host publicly accessible personal data have certain obligations with respect to third-party data-scraping, the statement says. "These obligations will generally apply to personal information whether that information is publicly accessible or not. Mass data-scraping of personal information can constitute a reportable data breach in many jurisdictions." The statement was sent directly to companies running the world's major social media platforms; Alphabet, Meta, ByteDance, Weibo, Microsoft and X Corp. The watchdogs say they are worried about identity fraud, spam marketing, and profiling and surveillance by authorities, and targeted cyberattacks carried about by malicious actors using swathes of personal data posted to hacking forums. Scraped data can also be exploited by foreign governments and intelligence agencies, or harvested without permission for dubious purposes, as with British consulting firm Cambridge Analytica, whose misuse of Facebook data for targeted political advertising triggered one of the most infamous data scandals in recent history. Privacy regulators outlined an array of measures companies should take to mitigate these risks, including cracking down on bots, limiting the number of times per day that an account can visit other account profiles, and dedicating in-house teams to monitor and respond to scraping activity. In an interview with Law.com, privacy scholar Omer Tene, a Goodwin Procter partner and senior fellow at the Future of Privacy Forum, said the statement reflects the attitude "that access to information, even if it's publicly available, if it's done at scale could lead to different harms." It also comes amid a surging commercial demand for data to train and machine learning algorithms and the attendant fight over data ownership. As lawsuits against AI companies alleging copyright and privacy violations pile up, social media platforms are looking to courts to prevent data-scrapers from accessing public information on their sites. "The data is incredibly valuable for the platforms especially today with generative AI and LLMs. A lot of players want to access data to teach algorithms," said Tene, who also noted that entire businesses have been built on scraping publicly accessible information. In his forthcoming "Field Guide to AI Law," scheduled to be published in January 2024, privacy expert Lothar Determann writes that data-scraping has been a longstanding practice. "Companies have been scraping so commonly that the Practicing Law Institute (PLI) hosted a conference in 2014 with the title, 'Everyone's Doing It, But Is It Legal? Web Scraping and Online Data Harvesting.'" He added: "Many online companies scrape content off other sites while complaining about being victims of scraping themselves…. Most companies welcome the robots deployed by search engines to ensure their websites are easily found. At the same time, however, they typically try to protect their sites from scraping and deep-linking that causes users to bypass portal sites (and their advertisements) or that otherwise affects their business interests adversely." In a recent interview, Determann said data-scraping in itself is neither good nor bad. "Accessing a website with automated tools is not per see illegal or problematic—far from it," he said. "So long as website users respect applicable terms and technical limitations, they may use automation to access information online." But the recent watchdog statement on privacy could be taken as an invitation for companies to restrict access to public data, clashing with the U.S. principle of open access to public information that federal case law has so far staunchly protected. Earlier this year, a federal judge in South Carolina ruled that the state court bureaucracy's blanket ban on data-scraping its repository of case records violated the First Amendment, as it undermined a local chapter of the NAACP's efforts to fight evictions and bring Fair Housing Act litigation. Business interests also collided in hiQ Labs' long-running court battle with LinkedIn, in which the now-defunct data analytics firm faced an anti-hacking Computer Fraud and Abuse Act claim for scraping LinkedIn members' public profiles. HiQ prevailed on that issue in 2022, when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in its favor on a motion for a preliminary injunction, noting that on a platform like LinkedIn "the default is free access." The appeals court panel also expressed deep concern over the risk of creating an "information monopoly" in the U.S. where companies have "free rein to decide, on any basis, who can collect and use data—data that the companies do not own, that they otherwise make publicly available to viewers, and that the companies themselves collect and use." Tene drew the distinction between American and European views on privacy and data protection. "In Europe, a company needs a legal basis, that is, positive permission, to process data. You are allowed to do only what the law explicitly sanctions," he wrote. "Whereas in the U.S., the opposite is true. A company — anyone really — is allowed to do anything with data, as long as the law doesn't prohibit it," he wrote in a blog post on the case for the International Association of Privacy Professionals. Without commenting on any specific case or company, Determann said the recent joint privacy statement presents a "conundrum," where "on one hand in the U.S. companies are being told they should be opening up more and for competition law purposes they should be sharing nicely. And on the other hand, they're being told to lock things down." Determann, who has argued that data shouldn't be subject to property rights, said the privacy regulators are "basically warning everyone that they should be more mindful of what other people do on their websites." While "no one owns data, companies own responsibilities with respect to personal data." Social media companies should reply by the end of the month, the regulators said, with feedback "demonstrating how they comply with the expectations outlined in this joint statement." Tene said it will be a tough for companies to balance with their commercial interests with the regulators' expectations that they protect public information from data-scraping. But they shouldn't brush it off, he said. "If I'm subject to the jurisdiction of any of these dozen regulators they tell you they view it as a privacy violation, I would take it seriously." article.title: In-House Lawyers Weigh In on How AI Will Revolutionize Dispute Resolution
article.description: For years, China has employed AI agents as online "robot judges." Could that happen here?
article.text: For years, China has employed artificial intelligence agents as online "robot judges" that can decide everything from copyright lawsuits to traffic tickets. Can such a thing be possible in America? For Jo Levy, former general counsel of Asia Pacific at Intel, it could very well be. "Concepts take a long time to be socially accepted. But there's a growing body of people in America who are ready and just want an answer," she said Thursday at Future Dispute Resolution, a conference at Stanford University hosted by the American Arbitration Association that explored how AI will revolutionize the dispute resolution process. In China, mobile courts are the norm. Litigants can even upload evidence to a mobile court on WeChat, China's ubiquitous messaging and payment app, and have a decision on their dispute in minutes. If they're not satisfied, the judgment can go directly to an actual judge to assess the AI's findings. Such a system is great for multinational tech firms like Alibaba, which has thousands of cases to deal with at any given time. Levy said people and companies alike love the system because it's fast, reliable and safe. Levy spoke on a panel of current and former in-house lawyers on how AI can help automate some of the most onerous parts of litigation and arbitration, arrive at decisions faster, and level the playing field between patent trolls and their targets. They came from companies large and small, but all had one thing in common: they have enormous litigation burdens and rely on arbitration to resolve disputes quickly. Matt Brown, associate general counsel and head of global litigation at peer-to-peer car-sharing startup Turo, said arbitration is crucial to managing all the issues that naturally arise when a stranger agrees to rent their car to another stranger via an app, from scratches and dents to a user smoking in someone else's car. "Without arbitration we wouldn't be able to deal with those issues at all," he said. Arbitration is a must for tech giants such as Cisco, where associate general counsel Bryan Sinclair heads its intellectual property litigation department. "We use mediation in 99% of our patent litigation matters as a vehicle to try to resolve disputes," he said. Lawsuits from so-called nonpracticing entities, or patent trolls as they're colloquially called, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits are exploding thanks to the backing of litigation funders. "When I started at Cisco seven years ago we had one case on my docket that had about 75 cases on it that we knew was funded," Sinclair said. "We suspect today that about 45% are funded at some level." NPEs and litigation funders are increasingly using AI to help them evaluate their cases before they file. Ken Korea, a transactions attorney and mediator at Colev Law who formerly headed the Silicon Valley IP office for Samsung, said NPEs are just as cost-conscious as companies when it comes to picking their legal battles. "AI is at some level the great equalizer," he said. "NPEs are afraid of the cost and you have to pick the right patents to sue, so it levels the playing field." Levy, now a partner at The Norton Law Firm, said it's just a matter of time before in-house counsel ask their outside firms to also start using AI for early case assessments. "NPEs are already using it. We're already behind," she said. AI has other benefits in litigation too, especially in discovery. Korea said he was floored when he was at Samsung and one expert quoted $100,000 to go through an 80,000 patent portfolio. "Now the same thing can be done for half the cost with AI," he said. "Small-sized firms usually don't have the resources to effectively review the documents in patent litigation. Getting a million+-page document is par for the course. How are you going to analyze it? With AI you can do it very effectively." Levy said AI may soon enable companies to simulate jury trials more efficiently, particularly helpful as impartial jurors in popular patent litigation jurisdictions like Texas are getting harder to find. "Pretty soon you'll have AI mock jurors which will enable you to do a mock trial online. You can even have mock lawyers and have 12 different personas for jurors," Levy said, adding that such tools will help companies decide if they should defend a case or try to settle. Brown added: "You'll learn very quickly about how much they believe in their case if they're willing to submit it to an objective machine." He noted that companies might be hesitant to try AI if arbitration is binding, but if not, what's the harm? "If mediation is not binding, that's maybe one way you can see early adoption," he said. Eric Tuchman, moderator and general counsel for the American Arbitration Association, then asked the trillion-dollar question of how the panelists are using AI internally in their own legal departments. Sinclair said the mandate from Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins has been that the company "is all in on AI, hard stop." Which means legal has been looking into what AI tools can help make their lives easier and cut outside counsel costs, but also mitigate the risk of AI use by its engineers. "Our job is to assess risk associated with engineering use of those tools and what could go wrong, but also getting our head around what is the most effective use of generative AI tools that are legal industry-facing. We have these things going on in parallel inside the company," Sinclair said. Perhaps a year from now, AI will provide an additional data point in assessing cases in mediation and providing predictive outcomes in certain venues and juror profiles. "I can tell you that getting a dispositive motion that goes our way in Marshall, Texas, now is 'no way,' and I don't need AI to tell me that," he laughed. "But there will be more predictive meaningful analysis, and I assume that I will integrate them into my own practice." Brown said he isn't using AI currently on a daily basis in his job, and the pressure to adopt it is still in its early stages. "For the most part the pressure is to keep costs down and be more efficient, and as I think about the advent of Westlaw taking over the library of research it's inevitable. But part of my concern or hesitation now is that I can't see exactly how we're going to be using it," he said. "This is moving very fast but I'm not seeing it just yet. But I'll be ready for it when it's here. I have the appetite for it." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. Levy spoke on a panel of current and former in-house lawyers on how AI can help automate some of the most onerous parts of litigation and arbitration, arrive at decisions faster, and level the playing field between patent trolls and their targets.

They came from companies large and small, but all had one thing in common: they have enormous litigation burdens and rely on arbitration to resolve disputes quickly.

Matt Brown, associate general counsel and head of global litigation at peer-to-peer car-sharing startup Turo, said arbitration is crucial to managing all the issues that naturally arise when a stranger agrees to rent their car to another stranger via an app, from scratches and dents to a user smoking in someone else's car.

"Without arbitration we wouldn't be able to deal with those issues at all," he said.

Arbitration is a must for tech giants such as Cisco, where associate general counsel Bryan Sinclair heads its intellectual property litigation department. "We use mediation in 99% of our patent litigation matters as a vehicle to try to resolve disputes," he said.

Lawsuits from so-called nonpracticing entities, or patent trolls as they're colloquially called, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits are exploding thanks to the backing of litigation funders. "When I started at Cisco seven years ago we had one case on my docket that had about 75 cases on it that we knew was funded," Sinclair said. "We suspect today that about 45% are funded at some level."

NPEs and litigation funders are increasingly using AI to help them evaluate their cases before they file. Ken Korea, a transactions attorney and mediator at Colev Law who formerly headed the Silicon Valley IP office for Samsung, said NPEs are just as cost-conscious as companies when it comes to picking their legal battles. "AI is at some level the great equalizer," he said. "NPEs are afraid of the cost and you have to pick the right patents to sue, so it levels the playing field."

Levy, now a partner at The Norton Law Firm, said it's just a matter of time before in-house counsel ask their outside firms to also start using AI for early case assessments. "NPEs are already using it. We're already behind," she said.

AI has other benefits in litigation too, especially in discovery. Korea said he was floored when he was at Samsung and one expert quoted $100,000 to go through an 80,000 patent portfolio. "Now the same thing can be done for half the cost with AI," he said. "Small-sized firms usually don't have the resources to effectively review the documents in patent litigation. Getting a million+-page document is par for the course. How are you going to analyze it? With AI you can do it very effectively."

Levy said AI may soon enable companies to simulate jury trials more efficiently, particularly helpful as impartial jurors in popular patent litigation jurisdictions like Texas are getting harder to find. "Pretty soon you'll have AI mock jurors which will enable you to do a mock trial online. You can even have mock lawyers and have 12 different personas for jurors," Levy said, adding that such tools will help companies decide if they should defend a case or try to settle.

Brown added: "You'll learn very quickly about how much they believe in their case if they're willing to submit it to an objective machine."

He noted that companies might be hesitant to try AI if arbitration is binding, but if not, what's the harm? "If mediation is not binding, that's maybe one way you can see early adoption," he said.

Eric Tuchman, moderator and general counsel for the American Arbitration Association, then asked the trillion-dollar question of how the panelists are using AI internally in their own legal departments.

Sinclair said the mandate from Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins has been that the company "is all in on AI, hard stop." Which means legal has been looking into what AI tools can help make their lives easier and cut outside counsel costs, but also mitigate the risk of AI use by its engineers.

"Our job is to assess risk associated with engineering use of those tools and what could go wrong, but also getting our head around what is the most effective use of generative AI tools that are legal industry-facing. We have these things going on in parallel inside the company," Sinclair said.

Perhaps a year from now, AI will provide an additional data point in assessing cases in mediation and providing predictive outcomes in certain venues and juror profiles.

"I can tell you that getting a dispositive motion that goes our way in Marshall, Texas, now is 'no way,' and I don't need AI to tell me that," he laughed. "But there will be more predictive meaningful analysis, and I assume that I will integrate them into my own practice."

Brown said he isn't using AI currently on a daily basis in his job, and the pressure to adopt it is still in its early stages. "For the most part the pressure is to keep costs down and be more efficient, and as I think about the advent of Westlaw taking over the library of research it's inevitable. But part of my concern or hesitation now is that I can't see exactly how we're going to be using it," he said. "This is moving very fast but I'm not seeing it just yet. But I'll be ready for it when it's here. I have the appetite for it."

article.title: What Executives Should Take From Ex-Uber Security Chief Joe Sullivan's Sentence
article.description: "What everyone in the industry wants to understand is, where is the line, and how can we be sure we're not crossing it?" said Ed McAndrew, a former cybercrime prosecutor.
article.text: Even as he spared ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan a prison sentence for concealing a massive data breach from authorities, a federal judge last week delivered a stern warning to the security industry. "If I had a similar case tomorrow, even if the defendant had the character of Pope Francis, they would be in custody," U.S. District Judge William Orrick said. While Sullivan's three-year probation sentence may have been a relief for security chiefs anxious about the outcome of his case, it is little consolation at a time when cyberattacks are increasing, and companies are being squeezed by regulators and law enforcement to report data breaches within short timeframes. "In some ways, Mr. Sullivan benefited from being first," said former cybercrime prosecutor Ed McAndrew, now a partner at BakerHostetler. "If there was another case, the outcome could be very different." Sullivan was convicted of both obstructing the Federal Trade Commission's ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices and misprision of a felony, a rare charge that involves taking active steps to conceal a crime. "I've seen hundreds of cases. I can count on one hand the number of times I even heard the words 'misprision of a felony.' That is seldom-used charge." McAndrew said. "It's a very indirect route to prosecuting failure to disclose a cyberattack. It gave everyone pause. This shows prosecutors have a lot of discretion in what conduct they choose to prosecute." While there were unique elements that differentiated Uber's situation from an everyday incident response, McAndrew said some of the facts of the case, like paying a ransom to hackers to try to secure stolen data, are now fairly commonplace, and cyber insurance policies even provide coverage for extortion payments. "What everyone in the industry wants to understand is, where is the line, and how can we be sure we're not crossing it?" He added that a data breach disclosure often isn't the end of the matter but just the beginning of a new phase of investigation and potential lawsuits over a company's cyber-incident response. "The noncustodial sentence is cold comfort to anyone who faces these types of choices on a daily basis," McAndrew said. Regulators are also demanding more information from companies on their security programs, and bearing down on those who aren't transparent enough. "We've observed several regulatory mandates, both at the state and federal level, with tight notification deadlines in the event of an incident, which indicate the move toward increased transparency," said Devon Ackerman, who was an FBI agent from 2018 to 2016. "This increased scrutiny was happening even during my time as a special agent with the FBI and I continue to see it today." There's also the heightened risk of civil litigation and regulatory penalties for failing to disclose security vulnerabilities. Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco has said the Justice Department will target federal contractors that misrepresent their cybersecurity practices with False Claims Act litigation. "That would be another potential line of liability for executives, not to mention shareholder derivative actions and securities actions you'll see in a civil context," said Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & Gray's data, privacy and cybersecurity practice. And the SEC, with strict data-breach-reporting rules for public companies that are expected to be finalized this year, may be a tougher enforcer than even the DOJ, McNicholas said. "All in all, there's a plethora of potential avenues for executives to be held personally liable both on civil and criminal grounds for failing to report a data breach; the effect of which will make executives much more likely to err on the side of reporting a data breach earlier." McNicholas said that while civil actions, not necessarily criminal charges, will be the primary driver of enforcement against executives, security chiefs will still be tested on how to best to handle data-breach reporting. "I think a security chief will be put in a much more difficult circumstance in terms of not wanting to disclose a vulnerability in their company but needing to comply with the law," he said. "It is, and will remain, a balancing act." It's been seven years since the 2016 hack that led to the DOJ's case against Sullivan, and cyberthreats have only grown in frequency and complexity since. Ackerman, now global head of investigations and risk at consulting firm Kroll, said ransomware attacks accounted for roughly a third of all the incidents Kroll handled in the past year. "The number of ransomware operators only continues to grow as large groups splinter into smaller and strategically coordinated groups and then themselves grow and enlarge their numbers only to repeat the cycle over and over again," he said. "It should never be a question of whether you'll be targeted, as all businesses will experience a cyberattack eventually." While data breaches have become more sophisticated, so have the procedures for dealing with them. Ackerman said he advises companies to create a post-breach plan for when the worst happens, which should involve senior senior management, the board of directors, communications team and outside counsel. Sullivan said one fatal error he made was in not consulting outside counsel on how to handle the breach. Uber's in-house legal team was also kept in the dark, aside from one in-house lawyer who testified against Sullivan in exchange for immunity. Security chiefs should work closely with legal, Ackerman said, "so in the event of an incident they know when and to whom to escalate, how to engage outside counsel, and how to enlist the help of an incident response provider with crisis comms and reputational management capabilities. "All that can be coordinated and arranged ahead of time through a retainer service that offers maximum flexibility to help alleviate the added pressure of trying to vet a consultant and subject matter experts 'in the heat' of an event." article.title: With the Rise of Generative AI, Legal Departments Lean on Law Firms as 'Business Partners' More Than Ever
article.description: Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they're placing similar expectations on their outside counsel.
article.text: Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they're placing similar expectations on their outside counsel. Certainly, caution reigns supreme in the ongoing dialogue between legal departments and law firms concerning the adoption of generative AI. Yet, in-house leaders are increasingly looking to outside counsel to at the very least understand the technology, if not use it to drive their own business efficiencies. "My growing expectation is that, if I'm going to outside counsel, they will be aware of [generative AI] and understand its use cases," said Colin Levy, director of legal at Malbek, noting he's looking for a combination of practicality and pragmatism. Even though law firms typically haven't been on the cutting edge of technology adoption, the way generative AI rushed into the public consciousness late last year has pushed client expectations higher, perhaps at a faster clip than ever before. "I'd hope a law firm in today's day and age would have the foresight to understand if they want to attract clients and retain their existing clients, they have to be up-to-date on the current state of tech as it pertains to the practice of law," Levy said. Laura Safdie, general counsel at CaseText, doubled down on the idea that law firms need to seriously consider the use of generative AI to improve their own business models for the benefit of their clients. "There's an expectation that outside counsel don't frivolously use human labor on the type of tasks that can be competently done by a machine," Safdie said, noting that there already is and will continue to be pressure from clients to keep billed time to a minimum on basic tasks. "If you see a 10-hour bill for a research memo where co-counsel can do the first draft in 10 minutes — it should be two hours. It should never be 10 [hours] anymore." Safdie said she's had conversations with several global firms that are asking important questions about how generative AI may change the practice of law, such as how associates are trained, the kind of substantive work that young associates can take on, as well as how quickly and efficiently they can produce a product or answer for the client. To the latter, Safdie said there is an awareness among law firms that generative AI can give them a competitive advantage by doing more work for their clients at a faster rate. "Being in-house, I can tell you there is nothing better than being able to provide a competent answer to the business stakeholder fast, as opposed to every contract review taking four hours," Safdie said. "When you can move at the speed of business, it creates a real opportunity to be seen as a business partner." Allen & Overy is one such law firm that embraced generative AI early on, as one of the first firms to adopt Harvey. Already, Karen Buzard, a partner and member of the firm's Markets Innovation Group, said Harvey is likely the firm's most utilized tool on a day-to-day basis. "It's becoming part of our day-to-day working and everybody is realizing that it didn't take their job, but it changed their job and took some mundane or low-value tasks off their plate," Buzard said. That early adoption spurred an immediate dialogue with clients, Buzard said, as companies reached to understand how Allen & Overy is using the technology and the challenges it encountered along the way. Generative AI is also contributing to a shift in discourse as it relates to law firm billing, as well as the quality and value of legal services, Buzard added. For instance, though it's still early days with respect to the adoption of AI, the cost of legal services has already been under pressure given the prevalence of alternative legal providers, she said. "Already, clients were starting to say I don't want to pay to have a first-year associate spending time on something that is not high value," she said. "That cost model of fixed fees (is) starting to become part of the vernacular," she said. "We haven't seen a complete shift. … But it is moving us in a direction that we can meet the demands of our clients at the pricing our clients were starting to demand." A 'Huge Opportunity' for Legal Departments to Step Up As legal departments' expectations shift, some in-house counsel are calling upon their outside counsel to help them navigate their role as a risk-mitigators within the confines of a much broader organization. About half a dozen law firm partners interviewed for this story flagged this issue, given that legal departments are viewed as cost centers, rather than revenue drivers, within a company. To put a finer point on that challenge, Mary Hildebrand, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler, explained: "Not every legal department will be aware of the use cases across different departments," she said. "That info can be difficult for legal departments to get because teams are engaged in multiple platforms and that info might not be readily available." Hildebrand recalled a conversation with a legal department leader, questioning if they'd know if AI was being used on any of their systems. They wouldn't necessarily, Hildebrand said. By contrast, "on our system, our [information security officer] would know. No question," she said. "But legal departments would have to make a credible business case to do that." Just as legal departments have to make a business case to acquire AI products, they'd have to make a business case to justify a process or product that'd give them oversight over the whole organization, Hildebrand explained. "There's a different set of imperatives for legal departments," she said. Yaron Dori, a partner at Covington & Burling, agreed that legal departments don't always have insights into what other departments are doing. "If there's a specific question from say, marketing, they may go to legal," he said. "But if they're not aware of legal considerations, they may just move forward. We're talking [to clients] about the importance of getting the word out internally and across departments." For some companies, it's uncharted territory, he added. "Some legal departments in highly regulated industries might have a better understanding of when new or novel technologies emerge, some thinking needs to be done and some policies need to be put in place," he said. In addition, "some cultures may be less centrally controlled or more entrepreneurial, and there may not be as much awareness." "In those environments, there might be a greater need for a law department to assert itself," Dori continued. "As to how they assert themselves, often they'll go to outside counsel to navigate that." Chris Mammen, a partner at Womble Bond Dickinson, said the firm has had lots of conversations with clients about the practical, useful and creative instances for generative AI. In particular, he said one area where the firm has been able to share its own learnings is with respect to creating a generative AI policy. "Generative AI is so new that all kinds of clients have not had an opportunity or a reason to implement a policy," he said. "We've adopted one, and we've brought that knowledge and insight to bear on conversations with clients." Nader Mousavi, a partner at Sullivan & Cromwell, said while legal departments are interested and engaged in conversations about adopting AI, multiple studies have shown there is also a significant perception of hurdles to adoption. That's where law firms can play a critical role, he said. "The answer to that from a legal perspective is: that is where we step in to figure out how best to enable the business to deploy AI while putting in good processes, governance, and other things within the toolbox of legal departments to enable the business to capture opportunities," Mousavi said. That, in turn, will enable legal departments to increase their value within a broader organization, he added. "There is a huge opportunity for legal to step up and help navigate an area where a lot of people don't understand the technology and there is a significant level of legal ambiguity," Mousavi said. "Legal departments can cut through the noise and provide meaningful guidance for businesses that need to make decisions and put in place procedures today." article.title: Regulators Say AI Enforcement Sweeps Are Reining in Hucksters, Not Innovation
article.description: Analysis "We're going after companies making deceptive claims in the sale of particular products and services. And if you don't like that because it doesn't jibe with your, you know, techno-optimist, quasi-religious or accelerationist views about the…
article.text: "We're going after companies making deceptive claims in the sale of particular products and services. And if you don't like that because it doesn't jibe with your, you know, techno-optimist, quasi-religious or accelerationist views about the tech, tough," said Michael Atleson, a Federal Trade Commission senior attorney. October 17, 2024 at 11:28 AM 7 minute read Artificial Intelligence By Maria Dinzeo "AI washing" is a relatively new addition to the regulatory lexicon, but it's really just plain-old grifting. Whether it's making bold, unfounded claims about your AI's capabilities or the accuracy of its outputs or downplaying the level of human involvement in an "automated" process, there is no AI exception to the consumer protection laws already on the books. "Whether you're in real life or in the metaverse or in some instance of the multiverse or it's all a giant computer simulation, guess what? Too bad. The FTC Act still applies," said Michael Atleson, senior attorney at the Federal Trade Commission's division of advertising practices. "Products and services that are new or innovative surely get no free pass."
