More than 2,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas last week for the 2024 CLOC Global Institute, with generative artificial intelligence taking center stage.

Legal industry professionals are shedding their initial fears that the burgeoning technology will come for everyone's jobs. Now, the conversation has shifted to how legal ops and in-house counsel can put it to use to automate rote tasks and solve complicated business problems.

A few of the panels featured practical discussions on how legal departments have experimented with generative AI in the past year, and what they envision for the future. Law firms also will be challenged to think more deeply about the value they bring to their client relationships, as the technology displaces some of the services outside lawyers currently provide.

Below are some observations and takeaways:

Legal Ops 3.0

The Corporate Legal Operations Consortium appointed Jenn McCarron as president in January, making this the first CGI where she ran the show. McCarron used the platform to showcase her vision to move the profession beyond being simply a support function for legal with "sharply defined limits" into becoming a true strategic business adviser.

In her opening keynote, McCarron said legal ops pros "have spent too much time on questions like 'what is the right contract life cycle management solution for my team?" instead of on the bigger picture.

"We need to take control of the technology and innovation agenda. We can't solely rely on our product teams anymore. All this transformation we're talking about, it goes through the technology. So if we aren't pushing the software development life cycle, then we aren't creating the impact that we need fast enough," she said.

McCarron went into more detail in a conversation with Law.com. Legal has always touched every aspect of the business, but is still siloed, she explained. McCarron said those who can use their positions effectively can deliver value beyond legal and grab the attention of the C-suite.

"If some of us are doing this right, and I'm starting to see this now, with some real senior thought leaders in our industry, your role will transcend legal. You'll be pulled up into a C-suite, advising, strategic, focused capacity, because you are driving an impact that is hundreds of millions of dollars or whatever it equates to in big numbers for your business," she said.

She pointed to Allison Silver, former head of legal ops at Zoom. Silver is now global head of operations and strategy and reports to Chief Operating Officer Aparna Bawa, who was herself chief legal officer before being promoted.

Legal Ops 3.0 is still in the nascent stage, and many CLOC goers are still puzzled over what it means in practice. One attendee predicted a backlash from general counsel, who have been fighting for years for that same C-suite attention. Another was too focused on the day-to-day job—taking on more legal work with fewer resources—to fixate on other ambitions.

And that's OK, McCarron said, noting that for a while there was a lot of buzz in legal ops around the chief of staff role. "I'm all of that, but that's not for me. That's not my archetype and I would not do well in that role," she said.

"But I love doing the technologist work inside of the legal department. What are the other endpoints? So stay in legal if that makes sense, if that's where your role starts, and that's where you are for the foreseeable future. And it's OK if it transcends in time," she said.

'The Future Is Written in Data'

Executive aspirations notwithstanding, everyone was talking about how to better use data.

"Data is the new gold," McCarron told the CLOC audience in her keynote. "It's the entire point of all this technology we spend our lives deploying. The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it."

Many of CLOC's panels focused on how legal can make the most of the swaths of data companies interact with every day. One blockbuster launch was the Legal Data Intelligence framework, a tool developed by a group of volunteers from companies such as Google, Moderna, Walgreens, Marsh McLennan and Edward Jones. It outlines how legal departments can identify and use data to complete legal tasks and solve business problems around disputes and investigations, contract review, data protection and privacy, and outside counsel management.

Jeremiah Weasenforth, assistant general counsel and ​​legal analytics director at Edward Jones, said the LDI model, with its step-by-step guidelines, can help legal teams put that underlying data to work.

At its core, it separates the sensitive, useful and necessary data from the redundant, obsolete and trivial, and transforms it into "answers, insights and advice."

He gave the example of litigation, where everyone has had the motion that never gets granted.

Weasenforth said legal data intelligence can help in-house teams figure out whether that motion is even worth filing. "You have your own internal data intelligence that you've done on the same question. You have law firm data of intelligence, you have opposing counsel data intelligence. So you could make an actual decision around 'do we push this motion forward? Do we file it?' That is a question that you could answer with the legal data intelligence model," he said.

The most important use case, he said, may be in the business of law. "Every challenge that we solve as legal operations professionals has a data intelligence component. If you want to make a business case for a new technology, a new resource, a new anything, how are you getting funding for that? You're using data, you're initiating, you're investigating, and you're implementing a data intelligence model to get that resource," he said.

"If you want to save money on outside counsel invoices, you're following the same process. You're using data intelligence to say, actually, I know this is litigation in Alabama, but historically it has not cost what we're expecting it to cost. Is there a reason or a nuance about this case that we can use in negotiations with outside counsel or with local counsel?"

It can also help in-house counsel transcend legal and act as true business advisers.

"You can think about a new product, a new service, a new offering that's coming in. And you understand from your data intelligence the common factors that have led to customer attrition, that have led to customer complaints, and that have ultimately led to litigation," Weasenforth said.

"And as you mature, you can start to develop models around the work that you're doing to start to predict where those issues are going to come up. It will give you opportunities to place guardrails around products that you may not have seen coming without that data intelligence background in the tool," he said.

Disrupting Client-Law Firm Relationships

In addition to harnessing the power of data, legal teams are looking to use generative AI in their everyday work.

While it hasn't obviated the need for outside counsel, clients are starting to question why they would pay upward of $800 an hour for tasks that take minutes. One attendee predicted that firms will be enlisted to sign off on work done in-house using generative AI-powered assistants, and they can charge a similar amount for the value of assuming the risk on behalf of their clients.

Law firms that rely heavily on high-volume litigation for revenue will be in trouble. "Technology and generative AI is testing the traditional relationship of client and outside counsel," a former law partner said. Firms need to start assuming now that anything that can be automated currently with generative AI, will be.

At a Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI, one in-house leader said corporate clients will no longer put up with the status quo from their firms. Another said in-house requests for proposal ask outside counsel how they are using generative AI and large language models, and that firms that do not have a satisfactory answer will lose business.

Experiment, Experiment, Experiment

Experimentation was a recurring theme, as in-house counsel were urged to play around with generative AI tools before making any big changes to their workflows.

McCarron told Law.com that she advises against going out and buying any off-the-shelf tech without doing proof of concept. "Pick one, do an RFP formally, or do what I do—call my 'fave five' in legal ops. And I go, 'what do you see who's on the cutting edge right now with the new product that wants to innovate with us?' And I'll do a proof of concept with them, a small use case, one use case, usually for a small amount of money."

Or as one in-house lawyer at the Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI put it, "Figure out what you want to do and find the tool that will get you there."

Getting Buy-In

Some legal ops leaders said they've encountered little resistance to generative AI on their teams. "I think people are just so interested in freeing up time that they're willing to try it out," said Jen Lenander, director of legal operations at enterprise search company Elastic.

For others who need a bit more convincing, Suffolk Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who gave the closing keynote, said in-house teams should "consider pilots."

It's hard to change an entire law department culture, he said, "but I can tell you from my own experience, even inside the law school, which traditionally law schools are considered very conservative when it comes to change, pilots make an enormous difference."

Hire Continual Learners

One in-house leader said his generative AI is not threatening jobs on his legal team, but the type of lawyers in-house teams are hiring is changing. The new priority is lawyers who have a "growth mindset" and are willing to adapt to new technology. "You cannot rely on what you learned a year ago," he said. "You have to keep changing your skill set."

One law firm partner said his firm is hiring more associates, not fewer, "but it will affect the kind of people we hire."

The complexity of the laws and state and federal AI regulations are actually producing more work than the firm can handle. But the firms want to see adaptability from candidates. "I want to see you embrace the revolution," he said.

article.title: 'This Is Not Going Away': Smackdown in Novel Cybersecurity Case Unlikely to Send SEC Into Retreat
article.description: The SEC last year sued the IT software company SolarWinds, calling its cyber risk disclosures overly general and its characterization of a massive 2020 breach misleading.A judge last week gutted most of the case, a big setback for the agency's push…
article.text: The SEC last year sued the IT software company SolarWinds, calling its cyber risk disclosures overly general and its characterization of a massive 2020 breach misleading.A judge last week gutted most of the case, a big setback for the agency's push to force companies to provide investors with more detail on their cybersecurity practices and potential vulnerabilities.But experts say that this was just one ruling in one case and that the SEC likely will continue to advance novel legal theories to assert authority over corporate cybersecurity controls. Security chiefs nationwide found solace in a federal judge’s recent gutting of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s civil fraud lawsuit against SolarWinds, a case that marked the first time the regulator took a public company to court over its handling of a cyberattack. The turn of events has drawn varied reactions from legal and security experts. While some see the dismissal as a blow to the SEC’s efforts to police companies’ cybersecurity practices, they’re not expecting regulators to back off their quest to force firms to provide greater transparency about their cybersecurity risks and how they’re managing them. “While the dismissal of most of the SEC charges against SolarWinds will be viewed as a win within the [chief information security officer] community, it is premature to think regulatory pressure and litigation against companies and individuals will desist in the future,” said Steve Martano, a faculty member at cybersecurity consulting firm IANS Research. Martano said that every cyber incident and response is unique, and while the SEC may pull back in the short term, it’s clear that regulators are willing to push boundaries and pursue cases premised on novel legal theories. The SEC’s suit, filed in October 2023 in the Southern District of New York, accused the Austin, Texas-based information technology software company and its CISO, Tim Brown, of concealing cybersecurity red flags and filing a “boilerplate” disclosure that cast as hypothetical cyber threats that its employees and Brown knew to be real. And once SolarWinds became aware of the breach, which occurred in 2020 and ranks among the most devastating cyberattacks ever, the SEC alleges the company misled the public about its magnitude. But in his 107-page ruling last Thursday, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer threw out the SEC’s claims that SolarWinds’ disclosures to investors before the attack were overly general and that disclosures afterward failed to convey its gravity. He said those disclosures represented the risks and the fallout from the attack accurately, observing that antifraud laws “do not require cautions to be articulated with maximum specificity.” An SEC spokesperson did not respond to Law.com’s request for comment on whether the ruling would have an impact on the agency’s cyber agenda. ‘Generic’ Filings and ‘Gamesmanship’ Cyber professionals had warned that overly detailed disclosures about vulnerabilities could have the unintended consequence of giving bad actors a road map to carry out attacks. Engelmayer agreed, writing that “spelling out a risk with maximal specificity may backfire in various ways, including by arming malevolent actors with information to exploit.” The ruling comes as companies wrestle with how to comply with SEC rules adopted last year requiring them to promptly disclose material cyberattacks and to detail their cyber risks and vulnerabilities in their annual reports. In advocating for the rules, SEC officials said they’d become fed up with “generic” filings and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers. Even in the wake of Engelmayer’s ruling, “bare minimum statements aren’t going to cut it,” said Michael Daniel, who serves as CEO of Cyber Threat Alliance and formerly was cybersecurity coordinator for the National Security Council, as well as special assistant to President Barack Obama. He said the SEC’s frustrations were well-founded. “A lot of companies would make a statement about their cybersecurity risk, which is just along the lines of ‘We have cybersecurity risk,’ which is not helpful to investors. The SEC does have an interest in ensuring that disclosures are accurate and useful to investors,” Daniel said. “The key thing is it has to be somewhere in between ‘we have some risk’ and ‘here are the holes in our controls.’ There has to be some kind of happy medium. In-house and outside counsel are going to have to figure out what is the language that will get you to the right place.” Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & Gray’s data, privacy and cybersecurity practice, said the ruling also gives companies and their legal advisers insight into how disclosures could be viewed by courts going forward. “If a company does a robust cybersecurity disclosure that considers all the reasonable risks and includes that as part of their filing, that this will be a very strong defense against suggestions that there was some sort of securities fraud after an incident,” he said. McNicholas said that another important aspect of Engelmayer’s ruling was that it sided with SolarWinds, not the SEC, on the question of whether provisions of the Securities Exchange Act giving the SEC authority to regulate internal accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls. SolarWinds had argued that those provisions “cannot reasonably be interpreted to cover a company’s cybersecurity controls such as its password and VPN protocols.” In his ruling, Engelmayer stated that “SolarWinds is clearly correct.” McNicholas said this suggests that the SEC “should not be trying to take a provision that requires appropriate internal accounting controls and use that as a hook to regulate cybersecurity.” ‘Not Every Little Thing Has to Be Disclosed’ This finding also stood out to Aravind Swaminathan, a strategic cybersecurity adviser for public companies and a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe. “That being an overstep by the SEC was pretty clear, which has a huge impact because I think companies have been worried about whether their internal controls actually extend to their cybersecurity controls, and the judge just resoundingly rejected that,” Swaminathan said. Engelmayer also shed light on when companies should be required to report material cybersecurity incidents, another heartburn-inducing aspect of the SEC’s new rules. The SEC contended in its lawsuit that SolarWinds should have updated the agency on two cybersecurity incidents it learned about from customers—the U.S. Trustee Program and PAN—as a result of the initial breach. But the judge said SolarWinds’ filings had already “captured the big picture,” that 18,000 customers, including government agencies, had been exposed. Swaminathan said SolarWinds did not need to update its risk disclosure to reflect details about the two downstream attacks. “I think that’s really important, and I don’t think that that should be overlooked. Not every little thing has to be disclosed,” he said. “I think the judge was saying that these two incidents, even if they disclosed them, wouldn’t have been material to the public.” ‘Licking My Wounds’ Experts diverge on what Engelmayer’s ruling means for the SEC’s cybersecurity agenda. “It creates the notion that the SEC isn’t just going to be able to do whatever it wants going forward and serve as an ‘overzealous’ regulator but one that has to abide by prudent principles,” said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio. He said the dismissal shows “that the practice of cybersecurity ought to just be subject to the general duty of care and fiduciary laws that governs so many aspects of organizational and enterprise behavior.” Companies also should focus on creating responsible security practices, rather than getting flummoxed by an uncertain and fluid regulatory landscape, Kannry said. “Building and practicing just a sound responsible security system tends to insulate you from ever-evolving regulations.” Swaminathan said the ruling suggests a limit on what the SEC can demand from companies in their disclosures. “The judge wholly rejected theories that are a significant extension of what the law is, and requires,” he said. “If I’m the SEC, I’m probably licking my wounds a little bit.” But he warned that companies shouldn’t assume that the regulator is going to stop aggressively investigating cyber incidents. “Notwithstanding the fact that this is a major win for SolarWinds, I don’t think that companies should say that the SEC has been put in its place, and we don’t have to worry about this,” Swaminathan said. “This is not going away. And while the judge has said these practices that SolarWinds engaged in are acceptable, if I were a client, I would not be resting on my rear and saying, ‘This is just not a big deal anymore,’” Swaminathan said. “This is one judge in one court on one very highly publicized action. But this is not going to necessarily stop the SEC.”
article.html:
• The SEC last year sued the IT software company SolarWinds, calling its cyber risk disclosures overly general and its characterization of a massive 2020 breach misleading.
  • A judge last week gutted most of the case, a big setback for the agency's push to force companies to provide investors with more detail on their cybersecurity practices and potential vulnerabilities.
  • But experts say that this was just one ruling in one case and that the SEC likely will continue to advance novel legal theories to assert authority over corporate cybersecurity controls.

Security chiefs nationwide found solace in a federal judge’s recent gutting of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s civil fraud lawsuit against SolarWinds, a case that marked the first time the regulator took a public company to court over its handling of a cyberattack.

The turn of events has drawn varied reactions from legal and security experts. While some see the dismissal as a blow to the SEC’s efforts to police companies’ cybersecurity practices, they’re not expecting regulators to back off their quest to force firms to provide greater transparency about their cybersecurity risks and how they’re managing them.

“While the dismissal of most of the SEC charges against SolarWinds will be viewed as a win within the [chief information security officer] community, it is premature to think regulatory pressure and litigation against companies and individuals will desist in the future,” said Steve Martano, a faculty member at cybersecurity consulting firm IANS Research.


Martano said that every cyber incident and response is unique, and while the SEC may pull back in the short term, it’s clear that regulators are willing to push boundaries and pursue cases premised on novel legal theories.

The SEC’s suit, filed in October 2023 in the Southern District of New York, accused the Austin, Texas-based information technology software company and its CISO, Tim Brown, of concealing cybersecurity red flags and filing a “boilerplate” disclosure that cast as hypothetical cyber threats that its employees and Brown knew to be real.

And once SolarWinds became aware of the breach, which occurred in 2020 and ranks among the most devastating cyberattacks ever, the SEC alleges the company misled the public about its magnitude.

But in his 107-page ruling last Thursday, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer threw out the SEC’s claims that SolarWinds’ disclosures to investors before the attack were overly general and that disclosures afterward failed to convey its gravity.

He said those disclosures represented the risks and the fallout from the attack accurately, observing that antifraud laws “do not require cautions to be articulated with maximum specificity.”

An SEC spokesperson did not respond to Law.com’s request for comment on whether the ruling would have an impact on the agency’s cyber agenda.

‘Generic’ Filings and ‘Gamesmanship’

Cyber professionals had warned that overly detailed disclosures about vulnerabilities could have the unintended consequence of giving bad actors a road map to carry out attacks. Engelmayer agreed, writing that “spelling out a risk with maximal specificity may backfire in various ways, including by arming malevolent actors with information to exploit.”

The ruling comes as companies wrestle with how to comply with SEC rules adopted last year requiring them to promptly disclose material cyberattacks and to detail their cyber risks and vulnerabilities in their annual reports.

In advocating for the rules, SEC officials said they’d become fed up with “generic” filings and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers.

Even in the wake of Engelmayer’s ruling, “bare minimum statements aren’t going to cut it,” said Michael Daniel, who serves as CEO of Cyber Threat Alliance and formerly was cybersecurity coordinator for the National Security Council, as well as special assistant to President Barack Obama.

He said the SEC’s frustrations were well-founded.

“A lot of companies would make a statement about their cybersecurity risk, which is just along the lines of ‘We have cybersecurity risk,’ which is not helpful to investors. The SEC does have an interest in ensuring that disclosures are accurate and useful to investors,” Daniel said.

“The key thing is it has to be somewhere in between ‘we have some risk’ and ‘here are the holes in our controls.’ There has to be some kind of happy medium. In-house and outside counsel are going to have to figure out what is the language that will get you to the right place.”

Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & Gray’s data, privacy and cybersecurity practice, said the ruling also gives companies and their legal advisers insight into how disclosures could be viewed by courts going forward.

“If a company does a robust cybersecurity disclosure that considers all the reasonable risks and includes that as part of their filing, that this will be a very strong defense against suggestions that there was some sort of securities fraud after an incident,” he said.

McNicholas said that another important aspect of Engelmayer’s ruling was that it sided with SolarWinds, not the SEC, on the question of whether provisions of the Securities Exchange Act giving the SEC authority to regulate internal accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls.

SolarWinds had argued that those provisions “cannot reasonably be interpreted to cover a company’s cybersecurity controls such as its password and VPN protocols.” In his ruling, Engelmayer stated that “SolarWinds is clearly correct.”

McNicholas said this suggests that the SEC “should not be trying to take a provision that requires appropriate internal accounting controls and use that as a hook to regulate cybersecurity.”

‘Not Every Little Thing Has to Be Disclosed’

This finding also stood out to Aravind Swaminathan, a strategic cybersecurity adviser for public companies and a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe.

“That being an overstep by the SEC was pretty clear, which has a huge impact because I think companies have been worried about whether their internal controls actually extend to their cybersecurity controls, and the judge just resoundingly rejected that,” Swaminathan said.

Engelmayer also shed light on when companies should be required to report material cybersecurity incidents, another heartburn-inducing aspect of the SEC’s new rules.

The SEC contended in its lawsuit that SolarWinds should have updated the agency on two cybersecurity incidents it learned about from customers—the U.S. Trustee Program and PAN—as a result of the initial breach.

But the judge said SolarWinds’ filings had already “captured the big picture,” that 18,000 customers, including government agencies, had been exposed. Swaminathan said SolarWinds did not need to update its risk disclosure to reflect details about the two downstream attacks.

“I think that’s really important, and I don’t think that that should be overlooked. Not every little thing has to be disclosed,” he said. “I think the judge was saying that these two incidents, even if they disclosed them, wouldn’t have been material to the public.”

‘Licking My Wounds’

Experts diverge on what Engelmayer’s ruling means for the SEC’s cybersecurity agenda.

“It creates the notion that the SEC isn’t just going to be able to do whatever it wants going forward and serve as an ‘overzealous’ regulator but one that has to abide by prudent principles,” said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio.

He said the dismissal shows “that the practice of cybersecurity ought to just be subject to the general duty of care and fiduciary laws that governs so many aspects of organizational and enterprise behavior.”

Companies also should focus on creating responsible security practices, rather than getting flummoxed by an uncertain and fluid regulatory landscape, Kannry said. “Building and practicing just a sound responsible security system tends to insulate you from ever-evolving regulations.”

Swaminathan said the ruling suggests a limit on what the SEC can demand from companies in their disclosures. “The judge wholly rejected theories that are a significant extension of what the law is, and requires,” he said. “If I’m the SEC, I’m probably licking my wounds a little bit.”

But he warned that companies shouldn’t assume that the regulator is going to stop aggressively investigating cyber incidents.

“Notwithstanding the fact that this is a major win for SolarWinds, I don’t think that companies should say that the SEC has been put in its place, and we don’t have to worry about this,” Swaminathan said.

“This is not going away. And while the judge has said these practices that SolarWinds engaged in are acceptable, if I were a client, I would not be resting on my rear and saying, ‘This is just not a big deal anymore,’” Swaminathan said. “This is one judge in one court on one very highly publicized action. But this is not going to necessarily stop the SEC.”

article.title: Prop. 8 Witness Says Gays Excluded
article.description: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) – Gays and lesbians possess the least political power of any minority group, said Stanford political scientist Gary Segura, whose testimony in the trial against California’s Proposition 8 began Wednesday and continued Thursday morning. Even the most stalwart of their allies falter in the face of political reprisals, Segura said, citing President
article.text: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) - Gays and lesbians possess the least political power of any minority group, said Stanford political scientist Gary Segura, whose testimony in the trial against California's Proposition 8 began Wednesday and continued Thursday morning. Even the most stalwart of their allies falter in the face of political reprisals, Segura said, citing President Obama's unfulfilled promise of repealing the Pentagon's "Don't ask, don't tell" policy. "President Obama is the best example of an ally that cannot be counted on," Segura said. "His rhetoric far exceeds his actions. Most gay activists and organizations feel that President Obama has been particularly disappointing." Gays and lesbians are subject to more political exclusion and discrimination than even black Americans were during the Civil Rights movement, Segura said. "Though some may argue that blacks suffered more discrimination than gays and lesbians, the 1965 Voting Rights Act allowed African-Americans to elect members of their community to political office. Prior to World War II, Executive Order 8803 prohibited the government from contracting with companies that discriminated against blacks, and in 1948, Truman desegregated the military," Segura said. "So they at least had some statutory protections and constitutionally established equality. "In contrast, gays and lesbians are in a very different position. In 1990, there was not a single constitutional establishment for equality for gays and lesbians." Most states do not have hate crime laws, Segura said, adding that homosexuals are the least able of all minority groups to advance their political causes and pass legislation in their favor. Voters have passed constitutional amendments prohibiting gays and lesbians from marrying in 30 states. "They simply do not have the numbers or resources to obtain politically favorable outcomes," Segura said. But it is religion, Segura said, that serves as the chief obstacle for gay and lesbian political progress. Segura said that religion was the driving force behind Prop. 8's success. David Thompson, an attorney for supporters of Prop. 8, objected to the introduction of letters and emails between "Yes on 8" campaign organizers and Evangelical and Mormon church leaders. But U.S. District Judge Vaughn Walker said the correspondence was not covered by constitutional privacy protections. The letters revealed the churches' plans to provide Prop. 8 supporters with campaign volunteers and donations, which Segura said showed a "fairly close connection between church hierarchy and leaders of the ballot initiative." While most churches supported the Civil Rights movement of the 1960s, they oppose homosexuality and same-sex marriage on moral grounds, Segura said, which translated to many "Yes on 8" votes among churchgoers in 2008. "The Bible teaches against homosexuality and religion views gays as morally inferior," he said. "And it's very hard to overcome that." SAN FRANCISCO (CN) - Gays and lesbians possess the least political power of any minority group, said Stanford political scientist Gary Segura, whose testimony in the trial against California's Proposition 8 began Wednesday and continued Thursday morning. Even the most stalwart of their allies falter in the face of political reprisals, Segura said, citing President Obama's unfulfilled promise of repealing the Pentagon's "Don't ask, don't tell" policy. "President Obama is the best example of an ally that cannot be counted on," Segura said.

"His rhetoric far exceeds his actions. Most gay activists and organizations feel that President Obama has been particularly disappointing."

Gays and lesbians are subject to more political exclusion and discrimination than even black Americans were during the Civil Rights movement, Segura said.

"Though some may argue that blacks suffered more discrimination than gays and lesbians, the 1965 Voting Rights Act allowed African-Americans to elect members of their community to political office. Prior to World War II, Executive Order 8803 prohibited the government from contracting with companies that discriminated against blacks, and in 1948, Truman desegregated the military," Segura said. "So they at least had some statutory protections and constitutionally established equality.

"In contrast, gays and lesbians are in a very different position. In 1990, there was not a single constitutional establishment for equality for gays and lesbians."

Most states do not have hate crime laws, Segura said, adding that homosexuals are the least able of all minority groups to advance their political causes and pass legislation in their favor. Voters have passed constitutional amendments prohibiting gays and lesbians from marrying in 30 states.

"They simply do not have the numbers or resources to obtain politically favorable outcomes," Segura said.

But it is religion, Segura said, that serves as the chief obstacle for gay and lesbian political progress. Segura said that religion was the driving force behind Prop. 8's success.

David Thompson, an attorney for supporters of Prop. 8, objected to the introduction of letters and emails between "Yes on 8" campaign organizers and Evangelical and Mormon church leaders. But U.S. District Judge Vaughn Walker said the correspondence was not covered by constitutional privacy protections.

The letters revealed the churches' plans to provide Prop. 8 supporters with campaign volunteers and donations, which Segura said showed a "fairly close connection between church hierarchy and leaders of the ballot initiative."

While most churches supported the Civil Rights movement of the 1960s, they oppose homosexuality and same-sex marriage on moral grounds, Segura said, which translated to many "Yes on 8" votes among churchgoers in 2008.

"The Bible teaches against homosexuality and religion views gays as morally inferior," he said. "And it's very hard to overcome that."

article.description: Business groups are urging northeastern states to rally around a single framework for data privacy, calling it the “New England model.” But lawmakers in Massachusetts, Maine and Vermont aren’t buying it, instead advancing stricter consumer protections that diverge from laws already on the books in Connecticut, Rhode Island and New Hampshire.
article.text: privacy, calling it the “New England model. ” But lawmakers in Massachusetts, Maine and Vermont aren’t buying it, instead advancing stricter consumer protections that diverge from laws already on the books in Connecticut, Rhode Island and New Hampshire. article.title: Consumers Say Facebook Invades Privacy, Sells Personal Information
article.description: SANTA ANA (CN) – Facebook invades the privacy of its customers and misappropriates people’s images and personal information, and sells that gold mine of information to other businesses, according to a class action filed in Southern California. Facebook uses the personal information for marketing and commercial purposes, the class claims in Orange County Superior
article.text: SANTA ANA (CN) - Facebook invades the privacy of its customers and misappropriates people's images and personal information, and sells that gold mine of information to other businesses, according to a class action filed in Southern California. Facebook uses the personal information for marketing and commercial purposes, the class claims in Orange County Superior Court. Facebook's "unconscionable" terms and conditions then allow it to compile an extraordinary amount of data from users, and permits third parties access to that information. "Data collected from Facebook users is the key commercial asset that Facebook uses for market valuation, internal marketing purposes, and for licensing and direct sale of data to third parties," according to the complaint. Professional photographer Elisha Melkonian says Facebook permitted her photos to be downloaded, copied and distributed without her permission, despite her fruitless attempts to stop it. Melkonian says she is concerned that Facebook has stored personal information posted by her 11-year-old son, including "partially clothed photographs of children aged 5 to 11" who were swimming. She claims Facebook has received "thousands" of complaints from users concerned about unauthorized use of their information and photos. Melkonian says that Facebook knows its users do not want their personal information circulated around cyberspace, yet its terms of use allow Facebook to retain users' posted data long after it has been taken off of the site. Melkonian says she recently removed one of her son's postings in which he revealed he might have swine flu, and has been "unable to learn where (his) medical information may have been stored, disseminated or sold by Facebook." She claims Facebook's terms and conditions are misleading, as they do not clearly specify how Facebook stores or uses such sensitive material as contact information, date of birth, email addresses and phone numbers, which puts users at risk of identity theft. "The statement that 'Facebook does not sell your information is misleading and false,'" Melkonian says. "Facebook has misled users with policies that imply that users are in control of their personal data." She wants Facebook enjoined from collecting or selling user data and from permitting downloading of copyrighted photos without permission. She also seeks class damages of $750 for every unauthorized use of names or photos. The class is represented in Orange County Court by Dana Taschner with the Lanier Law Firm of Los Angeles. article.html:
SANTA ANA (CN) - Facebook invades the privacy of its customers and misappropriates people's images and personal information, and sells that gold mine of information to other businesses, according to a class action filed in Southern California.

Facebook uses the personal information for marketing and commercial purposes, the class claims in Orange County Superior Court. Facebook's "unconscionable" terms and conditions then allow it to compile an extraordinary amount of data from users, and permits third parties access to that information.

"Data collected from Facebook users is the key commercial asset that Facebook uses for market valuation, internal marketing purposes, and for licensing and direct sale of data to third parties," according to the complaint.

Professional photographer Elisha Melkonian says Facebook permitted her photos to be downloaded, copied and distributed without her permission, despite her fruitless attempts to stop it.

Melkonian says she is concerned that Facebook has stored personal information posted by her 11-year-old son, including "partially clothed photographs of children aged 5 to 11" who were swimming.

She claims Facebook has received "thousands" of complaints from users concerned about unauthorized use of their information and photos.

Melkonian says that Facebook knows its users do not want their personal information circulated around cyberspace, yet its terms of use allow Facebook to retain users' posted data long after it has been taken off of the site.

Melkonian says she recently removed one of her son's postings in which he revealed he might have swine flu, and has been "unable to learn where (his) medical information may have been stored, disseminated or sold by Facebook."

She claims Facebook's terms and conditions are misleading, as they do not clearly specify how Facebook stores or uses such sensitive material as contact information, date of birth, email addresses and phone numbers, which puts users at risk of identity theft.

"The statement that 'Facebook does not sell your information is misleading and false,'" Melkonian says. "Facebook has misled users with policies that imply that users are in control of their personal data."

She wants Facebook enjoined from collecting or selling user data and from permitting downloading of copyrighted photos without permission. She also seeks class damages of $750 for every unauthorized use of names or photos.

The class is represented in Orange County Court by Dana Taschner with the Lanier Law Firm of Los Angeles.

article.title: Google, Chrome users spar over class certification in sweeping US privacy case
article.description: At a hearing today, a US federal judge overseeing a sweeping privacy lawsuit accusing Google of illegally collecting data on Chrome users weighed whether she should certify a potential class of millions of people. Certification hinges on whether users implicitly consented to Google's privacy policies and if that consent can be determined on a class-wide basis.

article.title: Prosecutorial Flip-Flop in Bribery Case of Ex-Cognizant CLO Highlights Confusion Over Trump Executive Order
article.description: The DOJ installed a new top prosecutor in New Jersey on Monday night, and hours later he asked a judge to put the trial on hold. His predecessor last month had told the judge the trial should proceed as scheduled, with jury selection starting this week.
article.text: Confusion over the implications of President Donald Trump’s executive order pausing Foreign Corrupt Practices Act enforcement is so thick that even officials within the Justice Department disagree on what it means. That became apparent Tuesday after the newly installed U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey asked a judge to delay the bribery trial for former Cognizant Chief Legal Officer Steven Schwartz and former Cognizant President Gordon Coburn for 180 days to give his office time to assess how Trump’s Feb. 10 FCPA order applies to the case. Jury selection had been set to begin this week.
article.html:

article.title: Report: High Court Ruling in Abortion Case More About Deceptive Speech
article.description: A 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that struck down a California law requiring faith-based pregnancy centers to provide women with information about family planning and abortions has far-reaching consequences for government regulation, public health and commercial disclosures, according to an analysis published Thursday by the NYU College of Global Public Health.
article.text: A 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that struck down a California law requiring faith-based pregnancy centers to provide women with information about family planning and abortions has far-reaching consequences for government regulation, public health and commercial disclosures, according to an analysis published Thursday by the NYU College of Global Public Health. (CN) – A 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that struck down a California law requiring faith-based pregnancy centers to provide women with information about family planning and abortions has far-reaching consequences for government regulation, public health and commercial disclosures, according to an analysis published Thursday by the NYU College of Global Public Health. While National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra was both hailed as a victory by anti-abortion advocates and caused ripples of anxiety among reproductive rights groups, the decision also signaled a shift in the court’s thinking on the government’s authority to regulate commercial speech and require disclosures, said Jennifer L. Pomeranz, assistant professor of public health policy and management at NYU. “The court is moving in a new direction for commercial speech,” she said. Specifically, Pomeranz is concerned about how the court applied the standards for commercial speech outlined in Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, a 1985 high court ruling that government-required disclosures be purely factual and noncontroversial, be reasonably related to the government’s interest, and not be “unduly burdensome.” The “factual and noncontroversial” element of the Zauderer test has paved the way for health warnings on tobacco, food labeling and calorie disclosures on restaurant menus, the NYU report says. But Pomeranz, who wrote the report, pointed out Justice Clarence Thomas wrote the majority’s opinion in NIFLA. “Thomas in the past has said he’s skeptical of Zauderer to begin with. My concern is that if that goes forward, we’re going to lose disclosure requirements,” Pomeranz said. NIFLA challenged California’s Reproductive FACT Act, passed in 2015, which mandated all pregnancy clinics – commonly called pregnancy crisis centers – to post this notice: “California has public programs that provide immediate free or low-cost access to comprehensive family planning services (including all FDA-approved methods of contraception), prenatal care, and abortion for eligible women. To determine whether you qualify, contact the county social services office at [insert the telephone number]." Many of these clinics are faith-based and actively oppose abortion. The majority mostly based its opinion on how California's’ law unconstitutionally targeted the clinics, with Thomas writing, “It targets speakers, not speech, and imposes an unduly burdensome disclosure requirement that will chill their protected speech.” But it also dealt with Zauderer, focusing on the controversial topic of abortion and the burdensomeness of the requirement that clinics notify women they are not licensed and had no licensed medical staff onsite. Pomeranz said the court’s interpretation of “controversial” is worrisome, as the term is usually applied to disputes over the facts, not about whether a topic is morally or politically contentious. “Federal courts before this case had always interpreted ‘controversial’ to be controversial about the facts, because everything can be politically controversial. That shouldn’t be a constitutional consideration,” she said. “I work in public health and every public health issue can be controversial.” For an example of scientific controversy, one need look no further than another public health on which Pomeranz has written: sugar sweetened beverages. An en banc panel of the Ninth Circuit is expected to rule soon in American Beverage Association v. The City and County of San Francisco, the soda industry’s challenge to a city ordinance requiring health warnings on ads for sugary beverages. In that case, the controversy has not been over whether soda contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay, as the industry has all but conceded that point, but whether it contributes more than other foods containing sugar. While the shift in interpretation of “controversy” in the NIFLA ruling is concerning, the NYU report said, purely factual disclosures should be safe.
article.html:
A 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that struck down a California law requiring faith-based pregnancy centers to provide women with information about family planning and abortions has far-reaching consequences for government regulation, public health and commercial disclosures, according to an analysis published Thursday by the NYU College of Global Public Health.

(CN) – A 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that struck down a California law requiring faith-based pregnancy centers to provide women with information about family planning and abortions has far-reaching consequences for government regulation, public health and commercial disclosures, according to an analysis published Thursday by the NYU College of Global Public Health.

While National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra was both hailed as a victory by anti-abortion advocates and caused ripples of anxiety among reproductive rights groups, the decision also signaled a shift in the court’s thinking on the government’s authority to regulate commercial speech and require disclosures, said Jennifer L. Pomeranz, assistant professor of public health policy and management at NYU.

“The court is moving in a new direction for commercial speech,” she said.

Specifically, Pomeranz is concerned about how the court applied the standards for commercial speech outlined in Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, a 1985 high court ruling that government-required disclosures be purely factual and noncontroversial, be reasonably related to the government’s interest, and not be “unduly burdensome.” The “factual and noncontroversial” element of the Zauderer test has paved the way for health warnings on tobacco, food labeling and calorie disclosures on restaurant menus, the NYU report says.

But Pomeranz, who wrote the report, pointed out Justice Clarence Thomas wrote the majority’s opinion in NIFLA. “Thomas in the past has said he’s skeptical of Zauderer to begin with. My concern is that if that goes forward, we’re going to lose disclosure requirements,” Pomeranz said.

NIFLA challenged California’s Reproductive FACT Act, passed in 2015, which mandated all pregnancy clinics – commonly called pregnancy crisis centers – to post this notice: “California has public programs that provide immediate free or low-cost access to comprehensive family planning services (including all FDA-approved methods of contraception), prenatal care, and abortion for eligible women. To determine whether you qualify, contact the county social services office at [insert the telephone number]."

Many of these clinics are faith-based and actively oppose abortion.

The majority mostly based its opinion on how California's’ law unconstitutionally targeted the clinics, with Thomas writing, “It targets speakers, not speech, and imposes an unduly burdensome disclosure requirement that will chill their protected speech.” But it also dealt with Zauderer, focusing on the controversial topic of abortion and the burdensomeness of the requirement that clinics notify women they are not licensed and had no licensed medical staff onsite.

Pomeranz said the court’s interpretation of “controversial” is worrisome, as the term is usually applied to disputes over the facts, not about whether a topic is morally or politically contentious.

“Federal courts before this case had always interpreted ‘controversial’ to be controversial about the facts, because everything can be politically controversial. That shouldn’t be a constitutional consideration,” she said. “I work in public health and every public health issue can be controversial.”

For an example of scientific controversy, one need look no further than another public health on which Pomeranz has written: sugar sweetened beverages. An en banc panel of the Ninth Circuit is expected to rule soon in American Beverage Association v. The City and County of San Francisco, the soda industry’s challenge to a city ordinance requiring health warnings on ads for sugary beverages. In that case, the controversy has not been over whether soda contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay, as the industry has all but conceded that point, but whether it contributes more than other foods containing sugar.

While the shift in interpretation of “controversy” in the NIFLA ruling is concerning, the NYU report said, purely factual disclosures should be safe.

article.title: High-Flying Genetics Testing Firm GeneDx Hires Ex-Zoetis GC as Legal Chief
article.description: Heidi Chen is a "celebrated and well-respected business leader and general counsel who brings extensive industry experience to GeneDx," CEO Katherine Stueland said.
article.text: The former general counsel of Pfizer's animal health spinoff Zoetis has been named chief legal officer of GeneDx, a genetic testing company whose rare-disease datasets are used to tailor precise medical treatments for pediatric patients. Stamford, Connecticut-based GeneDx announced on Monday that Heidi Chen will head legal and compliance functions, including regulatory matters and intellectual property.
article.html:

Stamford, Connecticut-based GeneDx announced on Monday that Heidi Chen will head legal and compliance functions, including regulatory matters and intellectual property.

article.title: From Tires to Tracks: Goodyear Chief Risk Officer Joins Union Pacific as Legal Chief
article.description: Christina Conlin is jumping aboard as the U.S. rail industry faces heightened regulatory scrutiny in the wake of a string of high-profile rail accidents.
article.text: Union Pacific will part ways with its chief legal officer in March 2025, the latest in a string of U.S. railroad giants changing out law department leadership. Craig Richardson, who's been with Union Pacific since 2016 and has been chief legal officer since 2020, will retire on March 31, 2025. He will be succeeded by Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. Chief Risk Officer Christina Conlin, who will join Union Pacific next month as deputy general counsel and step into the CLO post upon Richardson's exit.
article.html:

article.title: After Mysterious Parting With Last GC, Photronics Fills Vacancy
article.description: Photronics has said little about why it placed Richelle Burr on leave earlier this year or why she left the company last month. She will receive a year of salary under her separation agreement.
article.text: Photronics, the Brookfield, Connecticut-based maker of semiconductor components that recently parted with its longtime legal chief after putting her on leave, has hired in-house veteran Christopher Lutzo as general counsel. He replaces Richelle Burr, who suddenly retired last month. The company had put her on paid administrative leave four months earlier, citing an "ongoing internal review regarding certain Company transactions and other matters." It never elaborated on the nature of that review, or revealed what it found, and it has not responded to Law.com's inquiries.

article.title: People and Purpose: AbbVie's GC on Leading With Impact and Inspiring Change
article.description: "Being a good lawyer isn’t enough to be a successful general counsel. You need business sense, the ability to influence, and an understanding of how to protect the company’s reputation," AbbVie General Counsel Perry Siatis said.
article.text: "People and purpose" drive Perry Siatis’ leadership approach. As executive vice president, general counsel, and secretary at pharmaceutical company AbbVie, Siatis emphasizes the importance of caring for his team and living by the company's mission to transform patients’ lives. "It all comes down to caring for your people, being inclusive, trusting and inspiring them. When you do that, you create a team that's passionate about the company's mission," Siatis said.

article.description: "Internal control related to the preparation and review of the financial statements and footnotes was not properly designed and implemented to prevent, detect or correct errors and omissions," wrote Allmond & Co., a Lanham, Maryland-based accounting firm.
article.text: The Federal Trade Commission emotes a righteous tone in its crusade against corporate monetary misdeeds, whether excoriating an auto dealer for payment-packing or condeming competitors for improperly sharing pricing data. Now, in what may be cathartic to companies humbled by virtuous regulators, the commission has been called out for its own financial sins—some for inadequate communication with the agency's general counsel's office.

article.title: 'Black Box': Food Delivery Platform GrubHub Hit With Class Action Targeting Its Use of TikTok Software
article.description: GrubHub was slapped on Monday with a proposed class action lawsuit that accuses the food delivery service of allegedly siphoning consumer data to TikTok parent ByteDance.
article.text: GrubHub has been hit with a proposed class action lawsuit that accuses the app-based food ordering and delivery service of funneling consumer data to TikTok parent ByteDance and contributing to a national security threat from China. Pacific Trial Attorneys in Newport Beach filed the complaint, which alleged violations of California's "Trap and Trace" law under the California Invasion of Privacy Act, on Monday in the Superior Court for the State of California, County of Los Angeles. Counsel has not yet appeared for the defendant. Pacific Trial Attorneys declined to comment on pending litigation.

article.title: Dog Gone It, Target: Provider of Retailer's Mascot Dog Sues Over Contract Cancellation
article.description: Target had used English bull terriers supplied by California-based Worldwide Movie Animals for 22 years, according to the suit.
article.text: A California company that provides performing movie animals for commercials, TV, and movies is suing retailer Target, alleging breach of contract involving Target's beloved "Bullseye" dog mascot. Target had used English bull terriers supplied by Santa Clarita-based Worldwide Movie Animals for 22 years before the retailer abruptly ended the relationship last year without providing the six months of advance notice required under its contract, Worldwide alleges in a federal lawsuit filed Wednesday in the Central District of California. It says Target missed that cutoff by three days.
article.html:
A California company that provides performing movie animals for commercials, TV, and movies is suing retailer Target, alleging breach of contract involving Target's beloved "Bullseye" dog mascot.

Target had used English bull terriers supplied by Santa Clarita-based Worldwide Movie Animals for 22 years before the retailer abruptly ended the relationship last year without providing the six months of advance notice required under its contract, Worldwide alleges in a federal lawsuit filed Wednesday in the Central District of California. It says Target missed that cutoff by three days.

article.title: Porsche's Venture Capital Arm Adds General Counsel From Clifford Chance
article.description: Early-career attorney Lynn Nussbaum is taking the legal reins of Porsche Ventures as it hits the gas on its next phase of growth.
article.text: Porsche Ventures, the Luxembourg-based venture capital arm of the luxury carmaker Porsche AG, has hired Clifford Chance lawyer Lynn Nussbaum as general counsel, according to a LinkedIn announcement from Nussbaum. Nussbaum did not respond to a message from Law.com seeking comment on the move, and a Porsche spokesperson said the company "does not comment on personnel matters at this level." The role marks the first in-house job for the young lawyer, who joined Clifford Chance in 2020 after short stints as a legal intern at Luxembourg-based law firms Kleyr Grasso SCS, Trialys and Elvinger Hoss Prussen.

article.title: 'We’re Here to Empower People to Make Good Decisions': Why Compliance Chiefs Must Learn to Think Like a Businessperson
article.description: “The thrust of our jobs is when things in the business go right, because that’s when we gain trust within the company,” said Obiamaka Madubuko, chief ethics and compliance officer of Visa.
article.text: General counsel and chief compliance officers must build relationships across the company when times are good to earn the trust they'll need to navigate the business through future compliance and ethical challenges. That was a theme of Monday's opening keynote at ALM Global's two-day General Counsel Conference East at the Marriott Marquis in Midtown Manhattan. Discussing the topic with ALM's Heather Nevitt were Visa Chief Ethics and Compliance Officer Obiamaka Madubuko and Front-Line Anti-Bribery CEO Richard Bistrong.

article.title: Health Care Giants Sue FTC, Allege Lina Khan Using Loaded Process to Vilify Pharmacy Benefit Managers
article.description: CVS, Cigna and UnitedHealth are firing back at the FTC in the wake of an administrative complaint the agency filed in September accusing their PBMs of artificially inflating insulin prices through a process it likened to "bribes."
article.text: CVS Health, Cigna and UnitedHealth Group sued the Federal Trade Commission on Tuesday, alleging that the administrative process the Lina Khan-led agency is using to prosecute claims that their pharmacy benefit manager subsidiaries artificially inflated insulin prices violates their constitutional rights. Rhode Island-based CVS owns Caremark Rx, Connecticut-based Cigna owns Express Scripts and Minnesota-based UnitedHealth owns OptumRx, the nation's three largest pharmacy benefit managers. PBMs act as behind-the-scenes middlemen, negotiating discounts with drug manufacturers and reimbursement rates with insurers and determining which medications qualify for coverage.

article.title: Contract Software Unicorn Ironclad Hires Former Pinterest Lawyer as GC
article.description: Prior to her two years at Binti, Singh spent six months at Patreon, as deputy general counsel. She served as assistant general counsel of Pinterest from 2018 to 2022.
article.text: Former Patreon and Pinterest lawyer Jasmine Singh has climbed aboard San Francisco contract software firm Ironclad, filling the general counsel role held for six years by Chris Young. Young, who previously was general counsel of GoFundMe, left Ironclad in June, stating on LinkedIn that he wanted to "take a breather."

article.title: In-House Moves of Month: Discover Fills Awkward CLO Opening, Allegion GC Lasts Just 3 Months
article.description: The railroad industry saw a changing of the legal guard, with two of its largest players appointing new legal chiefs.
article.text: The general counsel moves that most grabbed readers in November were notable for their highly unusual aspects. For example, on Nov. 6, Discover announced it had hired former U.S. Department of Commerce General Counsel Kelly Welsh as interim chief legal officer—a role the company felt compelled to fill because its planned $35 billion sale to Capital One remains bogged down in regulatory scrutiny. The legal chief at the time, Hope Mehlman, who in September agreed to become legal chief of Ally Financial, had delayed her start date there as long as she could.

article.title: Three Reasons CLOs Are Critical to the Successful Adoption of Generative AI
article.description: CLOs have emerged as critical stakeholders who help drive GenAI decisions. Their ability to counsel the business to move GenAI projects forward and comply with laws and regulations are complementary skills to other executive-level leaders when it comes to executing on important decisions about the procurement, development, and implementation of GenAI-powered solutions.
article.text: CLOs are overwhelmingly bullish on Generative AI (GenAI). In fact, 93% of those surveyed believe it has the potential to bring value to their organizations in the next 12 months. Matching this optimism, 67% of surveyed business leaders in a complementary study indicate their organization has plans to expand investments in generative learning tools in the coming year. While the top two decision-makers at most U.S. companies for these investments are the CEO and chief information or technology officer (CIO/CTO), CLOs are not far behind in influence, ranking in third place.

article.description: "This is a pivotal moment, not just for Turing, but for the entire AI ecosystem," said Catherine Lacavera, chief legal oficer of Turing.Enterprises. "AI is reshaping industries, and companies need strong legal frameworks to navigate the challenges and opportunities it presents."
article.text: Former Google executive Catherine Lacavera has joined the artificial intelligence company Turing as its first chief legal officer. Lacavera joins Turing with two decades of legal experience and a background in computer engineering. She most recently was chief legal officer of ShipBob, a fulfillment and supply chain platform that helps e-commerce businesses manage logistics and scale operations.

article.title: Morrison & Foerster Doles Out Year-End and Special Bonuses, Raises Base Compensation for Associates
article.description: MoFo is among a handful of West Coast Am Law 200 outfits that have announced bonuses or plans to pay them out at the fiscal year’s end.
article.text: Morrison & Foerster is the latest West Coast Am Law 200 firm to match the annual bonus scale set by Milbank earlier this year, in addition to providing special bonuses based on merit and hours worked, according to an internal memo obtained by The American Lawyer. In addition to adopting the standard industry bonus scale, which ranges from $15,000 to $115,000, the firm is offering special bonuses, high hours bonuses and merit incentives. In total, the potential bonus amounts range from $21,000 to $218,200.

article.title: DEI Fallout: Florida AG Sues Target for Tens of Billions of Dollars
article.description: The suit claims the retailer knowingly “misled investors” by promoting diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives that prompted a backlash and hurt sales, ultimately costing shareholders.
article.text: In his first legal action as Florida's new attorney general, James Uthmeier announced a class action against Target, alleging the retailer misled investors by pushing diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, and LGBTQ+ Pride—which allegedly backfired, costing shareholders tens of billions of dollars. The lawsuit also claims Target hid risks, violating securities laws and threatening first responders’ and teachers’ retirement security.

article.title: United Soccer League Scores General Counsel
article.description: "The league's rapid growth is bringing increased interest from international investors and raised expectations for strong corporate governance, and I look forward to providing support in these crucial areas," said Andrew McIntosh, general counsel of the United Soccer League.
article.text: The United Soccer League has hired Tampa, Florida, attorney Andrew McIntosh as its executive vice president and general counsel, the USL announced. McIntosh is a business and transactions lawyer at Shumaker, Loop & Kendrick, where he will stay as of counsel and has worked for nearly a dozen years on matters including corporate governance and shareholder disputes.

article.title: CFIUS Is Locked and Loaded, but What Lies Ahead for CFIUS Enforcement Activity?
article.description: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (“CFIUS”) has published new details and guidance on its enforcement activities on the Department of Treasury’s website, including, for the first time, a comprehensive list of civil monetary penalties it has imposed.
article.text: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (“CFIUS”) has published new details and guidance on its enforcement activities on the Department of Treasury’s website, including, for the first time, a comprehensive list of civil monetary penalties it has imposed. CFIUS also provides insight on factors informing the issuance of Determination of Noncompliance Transmittal (“DONT”) Letters, which CFIUS sends to parties that CFIUS has determined violated CFIUS’ regulations or a national security risk-mitigation agreement. Enforcement Actions That Resulted in Penalties and DONT Letters CFIUS recently provided new insight into its new enforcement era by publishing on its website a list of eight enforcement actions involving monetary penalties pursuant to Section 721(h) of the Defense Production Act of 1950. CFIUS took into account the objectives of enforcement and national security, among other factors, when assessing these penalties. CFIUS also provided significant new insight via its website regarding its use of DONT Letters, with which CFIUS notifies parties of its determination that they have violated CFIUS’ regulations or a mitigation agreement. A DONT Letter itself does not impose a penalty, but could be a pre-cursor to CFIUS’ issuing a penalty, and will either inform the parties that CFIUS has elected not to issue a penalty or that CFIUS requires additional information to determine whether a penalty is warranted. Even if the DONT Letter does not result in a penalty, CFIUS at a later date could consider the existence of a violation identified in a DONT Letter as an aggravating factor in a subsequent enforcement proceeding.

article.title: FTC officials, other regulators, not protected from removal, US DOJ says | MLex | Specialist news and analysis on legal risk and regulation
article.description: Members of the Federal Trade Commission and other key regulatory officials can be fired by the president, and the US Department of Justice will no longer come to their defense, according to a letter the DOJ sent to Senator Richard Durbin, the top ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary committee. The move could very well force the US Supreme Court to revisit a decades-long precedent that limits the president's removal power.

article.title: Pressure mounts on Europe to address US shakeup of data privacy board | MLex | Specialist news and analysis on legal risk and regulation
article.description: A data-transfer pact between the US and Europe faces mounting scrutiny after President Trump fired three members of a key oversight body that keeps US surveillance measures in check. Privacy advocates and EU lawmakers are questioning whether this undermines US surveillance accountability and raises fresh questions about the adequacy of the pact.
article.text: Europe faces mounting scrutiny after President Trump fired three members of a key oversight body that keeps US surveillance measures in check. Privacy advocates and EU lawmakers are questioning whether this undermines US surveillance accountability and raises fresh questions about the adequacy of the pact. The foundation for transatlantic data transfers is facing new concerns over the independence of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (PCLOB) — a key body cited in the agreement as a safeguard against US surveillance overreach. . . .
