article.title: Panel Laments Politicization of Judiciary at High Court Preview
article.description: At the San Francisco Bar Association’s downtown headquarters Tuesday, a panel of experts weighed in on the cases they find most interesting, as well as how the newly constituted bench has been affected by the contentious confirmation process of its newest member, Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
article.text: (CN) – This year is shaping up to be a busy one for the U.S. Supreme Court: only a month into its oral argument session, the justices have begun tackling a slew of heavy legal questions from excessive fines and double jeopardy to when Congress can hand its power off to government agencies. At the San Francisco Bar Association’s downtown headquarters Tuesday, a panel of experts weighed in on the cases they find most interesting, as well as how the newly constituted bench has been affected by the contentious confirmation process of its newest member, Justice Brett Kavanaugh. For Ninth Circuit Judge Marsha Berzon, one high-stakes case is Gamble v. United States, where the high court will decide whether to overrule the double-jeopardy exemption that allows both the state and federal government to prosecute someone for the same crime because they are “separate sovereigns.” “The perhaps most recent prominent case where this question was critical was the Rodney King prosecution,” Berzon said, noting that the doctrine allowed federal prosecutors to go after the Los Angeles police officers who had been acquitted of state assault crimes for beating King during a traffic stop in 1991. In this case, Terance Martez Gamble contested his federal gun possession prosecution as double jeopardy, since he had already been convicted and sentenced to a year in prison in Alabama on the same charge. “He teed up this question from the outset. It was almost a set-up case,” said Berzon. Berzon added she finds a proposed civil-rights exception to double jeopardy compelling, not only because of the King case but because it allowed the federal prosecution of people previously acquitted of murdering civil rights activists in the 1950s. Another closely watched case is Timbs v. Indiana, involving criminal asset forfeiture. Indiana authorities confiscated a Land Rover belonging to small-time drug dealer Tyson Timbs because he had used it to transport a few grams of heroin. UC Hastings Law Professor Rory Little said the case presents an interesting question of whether an in rem forfeiture, or a seizure of property involved in a crime, should be proportional to the crime. Timbs’ lawyers have posited the forfeiture was not proportional since the drugs were worth about $400 and the car is worth $42,000. The Indiana Supreme Court reversed the trial and appellate courts, which found in Timbs’ favor. It ruled the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits excessive fines to punish criminal behavior, does not apply to the states. With the swell of criminal fines and forfeitures, a reversal from the Supreme Court would be significant. “It might be big news if they say in rem forfeitures have to meet the proportionality principle,” Little said, adding it’s pretty surprising the U.S. solicitor general has chosen not to get involved. The case is set for oral argument on Nov. 28. Also on Little’s list of impactful cases is Gundy v. United States, a challenge to the rule that Congress cannot delegate its authority to another executive branch agency without providing some guidance on how agencies should use that authority. The high court heard the case Oct. 3, and the justices asked a lot of questions. The challenge was brought by Herman Gundy, a sex offender indicated in 2013 under the Sex Offender Notification and Registration Act for traveling to New York from Pennsylvania and staying there without re-registering as a sex offender. In Gundy’s case, the Supreme Court took up the narrow issue of nondelegation regarding the attorney general’s power to apply the sex offender law to Gundy retroactively, since he was convicted a few months before the law took effect. If the justices find in Gundy’s favor, it will be the first case to use the nondelegation doctrine to strike down federal law since the New Deal era, when Congress butted heads with President Franklin Roosevelt. Some experts fear the court could decide Gundy in a way that drastically limits federal power, but Little said he believed the justices “seemed inclined to uphold.” Still, the nondelegation doctrine has been seen as a potential tool for the court to enact policy, and judicial activism was a concept raised during Kavanaugh’s political sideshow of a confirmation. On Tuesday, the panelists all seemed to agree the lifting of the veil to show the political machinations behind Supreme Court nominations was a terrible thing for both the court and the country. People like to think that the judiciary is above politics, but Kavanaugh’s confirmation process showed that’s far from true. At his hearing in September before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Kavanaugh raged that an accusation of sexual assault brought up at the eleventh hour was a conspiracy by Democrats to thwart his nomination. In his opening statement he said, “What goes around comes around.” Kristin Linsley, a partner at Gibson Dunn who clerked for the late Justice Antonin Scalia, said she lamented this kind of politicization of the court. “Scalia’s philosophy was that the role of the judiciary should be more limited than it has become. If that were the case, leaving policy to the elected branches, then you wouldn’t have as much focus on the nomination of justices to the Supreme Court. It wouldn’t be a political process,” Linsley said. “The process was becoming politicized because the court was becoming politicized. The way the general population was looking to the court, the Supreme Court was being looked at as the place where all these things were being decided,” she added. “The way that was exposed in this confirmation hearing, not only by Justice Kavanaugh but some other senators, was very unseemly and unfortunate and I think it illustrated Justice Scalia’s point.” Scalia was unanimously confirmed by the Senate in 1986, at least partly because Justice William Rehnquist’s appointment to chief justice after the retirement of Warren Burger was so hotly contested. Berzon said exposure of the process as political was unheard of until Kavanaugh. “It was at least extremely unfortunate that – either purposely or out of anger – the last hearing essentially pulled the veil off of the political underpinnings and characterized the process as an expressly partisan one,” she said. “That isn’t to say it hasn’t become partisan and that’s unfortunate, but on the other hand I think the veil is important for the independence and function of the courts. I’ve never seen something like that happen before and I thought it was extremely unfortunate.” Follow @MariaDinzeo Categories / Courts Subscribe to Closing Arguments Sign up for new weekly newsletter Closing Arguments to get the latest about ongoing trials, major litigation and hot cases and rulings in courthouses around the U.S. and the world. Additional Reads Ninth Circuit blocks California law protecting kids from social media addiction January 28, 2025
article.html:
(CN) – This year is shaping up to be a busy one for the U.S. Supreme Court: only a month into its oral argument session, the justices have begun tackling a slew of heavy legal questions from excessive fines and double jeopardy to when Congress can hand its power off to government agencies.

At the San Francisco Bar Association’s downtown headquarters Tuesday, a panel of experts weighed in on the cases they find most interesting, as well as how the newly constituted bench has been affected by the contentious confirmation process of its newest member, Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

For Ninth Circuit Judge Marsha Berzon, one high-stakes case is Gamble v. United States, where the high court will decide whether to overrule the double-jeopardy exemption that allows both the state and federal government to prosecute someone for the same crime because they are “separate sovereigns.”

“The perhaps most recent prominent case where this question was critical was the Rodney King prosecution,” Berzon said, noting that the doctrine allowed federal prosecutors to go after the Los Angeles police officers who had been acquitted of state assault crimes for beating King during a traffic stop in 1991.

In this case, Terance Martez Gamble contested his federal gun possession prosecution as double jeopardy, since he had already been convicted and sentenced to a year in prison in Alabama on the same charge.

“He teed up this question from the outset. It was almost a set-up case,” said Berzon.

Berzon added she finds a proposed civil-rights exception to double jeopardy compelling, not only because of the King case but because it allowed the federal prosecution of people previously acquitted of murdering civil rights activists in the 1950s.

Another closely watched case is Timbs v. Indiana, involving criminal asset forfeiture. Indiana authorities confiscated a Land Rover belonging to small-time drug dealer Tyson Timbs because he had used it to transport a few grams of heroin.

UC Hastings Law Professor Rory Little said the case presents an interesting question of whether an in rem forfeiture, or a seizure of property involved in a crime, should be proportional to the crime. Timbs’ lawyers have posited the forfeiture was not proportional since the drugs were worth about $400 and the car is worth $42,000.

The Indiana Supreme Court reversed the trial and appellate courts, which found in Timbs’ favor. It ruled the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits excessive fines to punish criminal behavior, does not apply to the states.

With the swell of criminal fines and forfeitures, a reversal from the Supreme Court would be significant.

“It might be big news if they say in rem forfeitures have to meet the proportionality principle,” Little said, adding it’s pretty surprising the U.S. solicitor general has chosen not to get involved.

The case is set for oral argument on Nov. 28.

Also on Little’s list of impactful cases is Gundy v. United States, a challenge to the rule that Congress cannot delegate its authority to another executive branch agency without providing some guidance on how agencies should use that authority.

The high court heard the case Oct. 3, and the justices asked a lot of questions. The challenge was brought by Herman Gundy, a sex offender indicated in 2013 under the Sex Offender Notification and Registration Act for traveling to New York from Pennsylvania and staying there without re-registering as a sex offender.

In Gundy’s case, the Supreme Court took up the narrow issue of nondelegation regarding the attorney general’s power to apply the sex offender law to Gundy retroactively, since he was convicted a few months before the law took effect.

If the justices find in Gundy’s favor, it will be the first case to use the nondelegation doctrine to strike down federal law since the New Deal era, when Congress butted heads with President Franklin Roosevelt. Some experts fear the court could decide Gundy in a way that drastically limits federal power, but Little said he believed the justices “seemed inclined to uphold.”

Still, the nondelegation doctrine has been seen as a potential tool for the court to enact policy, and judicial activism was a concept raised during Kavanaugh’s political sideshow of a confirmation. On Tuesday, the panelists all seemed to agree the lifting of the veil to show the political machinations behind Supreme Court nominations was a terrible thing for both the court and the country. People like to think that the judiciary is above politics, but Kavanaugh’s confirmation process showed that’s far from true.

At his hearing in September before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Kavanaugh raged that an accusation of sexual assault brought up at the eleventh hour was a conspiracy by Democrats to thwart his nomination. In his opening statement he said, “What goes around comes around.”

Kristin Linsley, a partner at Gibson Dunn who clerked for the late Justice Antonin Scalia, said she lamented this kind of politicization of the court.

“Scalia’s philosophy was that the role of the judiciary should be more limited than it has become. If that were the case, leaving policy to the elected branches, then you wouldn’t have as much focus on the nomination of justices to the Supreme Court. It wouldn’t be a political process,” Linsley said.

“The process was becoming politicized because the court was becoming politicized. The way the general population was looking to the court, the Supreme Court was being looked at as the place where all these things were being decided,” she added. “The way that was exposed in this confirmation hearing, not only by Justice Kavanaugh but some other senators, was very unseemly and unfortunate and I think it illustrated Justice Scalia’s point.”

Scalia was unanimously confirmed by the Senate in 1986, at least partly because Justice William Rehnquist’s appointment to chief justice after the retirement of Warren Burger was so hotly contested.

Berzon said exposure of the process as political was unheard of until Kavanaugh.

“It was at least extremely unfortunate that – either purposely or out of anger – the last hearing essentially pulled the veil off of the political underpinnings and characterized the process as an expressly partisan one,” she said. “That isn’t to say it hasn’t become partisan and that’s unfortunate, but on the other hand I think the veil is important for the independence and function of the courts. I’ve never seen something like that happen before and I thought it was extremely unfortunate.”

article.title: Trump bid to eject privacy board Democrats spurs EU-US data-transfer questions | MLex | Specialist news and analysis on legal risk and regulation
article.description: The Biden-era data deal between the U.S. and European Union, designed to enable billions of dollars in transatlantic digital trade, faces its first major test under President Donald Trump.
article.text: (January 24, 2025, 23:08 GMT | Comment) -- The beginning of the second Trump administration brought renewed questions this week about the future of transatlantic data transfers after President Donald Trump demanded the resignation of Democratic members of a key privacy oversight board. More than 3,000 companies, many of them smaller firms ranging from Abacus Information Technology to Zywave, are registered with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, the legal mechanism that since 2023 has allowed participants to legally transfer personal data between Europe and the US. The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board isn't a high-profile privacy watchdog, but within the Data Privacy Framework (DPF) it has a key role in overseeing the critical legal redress system that hears privacy complaints filed by Europeans about issues caused by US intelligence agencies or other elements of the US government. Soon after his inauguration on Monday, Trump demanded that three Democratic members of the five-member PCLOB resign by Thursday, raising questions in the view of European privacy advocates who twice successfully challenged two earlier transatlantic data transfer mechanisms. Max Schrems, the privacy advocate whose legal challenge to the EU-US Privacy Shield led to Europe’s top court annulling that data bridge in 2020 (see here), said this week that Trump’s action shows that the new DPF is a deal built “on sand” (see here). Despite that weak legal basis for the DPF, Schrems said, “the EU business lobby and the European Commission wanted it anyways. Instead of stable legal limitation, the EU was agreeing to executive promises that can be overturned in seconds. Now where the first Trump waves hit this deal, it may soon dissolve in seconds and bring many EU businesses into a legal limbo.” The reassuring news for companies that rely on the DPF is that it could take years for any legal challenge filed by Schrems or anyone else to work its way up to the European Court of Justice, and for the apex court to rule on that challenge. Until then, the DPF would remain in place. In short, there is no immediate crisis that data flows between Europe and the US might be disrupted because of Trump’s actions with the PCLOB. When the European Court of Justice annulled the EU-US Privacy Shield in July 2020 following a complaint by Schrems (see here), in large part because of the lack of a binding legal redress system for Europeans, it kicked off three years of legal uncertainty for data transfers between Europe and the US as the two jurisdictions worked out a successor dealing, including creation of the new redress court by the US Department of Justice. Like the DPF, Privacy Shield was meant to guarantee European residents equivalent protection for their data even when held inside US data centers. Privacy Shield was the successor to the EU-US Safe Harbor Framework, which was used by more than 5,000 US companies but which the European court invalidated in 2015. In its decisions on both Privacy Shield and Safe Harbor, the European court questioned the mechanism’s ability to protect Europeans’ data from US intelligence agency surveillance. The commission’s first annual review of the DPF, issued in September, notes that it will pay “particular attention to the upcoming reports of the PCLOB on the implementation” of the DPF in evaluating the transfer mechanism, and that review will include watching “the nomination and appointment of members to the PCLOB to fill upcoming vacancies." PCLOB members are chosen by the president and confirmed by Congress for six-year terms. There are currently four: Chair Sharon Bradford Franklin, who was appointed by Biden in 2022; Travis LeBlanc, a Democrat appointed to his first term by Trump and reappointed in 2022 by Biden; and Ed Felten, a Democrat appointed by Trump in 2018. The fourth member, Beth Williams, was appointed by Biden in 2022. But her Republican affiliation spared her from receiving an e-mail asking her to resign or be fired by end of day. LeBlanc is a lawyer who is a former enforcement director for the US Federal Communications Commission; Felten is a prominent Princeton University computer scientist. Trump’s resignation request was confirmed to MLex this week. As of today, the Democratic PCLOB members have not yet resigned, MLex has learned. PCLOB didn't respond to a request for comment from MLex today on the resignation demand. Trump’s purge of the Democrats on the independent advisory board, which must have at least three members to keep functioning, makes it unclear how the board could continue to function for the immediate future. However, if Trump appoints new members to the board that allows it to keep functioning, there likely would not be a significant issue from the point of view of the commission. If Trump fails to appoint enough members for the PCLOB to have a functioning quorum, it could be a different situation. A spokesman for the European Commission said Thursday that the DPF remains in place. Asked about Trump’s actions, the spokesman said the commission “will not speculate at this point, but let us be clear that we have worked closely with different US administrations on data flows arrangements in the past, and we will continue to do so.” The completion of the DPF in 2023 included a determination by the commission that the US provides an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the EU to companies that participate in the DPF. Under Europe’s GDPR, all adequacy decisions are subject to continuous monitoring. “We have all the necessary tools in place to react to any possible developments,” the commission spokesman said.
article.html:
(January 24, 2025, 23:08 GMT | Comment) -- The beginning of the second Trump administration brought renewed questions this week about the future of transatlantic data transfers after President Donald Trump demanded the resignation of Democratic members of a key privacy oversight board.


More than 3,000 companies, many of them smaller firms ranging from Abacus Information Technology to Zywave, are registered with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, the legal mechanism that since 2023 has allowed participants to legally transfer personal data between Europe and the US.

The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board isn't a high-profile privacy watchdog, but within the Data Privacy Framework (DPF) it has a key role in overseeing the critical legal redress system that hears privacy complaints filed by Europeans about issues caused by US intelligence agencies or other elements of the US government. Soon after his inauguration on Monday, Trump demanded that three Democratic members of the five-member PCLOB resign by Thursday, raising questions in the view of European privacy advocates who twice successfully challenged two earlier transatlantic data transfer mechanisms.

Max Schrems, the privacy advocate whose legal challenge to the EU-US Privacy Shield led to Europe’s top court annulling that data bridge in 2020 (see here), said this week that Trump’s action shows that the new DPF is a deal built “on sand” (see here). Despite that weak legal basis for the DPF, Schrems said, “the EU business lobby and the European Commission wanted it anyways. Instead of stable legal limitation, the EU was agreeing to executive promises that can be overturned in seconds. Now where the first Trump waves hit this deal, it may soon dissolve in seconds and bring many EU businesses into a legal limbo.”


The reassuring news for companies that rely on the DPF is that it could take years for any legal challenge filed by Schrems or anyone else to work its way up to the European Court of Justice, and for the apex court to rule on that challenge. Until then, the DPF would remain in place. In short, there is no immediate crisis that data flows between Europe and the US might be disrupted because of Trump’s actions with the PCLOB.

When the European Court of Justice annulled the EU-US Privacy Shield in July 2020 following a complaint by Schrems (see here), in large part because of the lack of a binding legal redress system for Europeans, it kicked off three years of legal uncertainty for data transfers between Europe and the US as the two jurisdictions worked out a successor dealing, including creation of the new redress court by the US Department of Justice.

Like the DPF, Privacy Shield was meant to guarantee European residents equivalent protection for their data even when held inside US data centers. Privacy Shield was the successor to the EU-US Safe Harbor Framework, which was used by more than 5,000 US companies but which the European court invalidated in 2015. In its decisions on both Privacy Shield and Safe Harbor, the European court questioned the mechanism’s ability to protect Europeans’ data from US intelligence agency surveillance.

The commission’s first annual review of the DPF, issued in September, notes that it will pay “particular attention to the upcoming reports of the PCLOB on the implementation” of the DPF in evaluating the transfer mechanism, and that review will include watching “the nomination and appointment of members to the PCLOB to fill upcoming vacancies."

PCLOB members are chosen by the president and confirmed by Congress for six-year terms. There are currently four: Chair Sharon Bradford Franklin, who was appointed by Biden in 2022; Travis LeBlanc, a Democrat appointed to his first term by Trump and reappointed in 2022 by Biden; and Ed Felten, a Democrat appointed by Trump in 2018.

The fourth member, Beth Williams, was appointed by Biden in 2022. But her Republican affiliation spared her from receiving an e-mail asking her to resign or be fired by end of day.

LeBlanc is a lawyer who is a former enforcement director for the US Federal Communications Commission; Felten is a prominent Princeton University computer scientist. Trump’s resignation request was confirmed to MLex this week. As of today, the Democratic PCLOB members have not yet resigned, MLex has learned.

PCLOB didn't respond to a request for comment from MLex today on the resignation demand. Trump’s purge of the Democrats on the independent advisory board, which must have at least three members to keep functioning, makes it unclear how the board could continue to function for the immediate future. However, if Trump appoints new members to the board that allows it to keep functioning, there likely would not be a significant issue from the point of view of the commission.

If Trump fails to appoint enough members for the PCLOB to have a functioning quorum, it could be a different situation.

A spokesman for the European Commission said Thursday that the DPF remains in place. Asked about Trump’s actions, the spokesman said the commission “will not speculate at this point, but let us be clear that we have worked closely with different US administrations on data flows arrangements in the past, and we will continue to do so.”

The completion of the DPF in 2023 included a determination by the commission that the US provides an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the EU to companies that participate in the DPF. Under Europe’s GDPR, all adequacy decisions are subject to continuous monitoring. “We have all the necessary tools in place to react to any possible developments,” the commission spokesman said.

article.title: Swedish Gen AI Assistant Leya Raises $10.5M in Seed Funding
article.description: On Thursday, Swedish legal tech startup Leya announced a $10.5 million investment round led by Benchmark’s Chetan Puttagunta, with participation from Hummingbird, SV Angel and Y-Combinator. Founded in 2023, Leya offers a generative AI assistant that…
article.text: On Thursday, Swedish legal tech startup Leya announced a $10.5 million investment round led by Benchmark’s Chetan Puttagunta, with participation from Hummingbird, SV Angel and Y-Combinator. Founded in 2023, Leya offers a generative AI assistant that looks to help streamline legal tasks such as document analysis, due-diligence review, data extraction, legal research and drafting legal documents like memos. A Leya spokesperson told Legaltech News in an email that the tool “integrates its AI system directly with the documents and knowledge that law firms have accumulated over the years, coupled with legal data from over 15 jurisdictions.” The AI assistant is already being used by a number of European law firms, including Spanish firms Pérez-Llorca and Araoz & Rueda, and Finnish firms Dittmar & Indrenius and Waselius, among others. “The company is currently being used by 70+ top law firms and companies in Europe with plans to expand to the U.S. in the future,” the spokesperson added. The company noted that it plans to leverage its new investment to grow its foothold in markets around the globe. “Leya plans to use the $10.5 million seed funding to expand its team, forge strategic partnerships, and shape the future of legal work,” the spokesperson said. “On top of this, geographical expansion is already well underway, as Leya was founded in the Nordics, but has quickly made its way to the U.K., France, Spain, Netherlands and Switzerland. This funding will also be used to establish a local presence in many of the markets where Leya already serves clients.” Though there are a number of other legal-focused generative AI assistants on the market, Leya looks to stand out via its focus on the European legal system specifically. “Our decision to choose Leya was influenced by its foundation in European and Spanish legal documentation,” Marisa Delgado, the head of knowledge management at Pérez-Llorca told Legaltech News in February. “This specialization makes Leya particularly adept at delivering precise and relevant results for the contexts in which we operate, and sets it apart from other tools that might not be as finely tuned to our specific legal environment.”
article.html:
On Thursday, Swedish legal tech startup Leya announced a $10.5 million investment round led by Benchmark’s Chetan Puttagunta, with participation from Hummingbird, SV Angel and Y-Combinator.

Founded in 2023, Leya offers a generative AI assistant that looks to help streamline legal tasks such as document analysis, due-diligence review, data extraction, legal research and drafting legal documents like memos. A Leya spokesperson told Legaltech News in an email that the tool “integrates its AI system directly with the documents and knowledge that law firms have accumulated over the years, coupled with legal data from over 15 jurisdictions.”

The AI assistant is already being used by a number of European law firms, including Spanish firms Pérez-Llorca and Araoz & Rueda, and Finnish firms Dittmar & Indrenius and Waselius, among others. “The company is currently being used by 70+ top law firms and companies in Europe with plans to expand to the U.S. in the future,” the spokesperson added.

The company noted that it plans to leverage its new investment to grow its foothold in markets around the globe. “Leya plans to use the $10.5 million seed funding to expand its team, forge strategic partnerships, and shape the future of legal work,” the spokesperson said. “On top of this, geographical expansion is already well underway, as Leya was founded in the Nordics, but has quickly made its way to the U.K., France, Spain, Netherlands and Switzerland. This funding will also be used to establish a local presence in many of the markets where Leya already serves clients.”

Though there are a number of other legal-focused generative AI assistants on the market, Leya looks to stand out via its focus on the European legal system specifically. “Our decision to choose Leya was influenced by its foundation in European and Spanish legal documentation,” Marisa Delgado, the head of knowledge management at Pérez-Llorca told Legaltech News in February. “This specialization makes Leya particularly adept at delivering precise and relevant results for the contexts in which we operate, and sets it apart from other tools that might not be as finely tuned to our specific legal environment.”

article.title: The Corporate Transparency Act’s First 100 Days
article.description: With the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) now in effect, the rubber has hit the road for corporate counsel seeking to evaluate their clients’ responsibilities and filing requirements. Adopted as part of the William M. Thornberry National Defense…
article.text: With the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) now in effect, the rubber has hit the road for corporate counsel seeking to evaluate their clients’ responsibilities and filing requirements. Adopted as part of the William M. Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, the CTA requires many U.S. businesses and foreign companies registered to do business in the U.S. to report beneficial ownership information to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a bureau of the Department of Treasury. These reports will be aggregated into a database to be used by U.S. law enforcement agencies in combatting money laundering and other illicit activity currently obscured through the opacity of business entities. The CTA, which took effect Jan. 1, 2024, has created significant new workflow for companies and the counsel who advise them. All domestic companies and foreign companies registered to do business in the U.S. are now generally required to report beneficial ownership information (BOI) unless one of a list of enumerated exemptions applies. BOI reporting requirements encompass any individual who exercises “substantial control” over the company, or who owns or controls at least 25% of the ownership interests of such reporting company.

article.title: Noncompete Ban Would Force Companies to Become Smarter About Data-Loss Strategies
article.description: Companies should focus most on securing data rather than on recovering stolen data. Enforcing a noncompete is time-consuming and expensive. Tracking where data moves can bring to light cyberattacks or questionable conduct by employees. Noncompetes…
article.text: Companies should focus most on securing data rather than on recovering stolen data. Enforcing a noncompete is time-consuming and expensive. Tracking where data moves can bring to light cyberattacks or questionable conduct by employees. Noncompetes were never a perfect way for companies to try to limit data loss, according to legal observers, who say an outright ban would force businesses to adopt more proactive measures. “It’s really a blunt instrument, and it’s inherently retrospective,” David Huberman said of noncompetes. Huberman is general counsel of Minneapolis-based Code42, a cybersecurity software company that specializes managing insider risk. This content has been archived. It is available through our partners, LexisNexis® and Bloomberg Law. • Companies should focus most on securing data rather than on recovering stolen data.
  • Enforcing a noncompete is time-consuming and expensive.
  • Tracking where data moves can bring to light cyberattacks or questionable conduct by employees.

Noncompetes were never a perfect way for companies to try to limit data loss, according to legal observers, who say an outright ban would force businesses to adopt more proactive measures.

“It’s really a blunt instrument, and it’s inherently retrospective,” David Huberman said of noncompetes. Huberman is general counsel of Minneapolis-based Code42, a cybersecurity software company that specializes managing insider risk.

article.title: The Financial and Cultural Costs in Providing Legal Tech Solutions to Clients
article.description: Professionals from Paul Hastings, Husch Blackwell, Redgrave and others discussed whether firms should buy or build and what the cultural costs are, if legal tech teams also develop client relationships. Law firms see increasing opportunities to…
article.text: Professionals from Paul Hastings, Husch Blackwell, Redgrave and others discussed whether firms should buy or build and what the cultural costs are, if legal tech teams also develop client relationships. Law firms see increasing opportunities to leverage both in-house and wider-market legal tech for their clients. But there are potential concerns, such as whether firms can support their own tech and whether partners will be willing to cede some degree of control over a client relationship to business teams. Big Law is exploring more tech solutions for clients, as law firms evolve to find business opportunities in generative AI, e-discovery tools and other software. But firms need to make sure their efforts in offering tech solutions to clients don’t upset the partnership and that the firm is capable of both scaling and supporting those tools for clients, according to law firm professionals and others speaking at a panel this week that focused on client-facing solutions that highlight firm expertise. The panel discussion, with experts from Paul Hastings, Redgrave, Husch Blackwell and Sente Advisors, was part of the technology-focused Legal Week conference in New York.

article.title: 'Very Problematic' Facebook Deposition Could Add to Gibson Dunn's Sanctionable Conduct
article.description: U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria scheduled a Sept. 1 hearing over Gibson Dunn’s 'dilatory discovery conduct' in the multidistrict litigation over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Plaintiffs' lawyers had alleged Facebook’s lawyers instructed a…
article.text: U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria scheduled a Sept. 1 hearing over Gibson Dunn’s 'dilatory discovery conduct' in the multidistrict litigation over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Plaintiffs' lawyers had alleged Facebook’s lawyers instructed a witness not to answer at least 22 times, with one objection lasting 17 minutes. Gibson Dunn's Rosemarie Ring insisted the problem was that plaintiffs’ attorneys continued to ask about 'incredibly overbroad' deposition topics. A federal judge already mulling possible sanctions against Facebook’s lawyers in privacy lawsuits excoriated the Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher team again for their conduct during a recent deposition. U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria, who earlier invited plaintiffs’ lawyers to bring a sanctions motion over Gibson Dunn’s “dilatory discovery conduct”, questioned firm partner Rosemarie Ring last week about a May 5 deposition in which Facebook’s lawyers allegedly instructed the witness not to answer at least 22 times.

article.title: Investors Want Companies to Prioritize Climate Change Over AI
article.description: "Boards should understand that even if climate change and environmental stewardship ranks low on their list of priorities for 2024, that may not be the case for their shareholders," the EY Center for Board Matters said in a new report. As business…
article.text: "Boards should understand that even if climate change and environmental stewardship ranks low on their list of priorities for 2024, that may not be the case for their shareholders," the EY Center for Board Matters said in a new report. As business leaders zero in on the risks and opportunities of artificial intelligence, investors remain focused on conventional priorities, such as climate change. And they want the companies they invest in on the same page, according to a new survey by the EY Center for Board Matters. EY said that its survey of institutional investors who represent $50 trillion in assets found that investors most wanted companies to focus on attracting and retaining talent in 2024, but “climate change and environmental stewardship” was close behind at No. 2.

article.title: SEC Escalates Fight With Robinhood, Sending Wells Notice Over Crypto Unit
article.description: Robinhood legal chief Dan Gallagher’s life just got harder. Over the weekend, the company disclosed in an 8-K that it received a “Wells Notice” from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, indicating that it is preparing to sue Robinhood over…
article.text: Robinhood legal chief Dan Gallagher’s life just got harder. Over the weekend, the company disclosed in an 8-K that it received a “Wells Notice” from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, indicating that it is preparing to sue Robinhood over its cryptocurrency unit. The notice said staff made a “preliminary determination” to recommend that the commission file an enforcement action against Robinhood Crypto for violating securities laws. This comes after Robinhood was hit with investigatory subpoenas earlier this year over its cryptocurrency listings and platform operations.

article.text: AI-powered HR platform Workday must face claims that its algorithmic screening tool was built with biased training data and disproportionately weeds out job applicants who are Black, disabled and over 40, a federal judge in San Francisco has ruled, The 20-page decision, issued Friday by Judge Rita Lin of the Northern District of California, tees up a legal showdown over the use of AI in making hiring decisions that could have sweeping implications for U.S. employers and HR vendors.
article.html:

The lawsuit was filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia against AJP Educational Foundation, also known as American Muslims for Palestine, a nonprofit corporation with its principal place of business in Falls Church, Virginia, and the National Students for Justice in Palestine (NSJP), an unincorporated association founded by AMP to provide on-campus management or control of hundreds of university chapters of Students for Justice in Palestine.

article.title: Tesla Sues Ex-Supplier Matthews International Corp. for Stealing EV Battery Trade Secrets
article.description: Electric vehicle giant Tesla, represented by its in-house counsel and Fish & Richardson, sued its ex-supplier Matthews International Corporation for stealing its trade secrets. Tesla's complaint alleges that Matthews, which formerly supplied Tesla…
article.text: Electric vehicle giant Tesla, represented by its in-house counsel and Fish & Richardson, sued its ex-supplier Matthews International Corporation for stealing its trade secrets. Tesla's complaint alleges that Matthews, which formerly supplied Tesla with equipment for its proprietary dry battery electrode (DBE) manufacturing process, used confidential information about the DBE tech to develop its own patents and shared it with Tesla's rivals. The complaint is filed in California, where Matthews and Tesla conducted business related to DBE technology over the past four years. Tesla is suing ex-supplier Matthews International Corp. for misappropriating trade secrets related to its dry battery electrode (DBE) manufacturing process. The electric vehicle manufacturer’s complaint, filed by its in-house counsel and Fish & Richardson last Friday in the California Northern District Court, accuses Matthews of flouting several nondisclosure agreements, filing patents that co-opt Tesla’s trade secrets and leaking confidential information to Tesla’s rivals. It alleges trade secret misappropriation, breach of contract and unfair competition under the Defend Trade Secrets Act and the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act.

article.text: Photo: Shutterstock According to the SEC filing, Maria Trainor was let go from her position as vice president, general counsel and secretary “as a result of a reduction in force.” The general counsel of the Carnegie, Pennsylvania-based Ampco-Pittsburgh Corp. has left her position as the company reduces its workforce. According to the Securities and Exchange Commission filing, Maria Trainor was let go from her position as vice president, general counsel and secretary “as a result of a reduction in force.” She will receive a severance package, however, the details of which were not outlined in the filing. It is not clear if someone else will be stepping up to the role of general counsel for the company.

article.title: Corporate Counsel Announces Its 2022 Women, Influence and Power in Law Awards
article.description: Corporate Counsel is excited to announce the honorees for our 2022 Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards! The WIPL awards honor general counsel, in-house leaders and law firm partners who have demonstrated a commitment to advancing the empowerment…
article.text: Corporate Counsel is excited to announce the honorees for our 2022 Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards! The WIPL awards honor general counsel, in-house leaders and law firm partners who have demonstrated a commitment to advancing the empowerment of women in law. These outstanding women will be recognized at an awards dinner on Oct. 18 as part of our Women, Influence & Power in Law Conference in Washington, D.C. These women leaders are business strategists, complex problem-solvers and, of course, great lawyers. But what particularly makes these women stand out is their personal dedication to the promotion of diversity in the legal industry. Our 2022 WIPL awards recognize legal department leaders for their work in leading through crisis as well as highlighting extraordinary leadership by female in-house counsel and law firm partners in the following categories: Innovative Leadership; Thought Leadership; Collaborative Leadership; Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Champion; Best Mentor; General Counsel of the Year or Managing Partner of the Year; and Lifetime Achievement. article.title: GCs Face Daunting Emerging Risk, Fanned by Global Economic Pessimism and Social Media Algorithms
article.description: As the public's trust in civic institutions declines, "individuals often seek out non-mainstream information sources that align with preexisting beliefs," the consulting firm Gartner said in a report. Political polarization, something many general…
article.text: As the public's trust in civic institutions declines, "individuals often seek out non-mainstream information sources that align with preexisting beliefs," the consulting firm Gartner said in a report. Political polarization, something many general counsel might have given little heed to a few years ago, has landed on consulting firm Gartner’s list of top five emerging risks for the first time—snagging the No. 2 slot, behind only mass generative artificial intelligence availability. Polarization was cited by 69% of the 347 senior risk executives Gartner surveyed in November. Mass gen AI availability came it at 76%, fueled in part by concern that adoption is occurring much faster than regulation. The remaining three were cloud concentration risk, which Law.com explored here (64%), market effects from higher borrowing costs (53%) and overzealous cost-cutting (52%).
article.html:
As the public's trust in civic institutions declines, "individuals often seek out non-mainstream information sources that align with preexisting beliefs," the consulting firm Gartner said in a report.

Political polarization, something many general counsel might have given little heed to a few years ago, has landed on consulting firm Gartner’s list of top five emerging risks for the first time—snagging the No. 2 slot, behind only mass generative artificial intelligence availability.

Polarization was cited by 69% of the 347 senior risk executives Gartner surveyed in November. Mass gen AI availability came it at 76%, fueled in part by concern that adoption is occurring much faster than regulation. The remaining three were cloud concentration risk, which Law.com explored here (64%), market effects from higher borrowing costs (53%) and overzealous cost-cutting (52%).

article.title: Tech Giants Have Halted Their Legal 'Hiring Frenzy,' but Specialists Will Still Be in Demand
article.description: In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory…
article.text: In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory road ahead. “The tech industry experienced unprecedented growth over the last couple of years, which is the reason for the incredible volume of hiring,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The current layoffs in the industry have been more of a market correction given the hiring frenzy over the last couple of years.” Want to continue reading?Become an ALM Digital Reader for Free! article.html:
In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory road ahead.

“The tech industry experienced unprecedented growth over the last couple of years, which is the reason for the incredible volume of hiring,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The current layoffs in the industry have been more of a market correction given the hiring frenzy over the last couple of years.”

article.title: Citigroup Deputy GC to Join HSBC as US General Counsel
article.description: HSBC has hired Citigroup veteran Curtis Tao as its U.S. general counsel, according to an internal memo shared with Law.com. Tao will be based in New York and will report to U.S. CEO Michael Roberts and Chief Legal Officer Bob Hoyt. He also will join…
article.text: HSBC has hired Citigroup veteran Curtis Tao as its U.S. general counsel, according to an internal memo shared with Law.com. Tao will be based in New York and will report to U.S. CEO Michael Roberts and Chief Legal Officer Bob Hoyt. He also will join HSBC’s U.S. executive and group legal executive committees. In the memo sent to employees, Roberts and Hoyt said that Tao went through a thorough selection process and that they’re confident that his expertise and leadership will “greatly benefit” HSBC’s U.S. organization.

article.title: Viewing AI Through Cheaper/Faster Lens Misses Its Full Potential
article.description: When Harvard law professor David Wilkins started teaching about technology and the law back in 2000, he invited a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor to speak to his class. This was at a time when architects and engineers were starting to…
article.text: When Harvard law professor David Wilkins started teaching about technology and the law back in 2000, he invited a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor to speak to his class. This was at a time when architects and engineers were starting to use software to create and build 3D models of physical structures, and computer-aided design and manufacturing were disrupting the world of design. “He walked into the class, and the very first thing he said was, ‘Professionals always think that technology allows them to do what they already do cheaper and faster. But, in fact, what technology does is it redefines what it means to be a professional,’” Wilkins recalled the professor saying.
article.html:
When Harvard law professor David Wilkins started teaching about technology and the law back in 2000, he invited a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor to speak to his class. This was at a time when architects and engineers were starting to use software to create and build 3D models of physical structures, and computer-aided design and manufacturing were disrupting the world of design.

“He walked into the class, and the very first thing he said was, ‘Professionals always think that technology allows them to do what they already do cheaper and faster. But, in fact, what technology does is it redefines what it means to be a professional,’” Wilkins recalled the professor saying.

article.title: Complexity Galore: New Merger Guidelines Will Add to M&A Uncertainty
article.description: "The draft guidelines would fundamentally remake how the agencies analyze potential mergers and antitrust violations," the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation said in a letter to the FTC and DOJ. Pulling the trigger on a merger will take a…
article.text: "The draft guidelines would fundamentally remake how the agencies analyze potential mergers and antitrust violations," the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation said in a letter to the FTC and DOJ. Pulling the trigger on a merger will take a steadier hand as increasingly hostile federal regulators stare down dealmakers with proposed new merger guidelines. Antitrust counsel who’ve reviewed the draft merger guidelines, released last month by the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice, say they would fundamentally remake how federal agencies analyze potential mergers, adding hurdles that boost deals’ costs and make them more time-consuming.

article.title: No Surprises: As Law Firms Double Down on Year-End Collections, GCs Detail Pet Peeves
article.description: General counsels do not like to be surprised with a law firm bill they are not expecting. GCs are willing to work with law firms if they miss a bill once there's clear communication. Outside counsel should tell their clients upfront how many lawyers…
article.text: General counsels do not like to be surprised with a law firm bill they are not expecting. GCs are willing to work with law firms if they miss a bill once there's clear communication. Outside counsel should tell their clients upfront how many lawyers will work on a matter. General counsels say that while firms often send bills in a timely manner, they will delay payment if a law firm sends them a surprise bill or higher bills than they expect because they’re trying to ramp up collections to close out the year.
article.html:
• General counsels do not like to be surprised with a law firm bill they are not expecting.
  • GCs are willing to work with law firms if they miss a bill once there's clear communication.
  • Outside counsel should tell their clients upfront how many lawyers will work on a matter.

General counsels say that while firms often send bills in a timely manner, they will delay payment if a law firm sends them a surprise bill or higher bills than they expect because they’re trying to ramp up collections to close out the year.

article.title: Feds Warn Companies Not to Delete Slack, Signal Chats
article.description: The FTC and DOJ said companies under investigation will have to turn over instant messages, or face criminal obstruction charges. Amazon and Google came under fire last year for deleting chat histories. Signal, Slack and Gchat messages always have…
article.text: The FTC and DOJ said companies under investigation will have to turn over instant messages, or face criminal obstruction charges. Amazon and Google came under fire last year for deleting chat histories. Signal, Slack and Gchat messages always have been considered documents subject to discovery, but companies haven't always properly retained them, the FTC said. Use Slack or Signal for work? Don’t delete your chat history. The Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice said Friday that companies under investigation will have to turn over these messages or face potential civil penalties and criminal obstruction charges. “These updates to our legal process will ensure that neither opposing counsel nor their clients can feign ignorance when their clients or companies choose to conduct business through ephemeral messages,” Manish Kumart, deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s antitrust division, said in a statement.
article.html:
• The FTC and DOJ said companies under investigation will have to turn over instant messages, or face criminal obstruction charges.
  • Amazon and Google came under fire last year for deleting chat histories.
  • Signal, Slack and Gchat messages always have been considered documents subject to discovery, but companies haven't always properly retained them, the FTC said.

Use Slack or Signal for work? Don’t delete your chat history. The Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice said Friday that companies under investigation will have to turn over these messages or face potential civil penalties and criminal obstruction charges.

“These updates to our legal process will ensure that neither opposing counsel nor their clients can feign ignorance when their clients or companies choose to conduct business through ephemeral messages,” Manish Kumart, deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s antitrust division, said in a statement.

article.title: As Cyberattacks Rise, Including Ga. Case, Firms Face 'Significantly Broadened' Duty to Protect Worker Data
article.description: Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information. Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally…
article.text: Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information. Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally bound to mitigate foreseeable risks to employee health and safety. But a ruling out of Georgia last month illustrates how that definition is evolving for the digital age. In Ramirez v. The Paradies Shops, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned a district court’s dismissal of a class action against a company that suffered a ransomware attack in 2020, where hackers made off with unencrypted Social Security numbers belonging to current and former employees. Employee Carlos Ramirez filed the case in 2021, after Paradies notified him of the attack and after he learned that his Social Security number had been used to file pandemic unemployment assistance claims in Kentucky and Rhode Island. The Eleventh Circuit revived his negligence claim, finding Georgia’s traditional negligence principles “flexible enough to cover Ramirez’s allegations. The court ruled Paradies had a duty under Georgia common law to protect Ramirez’s personal identifying information. In addition, the court found Ramirez had sufficiently shown that he had a “special relationship” with his employer, which has around 10,000 employees and more than $1 billion in sales, and that there was a foreseeable risk of harm as the company kept its employee information unencrypted. The case comes as more appeals courts are ruling in favor of employees in litigation showdowns over personal information swiped by hackers. Last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit found a former biopharmaceutical company employee had standing to bring a negligence class action against her old employer after a hacking group accessed its servers through a phishing attack in 2020, stealing a raft of personal information that the group later posted to the dark web. Event General Counsel Conference East 2023 General Counsel Conference addresses trends in regulatory, data protection, tech management, legal operations, and leadership. Get More Information “In an increasingly digitalized world, an employer’s duty to protect its employees’ sensitive information has significantly broadened,” Third Circuit Judge Joseph Greenaway wrote in Clemens v. ExecuPharm, adding that because the employee’s information was posted to the dark web, she faced a substantial risk of identify fraud that was more than hypothetical. These rulings come as ransomware attacks are becoming more sophisticated and frequent, said Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group. “And the harm that is coming out of the hacking events is also getting worse just because of the development of technology and the way the criminals can use the information that they now have access to in ways that maybe they couldn’t 10 years ago,” she said. “This is making it more risky for employers who hold personal information and don’t have adequate safeguards.” She pointed to yet another case, this one from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, where the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s status as a victim of cyber theft did not absolve it of its duty to ensure the protection the personal and financial information that its 62,000 current and former employees were required to provide as a condition of employment. “I think most employers and particularly large employers that are housing significant amounts of data can reasonably expect to be a target of these types of attacks,” Baker said. “The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania agreed with that and said, ‘Look, this is a relationship where you have a special responsibility. The employee is handing you this information so they can do their job as your employee. And so you have to take reasonable steps to protect it.” Andrew Gray, an associate with the employment law firm Littler Mendelson, said cases such as Ramirez indicate “a broader trend of individuals taking charge of their personal information,” empowered by a wave of state privacy laws that put the onus on companies to notify individuals affected by data breaches. While there isn’t a generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures, there are plenty of steps an employer can take. Gray said that in addition to encrypting sensitive data, companies should ensure passwords are secure and regularly changed. “They should also be sure not to retain personal information, particularly about former employees, for longer than is necessary or legally required,” Gray said, adding, “That’s a common issue my firm has seen recently. Some of the personal information dates back 10-20 years ago. As a precautionary step, it’s important before an incident arises that a business maintain a document retention schedule.” Employers should also communicate with employees after a breach. “In Ramirez, the plaintiff was an employee of this business. And when an employee raises concerns with the company, it’s important that they are heard and not ignored because they are a potential plaintiff,” Gray said. University of Southern California Gould School of Law professor Ronald Sarian said that it’s safe to assume that most courts nowadays would find that employers have a duty of care to protect employee data. “That’s ordinarily not going to be the issue. More often, the issue is damages. And the courts are split across the country on whether or not an actual data breach would automatically entitle you to damages.” Sarian said the analysis is always fact-specific, and plaintiffs that can show that their employers didn’t take reasonable security measures are more likely to prevail. “All anybody can do with regard to this is contact experts and have a good CISO [chief information security officer] who is continually keeping up with what is going on in the real world with the most current threats. It’s a constantly evolving field. The infosec people need to be on top of things, and employers have to be vigilant,” he said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2023 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. article.html:
Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information.

Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally bound to mitigate foreseeable risks to employee health and safety. But a ruling out of Georgia last month illustrates how that definition is evolving for the digital age.

In Ramirez v. The Paradies Shops, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned a district court’s dismissal of a class action against a company that suffered a ransomware attack in 2020, where hackers made off with unencrypted Social Security numbers belonging to current and former employees. Employee Carlos Ramirez filed the case in 2021, after Paradies notified him of the attack and after he learned that his Social Security number had been used to file pandemic unemployment assistance claims in Kentucky and Rhode Island.

The Eleventh Circuit revived his negligence claim, finding Georgia’s traditional negligence principles “flexible enough to cover Ramirez’s allegations. The court ruled Paradies had a duty under Georgia common law to protect Ramirez’s personal identifying information. In addition, the court found Ramirez had sufficiently shown that he had a “special relationship” with his employer, which has around 10,000 employees and more than $1 billion in sales, and that there was a foreseeable risk of harm as the company kept its employee information unencrypted.

The case comes as more appeals courts are ruling in favor of employees in litigation showdowns over personal information swiped by hackers. Last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit found a former biopharmaceutical company employee had standing to bring a negligence class action against her old employer after a hacking group accessed its servers through a phishing attack in 2020, stealing a raft of personal information that the group later posted to the dark web.

Event

General Counsel Conference East 2023

General Counsel Conference addresses trends in regulatory, data protection, tech management, legal operations, and leadership.

Get More Information

“In an increasingly digitalized world, an employer’s duty to protect its employees’ sensitive information has significantly broadened,” Third Circuit Judge Joseph Greenaway wrote in Clemens v. ExecuPharm, adding that because the employee’s information was posted to the dark web, she faced a substantial risk of identify fraud that was more than hypothetical.

These rulings come as ransomware attacks are becoming more sophisticated and frequent, said Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group.

“And the harm that is coming out of the hacking events is also getting worse just because of the development of technology and the way the criminals can use the information that they now have access to in ways that maybe they couldn’t 10 years ago,” she said. “This is making it more risky for employers who hold personal information and don’t have adequate safeguards.”

She pointed to yet another case, this one from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, where the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s status as a victim of cyber theft did not absolve it of its duty to ensure the protection the personal and financial information that its 62,000 current and former employees were required to provide as a condition of employment.

“I think most employers and particularly large employers that are housing significant amounts of data can reasonably expect to be a target of these types of attacks,” Baker said. “The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania agreed with that and said, ‘Look, this is a relationship where you have a special responsibility. The employee is handing you this information so they can do their job as your employee. And so you have to take reasonable steps to protect it.”

Andrew Gray, an associate with the employment law firm Littler Mendelson, said cases such as Ramirez indicate “a broader trend of individuals taking charge of their personal information,” empowered by a wave of state privacy laws that put the onus on companies to notify individuals affected by data breaches.

While there isn’t a generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures, there are plenty of steps an employer can take. Gray said that in addition to encrypting sensitive data, companies should ensure passwords are secure and regularly changed.

“They should also be sure not to retain personal information, particularly about former employees, for longer than is necessary or legally required,” Gray said, adding, “That’s a common issue my firm has seen recently. Some of the personal information dates back 10-20 years ago. As a precautionary step, it’s important before an incident arises that a business maintain a document retention schedule.”

Employers should also communicate with employees after a breach. “In Ramirez, the plaintiff was an employee of this business. And when an employee raises concerns with the company, it’s important that they are heard and not ignored because they are a potential plaintiff,” Gray said.

University of Southern California Gould School of Law professor Ronald Sarian said that it’s safe to assume that most courts nowadays would find that employers have a duty of care to protect employee data. “That’s ordinarily not going to be the issue. More often, the issue is damages. And the courts are split across the country on whether or not an actual data breach would automatically entitle you to damages.”

Sarian said the analysis is always fact-specific, and plaintiffs that can show that their employers didn’t take reasonable security measures are more likely to prevail.

“All anybody can do with regard to this is contact experts and have a good CISO [chief information security officer] who is continually keeping up with what is going on in the real world with the most current threats. It’s a constantly evolving field. The infosec people need to be on top of things, and employers have to be vigilant,” he said.

article.title: Did Boies Schiller Represent Theranos’ Elizabeth Holmes or Not?
article.description: Prosecutors in the federal fraud case against Elizabeth Holmes claim that more than a dozen communications between Holmes and Boies Schiller Flexner are not covered by the attorney-client privilege because the firm didn’t represent the Theranos…
article.text: Prosecutors in the federal fraud case against Elizabeth Holmes claim that more than a dozen communications between Holmes and Boies Schiller Flexner are not covered by the attorney-client privilege because the firm didn’t represent the Theranos founder personally and the company has waived its privileges. But Holmes’ attorneys claim her “unique” relationship with the firm means those communications are protected. These types of attorney-client privilege disputes arise with surprising frequency in corporate investigations, and the issue will continue to be litigated despite evolving case law, according to some white-collar lawyers.

article.title: Leading DEI with Practicality and Purpose
article.description: The Supreme Court’s affirmative action decisions and the current divisive political landscape have perpetuated skepticism about corporate Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (“DEI”) efforts, and undoubtedly have made corporate DEI programming…
article.text: The Supreme Court’s affirmative action decisions and the current divisive political landscape have perpetuated skepticism about corporate Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (“DEI”) efforts, and undoubtedly have made corporate DEI programming challenging. Corporate counsel should not allow these developments to derail DEI efforts. Instead, corporate counsel should take this opportunity to reinvigorate their companies’ commitments to DEI, in order to create workable and legally defensible programs that achieve robust representation and workforce success. Corporate counsel are well positioned to play a key role in focusing their companies on the case for DEI, whether premised on fundamental fairness, correcting for historical underrepresentation, or aligning with the shareholder goal of profitability. To do so effectively, they should approach DEI with a view to expanding and not restricting the workforce pipeline. In fact, an effective DEI program should always begin with the message that such programs create new, expansive, and more representative pipelines to the ultimate growth asset: talented people who achieve the corporate mission. Corporate counsel can take a few key steps to help their clients achieve a more diverse and inclusive workforce.

article.description: Layoffs could lead tech companies without the expertise they need to maintain cybersecurity. Staff cuts also could lead to leakage of information to the outside world. Whether it is due to over-hiring during the pandemic or budget constraints brought…
article.text: Layoffs could lead tech companies without the expertise they need to maintain cybersecurity. Staff cuts also could lead to leakage of information to the outside world. Whether it is due to over-hiring during the pandemic or budget constraints brought on by inflation, a stream of staff cuts has plagued the tech industry over the past few months. article.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence in the Workplace
article.description: As more and more companies begin to utilize Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the workplace, it becomes increasingly important for employers to understand both the risks and rewards that accompany this new technology. While the use of AI can be an…
article.text: As more and more companies begin to utilize Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the workplace, it becomes increasingly important for employers to understand both the risks and rewards that accompany this new technology. While the use of AI can be an efficient and cost effective means for employers to handle tasks such as talent acquisition, compensation analysis, and the completion of administrative duties, it is not without its challenges. Rather, as discussed below, the use of AI may also bring with it the potential for implicit bias and disparate impact toward protected categories, particularly in the context of gender and age. In addition, if AI is not properly introduced into the workforce, it may foster concerns among employees that the company no longer values their work or cause anxiety about employee job security. This article sets forth a high-level overview of some of the more prevalent challenges employers may encounter when deploying AI in the workplace, while also offering guidance on the proactive steps employers should consider when implementing or utilizing AI. AI is often used in the workplace to assist employers with recruitment through the use of algorithms to make hiring decisions. According to a 2017 survey by the talent software firm CareerBuilder, approximately 55 percent of U.S. human resource managers opined that AI will become a regular part of their work within the next five years. Similarly, as reported by the Society for Human Resource Management following a 2018 survey conducted of over 1,100 in-house counsel, human resource professionals and C-suite executives, 49 percent of respondents said that they already use AI and advanced data analytics for recruiting and hiring. While the use of AI may assist these companies, the technology may not always eliminate bias in the recruitment process.

article.title: Manchin Won’t Back Judicial Picks With No GOP Votes. What That Means for Biden's Nominees
article.description: Centrist Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin said this week that he won’t vote for judicial nominees who lack Republican support—a declaration court-watchers say could present an extra hurdle for party-line picks as the end of President Joe Biden’s first…
article.text: Centrist Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin said this week that he won’t vote for judicial nominees who lack Republican support—a declaration court-watchers say could present an extra hurdle for party-line picks as the end of President Joe Biden’s first term nears. Michigan State University political science professor Ian Ostrander said Manchin’s new rule could pose a slight challenge for some of Biden’s nominees in a Senate where Democrats have a 51-49 majority plus vice president Kamala Harris’ tie-breaking vote. It could slow down confirmations if uncertainty about a nominee forces Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, to wait for Harris’ presence when scheduling an expected close vote, Ostrander said.
article.html:

article.title: The Careerist: Asian-American Women Are Filling the GC Suite
article.description: Almost every Asian-American female lawyer I know has been told at some point that she’s too polite, demure or petite to be effective at her job. “How can anyone see you in a courtroom?” asked one of my ex-boyfriends when I started practicing law.…
article.text: Almost every Asian-American female lawyer I know has been told at some point that she’s too polite, demure or petite to be effective at her job. “How can anyone see you in a courtroom?” asked one of my ex-boyfriends when I started practicing law. “You’re tiny.” Despite putting up with such nonsense, female lawyers of Asian descent are on a tear—particularly in corporations. Of the 20 Asian-American lawyers now heading the legal departments of Fortune 500 companies, eight are women. And in China, where patriarchy rules and boys are still favored, over 50 percent of general counsel are women, reports legal consulting firm Acritas.

article.title: Unexplained Change to Hearing Date on eCourts Results in Remand by Appellate Division
article.description: The New Jersey Appellate Division sent a medical malpractice claim back to the Ocean County Superior Court after a notice of a hearing posted to eCourts was inexplicably changed, causing the plaintiff to miss a filing date. The plaintiff, Joan…
article.text: The New Jersey Appellate Division sent a medical malpractice claim back to the Ocean County Superior Court after a notice of a hearing posted to eCourts was inexplicably changed, causing the plaintiff to miss a filing date. The plaintiff, Joan Vanucci, appealed a trial court order dismissing her medical malpractice complaint with prejudice for failure to provide an affidavit of merit (AOM) required under the New Jersey Medical Care Access and Responsibility and Patients First Act. The case, Vanucci v. Schenker, was originally filed in October 2021, and alleged that Dr. Samuel D. article.text: An East Bay attorney has been charged with bank fraud in what federal prosecutors called the biggest criminal fraud scheme in the history of California’s Eastern District. A federal grand jury on Oct. 5 returned a 23-count indictment against Ari J. Lauer of Lafayette for his alleged role in a $912 million conspiracy involving the purported sales and leases of mobile generators, according to documents unsealed Tuesday following Lauer’s arrest. Lauer, a solo practitioner with an office in Walnut Creek, served as outside counsel for the generator company DC Solar.
