article.description: Deborah Hartnett, general counsel and senior vice president of Music Threatre International While she’s served as Music Theatre International’s top lawyer for a decade, Deborah Hartnett now has a title that more accurately reflects her starring legal…
article.text: Deborah Hartnett, general counsel and senior vice president of Music Threatre International While she’s served as Music Theatre International’s top lawyer for a decade, Deborah Hartnett now has a title that more accurately reflects her starring legal role at a theatrical licensing agency that has expanded its presence on the world stage in recent years. New York-based MTI announced Tuesday that it had promoted Hartnett from director of business and legal affairs to general counsel and senior vice president, effective Jan. 1. The group represents composers, lyricists and authors of hundreds of musicals, from “West Side Story” and “Annie” to “The Producers” and “Les Misérables.”

article.title: The New GDPR SCC Framework: What In-house Lawyers Must Do Today to Be Prepared
article.description: When the European Commission published its final guidance on new standard contractual clauses, it pinpointed several dates for compliance. The guidance took effect on June 27, 2021, and the final day for updating all new contracts was September 27,…
article.text: When the European Commission published its final guidance on new standard contractual clauses, it pinpointed several dates for compliance. The guidance took effect on June 27, 2021, and the final day for updating all new contracts was September 27, 2021. In that time, businesses across the European Union have come into compliance with the new SCCs, which in turn have brought them into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation. The clauses are contractual addendums that apply to both current and future agreements which pertain to how businesses manage, interact with and transfer user personal information. Europe’s status as a leader in data privacy means these clauses and the overall data privacy efforts are widely seen as best practices in the global race to protect data transfers.

article.title: AI Study Reveals How Employers Are Using the Tools, and With What Safeguards
article.description: Littler Mendelson surveyed 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals. The employment law firm found that companies are embracing artificial intelligence's predictive powers, but are cautious about using it for generating content. Most…
article.text: Littler Mendelson surveyed 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals. The employment law firm found that companies are embracing artificial intelligence's predictive powers, but are cautious about using it for generating content. Most respondents said they do not use generative AI at all for HR work. More companies are using artificial intelligence for hiring, recruiting and other human resource-related tasks, but have been slower to adopt generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for creating content, says a new report on AI in the workplace by employment law firm Littler Mendelson. San Francisco-based Littler’s survey of 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals found 56% do not use generative AI at all for HR work. But of those that do, 34% use the technology to write job descriptions, onboarding materials and employee memos. Others use it in much smaller numbers (12%) to answer workplace questions through internal chatbots, and 11% use it for employee development, such as personalized trainings. Only 8% use AI to interact with job candidates.
article.html:
• Littler Mendelson surveyed 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals.
  • The employment law firm found that companies are embracing artificial intelligence's predictive powers, but are cautious about using it for generating content.
  • Most respondents said they do not use generative AI at all for HR work.

More companies are using artificial intelligence for hiring, recruiting and other human resource-related tasks, but have been slower to adopt generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for creating content, says a new report on AI in the workplace by employment law firm Littler Mendelson.

San Francisco-based Littler’s survey of 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals found 56% do not use generative AI at all for HR work. But of those that do, 34% use the technology to write job descriptions, onboarding materials and employee memos. Others use it in much smaller numbers (12%) to answer workplace questions through internal chatbots, and 11% use it for employee development, such as personalized trainings. Only 8% use AI to interact with job candidates.

article.title: Former JCPenney General Counsel Joins Banged-Up Powersports Retailer
article.description: A former general counsel of JCPenney is taking the legal reins of powersports retailer RumbleOn, which has racked up rapid growth since going public in 2017 but experienced numerous setbacks, including a plunge in its stock price. The Dallas-based…
article.text: A former general counsel of JCPenney is taking the legal reins of powersports retailer RumbleOn, which has racked up rapid growth since going public in 2017 but experienced numerous setbacks, including a plunge in its stock price. The Dallas-based company announced Brandy Treadway’s appointment this week as chief legal officer. Treadway comes to the company from Martin Powers & Counsel, where she’s been a corporate partner for 17 months. Before that, she spent a decade at JCPenney, where she started as senior counsel and rapidly rose through the ranks.
article.html:

Treadway comes to the company from Martin Powers & Counsel, where she’s been a corporate partner for 17 months. Before that, she spent a decade at JCPenney, where she started as senior counsel and rapidly rose through the ranks.

article.title: FTC's Kroger-Albertsons Suit Premised on 'Fanciful' Definition of Grocery Market, Dissenting States Say
article.description: Attorneys general from Alabama, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio are urging a federal judge to allow Kroger’s $24.6 billion acquisition of rival Albertsons to go through, arguing that the Federal Trade Commission’s opposition to the deal is premised on an…
article.text: Attorneys general from Alabama, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio are urging a federal judge to allow Kroger’s $24.6 billion acquisition of rival Albertsons to go through, arguing that the Federal Trade Commission’s opposition to the deal is premised on an overly narrow definition of the grocery market that’s detached from reality and contradicts its own precedent. In an amicus brief filed in Oregon federal court Friday, the attorneys general say the merger actually is “procompetitive” because “it can be expected to strengthen Kroger’s ability to compete more effectively in the wide-open market for consumers’ retail grocery dollars,” a free-for-all that includes far larger companies such as Walmart and Amazon.

article.title: Meta Transfers AI-Related Patents to Midjourney to Thwart Patent Trolls
article.description: NEWS Meta Transfers AI-Related Patents to Midjourney to Thwart Patent Trolls "Sharing these assets makes our ecosystem stronger by allowing other operating companies to acquire patents that they can use to protect their innovation," said Jeremiah…
article.text: NEWS Meta Transfers AI-Related Patents to Midjourney to Thwart Patent Trolls "Sharing these assets makes our ecosystem stronger by allowing other operating companies to acquire patents that they can use to protect their innovation," said Jeremiah Chan, Meta's head of patents, licensing and open source. April 03, 2024 at 04:49 PM 5 minute read Patent Litigation The original version of this story was published on Legaltech News Meta has transferred three artificial intelligence-related patents to Midjourney, a research lab that uses generative AI to create images, a move the tech giant believes will bolster the startup’s intellectual property portfolio and spur more innovation in the AI space. The move also helps Midjourney defend itself from so-called nonparty entities, or NPEs, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits. "Sharing these assets makes our ecosystem stronger by allowing other operating companies to acquire patents that they can use to protect their innovation," said Jeremiah Chan, Meta's head of patents, licensing and open source.

April 03, 2024 at 04:49 PM

5 minute read

Patent Litigation

The original version of this story was published on Legaltech News

Meta has transferred three artificial intelligence-related patents to Midjourney, a research lab that uses generative AI to create images, a move the tech giant believes will bolster the startup’s intellectual property portfolio and spur more innovation in the AI space.

The move also helps Midjourney defend itself from so-called nonparty entities, or NPEs, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits.

article.title: Supercomputers Soon Will Crack Encryption. Is Your Company Ready?
article.description: Quantum computers under development will factor large numbers more easily. That will allow digital miscreants to crack public-key cryptography, putting data from highly regulated industries at risk. Experts say companies need to act now to update…
article.text: Quantum computers under development will factor large numbers more easily. That will allow digital miscreants to crack public-key cryptography, putting data from highly regulated industries at risk. Experts say companies need to act now to update their systems. Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet. The Cloud Security Alliance’s countdown to “Y2Q” clock will hit zero in 2030, the same year the U.S. Department of Homeland Security predicts that a quantum breakthrough will occur, posing a new threat to the means by which companies secure their customer data, business transactions and confidential communications. article.title: Michael Lynch Was a Titan of British Tech. Then He Got Crosswise With HP
article.description: A fraud trial for former Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch and former Vice President of Finance Stephen Chamberlain starts Monday in San Francisco and could last more than 10 weeks. HP wrote down the value of Autonomy by $8.8 billion in 2012, a year after…
article.text: A fraud trial for former Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch and former Vice President of Finance Stephen Chamberlain starts Monday in San Francisco and could last more than 10 weeks. HP wrote down the value of Autonomy by $8.8 billion in 2012, a year after buying it for $11 billion. HP says Autonomy overstated its revenues and profits, but Autonomy says HP is making it a scapegoat to cover up its own incompetence. It’s been more than a decade since British tech entrepreneur Michael Lynch sold his software company, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard for $11 billion. Now. he’s facing the risk of serious prison time. The blockbuster deal has landed him in criminal court alongside his former vice president of finance, Stephen Chamberlain, with each facing more than a dozen counts of wire fraud and other charges. Prosecutors say that, through a string of conference calls, news releases and emails, they presented a rosy picture of Autonomy at a time it actually was tanking, duping HP into massively overpaying in the process.

  • HP says Autonomy overstated its revenues and profits, but Autonomy says HP is making it a scapegoat to cover up its own incompetence.

article.title: Massive Stock Grant Pushes Pay for Zoom CLO/COO Into Stratosphere
article.description: Aparna Bawa received total compensation of $28 million in 2022, nearly all of it in the form of stock grants. The previous year, she did not receive grants, leaving her with compensation of just $419,940. The ultimate value of Bawa's grants will…
article.text: Aparna Bawa received total compensation of $28 million in 2022, nearly all of it in the form of stock grants. The previous year, she did not receive grants, leaving her with compensation of just $419,940. The ultimate value of Bawa's grants will depend on the company's long-term stock performance. The top lawyer at Zoom Video Communications, Aparna Bawa, who also serves as chief operating officer, saw her compensation rocket to $28 million in 2022, thanks to $27.6 million in stock grants, according to a newly filed proxy statement. The company awards periodic grants to executives, rather than making them every year. A year earlier, Bawa did not receive any grants, leaving her total pay at just $419,940.

article.title: Litigation Involving Failed Banks: What Litigators and In-House Counsel Should Be Thinking About
article.description: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in spectacular fashion earlier this month, with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation putting the bank into a federal receivership. This is the largest collapse of an FDIC-insured bank since the 2008 financial crisis…
article.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in spectacular fashion earlier this month, with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation putting the bank into a federal receivership. This is the largest collapse of an FDIC-insured bank since the 2008 financial crisis and the second largest in history, with more than $200 billion in assets involved. FDIC receiverships for two other large banks, Silvergate Bank and Signature Bank, quickly followed. The holding companies for all three banks are expected to enter bankruptcy soon. What is an FDIC receivership? Unlike most other businesses, an operating bank cannot seek relief in bankruptcy. (A bank holding company may reorganize in bankruptcy, though.) Rather, an operating bank is subject to its own insolvency regime, namely the FDIC receivership. You Might Like
article.html:
Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in spectacular fashion earlier this month, with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation putting the bank into a federal receivership. This is the largest collapse of an FDIC-insured bank since the 2008 financial crisis and the second largest in history, with more than $200 billion in assets involved. FDIC receiverships for two other large banks, Silvergate Bank and Signature Bank, quickly followed. The holding companies for all three banks are expected to enter bankruptcy soon.

What is an FDIC receivership?

Unlike most other businesses, an operating bank cannot seek relief in bankruptcy. (A bank holding company may reorganize in bankruptcy, though.) Rather, an operating bank is subject to its own insolvency regime, namely the FDIC receivership.

article.title: IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger
article.description: Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon. The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works…
article.text: Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon. The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works since August 2022, amid strong resistance from antitrust regulators in the European Union. In November, the EU’s competition authority said it was concerned that the acquisition, which would have added the Roomba to Amazon’s range of devices, would unfairly restrict competition in the market for robot vacuums. Amazon said it will pay iRobot a $94 million termination fee for walking way from the deal.

article.title: How Corporate Counsel Women of Color Became 'Sisterhood on a Grand Scale'
article.description: Before Corporate Counsel Women of Color was a global powerhouse of more than 4,500 diverse in-house lawyers. Before the group had members in more than 900 corporate legal departments around the world. Before it had connections with thousands of women…
article.text: Before Corporate Counsel Women of Color was a global powerhouse of more than 4,500 diverse in-house lawyers. Before the group had members in more than 900 corporate legal departments around the world. Before it had connections with thousands of women lawyers in Big Law. Before its annual conventions drew concert-level crowds of attendees and famous keynote speakers. Before all of that, CCWC was merely an idea that Laurie Robinson Haden was bringing to life as she sat in front of a laptop with dial-up internet in her kitchen in Harlem in the early 2000s. Haden had recently started her first in-house job as associate general counsel for ViacomCBS and, while studying her surroundings, didn’t see anyone who looked like her, a Black woman.

Haden had recently started her first in-house job as associate general counsel for ViacomCBS and, while studying her surroundings, didn’t see anyone who looked like her, a Black woman.

article.title: FTC Can Seek Monetary Relief From Government, Business Impersonators Under New Rule
article.description: NEWS FTC Can Seek Monetary Relief From Government, Business Impersonators Under New Rule The regulation, which went into effect Monday, marks the agency's latest effort to combat the illicit billion-dollar-a-year business. Consumer Protection Maydeen…
article.text: NEWS FTC Can Seek Monetary Relief From Government, Business Impersonators Under New Rule The regulation, which went into effect Monday, marks the agency's latest effort to combat the illicit billion-dollar-a-year business. Consumer Protection Maydeen Merino The Federal Trade Commission’s rule prohibiting government and business impersonations went into effect Monday, enabling the agency to seek monetary relief from scammers in an illicit billion-dollar-a-year industry that has become more difficult to combat amid improvements in artificial intelligence and related technologies. The new rule allows the FTC to seek financial penalties from scammers that “use government seals or business logos,” “spoof government and business emails and web addresses” and “falsely imply government or business affiliation” to fool consumers. FTC Can Seek Monetary Relief From Government, Business Impersonators Under New Rule

The regulation, which went into effect Monday, marks the agency's latest effort to combat the illicit billion-dollar-a-year business.

Consumer Protection

Maydeen Merino

The Federal Trade Commission’s rule prohibiting government and business impersonations went into effect Monday, enabling the agency to seek monetary relief from scammers in an illicit billion-dollar-a-year industry that has become more difficult to combat amid improvements in artificial intelligence and related technologies.

The new rule allows the FTC to seek financial penalties from scammers that “use government seals or business logos,” “spoof government and business emails and web addresses” and “falsely imply government or business affiliation” to fool consumers.

A Clinton appointee, Gilmore served as a U.S. District Judge in the Southern District of Texas from 1994 until her retirement from the bench.

article.title: What Dane Drobny Learned From Being GC of Groupon, Sears

Dane Drobny says that, when he was in law school, he thought being a lawyer was largely about advocacy and confrontation. He has since learned it’s more about problem-solving. “People are coming to you, and they’re trying to solve business problems. They’re not really trying to solve legal problems,” he said. “They’re trying to solve business problems in a compliant way that manages any legal risk.”

  • Drobny had been a litigator before broadening his legal experience with the in-house roles.

Dane Drobny says that, when he was in law school, he thought being a lawyer was largely about advocacy and confrontation. He has since learned it’s more about problem-solving.

“People are coming to you, and they’re trying to solve business problems. They’re not really trying to solve legal problems,” he said. “They’re trying to solve business problems in a compliant way that manages any legal risk.”

article.title: Head-Spinning Changes to Antitrust Enforcement Forcing Firms to Recalibrate Dealmaking
article.description: "You see significant enforcement where enforcement is meant to drive policy—policy as far as economic concerns, social concerns and stepping beyond the more traditional realm of merger review," said Peter Julian, a Jones Day partner. Expect federal…
article.text: "You see significant enforcement where enforcement is meant to drive policy—policy as far as economic concerns, social concerns and stepping beyond the more traditional realm of merger review," said Peter Julian, a Jones Day partner. Expect federal regulators to further escalate scrutiny of the antitrust landscape, experts say, as they unleash novel theories related to labor markets, roll-up deals and even seemingly innocuous exchanges of information within an industry. Jones Day partners Peter Julian and Kevin Hart highlighted those areas Thursday during a Level Legal-sponsored webinar on emerging antitrust issues. The pair say that the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission over the course of President Joe Biden’s presidency have recast antitrust enforcement in a dramatic and radical fashion.

article.title: 3 US Execs Indicted in Chiquita Terrorist Funding Probe in Colombia
article.description: Photo Credit: Mike Mozart Three American executives are among those indicted in Colombia for alleged crimes against humanity, related to a 2007 criminal case against Chiquita Brands International Inc. for funding right-wing terrorist groups in that…
article.text: Photo Credit: Mike Mozart Three American executives are among those indicted in Colombia for alleged crimes against humanity, related to a 2007 criminal case against Chiquita Brands International Inc. for funding right-wing terrorist groups in that country. The three, according to names published by UPI, are: John Olivo, formerly Chiquita’s controller for North America, and now president of its online Fresh Express unit, based in Orlando, which delivers fresh salads and produce. Dorn Wenninger, formerly chief administrative officer of Chiquita Colombia. Since 2016 he has been vice president of perishables for Walmart Mexico. Charles Keiser, formerly Chiquita’s vice president for global sourcing and production. Since 2015 he has been president and founder of Florida-based Tropical Agriculture Consulting, helping startups in developing countries improve existing supply chains from field to market delivery.
article.html:
Photo Credit: Mike Mozart

Three American executives are among those indicted in Colombia for alleged crimes against humanity, related to a 2007 criminal case against Chiquita Brands International Inc. for funding right-wing terrorist groups in that country.

The three, according to names published by UPI, are:

  •  John Olivo, formerly Chiquita’s controller for North America, and now president of its online Fresh Express unit, based in Orlando, which delivers fresh salads and produce.
  • Dorn Wenninger, formerly chief administrative officer of Chiquita Colombia. Since 2016 he has been vice president of perishables for Walmart Mexico.
  • Charles Keiser, formerly Chiquita’s vice president for global sourcing and production. Since 2015 he has been president and founder of Florida-based Tropical Agriculture Consulting, helping startups in developing countries improve existing supply chains from field to market delivery.

article.description: Shook has added Christopher Kondon and Saman Rejali, employment litigation partners from K&L Gates, in LA. The duo said they were looking for a more focused litigation and trial experience. Shook's LA office leader said he's looking for additional IP…
article.text: Shook has added Christopher Kondon and Saman Rejali, employment litigation partners from K&L Gates, in LA. The duo said they were looking for a more focused litigation and trial experience. Shook's LA office leader said he's looking for additional IP and regulatory expertise and wants to reach 'critical mass.' After growing from five to 27 lawyers over the last five years in Los Angeles, litigation-focused Shook, Hardy & Bacon is trying to reach “critical mass” in the city by adding roughly 20 more lawyers there over the next five years. “To have critical mass, to really have a presence in the Los Angeles market and be a litigation powerhouse, I think you need about 45 to 50 lawyers,” said Shook’s LA office managing partner, Michael Mallow, adding he’d like to have that number in the next five years.

article.title: Judge: Insurer Must Defend, Indemnify Contractor Accused of Negligence in Building Collapse
article.description: In an insurance coverage dispute, Capitol Specialty Insurance Corp. asked whether it was obligated to defend and indemnify a contractor accused of negligently causing the collapse of a four-story brick building during renovations. The contractor…
article.text: In an insurance coverage dispute, Capitol Specialty Insurance Corp. asked whether it was obligated to defend and indemnify a contractor accused of negligently causing the collapse of a four-story brick building during renovations. The contractor counterclaimed, seeking a declaration that Capitol has a duty to defend and indemnify in the underlying lawsuit. The federal judge sided with the contractor, finding that the policy pertaining to property damage applies to an occurrence, including an accident. A federal judge ruled Tuesday that an insurer is obligated to defend and indemnify a Boston contractor accused in an underlying $1.14 million lawsuit for negligently causing the collapse of a four-story brick building during renovations.

Conditions include 100 hours community service, legal ethics education, payment of $271,000 restitution. If Paxton successfully completes these and other conditions, the case will be dismissed in 18 months. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton entered a pretrial intervention agreement in a Harris County district court Tuesday morning to get felony securities fraud charges dismissed. The agreement requires Paxton complete 100 hours of community service, including 15 hours of legal ethics classes and he is to pay $271,000 in restitution to the victims, according to prosecutor Brian Wice.

Clinical-stage biopharma company BPGbio nabbed Ritesh Srivastava, former global compliance officer at publicly traded Spectrum Pharmaceuticals, as its first general counsel. Srivastava's public-company experience will help BPGbio as it moves to launch an IPO in the next three years. Two East Coast pharma companies are adding general counsel to their executive ranks, hiring compliance leaders with deep biotech industry experience to head their legal teams. Tris Pharma—a New Jersey-based drugmaker focused on treatments for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, addiction and other neurological diseases—hired Franchesca Fowler as its chief compliance officer and general counsel.
article.html:
• New Jersey-based Tris Pharma hired a compliance specialist as its chief compliance officer and general counsel.

  • Srivastava's public-company experience will help BPGbio as it moves to launch an IPO in the next three years.

Two East Coast pharma companies are adding general counsel to their executive ranks, hiring compliance leaders with deep biotech industry experience to head their legal teams.

Tris Pharma—a New Jersey-based drugmaker focused on treatments for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, addiction and other neurological diseases—hired Franchesca Fowler as its chief compliance officer and general counsel.

article.title: 'I’ve Never Had a Female General Counsel Before': How La-Z-Boy's New Chief Lawyer Reached the GC Seat
article.description: Raphael Richmond, general counsel and chief compliance officer at La-Z-Boy Inc. Courtesy photo "The first thing I’d say to anyone who doesn’t see themselves in the slate of general counsels is, 'You belong in the seat and go about your career with…
article.text: Raphael Richmond, general counsel and chief compliance officer at La-Z-Boy Inc. Courtesy photo "The first thing I’d say to anyone who doesn’t see themselves in the slate of general counsels is, 'You belong in the seat and go about your career with the assumption that you have the capability and potential to end up in that seat,'" said Raphael Richmond. On a recent rainy, windy and unseasonably cool afternoon in Michigan, with her “fabulous but somewhat grumpy cat” lurking in the background and wanting to go outside, Raphael Richmond sat in her kitchen for a video call and reflected on her path to becoming the next legal chief at La-Z-Boy Inc. Richmond confided that, earlier in her career, she had been reluctant to even entertain the idea of one day being a general counsel, all of whom seemed to be men at the time. Of course, her mindset changed over the years and now more women and minorities are running corporate legal departments for top companies than ever before, though the balance remains skewed toward white men.
article.html:
Raphael Richmond, general counsel and chief compliance officer at La-Z-Boy Inc. Courtesy photo

article.title: DocuSign Greeted New Legal Chief With a $13 Million Stock Award
article.description: DocuSign legal chief James Shaughnessy's total compensation was $13.6 million in 2022. Most of it came from a $13.2 million stock award. Shaughnessy joined DocuSign in May 2022 after its general counsel and senior vice president Trâm Phi left to take…
article.text: DocuSign legal chief James Shaughnessy's total compensation was $13.6 million in 2022. Most of it came from a $13.2 million stock award. Shaughnessy joined DocuSign in May 2022 after its general counsel and senior vice president Trâm Phi left to take the top lawyer job at Databricks. Former Workday, Lenovo and HP lawyer James Shaughnessy was paid $13.6 million, almost entirely in stock, when he joined DocuSign as head of its legal department in mid-2022, the electronic signature software company disclosed in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Shaughnessy, who took the legal reins at San Francisco-based DocuSign on May 31, received a $13.2 million stock award and a salary of $321,692, which was prorated because he joined mid-year, DocuSign’s proxy statement explains. article.title: Longtime Hormel General Counsel Making Sudden Exit
article.description: Lori Marco, Hormel Foods’ general counsel for nearly 13 years, will depart at the end of October. A Hormel spokesperson on Friday confirmed Marco’s planned departure and said the company is seeking a replacement, but declined to comment further. A…
article.text: Lori Marco, Hormel Foods’ general counsel for nearly 13 years, will depart at the end of October. A Hormel spokesperson on Friday confirmed Marco’s planned departure and said the company is seeking a replacement, but declined to comment further. A day earlier, Hormel said in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing that on Monday it “determined that … Marco … will separate from the company effective as of October 27, 2023.”
article.html:
Lori Marco, Hormel Foods’ general counsel for nearly 13 years, will depart at the end of October.

A Hormel spokesperson on Friday confirmed Marco’s planned departure and said the company is seeking a replacement, but declined to comment further. A day earlier, Hormel said in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing that on Monday it “determined that … Marco … will separate from the company effective as of October 27, 2023.”

article.title: National Rifle Association General Counsel Caught in Group's Firestorm
article.description: John Frazer, general counsel and secretary of National Rifle Association. Courtesy photo. A series of late April developments at the Fairfax, Virginia-based pro-gun organization have left general counsel John Frazer and his legal team dealing with an…
article.text: John Frazer, general counsel and secretary of National Rifle Association. Courtesy photo. A series of late April developments at the Fairfax, Virginia-based pro-gun organization have left general counsel John Frazer and his legal team dealing with an array of challenges. Internal financial and legal turmoil has gripped the National Rifle Association and its leadership over the past month, and at the center of the storm sits the general counsel office, headed by 21-year organization veteran John Frazer. A series of late April developments at the Fairfax, Virginia-based pro-gun organization have left Frazer and his legal team dealing with an array of challenges, including: New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into the NRA’s tax-exempt status. Fallout from the dismissal of the board of director’s longtime outside counsel, Steve Hart, who has declined to comment. Allegations of massive legal payments to other outside counsel over the past year that threaten to weaken the group. A bitter lawsuit between the organization and its Oklahoma-based advertising firm of 30 years, Ackerman McQueen, which operates NRATV. A yearlong legal battle with New York that has escalated to other states that are challenging a weapons-carry insurance program the organization sells to its members, which has been called crucial to the group’s existence.
article.html:
John Frazer, general counsel and secretary of National Rifle Association. Courtesy photo.

A series of late April developments at the Fairfax, Virginia-based pro-gun organization have left general counsel John Frazer and his legal team dealing with an array of challenges.

Internal financial and legal turmoil has gripped the National Rifle Association and its leadership over the past month, and at the center of the storm sits the general counsel office, headed by 21-year organization veteran John Frazer.

A series of late April developments at the Fairfax, Virginia-based pro-gun organization have left Frazer and his legal team dealing with an array of challenges, including:

  • New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into the NRA’s tax-exempt status.
  • Fallout from the dismissal of the board of director’s longtime outside counsel, Steve Hart, who has declined to comment.
  • Allegations of massive legal payments to other outside counsel over the past year that threaten to weaken the group.
  • A bitter lawsuit between the organization and its Oklahoma-based advertising firm of 30 years, Ackerman McQueen, which operates NRATV.
  • A yearlong legal battle with New York that has escalated to other states that are challenging a weapons-carry insurance program the organization sells to its members, which has been called crucial to the group’s existence.

article.text: Pendo has hired Bret DiMarco as chief legal officer. DiMarco comes from laser-maker Coherent, which was acquired for $7 billion in July. Pendo was valued at $2.6 billion in a funding round last year. Raleigh, North Carolina-based software unicorn Pendo has snagged as its first-ever chief legal officer a Bay Area attorney who recently helped sell his former employer for $7 billion. Bret DiMarco spent 16 years at Coherent, a laser-maker purchased by II-VI in July. article.title: AI Hype Needs To Come To An End
article.description: As we have seen the industry mature and get more involved and educated about AI, not many people still think that AI will replace lawyers. The idiom has changed to “lawyers who use AI will replace those who don’t.” It’s time to hold AI’s feet to the…
article.text: As we have seen the industry mature and get more involved and educated about AI, not many people still think that AI will replace lawyers. The idiom has changed to “lawyers who use AI will replace those who don’t.” It’s time to hold AI’s feet to the fire — it’s “come to Jesus” moment. In Cybersecurity Law & Strategy‘s end of 2023/look ahead to 2024, we asked experts if we are approaching AI overload and if it’s overhyped. The answers were mixed, but those who didn’t think so might change their minds if they were at Legalweek. As expected, Legalweek was AI heavy, both in the exhibit hall and in the conference sessions. The answer to the above question in the look ahead article that comes to mind is this one, from Richard Robbins, Epiq Managing Director, Applied Artificial Intelligence: The last year has been dominated by fascination with technology and consideration of what it might be. It has been time for initial experiments. Now we will learn from those experiments and for the leaders, move to adoption. We need to focus less on technology for the sake of technology and get back to the problems we want to solve. It’s time to stop the hype, stop talking up AI as if it’s the next best thing since sliced bread and prove that it’s a useful tool and technology that can actually be used in the actual practice of law. As we have seen the industry mature and get more involved and educated about AI, not many people still think that AI will replace lawyers, the idiom has changed to “lawyers who use AI will replace those who don’t.”
article.html:
• As we have seen the industry mature and get more involved and educated about AI, not many people still think that AI will replace lawyers.
  • The idiom has changed to “lawyers who use AI will replace those who don’t.”
  • It’s time to hold AI’s feet to the fire — it’s “come to Jesus” moment.

In Cybersecurity Law & Strategy‘s end of 2023/look ahead to 2024, we asked experts if we are approaching AI overload and if it’s overhyped. The answers were mixed, but those who didn’t think so might change their minds if they were at Legalweek. As expected, Legalweek was AI heavy, both in the exhibit hall and in the conference sessions. The answer to the above question in the look ahead article that comes to mind is this one, from Richard Robbins, Epiq Managing Director, Applied Artificial Intelligence:

The last year has been dominated by fascination with technology and consideration of what it might be. It has been time for initial experiments. Now we will learn from those experiments and for the leaders, move to adoption. We need to focus less on technology for the sake of technology and get back to the problems we want to solve.

It’s time to stop the hype, stop talking up AI as if it’s the next best thing since sliced bread and prove that it’s a useful tool and technology that can actually be used in the actual practice of law. As we have seen the industry mature and get more involved and educated about AI, not many people still think that AI will replace lawyers, the idiom has changed to “lawyers who use AI will replace those who don’t.”

article.title: EEOC Settles First AI-Bias Case, but Many More Are Likely
article.description: iTutorGroup will pay $365,000 to settle allegations it automatically disqualified female candidates over 55 and male candidates over 60. Employment attorneys say the allegations in that case were unusually straightforward, and future cases will be…
article.text: iTutorGroup will pay $365,000 to settle allegations it automatically disqualified female candidates over 55 and male candidates over 60. Employment attorneys say the allegations in that case were unusually straightforward, and future cases will be much more nuanced. An AI-bias-in-hiring lawsuit that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission settled this week was the first case of its kind brought by the agency. But employment lawyers expect many more to come, as well as more suits filed by job candidates who believe they were victims of AI bias.

article.title: Eighth Circuit: Intent Requirements in Iowa’s New 'Ag-Gag' Law Are Not Unconstitutional Restrictions on Speech
article.description: In Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Reynolds, 89 F.4th 1065 (8th Cir. 2024), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit upheld Iowa Code Section 717A.3B(1)(a)-(b) (2019), prohibiting (1) using deception to access an agricultural production facility…
article.text: In Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Reynolds, 89 F.4th 1065 (8th Cir. 2024), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit upheld Iowa Code Section 717A.3B(1)(a)-(b) (2019), prohibiting (1) using deception to access an agricultural production facility with intent to cause harm to the facility, and (2) using deception in an employment application, on a matter that would reasonably result in denial of employment at an agricultural facility, with the intent to cause harm to the facility. The statute’s intent requirements did not make the statute content-based or viewpoint-based such that it would trigger strict scrutiny. Judge Steven M. Colloton wrote the opinion, with Judge Raymond W. Gruender and Judge Jonathan A. Kobes joining. Previously, the Iowa legislature had passed a law prohibiting (1) accessing an agricultural production facility by false pretenses and (2) making a false statement as part of an employment application at such a facility. Iowa Code § 717A.3A(1)(a)-(b) (2012). When considering that law, the Eighth Circuit interpreted United States v. Alvarez, 567 U.S. 709 (2012), to mean “that intentionally false speech undertaken to accomplish a legally cognizable harm may be proscribed,” and found that the statute had done just that, proscribing false statements undertaken to accomplish trespass. Animal Legal Defense Fund v. Reynolds, 8 F.4th 781, 786 (8th Cir. 2021) (ALDF I). As such, the statute’s access provision did not violate the First Amendment. But the Eighth Circuit struck down the employment provision, concluding it was not narrowly tailored because it encompassed immaterial fabrications by an applicant, such as an applicant “inflat[ing] his past attendance at the hometown football stadium.”
article.html:

The statute’s intent requirements did not make the statute content-based or viewpoint-based such that it would trigger strict scrutiny. Judge Steven M. Colloton wrote the opinion, with Judge Raymond W. Gruender and Judge Jonathan A. Kobes joining.

Previously, the Iowa legislature had passed a law prohibiting (1) accessing an agricultural production facility by false pretenses and (2) making a false statement as part of an employment application at such a facility. article.title: 4 Longtime Netflix Legal Execs Out in Restructuring
article.description: Four attorneys who are senior members of Netflix’s legal and business affairs team are exiting as part of a restructuring, including 16-year company veteran Bryony Gagan, who oversaw global content production, acquisition and distribution. Gagan has…
article.text: Four attorneys who are senior members of Netflix’s legal and business affairs team are exiting as part of a restructuring, including 16-year company veteran Bryony Gagan, who oversaw global content production, acquisition and distribution. Gagan has the title vice president of legal affairs, as do nine-year company veteran Amy Paquette and 13-year veteran Tim Mizrahi, who also are leaving. The fourth departure is nine-year veteran Stephen Zager, vice president and associate general counsel. The news was first reported by Deadline.
article.html:
Four attorneys who are senior members of Netflix’s legal and business affairs team are exiting as part of a restructuring, including 16-year company veteran Bryony Gagan, who oversaw global content production, acquisition and distribution.

Gagan has the title vice president of legal affairs, as do nine-year company veteran Amy Paquette and 13-year veteran Tim Mizrahi, who also are leaving. The fourth departure is nine-year veteran Stephen Zager, vice president and associate general counsel. The news was first reported by Deadline.

article.title: 'Frustrated' Legal Department Leaders Want Law Firms to Improve Data Reporting
article.description: (l-r) Bill Deckelman, general counsel of DXC Technology; Lauren Chung, managing director at HBR Consulting; and Lindsey Haswell, chief administrative and legal officer of Blockchain.com. Courtesy photos General counsel want to see data from law firms…
article.text: (l-r) Bill Deckelman, general counsel of DXC Technology; Lauren Chung, managing director at HBR Consulting; and Lindsey Haswell, chief administrative and legal officer of Blockchain.com. Courtesy photos General counsel want to see data from law firms digitized and able to be analyzed. Law firms that are unable to digitize data and offer it to clients will likely lose out to competition. GCs want law firm data on budget and risks. General counsel are increasingly looking for law firms that can collect and deliver data so corporations can improve their decision-making about risks and spending. But they are often frustrated when outside counsel can’t meet these expectations, according to in-house sources. Law firms that are unable to digitize data and offer it to their clients will likely lose out to their more cutting-edge competition, some sources said.

article.title: Blizzard of New Laws, Covering Pot to Paid Leave, May Leave Employers in Fog
article.description: States are pushing up minimum wages, with the size of the increases sometimes varying by location and by industry. They're also getting into the antitrust enforcement game, particularly in relation to health care deals. California, Illinois and New…
article.text: States are pushing up minimum wages, with the size of the increases sometimes varying by location and by industry. They're also getting into the antitrust enforcement game, particularly in relation to health care deals. California, Illinois and New York are leading the way on worker-friendly measures, such as mandatory paid leave. In-house counsel will grapple with a heavy load of new laws taking effect in 2024, particularly in worker-friendly states such as California, Illinois and New York. For instance, several states and cities are rolling out new laws forcing employers to boost pay and to grant employees additional leave.

article.title: Study Reveals How Pedigree of Law Schools, Law Firms Influence In-House Pay
article.description: BarkerGilmore surveyed 3,800 U.S.-based corporate counsel, 48% of whom attended a top-50 U.S law school. The survey found in-house attorneys who went to a top-50 law school and worked at an Am Law 50 law firm earn 76% more than those who didn't.…
article.text: BarkerGilmore surveyed 3,800 U.S.-based corporate counsel, 48% of whom attended a top-50 U.S law school. The survey found in-house attorneys who went to a top-50 law school and worked at an Am Law 50 law firm earn 76% more than those who didn't. In-house attorneys who went to a Top 50 law school earn an average of 30% more than those attending schools ranked 100 or lower. If they went to a Top 50 law school and worked at an Am Law 50 law firm, they earned 76% more than those who didn’t. Those were among the findings from the recruiting firm BarkerGilmore’s recently released annual compensation report, which was based on responses from 3,800 U.S.-based corporate counsel, 48% of whom attended a top-50 U.S. law school. article.title: Foley & Lardner Hires Former SoftBank GC in San Francisco, Eyeing Fund Formation Opportunities
article.description: Foley & Lardner is bringing in a former investment fund GC to help build an investment fund team in California. The firm views California as an untapped market for investment fund advisory work. With a robust team already located in Boston, Foley is…
article.text: Foley & Lardner is bringing in a former investment fund GC to help build an investment fund team in California. The firm views California as an untapped market for investment fund advisory work. With a robust team already located in Boston, Foley is looking to re-create that success in California, starting with its latest hire. Foley & Lardner is bringing on a former managing partner and general counsel from SoftBank Investment Advisors in an attempt to fill gaps in California. Before joining Foley as a Silicon Valley-based partner in the firm’s transactions practice, Brian Wheeler spent more than two years working as general counsel for HENI, an art services and technology company, where he oversaw the company’s intellectual property portfolio as well as its venture investments. Before HENI, Wheeler also spent more than five years at SoftBank Investment Advisors, where he built a team of 40 lawyers managing more than $130 billion in investments. Before that, Wheeler served as general counsel for SoftBank Group International.

Before HENI, Wheeler also spent more than five years at SoftBank Investment Advisors, where he built a team of 40 lawyers managing more than $130 billion in investments. Before that, Wheeler served as general counsel for SoftBank Group International.

article.text: The Federal Trade Commission on Monday sued to block luxury fashion group Tapestry’s $8.5 billion purchase of rival Capri Holdings, saying it would quash direct competition between the firms and give Tapestry a dominant position in the market for “accessible luxury” handbags. The deal, announced in August, would combine Tapestry’s Coach, Stuart Weitzman and Kate Spade brands with Capri’s Michael Kors, Jimmy Choo and Versace labels.
article.html:
The Federal Trade Commission on Monday sued to block luxury fashion group Tapestry’s $8.5 billion purchase of rival Capri Holdings, saying it would quash direct competition between the firms and give Tapestry a dominant position in the market for “accessible luxury” handbags.

The deal, announced in August, would combine Tapestry’s Coach, Stuart Weitzman and Kate Spade brands with Capri’s Michael Kors, Jimmy Choo and Versace labels.

article.title: Copyright Infringement Damages Are Not Limited to Three Years, Supreme Court Says
article.description: But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely…
article.text: But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely filing of their infringement suits, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled Thursday. But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins: when the infringement occurred or when the holder discovered or should have discovered the copyright was infringed. So, in its decision regarding damages, the court “assume[d] without deciding that a claim is timely” if brought within three years of the infringement’s discovery regardless of when the infringement occurred. “We have never decided whether that assumption is valid—i.e., whether a copyright claim accrues when a plaintiff discovers or should have discovered an infringement, rather than when the infringement happened,” Justice Elena Kagan wrote for the majority. Nevertheless, she stated that there’s no reason to limit the availability of money damages for infringing conduct that has only occurred in the three years prior to filing, as a federal district court did in the proceedings below. “There is no time limit on monetary recovery,” Kagan wrote. “So a copyright owner possessing a timely claim for infringement is entitled to damages, no matter when the infringement occurred.” To the three dissenting justices, the majority’s exercise of assuming when the three-year clock begins for filing an infringement claim was a waste of the court’s time and energy. “The trouble is, the [Copyright] Act almost certainly does not tolerate a discovery rule,” Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote in a dissent joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito Jr. “And that fact promises soon enough to make anything we might say today about the rule’s operational details a dead letter.” The unusual procedural aspect of the case comes from the fact there is no acknowledged circuit split on the discovery rule, but there is one regarding how that rule is applied. Therefore, when the Supreme Court granted certiorari, or review, in the case, it assumed the existence of the discovery rule and asked whether the act allows for damages for “acts that allegedly occurred more than three years before the filing of a lawsuit.” The petitioner, Warner Chappell Music, had nevertheless encouraged the court to address the discovery rule, earning a mild rebuke from Kagan’s majority opinion Thursday. “Our reformulation of the question presented should have put an end to such arguments,” she wrote. Gorsuch, however, stated that the approach taken by the majority “does not strike me as the most sensible one.” “Nothing requires us to play along with these particular parties and expound on the details of a rule of law that they may assume but very likely does not exist,” he wrote. “Respectfully, rather than devote our time to this case, I would have dismissed it as improvidently granted and awaited another squarely presenting the question whether the Copyright Act authorizes the discovery rule,” Gorsuch wrote. “Better, in my view, to answer a question that does matter than one that almost certainly does not.” The lawsuit centers around a 1980s music venture between Sherman Nealy and Tony Butler called Music Specialist Inc., which recorded a number of songs during a brief period before Nealy went to prison from 1989 to 2008 for drug crimes. Butler later signed a deal with Warner Chappell Music to license Music Specialist Inc.’s works and found “quite a few takers,” as Kagan’s opinion explains. After a second prison term from 2012 to 2015, Nealy filed a copyright infringement lawsuit in 2018 covering alleged infringement acts that took place more than a decade prior. Nealy said his claims were timely because he did not learn of the infringement until after he was released from prison for the second time. A federal district court allowed the claims to proceed, but said Nealy could only seek damages for infringing conduct that occurred within three years of the lawsuit, a decision reversed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. Warner Chappell Music appealed, but the Supreme Court affirmed the Eleventh Circuit’s ruling. Kannon Shanmugam of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison argued the case on behalf of Warner Chappell Music in February. Joe Wesley Earnhardt of Cravath, Swaine & Moore appeared for respondent Nealy. Assistant to the U.S. Solicitor General Yaira Dubin appeared on behalf of the federal government in support of Nealy’s successful argument that damages are not limited to the prior three years. The case is Warner Chappell Music v. Nealy, No. 22-1078.
article.html:
But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins.

Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely filing of their infringement suits, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled Thursday.

But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins: when the infringement occurred or when the holder discovered or should have discovered the copyright was infringed. So, in its decision regarding damages, the court “assume[d] without deciding that a claim is timely” if brought within three years of the infringement’s discovery regardless of when the infringement occurred.

“We have never decided whether that assumption is valid—i.e., whether a copyright claim accrues when a plaintiff discovers or should have discovered an infringement, rather than when the infringement happened,” Justice Elena Kagan wrote for the majority.

Nevertheless, she stated that there’s no reason to limit the availability of money damages for infringing conduct that has only occurred in the three years prior to filing, as a federal district court did in the proceedings below.

“There is no time limit on monetary recovery,” Kagan wrote. “So a copyright owner possessing a timely claim for infringement is entitled to damages, no matter when the infringement occurred.”

To the three dissenting justices, the majority’s exercise of assuming when the three-year clock begins for filing an infringement claim was a waste of the court’s time and energy.

“The trouble is, the [Copyright] Act almost certainly does not tolerate a discovery rule,” Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote in a dissent joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito Jr. “And that fact promises soon enough to make anything we might say today about the rule’s operational details a dead letter.”

The unusual procedural aspect of the case comes from the fact there is no acknowledged circuit split on the discovery rule, but there is one regarding how that rule is applied. Therefore, when the Supreme Court granted certiorari, or review, in the case, it assumed the existence of the discovery rule and asked whether the act allows for damages for “acts that allegedly occurred more than three years before the filing of a lawsuit.”

The petitioner, Warner Chappell Music, had nevertheless encouraged the court to address the discovery rule, earning a mild rebuke from Kagan’s majority opinion Thursday.

“Our reformulation of the question presented should have put an end to such arguments,” she wrote.

Gorsuch, however, stated that the approach taken by the majority “does not strike me as the most sensible one.”

“Nothing requires us to play along with these particular parties and expound on the details of a rule of law that they may assume but very likely does not exist,” he wrote.

“Respectfully, rather than devote our time to this case, I would have dismissed it as improvidently granted and awaited another squarely presenting the question whether the Copyright Act authorizes the discovery rule,” Gorsuch wrote. “Better, in my view, to answer a question that does matter than one that almost certainly does not.”

The lawsuit centers around a 1980s music venture between Sherman Nealy and Tony Butler called Music Specialist Inc., which recorded a number of songs during a brief period before Nealy went to prison from 1989 to 2008 for drug crimes.

Butler later signed a deal with Warner Chappell Music to license Music Specialist Inc.’s works and found “quite a few takers,” as Kagan’s opinion explains. After a second prison term from 2012 to 2015, Nealy filed a copyright infringement lawsuit in 2018 covering alleged infringement acts that took place more than a decade prior.

Nealy said his claims were timely because he did not learn of the infringement until after he was released from prison for the second time.

A federal district court allowed the claims to proceed, but said Nealy could only seek damages for infringing conduct that occurred within three years of the lawsuit, a decision reversed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

Warner Chappell Music appealed, but the Supreme Court affirmed the Eleventh Circuit’s ruling.

Kannon Shanmugam of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison argued the case on behalf of Warner Chappell Music in February. Joe Wesley Earnhardt of Cravath, Swaine & Moore appeared for respondent Nealy.

Assistant to the U.S. Solicitor General Yaira Dubin appeared on behalf of the federal government in support of Nealy’s successful argument that damages are not limited to the prior three years.

The case is Warner Chappell Music v. Nealy, No. 22-1078.

article.title: Conservative States' Suit Accuses EEOC of Defining Gender-Identity Discrimination Way Too Broadly
article.description: Employers that refused to use transgender workers' preferred pronounces or barred them from using bathroom that match their gender identity would be committing workplace harassment, according to recently issued EEOC guidance. Eighteen…
article.text: Employers that refused to use transgender workers' preferred pronounces or barred them from using bathroom that match their gender identity would be committing workplace harassment, according to recently issued EEOC guidance. Eighteen Republican-leaning states have sued the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, alleging that the agency is defining gender-identity-based workplace harassment far more broadly than the landmark federal workplace-harassment law provides. Spurring the complaint was new EEOC guidance on workplace-harassment enforcement, issued in April, stating that employers that refused to use transgender workers’ preferred pronouns or barred them from using bathrooms that match their gender identity would be committing workplace harassment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
article.html:
Employers that refused to use transgender workers' preferred pronounces or barred them from using bathroom that match their gender identity would be committing workplace harassment, according to recently issued EEOC guidance.

Eighteen Republican-leaning states have sued the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, alleging that the agency is defining gender-identity-based workplace harassment far more broadly than the landmark federal workplace-harassment law provides.

Spurring the complaint was new EEOC guidance on workplace-harassment enforcement, issued in April, stating that employers that refused to use transgender workers’ preferred pronouns or barred them from using bathrooms that match their gender identity would be committing workplace harassment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

article.text: Hewlett-Packard legal chief Julie Jacobs received $6.1 million in pay in 2023, her first full year on the job. That included a $2 million cash bonus to offset compensation she lost by resigning as Yahoo's legal chief in the fall of 2022. In 2022, Jacobs received a $9 million stock grant from HP for the same reason. HP Chief Legal Officer Julie Jacobs received $6.2 million in compensation in her first full year on the job, a sum that includes a $2 million cash bonus. HP explains in its newly filed proxy statement that the bonus, paid out in fiscal year 2023, represents a one-time payment “in recognition of foregone compensation at her previous employer.” Julie Jacobs, HP CLO. Photo by Kira Gree

article.title: 'Be More Intentional': How GCs Are Building Camaraderie Amid Hybrid Work
article.description: "It is so much easier to trust someone at work when you know the whole person and trust them with your whole person," said Theresa Shea, general counsel of Utz Brands. GCs can't count on camaraderie to occur by happenstance. They especially need to…
article.text: "It is so much easier to trust someone at work when you know the whole person and trust them with your whole person," said Theresa Shea, general counsel of Utz Brands. GCs can't count on camaraderie to occur by happenstance. They especially need to help new employees feel part of the team. Making the most of in-person interactions is crucial. Shari Piré, chief legal and sustainability officer at Palo Alto, California-based Plume Design, said that because legal departments are the conduits through which all agreements and processes flow, they can exert a positive influence companywide. “The legal team is well-positioned to create camaraderie both in the legal team and across the company more broadly,” said Piré, whose company provides Wi-Fi and internet-connected smart home services. But GCs agree that camaraderie and mentorship that might have occurred by happenstance before the pandemic emptied out workplaces now requires intentionality. Timothy Brown, executive vice president and chief legal officer of West Chester, Pennsylvania-based Venerable, which owns legacy variable annuities cast off by insurance companies, said he makes a point of holding team meetings on in-office days to promote collaboration and the sharing of ideas. “This keeps everyone aligned on the progress toward department priorities and also helps our newer team members quickly integrate into the group,” he said. ‘Informal Conversations to Develop Were Not Happening’
article.html:
"It is so much easier to trust someone at work when you know the whole person and trust them with your whole person," said Theresa Shea, general counsel of Utz Brands.

  • GCs can't count on camaraderie to occur by happenstance.
  • They especially need to help new employees feel part of the team.
  • Making the most of in-person interactions is crucial.

Shari Piré, chief legal and sustainability officer at Palo Alto, California-based Plume Design, said that because legal departments are the conduits through which all agreements and processes flow, they can exert a positive influence companywide.

“The legal team is well-positioned to create camaraderie both in the legal team and across the company more broadly,” said Piré, whose company provides Wi-Fi and internet-connected smart home services.

But GCs agree that camaraderie and mentorship that might have occurred by happenstance before the pandemic emptied out workplaces now requires intentionality.

Timothy Brown, executive vice president and chief legal officer of West Chester, Pennsylvania-based Venerable, which owns legacy variable annuities cast off by insurance companies, said he makes a point of holding team meetings on in-office days to promote collaboration and the sharing of ideas.

“This keeps everyone aligned on the progress toward department priorities and also helps our newer team members quickly integrate into the group,” he said.

‘Informal Conversations to Develop Were Not Happening’

article.title: 'This Is a Rocket Ship': How Generative AI Will Transform Legal Departments
article.description: Generative AI could spur the biggest changes in how legal departments operate since the arrival of the internet. Attorneys will need to stop measuring their performance by the written work they're producing. Legal department leaders who fail to…
article.text: Generative AI could spur the biggest changes in how legal departments operate since the arrival of the internet. Attorneys will need to stop measuring their performance by the written work they're producing. Legal department leaders who fail to embrace the changes will imperil their careers. The Goldman Sachs report released this week saying generative AI could automate 44% of legal tasks in the U.S. is a watershed moment for legal departments, according to general counsel and other experts, signaling perhaps the biggest shift in how lawyers work since the arrival of the internet. In-house attorneys and consultants say the technology will accelerate attorneys’ transition away from rote work to high-value-add tasks. And while it’s difficult to predict exactly how changes will play out, they say legal departments likely will maintain and grow their workforces but in some cases scale back their reliance on pricey outside counsel.
article.html:
• Generative AI could spur the biggest changes in how legal departments operate since the arrival of the internet.
  • Attorneys will need to stop measuring their performance by the written work they're producing.
  • Legal department leaders who fail to embrace the changes will imperil their careers.

The Goldman Sachs report released this week saying generative AI could automate 44% of legal tasks in the U.S. is a watershed moment for legal departments, according to general counsel and other experts, signaling perhaps the biggest shift in how lawyers work since the arrival of the internet.

In-house attorneys and consultants say the technology will accelerate attorneys’ transition away from rote work to high-value-add tasks. And while it’s difficult to predict exactly how changes will play out, they say legal departments likely will maintain and grow their workforces but in some cases scale back their reliance on pricey outside counsel.

article.title: ‘Lead With Empathy,’ Not Indignation: How a Googler Fixes Outside Counsel Relationships in 4 Easy Steps
article.description: Every in-house counsel has been there, staring down the frustrating experience of managing an outside counsel relationship that just isn’t working. It can be emotionally exhausting. Nevertheless, difficult conversations must be had. But it need not…
article.text: Every in-house counsel has been there, staring down the frustrating experience of managing an outside counsel relationship that just isn’t working. It can be emotionally exhausting. Nevertheless, difficult conversations must be had. But it need not be as painful as it seems. Eager for practical advice, in-house attorneys convened Wednesday at the CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas for a session led by Matt Rubbelke, a senior associate in vendor strategy and governance management at Google, titled: “Can We Talk? How To Have Difficult Conversations With Your OC.”
article.html:
Every in-house counsel has been there, staring down the frustrating experience of managing an outside counsel relationship that just isn’t working. It can be emotionally exhausting. Nevertheless, difficult conversations must be had. But it need not be as painful as it seems.

Eager for practical advice, in-house attorneys convened Wednesday at the CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas for a session led by Matt Rubbelke, a senior associate in vendor strategy and governance management at Google, titled: “Can We Talk? How To Have Difficult Conversations With Your OC.”

article.title: Hackers Can Steal Encryption Keys From a Distance Using Video
article.description: On June 13, security researchers disclosed their findings that encryption keys for wireless devices are vulnerable to theft. This research found that cameras in cellular phones or commercial surveillance systems can be used to record power light…
article.text: On June 13, security researchers disclosed their findings that encryption keys for wireless devices are vulnerable to theft. This research found that cameras in cellular phones or commercial surveillance systems can be used to record power light emitting diodes (LEDs) from up to 60 feet away from a device, thus capturing encryption keys. This new weakness exploits two previously known side-channel attacks, a class of attacks measuring physical effects “leaking” from a device as it performs its operations. Companies should review their systems for this vulnerability, including smart card readers used for access or authentication. All industries are vulnerable to this exploitation; however, health care may be especially hard hit in the future due to the potential to expose electronic medical records. Defense contractors with sensitive information are also highly targeted and should review how this could impact their systems and networks. But the reality is that any secured physical area could be impacted by an attacker’s ability to physically break into buildings and facilities.
article.html:
On June 13, security researchers disclosed their findings that encryption keys for wireless devices are vulnerable to theft. This research found that cameras in cellular phones or commercial surveillance systems can be used to record power light emitting diodes (LEDs) from up to 60 feet away from a device, thus capturing encryption keys.

This new weakness exploits two previously known side-channel attacks, a class of attacks measuring physical effects “leaking” from a device as it performs its operations. Companies should review their systems for this vulnerability, including smart card readers used for access or authentication. All industries are vulnerable to this exploitation; however, health care may be especially hard hit in the future due to the potential to expose electronic medical records. Defense contractors with sensitive information are also highly targeted and should review how this could impact their systems and networks. But the reality is that any secured physical area could be impacted by an attacker’s ability to physically break into buildings and facilities.

article.title: Moving the Needle on Outside Counsel Team Diversity
article.description: The current profusion of outside counsel DEI surveys that law firms receive from their clients has hit an all-time high. While well intended, these surveys haven’t moved the needle at a rate commensurate with the work involved. And, at their worst,…
article.text: The current profusion of outside counsel DEI surveys that law firms receive from their clients has hit an all-time high. While well intended, these surveys haven’t moved the needle at a rate commensurate with the work involved. And, at their worst, they can actually work at cross-purposes with legal departments’ objective of fostering a culture of diversity and inclusivity by diverting valuable time from diversity leaders to repeatedly define the problem rather than working on solutions. This need not be the case. Most legal departments have neither the resources nor the scientific expertise to craft and conduct an effective assessment of their outside counsel DEI that produces more inclusive teams. Many have told us they don’t know where to start other than perhaps the raft of firmwide data produced annually by dozens of reputable third-party organizations. And even then, it takes substantial time and ability to analyze the data and successfully operationalize the findings to align with organizational values.
article.html:

article.title: Walgreens Goes Outside Retailing to Hire New Legal Chief
article.description: Walgreens Boots Alliance hired a successor legal chief, Danielle Gray, who left in December. Lanesha Minnix, general counsel at water treatment company Ecolab, will start her new role on April 15. Walgreens has made a raft of executive promotions and…
article.text: Walgreens Boots Alliance hired a successor legal chief, Danielle Gray, who left in December. Lanesha Minnix, general counsel at water treatment company Ecolab, will start her new role on April 15. Walgreens has made a raft of executive promotions and hires in recent months as it expands into health care. Walgreens Boots Alliance has found a new legal chief in Lanesha Minnix, an in-house veteran who has led legal teams spanning the building materials, electricity and industrial equipment industries. Walgreens global CLO Lanesha Minnix. (Courtesy photo) Minnix comes to Walgreens from the water treatment and purification company Ecolab, where she’s been the top lawyer since 2022. She’s was previously chief legal officer at FlowServe, the world’s largest maker of pumps, valves and seals. Prior to that, Minnix was general counsel at Building Materials and Construction Solutions and deputy general counsel and chief compliance officer at ABM Industries. Earlier in her career, she was in-house counsel at Shell Oil and Nextel.

article.title: Longtime Interim GC of Cloud Platform Scores Job on Permanent Basis
article.description: What You Need to Know Greenstein has been filling in since Paul Luongo left in June 2022 to become legal chief at e-commerce platform Narvar. Founded in 2011, Fastly helps heavily trafficked websites run faster. Fastly promoted Karen Greenstein to…
article.text: What You Need to Know Greenstein has been filling in since Paul Luongo left in June 2022 to become legal chief at e-commerce platform Narvar. Founded in 2011, Fastly helps heavily trafficked websites run faster. Fastly promoted Karen Greenstein to general counsel after she spent more than a year running its 16-person legal department on an interim basis. Greenstein joined the San Francisco-based cloud service provider as an assistant general counsel in 2019. In June 2022, she took over the legal department from chief legal and trust officer Paul Luongo, who resigned to become legal chief at e-commerce platform Narvar. Greenstein jumped into the role overseeing Fastly’s employment, privacy, intellectual property, litigation and commercial legal teams. She was previously general counsel at business news and advice site Business.com, and held senior in-house roles at Viacom, NBCUniversal and CNET. The company did not respond to a request for comment on Greenstein’s promotion. Fastly also hired Mozilla’s Marshall Erwin as chief information security officer and Check Point Software’s Peter Alexander as chief marketing officer. Founded in 2011, Fastly operates an “edge cloud platform” that helps highly trafficked websites run faster. It competes with Amazon Web Services, Cloudflare and Akamai. It had 493 enterprise customers as of year-end, according to a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Clients include GitHub, Yelp, Ticketmaster and Stripe, as well as news publishers Gannett and The New York Times. It made headlines in 2021 after an internal glitch brought down a host of major websites for an hour, including Amazon and Reddit.

article.title: California Prevails in X Corp.'s Early Challenge to Social Media Content Moderation Law
article.description: A federal judge declined to block California from enforcing a new law requiring social media companies to publicly disclose how they control content on their platforms and provide the attorney general with data on posts that contain “hate speech” and…
article.text: A federal judge declined to block California from enforcing a new law requiring social media companies to publicly disclose how they control content on their platforms and provide the attorney general with data on posts that contain “hate speech” and racism, extremism and foreign political interference. “While the reporting requirement does appear to place a substantial compliance burden on social media companies, it does not appear that the requirement is unjustified or unduly burdensome within the context of First Amendment law,” U.S. District Judge William Shubb wrote in his eight-page order.
article.html:
A federal judge declined to block California from enforcing a new law requiring social media companies to publicly disclose how they control content on their platforms and provide the attorney general with data on posts that contain “hate speech” and racism, extremism and foreign political interference.

“While the reporting requirement does appear to place a substantial compliance burden on social media companies, it does not appear that the requirement is unjustified or unduly burdensome within the context of First Amendment law,” U.S. District Judge William Shubb wrote in his eight-page order.
