article.title: Judge Throws Out Former In-House Lawyer's Age Bias Suit Against Accenture
article.description: Photo: Gints Ivuskans/Shutterstock.com A federal judge in Maryland has tossed a former Accenture in-house lawyer’s age discrimination suit against the global management consulting and professional services firm, ruling that the man was fired because…
article.text: Photo: Gints Ivuskans/Shutterstock.com A federal judge in Maryland has tossed a former Accenture in-house lawyer’s age discrimination suit against the global management consulting and professional services firm, ruling that the man was fired because of poor communication skills and aggressive emails to his boss. U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis of the District of Maryland, sitting in Greenbelt, Maryland, also rejected plaintiff Joseph Mott’s claim that firing him because of “his resistance to changes” was discriminatory. Mott was 61 when hired in December 2014 as senior manager in the global offerings support team in the compliance, offerings, regulatory and ethics division of Accenture’s legal department, according to Xinis’ April 29 memo supporting her grant of Accenture’s motion for summary judgment. Mott, who had worked as a lawyer for 35 years, including 10 years in the health care regulatory field, prior to joining Accenture, was 63 when fired in November 2016.

article.title: Uber CLO Tony West Receives Eight-Figure Compensation for Second Year in a Row
article.description: Those sorts of efforts have been central to Uber’s strategy since the company installed West and other new executives following the June 2017 departure of Travis Kalanick, who was widely criticized for fostering a problematic workplace culture and…
article.text: Those sorts of efforts have been central to Uber’s strategy since the company installed West and other new executives following the June 2017 departure of Travis Kalanick, who was widely criticized for fostering a problematic workplace culture and failing to address safety concerns. In recognition of West’s efforts to transform the culture and foster transparency and openness, Corporate Counsel last fall named West its 2023 General Counsel of the Year. Law.com reported in February that the company had recently reached the milestone of achieving a valuation of $120 billion for 90 consecutive days—unlocking a huge trove of stock options the company had granted West shortly after his hiring. Had the company failed to meet that threshold before the options expired in 2028, West never would have been eligible to exercise them. Options give holders the right to buy shares in the future at a preset price—$33.65 in West’s case. Uber’s stock price is now more than double that—about $76—giving him a paper profit on his option grant of $13 million.

article.title: Southwest Seeks Stay of Judge's Order Mandating 'Religious Liberty' Training for Senior In-House Counsel
article.description: Southwest wants a federal judge to stay his order for religious liberty training for three senior in-house attorneys. U.S. District Judge Brantley Starr held Southwest in contempt for failing to properly notify employees about federal laws…
article.text: Southwest wants a federal judge to stay his order for religious liberty training for three senior in-house attorneys. U.S. District Judge Brantley Starr held Southwest in contempt for failing to properly notify employees about federal laws prohibiting religious discrimination in the workplace. Southwest says the training will harm its reputation and that of its lawyers, while also violating the airline's First Amendment rights. Southwest is asking a federal judge to hold off on imposing his civil contempt order requiring three of its in-house counsel to undergo religious liberty training, saying the judge’s sanctions will irreparably harm the company’s and its lawyers’ reputations and will likely be overturned on appeal on First Amendment grounds. U.S. District Judge Brantley Starr’s unusual order followed a jury’s verdict in favor of flight attendant Charlene Carter, fired for violating the airline’s employee civility policy when she texted her co-worker a picture of an aborted fetus along with the message, “This is what you supported during your Paid Leave with others at the Women’s MARCH in DC. … You truly are Despicable in so many ways.”

article.title: FTC Shows Willingness to Use Extreme Measures to Tame AI
article.description: The FTC has grown more aggressive in punishing AI-driven companies that have profited off of customer data. A spate of recent settlements with Amazon, Everalbum and Weight Watchers shows the FTC's growing appetite for ordering companies to delete…
article.text: The FTC has grown more aggressive in punishing AI-driven companies that have profited off of customer data. A spate of recent settlements with Amazon, Everalbum and Weight Watchers shows the FTC's growing appetite for ordering companies to delete models trained on data collected in ways that violate privacy. FTC commissioners have said the remedy sends a clear message to companies that it's not worth it to illicitly collect data to train AI models. The Federal Trade Commission has one of the most potent tools to punish artificial intelligence-driven companies that disregard consumer privacy, and it’s not shy about using it. In recent years, the regulator has ramped up demands that companies destroy algorithms trained on “ill-gotten” data, signaling its growing urgency in trying to rein in AI. “The FTC is tinkering with new tools,” Holland & Knight warns in a recent client advisory. “The FTC hopes companies violating consumer privacy to cheaply train their AI may think twice because the punishment is becoming more severe.”
article.html:
• The FTC has grown more aggressive in punishing AI-driven companies that have profited off of customer data.

  • FTC commissioners have said the remedy sends a clear message to companies that it's not worth it to illicitly collect data to train AI models.

The Federal Trade Commission has one of the most potent tools to punish artificial intelligence-driven companies that disregard consumer privacy, and it’s not shy about using it. In recent years, the regulator has ramped up demands that companies destroy algorithms trained on “ill-gotten” data, signaling its growing urgency in trying to rein in AI.

“The FTC is tinkering with new tools,” Holland & Knight warns in a recent client advisory. “The FTC hopes companies violating consumer privacy to cheaply train their AI may think twice because the punishment is becoming more severe.”

article.title: Amazon Is Latest Target in FTC's Sweeping Probe of 'Dark Patterns' Marketing
article.description: The FTC alleges Amazon tricked customers into signing up for Prime, then forced them to navigate an arduous cancellation process. The suit, filed in federal court in Washington state, seeks unspecified damages. The enforcement action is part of a…
article.text: The FTC alleges Amazon tricked customers into signing up for Prime, then forced them to navigate an arduous cancellation process. The suit, filed in federal court in Washington state, seeks unspecified damages. The enforcement action is part of a broad inquiry into practices that coerce or deceive consumers into making purchases and make canceling them unduly difficult. In a further crackdown on what it dubs ”dark patterns” marketing, the Federal Trade Commission is taking aim at Amazon, accusing the e-commerce giant in a federal lawsuit of “tricking” customers into signing up for Prime and then thwarting their efforts to cancel the automatically renewing service. The heavily redacted lawsuit filed in Washington federal court Wednesday accuses Amazon of manipulating customers into enrolling in a $139 Prime membership during checkout, then knowingly complicating the cancellation process.

article.text: The New York Attorney General’s Office on Wednesday said that reports of alleged perjury by former Trump CFO Allen Weisselberg during his testimony in the AG’s civil fraud case against Donald Trump and others should not delay a decision from the presiding judge. The AG’s Office told Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Arthur Engoron that they were not involved or aware of any negotiations between Weisselberg and the Manhattan District Attorney’s office regarding possible charges of perjury.
article.html:
The New York Attorney General’s Office on Wednesday said that reports of alleged perjury by former Trump CFO Allen Weisselberg during his testimony in the AG’s civil fraud case against Donald Trump and others should not delay a decision from the presiding judge.

The AG’s Office told Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Arthur Engoron that they were not involved or aware of any negotiations between Weisselberg and the Manhattan District Attorney’s office regarding possible charges of perjury.

article.title: California High Court Holds AI Vendors Liable for Biased Job Screening
article.description: The California Supreme Court ruled that businesses that perform certain job-related functions for employers can be held directly liable for discrimination. The ruling will affect variety of industries, from AI vendors to recruiters and screeners.…
article.text: The California Supreme Court ruled that businesses that perform certain job-related functions for employers can be held directly liable for discrimination. The ruling will affect variety of industries, from AI vendors to recruiters and screeners. Outside counsel say they expect more litigation as a result. California’s highest court has handed down a landmark ruling with major implications for the AI industry: making vendors that use algorithms to target job ads, screen out applicants or perform other employment-related tasks for other companies directly liable for discrimination under state law. “The major impact of this is with outsourcing, and that’s what a lot of companies are doing for a lot of their employment-related functions,” said attorney Randy Erlewine of the San Francisco law firm Phillips, Erlewine, Given & Carlin. article.title: 'Ignore This Bill at Your Peril': Federal Privacy Legislation Has Teeth—and Real Shot at Passing
article.description: For years, the business community has been calling for a comprehensive federal privacy law, frustrated with operating under a patchwork of sometimes-conflicting state laws. Now, Congress is considering one that’s extremely wide-ranging and that…
article.text: For years, the business community has been calling for a comprehensive federal privacy law, frustrated with operating under a patchwork of sometimes-conflicting state laws. Now, Congress is considering one that’s extremely wide-ranging and that observers say has a legitimate chance of passage. The American Privacy Rights Act—unveiled over the weekend by Senate Commerce Committee chair Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and House Commerce Committee chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-Washington)—would cover every company with annual revenue topping $40 million, along with nonprofits, a realm previously untouched by the privacy regime.

article.title: M&A in the Era of Social Distancing—How Remote Work Affects Mergers & Acquisitions
article.description: Building relationships and taking in-person meetings have traditionally been quintessential actions for merger and acquisition dealmakers. Dealmakers normally focus their time on one-on-one meetings across different cities, as well as attending…
article.text: Building relationships and taking in-person meetings have traditionally been quintessential actions for merger and acquisition dealmakers. Dealmakers normally focus their time on one-on-one meetings across different cities, as well as attending conferences, dining out, and engaging in bonding activities. Now, with quarantines and common sense arguing against face-to-face meetings, how do we build the trust and confidence necessary to do a deal? Individuals in a myriad of industries, job functions, and levels worked from home long before the pandemic, facilitated by technological innovations that make remote work possible. Then, in 2013, working from home became a lightning rod of controversy when Yahoo! CEO Melissa Mayer decreed that remote workers would have to be in the office working side-by-side to deliver the best communication and collaboration. Her memo to all employees said, “The best decisions and insights come from hallway and cafeteria discussions, meeting new people, and impromptu team meetings.”

article.title: Big Law Salary War Throws Cold Water on In-House Recruiting
article.description: “The reality from where I sit as a recruiter is that when we approach in-house candidates with great opportunities, they often stop listening once they find out it could be a 30-50% pay cut," legal search consultant Stacy Humphries said. The pay…
article.text: “The reality from where I sit as a recruiter is that when we approach in-house candidates with great opportunities, they often stop listening once they find out it could be a 30-50% pay cut," legal search consultant Stacy Humphries said. The pay divide between Big Law and corporate legal departments continues to widen. In-house legal recruiters report that it's gotten more difficult to lure talent from top law firms. Some general counsel have given up on trying to hire Big Law lawyers, according to a recruiter. As Big Law showers associates with cash, corporate legal departments are going to have to get more creative about luring in-house legal talent from the most prestigious law firms—or wave the white flag and start looking elsewhere for recruits.
article.html:

article.title: In Big Law Partner Hiring, Business Plans Become 'Litmus Test' For Government Hires
article.description: Law firms are putting more emphasis on a candidates' business plan, particularly those leaving the government. A solid business plan can make a difference in who a firm hires, what title the attorney joins as and their compensation, according to…
article.text: Law firms are putting more emphasis on a candidates' business plan, particularly those leaving the government. A solid business plan can make a difference in who a firm hires, what title the attorney joins as and their compensation, according to recruiters. Recruiters and law firm practice leaders have noted an uptick in government attorneys on the job hunt, particularly from the DOJ, in recent weeks. When searching for lateral partners to hire, law firms are putting much more weight on candidates’ business plans, particularly government attorneys who are transitioning to private practice, according to recruiters for firms. Such business plans often incorporate a government candidate’s network and skills and how they expect to turn their expertise into revenue within the first years of practice, among other details.

article.title: Passport Snag Resolved for Key Witness in Bribery Trial of Ex-Cognizant Legal Chief
article.description: A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant president Gordon Coburn in 2019. Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building. The trial…
article.text: A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant president Gordon Coburn in 2019. Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building. The trial had been scheduled to start this week. A federal judge has set a new trial date for two former tech executives accused of bribing government officials in India, after a witness snafu caused the court to miss its chance to have the trial this year. Judge Kevin McNulty said the trial, scheduled to open this week, will now have to wait until at least mid-February. Prosecutors had asked for a brief postponement because its star witness was stuck in India. On Friday, a federal prosecutor, Sonali Patel, told McNulty that the witness had been cleared by the Indian government to travel and could be in court as early as the middle of next week, but McNulty said it was too late.
article.html:
• A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant president Gordon Coburn in 2019.
  • Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building.
  • The trial had been scheduled to start this week.

A federal judge has set a new trial date for two former tech executives accused of bribing government officials in India, after a witness snafu caused the court to miss its chance to have the trial this year.

Judge Kevin McNulty said the trial, scheduled to open this week, will now have to wait until at least mid-February. Prosecutors had asked for a brief postponement because its star witness was stuck in India. On Friday, a federal prosecutor, Sonali Patel, told McNulty that the witness had been cleared by the Indian government to travel and could be in court as early as the middle of next week, but McNulty said it was too late.

article.title: John Deere's GC Stepping Aside After a Prosperous but Quiet Quarter-Century With Farm-Equipment Giant
article.description: NEWS John Deere's GC Stepping Aside After a Prosperous but Quiet Quarter-Century With Farm-Equipment Giant Since Mary Jones took the legal reins in January 2013, the company has avoided major legal potholes, and its stock has risen more than…
article.text: NEWS John Deere's GC Stepping Aside After a Prosperous but Quiet Quarter-Century With Farm-Equipment Giant Since Mary Jones took the legal reins in January 2013, the company has avoided major legal potholes, and its stock has risen more than four-fold. In House Moves Mary Jones, a steady hand at Deere & Co. for more than a quarter-century who’s been general counsel during a golden age for the 187-year-old company, will retire later this year. The Moline, Illinois-based company—best known by the moniker John Deere—announced this week that Jones, 55, is stepping aside and will be succeeded as legal chief by Kellye Walker, whose been chief legal officer for the last four years at Eastman Chemical. Before that, she spent five years as chief legal officer of Huntington Ingalls Industries, America’s largest military shipbuilder. Both firms are in the Fortune 500. NEWS

John Deere's GC Stepping Aside After a Prosperous but Quiet Quarter-Century With Farm-Equipment Giant

Since Mary Jones took the legal reins in January 2013, the company has avoided major legal potholes, and its stock has risen more than four-fold.

In House Moves

Mary Jones, a steady hand at Deere & Co. for more than a quarter-century who’s been general counsel during a golden age for the 187-year-old company, will retire later this year.

The Moline, Illinois-based company—best known by the moniker John Deere—announced this week that Jones, 55, is stepping aside and will be succeeded as legal chief by Kellye Walker, whose been chief legal officer for the last four years at Eastman Chemical. Before that, she spent five years as chief legal officer of Huntington Ingalls Industries, America’s largest military shipbuilder. Both firms are in the Fortune 500.

article.title: Limitations of Generative AI in Civil Jury Trials
article.description: Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using…
article.text: Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using generative AI for drafting opening statements, closing arguments, direct and cross-examinations, creating graphics, and assisting with trial motions is strong. This allure and the marketing hype ignores a fundamental truth: Generative AI is not yet ready for the courtroom. Diverse Audiences With Unique Needs A jury trial is a multifaceted event, involving distinct audiences: the judge, the jury, client representatives, and witnesses. Each of these audiences have different needs and will require a tailored approach that will dynamically change throughout the trial. The Judge: Judges are concerned with the trial record, the potential for appeal, maintaining courtroom control, and efficient time use. They require clear, legally sound arguments. Understanding the judge’s experience and background is crucial. A seasoned judge may have a firm view of how a trial should proceed, while a newcomer might still be shaping their approach. Each judge’s unique viewpoint, philosophy, and rules play a significant role in the trial’s dynamics. Generative AI, however, lacks the nuance to adapt to these individualized needs effectively. The Jury: Comprising individuals from diverse backgrounds, jurors have no personal stake in the case outcome but are tasked with delivering a fair verdict. They must understand complex legal rules and concepts, making clear and relatable presentation of evidence crucial. Emotional appeals, compelling storytelling, and witness credibility are vital here—subtleties generative AI often misses. Client Representatives: These individuals, whether in-house legal counsel focused on costs and expectations or high-ranking corporate officers viewing the trial as an extended negotiation, have different goals and concerns. Their anxiety over trial outcomes is heightened by their limited control over courtroom proceedings. Generative AI cannot provide the reassurance and strategic updates these clients need. Witnesses: Witnesses, who range from nervous laypeople to compensated experts, are critical to the case. Their testimony needs to be clear, concise, and compelling. Preparing and managing witnesses requires a human touch. Many factors outside the courtroom and concerns about the future can have significant impact on the emotions, preparation and cooperation of witnesses. Generative AI lacks the information and capabilities to address these outside factors and concerns. Conflicting Goals and Contexts You Might Like
article.html:
Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using generative AI for drafting opening statements, closing arguments, direct and cross-examinations, creating graphics, and assisting with trial motions is strong. This allure and the marketing hype ignores a fundamental truth: Generative AI is not yet ready for the courtroom.

Diverse Audiences With Unique Needs

A jury trial is a multifaceted event, involving distinct audiences: the judge, the jury, client representatives, and witnesses. Each of these audiences have different needs and will require a tailored approach that will dynamically change throughout the trial.

  1. The Judge: Judges are concerned with the trial record, the potential for appeal, maintaining courtroom control, and efficient time use. They require clear, legally sound arguments. Understanding the judge’s experience and background is crucial. A seasoned judge may have a firm view of how a trial should proceed, while a newcomer might still be shaping their approach. Each judge’s unique viewpoint, philosophy, and rules play a significant role in the trial’s dynamics. Generative AI, however, lacks the nuance to adapt to these individualized needs effectively.
  1. The Jury: Comprising individuals from diverse backgrounds, jurors have no personal stake in the case outcome but are tasked with delivering a fair verdict. They must understand complex legal rules and concepts, making clear and relatable presentation of evidence crucial. Emotional appeals, compelling storytelling, and witness credibility are vital here—subtleties generative AI often misses.
  1. Client Representatives: These individuals, whether in-house legal counsel focused on costs and expectations or high-ranking corporate officers viewing the trial as an extended negotiation, have different goals and concerns. Their anxiety over trial outcomes is heightened by their limited control over courtroom proceedings. Generative AI cannot provide the reassurance and strategic updates these clients need.
  1. Witnesses: Witnesses, who range from nervous laypeople to compensated experts, are critical to the case. Their testimony needs to be clear, concise, and compelling. Preparing and managing witnesses requires a human touch. Many factors outside the courtroom and concerns about the future can have significant impact on the emotions, preparation and cooperation of witnesses. Generative AI lacks the information and capabilities to address these outside factors and concerns.

Conflicting Goals and Contexts

article.title: Federal Judge Dismisses Class Action Claim Over Data Breach for Lack of Relationship Between Plaintiff, Business
article.description: "Here, plaintiff fails to allege what parties are bound in contract to each other and which party plaintiff gave his PII to for safekeeping," the judge said. "Absent these allegations, the complaint fails to state a claim for breach of contract under…
article.text: "Here, plaintiff fails to allege what parties are bound in contract to each other and which party plaintiff gave his PII to for safekeeping," the judge said. "Absent these allegations, the complaint fails to state a claim for breach of contract under a third-party beneficiary theory or otherwise." A putative class action complaint alleging a data breach at information technology provider Maintech exposed the personal information of a group of individuals was dismissed last week by a federal judge after the plaintiffs failed to prove a direct relationship with the business. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey as Robinson v. Maintech, alleged that a data breach resulted in the unauthorized disclosure of the plaintiff’s personal information, including their names, Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses and financial information. The named plaintiff, Mark Robinson, alleged that he was a data breach victim, although, in his complaint, he stated that he does not know why Maintech possessed his personal information in the first place. Third parties provided Maintech with the PII, according to the opinion.

article.title: Come Back With a Warrant: State Court Deems Aerial Observation of Property Using Telephoto Lens Unconstitutional
article.description: The Alaska Supreme Court issued an opinion last week declaring the police practice of taking overhead pictures using telephoto lenses without a warrant to be an unreasonable search in violation of the Fourth Amendment’s and the Alaska Constitution’s…
article.text: The Alaska Supreme Court issued an opinion last week declaring the police practice of taking overhead pictures using telephoto lenses without a warrant to be an unreasonable search in violation of the Fourth Amendment’s and the Alaska Constitution’s protections of privacy. The Alaska high court relied on similar rulings from cases out of California, Hawaii and Vermont, in concluding a person’s home and surrounding land that are plainly visible from the sky “may nonetheless be subject to a reasonable expectation of privacy, making the ‘open view’ doctrine that applies at ground level inapplicable,’ according to the court’s majority opinion written by Justice Dario Borghesan, with Justices Daniel Winfree and Jennifer S. Henderson joining.

article.title: SEC Cybersecurity Rules Go Live in Days. Companies Still Aren't Sure What to Expect
article.description: The SEC's cybersecurity-disclosure rules kick in Dec. 18. Determining what to disclose will be tricky. Security chiefs may be inclined to disclose more, fearing personal liability for inadequate disclosures, while other C-suite executives might favor…
article.text: The SEC's cybersecurity-disclosure rules kick in Dec. 18. Determining what to disclose will be tricky. Security chiefs may be inclined to disclose more, fearing personal liability for inadequate disclosures, while other C-suite executives might favor revealing less, fearing negative fallout on the business. Any security professional who has dealt with a cyberattack can tell you that the early stages are often chaotic, with the extent of the damage and the magnitude of the intrusion difficult to immediately determine. The stakes will become even higher when new U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rules take effect in mid-December that demand prompt disclosure of material cyberattacks and annual reports about cyber risks and vulnerabilities. Tired of “generic” disclosures and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers, the SEC says it’s time to get tough.

Tired of “generic” disclosures and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers, the SEC says it’s time to get tough.

article.title: How Can Countries Prepare to Defend Against Deepfakes—and ‘Cheapfakes’—This Election Cycle?
article.description: 2024 has been dubbed the year of elections—and for good reason. Voters from at least 64 countries and the European Union are preparing to vote in national elections, all against the backdrop of a staggering rise in disinformation and misinformation…
article.text: 2024 has been dubbed the year of elections—and for good reason. Voters from at least 64 countries and the European Union are preparing to vote in national elections, all against the backdrop of a staggering rise in disinformation and misinformation increasingly fueled by artificial intelligence-generated content. Most parts of the world, including the United States, may not be prepared to face such waves of synthetic media, especially as investments in the development of large language models (LLMs) continue to outpace those made into detection-based approaches. As stakeholders from private companies and federal agencies start to collaborate to uncover robust solutions, experts during the “From Pixels to Policy: Defending Against AI-Generated Threats” session at the 2024 AI Expo for National Competitiveness in Washington, D.C., suggested it may be time to give up on the cat-and-mouse-game that has been the bane of many detection softwares and instead start to focus on content provenance. Retroactive Detection vs. Content Provenance Efforts to detect AI-generated content aren’t new. But more recently, they’ve involved steps from some of the leading AI providers. On May 7, OpenAI announced it joined the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity Steering Committee (C2PA), a standard used to prove that content comes from a particular source. The AI provider noted it began adding C2PA metadata “to all images created and edited by DALL·E 3, our latest image model, in ChatGPT and the OpenAI API.” It also announced the upcoming integration of C2PA metadata for its video generation model Sora. Earlier this year, Meta had made a similar announcement, noting that it was building tools to identify visible markers, including the C2PA and IPTC standards to “label images from Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Adobe, Midjourney, and Shutterstock.” “What that standard does is it simply exposes the origin and history of digital content over time, and it gives consumers the ability to view that, whether they’re looking at any photo or video, and understand and make their own decision around the credibility of that content,” explained Jeffrey McGregor, CEO at Truepic, a company which offers content transparency tools. There are currently two main approaches to content authenticity, McGregor noted. On one end, detection-based approaches often leverage some form of machine learning to analyze media retroactively and make what he called a “probabilistic determination” of whether it might be synthetic. “When you talk about the…pure scale of digital media, both synthetic and authentic, even a couple percentage points in terms of the model not being correct results in a massive amount of digital media that remains undetected as false,” McGregor said. “It’s also very much a cat-and-mouse game in terms of the ability for detection-based algorithms to keep up with the sheer investment into AI-generated content.” Instead, some are exploring approaches focusing on content provenance, meaning, the origin of a piece of media. This is akin to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificates—digital certificates that authenticate a website’s identity and security—by binding trusted data to a file. In practice, a content provenance standard would assign security credentials to a picture or video to show its origin. As iterations to the content are made—whether it be a simple crop, or an AI-generated background—these changes can be tracked in the metadata. “The robustness, the scale, the security of that all far outweighs what we believe is possible with detection,” McGregor explained. “The downside is, of course, it does need to be adopted by an ecosystem.” Deepfakes, ‘Cheapfakes’ and Media Literacy A truly scalable ecosystem of content provenance standards may still be a few years away, as it will require buy-in from leading AI providers as well as developers of open-source models. But in the meantime, a combination of multiple approaches may still help shield some of the impact of synthetic content. In addition, for authenticity markers to truly be effective, the onus will also have to fall on consumers to look for such markings—a task which some suggest many aren’t ready to tackle. “From a global standpoint, we’re not prepared from a media literacy standpoint to truly look for authenticity markers,” McGregor said. Isobel Coleman, Deputy Administrator for Policy and Programming at the United States Agency for International Development, has been monitoring the impact of AI-generated content across the globe, even in countries much smaller than the U.S. Take Moldova’s President Maia Sandu, for example, who in late 2023 was the target of deepfakes intended to show her pushing back on traditional values for the sake of her “pro-European Union agenda.” “Looking overseas in countries like Moldova, a country of two and a half million people, the stakes are big for Moldova, but are they as big as the stakes in our country? I’m not so sure,” Coleman said. “You could argue that the stakes are bigger here. The level of sophistication in what’s going on in Moldova, again, I say: Buckle up. Because if it’s happening in Moldova, it’s happening all around the world.” In fact, she noted that synthetic content is increasingly being leveraged by authoritarian regimes to manipulate information, especially in current conflict zones. “I think the most malign actor today in this dis/misinformation space is the Russian Federation. So countries that are really on the frontline of Putin’s various types of war that he is waging, I think are really most vulnerable,” she said. Russia is a primed player to wield deepfakes to its advantage, according to Coleman. As the one behind the original “bot factories and troll factories,” the Russian Federation now has access to more sophisticated and cheaper technology. “The impact of a deepfake can be huge, but it can be a pretty time-intensive process to create a deepfake,” she said. “Now we’re seeing cheapfakes have a huge impact.” While the production of realistic deepfakes used to require elaborate software, many tools today allow users to generate fake content with affordable applications that are easily accessible, sometimes even on phone applications—hence the new term: ’Cheapfakes.’ This means that, in addition to reliance on content authentication strategies, governments around the world will have to push for regulation or measures to educate their voters on what’s to come. This could include educational initiatives both in the U.S. and abroad, but also partnerships with independent news organizations to give them the technological tools to both authenticate incoming media and add authentic credentials to their own content. “I think regulation is necessary but not sufficient by any means,” Coleman said. “People are going to have to learn how to operate in a very fluid, dynamic environment, and to be able to evaluate for themselves. And the more they have the tools and the capacity, the analytical tools to do that, the better off they’ll be.”
article.html:
2024 has been dubbed the year of elections—and for good reason.

Voters from at least 64 countries and the European Union are preparing to vote in national elections, all against the backdrop of a staggering rise in disinformation and misinformation increasingly fueled by artificial intelligence-generated content.

Most parts of the world, including the United States, may not be prepared to face such waves of synthetic media, especially as investments in the development of large language models (LLMs) continue to outpace those made into detection-based approaches.

As stakeholders from private companies and federal agencies start to collaborate to uncover robust solutions, experts during the “From Pixels to Policy: Defending Against AI-Generated Threats” session at the 2024 AI Expo for National Competitiveness in Washington, D.C., suggested it may be time to give up on the cat-and-mouse-game that has been the bane of many detection softwares and instead start to focus on content provenance.

Retroactive Detection vs. Content Provenance

Efforts to detect AI-generated content aren’t new. But more recently, they’ve involved steps from some of the leading AI providers.

On May 7, OpenAI announced it joined the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity Steering Committee (C2PA), a standard used to prove that content comes from a particular source. The AI provider noted it began adding C2PA metadata “to all images created and edited by DALL·E 3, our latest image model, in ChatGPT and the OpenAI API.” It also announced the upcoming integration of C2PA metadata for its video generation model Sora.

Earlier this year, Meta had made a similar announcement, noting that it was building tools to identify visible markers, including the C2PA and IPTC standards to “label images from Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Adobe, Midjourney, and Shutterstock.”

“What that standard does is it simply exposes the origin and history of digital content over time, and it gives consumers the ability to view that, whether they’re looking at any photo or video, and understand and make their own decision around the credibility of that content,” explained Jeffrey McGregor, CEO at Truepic, a company which offers content transparency tools.

There are currently two main approaches to content authenticity, McGregor noted. On one end, detection-based approaches often leverage some form of machine learning to analyze media retroactively and make what he called a “probabilistic determination” of whether it might be synthetic.

“When you talk about the…pure scale of digital media, both synthetic and authentic, even a couple percentage points in terms of the model not being correct results in a massive amount of digital media that remains undetected as false,” McGregor said. “It’s also very much a cat-and-mouse game in terms of the ability for detection-based algorithms to keep up with the sheer investment into AI-generated content.”

Instead, some are exploring approaches focusing on content provenance, meaning, the origin of a piece of media. This is akin to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificates—digital certificates that authenticate a website’s identity and security—by binding trusted data to a file.

In practice, a content provenance standard would assign security credentials to a picture or video to show its origin. As iterations to the content are made—whether it be a simple crop, or an AI-generated background—these changes can be tracked in the metadata.

“The robustness, the scale, the security of that all far outweighs what we believe is possible with detection,” McGregor explained. “The downside is, of course, it does need to be adopted by an ecosystem.”

Deepfakes, ‘Cheapfakes’ and Media Literacy

A truly scalable ecosystem of content provenance standards may still be a few years away, as it will require buy-in from leading AI providers as well as developers of open-source models. But in the meantime, a combination of multiple approaches may still help shield some of the impact of synthetic content.

In addition, for authenticity markers to truly be effective, the onus will also have to fall on consumers to look for such markings—a task which some suggest many aren’t ready to tackle. “From a global standpoint, we’re not prepared from a media literacy standpoint to truly look for authenticity markers,” McGregor said.

Isobel Coleman, Deputy Administrator for Policy and Programming at the United States Agency for International Development, has been monitoring the impact of AI-generated content across the globe, even in countries much smaller than the U.S.

Take Moldova’s President Maia Sandu, for example, who in late 2023 was the target of deepfakes intended to show her pushing back on traditional values for the sake of her “pro-European Union agenda.”

“Looking overseas in countries like Moldova, a country of two and a half million people, the stakes are big for Moldova, but are they as big as the stakes in our country? I’m not so sure,” Coleman said. “You could argue that the stakes are bigger here. The level of sophistication in what’s going on in Moldova, again, I say: Buckle up. Because if it’s happening in Moldova, it’s happening all around the world.”

In fact, she noted that synthetic content is increasingly being leveraged by authoritarian regimes to manipulate information, especially in current conflict zones.

“I think the most malign actor today in this dis/misinformation space is the Russian Federation. So countries that are really on the frontline of Putin’s various types of war that he is waging, I think are really most vulnerable,” she said.

Russia is a primed player to wield deepfakes to its advantage, according to Coleman. As the one behind the original “bot factories and troll factories,” the Russian Federation now has access to more sophisticated and cheaper technology.

“The impact of a deepfake can be huge, but it can be a pretty time-intensive process to create a deepfake,” she said. “Now we’re seeing cheapfakes have a huge impact.” While the production of realistic deepfakes used to require elaborate software, many tools today allow users to generate fake content with affordable applications that are easily accessible, sometimes even on phone applications—hence the new term: ’Cheapfakes.’

This means that, in addition to reliance on content authentication strategies, governments around the world will have to push for regulation or measures to educate their voters on what’s to come. This could include educational initiatives both in the U.S. and abroad, but also partnerships with independent news organizations to give them the technological tools to both authenticate incoming media and add authentic credentials to their own content.

“I think regulation is necessary but not sufficient by any means,” Coleman said. “People are going to have to learn how to operate in a very fluid, dynamic environment, and to be able to evaluate for themselves. And the more they have the tools and the capacity, the analytical tools to do that, the better off they’ll be.”

article.title: Legal Chief Faces 40 Years for Alleged Role in Crypto Scam | Corporate Counsel
article.description: Irina Dilkinska was arrested in Bulgaria on Monday and extradited to the United States the next day. Prosecutors say she helped perpetuate a wide-ranging scheme with millions of victims and billions of dollars in losses.
article.text: The legal and compliance chief for Bulgaria-based crypto company OneCoin has been charged with running a pyramid scheme that conned global investors out of $4 billion. Prosecutors say Irina Dilkinska helped Mark Scott, a former equity partner at the law firm Locke Lord, launder $400 million in proceeds from the scam. She was arrested Monday in Bulgaria and extradited to the United States on Tuesday, where she faces the same charges as her alleged co-conspirator Scott, who was convicted of conspiracy to commit money laundering and bank fraud in 2019. "Irina Dilkinska, the supposed Head of Legal and Compliance for the OneCoin cryptocurrency pyramid scheme, accomplished the exact opposite of her job title and allegedly enabled OneCoin to launder millions of dollars of illegal proceeds through shell companies," U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York Damian Williams said in a statement. "Dilkinska helped perpetuate a wide-ranging scheme with millions of victims and billions of dollars in losses, and she will now face justice for her alleged crimes." This content has been archived. "Irina Dilkinska, the supposed Head of Legal and Compliance for the OneCoin cryptocurrency pyramid scheme, accomplished the exact opposite of her job title and allegedly enabled OneCoin to launder millions of dollars of illegal proceeds through shell companies," U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York Damian Williams said in a statement. "Dilkinska helped perpetuate a wide-ranging scheme with millions of victims and billions of dollars in losses, and she will now face justice for her alleged crimes."

article.text: Cisco paid chief legal officer Deborah 'Dev' Stahlkopf $13.3 million in the fiscal year that ended July 30. The package was driven up by a $9.5 million stock grant and a $2.2 million new-hire bonus. Stahlkopf joined the company last year after 14 years at Microsoft. ALM’s 2022 General Counsel Compensation Report dropped just a few months ago, but competition for a prime spot on next year’s list is already hot. According to a proxy filing this week, tech titan Cisco paid chief legal officer Deborah “Dev” Stahlkopf $13.3 million in the fiscal year that ended July 30. She received $675,000 in salary, $876,700 in nonequity incentive compensation, a $2.2 million cash bonus and $9.5 million in stock awards.

article.title: Passenger's Vicarious Liability Claims Proceed Against Uber Following Alleged Assault by Driver
article.description: "Here, based on the facts alleged in the Complaint, Micah was at the address as part of his business driving for Uber and assaulted Plaintiff to coerce payment of a debt owed to Uber; therefore, a reasonable jury could determine that ... the assault…
article.text: "Here, based on the facts alleged in the Complaint, Micah was at the address as part of his business driving for Uber and assaulted Plaintiff to coerce payment of a debt owed to Uber; therefore, a reasonable jury could determine that ... the assault was in furtherance of Uber’s business," U.S. District Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. said, denying Uber's motion to dismiss on the plaintiff's vicarious liability claims. A federal judge has found that Uber can be held vicariously liable after one of its drivers allegedly assaulted a passenger, who is now suing the rideshare giant for $15 million. Wading into an unsettled area of law, the federal judge relied on South Carolina law in making his ruling last week. Rommel Fuentes filed the negligence complaint against Uber Technologies and other Uber entities, as well as the driver at issue, Kehinde Idogho Micah, in Arlington County Circuit Court before it was moved to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia in April 2023. Fuentes claimed Micah dropped him and another passenger off at their desired location. However, as they exited the vehicle and started walking away, Micah allegedly got out of the vehicle to complain that he had not received payment, according to the complaint.
article.html:
"Here, based on the facts alleged in the Complaint, Micah was at the address as part of his business driving for Uber and assaulted Plaintiff to coerce payment of a debt owed to Uber; therefore, a reasonable jury could determine that ... the assault was in furtherance of Uber’s business," U.S. District Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. said, denying Uber's motion to dismiss on the plaintiff's vicarious liability claims.

article.title: Artists Sue Google, Alleging It Used Copyrighted Work in AI Training Database
article.description: This is the 22nd of 23 such lawsuits filed against AI developers for copyright infringement. Two more copyright infringement lawsuits were recently filed against Google, Microsoft and Open AI for using work they didn't have the rights to to train AI…
article.text: This is the 22nd of 23 such lawsuits filed against AI developers for copyright infringement. Two more copyright infringement lawsuits were recently filed against Google, Microsoft and Open AI for using work they didn't have the rights to to train AI models. The plaintiffs suing Google contend the company is purposefully opaque about the dataset used to train its AI image editing software so it doesn't get sued. Two of the artists named in the complaint also have a similar case pending against Stability AI. The wave of lawsuits pending against generative AI developers has reached another crest with new legal actions brought against Google, Microsoft and Open AI. Alphabet, the parent company of Google, and Google were named in a copyright class action on April 26 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Joseph Saveri Law Firm, Butterick Law and Lockridge Grindal Nauen filed the complaint on behalf of cartoonists Sarah Andersen, Hope Larson and Jessica Fink and photographer Jingna Zhang, who contend that Google used their registered copyrights to train Imagen, an AI photo editing assistant, without authorization.
article.html:
This is the 22nd of 23 such lawsuits filed against AI developers for copyright infringement.

  • Two more copyright infringement lawsuits were recently filed against Google, Microsoft and Open AI for using work they didn't have the rights to to train AI models.
  • The plaintiffs suing Google contend the company is purposefully opaque about the dataset used to train its AI image editing software so it doesn't get sued.
  • Two of the artists named in the complaint also have a similar case pending against Stability AI.

The wave of lawsuits pending against generative AI developers has reached another crest with new legal actions brought against Google, Microsoft and Open AI.

Alphabet, the parent company of Google, and Google were named in a copyright class action on April 26 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Joseph Saveri Law Firm, Butterick Law and Lockridge Grindal Nauen filed the complaint on behalf of cartoonists Sarah Andersen, Hope Larson and Jessica Fink and photographer Jingna Zhang, who contend that Google used their registered copyrights to train Imagen, an AI photo editing assistant, without authorization.

article.title: To Keep Zealous Privacy Regulators at Bay, Good Faith 'Goes a Long Way'
article.description: DataGrail hosted its inaugural privacy summit last week in San Francisco. The event occurred as companies struggle to comply with an evolving patchwork of privacy and data protection laws. California is prepping to unleash aggressive privacy…
article.text: DataGrail hosted its inaugural privacy summit last week in San Francisco. The event occurred as companies struggle to comply with an evolving patchwork of privacy and data protection laws. California is prepping to unleash aggressive privacy enforcement, with a baseline budget of $10 million, the same amount the Federal Trade Commission devotes to privacy regulation for the entire country. Companies are struggling to keep up with an evolving patchwork of laws and regulations around privacy and cybersecurity, even as enforcement actions over data breaches and privacy violations ramp up. Rick Arney, a co-author of the California Consumer Privacy Act, said last week that the state has allocated a baseline budget of $10 million to ensure that its privacy-rights enforcement has teeth, intentionally matching the amount the Federal Trade Commission spends to regulate privacy for the entire country.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission began cracking down on the use of WhatsApp, Signal and other messaging platforms two years ago. The agencies now have assessed fines totaling $2.5 billion. Federal regulators on Tuesday announced that they are fining 10 investment firms $549 million in their latest crackdown on regulated financial companies that failed to maintain and preserve electronic communications.

She will be a trusted resource for our leadership as we continue to drive towards winning championships on and off the court.”

“Zandria’s resume speaks for itself as she will bring two decades of experience to Rip City, including 15 years in the sports law space,” Dewayne Hankins, the NBA franchise’s president of business operations. She will be a trusted resource for our leadership as we continue to drive towards winning championships on and off the court.”

article.title: AI Legal Startup DoNotPay Reaches Settlement in 'Robot Lawyer' Class Action
article.description: A settlement has been reached in a class action against startup DoNotPay, which uses AI to offer legal advice and services. DoNotPay was accused in 2023 of misrepresenting itself as authorized to practice law in the state of California. DoNotPay has…
article.text: A settlement has been reached in a class action against startup DoNotPay, which uses AI to offer legal advice and services. DoNotPay was accused in 2023 of misrepresenting itself as authorized to practice law in the state of California. DoNotPay has faced controversy in the past over its since-abandoned plan to provide an AI-powered legal defense for a client in court. DoNotPay has reached a settlement in a class action alleging that the AI startup illegally claimed to practice law while billing itself as the “world’s first robot lawyer.” The original lawsuit was filed in March 2023 in the Superior Court of the State of California County of San Francisco. It alleged that DoNotPay flouted the State Bar Act, Cal. Bus. and Prof. Code §§ 6125, by falsely marketing its services as equivalent to those of lawyers authorized to practice law in the state of California.
article.html:
• A settlement has been reached in a class action against startup DoNotPay, which uses AI to offer legal advice and services.

  • DoNotPay has faced controversy in the past over its since-abandoned plan to provide an AI-powered legal defense for a client in court.

DoNotPay has reached a settlement in a class action alleging that the AI startup illegally claimed to practice law while billing itself as the “world’s first robot lawyer.”

The original lawsuit was filed in March 2023 in the Superior Court of the State of California County of San Francisco. It alleged that DoNotPay flouted the State Bar Act, Cal. Bus. and Prof. Code §§ 6125, by falsely marketing its services as equivalent to those of lawyers authorized to practice law in the state of California.

article.title: Fight or Fess Up? Starbucks, Uber GCs Chime In on How to Respond to Government Probes
article.description: Legal leaders at corporate heavyweights discussed how outside counsel can best approach a government investigation. The panelists mostly agreed it's best to fully cooperate, but there may be times when pushback is warranted. Companies should choose…
article.text: Legal leaders at corporate heavyweights discussed how outside counsel can best approach a government investigation. The panelists mostly agreed it's best to fully cooperate, but there may be times when pushback is warranted. Companies should choose their battles carefully. Starbucks General Counsel Brad Lerman said outside counsel are usually disliked on boards, and should tailor their message to their audience. Board members want the truth and realistic goals. Choose your battles carefully. Credibility is key. And for god’s sake, don’t bore the board of directors. This was some of the plainspoken advice an all-star lineup of general counsel had for outside counsel on how to best represent companies in the investigatory hot seat. Their remarks came Thursday at the American Bar Association’s white-collar crime conference in San Francisco, just hours after Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco announced a greater push to encourage people to report on companies by rewarding whistleblowing and incentivizing companies to disclose wrongdoing as early as possible.
article.html:
• Legal leaders at corporate heavyweights discussed how outside counsel can best approach a government investigation.
  • The panelists mostly agreed it's best to fully cooperate, but there may be times when pushback is warranted. Companies should choose their battles carefully.
  • Starbucks General Counsel Brad Lerman said outside counsel are usually disliked on boards, and should tailor their message to their audience. Board members want the truth and realistic goals.

Choose your battles carefully. Credibility is key. And for god’s sake, don’t bore the board of directors. This was some of the plainspoken advice an all-star lineup of general counsel had for outside counsel on how to best represent companies in the investigatory hot seat.

Their remarks came Thursday at the American Bar Association’s white-collar crime conference in San Francisco, just hours after Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco announced a greater push to encourage people to report on companies by rewarding whistleblowing and incentivizing companies to disclose wrongdoing as early as possible.

article.title: 'First-to-File' Rule Dooms Cardinal Health Executive's Qui Tam Action Against 5 Physician Practices
article.description: A federal judge in Massachusetts dismissed a former Cardinal Health executive’s qui tam action accusing five physician practices of accepting kickbacks because the allegations closely mirrored those laid out in a then-pending complaint against…
article.text: A federal judge in Massachusetts dismissed a former Cardinal Health executive’s qui tam action accusing five physician practices of accepting kickbacks because the allegations closely mirrored those laid out in a then-pending complaint against Cardinal by Omni Healthcare. U.S. District Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton for the District of Massachusetts concluded Sept. 7 that an amended complaint filed by Michael Mullen, former senior vice president and general manager of the Cardinal Health Specialty Solutions Group, against five physician practices, Birmingham Hematology and Oncology Associates, Oncology Specialties, Dayton Physicians, Northwest Medical Specialties, and Health First Medical Group, was barred by the “first-to-file rule” of the False Claims Act.

Gorton for the District of Massachusetts concluded Sept. 7 that an amended complaint filed by Michael Mullen, former senior vice president and general manager of the Cardinal Health Specialty Solutions Group, against five physician practices, Birmingham Hematology and Oncology Associates, Oncology Specialties, Dayton Physicians, Northwest Medical Specialties, and Health First Medical Group, was barred by the “first-to-file rule” of the False Claims Act.

She previously served as an in-house leader Ascena Retail Group, Boehringer Ingelheim, ITT Corp., GE Money and Credit Suisse. Wendy Hufford announced over the weekend that she’d “just started” her multifaceted legal boss role at the Fort Myers, Florida-based retailer, which also recently named a new chief financial officer. Chico’s brands include White House Black Market and Soma.

article.title: In-House Moves of Month: EBay, Estee Lauder, GE, Geico Grab Headlines
article.description: March saw a series of shakeups at prominent legal departments, from the sudden departure of longtime legal chiefs at eBay and Estee Lauder to big names in tech taking top lawyer roles at rising stars like Abnormal Security and mainstays like DXC…
article.text: March saw a series of shakeups at prominent legal departments, from the sudden departure of longtime legal chiefs at eBay and Estee Lauder to big names in tech taking top lawyer roles at rising stars like Abnormal Security and mainstays like DXC Technologies. The month began with a flurry of notable exits. EBay Chief Legal Officer Marie Oh Huber, who’d led the legal team since 2015, said she was leaving to explore other interests. EBay CEO Jamie Iannone didn’t give a reason for Huber’s exit, but it came on the heels of the company agreeing to pay $3 million to settle criminal charges that its employees in 2019 harassed a Massachusetts couple whose online newsletter had criticized the company. Huber was not implicated in the scandal, but it came on her watch.

article.title: Accused FTX 'Fixer' Silenced Whistleblowers, Enabled Fraud at Bankrupt Crypto Exchange, Lawsuit Claims
article.description: As a former top lawyer at bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, Daniel Friedberg helped Sam Bankman-Fried plunder billions of dollars from customer accounts and paid off whistleblowers as a “fixer” for the accused fraudster, according to a lawsuit…
article.text: As a former top lawyer at bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, Daniel Friedberg helped Sam Bankman-Fried plunder billions of dollars from customer accounts and paid off whistleblowers as a “fixer” for the accused fraudster, according to a lawsuit FTX Trading Ltd. filed this week in Delaware bankruptcy court. Friedberg, who was both FTX’s chief compliance officer and general counsel at crypto hedge fund Alameda Research, is accused of enabling a scheme in which Bankman-Fried and other higher-ups raided customer exchange deposits to enrich themselves, “lining their own and their families’ and friends’ pockets, and ingratiating themselves with numerous business prospects and potential allies,” the lawsuit says.

article.title: The Rise of Counter-Disinformation Litigation and What It Means for Business
article.description: In the past year, viral lies and conspiracies have saturated our public discourse, with concrete results. The scale and speed with which falsehoods have spread about everything from the outcome of the 2020 election to the Jan. 6 attack to COVID-19…
article.text: In the past year, viral lies and conspiracies have saturated our public discourse, with concrete results. The scale and speed with which falsehoods have spread about everything from the outcome of the 2020 election to the Jan. 6 attack to COVID-19 vaccines, and much else, have led to real-world consequences for companies and people—ruined reputations, lost business value, security expenses, and death threats, to name a few. The prevalence of disinformation can impact all kinds of businesses by affecting corporate brands, sales, partnerships, employee and customer retention, physical security, and even stockholder activism. Partly in response to the spread of false narratives, 2021 witnessed a new trend: the proliferation of counter-disinformation litigation. While many of these suits are still in the early stages, plaintiffs have seen notable (and surprising) successes thus far, suggesting the emergence of a specialized, potent tool to combat phony and harmful narratives. Both victims of false narratives and potential defendants should pay heed to these novel developments.

article.title: Court OKs $69B Microsoft-Activision Merger, Dealing Setback to Lina Khan's FTC
article.description: A federal judge denied the FTC's motion for a preliminary injunction halting the deal. The judge was not persuaded the merger would diminish competition or hurt consumers. The deal also faces opposition from the U.K.'s Competition Markets Authority,…
article.text: A federal judge denied the FTC's motion for a preliminary injunction halting the deal. The judge was not persuaded the merger would diminish competition or hurt consumers. The deal also faces opposition from the U.K.'s Competition Markets Authority, but the regulator on Tuesday invited Microsoft to modify the deal to address its concerns. In a big defeat for Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan, a federal judge on Tuesday rejected the agency’s attempt to derail Microsoft’s $69 billion acquisition of Santa Monica, California-based video game maker Activision Blizzard. In a 53-page decision rejecting the FTC’s request for a temporary injunction, U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley of the Northern District of California said she was not persuaded the merger would substantially reduce competition or harm consumers.
article.html:
• A federal judge denied the FTC's motion for a preliminary injunction halting the deal.
  • The judge was not persuaded the merger would diminish competition or hurt consumers.
  • The deal also faces opposition from the U.K.'s Competition Markets Authority, but the regulator on Tuesday invited Microsoft to modify the deal to address its concerns.

In a big defeat for Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan, a federal judge on Tuesday rejected the agency’s attempt to derail Microsoft’s $69 billion acquisition of Santa Monica, California-based video game maker Activision Blizzard.

In a 53-page decision rejecting the FTC’s request for a temporary injunction, U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley of the Northern District of California said she was not persuaded the merger would substantially reduce competition or harm consumers.

article.title: Ohio State Keeping Law Firms Busy With 2 #MeToo Probes, Lawsuits
article.description: Two separate, unrelated investigations of alleged sexual- or gender-related misconduct are unfolding at OSU: The first involves the school’s nationally prominent football program. The second concerns a sports doctor who examined hundreds of primarily…
article.text: Two separate, unrelated investigations of alleged sexual- or gender-related misconduct are unfolding at OSU: The first involves the school’s nationally prominent football program. The second concerns a sports doctor who examined hundreds of primarily male athletes and is alleged to have sexually abused them. Big league lawyers have been called in to help. The #MeToo movement has hit the Ohio State University athletic department with a double whammy, resulting in a flurry of legal activity in the past week, and one almost needs a program to keep straight who are the lawyers on which issue. The double whammy consists of two separate, unrelated investigations of alleged sexual or gender-related misconduct: The first involves the school’s nationally prominent football program and an investigation into coach Urban Meyer’s response after he learned of allegations of domestic abuse against one of his assistant coaches in 2015. OSU brought in Debevoise & Plimpton partner Mary Jo White, former U.S. attorney in Manhattan and ex-chair of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, to head that one.

article.title: 23andMe Breach Compounded by Theft of Ethnicity Data
article.description: 23andMe disclosed the theft of customer data in early October. The company says that rather than breaching its defenses, hackers gained access by amalgamating logins and passwords from other sites that were compromised. Customers have filed two dozen…
article.text: 23andMe disclosed the theft of customer data in early October. The company says that rather than breaching its defenses, hackers gained access by amalgamating logins and passwords from other sites that were compromised. Customers have filed two dozen lawsuits, and regulators have launched investigations. Genetic testing and ancestry company 23andMe is trying to rein in the fallout from a data breach that was especially dire. Not only did hackers gain access to standard personal information, such as dates of birth, but also to their genetic makeups, at a time when Jews and Asians are increasingly facing attacks. Just weeks after 23andMe disclosed the theft of customer data, the ancestry website has been slapped with two dozen lawsuits and has drawn the furrowed brows of regulators.

article.title: Supreme Court Lowers Bar for Title VII Discrimination Claims
article.description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a lower court ruling requiring Title VII plaintiffs to show that a discriminatory job transfer resulted in “significant” harm, reviving a lawsuit from a police officer claiming she was moved out of a…
article.text: The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a lower court ruling requiring Title VII plaintiffs to show that a discriminatory job transfer resulted in “significant” harm, reviving a lawsuit from a police officer claiming she was moved out of a prestigious task force because she is a woman. In Muldrow v. City of St. Louis, the Supreme Court unanimously vacated a U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruling that a Title VII claim over a discriminatory job transfer must result in “materially significant disadvantages” for the employee. Still, the Supreme Court required Title VII plaintiffs to show at least some harm to bring a discrimination lawsuit, a holding that could temper challenges to workplace DEI policies.
article.html:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a lower court ruling requiring Title VII plaintiffs to show that a discriminatory job transfer resulted in “significant” harm, reviving a lawsuit from a police officer claiming she was moved out of a prestigious task force because she is a woman.

In Muldrow v. City of St. Louis, the Supreme Court unanimously vacated a U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruling that a Title VII claim over a discriminatory job transfer must result in “materially significant disadvantages” for the employee. Still, the Supreme Court required Title VII plaintiffs to show at least some harm to bring a discrimination lawsuit, a holding that could temper challenges to workplace DEI policies.

article.description: Legal departments continue to struggle with being perceived negatively by other parts of the business, according to a newly released study that recommends departments unleash image overhauls. The findings are contained in Thomson Reuters’ “2024 State…
article.text: Legal departments continue to struggle with being perceived negatively by other parts of the business, according to a newly released study that recommends departments unleash image overhauls. The findings are contained in Thomson Reuters’ “2024 State of the Corporate Law Department,” which notes that some departments unwittingly fan those negative perceptions by measuring their performance by such metrics as cost and legal spend—in other words, casting legal as a cost center instead of a creator of value.

article.title: Evolving Rules Around Data Privacy in China Pose Challenges for Foreign Companies
article.description: Companies are buzzing about GDPR, but in-house lawyers can look beyond Europe and into Asia for another source of regulatory scrutiny around their data practices. As the May 2018 General Data Protection Regulation implementation date looms closer,…
article.text: Companies are buzzing about GDPR, but in-house lawyers can look beyond Europe and into Asia for another source of regulatory scrutiny around their data practices. As the May 2018 General Data Protection Regulation implementation date looms closer, global companies’ legal leaders have data privacy rights in Europe on the brain. But those familiar with China’s ever-evolving data rules and standards say it’s important global companies focus on more than just Europe. Though China’s Cybersecurity Law, which controls how data in the country can be collected and shared, has been around in some form since 2016, it’s been updated and clarified on an ongoing basis. On Jan. 25, the Standardization Administration of China published the full text of the Information Security Technology—Personal Information Security Specification, a set of best practices to ensure CSL compliance.
article.html:
Companies are buzzing about GDPR, but in-house lawyers can look beyond Europe and into Asia for another source of regulatory scrutiny around their data practices.

As the May 2018 General Data Protection Regulation implementation date looms closer, global companies’ legal leaders have data privacy rights in Europe on the brain. But those familiar with China’s ever-evolving data rules and standards say it’s important global companies focus on more than just Europe.

Though China’s Cybersecurity Law, which controls how data in the country can be collected and shared, has been around in some form since 2016, it’s been updated and clarified on an ongoing basis. On Jan. 25, the Standardization Administration of China published the full text of the Information Security Technology—Personal Information Security Specification, a set of best practices to ensure CSL compliance.

article.title: Judge Tosses Ex-Twitter Workers' $500M Severance Case
article.description: Thousands of Twitter employees fired after Elon Musk took control of the social media company in November 2022 are not entitled to $500 million in unpaid severance under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, a federal judge ruled. Lead…
article.text: Thousands of Twitter employees fired after Elon Musk took control of the social media company in November 2022 are not entitled to $500 million in unpaid severance under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, a federal judge ruled. Lead plaintiff Courtney McMillian, vice president of total rewards at Twitter before she was laid off in 2022, brought the case on behalf of about 6,000 employees terminated following Musk’s takeover.
article.html:
Thousands of Twitter employees fired after Elon Musk took control of the social media company in November 2022 are not entitled to $500 million in unpaid severance under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, a federal judge ruled.

Lead plaintiff Courtney McMillian, vice president of total rewards at Twitter before she was laid off in 2022, brought the case on behalf of about 6,000 employees terminated following Musk’s takeover.

article.title: Washington AG sues T-Mobile over 'avoidable' 2021 data breach
article.description: Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson says T-Mobile's lax security practices resulted in a 2021 data breach that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million Washingtonians.
article.text: By Maria Dinzeo (January 6, 2025, 21:30 GMT | Insight) -- The State of Washington is suing T-Mobile over lax cybersecurity practices in the lead up to a massive data breach back in August 2021 that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million residents, including their social security numbers and driver’s license information. "This significant data breach was entirely avoidable,” Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson said in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “T-Mobile had years to fix key vulnerabilities in its cybersecurity systems — and it failed.” Those vulnerabilities allegedly stemmed from inadequate risk management and security monitoring, including failure to store customers’ personal data in legacy Sprint databases maintained by T-Mobile after the two telecoms merged in 2020, according to the complaint filed in King County Superior Court today (see here). "T-Mobile knew of the risks from cyber-attacks and decided to accept the risks rather than adequately implement safeguards,” the lawsuit says. The complaint notes that T-Mobile even admitted in a securities filing that the merger introduced additional security risks. Security problems also preceded the merger, however, dating back to 2017 when an “ethical hacker” uncovered an Application Programming Interface vulnerability that could have exposed personal identifying information like customer names, email addresses and account numbers, just by knowing or guessing a customer’s phone number. Vulnerabilities persisted for years, the lawsuit says, resulting in several instances where hackers stole customer PII in 2018 and 2019. Employee credentials were also stolen by hackers in 2021 and 2022 and used to access call logs and proprietary source code. In August 2021, T-Mobile alerted customers that it had suffered a massive cyberattack. It eventually came out that the personal data of more than 79 million customers had been exposed and that PII had been posted for sale on the dark web. T-Mobile initially disclosed the breach to customers via text message, but the messages allegedly misled customers about its seriousness and omitted critical information like the fact that social security numbers were included in some of the leaked data. Ferguson’s office has been investigating the breach for years, though the office claimed in a 2023 court filing that T-Mobile impeded its efforts by failing to respond to numerous requests for documents and information related to its cybersecurity practices, past breaches and the revenue it derives from collecting user data. Ferguson’s office did not reply to questions from MLex about whether it ever received the requested documents. The 2021 data breach sparked a firestorm of privacy lawsuits across the country that were eventually consolidated in Washington federal court. Bellevue, Washington-based T-Mobile agreed to settle with the consolidated class for $350 million in a 2022 deal (see here) that was approved in 2023 (see here). T-Mobile also reached a $31.5 million settlement with the Federal Communications Commission last year. A T-Mobile spokesperson told MLex in an email that the company has had multiple conversations with the Washington AG's office about the 2021 data breach over the last several years "and even reached out in late November to continue discussions, so the office’s decision to file a lawsuit today came as a surprise." They added, "While we disagree with their approach and the filing’s claims, we are open to further dialogue and welcome the opportunity to resolve this issue, as we have already done with the FCC. We also look forward to sharing how T-Mobile has fundamentally transformed our approach to cyber security over the past four years to further protect our customers." The spokesperson did not address MLex's inquiry about whether it complied with Ferguson’s document requests prior to the lawsuit filed today, which seeks civil penalties and restitution, improved security practices and more transparency in T-Mobile’s communications about cybersecurity to its customers.
