article.html:
By Maria Dinzeo

(January 6, 2025, 21:30 GMT | Insight) -- The State of Washington is suing T-Mobile over lax cybersecurity practices in the lead up to a massive data breach back in August 2021 that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million residents, including their social security numbers and driver’s license information.

"This significant data breach was entirely avoidable,” Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson said in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “T-Mobile had years to fix key vulnerabilities in its cybersecurity systems — and it failed.”

Those vulnerabilities allegedly stemmed from inadequate risk management and security monitoring, including failure to store customers’ personal data in legacy Sprint databases maintained by T-Mobile after the two telecoms merged in 2020, according to the complaint filed in King County Superior Court today (see here).

"T-Mobile knew of the risks from cyber-attacks and decided to accept the risks rather than adequately implement safeguards,” the lawsuit says. The complaint notes that T-Mobile even admitted in a securities filing that the merger introduced additional security risks.

Security problems also preceded the merger, however, dating back to 2017 when an “ethical hacker” uncovered an Application Programming Interface vulnerability that could have exposed personal identifying information like customer names, email addresses and account numbers, just by knowing or guessing a customer’s phone number.

Vulnerabilities persisted for years, the lawsuit says, resulting in several instances where hackers stole customer PII in 2018 and 2019. Employee credentials were also stolen by hackers in 2021 and 2022 and used to access call logs and proprietary source code.

In August 2021, T-Mobile alerted customers that it had suffered a massive cyberattack. It eventually came out that the personal data of more than 79 million customers had been exposed and that PII had been posted for sale on the dark web.

T-Mobile initially disclosed the breach to customers via text message, but the messages allegedly misled customers about its seriousness and omitted critical information like the fact that social security numbers were included in some of the leaked data.

Ferguson’s office has been investigating the breach for years, though the office claimed in a 2023 court filing that T-Mobile impeded its efforts by failing to respond to numerous requests for documents and information related to its cybersecurity practices, past breaches and the revenue it derives from collecting user data.

Ferguson’s office did not reply to questions from MLex about whether it ever received the requested documents.

The 2021 data breach sparked a firestorm of privacy lawsuits across the country that were eventually consolidated in Washington federal court. Bellevue, Washington-based T-Mobile agreed to settle with the consolidated class for $350 million in a 2022 deal (see here) that was approved in 2023 (see here). T-Mobile also reached a $31.5 million settlement with the Federal Communications Commission last year.

A T-Mobile spokesperson told MLex in an email that the company has had multiple conversations with the Washington AG's office about the 2021 data breach over the last several years "and even reached out in late November to continue discussions, so the office’s decision to file a lawsuit today came as a surprise."

They added, "While we disagree with their approach and the filing’s claims, we are open to further dialogue and welcome the opportunity to resolve this issue, as we have already done with the FCC. We also look forward to sharing how T-Mobile has fundamentally transformed our approach to cyber security over the past four years to further protect our customers."

The spokesperson did not address MLex's inquiry about  whether it complied with Ferguson’s document requests prior to the lawsuit filed today, which seeks civil penalties and restitution, improved security practices and more transparency in T-Mobile’s communications about cybersecurity to its customers.

article.title: Wave of US state privacy bills taking effect in January
article.description: California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents.
article.text: A wave of state privacy laws taking effect in January will expand an already complicated patchwork of US privacy regulations and reflects an escalating trend among states to continue raising the bar for consumer privacy protections. 23 Dec 2024 | 23:48 GMT | Comment By Maria Dinzeo California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents. Regulations on annual cybersecurity audits, or CSAs, in the making since mid-2023, could finally get over the finish line this year. As currently written, the regulation requires that companies hire a third party to evaluate the strength of their cybersecurity programs and identify any gaps or weaknesses in baseline cybersecurity like multi-factor authentication, zero-trust architecture, account access controls, penetration testing and disaster-recovery plans. For any missing elements, the business and its auditor must explain why the component is not necessary to protect personal information. Stacey Higginbotham, a cybersecurity expert and policy fellow at Consumer Reports, said it’s remarkable how many companies currently don’t employ best cybersecurity practices. That became even more apparent earlier this year when Change Healthcare suffered one of the largest known data breaches of protected health information in a ransomware attack that exposed the personal, financial and healthcare records of some 100 million Americans. “That happened because someone didn't put multi-factor authentication, which is a bare bones best practice, on a remote admin server with data on it,” Higginbotham said. “It's bonkers that in the Year of our Lord 2024 that people aren't using MFA on a remote server. That's like leaving the house with the door unlocked and announcing on social media that you’ll be in Europe for the next two weeks.” She said California’s CSA requirement will get companies thinking about minimum standards at a time when so much consumer data is being disseminated across the dark web. “Broadly speaking, a CSA is a tool to help ensure that people are actually paying attention that they're taking the steps they need to,” Higginbotham said. “It's not going to magically prevent cybersecurity intrusions. It's going to ensure that they're employing best practices that will help prevent an intrusion or data extraction. It would be nice if anyone did this anyway, but you really need regulations to ensure people are doing them.” Data breaches also have staggering business costs. IBM’s 2024 data breach report puts the global average cost of a data breach at $4.88 million, up 10 percent from last year and the highest total ever. Customers suffer too. IBM’s report says that 63 percent of organizations said they planned to raise the price of goods and services following a data breach, up from 57 percent last year. But economic researchers from Berkeley and California State University Sacramento anticipate that Calfiornia’s CSA regulations will save companies money in avoided annual losses, approximately $734 million in 2027, and more than $32 billion by the end of 2036. The researchers also believe that absent a cybersecurity audit, businesses will be less likely to catch issues in internal controls and processes. But over time, the CSA will result in them being “more proficient in dealing with data breaches swiftly and effectively.” The rules apply to businesses that derive at least 50 percent of their revenue from selling data, or make $28 million or more in annual revenue and process the data of 250,000 consumers or the sensitive personal information of 50,000 or more consumers in the preceding calendar year. The California Privacy Protection Agency estimates that roughly 25,000 companies will be impacted by its CSA regulation. Importantly, the rules require that the company’s highest ranking executive or a member of the board sign off on the audit and attest that they have reviewed and understand its findings. Jeewon Serrato, a partner at Pillsbury Winthrop who handles enforcement actions and advises clients on complex security incident investigations, said regulatory agencies are asking more from C-suite executives. “The trend I’m seeing is personal liability,” she said. “We often talk to clients about how privacy and cybersecurity is now a C-suite and board-level responsibility.” While California’s CSA regulations do not penalize executives for cybersecurity failings, they demand that the most senior people in a business be informed about its security posture. “That there has to be executive-level sign off is really putting it onto the individual executives to be responsible and have oversight over these programs,” Serrato said. “To determine gaps and vulnerabilities and the remediation efforts you've signed off on requires the individual executives to take this seriously.” Higginbotham said she’s seeing a larger trend toward making it a company-wide responsibility to manage cyber risk. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, for example, this year released its updated cybersecurity guidance 2.0 to include an additional function that emphasizes the importance of cybersecurity governance and integrating cybersecurity into the overall organization and decision-making processes. “There is a trend toward making sure it's at the business level and not just throwing it over the fence to your CISO,” Higginbotham said. Lawmakers are also taking note of the staggering amount of data breaches US organizations have suffered in recent years and are taking steps to hold entire industries accountable. In response to the Change Healthcare breach, Democratic Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Mark Warner of Virginia introduced the Health Infrastructure Security and Accountability Act, which would establish “mandatory minimum cybersecurity standards for health care providers, health plans, clearinghouses and business associates.” According to a one-page summary of the bill from the Senate Finance Committee, the new law “sets tough minimum cybersecurity standards, requires annual audits for compliance, and creates serious accountability for companies that fail to meet those requirements.” It would also eliminate the statutory caps on the department of Health and Human Services’ fining authority and include enhanced penalties for lax cybersecurity. Hacks of the healthcare system “are entirely preventable and are the direct result of lax cybersecurity practices by health care providers and their business partners," the bill summary says. California’s new rules are not nearly as prescriptive, but early public comments reflect some consternation in the cybersecurity community. “Cybersecurity audits have significant limitations as a cybersecurity tool. They are a useful tool for an organization to capture a snapshot of the existence of cybersecurity plans, strategies, or controls; however, audit results are only reflective of a point in time and cannot reflect a real-time measure of the state of an organization’s security practices. While we recognize that it is the CPPA’s intention to create an auditing scheme, we would caution organizations against being overly reliant on the results,” Elizabeth Guillot, public policy manager at CrowdStrike, wrote in a preliminary comment to the CPPA. “In addition to a cybersecurity audit, organizations should deploy cybersecurity best practices to continuously protect themselves from cyberattacks and data breaches and reevaluate if those technologies are working to the best of their ability more regularly than a yearly audit.” The Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association, a trade group representing the wireless communications industry, said the CPPA should require companies to do cybersecurity audits “only when engaging in specific, enumerated activities that present a cybersecurity risk” and “should focus on processing activities that have significant, consequential effects on cybersecurity that impact consumers.” A high volume of CSAs, it cautions in its comment, “does not meaningfully improve cybersecurity protection, but rather detracts from it by diverting needed resources away from activities that actually raise impactful risks.” Higginbotham said the rules should bring companies up to a good baseline of cybersecurity, “however there are some companies that will meet these standards from a revenue or size perspective that probably haven't allocated enough resources to cybersecurity, and this could be expensive or difficult for them. But that doesn't mean it shouldn't be done, because it's better for everyone as a whole if people's data doesn't get compromised.” The CPPA will close its public comment period on Jan. 14, when it will meet in a public session to hear additional feedback on the rules. A spokesperson for the CPPA said its board will then determine whether to make any additional changes before releasing the final version. Please e-mail editors@mlex.com to contact the editorial staff regarding this story, or to submit the names of lawyers and advisers.
article.html:
A wave of state privacy laws taking effect in January will expand an already complicated patchwork of US privacy regulations and reflects an escalating trend among states to continue raising the bar for consumer privacy protections.

23 Dec 2024 |  23:48 GMT |  Comment

By Maria Dinzeo


California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents.


Regulations on annual cybersecurity audits, or CSAs, in the making since mid-2023, could finally get over the finish line this year. As currently written, the regulation requires that companies hire a third party to evaluate the strength of their cybersecurity programs and identify any gaps or weaknesses in baseline cybersecurity like multi-factor authentication, zero-trust architecture, account access controls, penetration testing and disaster-recovery plans.


For any missing elements, the business and its auditor must explain why the component is not necessary to protect personal information.


Stacey Higginbotham, a cybersecurity expert and policy fellow at Consumer Reports, said it’s remarkable how many companies currently don’t employ best cybersecurity practices. That became even more apparent earlier this year when Change Healthcare suffered one of the largest known data breaches of protected health information in a ransomware attack that exposed the personal, financial and healthcare records of some 100 million Americans.


“That happened because someone didn't put multi-factor authentication, which is a bare bones best practice, on a remote admin server with data on it,” Higginbotham said. “It's bonkers that in the Year of our Lord 2024 that people aren't using MFA on a remote server. That's like leaving the house with the door unlocked and announcing on social media that you’ll be in Europe for the next two weeks.”


She said California’s CSA requirement will get companies thinking about minimum standards at a time when so much consumer data is being disseminated across the dark web. “Broadly speaking, a CSA is a tool to help ensure that people are actually paying attention that they're taking the steps they need to,” Higginbotham said. “It's not going to magically prevent cybersecurity intrusions. It's going to ensure that they're employing best practices that will help prevent an intrusion or data extraction. It would be nice if anyone did this anyway, but you really need regulations to ensure people are doing them.”


Data breaches also have staggering business costs. IBM’s 2024 data breach report puts the global average cost of a data breach at $4.88 million, up 10 percent from last year and the highest total ever. Customers suffer too. IBM’s report says that 63 percent of organizations said they planned to raise the price of goods and services following a data breach, up from 57 percent last year.


But economic researchers from Berkeley and California State University Sacramento anticipate that Calfiornia’s CSA regulations will save companies money in avoided annual losses, approximately $734 million in 2027, and more than $32 billion by the end of 2036. The researchers also believe that absent a cybersecurity audit, businesses will be less likely to catch issues in internal controls and processes. But over time, the CSA will result in them being “more proficient in dealing with data breaches swiftly and effectively.”


The rules apply to businesses that derive at least 50 percent of their revenue from selling data, or make $28 million or more in annual revenue and process the data of 250,000 consumers or the sensitive personal information of 50,000 or more consumers in the preceding calendar year. The California Privacy Protection Agency estimates that roughly 25,000 companies will be impacted by its CSA regulation.


Importantly, the rules require that the company’s highest ranking executive or a member of the board sign off on the audit and attest that they have reviewed and understand its findings.


Jeewon Serrato, a partner at Pillsbury Winthrop who handles enforcement actions and advises clients on complex security incident investigations, said regulatory agencies are asking more from C-suite executives. “The trend I’m seeing is personal liability,” she said. “We often talk to clients about how privacy and cybersecurity is now a C-suite and board-level responsibility.”


While California’s CSA regulations do not penalize executives for cybersecurity failings, they demand that the most senior people in a business be informed about its security posture.


“That there has to be executive-level sign off is really putting it onto the individual executives to be responsible and have oversight over these programs,” Serrato said. “To determine gaps and vulnerabilities and the remediation efforts you've signed off on requires the individual executives to take this seriously.”


Higginbotham said she’s seeing a larger trend toward making it a company-wide responsibility to manage cyber risk. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, for example, this year released its updated cybersecurity guidance 2.0 to include an additional function that emphasizes the importance of cybersecurity governance and integrating cybersecurity into the overall organization and decision-making processes. “There is a trend toward making sure it's at the business level and not just throwing it over the fence to your CISO,” Higginbotham said.


Lawmakers are also taking note of the staggering amount of data breaches US organizations have suffered in recent years and are taking steps to hold entire industries accountable.


In response to the Change Healthcare breach, Democratic Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Mark Warner of Virginia introduced the Health Infrastructure Security and Accountability Act, which would establish “mandatory minimum cybersecurity standards for health care providers, health plans, clearinghouses and business associates.” According to a one-page summary of the bill from the Senate Finance Committee, the new law “sets tough minimum cybersecurity standards, requires annual audits for compliance, and creates serious accountability for companies that fail to meet those requirements.”


It would also eliminate the statutory caps on the department of Health and Human Services’ fining authority and include enhanced penalties for lax cybersecurity. Hacks of the healthcare system “are entirely preventable and are the direct result of lax cybersecurity practices by health care providers and their business partners," the bill summary says.


California’s new rules are not nearly as prescriptive, but early public comments reflect some consternation in the cybersecurity community.


“Cybersecurity audits have significant limitations as a cybersecurity tool. They are a useful tool for an organization to capture a snapshot of the existence of cybersecurity plans, strategies, or controls; however, audit results are only reflective of a point in time and cannot reflect a real-time measure of the state of an organization’s security practices. While we recognize that it is the CPPA’s intention to create an auditing scheme, we would caution organizations against being overly reliant on the results,” Elizabeth Guillot, public policy manager at CrowdStrike, wrote in a preliminary comment to the CPPA. “In addition to a cybersecurity audit, organizations should deploy cybersecurity best practices to continuously protect themselves from cyberattacks and data breaches and reevaluate if those technologies are working to the best of their ability more regularly than a yearly audit.”


The Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association, a trade group representing the wireless communications industry, said the CPPA should require companies to do cybersecurity audits “only when engaging in specific, enumerated activities that present a cybersecurity risk” and “should focus on processing activities that have significant, consequential effects on cybersecurity that impact consumers.” A high volume of CSAs, it cautions in its comment, “does not meaningfully improve cybersecurity protection, but rather detracts from it by diverting needed resources away from activities that actually raise impactful risks.”


Higginbotham said the rules should bring companies up to a good baseline of cybersecurity, “however there are some companies that will meet these standards from a revenue or size perspective that probably haven't allocated enough resources to cybersecurity, and this could be expensive or difficult for them. But that doesn't mean it shouldn't be done, because it's better for everyone as a whole if people's data doesn't get compromised.”


The CPPA will close its public comment period on Jan. 14, when it will meet in a public session to hear additional feedback on the rules. A spokesperson for the CPPA said its board will then determine whether to make any additional changes before releasing the final version.

article.title: Suits Flooding Courts Seize on Decades-Old Wiretapping Laws to Allege Data Breaches
article.text: Data privacy class actions focused on "session replay" software and other ad tech tools that track how users interact with websites are piling up by the day, unabated by a spate of rulings favoring defendants. Legal observers say the hitch in those defendant victories is that they have largely been on procedural or statute-of-limitation grounds, keeping alive plaintiffs' attorneys hopes that their legal strategy eventually will strike gold. The plaintiff attorneys are are putting decades-old state wiretap statutes to new use to go after a swath of retailers, insurers, airlines, and other businesses with public-facing websites, arguing that session replay tools—which track consumers' mouse movements, keystrokes, clicks and page visits—constitute illegal wiretapping or eavesdropping. The California Invasion of Privacy Act, which dates back to 1967, has been particularly popular with plaintiff attorneys, but they also have brought cases in Pennsylvania, Florida, Maryland, Illinois and Missouri. Lothar Determann, author of "Determann's Field Guide to Privacy Law," calls the complaints largely bogus, arguing that session replay software doesn't fit the definition of a wiretap, as there is no third-party interception of a communication. "Wiretap is intercepting communications between two parties. This is what it literally means. In these session replay cases, there isn't a third party who is intercepting something," said Determann, who teaches e-commerce law and data privacy law at Berkeley Law, the University of San Francisco Law School and Free University of Berlin. "This is the website operator trying to understand how users use their website to make their communication more effective. I do not think this consists of an an illegal wiretap illegal eavesdropping or illegal recording and I find these lawsuits and threats baseless, meritless and misrepresenting the communication situation and technology and how it works." Courts already have tossed dozens of privacy complaints at the pleading stage on jurisdictional or standing grounds—such as a failure to show plaintiffs actually were harmed by the practice. In another session replay ruling, a district court dismissed a session replay case against the wellness and weigh-loss company Noom, finding it can't be held liable under the California Invasion of Privacy Act for recording communications on its own website. But two recent appellate rulings have given plaintiffs' attorneys renewed confidence in their theories. Last May, the Ninth Circuit reversed a district court's dismissal of a session replay lawsuit, holding that a life insurance company failed to get prior consent from a prospective customer before using a session replay tool called ActiveProspect to record health information he entered into an online questionnaire. That he clicked "view my quote" after filling out the questionnaire and retroactively consented to the company's privacy was not enough, the panel found. The case ended up back before another district judge, who recently dismissed it as barred by CIPA's one-year statute of limitations. In another case, the Third Circuit last August overturned a district judge and revived a woman's claims that she was unlawfully surveilled by marketing platform NaviStone's session replay technology while browsing an online store for pet stairs. The court ruled that NaviStone had "intercepted" the woman's online activities in violation of Pennsylvania's Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act. "There are areas of state law that remain untested, and the plaintiffs' bar has been emboldened in the last year or so by a couple of circuit opinions that directly address session replay," said Rebekah Guyon, a Greenberg Traurig shareholder. "Plaintiffs have argued that those decisions opened up potential ambiguity around when the use of session replay could be a wiretap." She added: "For session replay cases as a whole in 2023, we're on track to have more filed cases filed this year than last year, which was a record year for session replay cases nationwide." Plaintiffs have racked up victories in the district courts, as well. This month, U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer ruled against Prudential Financial, upholding privacy claims asserted by a group of consumers who argued that the company used marketing software from ActiveProspect that collected their information without consent while they sought life insurance quotes. District courts also have found that Nike and Lululemon aided and abetted wiretapping by using third-party session replay software. Litigator Michael Bahar, a partner at Eversheds Sutherland, said companies still face a "tremendous risk" from lawsuits based on CIPA and other state wiretapping laws. "What we're seeing is a lot of boilerplate complaints, which are likely the reason we're seeing a lot of these falling part. But that's part of the risk, as it's very easy for any company to get slapped with one of these disputes," he said. "A lot of these things are getting kicked based on standing and statute of limitations. We have yet to see a ruling at the heart of the matter, and until we see such a ruling, we're not going to see these things go away." Eric Goldman, a law professor at Santa Clara University, said it only takes one case to spur a torrent of copycats. "It only takes one plaintiff win to crack open the floodgates," he said. "That one will spark another 1,000 lawsuits." For Goldman, what's old is new again. "I teach a case in my internet law class called In re: Pharmatrak. It was basically the exact same issue being litigated in session replay cases," he said. In that early 2000s case, a web analytics company called Pharmatrak that collected website traffic data for pharmaceutical companies was accused of violating the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. The First District held that Pharmatrak "intercepted" communications under the law. "We're litigating the same damn issue 20 years later," Goldman said. While the district court later dismissed the case on remand, Goldman said Pharmatrak was eventually driven out of business when its customers stopped using it. Cases like this present a "double-whammy" for ad tech companies, Goldman said. Even if they win in court, companies might still drop them out of fear of being sued. Plaintiff attorneys are diving into the nitty-gritty of ad tech technology to find creative ways to fit new ad tech tools into Cold War-era laws. Michael Stortz, a partner at K&L Gates who specializes in consumer protection and data privacy cases, said he's seen a spike in cases involving tracking pixels, chatbot features and video recordings, all brought under older statutes like CIPA and the federal Video Privacy Protection Act, which was originally enacted to protect the privacy of consumers' video tape rentals. "The plaintiffs' bar had high hopes that state privacy statutes like the California Consumer Protection Act would support a broader regime of data privacy claims and that hasn't happened. So what we're seeing—whether its wiretapping or the VPPA—is an attempt to shoehorn these old statues, which date back decades, as a vehicle to challenge modern technologies," Stortz said. Greenberg Traurig's Guyon said she doesn't think VPPA ever was intended to apply online, "let alone to a website operator that happens to have videos online. But wherever there is new technology, the plaintiffs' bar will try to expand the case law." Enterprising attorneys also are looking to expand other areas of CIPA, Guyon said. For instance, section 637.3 of the statute, originally written to protect people from being subjected to non-consensual polygraphs by their employers, is now being applied to voice recordings. "We've seen efforts by plaintiffs to expand that to voice recognition technology," she said. "That speaks to the commonality of where there's a privacy statute with statutory damages we are seeing more litigation." Guyon said she advises companies to understand how their online advertising tools and consents work. "A lot of areas of risk can be avoided by having a really cohesive working relationship with the marketing team, which always knows what is being done with ad tech tools," she said. "Have fulsome discussions with your marketing team, and see who is customizing the technology, and does your consent flow line up with what you're doing." Bahar said that while companies have robust defenses to these lawsuits, a strong disclosure and consent policy can help them avoid drawing the attention of the plaintiffs' bar. "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure," he said.

article.title: California's Data-Deletion Legislation Threatens to Shake Up Digital Ad Industry
article.description: "We think that this will have a tremendous impact on the small business and startup community in California," said Lartease Tiffith of the Interactive Advertising Bureau.
article.text: A California privacy bill that will give consumers the power to delete their personal information through a single request may soon become law, and could upend the way data brokers, advertisers and publishers do business in the Golden State. The Delete Act, now on Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, tasks California's privacy regulator with setting up a "simple" way for people to direct companies to delete their information through a single request by 2026. Data brokers, of which there are about 500 registered with the California Department of Justice, will also have to disclose what kind of information they collect on consumers—including precise geolocation and women's reproductive health data—beginning Jan. 1, 2029. They'll also have to undergo compliance audits every three years, starting in 2028. The California Privacy Protection Agency will have the authority to levy stiff penalties of $200 for each failure to delete, and a $200 fine for each day the data broker fails to register with the CPPA. The law defines "data brokers" as any company that knowingly collects personal information on a consumer with whom it doesn't have a direct relationship to sell to third parties. It would not apply to first-party data, or information that companies collect directly from consumers. Third-party data brokers aggregate public records, mobile apps, social media activity, online purchases and browser cookies to create profiles (third-party data) on consumers that they can sell to others. Some companies, like the credit bureaus Experian and Transunion, operate in the credit and risk mitigation arena, while others work to prevent fraud, perform background checks or build online directories. Many more track consumers' shopping habits and preferences to give other businesses insight to into what products and services they might be interested in buying. CPPA executive director Ashkan Soltani said the bill mirrors an existing state requirement under the California Consumer Privacy Act that businesses honor consumers' requests to opt out of sharing their information with third parties. Last year, retail cosmetics giant Sephora was hit with a $1.2 million fine for failing to process opt-out requests in the first public enforcement action under the state's landmark consumer privacy law. The Delete Act, Soltani said, will make it even easier for consumers to exercise their privacy rights. Ryan O'Leary, a research director at International Data Corp., said there hasn't been much enforcement of the CCPA's opt-out provision apart from the Sephora action, which the Delete Act should help address. "There still leaves a lot to be desired, and this gives them an actual mechanism," he said. The question remains how accessible the mechanism will be for consumers. "The education has to be there for consumers because you can have this law but what if no one requests that their data be deleted?" O'Leary said advertisers and marketing firms will likely lose access to fresh data, but he doesn't see a wholesale crippling of the industry. "I think there will still be a non-negligible amount of people that allow data brokers to sell their data. I don't think there are going to be folks going out of business because of this. They just won't have as much data or they won't be able to be as efficient and narrowly-targeted with their marketing," he said, "The advertising world existed before data was collected. It will exist long after." But the prospect of consumers scrubbing their data en masse has data brokers and digital advertisers on edge, and industry groups have vigorously lobbied in opposition to the bill, saying it will cut off access to free and low-cost digital content and keep small and medium-sized businesses from finding potential customers. "We think that this will have a tremendous impact on the small business and startup community in California," said Lartease Tiffith, executive vice president for public policy for the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Direct-to-consumer businesses may be the most affected, he said, as they rely heavily on third-party data purchased from data brokers for targeted advertising. "Everybody who is using third-party data is using data brokers," Tiffith said. "There's a rush to get more first party data, mostly because there seems to be an anti-third-party data thing going on, but not everyone can afford to." It may also force publishers to put more online content behind a paywall. "If you're a publisher and you rely on advertising and you're realizing you're getting less revenue and advertisers are seeing less conversions, at some point businesses will have to decide whether to keep their content free or go to subscription," Tiffith said. "That's something a lot of companies, especially publishers, are going to have to decide." Julie Rubash, chief privacy officer and general counsel for privacy software firm Sourcepoint, said mass deletion will likely be complicated. "If there is wide adoption of it, it very well could be extremely burdensome, especially for small companies to put mechanisms in place to listen for these signals and respond to them," she said. "Some companies have automated processes to find that information if you're interacting directly with a portal that is able to pull that information from your device, but I don't know if this automated mechanism is going to have the ability to pull that information. It may end up being a lot of time and money spent by these companies to achieve potentially very little of the intended effect." Opponents have also noted that the bill could thwart identity verification and fraud detection because it doesn't allow data brokers to transfer data to businesses or government agencies for anti-fraud purposes. It also permits "authorized agents" to submit requests on behalf of consumers, potentially opening the door to a cottage industry of lawyers and other enterprising "agents" to exploit Californians' privacy rights. To address some of these concerns, the bill was amended to allow consumers to selectively exclude certain data brokers from their deletion request, allow people to control precisely which brokers may continue to maintain the consumer's personal information." Rubash said a lot hinges on how the CPPA decides to implement the law. "The more control they give users the better, and perhaps working with companies to enable that control may be one method of doing that," she said. "There needs to be a lot of transparency. Users need to understand the consequences of what they're doing, and have a good understanding of what a data broker is and what different types of data brokers are, and perhaps where the data is collected from. I don't know if it would be possible to do that level of granularity, but I think it's important to educate consumers." Some CPPA board members have already shown a disposition toward not unduly burdening small businesses. Rubash said she hopes the agency will also consider exempting certain data brokers that are involved in preventing fraud. "These are all things the CPPA will have to think through when they implement this, as well as impacts it will have on smaller businesses and doing everyone they can to provide resources to those businesses to make it easier for them."

article.title: Tech giants must face largest personal injury litigation in US over social media harm
article.description: Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward.
article.text: 14 Dec 2024 | 00:25 GMT | Insight By Maria Dinzeo Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward. Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward. Meta Platform’s Facebook and Instagram, ByteDance’s TikTok, Google’s YouTube and Snap’s Snapchat petitioned the appellate court last December, asking the judges to review Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn B. Kuhl’s October 2023 ruling that the companies aren't shielded by the First Amendment or Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which provides online platforms immunity from liability over third-party content. The plaintiffs, a group of individuals, school districts and local governments, claim Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Snap are all designed to get young people addicted without regard for the deleterious consequences for kids’ mental health. They’ve also used a unique tack to skirt Section 230 and First Amendment protections by alleging that social media platforms are defectively designed products. Kuhl reasoned that the platforms are not “products” in the product liability sense, but the plaintiffs nevertheless sufficiently alleged that the companies were careless about the design of their algorithms. “Plaintiffs have adequately pled a cause of action for negligence that is not barred by federal immunity or the First Amendment,” Kuhl wrote in her 89-page ruling (see here). In their petition (see here), the social media giants argued that Kuhl had violated the “core principles” of Section 230 and the First Amendment as a means of immunizing platforms from protracted litigation, “not just from liability.” California’s Second Appellate District rejected the petition in a two-sentence order last week, saying it had read and considered the petition for writ of mandate and that “the petition is denied.” The companies didn't respond to messages seeking comment on the brief order. In a statement, Beasley Allen, which is representing the plaintiffs, said it was pleased with the most recent development in the litigation, saying the appellate courts’ refusal to weight in puts the case “one step closer to trials seeking to hold the tech giants liable for the mental physical harm suffered by youth as a result of social media addiction.” Kuhl is overseeing the largest personal injury litigation in the nation against the social media giants, encompassing 1,900 cases from 44 states, which has been consolidated into a Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding — the state equivalent of multidistrict litigation in federal court. Meanwhile, a massive MDL is playing out in the US Northern District of California before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who in November largely denied the social media companies’ motion to dismiss nuisance claims. Please e-mail editors@mlex.com to contact the editorial staff regarding this story, or to submit the names of lawyers and advisers. Related Portfolio(s): Data Privacy & Security - Meta - Google - TikTok - Litigation in California state court alleging Meta Platforms algorithms are defective, addictive product (US) Areas of Interest: Data Privacy & SecurityDownloaded on 16 Dec 2024 by maria.dinzeo@mlex.com Redistribution authorized in accordance with User Terms in the MLex General Terms of Business. appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move

forward.

Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California

appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward.

Meta Platform’s Facebook and Instagram, ByteDance’s TikTok, Google’s YouTube and Snap’s Snapchat petitioned the

appellate court last December, asking the judges to review Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn B. Kuhl’s October

2023 ruling that the companies aren't shielded by the First Amendment or Section 230 of the Communications Decency

Act, which provides online platforms immunity from liability over third-party content.

The plaintiffs, a group of individuals, school districts and local governments, claim Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube

and Snap are all designed to get young people addicted without regard for the deleterious consequences for kids’ mental

health. They’ve also used a unique tack to skirt Section 230 and First Amendment protections by alleging that social

media platforms are defectively designed products.

Kuhl reasoned that the platforms are not “products” in the product liability sense, but the plaintiffs nevertheless sufficiently

alleged that the companies were careless about the design of their algorithms. “Plaintiffs have adequately pled a cause of

action for negligence that is not barred by federal immunity or the First Amendment,” Kuhl wrote in her 89-page ruling

(see here).

In their petition (see here), the social media giants argued that Kuhl had violated the “core principles” of Section 230 and

the First Amendment as a means of immunizing platforms from protracted litigation, “not just from liability.”

California’s Second Appellate District rejected the petition in a two-sentence order last week, saying it had read and

considered the petition for writ of mandate and that “the petition is denied.”

The companies didn't respond to messages seeking comment on the brief order.

In a statement, Beasley Allen, which is representing the plaintiffs, said it was pleased with the most recent development in

the litigation, saying the appellate courts’ refusal to weight in puts the case “one step closer to trials seeking to hold the

tech giants liable for the mental physical harm suffered by youth as a result of social media addiction.”

Kuhl is overseeing the largest personal injury litigation in the nation against the social media giants, encompassing 1,900

cases from 44 states, which has been consolidated into a Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding — the state

equivalent of multidistrict litigation in federal court. Meanwhile, a massive MDL is playing out in the US Northern District of

California before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who in November largely denied the social media

companies’ motion to dismiss nuisance claims.

advisers.

article.title: Autonomy CEO Acquitted on All Counts in HP Fraud Trial
article.description: Mike Lynch has spent more than a decade defending the sale of his software startup Autonomy to HP. Now he’s been vindicated. A federal jury on Thursday found the British tech tycoon not guilty of 14 counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy…
article.text: Mike Lynch has spent more than a decade defending the sale of his software startup Autonomy to HP. Now he’s been vindicated. A federal jury on Thursday found the British tech tycoon not guilty of 14 counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy for padding the revenues of his software startup Autonomy ahead of its $11 billion sale to HP more than a decade ago. His co-defendant, former vice president of finance Stephen Chamberlain, was also acquitted on all counts.

article.text: ANALYSIS United States v. Napout The U.S. government’s lead role in the prosecution of corruption within the Zurich-based FIFA may be a paradigmatic example of U.S. law enforcement acting as the world’s policeman. article.title: 'Everyone Is Swamped': In-House Lawyers Hopeful Gen AI Will Help Them Come Up for Air
article.description: "Everyone is constantly telling us how buried they are and there's too much work to be done. And you're a cost center by nature, you can't deny it. So, your incentive is always to get more done, faster," said Mary O'Carroll, chief community officer…
article.text: "Everyone is constantly telling us how buried they are and there's too much work to be done. And you're a cost center by nature, you can't deny it. So, your incentive is always to get more done, faster," said Mary O'Carroll, chief community officer at Ironclad. For all the anxiety over generative AI’s uncertain legal implications—even its perceived threat to job security in the legal department—the technology making lawyers go mental may actually help their mental health. This apparent contradictory finding by contract management platform Ironclad, in its 2024 State of AI in Legal report, is predicated on AI’s potential to take over mundane and unsatisfying tasks contributing to lawyer burnout.
article.html:

article.title: Antitrust Regulators Poised to Pounce as AI Firms Jostle for Dominance
article.description: The Federal Trade Commission is concerned that AI's rise will further the dominance of existing tech giants. G7 authorities are expressing similar anxieties. While tech giants say they champion innovation, they have an incentive to maintain the…
article.text: The Federal Trade Commission is concerned that AI's rise will further the dominance of existing tech giants. G7 authorities are expressing similar anxieties. While tech giants say they champion innovation, they have an incentive to maintain the established order. Does AI have a competition problem? That’s what regulators are trying to figure out, and with growing urgency, as the technology advances at a stunning pace and fears mount about already-dominant digital giants entrenching their market power. At its first developer conference earlier this month, OpenAI—whose biggest backer is Microsoft—unveiled an update to ChatGPT whose new features for its paying users, like the ability to read PDFs, threaten to wipe out small startups that built their businesses around filling a gap in ChatGPT’s functionality.
article.html:
• The Federal Trade Commission is concerned that AI's rise will further the dominance of existing tech giants.
  • G7 authorities are expressing similar anxieties.
  • While tech giants say they champion innovation, they have an incentive to maintain the established order.

Does AI have a competition problem? That’s what regulators are trying to figure out, and with growing urgency, as the technology advances at a stunning pace and fears mount about already-dominant digital giants entrenching their market power.

At its first developer conference earlier this month, OpenAI—whose biggest backer is Microsoft—unveiled an update to ChatGPT whose new features for its paying users, like the ability to read PDFs, threaten to wipe out small startups that built their businesses around filling a gap in ChatGPT’s functionality.

article.title: Audubon Society Fills GC Slot After Longtime Legal Chief's Quiet Exit Amid Renaming Controversy
article.description: The nonprofit's rejection of a name change sparked the resignation of three directors, but it isn't clear whether it played a role in Sciarra's decision to depart. Sciarra had been legal chief for nearly 12 years. The organization has nearly 1,000…
article.text: The nonprofit's rejection of a name change sparked the resignation of three directors, but it isn't clear whether it played a role in Sciarra's decision to depart. Sciarra had been legal chief for nearly 12 years. The organization has nearly 1,000 employees and annual revenue of $150 million. Overshadowed by the resignations in March of three National Audubon Society directors after it rejected changing its name over concerns about racist views held by namesake John James Audubon was the departure that same month of longtime general counsel Lorraine Sciarra. The nonprofit didn’t announce Sciarra’s departure after nearly 12 years as legal chief, but it came to light Monday after Lochlin Partners, a recruiting firm that assisted the Audubon Society with its GC search, announced that veteran environmental attorney Charlotte Young had landed the role.

article.title: Charlie Rose Lawsuit Sees Several Major Claims Dismissed
article.description: A state appeals court has thrown out several major claims that a former head makeup artist who spent 22 years working for the Charlie Rose Show had leveled against the once-famed talk show host in a discrimination, harassment and labor lawsuit. Much…
article.text: A state appeals court has thrown out several major claims that a former head makeup artist who spent 22 years working for the Charlie Rose Show had leveled against the once-famed talk show host in a discrimination, harassment and labor lawsuit. Much of the former makeup artist’s 2019-filed suit, in which she details Rose allegedly “preying” on female staff for years at a TV studio described as a “sexual hunting ground,” is no longer alive. The makeup artist, Gina Riggi, previously withdrew age discrimination and retaliation claims, along with one of her state Labor Law claims, from the action, according to a lower-court ruling.

article.title: McKesson's Compliance Chief Joins Alphabet's Verily Life Sciences as GC
article.description: Laura O'Donnell succeeds Cynthia Patton, who left to become general counsel of Tessera Therapeutics. O'Donnell has a long resume in health care law and earlier was general counsel of GE Healthcare. Verily recently laid off workers and pared its…
article.text: Laura O'Donnell succeeds Cynthia Patton, who left to become general counsel of Tessera Therapeutics. O'Donnell has a long resume in health care law and earlier was general counsel of GE Healthcare. Verily recently laid off workers and pared its portfolio of projects, which once ranged from insurance to mosquito breeding. Verily Life Sciences, an Alphabet subsidiary that’s using artificial intelligence and data science to make a splash in precision medicine, hired drug distributor McKesson’s chief compliance officer as general counsel. Laura O’Donnell is coming aboard at a time of rapid-fire change for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company. Since last fall, Verily has made sweeping leadership changes, including the appointment of a new CEO, narrowed its focus, laid off 15% of its 1,600 employees and received a $1 billion infusion from Alphabet to fund its next phase of growth.

article.title: Beyond Borders: Navigating Global Business Compliance With the FCPA
article.description: On March 7, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a new whistleblower reward program intended to help prosecutors bring more foreign corruption cases. Under the new program, individuals who report corporate misconduct can earn a share of any…
article.text: On March 7, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a new whistleblower reward program intended to help prosecutors bring more foreign corruption cases. Under the new program, individuals who report corporate misconduct can earn a share of any resulting DOJ forfeiture. This comes on the heels of one of the world’s largest commodity trading firms agreeing to pay about $661 million after admitting to bribing Ecuadorean officials. These events reinforce anti-bribery and corruption laws as one of the significant compliance risks companies face in an increasingly competitive global marketplace.

article.description: The U.S. Supreme Court has turned to Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan partner Christopher Michel to defend an Oklahoma murder conviction—and death sentence—that the state’s own attorney general argues was tainted by prosecutorial misconduct. The…
article.text: The U.S. Supreme Court has turned to Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan partner Christopher Michel to defend an Oklahoma murder conviction—and death sentence—that the state’s own attorney general argues was tainted by prosecutorial misconduct. The high court on Friday announced Michel’s appointment as “amicus curiae,” Latin for “friend of the court,” to brief and argue for the state in Glossip v. Oklahoma. The case involves claims by condemned murdered Richard Glossip—who has spent the last quarter century on death row— that prosecutors withheld crucial evidence about the reliability of their star witness.

Recognizing the important role of an in-house attorney during a crisis, few organizations made cuts from their legal departments in the middle of the pandemic, according to the 2020 Law Department Compensation Policies and Practices Report published by the Association of Corporate Counsel and Empsight International on Thursday. Between 0.5 and 1.8% of respondents to the survey said they implemented a layoff because of the pandemic and only 0.6% to 4.3% of companies have implemented a furlough in the legal department, the report states.

NEWS

Meta Transfers AI-Related Patents to Midjourney to Thwart Patent Trolls

"Sharing these assets makes our ecosystem stronger by allowing other operating companies to acquire patents that they can use to protect their innovation," said Jeremiah Chan, Meta's head of patents, licensing and open source.

Maria Dinzeo

Meta has transferred three artificial intelligence-related patents to Midjourney, a research lab that uses generative AI to create images, a move the tech giant believes will bolster the startup’s intellectual property portfolio and spur more innovation in the AI space.

The move also helps Midjourney defend itself from so-called non-practicing entities, or NPEs, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits.

article.title: 'Patently Unreasonable': Twitter Blasts Vijaya Gadde's $1.1M Legal-Fee-Reimbursement Request
article.description: What You Need to Know Twitter is asking the court to slash the reimbursement to $109,203. Sidley Austin says the fees are completely justified, given the uncertainties surrounding the hearing, which focused on Twitter's decision to suppress a report…
article.text: What You Need to Know Twitter is asking the court to slash the reimbursement to $109,203. Sidley Austin says the fees are completely justified, given the uncertainties surrounding the hearing, which focused on Twitter's decision to suppress a report about Hunter Biden's laptop. The legal clash between Twitter and former legal chief Vijaya Gadde is heating up, with the company’s lawyers blasting her request to be reimbursed $1.1 million for legal fees she rung up preparing to testify before a U.S. House committee as “unreasonable in the extreme.” Gadde and two other former Twitter executives sued the San Francisco-based company in the Delaware Court of Chancery in April seeking reimbursement for legal fees they’d racked up on Twitter-related matters, including lawsuits and investigations, since Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the company in October and immediately fired them. What You Need to Know

  • Twitter is asking the court to slash the reimbursement to $109,203.
  • Sidley Austin says the fees are completely justified, given the uncertainties surrounding the hearing, which focused on Twitter's decision to suppress a report about Hunter Biden's laptop.

The legal clash between Twitter and former legal chief Vijaya Gadde is heating up, with the company’s lawyers blasting her request to be reimbursed $1.1 million for legal fees she rung up preparing to testify before a U.S. House committee as “unreasonable in the extreme.”

Gadde and two other former Twitter executives sued the San Francisco-based company in the Delaware Court of Chancery in April seeking reimbursement for legal fees they’d racked up on Twitter-related matters, including lawsuits and investigations, since Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the company in October and immediately fired them.

article.text: Eleven of the 20 highest-paid legal chiefs were from the tech industry. The average tech GC earned $6 million—25% more than the average financial services or entertainment GC. The nine-highest paid tech GCs all received at least 80% of their total pay in stock grants. Legal chiefs in tech vastly out-earned their counterparts in other industries in 2022, even though tech underwent a retrenching last year marked by tens of thousands of layoffs and plunging stock prices. Eleven of the 20 highest-paid general counsel were from tech companies, and the tech industry held the top four slots, according to Corporate Counsel and ALM Intelligence’s 2023 General Counsel Compensation Report, based on Securities and Exchange Commission pay disclosures of the Fortune 1000 for fiscal 2022.

article.title: 'Heavily Publicized and Scrutinized': Tech Leaders' Concerns Over Reputational Risks Soar
article.description: Reputational risks ranked as the fourth-biggest risk facing organizations. A year earlier, it ranked 10th. More than one-third of respondents said managing reputational risk will become more complex over the next three to five years. Reputational…
article.text: Reputational risks ranked as the fourth-biggest risk facing organizations. A year earlier, it ranked 10th. More than one-third of respondents said managing reputational risk will become more complex over the next three to five years. Reputational risk is rocketing up the list of major concerns for risk leaders, according to a new study by insurance broker Marsh. Eighty percent of respondents in the study, which surveyed 300 risk leaders at tech companies in 29 countries, said reputational risk had become something to worry about, and they ranked it as the fourth-biggest risk facing their organizations, beating other concerns such as regulatory compliance and supply chain disruption.

Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia have introduced AI-related legislation since ChatGPT debuted in November, Lawmakers want to protect their constituents while encouraging innovation. AI is capturing the attention of statehouses across the country. Lawmakers are racing to put up guardrails around the rapidly advancing technology, grappling with how to embrace its massive innovation potential while protecting their constituents from its harms. Carrie Schiff recently departed Sage Law, where she was founding partner, to become chief legal officer of Pax8. Pax8 simplifies the way organizations buy, sell and manage cloud solutions. She has more than three decades of legal experience. Pax8′s chief legal officer, Carrie Schiff, said the most rewarding part of her career is building teams and helping younger lawyers realize their dreams. article.title: Companies' Push to Attract Millennials Fueling Age-Discrimination Suits
article.description: "If companies want to avoid this trap, they should probably refrain from being explicit in looking for members of certain age demographics in general," said Michael North, an assistant professor at New York University. The EEOC and an Eli Lilly and…
article.text: "If companies want to avoid this trap, they should probably refrain from being explicit in looking for members of certain age demographics in general," said Michael North, an assistant professor at New York University. The EEOC and an Eli Lilly and Co. sales rep allege in lawsuits that the company illegally favored younger employees. PricewaterhouseCoopers settled an age discrimination suit in 2021 for $11.6 million. Former IBM workers who say they were fired in favor of younger workers may be nearing a settlement with the company. Diversity, equity and inclusion is all the rage in the corporate world. But seeking age diversity by appealing to a particular age group in hiring and promotions is proving to be a legal quagmire for some of the nation’s biggest companies. Pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly and Co. is the latest to see litigation mount, following an initiative it launched in 2017 to increase millennials in its workforce. The case comes as IBM continues to fight allegations by ex-workers who allege they were fired in favor of younger workers, and as PricewaterhouseCoopers licks its wounds from a 2021 settlement in an age discrimination suit that will cost it $11.6 million.
article.html:
"If companies want to avoid this trap, they should probably refrain from being explicit in looking for members of certain age demographics in general," said Michael North, an assistant professor at New York University.

article.title: 'I'm Aghast': Viral Paul Hastings Presentation Garners Strong In-House Reaction
article.description: A slide prepared by a senior Paul Hastings associate listing nonnegotiable expectations for junior colleagues touched a nerve in the legal community. Some in-house attorneys said it exposed a deep misunderstanding of what clients actually want. Some…
article.text: A slide prepared by a senior Paul Hastings associate listing nonnegotiable expectations for junior colleagues touched a nerve in the legal community. Some in-house attorneys said it exposed a deep misunderstanding of what clients actually want. Some called the expectations appalling; others said that young lawyers tend to be coddled and need reminding that the client comes first. A presentation by a senior Paul Hastings associate with a demanding list of “nonnegotiable expectations” for junior colleagues is sparking a broad range of reactions in the in-house community, from a shrug to outrage. The debate reverberated across social media in recent days, with the outcry on Twitter especially spirited. “Definite big time Glengarry Glen Ross energy coming through on this one,” one commenter tweeted. “Reason 6,540,329 I am so glad I had nothing to do with these firms,” said another. Others ridiculed the firm’s $850-per-hour rack rate for a junior associate.

article.title: The AI Revolution Is Here. Who Will Be the Winners and Losers in Legal Services?
article.description: Law firms, alternative legal service providers and legal tech companies are racing to attract in-house counsel dollars amid the generative AI explosion. AI promises to move a lot of previously outsourced work in-house, so firms will have to change…
article.text: Law firms, alternative legal service providers and legal tech companies are racing to attract in-house counsel dollars amid the generative AI explosion. AI promises to move a lot of previously outsourced work in-house, so firms will have to change out they provide services to clients. Some lawyers predict that AI will force firms to combine their specialized expertise and AI to solve the most complex client-specific problems. The explosion of generative AI has triggered endless speculation about the extent to which technology threatens the law firm business model. Empowered by the ability to automate more routine work, corporate legal departments could do more in-house and depend less on outside counsel. Legal teams would also have more choices, working directly with tech vendors to subscribe directly to AI tools that can help inform their decisions on everything from litigation strategy to changes in employment law.

article.title: Employers Try Novel Tactic to Blunt New Rules Lowering Hurdles to Unionizing
article.description: The Democrat-controlled National Labor Relations Board last August overhauled unionizing rules. The new process provides a path for workers to unionize without having to vote. Employers are trying to foreclose that possibility by petitioning for…
article.text: The Democrat-controlled National Labor Relations Board last August overhauled unionizing rules. The new process provides a path for workers to unionize without having to vote. Employers are trying to foreclose that possibility by petitioning for elections themselves. Employers are flooding the National Labor Relations Board with requests for union elections in the wake of an historic agency ruling last August that makes it far easier for worker unionizing efforts to succeed. While making the first move might leave the impression that employers are egging on unionizing efforts, in fact, the tactic is aimed at gaining a competitive advantage in hopes of blocking efforts to unionize, employment attorneys say.
article.html:
• The Democrat-controlled National Labor Relations Board last August overhauled unionizing rules.
  • The new process provides a path for workers to unionize without having to vote.
  • Employers are trying to foreclose that possibility by petitioning for elections themselves.

Employers are flooding the National Labor Relations Board with requests for union elections in the wake of an historic agency ruling last August that makes it far easier for worker unionizing efforts to succeed.

While making the first move might leave the impression that employers are egging on unionizing efforts, in fact, the tactic is aimed at gaining a competitive advantage in hopes of blocking efforts to unionize, employment attorneys say.

article.title: Creating a Roadmap to Success: Five Questions Every Change Champion Should Ask
article.description: Change management is a constant for corporate legal departments, as it is for everyone else in today’s rapidly changing business world. Companies are in a constant state of transformation, be it organic or as a function of structural changes such as…
article.text: Change management is a constant for corporate legal departments, as it is for everyone else in today’s rapidly changing business world. Companies are in a constant state of transformation, be it organic or as a function of structural changes such as a merger/acquisition/divestment, restructuring, leadership change, technology adoption, or evolving corporate priorities. Corporate legal departments are increasingly expected to manage these transitions in a way that is nimble, efficient, and aligned with the often-shifting strategic goals of the business. Legal departments face two primary challenges to intentional and sustainable organizational change. First, time and money are limited. Legal departments are increasingly asked to do more with less, and deliberate change management can divert already-limited resources to longer-term goals at the expense of short-term productivity.

article.title: NPR Attorney for Quarter-Century Takes Legal Reins of Public TV Advocacy Group
article.description: Michelle Shanahan has joined America's Public Television Stations as general counsel. When Shanahan left NPR last year, the board issued a resolution saying she'd played a pivotal role in the network's successful digital transformation. America's…
article.text: Michelle Shanahan has joined America's Public Television Stations as general counsel. When Shanahan left NPR last year, the board issued a resolution saying she'd played a pivotal role in the network's successful digital transformation. America's Public Television Stations represents the interests of public TV's 170 licensees, which operate more than 350 stations. Michelle Shanahan, a nonprofit attorney who spent a quarter century in senior roles at National Public Radio, has joined the advocacy organization America’s Public Television Stations as general counsel. Shanahan joined NPR in January 1997 as assistant general counsel. Through the years, she rose to associate general counsel, senior associate general counsel to deputy general counsel, the title she held when she departed the Washington, D.C.-based news and entertainment provider in February 2022. She also served a four-month stint as acting general counsel a year before she left.

article.title: Ex-Cognizant Legal Chief's Bribery Trial Delayed as DOJ Scrambles to Get Star Witness to Court
article.description: A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant President Gordon Coburn in 2019. Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building. A judge…
article.text: A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant President Gordon Coburn in 2019. Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building. A judge last week delayed their trial, which was to have started Monday. Prosecutors are facing a major hitch in their case against two former tech company executives accused of paying bribes in India: They can’t get their star witness into the country. The long-awaited trial of ex-Cognizant President Gordon Coburn and ex-chief legal officer Steven Schwartz over allegations that they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite the construction of an office building was scheduled to begin Monday in federal court for the District of New Jersey. But a key witness, former Cognizant vice president of administration Srimanikadan Ramamoorthy, is currently under investigation by Indian authorities over his role in the bribery scheme and had surrendered his passport.
article.html:
• A grand jury indicted ex-Cognizant chief legal officer Steven Schwartz along with ex-Cognizant President Gordon Coburn in 2019.
  • Investigators allege they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite construction of an office building.
  • A judge last week delayed their trial, which was to have started Monday.

Prosecutors are facing a major hitch in their case against two former tech company executives accused of paying bribes in India: They can’t get their star witness into the country.

The long-awaited trial of ex-Cognizant President Gordon Coburn and ex-chief legal officer Steven Schwartz over allegations that they bribed Indian officials $3.6 million to expedite the construction of an office building was scheduled to begin Monday in federal court for the District of New Jersey. But a key witness, former Cognizant vice president of administration Srimanikadan Ramamoorthy, is currently under investigation by Indian authorities over his role in the bribery scheme and had surrendered his passport.

article.title: How to Identify Bias in the Courtroom
article.description: In the age of the vanishing jury trial, “litigators” spend a small fraction of the time in the courtroom that their predecessors did in decades past. With so few jury trials, lawyers have become tone deaf to the nuances of bias that pervades trial…
article.text: In the age of the vanishing jury trial, “litigators” spend a small fraction of the time in the courtroom that their predecessors did in decades past. With so few jury trials, lawyers have become tone deaf to the nuances of bias that pervades trial practice. Some proponents of tort reform have argued against jury trials, as if some utopian policy could purge dispute resolution of all bias. Yet psychologists have identified many types of biases and as well as many other shortcuts people use in everyday decisions that trial lawyers should understand. For example, a landmark 1954 article, “They Saw A Game,” published in the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, addressed the emerging study of biases in its evaluation of wildly divergent opinions about who played dirty and who played clean in a football game. article.title: Former Pfizer Lawyer, Blue Buffalo GC Takes Legal Reins at Bioweapon Fighting Pharma Company
article.description: SIGA Technologies has a new general counsel in Larry Miller, former GC at Blue Buffalo. Miller previously led negotiations for Blue Buffalo's $8 billion sale to General Mills. He was also a senior corporate counsel at Pfizer, where he headed legal…
article.text: SIGA Technologies has a new general counsel in Larry Miller, former GC at Blue Buffalo. Miller previously led negotiations for Blue Buffalo's $8 billion sale to General Mills. He was also a senior corporate counsel at Pfizer, where he headed legal for two critical business units. Larry Miller, a former senior in-house attorney at Pfizer and general counsel of Blue Buffalo, has been tapped to lead the legal department at SIGA Technologies, a pharmaceutical company best known for its smallpox drug Tpoxx. Miller’s in-house experience is almost entirely in pharmaceuticals and biotech, aside from the three years he spent at Blue Buffalo, where he led negotiations and due diligence on its $8 billion sale to General Mills in 2018.

article.title: 'We're Seeing the Floodgates Open': EEOC's Flip to Democratic Control Already Turbocharging Agency
article.description: "We sometimes hear employers sort of downplay the concern with the EEOC, believing they're going to slip under the agency's radar. But it's important to remember that where the EEOC leads, the private plaintiffs bar follows," Seyfarth Shaw partner…
article.text: "We sometimes hear employers sort of downplay the concern with the EEOC, believing they're going to slip under the agency's radar. But it's important to remember that where the EEOC leads, the private plaintiffs bar follows," Seyfarth Shaw partner Christopher DeGroff said. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s flip to Democratic control at the tail end of fiscal 2023 sets the table for the agency to further ratchet up litigation and investigations this year. That’s the take of attorneys at Seyfarth Shaw, which has just released its annual “EEOC-Initiated Litigation” report. The law firm notes the Senate’s July 14 confirmation of Kalpana Kotagal as an EEOC commissioner was a watershed moment because it flipped the commission to Democratic control for the first time since President Joe Biden, a champion of pro-labor policies, took office in 2021.

article.title: Juul Lawyer's Suit Buttresses Concerns Pregnancy Discrimination Lives On, Just in Subtler Ways
article.description: Elizabeth Johannessen was senior corporate compliance director at Juul before the company laid her off in May 2020. Johannessen says she was marginalized after returning from a four-week maternity leave in September 2019. The company and its law firm…
article.text: Elizabeth Johannessen was senior corporate compliance director at Juul before the company laid her off in May 2020. Johannessen says she was marginalized after returning from a four-week maternity leave in September 2019. The company and its law firm did not respond to requests for comment. A former Juul in-house lawyer charges in a lawsuit that after she returned from maternity leave the e-cigarette company took a series of small steps that added up to a substantial reduction in her authority before finally laying her off in May 2020. The allegations in Elizabeth Johannessen’s pregnancy-discrimination suit closely align with what legal observers and attorneys who bring such cases say they’re seeing in the trenches: While the days of supervisors making blatantly discriminatory statements or taking overt steps to derail careers may be largely over, pregnancy discrimination is still a serious problem and remains remarkably common.

article.title: All Eyes on Pennsylvania After Texas Court's Limited Injunction Against FTC Noncompete Ban
article.description: A first-in-nation ruling in Texas federal court casts serious doubt on the enforceability of the broad-reaching new Federal Trade Commission (FTC) noncompete rule. For any company seeking to legitimately protect its hard-earned competitive position,…
article.text: A first-in-nation ruling in Texas federal court casts serious doubt on the enforceability of the broad-reaching new Federal Trade Commission (FTC) noncompete rule. For any company seeking to legitimately protect its hard-earned competitive position, this opinion and the FTC’s rule must be considered and understood. While the Texas decision was limited to the parties before that court, the reasoning is important in predicting whether the FTC’s noncompete rule is likely to go into effect, and all companies need to be constantly reevaluating how they are protecting their corporate secrets. On April 23, 2024, the FTC issued its noncompete rule, a rule that largely banned worker noncompete agreements with limited exceptions, based on the FTC’s position that nearly all noncompetition agreements constitute an “unfair method of competition” under Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. Section 45(a). The FTC estimated that, upon the noncompete rule’s planned effective date of Sept. 4, 2024, the rule would invalidate 30 million contracts. Baker Donelson’s attorneys initially covered the decision and its significance for employers shortly after it was issued.
