article.title: The Strategy Behind a $525M Patent Infringement Verdict Against Amazon Web Services
article.description: “In massive, high-stakes litigation, it’s really, really difficult to try cases [against] somebody like Amazon who’s got, for all intents and purposes, unlimited resources,” said the plaintiff’s counsel, Courtland Reichman, noting his team put more…
article.text: “In massive, high-stakes litigation, it’s really, really difficult to try cases [against] somebody like Amazon who’s got, for all intents and purposes, unlimited resources,” said the plaintiff’s counsel, Courtland Reichman, noting his team put more than 30,000 hours into the suit. A computer storage and data management company sued Amazon Web Services for infringing on three patents in 2018. It argued that AWS was able to grow to prominence because of the technology, ultimately generating $1.03 billion as a result. While the jury didn't find the infringement was willful, it awarded the jury $525 million in compensation. Reichman Jorgensen Lehman & Feldberg recently secured a $525 million patent infringement verdict for small tech company Kove IO against Amazon Web Services in a case out of the Northern District of Illinois. Though Amazon’s counsel declined to comment on the record, a spokesperson for the company told CBS News, the defense plans to appeal.

article.text: Who are the lead rainmakers of M&A in Big Law? A look at the top law firm partners based on the value of their deals shows the typical crowd of New York elites—along with a couple others who have edged out competitors in recent years to enter the top tier of M&A work. Mergerlinks, a financial data provider, generated the rankings based on total deal value of the deals they led. With the caveat that those who drive a deal are known really only to the deal teams, there are seven different dealmaker firms on the chart, with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz taking three of those spots and Sullivan & Cromwell taking two.

article.title: How a Few Business Basics Can Heal Legal Department-Law Firm Relationships
article.description: "The challenge with a lot of legal-ops departments is they are populated by lawyers who are intimidated by external counsel. So it's hard to step away and actually put a real business lens on it," said Bindu Cudjoe, chief legal officer of Laurentian…
article.text: "The challenge with a lot of legal-ops departments is they are populated by lawyers who are intimidated by external counsel. So it's hard to step away and actually put a real business lens on it," said Bindu Cudjoe, chief legal officer of Laurentian Bank. Michael Lordi, head of law department operators at Equitable, said working with law firms has gotten a lot easier. He remembers when his efforts to take advantage of tech tools to boost efficiency drew responses like, “I hate this. Don’t ever say this to me. Or we’ve always done it that way.” Lordi would reply, “It’s better for both of us. It’s not just a benefit to me; it’s going to be a benefit to you.”
article.html:
"The challenge with a lot of legal-ops departments is they are populated by lawyers who are intimidated by external counsel. So it's hard to step away and actually put a real business lens on it," said Bindu Cudjoe, chief legal officer of Laurentian Bank.

Michael Lordi, head of law department operators at Equitable, said working with law firms has gotten a lot easier. He remembers when his efforts to take advantage of tech tools to boost efficiency drew responses like, “I hate this. Don’t ever say this to me. Or we’ve always done it that way.”

Lordi would reply, “It’s better for both of us. It’s not just a benefit to me; it’s going to be a benefit to you.”

TikTok General Counsel Stepping Down to Focus on Fighting Ban

Erich Andersen had held the legal reins of the wildly popular social media app for four years. He previously spent more than two decades at Microsoft.

General Counsel and In House Counsel

Maria Dinzeo

Embattled social media platform TikTok said Friday that General Counsel Erich Andersen has stepped down to focus on the company’s fight against a new federal law that will ban the app in the United States if its Chinese owner doesn’t sell its stake within a year.

Andersen, who is based in the United States and is a former deputy general counsel at Microsoft, said in a statement that it was a “difficult decision” to step down from a role he’s held for four years.

article.text: "The more you procrastinate, the more you're hesitant, the bigger the opportunity cost of not essentially moving the needle,” said Murtuza Vohra, managing director of legal consulting firm Morae Global. By now, every in-house lawyer has heard the persistent buzz around generative AI’s potential to deliver unprecedented efficiency for overworked legal teams bogged down in mundane and repetitive work. Along with saving time and money, AI also promises to give companies a sustainable competitive edge. But how exactly can it do that? Samir Raiyani, co-founder and CEO of IP market research firm Dolcera, said clients are quickly figuring it out, finding real uses and realizing actual returns.

article.title: Former Uber Security Chief Joe Sullivan Avoids Prison Time
article.description: Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan was sentenced to three years of probation for obstruction justice and covering up a felony after a 2016 data breach U.S. District Judge William Orrick said the case was not a typical white collar crime case,…
article.text: Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan was sentenced to three years of probation for obstruction justice and covering up a felony after a 2016 data breach U.S. District Judge William Orrick said the case was not a typical white collar crime case, as it did not involve money or greed. Sullivan said he hopes his case will help other security chiefs gather the courage to speak up to the C-suite. Former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan will serve three months of probation for concealing a 2016 data breach from authorities and obstructing a regulator’s investigation into Uber’s security practices, bringing an end to a novel criminal case that has rattled the security industry. “I hope everyone in the CISO community takes this as a lesson, and not leniency,” said U.S. District Judge William Orrick Thursday afternoon in San Francisco. article.title: When Politics and Employment Mix: What Speech Is Protected at Work?
article.description: It is well known that the law protects employees from harassment and discrimination based on race, gender, age, and disability, among other protected statuses. But what about political opinions? The extent to which federal and state law give…
article.text: It is well known that the law protects employees from harassment and discrimination based on race, gender, age, and disability, among other protected statuses. But what about political opinions? The extent to which federal and state law give employees a right to engage in political activity is less well known. Below are some broad legal principles for employers to keep in mind as the election approaches and comments about cultural, social and religious topics take on a political hue. Public Employers and the First Amendment Public employers are subject to the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which means public employees have free speech rights.

article.title: California DOJ Fines Robinhood $3.9M in First-Ever Crypto Enforcement Action
article.description: The California Department of Justice said it has slapped Robinhood with a $3.9 million penalty after finding that the crypto and stock trading platform did not allow customers access to the cryptocurrency in their wallets, misled customers about the…
article.text: The California Department of Justice said it has slapped Robinhood with a $3.9 million penalty after finding that the crypto and stock trading platform did not allow customers access to the cryptocurrency in their wallets, misled customers about the best crypto trade rates, and was not transparent about who held their assets. The settlement marks the first public enforcement action by the state DOJ against a crypto company.
article.html:
The California Department of Justice said it has slapped Robinhood with a $3.9 million penalty after finding that the crypto and stock trading platform did not allow customers access to the cryptocurrency in their wallets, misled customers about the best crypto trade rates, and was not transparent about who held their assets.

The settlement marks the first public enforcement action by the state DOJ against a crypto company.

article.title: 'It Was a Bunch of Spooked Wildebeests': How Tech GCs Survived the SVB Panic
article.description: Tech GCs realized pulling money from troubled banks exacerbated those institutions' troubles, but they concluded they had to put their own companies first. The fact startups were worried whether they could make payroll suggests they need to rethink…
article.text: Tech GCs realized pulling money from troubled banks exacerbated those institutions' troubles, but they concluded they had to put their own companies first. The fact startups were worried whether they could make payroll suggests they need to rethink their capital-management strategies. Going forward, startups are less likely to let their VC funders decide where they bank. Silicon Valley Bank’s astonishingly rapid meltdown tested tech’s top in-house lawyers, who flew into emergency response mode to help steer their companies through the chaos. Greg Raiten, co-founder of the general counsel network and platform TechGC, said the upheaval wrought by SVB’s collapse within the tech in-house community was on par only with the COVID-19 pandemic. Greg Raiten, co-founder of the general counsel network and platform TechGC, said the upheaval wrought by SVB’s collapse within the tech in-house community was on par only with the COVID-19 pandemic.

article.title: 'I'd Wake Up and Put on That Face': Former General Counsel Shares Story of Mental Health Battle and Recovery
article.description: Tara Trantham is a former legal and compliance chief based in South Carolina. Trantham spent years trying to hide her struggles with anxiety and depression. Now, she's sharing her story to empower others to speak up and seek help. Tara Trantham was…
article.text: Tara Trantham is a former legal and compliance chief based in South Carolina. Trantham spent years trying to hide her struggles with anxiety and depression. Now, she's sharing her story to empower others to speak up and seek help. Tara Trantham was driving home after attending her 11-year-old son’s football game, a cheer bow still in her hair, when she looked up and saw flashing blue lights in the rearview mirror. Her son had gone home with his grandparents, which was good—he’d be spared the sight of his mom getting arrested. She says the officer bent her over the hood of his cruiser, handcuffed her and took her to jail, where she remained for nearly 30 hours last August. The experience threw Trantham into what she now describes as a rapid “downward spiral” that ended with her finally peeling away the mask she’d spent years constructing to hide her mental health struggles from colleagues, friends and family.

But the prevalence of counterfeit cosmetics has increased significantly over the past few years, ranking in the top 10 of fake items imported into the United States in fiscal year 2017. Evan Feldstein, vice general manager and general counsel at FOREO North America, attributes the increase to a growing luxury beauty product market, citing as examples skin serums that cost more than $100 and FOREO facial devices that can run up to $200.

article.text: VerdictSearch strives to report as many jury verdicts, decisions and settlements as possible. Although a great many cases are submitted by attorneys, we also rely on a diligent team of assignment editors who scour docket lists, cultivate relationships with law firms, and search the internet and news sources, including the ALM family of legal publications. Our exhaustive efforts allow us to present what we believe is a comprehensive list of the top 100 jury awards of 2023. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologize to anyone whose case may have been inadvertently omitted. The Top 100 verdicts are ranked by gross award calculated by the jury. They do not reflect reductions for comparative negligence or assignment of fault to settling defendants or nonparties; additurs, remittiturs or reversals; or attorney fees and costs, unless awarded by the jury. In cases in which awards were automatically doubled or trebled by statute, the doubled or trebled amount determined rank. We do not consider cases in which the jury only determined per-plaintiff or per-year damages that a judge later used to calculate the gross award, cases in which the jury’s instructions permitted it to determine damages against a party that it had already deemed not liable, or cases in which a jury awarded damages against one or more parties while one or more other parties awaited trial in the same matter. The editors retain sole discretion to make adjustments in rank when necessary to reflect statutes that provide for election of remedies or other types of overlapping awards. You Might Like

article.title: Challenges to Noncompete Ban Already Hitting Courts, Setting Up Showdown Over FTC's Powers
article.description: The first legal challenges to the Federal Trade Commission’s nationwide ban on noncompetes are flooding in from business groups claiming the commission overstepped its authority on Tuesday by approving the new regulation. The U.S. Chamber of…
article.text: The first legal challenges to the Federal Trade Commission’s nationwide ban on noncompetes are flooding in from business groups claiming the commission overstepped its authority on Tuesday by approving the new regulation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, which was promising to challenge the restriction even before the commission’s 3-2 vote approving it, filed the first lawsuit in the Eastern District of Texas, followed closely by the tax services firm Ryan LLC in the Northern District. The chamber was joined in its lawsuit by Business Roundtable, which is an association of CEOs from many of the nation’s largest companies, and the Texas Association of Business.

article.title: Is Your Company’s NDA Up to Date With Robust IP Provisions?
article.description: Companies routinely work together, signing stock non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) before collaboration. One challenge is that most company employees just assume that the stock NDA will cover all subsequent activities during such collaboration. But…
article.text: Companies routinely work together, signing stock non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) before collaboration. One challenge is that most company employees just assume that the stock NDA will cover all subsequent activities during such collaboration. But stock NDAs seldom include robust provisions that address common intellectual property (IP) issues that arise from intercompany collaboration. For example, who owns the IP resulting from the collaboration (new IP)? If your company’s or your client’s NDA does not answer that question or address any of the other following common IP questions, it may be time to update that NDA. Why Do Robust NDAs Matter?
article.html:

If your company’s or your client’s NDA does not answer that question or address any of the other following common IP questions, it may be time to update that NDA.

article.title: Finding Contributor-Level Work as a Truly Senior Counsel
article.description: I have addressed the topic of age discrimination a few times in this space, usually in the context of displaced (via M&A activity, RIF, or incentivized early retirement) in-house counsel who struggle over age 60 to find traditional direct hire…
article.text: I have addressed the topic of age discrimination a few times in this space, usually in the context of displaced (via M&A activity, RIF, or incentivized early retirement) in-house counsel who struggle over age 60 to find traditional direct hire positions. Former general counsels find it particularly difficult to land contributor level roles, such as Senior Counsel, where they are viewed as overqualified. I do understand when a company rejects a candidate over this concern. This topic often feels personal to me, as I get many calls from older attorneys who have been good to me, either as former client contacts or as candidates placed into positions by my search firm. I want to help, but often that is limited to advice and counsel. And I know that falls short of what the person really wants, which is to be presented for an opening.
article.html:
I have addressed the topic of age discrimination a few times in this space, usually in the context of displaced (via M&A activity, RIF, or incentivized early retirement) in-house counsel who struggle over age 60 to find traditional direct hire positions.  Former general counsels find it particularly difficult to land contributor level roles, such as Senior Counsel, where they are viewed as overqualified.  I do understand when a company rejects a candidate over this concern.

This topic often feels personal to me, as I get many calls from older attorneys who have been good to me, either as former client contacts or as candidates placed into positions by my search firm.  I want to help, but often that is limited to advice and counsel.  And I know that falls short of what the person really wants, which is to be presented for an opening.

article.description: The suit comes just as an assortment of free or inexpensive online tools is launched online to help users generate images of people, including some that offer to "nudify" subjects. Clothes Off is available for Apple and Android apps but its website…
article.text: The suit comes just as an assortment of free or inexpensive online tools is launched online to help users generate images of people, including some that offer to "nudify" subjects. Clothes Off is available for Apple and Android apps but its website gives no indication where the company is located or who owns it. A new suit in federal court in New Jersey will test the waters for obtaining compensation for victims of “deepfake” pornography generated by artificial intelligence. A 15-year-old girl says in the suit that a high school classmate used an AI application to create and distribute nonconsensual nude images of her. The girl, identified as Jane Doe, is a high school student from Westfield. Around last August she accepted an Instagram friend request from a male classmate, who then downloaded a fully clothed photo of the girl that he used to generate those images, according to the suit.

article.title: The Future of Partner Compensation: How Profit-Sharing Systems Shape the Firm’s Culture and Success
article.description: The likes of Paul Weiss and Linklaters have to decide on a remuneration system that reflects their culture and strategic objectives. It has been reported that Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison has moved to a ‘black box’ style profit sharing…
article.text: The likes of Paul Weiss and Linklaters have to decide on a remuneration system that reflects their culture and strategic objectives. It has been reported that Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison has moved to a ‘black box’ style profit sharing system. A black box system allows the firm to allocate profits between partners confidentially. In short, no-one knows what anyone else is being paid. In many ways, the appeal is obvious. A black box approach addresses the inevitable comparisons that partners draw between themselves. These comparisons can be divisive and distract from client service. In the case of lateral hires, who are often rewarded handsomely at the outset to lure them from their previous firm, comparisons can impede their effective integration into the firm.

article.title: CrowdStrike Glitch Highlights Risk of Single Point of Failure in Cybersecurity
article.description: The recent IT outage caused by a bug in CrowdStrike’s software has highlighted the risks associated with too much market concentration.The cybersecurity market is heavily dominated by a few key players, with CrowdStrike and Microsoft holding…
article.text: The recent IT outage caused by a bug in CrowdStrike’s software has highlighted the risks associated with too much market concentration.The cybersecurity market is heavily dominated by a few key players, with CrowdStrike and Microsoft holding significant shares.In response to the outage, lawmakers and the Federal Trade Commission are scrutinizing the cybersecurity market's concentration and its implications for critical infrastructure. Competition regulators have been on high alert for risks posed by too much market concentration, where a single point of failure can disrupt business worldwide. A cascading information technology outage that recently grounded hundreds of flights, upended health care and halted banking across the globe has been no exception. The recent outage was triggered by a bug in a routine update to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike’s flagship software Falcon, resulting in a “blue screen of death” across thousands of enterprise computer systems running on Microsoft Windows. Even though CrowdStrike had issued a fix within hours, some companies took days to recover. Lawmakers immediately pounced, calling on CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz to testify before a House Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure. “Protecting our critical infrastructure requires us to learn from this incident and ensure that it does not happen again,” said a letter from Reps. Mark Green, R-Tennessee, and Andrew Gabarino, R-New York. The outage also drew the attention of the Federal Trade Commission, which lately has taken a keen interest in how competition issues across layers of the technology stack can cause resiliency problems that wreak widescale havoc. “All too often these days, a single glitch results in a system-wide outage, affecting industries from healthcare and airlines to banks and auto-dealers. Millions of people and businesses pay the price. These incidents reveal how concentration can create fragile systems,” FTC Chair Lina Khan posted on X shortly after the outage. Meanwhile, competition and cyber experts are wondering what to make of the debacle, and whether the market for threat detection software has become too heavily concentrated in a few dominant players. “If the market doesn’t have competition, then essentially what you find is that one standard, one dominant way of doing it kind of emerges. And that’s exactly what you’re seeing with CrowdStrike,” said Ramnath Chellappa, a professor of information systems and operations management at Emory University’s Goizueta Business School. He said CrowdStrike, which works on the cloud and on-prem, has become an industry standard for remote and local monitoring of computer systems throughout a company. “CrowdStrike has just become a nice way to put a little sensor on every single machine and monitor that nobody’s changing anything. Basically, they almost become like a monopoly when it comes to thinking about what is a good way to address these things,” he said. Microsoft Blames European Competition Regulator for Meltdown Chellappa explained that CrowdStrike’s Falcon runs at the deepest level of the Windows operating system, the kernel, which gives it privileged access to the system’s core functions and memory. This should allow Falcon to provide stronger protection because it can more closely monitor system activities and intercept threats before they can cause harm. But it also means that an entire system can be brought down if one little thing goes wrong. Chellappa said this unique level of access also means that while Microsoft computers crashed, Macs were unaffected. “Apple is very tight with its ecosystem,” he said. Microsoft has said that it’s not allowed to wall off Windows the way Apple has because it agreed to give third-party developers greater access to its operating system under a 2009 agreement with the European Union. “Microsoft is saying that it cannot legally implement the same protections as Apple, simply because it’s opened it up so much,” Chellappa said. He noted that the outage also didn’t affect computers that run on Linux, which has a completely open operating system. However, he said that could be because most companies don’t use Linux. Ironically, the EU agreement designed to promote competition may have caused a bigger problem, said Anant Raut, Meta’s former director of global competition policy and a public adviser to the National Institute of Standards and Technology. “If it exposed Microsoft Windows at a more dangerous level that would be an argument against mandated interoperability.” CrowdStrike Dominates in the Cybersecurity Services Market CrowdStrike is a behemoth in the cybersecurity world. It ranks second after Microsoft in market share for endpoint protection platform services, with 14.74% share of the market and about $2 billion in sales last year, according to Gartner, a technological research and consulting firm based in Stamford, Connecticut. Microsoft’s share was about 40% in that market. Trellix is CrowdStrike’s next largest competitor with a 6.6% market share in 2023, down from 7.9% in 2022. In addition, Trend Micro has a 3.9% share, down from 4.2%, and Sophos’ market share remains at 3.7%. CrowdStrike also had 18% of the market share for endpoint security suites in 2023, according to data provided by IDC, followed by Trellix and Broadcom each with 5.8% and Sophos with 4.5%. Microsoft had the largest share at 25%. Cybersecurity market concentration may not be a bad thing, so long as major players don’t grow too stagnant. “While competition is a good thing and keeps people on their toes. On the flip side, you could argue that because of the sheer resources and ultimate survivability of these companies, they can actually do a better job, even if they are a big concentrated dominant player, because they have to, because of who they are. But do they get so big and so concentrated that they can take a more lackadaisical approach to things because they could rest on the notion that nobody has a choice, they have to use us?” said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio. Kannry said there has been a lot of consolidation in the cybersecurity industry over the past 12 to 24 months. “Candidly, I think there will be more because it’s a necessity. The cybersecurity market is so overcharged. You have dozens and dozens of companies in similar categories and there’s a lot of lemons out there. Market consolidation can be helpful towards that problem, and then you go too far and the dynamic we talked about takes hold.” CrowdStrike says 82% of state governments and 48% of the 50 largest cities in the U.S. have purchased its products. It also works with half the Fortune 500, about 25% of which were disrupted by the outage, according to a report on the incident from cloud monitoring and insurance firm Parametrix, which estimated financial losses of about $5.4 billion. CrowdStrike, which said 97% of its Windows sensors are back up and running as of late last week, told Law.com, “We compete every day in a highly competitive and fragmented market by proving to our customers why our industry-leading cyber protection services are effective.” Raut said the outage was most striking because of how far-reaching it was. “Perhaps if there was more competition, the outage wouldn’t have affected this many companies,” he said. “If there were a more robust market for cybersecurity services, you wouldn’t have these entire industries going down. In theory, it would avoid this level of catastrophe.” Resiliency concerns have also prompted the FTC to probe the cybersecurity implications of concentration in the market for cloud services, which is currently dominated by a handful of big tech firms. But Raut said he doesn’t see the CrowdStrike outage as an indication of a major competition issue yet. “This is such a one-off accidental buggy thing that I don’t know if it’s indicative of CrowdStrike being this terrible monopolist,” he said. “It comes down to how are they getting this concentration and are they engaging in behavior that is stifling competition? Cloud is different because there are high capital requirements and it’s hard to be a new entrant in the market. You have to come from a position of strength, whereas CrowdStrike is more like an application and barriers to entry should be low.” Still, Kannry said the outage should serve as a warning for cybersecurity teams not to rely on a single vendor. “The lesson is just don’t get comfortable with putting your eggs in the smallest amount of baskets possible,” he said. “Don’t just go with the 800-pound gorilla. Think hard about it.”
article.html:
• The recent IT outage caused by a bug in CrowdStrike’s software has highlighted the risks associated with too much market concentration.
  • The cybersecurity market is heavily dominated by a few key players, with CrowdStrike and Microsoft holding significant shares.
  • In response to the outage, lawmakers and the Federal Trade Commission are scrutinizing the cybersecurity market's concentration and its implications for critical infrastructure.

Millions of people and businesses pay the price. These incidents reveal how concentration can create fragile systems,” FTC Chair Lina Khan posted on X shortly after the outage.

Meanwhile, competition and cyber experts are wondering what to make of the debacle, and whether the market for threat detection software has become too heavily concentrated in a few dominant players.

“If the market doesn’t have competition, then essentially what you find is that one standard, one dominant way of doing it kind of emerges. And that’s exactly what you’re seeing with CrowdStrike,” said Ramnath Chellappa, a professor of information systems and operations management at Emory University’s Goizueta Business School.

He said CrowdStrike, which works on the cloud and on-prem, has become an industry standard for remote and local monitoring of computer systems throughout a company. “CrowdStrike has just become a nice way to put a little sensor on every single machine and monitor that nobody’s changing anything. Basically, they almost become like a monopoly when it comes to thinking about what is a good way to address these things,” he said.

Microsoft Blames European Competition Regulator for Meltdown

Chellappa explained that CrowdStrike’s Falcon runs at the deepest level of the Windows operating system, the kernel, which gives it privileged access to the system’s core functions and memory. This should allow Falcon to provide stronger protection because it can more closely monitor system activities and intercept threats before they can cause harm. But it also means that an entire system can be brought down if one little thing goes wrong.

Chellappa said this unique level of access also means that while Microsoft computers crashed, Macs were unaffected. “Apple is very tight with its ecosystem,” he said.

Microsoft has said that it’s not allowed to wall off Windows the way Apple has because it agreed to give third-party developers greater access to its operating system under a 2009 agreement with the European Union. “Microsoft is saying that it cannot legally implement the same protections as Apple, simply because it’s opened it up so much,” Chellappa said. He noted that the outage also didn’t affect computers that run on Linux, which has a completely open operating system. However, he said that could be because most companies don’t use Linux.

Ironically, the EU agreement designed to promote competition may have caused a bigger problem, said Anant Raut, Meta’s former director of global competition policy and a public adviser to the National Institute of Standards and Technology. “If it exposed Microsoft Windows at a more dangerous level that would be an argument against mandated interoperability.”

CrowdStrike Dominates in the Cybersecurity Services Market

CrowdStrike is a behemoth in the cybersecurity world. It ranks second after Microsoft in market share for endpoint protection platform services, with 14.74% share of the market and about $2 billion in sales last year, according to Gartner, a technological research and consulting firm based in Stamford, Connecticut.

Microsoft’s share was about 40% in that market. Trellix is CrowdStrike’s next largest competitor with a 6.6% market share in 2023, down from 7.9% in 2022. In addition, Trend Micro has a 3.9% share, down from 4.2%, and Sophos’ market share remains at 3.7%.

CrowdStrike also had 18% of the market share for endpoint security suites in 2023, according to data provided by IDC, followed by Trellix and Broadcom each with 5.8% and Sophos with 4.5%. Microsoft had the largest share at 25%.

Cybersecurity market concentration may not be a bad thing, so long as major players don’t grow too stagnant.

“While competition is a good thing and keeps people on their toes. On the flip side, you could argue that because of the sheer resources and ultimate survivability of these companies, they can actually do a better job, even if they are a big concentrated dominant player, because they have to, because of who they are. But do they get so big and so concentrated that they can take a more lackadaisical approach to things because they could rest on the notion that nobody has a choice, they have to use us?” said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio.

Kannry said there has been a lot of consolidation in the cybersecurity industry over the past 12 to 24 months. “Candidly, I think there will be more because it’s a necessity. The cybersecurity market is so overcharged. You have dozens and dozens of companies in similar categories and there’s a lot of lemons out there. Market consolidation can be helpful towards that problem, and then you go too far and the dynamic we talked about takes hold.”

CrowdStrike says 82% of state governments and 48% of the 50 largest cities in the U.S. have purchased its products. It also works with half the Fortune 500, about 25% of which were disrupted by the outage, according to a report on the incident from cloud monitoring and insurance firm Parametrix, which estimated financial losses of about $5.4 billion.

CrowdStrike, which said 97% of its Windows sensors are back up and running as of late last week, told Law.com, “We compete every day in a highly competitive and fragmented market by proving to our customers why our industry-leading cyber protection services are effective.”

Raut said the outage was most striking because of how far-reaching it was. “Perhaps if there was more competition, the outage wouldn’t have affected this many companies,” he said. “If there were a more robust market for cybersecurity services, you wouldn’t have these entire industries going down. In theory, it would avoid this level of catastrophe.”

Resiliency concerns have also prompted the FTC to probe the cybersecurity implications of concentration in the market for cloud services, which is currently dominated by a handful of big tech firms.

But Raut said he doesn’t see the CrowdStrike outage as an indication of a major competition issue yet. “This is such a one-off accidental buggy thing that I don’t know if it’s indicative of CrowdStrike being this terrible monopolist,” he said. “It comes down to how are they getting this concentration and are they engaging in behavior that is stifling competition? Cloud is different because there are high capital requirements and it’s hard to be a new entrant in the market. You have to come from a position of strength, whereas CrowdStrike is more like an application and barriers to entry should be low.”

Still, Kannry said the outage should serve as a warning for cybersecurity teams not to rely on a single vendor. “The lesson is just don’t get comfortable with putting your eggs in the smallest amount of baskets possible,” he said. “Don’t just go with the 800-pound gorilla. Think hard about it.”

article.title: $14M Severance Eases Activision Blizzard Legal Chief's Exit
article.description: Dixton is among a slate of Activision executives set to depart at the end of March. Before taking the post, he was general counsel of Boeing and assistant counsel to President George W. Bush. Dixton helped usher the Microsoft deal to completion and…
article.text: Dixton is among a slate of Activision executives set to depart at the end of March. Before taking the post, he was general counsel of Boeing and assistant counsel to President George W. Bush. Dixton helped usher the Microsoft deal to completion and manage the legal fallout from allegations Activision fostered a frat boy culture. A $14.2 million golden parachute awaits Activision Blizzard chief legal officer Grant Dixton when he steps aside at the end of March in the wake of the video game maker’s $69 billion sale to Microsoft. Dixton’s compensation last year totaled $5.5 million, according to Activision Blizzard’s latest proxy statement, which also lays out details of his severance package in the event of his departure “following a change of control of the company involving Microsoft.” His employment contract already was set to expire on June 30.

article.title: What Executives Should Take From Ex-Uber Security Chief Joe Sullivan's Sentence
article.description: Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan was spared prison time by a federal judge for concealing a 2016 data breach. Legal observers say Sullivan might have received a harsher sentence had he not been the first security chief to be held criminally…
article.text: Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan was spared prison time by a federal judge for concealing a 2016 data breach. Legal observers say Sullivan might have received a harsher sentence had he not been the first security chief to be held criminally liable. Cyberattacks continue to grow in frequency and sophistication, which suggests more security chiefs will face difficult disclosure decisions. Even as he spared ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan a prison sentence for concealing a massive data breach from authorities, a federal judge last week delivered a stern warning to the security industry. “If I had a similar case tomorrow, even if the defendant had the character of Pope Francis, they would be in custody,” U.S. District Judge William Orrick said. article.title: Microsoft Deepens Commitment to Unions Amid Workers' AI Anxiety
article.description: Artificial intelligence will change many people’s jobs, but unionized workers will have a voice in how the technology develops, Microsoft President Brad Smith said Monday in announcing a historic partnership with the AFL-CIO, the largest federation…
article.text: Artificial intelligence will change many people’s jobs, but unionized workers will have a voice in how the technology develops, Microsoft President Brad Smith said Monday in announcing a historic partnership with the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the United States. Microsoft President Brad Smith. Standing alongside AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler and other labor leaders, Smith said Microsoft will respect “the fundamental right to organize” by AFL-CIO’s 60 affiliate unions. Workers will also have a chance to give Microsoft developers feedback on how AI tools are created and train for new jobs in the AI-powered economy. The deal was announced at the AFL-CIO headquarters in Washington, D.C., at an event billed as a conversation about AI and the future of work.

article.title: 'Existential Risks': AI Anxiety Fueling Stream of Shareholder Proposals
article.description: "Because this is such a new space, a lot of the proposals will be about more transparency, and about what companies are doing with AI, and how boards are overseeing risks," said Jamie Smith of the EY Americas Center for Board Matters. Public company…
article.text: "Because this is such a new space, a lot of the proposals will be about more transparency, and about what companies are doing with AI, and how boards are overseeing risks," said Jamie Smith of the EY Americas Center for Board Matters. Public company shareholders this spring will vote on a bevy of investor proposals related to artificial intelligence, a topic that rarely came up during the confabs a year ago. Investors already were deep into the process of crafting their 2023 proposals when AI burst into the public consciousness in November 2022 with OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT. But investors are ready his time around and are thrusting the topic alongside other hot-button issues such as executive compensation and climate change.

article.title: Longtime Law Firm Partner Going In-House to Help Companies Control Legal Bills
article.description: Brian Arbetter is joining LegalBillReview.com as its first general counsel. Arbetter was previously an equity partner at Baker McKenzie, Sheppard Mullin and Norton Rose Fulbright. He was most recently a partner emeritus at Seddigh Arbetter. After 30…
article.text: Brian Arbetter is joining LegalBillReview.com as its first general counsel. Arbetter was previously an equity partner at Baker McKenzie, Sheppard Mullin and Norton Rose Fulbright. He was most recently a partner emeritus at Seddigh Arbetter. After 30 years as a partner at some of the world’s most prominent law firms, Brian Arbetter is going in-house, leveraging decades of law firm experience to help corporate clients control their outside counsel spend as the first general counsel and vice president of law firm relations for LegalBillReview.com. Arbetter got his start doing labor and employment work at Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp in the early 1990s. Since then, he’s been an equity partner at such prestigious firms as Baker McKenzie, Sheppard Mullin and Norton Rose Fulbright, where he specialized in international labor and employment law.

article.title: More People Are Bringing Politics, Religion to Workplace, Testing Employers on Civility
article.description: COVID-19 blurred the lines between home and work, upending long-established workplace boundaries. Meanwhile, a larger cultural push is encouraging employees to bring their whole selves to work. But the new environment can leave some employees feeling…
article.text: COVID-19 blurred the lines between home and work, upending long-established workplace boundaries. Meanwhile, a larger cultural push is encouraging employees to bring their whole selves to work. But the new environment can leave some employees feeling uncomfortable and threatened. Southwest Airlines thought it was getting rid of a workplace bully when it fired a flight attendant for sending abusive messages to a colleague on social media. But her termination turned into a legal nightmare, with the airline ordered to reinstate the flight attendant, pay $5 million in damages and send a team of its top lawyers to “religious liberty” training. The episode underscores the predicament companies face in maintaining a workplace culture of mutual respect and civility. While never an easy proposition, it’s getting even harder as employees shed reservations about loudly sharing their strongly held religious and political beliefs, emboldened by a larger cultural push to bring their “whole” selves to work.

article.title: Meta Blasts FTC After Agency Moves to Block It From Monetizing Child and Teen Data
article.description: The FTC says Facebook parent Meta is a serial violator of privacy rules. The agency fined Facebook $5 billion in 2020 after Cambridge Analytics accessed the data of 87 million users worldwide without their consent. Meta says it will challenge the…
article.text: The FTC says Facebook parent Meta is a serial violator of privacy rules. The agency fined Facebook $5 billion in 2020 after Cambridge Analytics accessed the data of 87 million users worldwide without their consent. Meta says it will challenge the FTC's latest proposed actions and expects to prevail. The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday proposed a fresh round of sanctions on Facebook parent Meta, including a blanket ban on monetizing the data it collects on children and teens, after determining that the company hasn’t lived up to its promises to protect user privacy. Meta has 30 days to respond to allegations that it continued to share its users’ private information with third-party apps well into 2020, even after touting a privacy policy in 2018 that said it would no longer share information with so-called expired apps, or apps that hadn’t been used in 90 days. article.description: Nearly one-quarter of in-house attorneys surveyed by Norton Rose Fulbright say their companies’ ESG-related risk exposure increased in 2023, and 27% expect it to get worse in 2024. The firm’s recently released “2024 Litigation Trends Survey,” based…
article.text: Nearly one-quarter of in-house attorneys surveyed by Norton Rose Fulbright say their companies’ ESG-related risk exposure increased in 2023, and 27% expect it to get worse in 2024. The firm’s recently released “2024 Litigation Trends Survey,” based on interviews with 400 in-house attorneys late last year, found that 1 in 10 respondents worked for legal departments that faced ESG-related litigation last year. That compared with 2 of every 100 legal departments a year earlier.

article.title: Big Law Opts for Smaller but New Space in NY, as Law Firm Leasing Activity Ticks Up
article.description: Law firm leasing deals were up in the second quarter of 2024, compared with the first. Firms like Willkie Farr & Gallagher and Covington & Burling signed big leases in the second quarter. The first half of 2024 saw more firms relocating rather than…
article.text: Law firm leasing deals were up in the second quarter of 2024, compared with the first. Firms like Willkie Farr & Gallagher and Covington & Burling signed big leases in the second quarter. The first half of 2024 saw more firms relocating rather than staying in place, compared with 2023. More law firms are signing office leases in Manhattan this year, as firms commit to attendance policies and look for efficiencies in office space. Some of the latest lease transactions include Covington & Burling, which signed for a new office at Hudson Yards, and Willkie Farr & Gallagher, which renewed its headquarters space, according to brokers. Overall this year, law firms have been more likely to leave their current spaces and relocate, but they continue opting for smaller spaces, according to leasing data from real estate firms Savills and Cushman & Wakefield.
article.html:
• Law firm leasing deals were up in the second quarter of 2024, compared with the first.
  • Firms like Willkie Farr & Gallagher and Covington & Burling signed big leases in the second quarter.
  • The first half of 2024 saw more firms relocating rather than staying in place, compared with 2023.

More law firms are signing office leases in Manhattan this year, as firms commit to attendance policies and look for efficiencies in office space. Some of the latest lease transactions include Covington & Burling, which signed for a new office at Hudson Yards, and Willkie Farr & Gallagher, which renewed its headquarters space, according to brokers.

Overall this year, law firms have been more likely to leave their current spaces and relocate, but they continue opting for smaller spaces, according to leasing data from real estate firms Savills and Cushman & Wakefield.

article.title: Controversy, Criticism, Profit: PGA and LIV Golf Merger Leaves Many Unanswered Questions
article.description: In a stunning “about face” that shocked the sports world, on June 6, 2023, the PGA Tour announced that it would team up with its bitter rival, LIV Golf, and enter into a business combination to settle the rancorous disputes between the competing…
article.text: In a stunning “about face” that shocked the sports world, on June 6, 2023, the PGA Tour announced that it would team up with its bitter rival, LIV Golf, and enter into a business combination to settle the rancorous disputes between the competing tours that have fractured the golf world along economic, and even political lines. The details regarding this business combination have not been released publicly; however, it is known that this partnership will also include the DP World Tour (i.e., the European golf tour). It seems more than likely that the consummation of this transaction will result in the creation of a new golf super league, which has sparked both outrage among observers and even government scrutiny.

article.title: Layoff Season Winds Down as Law Firms Firms Prepare for Demand Uptick
article.description: Katten Muchin Rosenman and Armstrong Teasdale announced layoffs this week, following cuts earlier this summer at Reed Smith and Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe. However, recruiters predict fewer layoffs this fall as demand for corporate associates…
article.text: Katten Muchin Rosenman and Armstrong Teasdale announced layoffs this week, following cuts earlier this summer at Reed Smith and Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe. However, recruiters predict fewer layoffs this fall as demand for corporate associates begins to tick up. With the associate talent wars fresh in their minds, firm leaders are also hesitant to cut associates they may need in the next year. Layoffs hit two Midwestern firms in the Am Law 200 this week, with Katten Muchin Rosenman announcing cuts of fewer than 5% of attorneys and staff amid a slump in demand and Armstrong Teasdale dismissing 24 staffers due to a desire to streamline operations. The latter firm also cut 11 lawyers following performance reviews. The cuts followed June layoffs at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe and Reed Smith, which impacted a total of 90 attorneys and staff at Orrick and 50 total employees at Reed Smith. Law firms that service Silicon Valley saw more turmoil earlier in this year as Gunderson Dettmer Stough Villeneuve Franklin & Hachigian let go of 10% of U.S. attorneys and staff in April. article.title: Biden’s AI Executive Order: 6 Actions for Legal Leaders
article.description: In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology. “Artificial Intelligence must be…
article.text: In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology. “Artificial Intelligence must be safe and secure. Meeting this goal requires robust, reliable, repeatable, and standardized evaluations of AI systems, as well as policies, institutions, and as appropriate, other mechanisms to test, understand, and mitigate risks from these systems before they are put to use. It also requires addressing AI systems’ most pressing security risks — including with respect to biotechnology, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and other national security dangers — while navigating AI’s opacity and complexity.” Much of the order pertains to U.S. government requirements and specific industries such as healthcare, financial services, and critical infrastructure owners and operators. However, it also reflects principles aligned with global regulatory efforts initiated by the European Union and others, which include: Transparency: Highlights new guidance and standards on disclosing to individuals and relevant regulatory agencies when and how AI is being used. Fairness: Calls for cabinet and regulatory agencies to set standards and guidance to minimize bias in areas such as hiring, housing, and healthcare. Human oversight: Recognizes the importance of having human oversight in AI decisions, especially higher-risk situations where discrimination or unintentional bias may pose an issue in automated decision making. Risk management: Introduces new risk management practices specifically for AI with a particular focus on third-party usage and monitoring. It also calls for an updated National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) risk framework. Privacy: Renews a call for federal legislation in this area and calls out specific privacy risks that are potentially exacerbated by AI.
article.html:
In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology.

“Artificial Intelligence must be safe and secure. Meeting this goal requires robust, reliable, repeatable, and standardized evaluations of AI systems, as well as policies, institutions, and as appropriate, other mechanisms to test, understand, and mitigate risks from these systems before they are put to use. It also requires addressing AI systems’ most pressing security risks — including with respect to biotechnology, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and other national security dangers — while navigating AI’s opacity and complexity.”

Much of the order pertains to U.S. government requirements and specific industries such as healthcare, financial services, and critical infrastructure owners and operators. However, it also reflects principles aligned with global regulatory efforts initiated by the European Union and others, which include:

  • Transparency: Highlights new guidance and standards on disclosing to individuals and relevant regulatory agencies when and how AI is being used.
  • Fairness: Calls for cabinet and regulatory agencies to set standards and guidance to minimize bias in areas such as hiring, housing, and healthcare.
  • Human oversight: Recognizes the importance of having human oversight in AI decisions, especially higher-risk situations where discrimination or unintentional bias may pose an issue in automated decision making.
  • Risk management: Introduces new risk management practices specifically for AI with a particular focus on third-party usage and monitoring. It also calls for an updated National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) risk framework.
  • Privacy: Renews a call for federal legislation in this area and calls out specific privacy risks that are potentially exacerbated by AI.

article.title: Tech Giants Take a Beating at FTC's AI Summit
article.description: “Will this be a moment of opening up markets to fair and free competition, unleashing the full potential of emerging technologies? Or will a handful of dominant firms concentrate control over these key tools locking us into a future of their…
article.text: “Will this be a moment of opening up markets to fair and free competition, unleashing the full potential of emerging technologies? Or will a handful of dominant firms concentrate control over these key tools locking us into a future of their choosing?” Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan said. The FTC hosted a virtual summit Thursday focused on competition problems in the burgeoning AI industry. The outlook is grim for new entrants into the market for chips and cloud computing services, and experts said it may be too late to level the playing field. Undeterred, the FTC launched an inquiry Thursday into the investments and partnerships between AI developers Open AI and Anthropic and tech titans Microsoft, Google and Amazon. Dominant tech firms have the advantage when it comes to the data, chips and cloud computing infrastructure necessary to compete on the AI playing field. But antitrust authorities are determined to level it. Speaking at a summit hosted by the Federal Trade Commission’s technology office Thursday, chair Lina Khan framed the fight for fair competition in artificial intelligence as an existential one, pitting the biggest tech companies against the regulators holding them at bay.
article.html:
“Will this be a moment of opening up markets to fair and free competition, unleashing the full potential of emerging technologies? Or will a handful of dominant firms concentrate control over these key tools locking us into a future of their choosing?” Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan said.

article.title: Law Firm Partner Hourly Rates Rose Last Year at Biggest Clip in at Least a Decade
article.description: What You Need to Know LexisNexis CounselLink analyzed $52 billion in legal spending across 420,000 timekeepers and 1.4 million legal matters. The 50 largest law firms increased their market share to 47.3%. Alternative fee arrangements held steady at…
article.text: What You Need to Know LexisNexis CounselLink analyzed $52 billion in legal spending across 420,000 timekeepers and 1.4 million legal matters. The 50 largest law firms increased their market share to 47.3%. Alternative fee arrangements held steady at 6.3% of legal billings. Hourly rates for law firm partners jumped 4.5% in 2022, driven in part by law firms’ fears of profitability losses from inflation and a drop in M&A activity, according to a report from the e-billing platform LexisNexis CounselLink. The report, based on $52 billion in legal spending across 420,000 timekeepers and 1.4 million legal matters, says that annual percentage increase was the largest since CounselLink put out its first report in 2013. article.title: Historic NLRB Ruling Gives Workers Path to Unionize Without Having to Vote
article.description: An NLRB decision issued last Thursday shifts many of the burdens in union representation efforts to employers—and sets traps for any missteps. The changes are expected to open the floodgates on unionization efforts. This is the NLRB's most aggressive…
article.text: An NLRB decision issued last Thursday shifts many of the burdens in union representation efforts to employers—and sets traps for any missteps. The changes are expected to open the floodgates on unionization efforts. This is the NLRB's most aggressive pro-union move since it came under Democratic control in 2021. In what some attorneys are calling the most significant change in federal labor law in a half-century, the National Labor Relations Board has issued new rules that put employers in the onerous position of being forced to recognize and bargain with a union—unless they take swift action to request an employee election and prevail in that election. “These changes radically shift the legal landscape for companies,” Morgan, Lewis & Bockius wrote in a note to corporate clients, and “make it much easier for unions to organize.”
article.html:
• An NLRB decision issued last Thursday shifts many of the burdens in union representation efforts to employers—and sets traps for any missteps.
  • The changes are expected to open the floodgates on unionization efforts.
  • This is the NLRB's most aggressive pro-union move since it came under Democratic control in 2021.

In what some attorneys are calling the most significant change in federal labor law in a half-century, the National Labor Relations Board has issued new rules that put employers in the onerous position of being forced to recognize and bargain with a union—unless they take swift action to request an employee election and prevail in that election.

“These changes radically shift the legal landscape for companies,” Morgan, Lewis & Bockius wrote in a note to corporate clients, and “make it much easier for unions to organize.”

article.text: Tesla senior director of legal Dinna Eskin made it clear that she's now in charge of the EV maker's legal department, but her predecessor's status remains murky. Tesla senior director of legal Dinna Eskin is the company's latest legal chief. Eskin disclosed her new GC role in an affidavit in Twitter's suit against Elon Musk. Tesla has disputed reports that Eskin's apparent predecessor exited the company. Tesla Inc. senior director of legal Dinna Eskin is acting as the electric vehicle maker’s general counsel, according to an affidavit she filed in connection with Twitter’s lawsuit to prevent Elon Musk from backing out of a deal to buy the social media company. Eskin revealed in the filing earlier this month in the Delaware Court of Chancery that Tesla has no “employee with the formal title of ‘General Counsel,’ and my role as Senior Director of Legal is functionally equivalent to the role commonly known as ‘General Counsel.’
article.html:
Tesla senior director of legal Dinna Eskin made it clear that she's now in charge of the EV maker's legal department, but her predecessor's status remains murky.

  • Tesla senior director of legal Dinna Eskin is the company's latest legal chief.
  • Eskin disclosed her new GC role in an affidavit in Twitter's suit against Elon Musk.
  • Tesla has disputed reports that Eskin's apparent predecessor exited the company.

Tesla Inc. senior director of legal Dinna Eskin is acting as the electric vehicle maker’s general counsel, according to an affidavit she filed in connection with Twitter’s lawsuit to prevent Elon Musk from backing out of a deal to buy the social media company. 

Eskin revealed in the filing earlier this month in the Delaware Court of Chancery that Tesla has no “employee with the formal title of ‘General Counsel,’ and my role as Senior Director of Legal is functionally equivalent to the role commonly known as ‘General Counsel.’

article.title: Conflict? Guyana Hires Exxon Mobil’s Lobbyist to Rewrite Country's Petroleum Law
article.description: One business ethics professor called the conflict of interest obvious. A World Bank representative said the organization doesn't see it, and is just trying to help a poor country improve its legal and institutional frameworks. The World Bank, which…
article.text: One business ethics professor called the conflict of interest obvious. A World Bank representative said the organization doesn't see it, and is just trying to help a poor country improve its legal and institutional frameworks. The World Bank, which has pledged not to fund fossil fuel extraction, has agreed to pay nearly $2 million to Hunton Andrews Kurth to revise Guyana’s petroleum law. The catch: Hunton has represented Exxon Mobil Corp. for decades, and Exxon Mobil is leading the pack in oil production in Guyana. At least one German environmental rights group, Urgewald, is objecting to the funding for Hunton both as environmentally unsound and as a conflict of interest.
article.html:

At least one German environmental rights group, Urgewald, is objecting to the funding for Hunton both as environmentally unsound and as a conflict of interest.

article.title: Autonomy CEO Denies Misleading HP, Says Its Own Blunders Made $11B Buyout a Flop
article.description: Former Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch, standing trial in San Francisco on charges he used accounting trickery to dupe Hewlett-Packard into buying his company for $11 billion in 2011, testified Tuesday that he actually would have preferred to keep it…
article.text: Former Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch, standing trial in San Francisco on charges he used accounting trickery to dupe Hewlett-Packard into buying his company for $11 billion in 2011, testified Tuesday that he actually would have preferred to keep it independent. Prosecutors say the British tech tycoon orchestrated what they call the biggest fraud in Silicon Valley history through a range of tactics, including padding Autonomy revenues and issuing false and misleading annual reports.
article.html:
Former Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch, standing trial in San Francisco on charges he used accounting trickery to dupe Hewlett-Packard into buying his company for $11 billion in 2011, testified Tuesday that he actually would have preferred to keep it independent.

Prosecutors say the British tech tycoon orchestrated what they call the biggest fraud in Silicon Valley history through a range of tactics, including padding Autonomy revenues and issuing false and misleading annual reports.

article.title: Playing 'Catch-Up in the AI Race,' Panicked Amazon Cast Aside Worker Rights, Suit Alleges
article.description: A high-performing AI researcher and engineer claims she was sidelined and eventually fired over her pregnancy. She also says she was told to ignore internal copyright policies in favor of getting better results for her AI related project. The lawsuit…
article.text: A high-performing AI researcher and engineer claims she was sidelined and eventually fired over her pregnancy. She also says she was told to ignore internal copyright policies in favor of getting better results for her AI related project. The lawsuit claims that the AI arms race caused Amazon to put productivity over employee rights. Amid the mad dash to catch up to its rivals in AI, Amazon pressured an artificial intelligence researcher to quit after she disclosed her pregnancy and then fired her while her pregnancy discrimination and retaliation claims were pending, according to a lawsuit filed this week against the tech giant in Los Angeles Superior Court. Viviane Ghaderi, who was responsible for spotting violations of Amazon’s internal copyright policies and bringing them to its legal department, also claims she was told by Amazon’s director of web Information services and structured knowledge to ignore the policies and applicable copyright laws to keep pace with the company’s competitors.
article.html:
• A high-performing AI researcher and engineer claims she was sidelined and eventually fired over her pregnancy.
  • She also says she was told to ignore internal copyright policies in favor of getting better results for her AI related project.
  • The lawsuit claims that the AI arms race caused Amazon to put productivity over employee rights.

Amid the mad dash to catch up to its rivals in AI, Amazon pressured an artificial intelligence researcher to quit after she disclosed her pregnancy and then fired her while her pregnancy discrimination and retaliation claims were pending, according to a lawsuit filed this week against the tech giant in Los Angeles Superior Court.

Viviane Ghaderi, who was responsible for spotting violations of Amazon’s internal copyright policies and bringing them to its legal department, also claims she was told by Amazon’s director of web Information services and structured knowledge to ignore the policies and applicable copyright laws to keep pace with the company’s competitors.

article.title: 'There Are Headaches Galore': 3 Risk Areas That Will Reign in 2023
article.description: What You Need to Know The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come. The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies. The Biden administration stepped up antitrust…
article.text: What You Need to Know The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come. The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies. The Biden administration stepped up antitrust enforcement in 2022 and likely will escalate those efforts this year. General counsel are entering 2023 facing a raft of global uncertainty, regulatory risks, and legal battles with major implications for the digital economy. Lawmakers, regulators and the courts have all ramped up pressure on the tech industry and show no sign of letting up this year. How companies deal with climate change, compete for business, and collect and protect user data will be top risk areas in 2023. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come.
  • The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies.
  • The Biden administration stepped up antitrust enforcement in 2022 and likely will escalate those efforts this year.

General counsel are entering 2023 facing a raft of global uncertainty, regulatory risks, and legal battles with major implications for the digital economy.

Lawmakers, regulators and the courts have all ramped up pressure on the tech industry and show no sign of letting up this year. How companies deal with climate change, compete for business, and collect and protect user data will be top risk areas in 2023.

article.title: Lionsgate Hires O’Melveny and Myers Dealmaker as General Counsel
article.description: Bruce Tobey has joined Lionsgate as executive vice president and general counsel. He's a former senior executive at CBS Films and Paramount Pictures. Tobey's employment agreement entitles him to annual cash and equity compensation approaching $3…
article.text: Bruce Tobey has joined Lionsgate as executive vice president and general counsel. He's a former senior executive at CBS Films and Paramount Pictures. Tobey's employment agreement entitles him to annual cash and equity compensation approaching $3 million. The media company Lionsgate has quietly brought aboard a new general counsel, Bruce Tobey, who spent the past decade as a partner at O’Melveny & Myers and before that was chief operating officer of CBS Films and executive vice president at Paramount Pictures.
article.html:
• Bruce Tobey has joined Lionsgate as executive vice president and general counsel.
  • He's a former senior executive at CBS Films and Paramount Pictures.
  • Tobey's employment agreement entitles him to annual cash and equity compensation approaching $3 million.

The media company Lionsgate has quietly brought aboard a new general counsel, Bruce Tobey, who spent the past decade as a partner at O’Melveny & Myers and before that was chief operating officer of CBS Films and executive vice president at Paramount Pictures.

article.title: Former GC and CEO of Merck Joins Harvard Governing Board, Jumping Into Fray
article.description: A Harvard-trained lawyer who later became the first Black man to serve as CEO of a major pharmaceutical company has joined the 13-person governing board of Harvard University, which is still reeling from accusations that it failed to condemn calls…
article.text: A Harvard-trained lawyer who later became the first Black man to serve as CEO of a major pharmaceutical company has joined the 13-person governing board of Harvard University, which is still reeling from accusations that it failed to condemn calls for the genocide of Jews. Kenneth Frazier, who was general counsel of Merck before serving as CEO from 2011 to 2021, will fill a vacant seat on the board as it grapples with reputational damage and boycotts by a number of financial donors accusing the school of going soft on antisemitism. One sign of that discontent was a sharp drop in early undergraduate applications.
article.html:
A Harvard-trained lawyer who later became the first Black man to serve as CEO of a major pharmaceutical company has joined the 13-person governing board of Harvard University, which is still reeling from accusations that it failed to condemn calls for the genocide of Jews.

Kenneth Frazier, who was general counsel of Merck before serving as CEO from 2011 to 2021,  will fill a vacant seat on the board as it grapples with reputational damage and boycotts by a number of financial donors accusing the school of going soft on antisemitism. One sign of that discontent was a sharp drop in early undergraduate applications.

article.title: SVB's Failure May Constrict Flow of Capital to Some Startups | Corporate Counsel
article.description: “The most important thing is it seems like payroll is going to get hit on time, but there are still plenty of things to be concerned about,” said Healy Jones, vice president of financial strategy at the accounting firm Kruze Consulting.
article.text: The government's move to protect uninsured deposits at Silicon Valley Bank was a relief for many company founders, but the bank's demise likely will leave a trail of challenges for startups, including making cash to fund growth a little harder to come by. "The most important thing is it seems like payroll is going to hit on time, but there are still plenty of things to be concerned about," said Healy Jones, vice president of financial strategy at startup-focused accounting firm Kruze Consulting, which counts nearly 800 venture-backed startups as clients. Though the government guaranteed all deposits at SVB, including those above the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.'s $250,000 limit, it remains unclear whether companies will be able to draw on funds from venture debt loans. SVB touted itself as the first bank to offer such loans, which startups use to give themselves breathing room before they need more funding from investors. "Many startups were probably planning to use that money to extend their runway and finance operations," Jones said. "It's definitely messing up financing plans and strategy for some clients." The effects will be felt mostly by later stage startups, as 20%-30% of series B to series D companies have some venture debt or have paid a fee to make it available later, Jones said. He estimated that just 10% of those companies actually choose to draw on venture debt. Even so, given that SVB had more than half the market share of venture debt, whether those agreements are still good will be a big concern. "For sure, there will be some companies that it will hurt," he said. "It's important to be able to stretch your runway and grow your valuation, and this is a major partner that has disappeared from the ecosystem." Alex Meshkin, CEO of the tech-enabled medical laboratory FlowHealth, said SVB's collapse calls into question that entire financing tool for startups. "Who wants those loans? They're basically subprime business loans. You're talking about companies that have no credit profile, they're burning cash and are unlikely to raise the same type of capital because of interest rates." Meshkin, who started his company in 2014 without venture backing, said SVB's business model was a turnoff. "I met with SVB many times throughout my career, and I never understood why anyone would bank with them. It was basically social credit. 'If you're backed by Sequoia we're going to lend you money.' That's how it worked." Companies don't need a "friendly bank," he added. "I don't understand why a company with $10 million in funding want more risk than they already have. What do you need as a startup? A bank that you can put your money in that's safe. That's really all you need. SVB provided credit. Do we need credit? VCs have so much money, so why do startups need debt?" Even so, Meshkin said, "SVB was kind of a key aspect of the entire technology ecosystem— not just in Silicon Valley, but other aspiring startup markets as well. Let's just face it, it would do things for startups that very few things other banks would consider doing, because startups are very risky." Jay Jung, founder and managing partner for consulting firm Embarc Advisors, said the VCs' sponsorship of the startups mitigated the risk of the venture debt loans, in addition to making it easier for the companies to raise additional venture rounds. "There's no doubt they were lending to riskier companies, but they were looking at the VC investors when they invest in a startup as well," he said. In cases where a company runs into financial difficulties, Jung said he's seen SVB "work closely with the investors to make the best of the situation and try to salvage what they can. A lot of the people in the startup ecosystem appreciated SVB and liked working with them, and that's why a lot of people are sad to see them go away, at least temporarily." Jung said the venture debt loans that SVB provided aren't necessarily easy to get elsewhere, and alternatives like venture debt funds are more expensive. "It's kind of adding insult to injury because in the last 12 months, it's been a lot lot more difficult to raise equity. They're getting hit on both the equity side and debt side. Equity investors are investing less frequently and in smaller amounts," Jung said. Eighteen months ago, a company that raised $50 million in venture capital might be able to borrow $20 million from SVB, he said. If the company was burning through $14 million a year, the $70 million would allow it to operate for five years before it ran out of money. Today, that company might be able to raise $35 million, he said. Without a venture debt loan, it would be out of money in less than three years. Jones said another issue companies will need to consider is whether they would be violating their loan agreements if they move money out of SVB. "A founder may not want to stay with SVB for all of their banking needs. It would be reasonable to take some cash and move it to another bank right now. But if you do that, have you triggered a default?" he asked. "SVB may not want to screw founders over, but what if that business gets sold to more predatory distressed fund? They might call default on those companies to try to extract a pound of flesh." Joseph Cioffi, chair of Davis + Gilbert's insolvency and finance practice in New York, agreed. "You just can't terminate a contract freely with a bank in receivership," he said. Cioffi said he's generally bullish about the future financial landscape for tech companies, "tempered only by the fact that we've got to have a full understanding of what's happened and how deep the issues might be." He added: "You may have to adjust your practices in terms of your risk, knowing this type of event can happen. Even though the government stepped in, you can't take that for granted. I think that panic will linger, and people will adjust their behavior—the startups, the lenders, the VC firms. Anybody who is funding a VC firm is realizing this could happen again." In the meantime, Jung said companies will need to spend less and move away from the growth-at-all-costs mindset of years past. "What companies have to do now is reduce their burn. Companies are going have to be much more judicious about how they hire and when they hire, and make sure everyone is performing at 80%-plus," he said. "Maybe before you hired three to four marketing people, one for social, one for events, you'll start seeing companies hire maybe one or two people taking on more generalized roles. There will be less specialization and more generalists." He said companies might consider offshoring some customer service and engineering functions and turning to part-time freelancers for some roles. "Maybe you don't need a full-time CFO. Maybe you're fine with a fractional team to make sure things get done," he said. Cioffi said he expects the tech sector to be resilient. "There is going to be a lot of enthusiasm, still, for lending to the tech industry," with other players, including non-U.S. lenders and non-bank investors, becoming more aggressive in a quest to gain market share. Meshkin said venture capital will continue to flow as well. "Any company that's good can raise more equity," he said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. A bank that you can put your money in that's safe. That's really all you need. SVB provided credit. Do we need credit? VCs have so much money, so why do startups need debt?"

In cases where a company runs into financial difficulties, Jung said he's seen SVB "work closely with the investors to make the best of the situation and try to salvage what they can. A lot of the people in the startup ecosystem appreciated SVB and liked working with them, and that's why a lot of people are sad to see them go away, at least temporarily."

"It's kind of adding insult to injury because in the last 12 months, it's been a lot lot more difficult to raise equity. They're getting hit on both the equity side and debt side. Equity investors are investing less frequently and in smaller amounts," Jung said.
