Joseph Cioffi, chair of Davis + Gilbert's insolvency and finance practice in New York, agreed. "You just can't terminate a contract freely with a bank in receivership," he said.

Cioffi said he's generally bullish about the future financial landscape for tech companies, "tempered only by the fact that we've got to have a full understanding of what's happened and how deep the issues might be."

He added: "You may have to adjust your practices in terms of your risk, knowing this type of event can happen. Even though the government stepped in, you can't take that for granted. I think that panic will linger, and people will adjust their behavior—the startups, the lenders, the VC firms. Anybody who is funding a VC firm is realizing this could happen again."

In the meantime, Jung said companies will need to spend less and move away from the growth-at-all-costs mindset of years past.

"What companies have to do now is reduce their burn. Companies are going have to be much more judicious about how they hire and when they hire, and make sure everyone is performing at 80%-plus," he said.

"Maybe before you hired three to four marketing people, one for social, one for events, you'll start seeing companies hire maybe one or two people taking on more generalized roles. There will be less specialization and more generalists."

He said companies might consider offshoring some customer service and engineering functions and turning to part-time freelancers for some roles.

Cioffi said he expects the tech sector to be resilient. "There is going to be a lot of enthusiasm, still, for lending to the tech industry," with other players, including non-U.S. lenders and non-bank investors, becoming more aggressive in a quest to gain market share.

article.title: Seyfarth’s New Chief D&I Officer Aims to Maximize Benefits of Diverse Workforce
article.description: Seyfarth Shaw recently hired Mira Dewji as its new chief diversity & inclusion officer. Dewji replaces the firm’s first D&I leader, who founded her own consulting firm. Dewji’s background in behavioral science will help her get the most out of…
article.text: Seyfarth Shaw recently hired Mira Dewji as its new chief diversity & inclusion officer. Dewji replaces the firm’s first D&I leader, who founded her own consulting firm. Dewji’s background in behavioral science will help her get the most out of Seyfarth’s diverse team, she said. Seyfarth Shaw recently named a new chief diversity and inclusion officer, hiring Mira Dewji, the former DEI director at Fenwick & West, who started at Seyfarth’s New York office this week. Dewji, who left Fenwick in 2022, said her hiring was the product of an extended search after Seyfarth’s first D&I leader, Kori Karew, departed the firm to launch her own consultancy at the end of 2022.

article.title: Perkins Coie Hires Former Patent Judge to Tackle High-Stakes IP Litigation
article.description: Jessica Kaiser joined Perkins Coie as a partner. Kaiser previously led Arnold & Porter's post-grant patent proceedings practice. During her time at the USPTO, Kaiser decided hundreds of cases before the PTAB. More and more, IP lawyers are flocking to…
article.text: Jessica Kaiser joined Perkins Coie as a partner. Kaiser previously led Arnold & Porter's post-grant patent proceedings practice. During her time at the USPTO, Kaiser decided hundreds of cases before the PTAB. More and more, IP lawyers are flocking to tech-focused firms. In the latest in a series of moves, Perkins Coie has hired Jessica Kaiser, a former lead administrative patent judge at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Kaiser, most recently a partner and co-chair of the post-grant patent proceedings practice at Arnold & Porter, joined Perkins Coie as a partner in its intellectual property and patent litigation practices. She is based in Denver, though her practice often takes her to Washington, D.C. as well.

• Jessica Kaiser joined Perkins Coie as a partner.
  • Kaiser previously led Arnold & Porter's post-grant patent proceedings practice.

article.title: Disney's Black Eye Over Arbitration Gambit Likely to Linger, Underscoring PR Risks of Spurning Courts
article.description: The public relations drubbing that beset The Walt Disney Co. recently after the entertainment giant tried to force a wrongful-death lawsuit into arbitration for the quirkiest of reasons—in signing up for a Disney+ trial in 2019, the plaintiff had…
article.text: The public relations drubbing that beset The Walt Disney Co. recently after the entertainment giant tried to force a wrongful-death lawsuit into arbitration for the quirkiest of reasons—in signing up for a Disney+ trial in 2019, the plaintiff had agreed to settle all disputes with the company out of court—should serve as a cautionary tale for other companies, legal observers say. Companies often prefer to resolve disputes through binding arbitration, rather than in court, in part because of the efficiency and confidentiality of the process. But in this matter, Disney found itself a social media punching bag because of the legal tactics it used in a dispute that otherwise might have garnered little or no public attention.

article.title: In First-of-Kind Case, DOJ Alleges CEO Filed Trading Plans to Pull Off Vast Insider Trading Scheme | Corporate Counsel
article.description: Few things undermine trust in the markets more than insiders abusing their positions for personal advantage, SEC enforcement division director Gurbir Grewal said.
article.text: The Department of Justice for the first time has charged an executive with fraudulent use of so-called 10b5-1 trading plans to commit criminal insider trading—the latest sign of regulators' concern that the plans, created more than two decades ago to tamp down the potential for illegal trading on nonpublic information, are being abused. The DOJ on Wednesday unsealed an indictment alleging that Terren Peizer, chairman and former CEO of Los Angeles-based Ontrak, dumped more than $20 million in company stock between May 2021 and August 2021 based on inside knowledge that it was about to lose a contract with Cigna, its largest customer. Authorities allege that Peizer, 63, dodged more than $12.7 million in losses by creating and trading on two 10b5-1 plans after learning that Cigna was going to cease doing business with Ontrak, which provides behavioral health services to large insurers. This content has been archived. It is available through our partners, LexisNexis® and Bloomberg Law. To view this content, please continue to their sites.
article.html:
The Department of Justice for the first time has charged an executive with fraudulent use of so-called 10b5-1 trading plans to commit criminal insider trading—the latest sign of regulators' concern that the plans, created more than two decades ago to tamp down the potential for illegal trading on nonpublic information, are being abused.

The DOJ on Wednesday unsealed an indictment alleging that Terren Peizer, chairman and former CEO of Los Angeles-based Ontrak, dumped more than $20 million in company stock between May 2021 and August 2021 based on inside knowledge that it was about to lose a contract with Cigna, its largest customer.

Authorities allege that Peizer, 63, dodged more than $12.7 million in losses by creating and trading on two 10b5-1 plans after learning that Cigna was going to cease doing business with Ontrak, which provides behavioral health services to large insurers.

article.title: 'Patently Unreasonable': Twitter Blasts Vijaya Gadde's $1.1M Legal-Fee-Reimbursement Request
article.description: Twitter rapped its former legal chief for enlisting eight Sidley Austin professionals—five partners, two associates and a policy adviser—in connection with her one-day appearance before a House committee. "This is not a case of mere duplication of…
article.text: Twitter rapped its former legal chief for enlisting eight Sidley Austin professionals—five partners, two associates and a policy adviser—in connection with her one-day appearance before a House committee. "This is not a case of mere duplication of effort," its filing said. "This is a case of quadruplication of effort." Twitter is asking the court to slash the reimbursement to $109,203. Sidley Austin says the fees are completely justified, given the uncertainties surrounding the hearing, which focused on Twitter's decision to suppress a report about Hunter Biden's laptop. The legal clash between Twitter and former legal chief Vijaya Gadde is heating up, with the company’s lawyers blasting her request to be reimbursed $1.1 million for legal fees she rung up preparing to testify before a U.S. House committee as “unreasonable in the extreme.” Gadde and two other former Twitter executives sued the San Francisco-based company in the Delaware Court of Chancery in April seeking reimbursement for legal fees they’d racked up on Twitter-related matters, including lawsuits and investigations, since Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the company in October and immediately fired them.

article.title: 9th Circuit Denies Family's En Banc Request in Nazi-Looted Art Case
article.description: A Southern California family trying to recover a painting stolen by Nazis in 1939 was dealt another legal blow Tuesday when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit declined to rehear its case en banc. Ninth Circuit Judges Consuelo Callahan,…
article.text: A Southern California family trying to recover a painting stolen by Nazis in 1939 was dealt another legal blow Tuesday when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit declined to rehear its case en banc. Ninth Circuit Judges Consuelo Callahan, Carlos Bea and Sandra Ikuta denied a petition by the descendants of Lilly Neubauer to reconsider its ruling that Spanish law, not California law, should determine who owns the Camille Pissarro painting “Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon. Effect of Rain.” The case also failed to secure enough votes in the circuit for a full court, en banc, consideration.
article.html:

Effect of Rain.” The case also failed to secure enough votes in the circuit for a full court, en banc, consideration.

article.title: Forgiveness or Permission?: What LeBron James’ Copyright Infringement Defense Win Means
article.description: An artist who tattooed LeBron James sued 2K Games for including the tattoos as part of James' character model without getting the artists permission. However, the jury found in favor of James, reasoning he had an implied license to art on his body.…
article.text: An artist who tattooed LeBron James sued 2K Games for including the tattoos as part of James' character model without getting the artists permission. However, the jury found in favor of James, reasoning he had an implied license to art on his body. This is the latest decision in a relatively new area of case law clarifying when tattoo artists do and don't have copyrights to their designs. A Northern District of Ohio jury recently held that people with tattoos have an implied license to include their body art as part of their appearance when depicted in video games, further drawing the line between infringement and noninfringement in tattoo copyright claims. The result comes after tattoo artist James Hayden sued LeBron James and 2K Games for copyright infringement for not getting permission from him to use his tattoo designs before including them on LeBron’s character model in a basketball video game.

article.title: Is Big Tech's Cloud Dominance Scary or Impressive?
article.description: There is a fine line between anti-competitive conduct and customers simply gravitating toward the big three cloud providers. One reason for concern is that once a company picks a cloud provider, it is difficult to unwind that relationship. Some…
article.text: There is a fine line between anti-competitive conduct and customers simply gravitating toward the big three cloud providers. One reason for concern is that once a company picks a cloud provider, it is difficult to unwind that relationship. Some experts fear that investments by cloud giants in machine-learning startups will stifle innovation. The machine learning revolution has produced hundreds of artificial intelligence startups, but experts warn that putting all the power in the hands of a few big cloud providers to host their data will be terrible for society and the economy. “AI is now the leading application shaping competition, and increasingly security, in the cloud,” said Steven Weber, faculty director for the UC Berkeley Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity. article.title: In-House Lawyers Say AI Well-Suited for Some Tasks, Dangerous for Others
article.description: "I am ... more likely to trust the use of [AI] by someone who is more seasoned because they have the experience to know whether it is a legitimate response," said one participant in a newly released survey of general counsel. In-house legal leaders…
article.text: "I am ... more likely to trust the use of [AI] by someone who is more seasoned because they have the experience to know whether it is a legitimate response," said one participant in a newly released survey of general counsel. In-house legal leaders are comfortable letting artificial intelligence help with e-discovery and compliance monitoring, but are uneasy using it on internal investigations, according to a report released Wednesday by FTI Consulting and the compliance tech company Relativity. Eighty percent of in-house attorneys surveyed said they were comfortable with AI-powered e-discovery tools, while 67% said the same about using AI to help with compliance monitoring. Document review and legal research also ranked highly.

article.title: Snapchat Faces Wrongful-Death Suit Following 'Sextortion' Scheme Involving 13-Year-Old Boy
article.description: Snapchat is accused of strict liability and negligence in a wrongful death suit where a 13-year-old boy allegedly committed suicide after he was a victim of a “sextortion” scheme, according to the federal lawsuit filed in South Carolina. This suit…
article.text: Snapchat is accused of strict liability and negligence in a wrongful death suit where a 13-year-old boy allegedly committed suicide after he was a victim of a “sextortion” scheme, according to the federal lawsuit filed in South Carolina. This suit was surfaced by Law.com Radar, ALM’s source for immediate alerting on just-filed cases in state and federal courts. Law.com Radar now offers state court coverage nationwide. Sign up today and be among the first to know about new suits in your region, practice area or client sector. Snap Inc., the creator of messaging app Snapchat, was hit with a wrongful-death lawsuit on May 17 in U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina. The lawsuit was filed by Griffin Humphries and Joe Cunningham Law on behalf of the estate of the teenager, Timothy Isaiah Barnett. Barnett died by suicide after being the victim of “sextortion,” which is the practice of a predator threatening to circulate the sexual images of an individual unless the predator is paid to keep the images hidden, according to the complaint. The complaint alleged that a predator posing as a young girl manipulated Barnett into sending sexually explicit photos. The predator then threatened to share the images unless certain demands were met, allegedly leading Barnett to commit suicide, the complaint said. Snap is accused of knowingly facilitating the exploitation via its defective practices and design, including features that make the platform dangerous for minors, such as the “My Eyes Only” and disappearing photos features. Snap allegedly failed to implement adequate age verification and additional safeguards to protect vulnerable minors from being exploited, and is instead accused of facilitating and exacerbating the risk of exploitation by implementing features which help sexual predators connect with children. “Defendant’s product is designed in unsafe ways—including, as to some or all Defendants, flawed age verification, lack of meaningful mechanisms to prevent sham accounts, default-public profiles, matching and recommending connections between adults and minors, promoting unsolicited messages and interactions from adults, and wholly inadequate and ineffective parental controls, among others—that allow children to be easily identified, targeted, accessed, and exploited,” the complaint said. The complaint brings claims for strict liability, design defect and failure to warn, negligence, and negligence per se. The estate requests more than $10 million in compensatory damages, punitive and exemplary damages, attorneys fees and costs, and pre- and post-judgment interest. Neither the estate’s attorney, James M. Griffin of Griffin Humphries in Columbia, nor Snap immediately responded to requests for comment. Counsel have not yet appeared for the defendant.

article.text: Phil Weinberg had served as chief legal counsel of Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the NHL’s Flyers and their home arena, Wells Fargo Center, since 1996 and played a pivotal role in the organization's growth. Phil Weinberg served for 25 years as chief legal counsel for Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the Philadelphia Flyers and Wells Fargo Center. Weinberg advised the company on the Spectacor-Comcast merger and sale of the NBA's 76ers. He died unexpectedly Wednesday while recovering from hernia surgery. Philadelphia sports fans and legal and business leaders in the city and elsewhere are mourning the loss of Phil Weinberg, longtime legal chief of Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the NHL’s Flyers and their home arena, Wells Fargo Center.
article.html:
Phil Weinberg had served as chief legal counsel of Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the NHL’s Flyers and their home arena, Wells Fargo Center, since 1996 and played a pivotal role in the organization's growth.

  • Phil Weinberg served for 25 years as chief legal counsel for Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the Philadelphia Flyers and Wells Fargo Center.
  • Weinberg advised the company on the Spectacor-Comcast merger and sale of the NBA's 76ers.
  • He died unexpectedly Wednesday while recovering from hernia surgery.

Philadelphia sports fans and legal and business leaders in the city and elsewhere are mourning the loss of Phil Weinberg, longtime legal chief of Comcast Spectacor, parent company of the NHL’s Flyers and their home arena, Wells Fargo Center.

article.title: Legal Departments Frustrated SCOTUS Sidestepped Attorney-Client Privilege
article.description: What You Need to Know The U.S. Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order disposing of a case that could have brought clarity to when communication with clients is protected.It was the first time the high court had taken up attorney-client privilege…
article.text: What You Need to Know The U.S. Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order disposing of a case that could have brought clarity to when communication with clients is protected.It was the first time the high court had taken up attorney-client privilege in 40 years.At issue in the case was so-called dual-purpose communication covering both legal and nonlegal matters. In a blow for in-house counsel seeking clarity on attorney-client privilege, the U.S. Supreme Court tossed what could have been a decisive case for when attorney’s communications with clients are protected. In an unsigned, one-sentence order, the court dismissed an appeal in the case as “improvidently granted” just two weeks after hearing oral arguments, which marked the first time the high court had taken up the issue of attorney-client privilege in 40 years. (Find full coverage of the ruling here.) The case, In re Grand Jury, No. 21-1397, involved a district judge’s denial of attorney-client privilege sought by a law firm hired to prepare tax returns for a client who was “an early promoter of Bitcoin” and left the United States in early 2014, according to a U.S. brief in the case. In a SCOTUS petition In In re Grand Jury, the law firm, which bills itself as specializing in international tax issues, says it provided the client with “legal advice regarding the tax consequences of their anticipated expatriation” and prepared their tax returns and forms to ensure they complied with expatriation tax requirements. A federal grand jury sought records from the firm in its criminal investigation of the client, but the firm refused to hand them over, claiming the communications the grand jury wanted to see were privileged. A federal judge held the firm in contempt for failing to comply with the grand jury’s subpoenas, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed, finding that, while the records addressed both legal and tax matters, they were not privileged, because their “primary purpose” concerned “normal tax return preparation assistance.” In a statement Monday, the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC) said it was disappointed with the court’s decision to dismiss the case. Susanna McDonald, ACC vice president and chief legal officer, said the court missed an opportunity to weigh in on whether attorney-client privilege applies to “dual purpose” communications that contain advice on multiple legal and nonlegal issues. “In-house counsel need clarity on how all courts will view their client communications so that they can provide the best possible legal advice while also fulfilling their role as a strategic business partner,” McDonald said. In an ACC amicus brief filed jointly with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the ACC argued that the demands placed on in-house counsel to advise on compliance, risk mitigation, human resources and government affairs issues require a more predictable standard for determining when attorney-client privilege protections apply. “This predictability is necessary to ensure the full and frank communication between lawyers and their clients that effective legal practice requires,” the groups wrote, shunning the “primary purpose” test used by the appellate court as “completely unworkable for attorneys” and their clients. “Without guidance from the Supreme Court, the legal landscape for dual purpose communications remains murky. In-house counsel routinely engage in communications that have both legal and business purposes that cannot easily be untangled,” McDonald said. “Because the circuit courts are split over which test should be used to determine privilege in these situations, in-house counsel are left wondering what test will apply when so many transactions are across state borders and many companies have operations in multiple states.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • The U.S. Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order disposing of a case that could have brought clarity to when communication with clients is protected.
  • It was the first time the high court had taken up attorney-client privilege in 40 years.
  • At issue in the case was so-called dual-purpose communication covering both legal and nonlegal matters.

In a blow for in-house counsel seeking clarity on attorney-client privilege, the U.S. Supreme Court tossed what could have been a decisive case for when attorney’s communications with clients are protected.

In an unsigned, one-sentence order, the court dismissed an appeal in the case as “improvidently granted” just two weeks after hearing oral arguments, which marked the first time the high court had taken up the issue of attorney-client privilege in 40 years. (Find full coverage of the ruling here.)

The case, In re Grand Jury, No. 21-1397, involved a district judge’s denial of attorney-client privilege sought by a law firm hired to prepare tax returns for a client who was “an early promoter of Bitcoin” and left the United States in early 2014, according to a U.S. brief in the case.

In a SCOTUS petition In In re Grand Jury, the law firm, which bills itself as specializing in international tax issues, says it provided the client with “legal advice regarding the tax consequences of their anticipated expatriation” and prepared their tax returns and forms to ensure they complied with expatriation tax requirements.

A federal grand jury sought records from the firm in its criminal investigation of the client, but the firm refused to hand them over, claiming the communications the grand jury wanted to see were privileged. A federal judge held the firm in contempt for failing to comply with the grand jury’s subpoenas, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed, finding that, while the records addressed both legal and tax matters, they were not privileged, because their “primary purpose” concerned “normal tax return preparation assistance.”

In a statement Monday, the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC) said it was disappointed with the court’s decision to dismiss the case.

Susanna McDonald, ACC vice president and chief legal officer, said the court missed an opportunity to weigh in on whether attorney-client privilege applies to “dual purpose” communications that contain advice on multiple legal and nonlegal issues.

“In-house counsel need clarity on how all courts will view their client communications so that they can provide the best possible legal advice while also fulfilling their role as a strategic business partner,” McDonald said.

In an ACC amicus brief filed jointly with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the ACC argued that the demands placed on in-house counsel to advise on compliance, risk mitigation, human resources and government affairs issues require a more predictable standard for determining when attorney-client privilege protections apply.

“This predictability is necessary to ensure the full and frank communication between lawyers and their clients that effective legal practice requires,” the groups wrote, shunning the “primary purpose” test used by the appellate court as “completely unworkable for attorneys” and their clients.

“Without guidance from the Supreme Court, the legal landscape for dual purpose communications remains murky. In-house counsel routinely engage in communications that have both legal and business purposes that cannot easily be untangled,” McDonald said.

“Because the circuit courts are split over which test should be used to determine privilege in these situations, in-house counsel are left wondering what test will apply when so many transactions are across state borders and many companies have operations in multiple states.”

article.title: What the 5th Circuit's Content-Moderation Ruling Means for Social Media
article.description: Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the Biden administration had likely violated the First Amendment for “coercing” social media platforms to take down “disfavored” content from their sites that it deemed to…
article.text: Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the Biden administration had likely violated the First Amendment for “coercing” social media platforms to take down “disfavored” content from their sites that it deemed to be misinformation about topics such as COVID-19 or the 2020 elections. Following that ruling, the court issued an injunction against several members of the Biden White House, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the FBI. The Supreme Court, however, quickly put a pause on the injunction, which was still in effect at press time.
article.html:
Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the Biden administration had likely violated the First Amendment for “coercing” social media platforms to take down “disfavored” content from their sites that it deemed to be misinformation about topics such as COVID-19 or the 2020 elections.

Following that ruling, the court issued an injunction against several members of the Biden White House, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the FBI. The Supreme Court, however, quickly put a pause on the injunction, which was still in effect at press time.

article.title: How to Stay on Top of Cybersecurity Disclosures as SEC Ramps Up Enforcement
article.description: It is no secret among public companies and their counsel that the US Securities and Exchange Commission has steadily adopted a more aggressive stance on cybersecurity controls and disclosure and incident response recordkeeping. SEC Senior Counsel…
article.text: It is no secret among public companies and their counsel that the US Securities and Exchange Commission has steadily adopted a more aggressive stance on cybersecurity controls and disclosure and incident response recordkeeping. SEC Senior Counsel Arsen Ablaev recently highlighted the Commission’s cybersecurity priorities at the annual Incident Response Forum Masterclass. SEC Chair Gary Gensler also emphasized risks in cyber and information security in the March 29 budget hearing with the House Appropriations Committee, and endorsed U.S. President Joe Biden’s request to earmark a record $2.4 billion in funding for the regulator in 2024. Last month saw yet another example of the SEC’s mounting focus on cyber disclosures as an enforcement priority with the announcement that cloud computing company Blackbaud agreed to pay a $3-million civil penalty to settle administrative charges for alleged “materially misleading disclosures” about a 2020 ransomware attack. As we foreshadowed in our 2023 U.S. Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Outlook and Review, the increase in SEC enforcement resources (e.g., doubling the size of its Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit Ablaev sits in), in combination with the promulgation of cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incident disclosure rules Ablaev confirmed will be finalized in coming months, signal that cybersecurity will continue to be an area of heightened enforcement activity for the SEC. In light of these developments, it is critical companies take stock of their cyber hygiene policies and incident response protocols, and not only manage cybersecurity risks and prevent attacks, but also respond to them with proper disclosures. Ablaev at Incident Response Forum: SEC’s Priorities and Blackbaud as a Masterclass In What Not To Do
article.html:
It is no secret among public companies and their counsel that the US Securities and Exchange Commission has steadily adopted a more aggressive stance on cybersecurity controls and disclosure and incident response recordkeeping. SEC Senior Counsel Arsen Ablaev recently highlighted the Commission’s cybersecurity priorities at the annual Incident Response Forum Masterclass. SEC Chair Gary Gensler also emphasized risks in cyber and information security in the March 29 budget hearing with the House Appropriations Committee, and endorsed U.S. President Joe Biden’s request to earmark a record $2.4 billion in funding for the regulator in 2024. Last month saw yet another example of the SEC’s mounting focus on cyber disclosures as an enforcement priority with the announcement that cloud computing company Blackbaud agreed to pay a $3-million civil penalty to settle administrative charges for alleged “materially misleading disclosures” about a 2020 ransomware attack.

As we foreshadowed in our 2023 U.S. Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Outlook and Review, the increase in SEC enforcement resources (e.g., doubling the size of its Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit Ablaev sits in), in combination with the promulgation of cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incident disclosure rules Ablaev confirmed will be finalized in coming months, signal that cybersecurity will continue to be an area of heightened enforcement activity for the SEC. In light of these developments, it is critical companies take stock of their cyber hygiene policies and incident response protocols, and not only manage cybersecurity risks and prevent attacks, but also respond to them with proper disclosures.

Ablaev at Incident Response Forum: SEC’s Priorities and Blackbaud as a Masterclass In What Not To Do

article.title: Match.com Legal Chief Splits for GoDaddy and Its $10M Stock Grant
article.description: Jared Sine, chief legal and business affairs officer for Match Group, the Dallas-based owner of Match.com, Tinder, OkCupid and other online dating apps, is taking the top lawyer job at web hosting giant GoDaddy. He’ll receive an initial equity grant…
article.text: Jared Sine, chief legal and business affairs officer for Match Group, the Dallas-based owner of Match.com, Tinder, OkCupid and other online dating apps, is taking the top lawyer job at web hosting giant GoDaddy. He’ll receive an initial equity grant of $10 million, according to his employment agreement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission Thursday. That ranks in the upper tier of inducements companies have used in recent years to help lure a legal chief aboard. In January 2022, Dana Wagner received a $12.8 million hiring stock grant from Twilio after the jumped to the customer-engagement-software company from Impossible Foods.
article.html:
Jared Sine, chief legal and business affairs officer for Match Group, the Dallas-based owner of Match.com, Tinder, OkCupid and other online dating apps, is taking the top lawyer job at web hosting giant GoDaddy.

He’ll receive an initial equity grant of $10 million, according to his employment agreement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission Thursday. That ranks in the upper tier of inducements companies have used in recent years to help lure a legal chief aboard. In January 2022, Dana Wagner received a $12.8 million hiring stock grant from Twilio after the jumped to the customer-engagement-software company from Impossible Foods.

article.title: Judge Blasts Authors' Lawyers in Key AI Suit, Says Case Doomed Without Upgraded Team
article.description: The San Francisco federal judge overseeing prominent authors’ artificial intelligence copyright lawsuit against Meta said he’s completely lost confidence in the plaintiffs’ legal team and that he won’t grant class certification unless plaintiffs hire…
article.text: The San Francisco federal judge overseeing prominent authors’ artificial intelligence copyright lawsuit against Meta said he’s completely lost confidence in the plaintiffs’ legal team and that he won’t grant class certification unless plaintiffs hire a new one. The team, led by San Francisco antitrust and class action lawyer Joseph Saveri of the Joseph Saveri Law Firm and Los Angeles lawyer Matthew Butterick, has “failed to adequately and diligently litigate” the case, U.S. District Judge Vincent Chhabria said during an hourlong video hearing Friday. He expressed frustration that the case had not advanced further 11 months after its filing.
article.html:
The San Francisco federal judge overseeing prominent authors’ artificial intelligence copyright lawsuit against Meta said he’s completely lost confidence in the plaintiffs’ legal team and that he won’t grant class certification unless plaintiffs hire a new one.

The team, led by San Francisco antitrust and class action lawyer Joseph Saveri of the Joseph Saveri Law Firm and Los Angeles lawyer Matthew Butterick, has “failed to adequately and diligently litigate” the case, U.S. District Judge Vincent Chhabria said during an hourlong video hearing Friday. He expressed frustration that the case had not advanced further 11 months after its filing.

article.title: 'It's Just Really Frustrating': Microsoft IP Contract Dispute Removed to Federal Court on Eve of Pretrial Conference
article.description: “I think [Microsoft is] trying to avoid a trial and an adverse ruling on summary judgment," said Mark Walters of Lowe Graham Jones. Microsoft recently asked the Western District of Washington to issue a declaratory judgment of non-infringement…
article.text: “I think [Microsoft is] trying to avoid a trial and an adverse ruling on summary judgment," said Mark Walters of Lowe Graham Jones. Microsoft recently asked the Western District of Washington to issue a declaratory judgment of non-infringement concerning a former employee's patents. However, the employee's counsel contend the underlying issue isn't about patent infringement, it's a contractual dispute. Now, the other side is trying to get the case remanded back to state court. An ongoing contractual dispute between Microsoft and a former employee took on a new dimension when it was removed from the State Court of King County to the Western District of Washington on Wednesday. There, the tech giant also asked the federal court for a declaratory judgment of patent non-infringement. However, according to the former employee’s attorney, Mark Walters of Lowe Graham Jones, that’s not what the case is about.
article.html:

article.title: Legal Departments' Spending Soared Last Year, Fueled by Merger Frenzy, Outside Counsel Rate Hikes
article.description: LexisNexis CounselLink has its 2022 Enterprise Legal Management Trends Report. Corporate legal department spending shot up in 2021. The median hourly billing rate for partners at the 50 largest law firms was $895. The biggest chunk of spending went…
article.text: LexisNexis CounselLink has its 2022 Enterprise Legal Management Trends Report. Corporate legal department spending shot up in 2021. The median hourly billing rate for partners at the 50 largest law firms was $895. The biggest chunk of spending went to the 50 largest law firms, which all have at least 750 lawyers. They took in 46% of outside counsel spending, according to the report from LexisNexis CounselLink. Partners in firms with more than 750 lawyers have a median hourly billing rate of $895, 54% higher than the median hourly billing rate of the next tier of firms, the report found. The 2022 Enterprise Legal Management Trends Report, which is in its ninth year, is based on $49 billion in legal spending across 350,000 timekeepers, 8 million invoices and 1.2 million legal matters. The median partner rate for firms with 51 to 100 lawyers was $400, while the rate was $405 for firms with 101 to 200 lawyers. Kris Satkunas, director of strategic consulting for CounselLink and author of the report, said the largest firms’ expertise across many practices areas and geographies allows them to command higher rates. “Legal departments typically choose larger firms to handle more critical, strategic, or high-value work,” she said. “For example, bet the farm matters that are M&A, IP litigation, or regulatory issue related, are most often handled by the largest firms because they often have a lot of expertise in these areas, and that expertise continues to grow because they continue to handle most of that work.” Also driving up legal department spending was the record-shattering year for M&A. M&A-related legal fees rose from 4.3% of total legal billing in 2020 to 7.4% in 2021. The median partner rate billed for M&A work jumped 6.1% in 2021, reaching $878. The report documented the growing use of alternative fee arrangements, continuing a 10-year growth trend. Last year, 14.8% of matters were billed at least partly on a non-hourly basis, while 9.6% of all fees were non-hourly. “While [less than] 15% of matters being billed under an AFA may not be huge, it is a continuation of a gradual trend that does indicate a willingness to find creative pricing strategies,” Satkunas said. AFAs were used mainly when billing for intellectual property, labor and employment, and insurance. Nearly 60% of companies consolidated 80% or more of their legal work with 10 or fewer law firms, the report found. Satkunas said that, although some legal departments will bring more work in-house to reduce outside counsel spending, the most premium work likely will continue to be handled by outside counsel at the largest firms. “I think that savvy GCs will look to leverage both benchmarking data and the volume of work they provide these firms to minimize continued rate increases,” she said. Satkunas added: “In the current inflationary environment, it is increasingly important for corporate counsel to keep an eye on rate trends and work closely with outside counsel to manage costs.”
article.html:
• LexisNexis CounselLink has its 2022 Enterprise Legal Management Trends Report.
  • Corporate legal department spending shot up in 2021.
  • The median hourly billing rate for partners at the 50 largest law firms was $895.

The biggest chunk of spending went to the 50 largest law firms, which all have at least 750 lawyers. They took in 46% of outside counsel spending, according to the report from LexisNexis CounselLink.

Partners in firms with more than 750 lawyers have a median hourly billing rate of $895, 54% higher than the median hourly billing rate of the next tier of firms, the report found.

The 2022 Enterprise Legal Management Trends Report, which is in its ninth year, is based on $49 billion in legal spending across 350,000 timekeepers, 8 million invoices and 1.2 million legal matters.

The median partner rate for firms with 51 to 100 lawyers was $400, while the rate was $405 for firms with 101 to 200 lawyers.

Kris Satkunas, director of strategic consulting for CounselLink and author of the report, said the largest firms’ expertise across many practices areas and geographies allows them to command higher rates.

“Legal departments typically choose larger firms to handle more critical, strategic, or high-value work,” she said. “For example, bet the farm matters that are M&A, IP litigation, or regulatory issue related, are most often handled by the largest firms because they often have a lot of expertise in these areas, and that expertise continues to grow because they continue to handle most of that work.”

Also driving up legal department spending was the record-shattering year for M&A. M&A-related legal fees rose from 4.3% of total legal billing in 2020 to 7.4% in 2021. The median partner rate billed for M&A work jumped 6.1% in 2021, reaching $878.

The report documented the growing use of alternative fee arrangements, continuing a 10-year growth trend. Last year, 14.8% of matters were billed at least partly on a non-hourly basis, while 9.6% of all fees were non-hourly.

“While [less than] 15% of matters being billed under an AFA may not be huge, it is a continuation of a gradual trend that does indicate a willingness to find creative pricing strategies,” Satkunas said.

AFAs were used mainly when billing for intellectual property, labor and employment, and insurance.

Nearly 60% of companies consolidated 80% or more of their legal work with 10 or fewer law firms, the report found.

Satkunas said that, although some legal departments will bring more work in-house to reduce outside counsel spending, the most premium work likely will continue to be handled by outside counsel at the largest firms.

“I think that savvy GCs will look to leverage both benchmarking data and the volume of work they provide these firms to minimize continued rate increases,” she said.

Satkunas added: “In the current inflationary environment, it is increasingly important for corporate counsel to keep an eye on rate trends and work closely with outside counsel to manage costs.”

article.text: Wholesale building materials distributor Blue Linx has lured away ServiceMaster legal chief Tricia Kinney to serve as its chief legal officer. Blue Linx disclosed that Gibson had left the company and vacated his board seat in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing, saying only that his departure would be treated as termination without cause. Gibson was paid a little more than $1.5 million in severance, according to the filing.

article.title: OpenAI's General Counsel Weighs In on How to Regulate AI, Why His Firm's Unique Structure Matters
article.description: OpenAI in August promoted Deputy General Counsel Che Chang to GC. A former senior corporate counsel at Amazon, Chang joined OpenAI in 2021. He said OpenAI's unique structure—a nonprofit owns a for-profit with capped profits—causes it to view…
article.text: OpenAI in August promoted Deputy General Counsel Che Chang to GC. A former senior corporate counsel at Amazon, Chang joined OpenAI in 2021. He said OpenAI's unique structure—a nonprofit owns a for-profit with capped profits—causes it to view regulation and profitability differently from other AI companies. OpenAI General Counsel Che Chang says he’s a strong proponent of artificial intelligence regulation, a view that puts him in line with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman but less so with other AI industry executives. He said regulators are “trying to make sure humanity stays at the forefront of technology, not the other way around,” Chang said. “I think that’s what we all want.”

article.title: FTC Claims Genetic Testing Company Publicly Exposed Health Data
article.description: Genetic testing company 1Health.io has been charged with exposing customers' private health data, the FTC claims in a first-of-its-kind complaint The company stored the unencrypted information in publicly accessible AWS buckets in the cloud. A…
article.text: Genetic testing company 1Health.io has been charged with exposing customers' private health data, the FTC claims in a first-of-its-kind complaint The company stored the unencrypted information in publicly accessible AWS buckets in the cloud. A proposed settlement requires 1Health.io to pay $75,000 in refunds. In its first case focused on the security and privacy of genetic information, the Federal Trade Commission has charged genetic testing company 1Heath.io with failing to secure its customers’ genetic data by storing health reports of more than 2,000 of its customers in the cloud without encryption or access controls. The San Francisco-based firm, called Vitagene prior to a 2020 name change, sold “DNA Health Test Kits” that instructed customers to send in a saliva sample by mail and fill out an online questionnaire about their health, ancestry and lifestyle. It used the information to generate health and wellness reports identifying a customer’s risk of developing certain health conditions like high cholesterol or obesity based on their genetics, bundling the data along with vitamin subscriptions and nutritional coaching for a product package that could cost up to $259.
article.html:
• Genetic testing company 1Health.io has been charged with exposing customers' private health data, the FTC claims in a first-of-its-kind complaint
  • The company stored the unencrypted information in publicly accessible AWS buckets in the cloud.
  • A proposed settlement requires 1Health.io to pay $75,000 in refunds.

In its first case focused on the security and privacy of genetic information, the Federal Trade Commission has charged genetic testing company 1Heath.io with failing to secure its customers’ genetic data by storing health reports of more than 2,000 of its customers in the cloud without encryption or access controls.

The San Francisco-based firm, called Vitagene prior to a 2020 name change, sold “DNA Health Test Kits” that instructed customers to send in a saliva sample by mail and fill out an online questionnaire about their health, ancestry and lifestyle. It used the information to generate health and wellness reports identifying a customer’s risk of developing certain health conditions like high cholesterol or obesity based on their genetics, bundling the data along with vitamin subscriptions and nutritional coaching for a product package that could cost up to $259.

article.title: Aspartame Study Results May Take Fizz Out of Push to File Tsunami of Suits
article.description: "Proving that any particular plaintiff's cancer was caused by aspartame, as distinguished from the many other possible causes, could prove to be an insuperable obstacle to recovery," said Kenneth Abraham, a University of Virginia law professor. Last…
article.text: "Proving that any particular plaintiff's cancer was caused by aspartame, as distinguished from the many other possible causes, could prove to be an insuperable obstacle to recovery," said Kenneth Abraham, a University of Virginia law professor. Last week’s news on aspartame might have sounded bad for Coca-Cola and other consumer-product companies that widely use the artificial sweetener. After all, no manufacturer wants this kind of headline about one of its key ingredients, “Aspartame May Be a Carcinogen: How Worried Should You Be?” But attorneys in the food and beverage industry and academia say the mixed messages released on Friday about aspartame are unlikely to trigger the torrent of litigation that some class action lawyers had been gearing up for.

article.title: High-Profile Exxon Mobil Attorney Departs Despite Company's Looming GC Opening
article.description: Assistant General Counsel David Woodcock is leaving Exxon Mobil just a year before its prized general counsel job is set to open up. Woodcock said he's leaving because the company is moving from suburban Dallas to Houston, and he doesn't want to…
article.text: Assistant General Counsel David Woodcock is leaving Exxon Mobil just a year before its prized general counsel job is set to open up. Woodcock said he's leaving because the company is moving from suburban Dallas to Houston, and he doesn't want to relocate while he has children in high school. David Woodcock’s announcement this week that he is stepping down as assistant general counsel of Exxon Mobil and joining Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher seemingly eliminates from contention a strong candidate to become the next general counsel of the oil giant. Woodcock told Law.com that he never set out as a career goal to become Exxon Mobil’s general counsel and doesn’t know whether the board and CEO Darren Woods would have chosen him. But the Dallas Business Journal and a source close to the company said Woodcock’s departure surprised colleagues, in part because the GC job is set to open up in just one year.

article.title: Managing Global Legal Departments, Risk and Gender Discrimination: A Q&A with Veteran General Counsel Susie Flook
article.description: Susie Flook, former general counsel of The Body Shop. With more than four decades of experience as an in-house leader and executive for several prominent global companies, Susie Flook is an expert at fostering collaboration among members of far-flung…
article.text: Susie Flook, former general counsel of The Body Shop. With more than four decades of experience as an in-house leader and executive for several prominent global companies, Susie Flook is an expert at fostering collaboration among members of far-flung legal departments and other business teams within a firm. Flook began her in-house career with The Coca-Cola Export Corp. in Sydney before joining CPC UK Ltd., where she focused on global merger and acquisition deals. She moved on to beer maker Guinness and helped the company prepare for a $22 billion merger deal with Grand Metropolitan.
article.html:
Susie Flook, former general counsel of The Body Shop.

article.title: After Trial by Fire, Robinhood Legal Chief Knows Keys to Getting Along With SEC
article.description: Dan Gallagher took the legal reins at Robinhood in 2020, just before the meme stock trading frenzy roiled the company. Gallagher said companies mistakenly think the SEC should be feared and avoided, when engagement is a better long-term strategy. He…
article.text: Dan Gallagher took the legal reins at Robinhood in 2020, just before the meme stock trading frenzy roiled the company. Gallagher said companies mistakenly think the SEC should be feared and avoided, when engagement is a better long-term strategy. He said outside counsel were critical in helping Robinhood weather regulatory and congressional investigations. The past three years have been a roller coaster for Robinhood chief legal compliance and corporate affairs officer Dan Gallagher, who grabbed the legal reins at the online brokerage only months before the meme stock-trading craze plunged the company into chaos. During his tenure, Gallagher has weathered investigations by both Congress and the Securities and Exchange Commission, an IPO that drew allegations of false and misleading statements by investors (recently dismissed by a federal judge) and a severe market downturn that sent its stock plummeting. article.title: New Corporate-Transparency Laws to Require 'Mountain of Filings'
article.description: People looking for anonymity in their business dealings might be shocked to find they no longer can use limited liability companies to hide their ownership interests under the Corporate Transparency Act, a federal law aimed at curtailing money…
article.text: People looking for anonymity in their business dealings might be shocked to find they no longer can use limited liability companies to hide their ownership interests under the Corporate Transparency Act, a federal law aimed at curtailing money laundering that went into effect on Jan. 1. The feds aren’t the only ones going after shell companies. In December, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed into law the New York LLC Transparency Act, a similar measure that requires beneficial owners of LLCs to file personal information with the New York Department of State. California’s legislature has its own version of the law in the works.

article.title: With the Rise of Generative AI, Legal Departments Lean on Law Firms as ‘Business Partners’ More Than Ever
article.description: Legal departments expect law firms to consider the use of generative AI to improve their own business models for the benefit of their clients. Multiple studies have shown there is also a significant perception of hurdles to adoption. At the same…
article.text: Legal departments expect law firms to consider the use of generative AI to improve their own business models for the benefit of their clients. Multiple studies have shown there is also a significant perception of hurdles to adoption. At the same time, some in-house counsel are calling upon outside counsel to help them navigate their role as a risk-mitigators. Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they’re placing similar expectations on their outside counsel. Certainly, caution reigns supreme in the ongoing dialogue between legal departments and law firms concerning the adoption of generative AI. Yet, in-house leaders are increasingly looking to outside counsel to at the very least understand the technology, if not use it to drive their own business efficiencies.

article.title: FTC Preps for Crackdown on the Wild West of Social Media Influencers
article.description: The FTC recently released updated guidelines for companies that use social media influencers. Issuing guidelines is a step the agency typically takes before unleashing a wave of enforcement actions in an industry. The FTC has been relatively quiet in…
article.text: The FTC recently released updated guidelines for companies that use social media influencers. Issuing guidelines is a step the agency typically takes before unleashing a wave of enforcement actions in an industry. The FTC has been relatively quiet in this arena previously, resolving about two dozen investigations since 2011. The Federal Trade Commission recently issued new regulatory-compliance guidelines for the social media influencer market, a step it typically takes to put an industry on notice before it substantially ramps up enforcement actions. The FTC’s increased attention to the sector comes as it grows explosively. A report this year from Data Bridge Market Research projects the market will grow from $7.4 billion in 2021 to $70.0 billion by 2029.

article.title: U.S. Regulators Lift the Curtain on Data Privacy Practices
article.description: In the second generation of state consumer privacy laws and regulations, numerous states require affirmative due diligence and a structured approach for conducting and documenting risk assessments. Companies subject to the applicable state privacy…
article.text: In the second generation of state consumer privacy laws and regulations, numerous states require affirmative due diligence and a structured approach for conducting and documenting risk assessments. Companies subject to the applicable state privacy laws need to develop or refine their data inventory and assessment practices as a top priority in 2024. California enacted the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018, which was the first of its kind in the U.S. and drew inspiration from Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Following California’s lead, other states, including Colorado, implemented their own laws and regulations. California further strengthened its legislation in 2020 through a ballot initiative known as the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA). Unlike the GDPR, the first generation CCPA was light on affirmative due diligence requirements and many companies designed data privacy and protection programs that were little more than window dressing (e.g., privacy policies and a consumer rights request process). In the second generation of state consumer privacy laws and regulations, as well as in recent laws pertaining to the privacy of minors (such as in California and Connecticut), numerous states require affirmative due diligence and a structured approach for conducting and documenting risk assessments and associated remediation. The assessment documentation must be available for review by regulators, and the CPRA requires risk assessments to be filed with the state, a requirement that is currently under consideration in a condensed form with certification by the executive officer. This means that companies subject to the applicable state privacy laws need to develop or refine their data inventory and assessment practices as a top priority in 2024 to be prepared for the coming enforcement of these requirements. How Did We Get Here?
article.html:
• In the second generation of state consumer privacy laws and regulations, numerous states require affirmative due diligence and a structured approach for conducting and documenting risk assessments.
  • Companies subject to the applicable state privacy laws need to develop or refine their data inventory and assessment practices as a top priority in 2024.

California enacted the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018, which was the first of its kind in the U.S. and drew inspiration from Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Following California’s lead, other states, including Colorado, implemented their own laws and regulations. California further strengthened its legislation in 2020 through a ballot initiative known as the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA).

Unlike the GDPR, the first generation CCPA was light on affirmative due diligence requirements and many companies designed data privacy and protection programs that were little more than window dressing (e.g., privacy policies and a consumer rights request process). In the second generation of state consumer privacy laws and regulations, as well as in recent laws pertaining to the privacy of minors (such as in California and Connecticut), numerous states require affirmative due diligence and a structured approach for conducting and documenting risk assessments and associated remediation. The assessment documentation must be available for review by regulators, and the CPRA requires risk assessments to be filed with the state, a requirement that is currently under consideration in a condensed form with certification by the executive officer. This means that companies subject to the applicable state privacy laws need to develop or refine their data inventory and assessment practices as a top priority in 2024 to be prepared for the coming enforcement of these requirements.

article.title: U-Haul Names Successor to Retiring Legal Chief
article.description: Kristine Campbell will take the legal reins from Larry De Respino when he retires on May 12. De Respino was general counsel at U-Haul for 18 years. Campbell has served as assistant general counsel for nine years and also is director of litigation.…
article.text: Kristine Campbell will take the legal reins from Larry De Respino when he retires on May 12. De Respino was general counsel at U-Haul for 18 years. Campbell has served as assistant general counsel for nine years and also is director of litigation. Kristine Campbell will succeed veteran U-Haul general counsel Larry De Respino when he retires in May, the company announced Wednesday. Campbell was a member of Greenberg Traurig’s class action team in Phoenix, where U-Haul has its headquarters, before joining U-Haul in 2011. She has spent the last nine years working under De Respino as assistant general counsel, and has headed litigation at the company since 2020. This content has been archived. article.title: Evolving Standards for Remote Lawyers
article.description: During the pandemic, remote work became the norm, with some lawyers even making such choices permanent by moving their homes to locations where they are not admitted to practice law. This shift has raised a number of ethical issues for courts and…
article.text: During the pandemic, remote work became the norm, with some lawyers even making such choices permanent by moving their homes to locations where they are not admitted to practice law. This shift has raised a number of ethical issues for courts and bars. The Georgia Bar addressed this question involving a hypothetical lawyer working in Georgia in Formal Advisory Opinion No. 22-1 (“FAO”): “[u]nder Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 5.5, may a Domestic Lawyer or a Foreign Lawyer provide legal services by remote means from Georgia while residing in Georgia, when the services have no relationship with Georgia other than the lawyer’s physical location?”
article.html:
During the pandemic, remote work became the norm, with some lawyers even making such choices permanent by moving their homes to locations where they are not admitted to practice law. This shift has raised a number of ethical issues for courts and bars.

The Georgia Bar addressed this question involving a hypothetical lawyer working in Georgia in Formal Advisory Opinion No. 22-1 (“FAO”): “[u]nder Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 5.5, may a Domestic Lawyer or a Foreign Lawyer provide legal services by remote means from Georgia while residing in Georgia, when the services have no relationship with Georgia other than the lawyer’s physical location?”

article.title: Tesla Legal Chief Aims to Build In-House Litigation Powerhouse
article.description: General counsel Brandon Ehrhart raised eyebrows by encouraging Big Law litigators to apply to work at Tesla. Ehrhart said in a tweet that the company is building a full-scale internal litigation and trial team. Elon Musk said in his own tweet the the…
article.text: General counsel Brandon Ehrhart raised eyebrows by encouraging Big Law litigators to apply to work at Tesla. Ehrhart said in a tweet that the company is building a full-scale internal litigation and trial team. Elon Musk said in his own tweet the the team's targets would include short-sellers, certain law firms and corrupt regulators. Tesla’s new legal chief is on the hunt for Big Law partners with litigation and trial experience to beef up its in-house team. General counsel Brandon Ehrhart, who joined the company in January from DISH Network, put out a call for applicants on LinkedIn last week, writing, “Are you an experienced partner at a top law firm? Do you enjoy handling sophisticated litigation and trials but are frustrated by internal issues like conflicts and passing on work for clients you love? Tesla Legal is building something unique: a full-scale internal litigation and trial team that can handle all aspects of litigation and trial work, including briefings, hearings, discovery, depositions and trials, completely in-house.” This content has been archived. article.title: Why Do Large Companies Have So Many Empty General Counsel Seats?
article.description: A dozen of the largest companies in the U.S. were operating without an official chief lawyer as the firms entered 2021, which is the highest number of general counsel vacancies that John Gilmore, co-founder and managing partner of BarkerGilmore, has…
article.text: A dozen of the largest companies in the U.S. were operating without an official chief lawyer as the firms entered 2021, which is the highest number of general counsel vacancies that John Gilmore, co-founder and managing partner of BarkerGilmore, has ever seen. Gilmore attributes the empty GC seats, at least in part, to the unprecedented demands and stress that top lawyers have faced over the past year. Those factors, combined with soaring stock prices, might have enticed more general counsel to cash out, he said.

article.title: AI Chipmaker Cerebras Gets New Legal Chief
article.description: Cerebras, a chipmaker specializing in designing artificial intelligence processors and supercomputer hardware, has hired Shirley Li, the former legal chief at Snapdocs, to head its legal department. Li was with Snapdocs, a mortgage startup that helps…
article.text: Cerebras, a chipmaker specializing in designing artificial intelligence processors and supercomputer hardware, has hired Shirley Li, the former legal chief at Snapdocs, to head its legal department. Li was with Snapdocs, a mortgage startup that helps realtors manage the home-buying process in the cloud, for nearly two years, starting as general counsel then becoming chief legal and people officer in late 2022. Before that, she was with software firm Cadence Design systems, where she served in various in-house roles, including senior corporate counsel and associate general counsel focusing on securities, mergers and acquisitions, corporate governance and compliance.

article.text: A federal judge late Monday trimmed claims against AI-powered image creators accused of ripping off artists’ work but said the artists’ direct copyright infringement theories should be put to the test on summary judgment. His ruling is the latest turn in a high-profile class action brought by a slew of cartoonists, painters and illustrators who say AI startups Stability AI, Midjourney, Runway AI and DeviantArt used their art to train machine learning models Stable Diffusion and AI image generators Dream Up and AI Magic Tools without paying the artists or getting their consent.

article.title: Protecting Technology-Assisted Works and Inventions: Where Does Smart Technology End and AI Begin?
article.description: With the widespread adoption of AI technologies will come the need for companies and innovators to protect AI technologies under then-current intellectual property frameworks. Efforts to protect and enforce intellectual property on AI-based…
article.text: With the widespread adoption of AI technologies will come the need for companies and innovators to protect AI technologies under then-current intellectual property frameworks. Efforts to protect and enforce intellectual property on AI-based technologies are likely to be hampered by a lack of both a unified governing framework and a common understanding of the technology. These complex issues will probably be decided upon by courts, and subsequently the Federal Circuit or the Supreme Court.

article.title: Mike Lynch's Brush With Prison Taught Him Life Is Precious. Then a Yacht Accident Proved Him Right
article.description: Mike Lynch spent years fighting to exonerate himself of charges of fraud and conspiracy over the sale of his British software startup, Autonomy. When a clerk at the San Francisco federal courthouse read out the verdict of “not guilty” on June 6,…
article.text: Mike Lynch spent years fighting to exonerate himself of charges of fraud and conspiracy over the sale of his British software startup, Autonomy. When a clerk at the San Francisco federal courthouse read out the verdict of “not guilty” on June 6, Lynch, who had remained largely stoic throughout his three-month criminal trial, began to cry. His co-defendant, former finance executive Stephen Chamberlain, had been acquitted, too. And before the clerk had even finished speaking, the courtroom erupted into a flurry of sobs, hugs and handshakes. Cries of elation and relief rang out through the gallery. In the hallway, Chamberlain sat on a bench, holding up his phone and beaming. He told the person on the other end that he couldn’t wait to get home.

article.title: Former Facebook Security Chief Sounds Off on the Case that Rocked the Cybersecurity World
article.description: A jury found former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan guilty of covering up a 2016 data breach, in an unprecedented prosecution of a company executive. Sullivan is set to be sentenced on May 4 and faces significant jail time. Former Facebook…
article.text: A jury found former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan guilty of covering up a 2016 data breach, in an unprecedented prosecution of a company executive. Sullivan is set to be sentenced on May 4 and faces significant jail time. Former Facebook security chief Alex Stamos said the prosecution sets a terrible precedent. Companies of all sizes are under assault from sophisticated ransomware groups, and the government’s recent prosecution of a former Uber executive for failing to disclose a data breach to law enforcement has company executives, and security chiefs in particular, anxious that they might be next. Alex Stamos, former chief security officer at Facebook and now director at the Stanford Internet Observatory, said Tuesday that the unprecedented criminal case against ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan, the first of its kind against a company executive, is problematic on several fronts. article.title: Nonpracticing Entity Spikes Patent Infringement Filings in California
article.description: The company has filed 45 patent infringement actions against businesses, including Walmart, Guitar Center and Big Lots, since 2021. Nonpracticing entity Linfo IP triggered a litigation trend this week after filing several patent infringement lawsuits…
article.text: The company has filed 45 patent infringement actions against businesses, including Walmart, Guitar Center and Big Lots, since 2021. Nonpracticing entity Linfo IP triggered a litigation trend this week after filing several patent infringement lawsuits in the Central District of California on Tuesday. The lawsuits claimed the defendants' websites' customer review portals allegedly infringed on the plaintiff's patent. So far, Linfo IP has filed at least 45 patent infringement claims across the country. Patent defense attorneys in the Southern District of New York and Central District of California have their work cut out for them after Texas-based nonpracticing entity Linfo IP unleashed a flurry of four new patent infringement suits on Tuesday, alleging several companies have customer review portals that infringe on its intellectual property. The current alleged infringers include business review platform Trustpilot and timepiece retailer MVMT Watches. This isn’t Linfo’s first foray with alleged infringers. According to CourtListener, the company has filed 45 patent infringement actions against businesses, including Walmart, Guitar Center and Big Lots, since 2021. The company was and continues to be represented by William “Bill” Ramey III and sometimes Susan Kalra of the Texas-based Ramey Firm.

article.title: Who Got the Work: Sheppard Mullin Team Steps In to Defend Visionox in Patent Case
article.description: Sheppard Mullin partners Batts, Liang and Ponder appeared on behalf of Visionox Technology. The China-based company and its U.S. subsidiary allegedly violated patents held by SEL of Japan. The case centers on technology used in smartphones sold by…
article.text: Sheppard Mullin partners Batts, Liang and Ponder appeared on behalf of Visionox Technology. The China-based company and its U.S. subsidiary allegedly violated patents held by SEL of Japan. The case centers on technology used in smartphones sold by U.K.-based Nothing Technology. Sheppard Mullin partners Harper Batts, Jeffrey Liang and Chris Ponder on July 3 entered appearances for Visionox Technology and Visionox America in a pending patent infringement lawsuit. A complaint filed on May 7 by Fish & Richardson on behalf of Semiconductor Energy Laboratory in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California alleged that Visionox and co-defendant Nothing Technology have made, sold and marketed smartphones with displays that infringe on three U.S. patents.

article.title: Generative AI Tools Threaten Big Tech's Digital Advertising Dominance | Corporate Counsel
article.description: “Data is not oil. It’s water that will be shared by everyone. Every company is trying to figure out how to build a relationship with the customer and provide something of value to them, said Vijay Viswanathan, a marketing professor at Northwestern University.
article.text: Generative AI has changed the advertising game, upping the pressure on Silicon Valley heavyweights to fight harder for online advertising dollars. Long a dominant player in the ad business, Google is under particular strain not to be left behind by the chatbot takeover, as brands are figuring out how to use tools like ChatGPT to engage directly with consumers. "Google will have to fight it out," said Vijay Viswanathan, associate dean of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University. "Many brands will try to figure out how they can go directly to customers and how they can create personalized content with ChatGPT. We might see a shift, and companies like the Googles of the world will have to figure out their value in the marketplace." This content has been archived. article.title: Cybersecurity Startup Hires GC, Rebuilds Legal Team After Mass Layoffs
article.description: What You Need to Know Snyk's legal chief and legal ops chief got the ax in last fall's retrenchment. The company raised nearly $200 million in December, an infusion that rekindled growth. The funding round was at a valuation of $7.4 billion. In-house…
article.text: What You Need to Know Snyk's legal chief and legal ops chief got the ax in last fall's retrenchment. The company raised nearly $200 million in December, an infusion that rekindled growth. The funding round was at a valuation of $7.4 billion. In-house veteran David Morris joined cybersecurity platform Snyk as general counsel as it continues to rebuild its legal team after a wave of layoffs last year that included its chief legal officer and head of legal operations. Morris shared the news on LinkedIn. “Since 2015, Snyk has led the way for developer security to make the digital world a safer place. I’m proud to take part in their mission to help organizations worldwide develop applications securely,” he wrote. He most recently was general counsel at online-ticketing platform Vivid Seats, which he departed in December. Before that, he spent 13 years as associate general counsel at Tripadvisor. Morris is among a string of executive hires recently announced by Snyk. Also coming aboard are Als Myke Lyons as chief information security officer, Jonaki Egenolf as chief marketing officer and Michael Durso as senior vice president of sales. In a blog post, CEO Peter McKay said the hires will help Snyk further its mission of helping enterprises strengthen their developer security. “Jonaki, Myke, David and Michael each bring an incredibly valuable point of view and the right relevant experience to best position us for growing success as we continue to lead the developer security category we invented,” McKay said. “As DevSecOps becomes increasingly mainstream, together we look forward to helping more global brands shift away from a legacy cybersecurity mindset and fully embrace this cultural revolution,” McKay said. The hires follow a tumultuous year for Snyk, which cut 14% of its global workforce last October in a round of restructuring that McKay said was necessary for the company to operate more efficiently in the face of global economic headwinds. Caught in the layoffs were CLO Karyn Smith, who joined Snyk in January 2022 after seven years as legal chief at San Francisco-based Twilio, and Susan Packal, who stepped down as Twilio’s senior director of legal operations and chief of staff in May 2022 to become vice president of legal operations at Snyk. According to LinkedIn, Smith has not taken a new post while Packal this month become the head of global legal operations for the software firm Atlassian. Snyk shifted back into growth mode after it closed in December on a $196 million Series G funding round at a valuation of $7.4 billion. The round was led by Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund Qatar Investment Authority. Snyk has since added to its legal team, hiring Krista Matthews as vice president of commercial legal in February and Kathryn “Kate” Helin as privacy lead counsel in April. Legal operations specialist Katie Corso joined in March, along with lead counsel Lauren Wilk. On LinkedIn, Morris said a few more additions to the team will be coming soon. “One of the many reasons that I was so enthusiastic about the General Counsel role at Snyk was the opportunity to build a diverse, global team of well rounded legal ‘athletes,’ who are both responsive to a fast moving, growing organization as well as true partners to the business with deep enterprise tech knowledge,” Morris said in an email to Law.com. “As we continue to build the Snyk team and our legal function further matures, I’m personally committed to identifying diverse, passionate candidates who care deeply about building Snyk’s business through a deep understanding of the company’s mission and cybersecurity solutions,” Morris said. He said he’s embraced team-building throughout his career, including at Tripadvisor, where he was the company’s first legal hire in 2008. When he left in 2021, it was publicly traded and had 4,000 employees. Snyk also announced a series of business moves in recent months, including buying the application security management firm Enso Security for more than $50 million. Cooley, which advised Snyk on the last two of its 13 funding rounds, worked on the deal. In April, Snyk launched a series of enhancements to its developer security platform intended to help other businesses create a secure software supply chain. The company made CNBC’s Disruptor 50 List this year, and also was favorably recognized by consulting firms Gartner and Forrester. Morris said Snyk is adding to its legal ranks on the heels of these milestones. “We are adding multiple people to the legal team over the next few months, and expect further growth in the future,” he said.
