article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Snyk's legal chief and legal ops chief got the ax in last fall's retrenchment.
  • The company raised nearly $200 million in December, an infusion that rekindled growth.
  • The funding round was at a valuation of $7.4 billion.

In-house veteran David Morris joined cybersecurity platform Snyk as general counsel as it continues to rebuild its legal team after a wave of layoffs last year that included its chief legal officer and head of legal operations.

Morris shared the news on LinkedIn. “Since 2015, Snyk has led the way for developer security to make the digital world a safer place. I’m proud to take part in their mission to help organizations worldwide develop applications securely,” he wrote.

He most recently was general counsel at online-ticketing platform Vivid Seats, which he departed in December. Before that, he spent 13 years as associate general counsel at Tripadvisor.

Morris is among a string of executive hires recently announced by Snyk. Also coming aboard are Als Myke Lyons as chief information security officer, Jonaki Egenolf as chief marketing officer and Michael Durso as senior vice president of sales.

In a blog post, CEO Peter McKay said the hires will help Snyk further its mission of helping enterprises strengthen their developer security. “Jonaki, Myke, David and Michael each bring an incredibly valuable point of view and the right relevant experience to best position us for growing success as we continue to lead the developer security category we invented,” McKay said.

“As DevSecOps becomes increasingly mainstream, together we look forward to helping more global brands shift away from a legacy cybersecurity mindset and fully embrace this cultural revolution,” McKay said.

The hires follow a tumultuous year for Snyk, which cut 14% of its global workforce last October in a round of restructuring that McKay said was necessary for the company to operate more efficiently in the face of global economic headwinds.

Caught in the layoffs were CLO Karyn Smith, who joined Snyk in January 2022 after seven years as legal chief at San Francisco-based Twilio, and Susan Packal, who stepped down as Twilio’s senior director of legal operations and chief of staff in May 2022 to become vice president of legal operations at Snyk. According to LinkedIn, Smith has not taken a new post while Packal this month become the head of global legal operations for the software firm Atlassian.

Snyk shifted back into growth mode after it closed in December on a $196 million Series G funding round at a valuation of $7.4 billion. The round was led by Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund Qatar Investment Authority.

Snyk has since added to its legal team, hiring Krista Matthews as vice president of commercial legal in February and Kathryn “Kate” Helin as privacy lead counsel in April. Legal operations specialist Katie Corso joined in March, along with lead counsel Lauren Wilk. On LinkedIn, Morris said a few more additions to the team will be coming soon.

“One of the many reasons that I was so enthusiastic about the General Counsel role at Snyk was the opportunity to build a diverse, global team of well rounded legal ‘athletes,’ who are both responsive to a fast moving, growing organization as well as true partners to the business with deep enterprise tech knowledge,” Morris said in an email to Law.com.

“As we continue to build the Snyk team and our legal function further matures, I’m personally committed to identifying diverse, passionate candidates who care deeply about building Snyk’s business through a deep understanding of the company’s mission and cybersecurity solutions,” Morris said.

He said he’s embraced team-building throughout his career, including at Tripadvisor, where he was the company’s first legal hire in 2008. When he left in 2021, it was publicly traded and had 4,000 employees.

Snyk also announced a series of business moves in recent months, including buying the application security management firm Enso Security for more than $50 million.

Cooley, which advised Snyk on the last two of its 13 funding rounds, worked on the deal. In April, Snyk launched a series of enhancements to its developer security platform intended to help other businesses create a secure software supply chain. The company made CNBC’s Disruptor 50 List this year, and also was favorably recognized by consulting firms Gartner and Forrester.

Morris said Snyk is adding to its legal ranks on the heels of these milestones. “We are adding multiple people to the legal team over the next few months, and expect further growth in the future,” he said.

article.title: Iron Mountain General Counsel Says CEOs Putting More Pressure on In-House Leaders to Drive Diversity
article.description: For the last several years, general counsels have been putting pressure on outside law firms to hire more diverse lawyers. Now, CEOs are leaning on their in-house leaders to drive corporate diversity initiatives amid heightened public awareness and…
article.text: For the last several years, general counsels have been putting pressure on outside law firms to hire more diverse lawyers. Now, CEOs are leaning on their in-house leaders to drive corporate diversity initiatives amid heightened public awareness and outrage over inequality and systemic racism, according to Deborah Marson, general counsel, executive vice president and secretary of Iron Mountain Inc.
article.html:
For the last several years, general counsels have been putting pressure on outside law firms to hire more diverse lawyers.

Now, CEOs are leaning on their in-house leaders to drive corporate diversity initiatives amid heightened public awareness and outrage over inequality and systemic racism, according to Deborah Marson, general counsel, executive vice president and secretary of Iron Mountain Inc.

article.title: AG Garland Calls Prosecuting Execs 'Greatest Deterrent' to Corporate Fraud
article.description: Speaking at a white-collar crime conference in San Francisco, AG Merrick Garland also discussed the rising use of AI by cybercriminals and "the heightened level of threats and the hyperspeed of threats against everyone who works in public spaces."
article.text: That Attorney General Merrick Garland is a Swiftie is well-known. So it wasn't surprising that when he was asked at the American Bar Association's institute on white-collar crime Wednesday to name his favorite Taylor Swift song, he drew from the lyrics of multiple hits. "Vigilante S***" from Swift's "Midnights" album "should be the theme song for white-collar crime," Garland said. He added that he chose it as the "anthem for this group" but that his favorite song remains "Shake It Off." "Shake off the outside attacks, shake off the political stuff that's going on," he said. "Do your job and follow the principles of prosecution and follow the rule of law." Addressing a packed ballroom at downtown San Francisco's Marriott Marquis, Garland said he's focused more than ever on preserving the integrity of the country's economic and democratic institutions. On the white-collar front, he said the Department of Justice will make it a priority to prosecute individual bad actors and send the message that the rich and powerful are not above the law. "If people think there is a different rule for the powerless and the powerful, the rich and the poor, they lose respect not only for the DOJ, for prosecutors, but for the rule of law and the country," he said. "That's why our first priority in white-collar crime is going after individual bad actors," he said. "All of us know that the acts of corporations are the acts of individuals. The greatest deterrent to white-collar crime is fear of individual prosecutions of the executives of companies." Garland made the remarks as part of a broader conversation with Kenneth Polite, a former assistant attorney general for the DOJ's Criminal Division, who observed that Garland is now on his fourth tour of duty with the agency, having served under five attorneys general before President Bill Clinton appointed him to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in 1997. Garland said little has changed with respect to the dedication of the DOJ's lawyers and staff, who "had to do the right thing, had to do it in the right way, filtering out the noise of Washington and the politics just to do what our job is supposed to do." "I'm really proud to find that the department is still the way it was when I was last there. On the changed side, what concerns me is the heightened level of threats and the hyperspeed of threats against everyone who works in public spaces; against our judges, against our prosecutors, against our agents, against cops, against local law enforcement of every kind and against election workers, the volunteers who run our elections." Garland said he's well aware that domestic terrorism is hardly new—he worked on such high-profile domestic terrorism cases as the Oklahoma City and Atlanta Olympics bombings—"but what's different now is the speed at which these attacks are accelerating, the speed at which we accelerate from threats to actual kinetic action. That's what worries me. And that's why our priority is to fight these attacks." Every day, his office holds an "all-threats meeting" with the FBI, intelligence agencies and the DOJ's National Security Division. "We call it the scary meeting," he said. "We're just spending the entire day allocating our resources to respond to the kind of threats that we're facing— domestic terrorism, foreign terrorism and foreign nation states." He also addressed an emerging new threat—artificial intelligence, which he said has supercharged cyberattacks against companies, law firms, the government and the military. "We're worried about the ways in which it can accelerate the cyberattacks that are happening daily, almost minute-ly," he said. "On the positive side, it also enables us to react at light speed to the attacks on our system. Where it's no longer possible for human computer operators to fight off the enormous number of hacks that occur constantly, AI can make it easier for us to defend our systems." He also said the DOJ would aggressively pursue cases against foreign nationals who try to steal trade secrets from American tech firms working on AI. Just hours before Garland spoke, the DOJ charged Linwei Ding, a Chinese national who worked as a software engineer at Google, with stealing the company's proprietary AI information. Ding, who helped Google develop software for its supercomputing data centers, was charged with four counts of trade secrets theft. The DOJ alleged that Ding downloaded confidential information about Google's hardware infrastructure, its machine-learning software platform, and the AI models and applications they supported, and planned to use those secrets for his own startup based in China. The feds also said that Ding was secretly affiliated with another China-based startup while he worked at Google, serving as its chief technology officer and tasked with developing software for machine learning on graphics processing unit chips, the same thing he was simultaneously doing at Google. At the outset of his conversation with Polite, Garland dropped the news that an indictment against Ding had just been unsealed. "The Justice Department just will not tolerate the theft of our trade secrets in the area of AI," Garland said. U.S. Attorney Ismail Ramsey, who also spoke at the ABA's institute Wednesday, said in a statement that his office "is committed to protecting the innovation of our Silicon Valley companies" and that he "will aggressively investigate and prosecute the theft of sensitive trade secrets by insiders like Ding, particularly when the theft endeavors to jump start illegitimate competition." Media outlets have been unable to locate an attorney for Ding for comment.

article.title: What to Expect From the SEC Under Trump 2.0
article.description: Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority.
article.text: Donald Trump's reclaiming of the White House could spell the end of one of the most aggressive SEC rulemaking and enforcement regimes in history. Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority and more concerned with issues affecting Main Street and everyday retail investors. "We've already seen what the SEC in a Trump 1.0 administration looked like, where the SEC focused on bread-and-butter cases focused on addressing harm to retail investors, such as offering frauds, Ponzi schemes and excessive fees charged by investment advisory firms," said Jennifer Lee, a Jenner & Block partner who formerly spent 12 years with the SEC, rising to assistant regional director of its enforcement division. By contrast, the SEC under current Chair Gary Gensler has been more willing to bring individual compliance cases against public companies and investment firms it regulates, even if there is no investor harm," she said. In his three years as chair, Gensler has steered the commission into uncharted territory, pushing initiatives on climate change disclosure, environmental, social and governance investing and corporate greenwashing. Preemptive compliance measures were at the center of Gensler's ambitious regulatory agenda. Observers said he wanted to get ahead of issues that, if left unchecked, could lead to greater fraud or investor harm down the road. To that end, the commission expanded its authority into policing data-security incidents and cyber-risk disclosures, greenhouse gas emission reporting and regulating the use of AI and other types of predictive analytics by broker-dealers and investment advisers. "The SEC under Chair Gensler has been aggressive in terms of really putting in prospective requirements in emerging substance areas like cybersecurity, ESG and also AI," Lee said. She expects that, under the Trump administration, the SEC will likely pull back on rulemaking and adopt a less stringent stance on enforcement, particularly when it comes to pushing the bounds of existing rules. Trump already has vowed to fire Gensler "on day one" and appoint a replacement. One credible successor is Robinhood Chief Legal, Compliance and Corporate Affairs Officer Dan Gallagher, who was an SEC commissioner from 2011 to 2015, according to people familiar with the discussions, Also well-respected in the legal community and a potential to successor are Hester Pierce, who has been a Republican GOP commissioner since 2017 and is known for her incisive dissents, and Chris Giancarlo, a former chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, who is now a partner at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Legal observers say that, under a new chair, the SEC likely will abandon ESG rulemaking and will stop trying to implement its new rule requiring public companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions. That rule is on holding amid challenges by industry groups and Republican-run states. Novel legal theories also likely will be out, including its controversial push to apply internal accounting controls to cybersecurity, legal observers said. In July, a federal judge sided with software firm SolarWinds on the question of whether the provisions of the the Securities Exchange Act that give the SEC authority to regulate accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls. The judge "resoundingly rejected" that premise, finding that the SEC was overreaching. Aravind Swaminathan, a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, told Law.com at the time. Lee said the SEC under its next chair will be less likely to test its legal boundaries. "There will be more of a hewing to tried and true legal theories," she said. "The SEC under Trump will generally be more skeptical of novel theories in enforcement actions. The posture will also matter—the SEC may be more open to novel theories that will be litigated before a court or tried in front of a jury, versus theories that companies may feel they have to settle just to move on from an issue." She also anticipates that the SEC will be less exacting in its demands around cyber-incident disclosures and will shy away from bringing enforcement actions in instances where regulatory violations may have occurred but there is no evidence of consumers being harmed. Last month, the commission fined four companies that it said downplayed intrusions into their systems and misled investors about their cybersecurity risks, an action that brought a strong dissent from Pierce and fellow GOP commissioner Mark Uyeda. Lee said that, in the future, the SEC might not require minute details like the identity of a threat actor or the percentage of data exfiltrated from a company's systems, issues that came into play in its enforcement action against the four companies. Instead, she and other attorneys expect the SEC's focus to shift back to staple issues like retail fraud, calculation of fees and conflicts of interest associated with financial incentives, as well as ensuring that firms aren't misrepresenting themselves to consumers. "While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates and member of its asset management and investment funds practice. "Ultimately what the SEC's priorities are is going to depend on the new chair, but I would expect that their approach to rulemaking and enforcement would be more consistent with what we saw during the first Trump administration."

article.title: Lawyers Drowning in Cases Are Embracing AI Fastest—and Say It's Yielding Better Outcomes for Clients
article.description: “This is the first technology wave that no lawyer can ignore," said Aaref Hilaly, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures, which invests in legal document automation companies.
article.text: Lawyers with sky-high caseloads are adopting generative artificial intelligence with the greatest zeal—embracing the technology to screen cases, draft demand letters, pull together medical records and refine litigation strategies. And they're finding it's giving them a big advantage over those mired in traditional ways of working. They’re able to do more with less, resolve cases faster and achieve better outcomes. It’s also supercharging their output. “It's an advantage available to both sides, and it’s sort of an arms race to a certain extent, where when one side gets equipped with one advantage, the other side will have to essentially respond,” said James Lee, a former litigator at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan and at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius who two decades ago started his own boutique firm, LTL Attorneys. He said litigation departments have historically been the least productive in terms of producing revenue. An old-timer at Morgan Lewis once told him this all changed with the advent of the Xerox machine. “Because when the Xerox machine was invented, people made copies of copies of copies of documents, memos, and reports, and guess who had to review them all? Litigators. And then at that point you had the number of billable hours on litigation cases go up.” Email and e-discovery likewise increased the volume of data lawyers had to deal with, and now AI is amping things up even more. Which can be good for lawyers who know how to exploit it. “If you truly are part of the elite, you're going to do fine. If you truly admit that you are a commodity firm, you're going to do fine. These firms in the middle are going to struggle, and at some point they'll just disappear." Lee saw the revolution coming six years ago when he attended a week-long program for AM Law 200 partners and practice heads at Harvard Law School. “On one of the days, they talked about how AI had already started to take over portions of the medical world, and it was just a matter of time before it would start taking over portions of law,” he said. Lee remembered looking around the room. “I could see the look of fear in their eyes,” he said. “Lawyers are motivated by two things, fear or greed. Mostly fear. And you could just see the fear in their eyes. And I had that fear too, by the way—that I thought these bigger firms were going to steal our lunch.” 'This Is Nuts' When Lee returned to LTL's Los Angeles headquarters, he told his partners to experiment with AI platforms. Soon, they were able to do work in two minutes that junior lawyers required eight hours to complete—answering a lawsuit, coming up with affirmative defenses, and drafting very targeted discovery questions based on the complaint. “Six years ago, people were going, ‘This is nuts,' because it really is replicating the work of what a junior lawyer would be doing,” Lee said. But it became so successful that he and LTL partners Enoch Liang and Thomas Suh spun out those services into a new company, LegalMation, which provides AI tools that automate the creation of legal documents, streamlining the early phases of a lawsuit. Walmart became its first client. Later, U.S. auto companies and large insurance companies signed on, as did a handful of high-volume litigation firms. Lee said the services make the most sense for litigators with high-volume caseloads. “I'm doing dishes one night, and my wife says, ‘Hey, you run an automation company. Why aren't you using a dishwasher?’ And I couldn't answer this question, and it took me two weeks before I realized I just don't do enough dishes. ... I see automation the same way.” Automation has been a particular game-changer for insurers. “There's one large national insurance carrier where, in 33 states, we are handling all of their motor vehicle accident claims,” Lee said. “That works out to about 60,000 cases. That’s a lot of dirty dishes. And it’s where it begins to make sense, getting a number of these dishwashers all over the country for their teams.” LegalMation launched in 2016 as the first AI company to automate and enhance litigation tasks. Today, the landscape is vastly different, with more than 500 legal document automation companies globally, 85 of which have received venture capital funding, according to the technology research firm Tracxn. The 85 firms have raised $27.3 billion, with LegalMation scooping up nearly $24 million, including $15 million in a funding round last year. Investors are wowed by the sector's potential. “This is the first technology wave that no lawyer can ignore. Any lawyer who doesn't embrace AI will get swept away ... because the way to succeed in law will be to leverage it,” said Aaref Hilaly, a Bay Area-based partner at Bain Capital Ventures, an investor in legal document automation companies. He said that while lawyers today are still struggling with how to use AI in the right way, within a couple of years "it will become a standard part of the workflow.” 'Medical Records Are Everything' One of the legal automation companies Bain is backing is San Francisco-based EvenUp, a four-year-old startup that's raised $235 million. The company sells software that helps level the playing field for plaintiffs' attorneys as they litigate personal injury lawsuits against big corporate defendants. EvenUp says its AI platform allows PI attorneys to settle cases faster and for larger amounts, based on its analysis of case details and its large database of past verdicts and settlements. The platform also provides medical summaries, robust estimates for losses, and storytelling to support settlement proposals. “It’s an industry where you have about 20 million claims every year that range from motor vehicle accidents to dog bite cases, even police brutality cases," Rami Karabibar, co-founder and CEO of EvenUp, told Law.com. "There are many different ways folks get injured, and there's a pretty big distribution in terms of what these cases settle for and how long it takes these cases to settle. We’re making sure that these cases are won purely for their merit and settle as fast as they can." The idea grew out of dissatisfaction co-founder Ray Mieszaniec felt after his father was permanently disabled in a car accident and then went through a protected court battle that yielded a settlement that was minuscule compared with what he could have received had his attorney known how much to demand. Karabibar said the database of settlements and verdicts helps both sides, since enabling personal injury attorneys to make data-supported settlement demands resolves cases faster, sparing defendants of the costs of carrying a case for months or years. "It's actually a process that we took from the insurance world and the defense side. We're leveraging it on the plaintiff side, because they don't typically have access to the same data and resources," he said. Bob Simon, a personal injury attorney in California who uses EvenUp, said writing his own demand letters was a huge pain point when he was starting out as a solo practitioner. He estimated it would take 20 hours to write the letter and find all the missing medical records and bills to submit to the insurance company. He said having all the right documentation at his fingertips is a critical advantage. “Medical records are everything to win that case. We have to know them very well, we have to know them quickly, and we have to be organized. So when we're going to a trial, if somebody throws a punch you didn't see coming, I have to go back to the medical records very quickly and see it. But that doesn't really happen anymore because we have Even Up when we’re at trial." As a lawyer who receives a lot of referrals from other firms, the technology has also helped him screen incoming cases to determine whether they’re worth his time. “We call it finding the grenade,” Simon said. “Are there prior medical records they're missing? Are there big red flags in the medical records that this lawyer that's shopping us the case didn't see or was trying to hide? It actually happens a lot. And EvenUp makes it a lot easier to find that grenade.” Bain Capital's Hilaly, whose firm led EvenUp’s $135 million funding round that closed in October, said the company focuses on an area of the law that’s tailor-made to reap AI’s benefits. “You have the lawyers receiving vast volumes of information which they have to make sense of very quickly in terms of medical case histories and interview notes and police records and whatever else is involved. And then all of that has to be distilled quickly and efficiently down into a single legal document, the demand letter. "And then you have to kind of follow the progress of that case over time and kind of keep track of it and all the follow-ups. And you have to create other exhibits like medical chronologies to show a timeline of events. So it felt to us as we looked at it that personal injury is the perfect starting point for AI.” Simon said using the EvenUp platform has made him a better lawyer. “I truly believe that if you were leveraging artificial intelligence, you could spend more time in your client's living room than the mail room,” Simon said. “That's where we make our cases more valuable. We are sitting down with our clients, learning their damages story, what makes what they lost important, and then being able to communicate that story to a jury. If you leverage artificial intelligence, it makes it so much easier to do that stuff.”
article.html:
Lawyers with sky-high caseloads are adopting generative artificial intelligence with the greatest zeal—embracing the technology to screen cases, draft demand letters, pull together medical records and refine litigation strategies. And they're finding it's giving them a big advantage over those mired in traditional ways of working.

They’re able to do more with less, resolve cases faster and achieve better outcomes. It’s also supercharging their output.

“It's an advantage available to both sides, and it’s sort of an arms race to a certain extent, where when one side gets equipped with one advantage, the other side will have to essentially respond,” said James Lee, a former litigator at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan and at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius who two decades ago started his own boutique firm, LTL Attorneys.

An old-timer at Morgan Lewis once told him this all changed with the advent of the Xerox machine. “Because when the Xerox machine was invented, people made copies of copies of copies of documents, memos, and reports, and guess who had to review them all? Litigators. And then at that point you had the number of billable hours on litigation cases go up.”

Email and e-discovery likewise increased the volume of data lawyers had to deal with, and now AI is amping things up even more. Which can be good for lawyers who know how to exploit it.

article.title: How General Counsel Jennifer McGlinn Drives Diversity in the Construction Industry
article.description: Jennifer McGlinn, general counsel for Power Home Remodeling. Courtesy photo Jennifer McGlinn has served as general counsel for Power Home Remodeling for only about a year. But in that short time, the company has welcomed about 100 new female…
article.text: Jennifer McGlinn, general counsel for Power Home Remodeling. Courtesy photo Jennifer McGlinn has served as general counsel for Power Home Remodeling for only about a year. But in that short time, the company has welcomed about 100 new female employees to its national workforce. When McGlinn joined the Chester, Pennsylvania-based company in 2019, Power launched a gender diversity initiative that added $1,000 to an existing $2,000 general referral bonus for employees who referred women who ended up being hired.
article.html:
Jennifer McGlinn, general counsel for Power Home Remodeling. Courtesy photo

Jennifer McGlinn has served as general counsel for Power Home Remodeling for only about a year. But in that short time, the company has welcomed about 100 new female employees to its national workforce.

When McGlinn joined the Chester, Pennsylvania-based company in 2019, Power launched a gender diversity initiative that added $1,000 to an existing $2,000 general referral bonus for employees who referred women who ended up being hired.

article.title: AI Boom Has Left Employers With Head-Spinning Governance Challenges
article.description: With the artificial intelligence genie out of the bottle, government and industry now must get their arms around another topic that’s nearly as complicated as the technology itself: AI governance, the policies, laws and regulations that will guide…
article.text: With the artificial intelligence genie out of the bottle, government and industry now must get their arms around another topic that’s nearly as complicated as the technology itself: AI governance, the policies, laws and regulations that will guide the development, use and deployment of AI systems. The “AI Governance in Practice Report 2024,” released Tuesday by FTI Consulting and the International Association of Privacy Professionals, lists 31 of what the report calls “some of the most prominent and consequential” AI governance efforts in the world—from the EU AI Act and the White House “Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights” to the Digital India Act and The OECD Framework for Classifying AI Systems.
article.html:
With the artificial intelligence genie out of the bottle, government and industry now must get their arms around another topic that’s nearly as complicated as the technology itself: AI governance, the policies, laws and regulations that will guide the development, use and deployment of AI systems.

The “AI Governance in Practice Report 2024,” released Tuesday by FTI Consulting and the International Association of Privacy Professionals, lists 31 of what the report calls “some of the most prominent and consequential” AI governance efforts in the world—from the EU AI Act and the White House “Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights” to the Digital India Act and The OECD Framework for Classifying AI Systems.

article.title: Merill Lynch Alum to Head Legal Team at Mortgage Giant
article.description: Carlos Pelayo has joined Mr. Cooper Group as executive vice president and chief legal officer. Mr. Cooper Group is the nation's largest nonbank home loan servicer. Pelaya is succeeding Eldridge Burns Jr., who became general counsel of Exeter Finance…
article.text: Carlos Pelayo has joined Mr. Cooper Group as executive vice president and chief legal officer. Mr. Cooper Group is the nation's largest nonbank home loan servicer. Pelaya is succeeding Eldridge Burns Jr., who became general counsel of Exeter Finance last year. The nation’s largest nonbank home loan servicer, Mr. Cooper Group, has appointed Merrill Lynch’s Carlos Pelayo to lead its in-house legal team, replacing executive vice president and Chief Legal Officer Eldridge Burns Jr., who departed last year. Pelayo comes from Merrill Lynch Wealth Management, acquired by Bank of America in 2009, where he spent eight years as managing director of its legal and compliance division. article.title: Senior Boeing Attorney Steps In to HR Chief Role as Contentious Labor Talks Loom
article.description: Uma Amuluru, who has rapidly climbed the leadership rungs in Boeing's legal department, will become chief human resources officer. She'll replace Michael D'Ambrose, who is retiring. Boeing in March will kick off contract talks with its largest union.…
article.text: Uma Amuluru, who has rapidly climbed the leadership rungs in Boeing's legal department, will become chief human resources officer. She'll replace Michael D'Ambrose, who is retiring. Boeing in March will kick off contract talks with its largest union. Uma Amuluru, general counsel for Boeing Co.’s defense and aerospace division, is headed for the C-suite this spring. She’ll replace current HR chief Michael D’Ambrose when her job starts on April 1, Boeing said. D’Ambrose said he plans to retire in July, capping a career extending back to the 1970s that included senior leadership roles at Ingersoll Rand, The Travelers, Citigroup, Toys R Us and ADM.
article.html:
• Uma Amuluru, who has rapidly climbed the leadership rungs in Boeing's legal department, will become chief human resources officer.
  • She'll replace Michael D'Ambrose, who is retiring.
  • Boeing in March will kick off contract talks with its largest union.

Uma Amuluru, general counsel for Boeing Co.’s defense and aerospace division, is headed for the C-suite this spring.

She’ll replace current HR chief Michael D’Ambrose when her job starts on April 1, Boeing said. D’Ambrose said he plans to retire in July, capping a career extending back to the 1970s that included senior leadership roles at Ingersoll Rand, The Travelers, Citigroup, Toys R Us and ADM.

article.title: Facebook Taps Former Deputy HP General Counsel to Head App Legal
article.description: Willie Hernandez already had IBM, Amazon.com Inc. and Hewlett Packard on his stellar resume. Now he’s added another big firm: Facebook Inc., which he credits with a global reach that can change how communities—no matter how far apart—interact with…
article.text: Willie Hernandez already had IBM, Amazon.com Inc. and Hewlett Packard on his stellar resume. Now he’s added another big firm: Facebook Inc., which he credits with a global reach that can change how communities—no matter how far apart—interact with each other. Hernandez joined the Menlo Park, California-based firm this week as director and associate general counsel of product. He will lead the legal team for Facebook’s core app. His first day on the job was June 29.

article.title: Laid-Off In-House Lawyers Still Finding Jobs, But Could Face Stiffer Competition
article.description: What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire. Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs…
article.text: What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire. Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs pummeling the tech industry. And while there are still jobs aplenty for those seeking reemployment, legal recruiters warn that the tide could be turning. “We haven’t seen a lot of in-house lawyers desperately looking for jobs,” said Sean Burke, founding partner at legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. However, he added, there’s been a marked increase in applications from law firm lawyers looking to go in-house, leading him to suspect that layoffs have mostly affected the other side. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.
  • Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions.

In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs pummeling the tech industry. And while there are still jobs aplenty for those seeking reemployment, legal recruiters warn that the tide could be turning.

“We haven’t seen a lot of in-house lawyers desperately looking for jobs,” said Sean Burke, founding partner at legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. However, he added, there’s been a marked increase in applications from law firm lawyers looking to go in-house, leading him to suspect that layoffs have mostly affected the other side.

article.title: Despite Cuts, Fenwick Sees Revenue Growth and Remains Bullish on Tech Business Bounceback
article.description: "Some uncertainty remains. But it will come back, and come back stronger," said firm chair Richard Dickson about the firm's scope of work. "We just don’t know exactly when." Fenwick, which announced a reduction of nearly 10% of its professionals a…
article.text: "Some uncertainty remains. But it will come back, and come back stronger," said firm chair Richard Dickson about the firm's scope of work. "We just don’t know exactly when." Fenwick, which announced a reduction of nearly 10% of its professionals a month ago, still grew by about 3% across several categories in 2023. The California-headquartered firm grossed nearly $770 million, up from $750.4 million the previous year. The firm's equity and nonequity ranks expanded. And the firm's chair is expecting 2024 to be 'another growth year.' While Fenwick & West announced layoffs amounting to nearly 10% of its professionals a month ago, the law firm still grew by roughly 3% in revenue, revenue per lawyer and net income in 2023. The California-headquartered firm grossed nearly $770 million, with revenue per lawyer rising to $1.6 million and net income reaching $365.1 million.
article.html:
"Some uncertainty remains. But it will come back, and come back stronger," said firm chair Richard Dickson about the firm's scope of work. "We just don’t know exactly when."

  • Fenwick, which announced a reduction of nearly 10% of its professionals a month ago, still grew by about 3% across several categories in 2023.
  • The California-headquartered firm grossed nearly $770 million, up from $750.4 million the previous year.
  • The firm's equity and nonequity ranks expanded. And the firm's chair is expecting 2024 to be 'another growth year.'

While Fenwick & West announced layoffs amounting to nearly 10% of its professionals a month ago, the law firm still grew by roughly 3% in revenue, revenue per lawyer and net income in 2023.

The California-headquartered firm grossed nearly $770 million, with revenue per lawyer rising to $1.6 million and net income reaching $365.1 million.

article.title: Amid Executive Shakeup, Rivian Taps Former LinkedIn, Yahoo GC as Legal Chief
article.description: Before entering academia, Callahan was senior vice president and general counsel at LinkedIn, where he had global responsibility for legal, regulatory and public policy matters, including corporate governance. Before that, he was executive vice…
article.text: Before entering academia, Callahan was senior vice president and general counsel at LinkedIn, where he had global responsibility for legal, regulatory and public policy matters, including corporate governance. Before that, he was executive vice president and chief legal officer at Ten-X and executive vice president and general counsel at Yahoo. Callahan replaces Neil Sitron, who was the Irvine, California-based company’s first general counsel. Sitron’s departure from the company in September was the beginning of an executive exodus that continued to the start of the year. The executive departures came after the company fell short of its production targets.
article.html:
Before entering academia, Callahan was senior vice president and general counsel at LinkedIn, where he had global responsibility for legal, regulatory and public policy matters, including corporate governance. Before that, he was executive vice president and chief legal officer at Ten-X and executive vice president and general counsel at Yahoo.

Callahan replaces Neil Sitron, who was the Irvine, California-based company’s first general counsel. Sitron’s departure from the company in September was the beginning of an executive exodus that continued to the start of the year. The executive departures came after the company fell short of its production targets.

article.title: Split Maryland High Court Approves Lewis Brisbois Associate for Admission to State Bar Following Cheating Scandal
article.description: In a 5-2 majority order Tuesday, the Maryland Supreme Court followed two other jurisdictions in approving an applicant to the state bar after his character was flagged for cheating on a University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law bar…
article.text: In a 5-2 majority order Tuesday, the Maryland Supreme Court followed two other jurisdictions in approving an applicant to the state bar after his character was flagged for cheating on a University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law bar preparation exam during his final semester. Samuel Edward Howie, who is now a labor and employment law associate in Lewis Brisbois Bisgaard & Smith’s Newark, New Jersey, office, has previously been granted admission to both the New Jersey and New York state bars. He had applied to the Maryland State Bar in July 2021, and in a split decision Tuesday, the state high court’s majority concluded that Howie should also admitted to practice law in the third state.
article.html:
In a 5-2 majority order Tuesday, the Maryland Supreme Court followed two other jurisdictions in approving an applicant to the state bar after his character was flagged for cheating on a University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law bar preparation exam during his final semester.

Samuel Edward Howie, who is now a labor and employment law associate in Lewis Brisbois Bisgaard & Smith’s Newark, New Jersey, office, has previously been granted admission to both the New Jersey and New York state bars. He had applied to the Maryland State Bar in July 2021, and in a split decision Tuesday, the state high court’s majority concluded that Howie should also admitted to practice law in the third state.

article.title: UPDATE: In Georgia Case, Ex-Law Partner Says He Doesn't Know When Willis and Wade's Relationship Began
article.description: A potential key witness for lawyers seeking to derail the Georgia election interference case against former President Donald Trump and others returned to the witness stand Tuesday, but repeatedly said he couldn’t remember when pressed about details…
article.text: A potential key witness for lawyers seeking to derail the Georgia election interference case against former President Donald Trump and others returned to the witness stand Tuesday, but repeatedly said he couldn’t remember when pressed about details of the romantic relationship between District Attorney Fani Willis and another top prosecutor. Special prosecutor Nathan Wade’s former law partner and onetime divorce attorney, Terrence Bradley, testified that he does not know when Wade’s relationship with Willis began, adding: “I do not have knowledge of it starting or when it started.”

article.title: Use of SCOTUS Foreign Corporation Ruling Fails in Non-Compete Suit
article.description: Norton Rose Fulbright won a foreign defendant jurisdiction issue where the plaintiff tried to use a U.S. Supreme Court decision sue in a Texas court. Repairify, a Plano-based firm, sued Michigan-based Opus IVS for tortious interference. The Dallas…
article.text: Norton Rose Fulbright won a foreign defendant jurisdiction issue where the plaintiff tried to use a U.S. Supreme Court decision sue in a Texas court. Repairify, a Plano-based firm, sued Michigan-based Opus IVS for tortious interference. The Dallas Court of Appeals ruled a SCOTUS 2023 opinion was specific to a Pennsylvania law and did not apply in Texas. A Norton Rose Fulbright litigation team prevailed on appeal in a tortious-interference lawsuit where the plaintiff tried to use a recent Supreme Court of the United States decision to sue a Michigan-based defendant in Texas. In a prepared statement, Norton Rose said this was the first time a Texas court of appeals tested the Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co., a case where the court concluded a Pennsylvania’s business registration statute—which expressly provided that registered foreign corporations consented to the personal jurisdiction of Pennsylvania courts—did not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
article.html:
• Norton Rose Fulbright won a foreign defendant jurisdiction issue where the plaintiff tried to use a U.S. Supreme Court decision sue in a Texas court.
  • Repairify, a Plano-based firm, sued Michigan-based Opus IVS for tortious interference.
  • The Dallas Court of Appeals ruled a SCOTUS 2023 opinion was specific to a Pennsylvania law and did not apply in Texas.

A Norton Rose Fulbright litigation team prevailed on appeal in a tortious-interference lawsuit where the plaintiff tried to use a recent Supreme Court of the United States decision to sue a Michigan-based defendant in Texas.

Norfolk Southern Railway Co., a case where the court concluded a Pennsylvania’s business registration statute—which expressly provided that registered foreign corporations consented to the personal jurisdiction of Pennsylvania courts—did not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

article.title: IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger
article.description: Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon. The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works…
article.text: Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon. The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works since August 2022, amid strong resistance from antitrust regulators in the European Union. In November, the EU’s competition authority said it was concerned that the acquisition, which would have added the Roomba to Amazon’s range of devices, would unfairly restrict competition in the market for robot vacuums. Amazon said it will pay iRobot a $94 million termination fee for walking way from the deal.

article.title: Cash Is King for Startups as Venture Capital Pulls Back
article.description: Startups face a more challenging fundraising environment and more scrutiny from investors. Founders used to hold the cards, but the tables have turned. Some observers say this is a healthier environment. The balance of power has shifted in the…
article.text: Startups face a more challenging fundraising environment and more scrutiny from investors. Founders used to hold the cards, but the tables have turned. Some observers say this is a healthier environment. The balance of power has shifted in the startup realm. Entrepreneurs who once had their pick of investors will have a harder time raising money in 2023. Venture capital firms are also pushing back, insisting on due diligence and demanding better terms. The market is looking quite different than it did in 2021, when founders could command higher valuations, fewer restrictions on share sales and more of a say in board composition. article.title: Disney's Impending Restructuring Presents a Test for Its Star General Counsel
article.description: What You Need to Know Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page.…
article.text: What You Need to Know Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page. Horacio Gutierrez landed one of the top legal jobs in the world last December—general counsel of The Walt Disney Co. But just months into the job, the board has fired Bob Chapek—the man who hired him—a sudden shift that presents the first big test for the former Spotify chief legal officer. Legal observers say the big question is whether Gutierrez can conform to new CEO Bob Iger’s vision as he undos some changes by Chapek, whom the board dismissed Sunday after nearly three years at the helm. The change-out occurred after the company reported terrible fiscal fourth-quarter results on Nov. 8, and Chapek was widely criticized for nonetheless striking an upbeat tone during a conference call with analysts later that day. While Iger hasn’t revealed specifics, he said in a staff memo that he will be instituting “organizational and operating changes,” adding, “It is my intention to restructure things in a way that honors and respects creativity as the heart and soul of who we are,” with more control shifting to content-creating teams. Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said Iger will assess whether Gutierrez fits into his new vision of the company. “Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around? A lot of times when you have CEO changes, the CEO likes to ensure their direct reports and executive management team are all in alignment and can work well together, especially in a situation where you are trying to right the ship,” he said. “The reality of it is, when you’re steering a large ship like this, the executive team needs to be a well-oiled machine and all be on the same page on where the company is going to go and how it’s going to get there. If that’s not the case, the strategy is sort of doomed to failure.” Randy Milch, a former executive vice president and general counsel of Verizon, said Gutierrez has the chops to weather the changes. Gutierrez has more than 35 years of legal experience. He joined Spotify in 2016, starting out as vice president of business and legal affairs. Three years later, the company promoted him to head of global affairs and chief legal officer. He came to Spotify from Microsoft, where he’d spent 17 years, rising to general counsel. This is Iger’s second go-round as Disney CEO. He spent 15 years at the helm of the Burbank, California-based company, a period when it prospered, before retiring in 2020. He remained on the board until stepping down as executive chairman at the end of last year, nine days after the company announced the hiring of Gutierrez as senior executive vice president and general counsel. “Gutierrez has been a senior lawyer at a bunch of companies for quite a long time. I think he’s as well positioned as anyone to understand what happens in the corporate structure when the CEO changes,” Milch said. “The thing that is a little bit different here is that Iger was the CEO for a very long time, very successfully. He had a structure in place and his successor changed that structure, and Iger seems to be saying more or less that he’s going to change the structure back to the way it was.” Gutierrez succeeded Alan Braverman, who retired after nearly two decades as general counsel. Braverman regularly ranked among the highest-paid GCs in the country. In 2021, he received total compensation of $16.6 million. That included $8.8 million in cash—more than any other legal chief. Gutierrez has a rich pay package, as well. His employment agreement shows he could earn more than $22 million in his first year, including an initial stock grant of $10 million and a $2 million signing bonus. Gutierrez, who could not be reached for comment for this story, started his new job in February. He is one of the newer faces on Disney’s leadership roster, which includes longtime executives Alan Bergman, Rebecca Campbell, James Pitaro and Christine McCarthy. Milch, the former Verizon general counsel, said Chapek’s ouster fundamentally changes Gutierrez’s job. “When you’re a new general counsel, you come in and you have a CEO who has not been there very long who is remolding the place. That means there’s time to bond with that new CEO and become an effective executor of that vision he has. And that vision is now going to be changed,” Milch said. “And [Iger] had the benefit of working with Braverman for a very long time.” Gutierrez’s Spotify background should serve him well as the company tries to wring profitably out of its streaming platform, an area Iger made a priority when he unveiled Disney+ in 2019. “My prediction is not that there’s going to be further turmoil, but there is going to be a successful effort to work together,” Milch said. Foehl—who spent nearly a decade in-house at Target, including serving as its first director of corporate compliance and ethics—said one of Gutierrez’s biggest challenges will be ensuring the company meets its compliance obligations as it restructures and resets priorities. “You have a company who is reporting concerning financial numbers, and you have changes that are happening and more that are to come. The opportunities tend to be increased a bit in maybe taking ethical or compliance shortcuts,” he said. “They need to makes sure they are on guard. When the seas are stormy and everyone’s eyes are on ‘what’s going to happen to me’ and that sort of thing, it’s important that companies have a heightened vigilance when it comes to ethical and compliance issues.” Disney’s in-house team also will have to see the company through any plans for asset sales or purchases. Some investors have suggested the company sell ESPN or accelerate the purchase of the one-third of Hulu it doesn’t already own. The stake is held by Comcast. Under the existing agreement between the two companies, Disney has the right to buy it starting in 2024. “Whatever the new strategy is will have to be navigated from a legal perspective,” Foehl said. “Change can be concerning and it can be anxiety inducing. But the flip side for that is change can be exciting and incredibly fulfilling from a professional perspective.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.
  • The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.
  • Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page.

“The reality of it is, when you’re steering a large ship like this, the executive team needs to be a well-oiled machine and all be on the same page on where the company is going to go and how it’s going to get there. If that’s not the case, the strategy is sort of doomed to failure.”

“Gutierrez has been a senior lawyer at a bunch of companies for quite a long time. I think he’s as well positioned as anyone to understand what happens in the corporate structure when the CEO changes,” Milch said.

“The thing that is a little bit different here is that Iger was the CEO for a very long time, very successfully. He had a structure in place and his successor changed that structure, and Iger seems to be saying more or less that he’s going to change the structure back to the way it was.”

“When you’re a new general counsel, you come in and you have a CEO who has not been there very long who is remolding the place. That means there’s time to bond with that new CEO and become an effective executor of that vision he has. And that vision is now going to be changed,” Milch said. “And [Iger] had the benefit of working with Braverman for a very long time.”

Gutierrez’s Spotify background should serve him well as the company tries to wring profitably out of its streaming platform, an area Iger made a priority when he unveiled Disney+ in 2019.

“My prediction is not that there’s going to be further turmoil, but there is going to be a successful effort to work together,” Milch said.

Foehl—who spent nearly a decade in-house at Target, including serving as its first director of corporate compliance and ethics—said one of Gutierrez’s biggest challenges will be ensuring the company meets its compliance obligations as it restructures and resets priorities.

“You have a company who is reporting concerning financial numbers, and you have changes that are happening and more that are to come. The opportunities tend to be increased a bit in maybe taking ethical or compliance shortcuts,” he said.

“They need to makes sure they are on guard. When the seas are stormy and everyone’s eyes are on ‘what’s going to happen to me’ and that sort of thing, it’s important that companies have a heightened vigilance when it comes to ethical and compliance issues.”

Disney’s in-house team also will have to see the company through any plans for asset sales or purchases. Some investors have suggested the company sell ESPN or accelerate the purchase of the one-third of Hulu it doesn’t already own. The stake is held by Comcast. Under the existing agreement between the two companies, Disney has the right to buy it starting in 2024.

“Whatever the new strategy is will have to be navigated from a legal perspective,” Foehl said. “Change can be concerning and it can be anxiety inducing. But the flip side for that is change can be exciting and incredibly fulfilling from a professional perspective.”

article.title: Will Legal Chief Be Next to Go at Embattled National Association of Realtors?
article.description: National Association of Realtors CEO Bob Goldberg stepped down Thursday following a $1.8 billion jury verdict in a pricing-conspiracy lawsuit. Even before that stinging legal loss, NAR members were blasting top executives, including chief legal…
article.text: National Association of Realtors CEO Bob Goldberg stepped down Thursday following a $1.8 billion jury verdict in a pricing-conspiracy lawsuit. Even before that stinging legal loss, NAR members were blasting top executives, including chief legal officer Katie Johnson, saying they'd fostered a toxic workplace culture and should resign. Johnson, who has been legal chief since 2014, earned $963,164 in 2021, the latest year publicly available. The National Association of Realtors says CEO Bob Goldberg’s sudden departure has nothing to reawith a $1.8 billion jury verdict against the organization handed down this week for inflating agent commissions, or widespread complaints of sexual harassment against NAR’s former president. But there’s no mistaking that the timing was uncanny. And it raises questions about the fate of other top executives—including chief legal officer Katie Johnson, who even before the verdict was facing calls to resign from a group of vocal NAR members who say the organization is in dire need of a leadership and workplace-culture overhaul.

article.text: The EEOC flipped to Democratic control in August, one of several developments leading employment lawyers to predict the agency will be filing more transgender-discrimination cases. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission recently settled a transgender-harassment lawsuit, extracting $25,000 from an upstate New York pizzeria accused of forcing an employee to quit to escape endless harassment. While that suit against T.C. Wheelers Bar & Pizzeria was the first trans-discrimination case the agency had filed since 2017, employment attorneys expect many more as the EEOC files more lawsuits overall, follows through on its new Strategic Enforcement Plan’s focus on protecting vulnerable workers, and as the number of Americans identifying themselves as trans swells.

article.title: Boeing Turns to String of Big Law Firms for Latest Legal Troubles
article.description: While the aviation giant retained Perkins Coie to handle a new suit related to a door plug blowout, Boeing is also working with several others, such as Kirkland & Ellis and McGuireWoods, for ongoing matters. Boeing has retained Perkins Coie for a new…
article.text: While the aviation giant retained Perkins Coie to handle a new suit related to a door plug blowout, Boeing is also working with several others, such as Kirkland & Ellis and McGuireWoods, for ongoing matters. Boeing has retained Perkins Coie for a new class action lawsuit stemming from the door plug blowout. The firm has turned to Kirkland & Ellis, McGuireWoods, Jones Day, Mayer Brown for counsel on other matters, according to court records. Ken Callander, founder of Value Strategies, indicated that while Boeing's legal troubles will be costly, it may turn to firms it has used in the past. As Boeing’s legal woes mount, the aviation giant has retained a number of Big Law firms to handle litigation and investigations. The company’s recent legal counsel include Perkins Coie, Kirkland & Ellis, McGuireWoods, Jones Day, Mayer Brown and Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, according to court records. Recently, Boeing turned to Perkins Coie to handle a new class action lawsuit related to a door plug blowout on a 737 Max 9 flight last month.

article.title: Female GCs Who Break Into Fortune 1000 Earn Big Bucks, But Men Hold Most of the Jobs
article.description: Corporate Counsel and ALM Intelligence have released their 2023 General Counsel Compensation Report. It shows that women GCs in the Fortune 1000 earn slightly more than men, but men hold far more of the jobs. The report includes compensation for…
article.text: Corporate Counsel and ALM Intelligence have released their 2023 General Counsel Compensation Report. It shows that women GCs in the Fortune 1000 earn slightly more than men, but men hold far more of the jobs. The report includes compensation for legal chiefs at 505 companies, more than half of the Fortune 1000. Female general counsel at Fortune 1000 companies received slightly higher total compensation than their male counterparts last year, but they continued to be drastically outnumbered. That was among the key findings of Corporate Counsel’s analysis of female representation on its 2023 list of highest-paid general counsel. The list, created in partnership with ALM Intelligence, was based on U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission pay disclosures of the Fortune 1000 for fiscal 2022.

article.title: Antitrust Laws and Their Interpretive Dilemmas: A Counseling Scenario (Part 1)
article.description: But what of the situation in which a client seeks counseling, rather than presentation of a dispute to a figure authorized to make a decision? In this context, Brad Wendel foregrounds the difficulty that “must be faced in any complex regulatory arena…
article.text: But what of the situation in which a client seeks counseling, rather than presentation of a dispute to a figure authorized to make a decision? In this context, Brad Wendel foregrounds the difficulty that “must be faced in any complex regulatory arena in which a client may seek the assistance of a lawyer to avoid a legal prohibition or penalty through careful planning.” As already noted earlier in this series, one of Wendel’s targets is abusive tax shelters that are supported by spurious legal advice. In my career as a Dallas practitioner, I saw the collapse of a very fine competitor firm for this very type of conduct and one of its responsible partners sentenced to a lengthy prison stay. In some ways, these cases are easy to analyze in ethical terms ex post facto because they are threaded with bogus transactions. Such is not always the case, though—there are plenty of regulatory regimes in which transactional structures can be manipulated so as to defeat a rule’s background justifications.

article.title: Judge Refuses to Halt Southwest's 'Religious Liberty' Training, Says Airline 'Direly' Needs It
article.description: Federal Judge Brantley Starr denied Southwest Airlines' motion to stay religious liberty training for three senior Southwest attorneys. The judge had ordered the training to sanction Southwest for not complying with an earlier order in the case,…
article.text: Federal Judge Brantley Starr denied Southwest Airlines' motion to stay religious liberty training for three senior Southwest attorneys. The judge had ordered the training to sanction Southwest for not complying with an earlier order in the case, which was brought by a flight attendant alleging religious discrimination. Southwest said it will appeal Starr's denial. A federal judge ruled that three senior Southwest Airlines attorneys must undergo “religious liberty” training by Sept. 26, rejecting the airline’s pleas that he put the training on hold while it appeals. In a 23-page order, Dallas Judge Brantley Starr disagreed that his sanctions—which Southwest had called “unprecedented” and ideological—violated the First Amendment or likely would be overturned on appeal.
article.html:
• Federal Judge Brantley Starr denied Southwest Airlines' motion to stay religious liberty training for three senior Southwest attorneys.

  • Southwest said it will appeal Starr's denial.

article.title: VantageScore Snags Former Visa Counsel for GC Role
article.description: VantageScore is a credit score model that competes with FICO as a resource for lenders. Schmid previously spent four years at Visa and four years at Netspend. She replaces Bill Sakkab, who departed in April. VantageScore, a credit-scoring model…
article.text: VantageScore is a credit score model that competes with FICO as a resource for lenders. Schmid previously spent four years at Visa and four years at Netspend. She replaces Bill Sakkab, who departed in April. VantageScore, a credit-scoring model designed by major credit bureaus Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, hired former Visa lawyer Kimberly Schmid as executive vice president and general counsel. Schmid was senior counsel at Visa from January 2018 until January 2022, starting on its global regulatory affairs team before moving to senior managing counsel for global product, technology and business solutions. Before Visa, Schmid spent four years at paid debit card purveyor Netspend, where she was vice president and counsel. She also spent six years as an attorney adviser for the U.S. Department of Justice’s national security division.

article.text: NEWS TikTok General Counsel Stepping Down to Focus on Fighting Ban Erich Andersen had held the legal reins of the wildly popular social media app for four years. TikTok General Counsel Stepping Down to Focus on Fighting Ban

Erich Andersen had held the legal reins of the wildly popular social media app for four years. He previously spent more than two decades at Microsoft.

General Counsel and In House Counsel

The original version of this story was published on Corporate Counsel

Embattled social media platform TikTok said Friday that General Counsel Erich Andersen has stepped down to focus on the company’s fight against a new federal law that will ban the app in the United States if its Chinese owner doesn’t sell its stake within a year.

Andersen, who is based in the United States and is a former deputy general counsel at Microsoft, said in a statement that it was a “difficult decision” to step down from a role he’s held for four years.

article.title: New DOL Regulation on Employees Versus Independent Contractors Restores Multifactor Test While Leaving Some Important Questions Unanswered
article.description: On Jan. 1, 2024, the Biden administration’s Department of Labor (DOL) issued its final regulation on who is an employee versus who is an independent contractor, Part 795 – Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor…
article.text: On Jan. 1, 2024, the Biden administration’s Department of Labor (DOL) issued its final regulation on who is an employee versus who is an independent contractor, Part 795 – Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 89 F.R. 1741, No. 7 (Jan. 10, 2024). The regulation rescinds the Trump administration rule because, according to the administration, it emphasized two factors—employer control over how the work is done and opportunity to engage in entrepreneurial activity—in a manner unsupported by the agency’s traditional multifactor view and case law, and was inconsistent with the DOL’s emphasis on “economic dependence” as a principal guidepost. The regulation brings back the traditional, flexible multifactor approach but leaves some important questions unanswered.
article.html:
On Jan. 1, 2024, the Biden administration’s Department of Labor (DOL) issued its final regulation on who is an employee versus who is an independent contractor, Part 795 – Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 89 F.R. 1741, No. 7 (Jan. 10, 2024). The regulation rescinds the Trump administration rule because, according to the administration, it emphasized two factors—employer control over how the work is done and opportunity to engage in entrepreneurial activity—in a manner unsupported by the agency’s traditional multifactor view and case law, and was inconsistent with the DOL’s emphasis on “economic dependence” as a principal guidepost.

The regulation brings back the traditional, flexible multifactor approach but leaves some important questions unanswered.

article.title: Climate Change Will Up Pressure on Tech Over Energy-Hungry Data Centers
article.description: Data center demand is soaring just as pressure grows on tech companies to reduce their carbon footprint. Data centers account for about 2% of worldwide greenhouse gas emissions. A proposed SEC climate-impact disclosure rule would put additional…
article.text: Data center demand is soaring just as pressure grows on tech companies to reduce their carbon footprint. Data centers account for about 2% of worldwide greenhouse gas emissions. A proposed SEC climate-impact disclosure rule would put additional public scrutiny on tech companies' environmental footprint. Data centers, the giant facilities that form the backbone of the internet, soon will fall under more scrutiny as climate risk disclosure rules and investor expectations put more pressure on tech to reduce its environmental footprint. With the rise of social media, video streaming, self-driving vehicles and generative artificial intelligence tools, the amount of digital data being created, replicated and processed every year is escalating, and with it the global demand for storage. The market research firm International Data Corp. estimates that the “datasphere” will grow to 175 zettabytes by 2025, likening the world’s entire data collection to a stack of DVDs that could circle the Earth 222 times.

article.title: How Will the Federal Reclassification of Marijuana Affect New Jersey's Cannabis Industry?
article.description: Marijuana has been classified as a Schedule I drug since Congress enacted the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) in 1970. Under the CSA, Schedule I drugs are deemed to have a high potential for abuse and have no accepted medical use. For perspective,…
article.text: Marijuana has been classified as a Schedule I drug since Congress enacted the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) in 1970. Under the CSA, Schedule I drugs are deemed to have a high potential for abuse and have no accepted medical use. For perspective, other drugs listed as a Schedule I drug include, but are not limited to, heroin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and ecstasy. However, as of the writing of this column, 38 states have legalized medical marijuana and 24 states have legalized recreational, adult-use marijuana. Perhaps you are thinking—if 38 states have already legalized medical marijuana in the U.S., then the U.S. government must have previously recognized that there is at least some accepted medical use … right? Wrong.
article.html:
Marijuana has been classified as a Schedule I drug since Congress enacted the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) in 1970. Under the CSA, Schedule I drugs are deemed to have a high potential for abuse and have no accepted medical use. For perspective, other drugs listed as a Schedule I drug include, but are not limited to, heroin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and ecstasy. However, as of the writing of this column, 38 states have legalized medical marijuana and 24 states have legalized recreational, adult-use marijuana.

Perhaps you are thinking—if 38 states have already legalized medical marijuana in the U.S., then the U.S. government must have previously recognized that there is at least some accepted medical use … right? Wrong.

article.title: FTC Statements on Reporting Misconduct and Guidance on Undisclosed Fees in Franchising
article.description: The Federal Trade Commission recently issued a policy statement regarding the franchise industry. The FTC is charged with protecting franchisees from unfair methods of competition and unfair and deceptive practices. The policy statement from the…
article.text: The Federal Trade Commission recently issued a policy statement regarding the franchise industry. The FTC is charged with protecting franchisees from unfair methods of competition and unfair and deceptive practices. The policy statement from the commission addresses restrictions on the ability to report and collect information about potential law violations. The FTC staff also issued guidance about the charging of fees not disclosed when a franchisee purchases a franchise. The response to these statements are mixed. Policy Statement Pertaining to Communications Regarding Potential Law Violations The FTC is concerned that franchisors suppress the ability of franchisees to voluntarily discuss or file reports about their experiences with franchisors, even if the franchisees believe a law violation has occurred. The policy statement was issued to express the FTC’s “view that provisions included in franchise agreements or other contractual documents between franchisors and franchisees may not restrict franchisees’ communications with the commission or any other or federal law enforcer or regulator about potential law violations.”
article.html:

The policy statement from the commission addresses restrictions on the ability to report and collect information about potential law violations. The FTC staff also issued guidance about the charging of fees not disclosed when a franchisee purchases a franchise. The response to these statements are mixed.

Policy Statement Pertaining to Communications Regarding Potential Law Violations

The FTC is concerned that franchisors suppress the ability of franchisees to voluntarily discuss or file reports about their experiences with franchisors, even if the franchisees believe a law violation has occurred. The policy statement was issued to express the FTC’s “view that provisions included in franchise agreements or other contractual documents between franchisors and franchisees may not restrict franchisees’ communications with the commission or any other or federal law enforcer or regulator about potential law violations.”

Monteleone has been with the Austin, Texas-based online dating and networking app since 2018, when she met one of its earliest employees on its Bumble For Friends site. It was her first in-house role; Monteleone was previously an associate with Winstead in Austin and an associate with Proskauer Rose in New York.

article.title: In Deposition, Fox Legal Chief Says He 'Allowed the Possibility' Rigged-Election Claims Were True | Corporate Counsel
article.description: “I was skeptical but I had to reserve some mind space to—for them to be proven right, Viet Dinh said in the newly released deposition.
article.text: Viet Dinh, chief legal and policy officer of Fox Corp., said he was "skeptical" of allegations that the 2020 presidential election had been rigged by two voting companies, but didn't dismiss them. "There was a period of time when allegations were made that I was skeptical of, but I allowed the possibility that they may be true," Dinh said in a deposition made public Tuesday evening by Susman Godfrey, the firm representing Dominion Voting Systems in a $1.6 billion defamation lawsuit against Fox News. Under questioning from Dominion attorney Stephen Shackelford, Dinh said he "allowed room for the allegations to be shown" that Dominion's software and algorithms had manipulated vote counts, at least from November through mid-December, when the election results were certified.
article.html:

article.title: Sanctions Sought for Ex-In-House Lawyer Representing Client in Alleged 'Substantially Related' Matter
article.description: Retailer Conn Appliances Inc. has asked a federal judge to sanction its former senior legal counsel, Trista Johnson, for representing a plaintiff now suing the company on causes of action similar to those that the in-house attorney defended during…
article.text: Retailer Conn Appliances Inc. has asked a federal judge to sanction its former senior legal counsel, Trista Johnson, for representing a plaintiff now suing the company on causes of action similar to those that the in-house attorney defended during her 18 months there. Retailer Conn Appliances Inc. has asked a federal judge to sanction its former senior legal counsel for representing a plaintiff now suing the company on causes of action similar to those that the in-house attorney defended during her time there. According to The Woodlands, Texas-based seller of furniture, mattresses, home appliances and consumer electronics, attorney Trista Johnson, the retailer’s No. 2 in-house lawyer from December 2016 to February 2018, “willfully ignored her ethical and professional obligations” when she filed Telephone Consumer Protection Act and Texas Debt Collection Act claims against Conn’s in May on behalf of a client. That’s because, as Conn’s in-house counsel, Johnson, the company alleges, handled the exact same consumer claims on a daily basis.
