article.title: Ethical 'Fails': Social Media Pitfalls and In-House Counsel
article.description: It’s an incredibly wired world we live in. Over 82% of the adult American population has at least one social networking profile, and in a single minute we’ll witness 293,000 status updates posted to Facebook, more than 360,000 tweets on Twitter, and…
article.text: It’s an incredibly wired world we live in. Over 82% of the adult American population has at least one social networking profile, and in a single minute we’ll witness 293,000 status updates posted to Facebook, more than 360,000 tweets on Twitter, and roughly 400 hours of video uploaded to YouTube. And while lawyers have yet to catch up with the social media usage of the general population, the rate at which lawyers use social networking platforms has been climbing steadily every year. In-house lawyers are no different; according to a 2017 survey conducted by Zeughauser Group and Greentarget, 73% of corporate counsel report using social media sites like LinkedIn and Facebook for professional reasons. But perhaps the most important question in an era in which attorneys are just one viral post or inflammatory tweet away from the unemployment line or even the disciplinary board, is whether in-house lawyers are using social media ethically and responsibly. As with their counterparts in private firms and government entities, there is no shortage of “cautionary tales for the Digital Age” originating from corporate legal departments.

article.title: Fox Legal Chief Rips Judge in Dominion Case, Says 'Illogical' Pre-Trial Rulings 'Hamstrung' Company
article.description: "At some point, it became not just a matter of reversible error. It called into question the fundamental fairness and integrity of the Delaware civil justice system," Viet Dinh said during an appearance at Harvard Monday. Fox Corp. legal chief Viet…
article.text: "At some point, it became not just a matter of reversible error. It called into question the fundamental fairness and integrity of the Delaware civil justice system," Viet Dinh said during an appearance at Harvard Monday. Fox Corp. legal chief Viet Dinh, who has been widely criticized for his handling of the Dominion Voting Systems’ defamation lawsuit, this week blasted the judge who handled the case, saying his “illogical” rulings had “hamstrung” the company’s defense. Dinh, a 1993 graduate of Harvard Law School, was the featured speaker at an hourlong event at the university on Monday. In his address, he never mentioned by name the judge who handled the case—Eric Davis of Delaware Superior Court—but said his handling of it undermined the “fairness and integrity of the legal system.”

article.title: Justices Seemingly Balk at Deferring to NLRB in Starbucks Appeal of Injunction
article.description: The U.S. Supreme Court appeared open to the idea Tuesday that some courts have been too deferential to the National Labor Relations Board in unfair labor practice cases, as justices seemed to lean in favor of Starbucks in litigation over fired…
article.text: The U.S. Supreme Court appeared open to the idea Tuesday that some courts have been too deferential to the National Labor Relations Board in unfair labor practice cases, as justices seemed to lean in favor of Starbucks in litigation over fired workers who had been trying to start a union. In Starbucks Corp. v. M. Kathleen McKinney, the high court is considering the coffee giant’s appeal of a ruling for seven fired baristas who had been engaged in a campaign to unionize their coffee shop in Memphis, Tennessee. The case deals with the proper test courts should impose before hitting employers with injunctions pending an NLRB investigation into whether they violated labor laws.

article.title: Michael Lynch Was a Titan of British Tech. Then He Got Crosswise With HP
article.description: It’s been more than a decade since British tech entrepreneur Michael Lynch sold his software company, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard for $11 billion. Now. he’s facing the risk of serious prison time. The blockbuster deal has landed him in criminal…
article.text: It’s been more than a decade since British tech entrepreneur Michael Lynch sold his software company, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard for $11 billion. Now. he’s facing the risk of serious prison time. The blockbuster deal has landed him in criminal court alongside his former vice president of finance, Stephen Chamberlain, with each facing more than a dozen counts of wire fraud and other charges. Prosecutors say that, through a string of conference calls, news releases and emails, they presented a rosy picture of Autonomy at a time it actually was tanking, duping HP into massively overpaying in the process.

article.title: As Companies' Fears of Data-Breach Litigation Soar, Legal Terrain Rife With Uncertainty
article.description: What You Need to Know Court rulings have created uncertainty over who has standing to bring data-breach claims. Cybercriminals are unleashing more attacks and using more sinister methods. A new survey of corporate litigation attorneys ranked…
article.text: What You Need to Know Court rulings have created uncertainty over who has standing to bring data-breach claims. Cybercriminals are unleashing more attacks and using more sinister methods. A new survey of corporate litigation attorneys ranked cybersecurity as their top concern. Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims. The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Court rulings have created uncertainty over who has standing to bring data-breach claims.
  • Cybercriminals are unleashing more attacks and using more sinister methods.
  • A new survey of corporate litigation attorneys ranked cybersecurity as their top concern.

Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims.

The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies.

article.title: 'We’re Going to Tear the Barriers Down': Judge Prepares to Open App Market Floodgates on Google
article.description: A federal judge indicated he will impose sweeping changes to how Google operates its app store. Epic Games wants the court to allow third party app stores on Android devices and to give the stores access to Google Play's massive trove of apps. Google…
article.text: A federal judge indicated he will impose sweeping changes to how Google operates its app store. Epic Games wants the court to allow third party app stores on Android devices and to give the stores access to Google Play's massive trove of apps. Google argued that implementing what Epic wants would be excessive, as well as burdensome and time-consuming to implement. The federal judge in charge of imposing wide-scale changes to how Google runs its app store said he has no intention of micromanaging the tech giant but warned that Google should get ready to open the floodgates. “We’re going to tear the barriers down. When you have a mountain that’s built out of bad conduct, you’re going to have to move that mountain,” U.S. District Judge James Donato said.

“We’re going to tear the barriers down. When you have a mountain that’s built out of bad conduct, you’re going to have to move that mountain,” U.S. District Judge James Donato said.

article.title: $2B Settlement in Cummins Environmental Probe Signals End to Era of Lax Enforcement
article.description: The agreement "sends a signal the EPA is making an example of someone. Make sure your house is in order," said Joshua Van Eaton, a principal at Beveridge & Diamond. Cummins is paying the largest Clean Air Act settlement ever to settle allegations it…
article.text: The agreement "sends a signal the EPA is making an example of someone. Make sure your house is in order," said Joshua Van Eaton, a principal at Beveridge & Diamond. Cummins is paying the largest Clean Air Act settlement ever to settle allegations it installed devices in Ram pickup engines that circumvented emissions tests. The company does not admit wrongdoing and says it has seen no evidence that anyone acted in bad faith. The EPA recently installed as enforcement chief David Uhlmann, who's long bemoaned the agency's record of declining enforcement. The $2 billion settlement that the Department of Justice and Environmental Protection Agency finalized with diesel engine-maker Cummins on Wednesday serves as a cautionary tale for all companies after years of lax enforcement of the Clean Air Act. Regulators alleged Cummins installed emissions-control-defeat devices on diesel engines it supplied for more than 600,000 Ram pickup trucks over the course of a decade. Under the consent agreement, which concludes a regulatory review that began four years ago, Cummins did not admit wrongdoing.

article.title: Swelling Workloads Taking Toll on In-House Lawyers' Mental Health
article.description: In-house lawyers generally like their jobs but are nonetheless anxious, exhausted and stressed. according to Law.com and ALM Intelligence’s 2024 Mental Health Survey. It found that crushing workloads, understaffed teams and dysfunctional company…
article.text: In-house lawyers generally like their jobs but are nonetheless anxious, exhausted and stressed. according to Law.com and ALM Intelligence’s 2024 Mental Health Survey. It found that crushing workloads, understaffed teams and dysfunctional company culture are largely to blame. Seventy-nine in-house counsel responded to the survey, up from last year’s two dozen. While it’s too small a sample to be statistically significant, the results are consistent with observations from in-house experts who say the job has grown increasingly demanding.
article.html:
In-house lawyers generally like their jobs but are nonetheless anxious, exhausted and stressed. according to Law.com and ALM Intelligence’s 2024 Mental Health Survey. It found that crushing workloads, understaffed teams and dysfunctional company culture are largely to blame.

Seventy-nine in-house counsel responded to the survey, up from last year’s two dozen. While it’s too small a sample to be statistically significant, the results are consistent with observations from in-house experts who say the job has grown increasingly demanding.

article.description: The founder of electric truck maker Nikola, convicted last year of defrauding investors about his company’s technology, now is suing his legal chief and other insiders, saying they praised him for aggressively promoting the company before turning on…
article.text: The founder of electric truck maker Nikola, convicted last year of defrauding investors about his company’s technology, now is suing his legal chief and other insiders, saying they praised him for aggressively promoting the company before turning on him when scrutiny of the business increased. Trevor Milton, who in December was sentenced to four years in prison, says in the June 6 lawsuit that he relied heavily on Chief Legal Officer Britton Worthen, who also was his personal attorney, to advise him on what he should or shouldn’t say on social media and in other public forums about the Phoenix-based company.

article.title: 'Follow the Money': Feds Close Case Against Michael Lynch in HP Fraud Trial
article.description: Prosecutors allege Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch used accounting trickery to dupe Hewlett-Packard into buying his company for $11 billion. Lynch's defense portrays him as a tech visionary who delegated financial details to others. Lynch testified that…
article.text: Prosecutors allege Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch used accounting trickery to dupe Hewlett-Packard into buying his company for $11 billion. Lynch's defense portrays him as a tech visionary who delegated financial details to others. Lynch testified that HP overpaid and then frittered away Autonomy's value by bungling the merger integration. Autonomy CEO Michael Lynch “had more than $500 million reasons to lie to HP” when he sold the U.K. company to the Silicon Valley giant in 2011, federal prosecutors said during closing arguments Monday in Lynch’s fraud case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Leach spent four hours walking the jury through a complex web of transactions constituting the 14 counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy with which Lynch and his former vice president of finance, Stephen Chamberlain, are charged. “There’s an old saying for our line of work: Follow the money. It’s easy in this case,” Leach said.
article.html:

  • Lynch testified that HP overpaid and then frittered away Autonomy's value by bungling the merger integration.

It’s easy in this case,” Leach said.

article.title: Supreme Court Delays Trump Trial, Will Review Immunity Defense
article.description: The U.S. Supreme Court said Wednesday that it will decide whether former President Donald Trump can stand trial on charges related to his efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election, setting arguments on the issue for the week of April 22.…
article.text: The U.S. Supreme Court said Wednesday that it will decide whether former President Donald Trump can stand trial on charges related to his efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election, setting arguments on the issue for the week of April 22. Specifically, the court will address the question of “whether and if so to what extent does a former President enjoy presidential immunity from criminal prosecution for conduct alleged to involve official acts during his tenure in office.”

article.title: Food-Waste Company Divert—Backed by $1.1B in Funding—Hires First General Counsel
article.description: Kathleen Patton has taken the legal reins of the Massachusetts company as it builds facilities that combine spoiled food with bacteria to create energy. Divert, a Massachusetts-based startup focused on converting food waste into renewable energy, has…
article.text: Kathleen Patton has taken the legal reins of the Massachusetts company as it builds facilities that combine spoiled food with bacteria to create energy. Divert, a Massachusetts-based startup focused on converting food waste into renewable energy, has hired a seasoned in-house leader with IPO and M&A experience as its first general counsel. Kathleen Patton, former general counsel at job marketplace and social platform Jobcase, took the legal reins at Divert earlier this month. She was also previously general counsel at CarGurus, where she oversaw its 2017 debut on the public market, as well as its purchase of car shopping and trading platforms Autolist and CarOffer.

article.title: Bain-Backed Software Firm Hires Startup Veteran as Legal Chief
article.description: Bain Capital-backed Rocket Software added three executives, including chief legal officer Liz Fischer. Fischer previously was general counsel at two other venture-backed tech startups. Rocket Software, an enterprise software development firm owned by…
article.text: Bain Capital-backed Rocket Software added three executives, including chief legal officer Liz Fischer. Fischer previously was general counsel at two other venture-backed tech startups. Rocket Software, an enterprise software development firm owned by Bain Capital, is building up its executive ranks to help boost growth, hiring seasoned tech industry lawyer Liz Fischer as its first chief legal officer. Fischer will report to Rocket Software CEO Milan Shetti. She joins Rocket Software from Perch, a venture-backed e-commerce platform that sells direct-to-consumer products made by its more than 100 brands. Fischer handled all legal functions as Perch’s general counsel, including managing litigation, negotiating mergers and acquisitions and debt transactions, and overseeing its intellectual property portfolio.

article.title: 'Match Made in Heaven': Meet Obama Foundation's New General Counsel
article.description: Shawn Ray White, the incoming general counsel at the Obama Foundation, recalls one aspect of being a summer associate in New York very clearly. She remembers the long, black town car that picked her up at the Manhattan office of Schulte Roth & Zabel…
article.text: Shawn Ray White, the incoming general counsel at the Obama Foundation, recalls one aspect of being a summer associate in New York very clearly. She remembers the long, black town car that picked her up at the Manhattan office of Schulte Roth & Zabel to drive her to the Bronx Legal Foundation every morning. In the poorest borough of New York she worked on a fellowship from Schulte Roth on landlord/tenant issues, asbestos, and lead paint in housing. The town car drove her home every night. “I made sure the fancy car dropped my legal assistant at home as well!” she remembers. Colleagues in the nonprofit organization didn’t mind her unusual form of transportation, she said, since the law firm also provided research, analysis and resources that otherwise would not have been available to the foundation.

article.title: Workers Have New Incentives to Snitch to Feds, Skipping Internal Ethics Hotlines
article.description: New DOJ programs are further complicating companies' already-agonizing decision on whether to self-report wrongdoing. The agency wants employers to fear that if they stay silent, one of their employees will blow the whistle, or maybe already has.…
article.text: New DOJ programs are further complicating companies' already-agonizing decision on whether to self-report wrongdoing. The agency wants employers to fear that if they stay silent, one of their employees will blow the whistle, or maybe already has. Companies count on their workers to help ferret out wrongdoing, but their hotlines don't offer the potential for multimillion-dollar rewards that government programs do. A new Department of Justice program that offers cash rewards to whistleblowers will give employees an additional incentive to take allegations of misconduct straight to the feds, bypassing internal ethics hotlines companies count on to ferret out suspicious behavior before it becomes a crisis. It “creates the risk of disincentivizing internal reporting,” said Carolyn Small, special counsel at Jenner & Block and a former assistant U.S. attorney.

article.title: CLO to Retire After Helping Auto Dealership Giant Triple Revenue
article.description: The nation’s fourth-largest auto dealership group is losing its longtime legal chief. George Villasana will step down in June and retire in March 2025. Duluth, Georgia-based Asbury Automotive disclosed the news in a securities filing on Friday.…
article.text: The nation’s fourth-largest auto dealership group is losing its longtime legal chief. George Villasana will step down in June and retire in March 2025. Duluth, Georgia-based Asbury Automotive disclosed the news in a securities filing on Friday. Villasana has led its legal department since 2012. He came to Asbury from Swisher Hygiene, a sanitation company, where he was senior vice president and general counsel for two years. Before that, Villasana was general counsel at veterinary hospital chain Pet DRx. He started his in-house career at AutoNation, where he was promoted to senior counsel shortly after joining the then-fledgling car dealership chain.

He came to Asbury from Swisher Hygiene, a sanitation company, where he was senior vice president and general counsel for two years. He started his in-house career at AutoNation, where he was promoted to senior counsel shortly after joining the then-fledgling car dealership chain.

article.title: Paramount General Counsel Heads for Exit in Wake of Failed Merger
article.description: Christa D’Alimonte is stepping down as general counsel of New York-based Paramount Global after more than a decade with the media conglomerate. D’Alimonte broke the news to her team in an internal memo this week that was published by entertainment…
article.text: Christa D’Alimonte is stepping down as general counsel of New York-based Paramount Global after more than a decade with the media conglomerate. D’Alimonte broke the news to her team in an internal memo this week that was published by entertainment news sites Deadline and Variety. Her last day will be June 28. Deadline reported that she will be succeeded by 15-year Paramount veteran Caryn Groce, who’s been deputy general counsel for four years.
article.html:

Deadline reported that she will be succeeded by 15-year Paramount veteran Caryn Groce, who’s been deputy general counsel for four years.

ANALYSIS

What Have We Learned From 20 AI Copyright Lawsuits?

In less than two years, generative AI providers have racked up at least 20 lawsuits alleging copyright infringement. Experts narrowed down three main commonalities between them.

Copyrights

From the big-name brands to smaller, independent creators, the oftentimes David vs. Goliath nature of tech litigation in the arena of AI and copyright has shown few signs of slowing down.

In less than two years, AI companies have racked up at least 20 lawsuits from plaintiffs alleging that AI providers used their works to train their algorithms, and therefore violated their copyright protections.

article.title: Litigators' Advice to Companies on FTC Non-Compete Ban
article.description: What You Need to Know Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance. Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential. FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes…
article.text: What You Need to Know Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance. Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential. FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes with low-wage workers. With the Federal Trade Commission poised to sharply curtail non-compete clauses, litigation experts say now is the time for companies to take stock of their employment agreements. “You want to have a clear message when the FTC or anyone else comes calling and asks, ‘Why do you have these agreements?’” said John Barry, who heads Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ employment litigation practice and co-authored a recent client_briefing on the issue. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance.
  • Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential.
  • FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes with low-wage workers.

With the Federal Trade Commission poised to sharply curtail non-compete clauses, litigation experts say now is the time for companies to take stock of their employment agreements.

“You want to have a clear message when the FTC or anyone else comes calling and asks, ‘Why do you have these agreements?’” said John Barry, who heads Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ employment litigation practice and co-authored a recent client_briefing on the issue.

article.title: 'You Can’t Do a First Draft of Common Sense': Microsoft GC Jon Palmer Talks AI, Litigation, and Leadership
article.description: The company recently said that its deal to invest $40 million in the ailing Container Store chain is on the rocks. "In a time of AI and technology and innovation, maybe some of the most important qualities to build on and to really dig in on are thos
article.text: Jon Palmer didn’t expect to wind up the general counsel at Microsoft when he joined as senior attorney back in 2010. He hadn’t even expected to go in-house. But after decades as outside counsel the opportunity to work for his favorite client was too good to pass up. “I was always super impressed by the litigators that I worked with there, how strategic they were, the role they played at the company and how thoughtful they were,” he said. “I loved being at law firms and I never really thought much about going in house, but because I knew the litigation group so well, it was really interesting and attractive. So that's why I made the jump.” Ten years later, he was head of litigation. And as a self-described “lifelong generalist,” that suited him just fine. “If you're a litigator at Microsoft, you're not just representing the gaming Xbox division. You're not just representing one particular subsidiary. You really have a side-to-side view of the whole company. The ability just to work in different substantive areas across different businesses really appealed to me,” Palmer said. One of the most fascinating cases he worked on was actually a contempt proceeding, where Microsoft challenged an FBI search warrant demanding that it turn over customer emails stored on a server in Ireland. Another was when Microsoft sued the federal government over its gag order policies that prevented the company from telling their customers when the government tried to access their data. Palmer recalls those cases fondly as ones where the company was able to help shape resulting legislation—the CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act) of 2018—that had an impact in changing those practices. Palmer recounted his career journey in an interview this week with Berkeley Law’s executive-in-residence Irene Liu as part of its executive education program. “Probably the high point of my life, frankly, was being a litigator at Microsoft. It's just such a great job,” he told Liu. “And it did prepare me ultimately for the general counsel role because I really did have this chance to work with so many businesses, so many subsidiaries, so many executives across the company and on so many different types of matters.” At other times, it wasn’t so fun, especially when high-profile lawsuits get filed right around the holidays. Liu reminded him that it was right around Christmas when The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft last year. Palmer said that kind of timing is not unusual, as 30%-40% of lawsuits are filed against the company between Thanksgiving and New Year's. “I think plaintiffs lawyers in particular think that they're being tricky or that they're somehow getting some advantage by doing that,” he said. “It’s become a joke in my family—it’s the holidays, what's gonna make Dad be on the phone for 12 hours straight? It's become almost routine. It will probably happen this year too, I’m sure it will.” Palmer has a lot more on his plate now than litigation, especially as Microsoft has transformed over the decades from primarily a software company with some hardware offerings into a diversified tech powerhouse with a footprint in cloud computing, video games, social media, and now artificial intelligence. “The level of complexity has increased and of course, there's been a backlash and increase in regulation and accountability with respect to big tech. And we understand that,” he said. But the only way Microsoft can pursue its mission is “to be a trustworthy company,” he said. “There's a lot more regulatory scrutiny. We embrace that in many ways we feel we need to be accountable and subject to the rules of law and rules of society. That's expected when you get big and when you get complicated, regulation follows. So we just basically try to keep up.” Keeping up has been about as easy as you might expect for a legal team that numbers in the thousands. “I won't lie, it's difficult sometimes to really stay coordinated and not work in silos,” Palmer said, adding that how issues like how trade and export controls, labor, copyright, antitrust and competition affect the different layers of Microsoft’s business is a regular agenda item in meetings with his leadership team. “We'll also set up a series of meetings that pull in different pieces so that we can all sort of learn together. So we may have a meeting just on copyright, for instance, and not just IP lawyers attending that meeting, but people from across the legal team to really understand and get grounded in those issues,” he said. They’re also keeping a close eye on the incipient regulation around artificial intelligence, an increasingly critical part of the tech giant’s longterm strategy. Palmer said the company knows regulation is coming, and even wants it. “Ultimately, we're under no illusion. We want regulation. We don't think the world should just leave it to tech companies to figure this out for themselves and act responsibly,” he said. “We think there's definitely a role, there has to be a role for the government to regulate, but it will trail a little bit. And in that intervening time, companies have to act responsibly and help develop the norms that ultimately will bind us.” Now in his 14th year at Microsoft, Palmer said he’s always thinking about whether he’s learning and growing in whatever role he’s in. It’s something he’ll often ask those who come to him for career advice, including his own children, who are now in their 20s. "If you feel stuck and you're not learning, why is that? Is there something you can do about that? You know, you're the governor of your own career,” he said. Liu remarked that this tip could apply to learning on an emotional level as well. Palmer agreed. “In a time of AI and technology and innovation, maybe some of the most important qualities to build on and to really dig in on are those things that AI can't do,” he said, laughing that you can’t offload things like common sense and good judgment to AI. “You can't do a first draft of common sense,” he said. “Things like common sense and good judgment, which is just the experience that you get from life and from your job—how to get along with different kinds of people, how to lead and influence people. These are important skills that I believe people literally can build these skills no matter where they sit in the organization. I really believe that.”

article.title: How Marsh McLennan's Small But Mighty Legal Innovation Team Builds Solutions That Bring Joy
article.description: "Everything that we do and we build is…to help our colleagues achieve their dreams," said Farrah Pepper, chief legal innovation counsel at Marsh McLennan.
article.text: LIT Lab started as a concept. Now it’s a verb. For Marsh McLennan chief legal innovation counsel Farrah Pepper, there’s no higher praise for the Legal Innovation & Technology (LIT) framework she helped launch in 2019 to drive new ideas for how to better run legal and compliance at a global company. Legal has long suffered under the sometimes unfair designation as the “place where good ideas go to die.” But it’s recently started to turn that label on its head. For Pepper, who was hired back in 2018, it’s about finding better ways of working. “Innovation doesn't have to always be a moonshot," she said. "I define it as incremental change that adds value. And that's what our LIT Lab is doing all the time; looking at the processes we have now. How do we make them better?” Marsh McLennan’s commitment to modernizing its legal and compliance department through its own innovation lab earned it this year’s Corporate Counsel award for Best Use of Technology. She and other Corporate Counsel winners were recognized for their achievements on Nov. 13 at The American Lawyer Industry Awards in New York City. (Read the full list of winners here.) With the blessing of General Counsel Kate Brennan, Pepper said she and her team have gone about rooting out mundane, repetitive tasks and cumbersome processes, and applying practical, streamlined solutions. "It is possible to teach an old lawyer new tricks," Brennan told Law.com for a LIT Lab profile back in 2022. "I think it's easy when you're in-house for a number of years to just become complacent and resort to 'that's always just how we've done it and it works fine, so don't break it.'" Projects have to meet four principles—save time, save money, improve quality and bring joy. “That last one is my personal favorite,” Pepper said. “Is it making our colleagues day better? Is it making them enjoy their job more?” Though some might think of Pepper’s role as primarily data- or tech-based, she said that it’s really about people. “I will have conversations all day long with colleagues, and I will hear them say something which embedded in their statement is a hope or a wish," she said. "Maybe something like, 'I wish this process were easier, but it's not.' And to me, that's the antenna up moment where I say, 'Well, maybe we can help you. Let's have a LIT Lab conversation about whether there's something we can do to make that better.’ And we find opportunities everywhere.” She said one of the recurring pain points her team heard from legal colleagues was translation services. Microsoft already has translation capabilities embedded in its software suite, Pepper said, “But we found that sometimes that wasn't enough, and people needed something that was more specific to legal terms.” So they also started using an artificial intelligence-based translation tool through Marsh McLennan’s own internal generative AI solution, dubbed “LenAI.” When legal wanted the tool to be able to learn specific legal terms and clauses, the company partnered with Alexa Translations to “build a translation brain for our department of key terms and clauses," she said. "That's one example of something that may sound simple, but in reality, it's a multipronged approach with different solutions depending on different use cases,” as well as “an external relationship and partnership where we are collaborating to add capabilities and features.” Another strategic partnership has been with Priori Legal to design and test a new outside counsel management program called Scout. Pepper said Scout pulls together all the data points on a firm, including billing, diversity initiatives and reviews, traditionally information that lives in a bunch of places, and puts them all together in one place. “You're looking at actual real matters and associated cost structures. We've also got reviews and testimonials,” Pepper said. “As much as we want to think our colleagues will stay with us forever, sometimes there can be a change in who those relationship leads are. We wanted to prevent a situation where years of excellent work from a law firm and institutional knowledge walked out the door with a relationship lead on the in-house side and vice-versa.” LIT Lab also created an ideas portal called FIRE, an acronym for “fabulous ideas, requests, and enhancements," where legal and compliance colleagues can submit ideas, crowdsource, and vote on one others' ideas about how to work better and smarter. “We have a simple intake form for our colleagues to present their idea, it gets posted into the portal, and others can review it, comment, vote on it,” Pepper said. Though they serve an enormous client, a legal and compliance department of more than 600, Pepper’s team is surprisingly lean. It currently stands at five members, including herself. Three—Joyce Murray, JP Chaplen, and Scott Stower— were recruited from Marsh McLennan’s information technology department and combine decades of tech experience with an affinity for legal. The most recent hire is Sean Raven, previously counsel at Sidley who specializes in discovery and information governance. “We're a mix of tech, project management, legal— varied, substantive skills all blended together in one team,” Pepper said. Brennan, along with Deputy General Counsel Connor Kuratek, have also lent tremendous support. “I know from talking to colleagues in other organizations that without that kind of sponsorship and championship, innovation work can be a really hard sell. So part of what has made our ability to thrive happen is very much that tone from the top," Pepper said, "and that commitment and saying to our colleagues, ‘this matters.'" Pepper said she and her team spend a lot of time making sure their solutions are solving real problems. One person she asked for advice when she took the job at Marsh McLennan told her something that really stuck, “which is that innovation has to come from a place of desirability," she said. "You do not want to be in the business of forcing people to do changes, processes, or use tech that they don't want. So everything that we do and we build is predicated on a position of working with our colleagues to help them achieve their dreams.” Besides, the LIT Lab is so leanly staffed they have to make sure that everything they do adds value. “We can't afford to devote time to folly,” Pepper said.

article.title: So You Want to Be a Tech Lawyer? Consider Product Counseling
article.description: Veteran product lawyers are realizing they have a lot of wisdom—gathered from years in the trenches at tech companies—to impart to the next generation of in-house counsel.
article.text: The truism that law school doesn’t prepare you to be an in-house lawyer in tech is quickly changing. Veteran product attorneys are translating their years of experience in the trenches of Silicon Valley into practical lessons that will equip the next generation of in-house counsel with the skills to navigate the fast-paced world of tech. “Part of it is coming into law school wanting to give information to students that I didn't necessarily see when I went to law school and had to figure out myself,” said adjunct UC Law San Francisco professor John Didday, who just wrapped his inaugural semester teaching “Product Counseling: Actionable Legal Advice for Tech Companies.” The basic idea is to “introduce people to the realities of tech companies,” Didday said, something he learned on the fly as a young product and technology counsel. Didday, an associate general counsel of product and privacy at Zendesk, grew up in the Bay Area and was familiar with the boom-and-bust cycle of tech. But it wasn’t until he went in-house at cloud-based electronic health record company Practice Fusion after four years in Big Law that he got a crash course in how those companies actually operate, and what being an “effective and helpful” in-house lawyer really means. “Listening to how the business operates and advising on how they can comply with the law is the core definition of what it is to be a lawyer.” Didday said. The product counsel's job is to figure out what the company is planning to do and ensure that the path to that goal from idea to launch is legal, he added. Didday said lawyers tend to think of the world as “two sided”: There are plaintiffs and defendants, winners and losers; someone is right and someone is wrong. “A tech company is more complex," he added. "It's not my job to say finance is right and engineering is wrong. It's more like, 'What are all those departments, and what are they trying to do as a company?' That skill set of learning about and being curious about and communicating with those departments is the crux of the skill that I realized was going to be so important.” Fortunately, Didday had a mentor early on “who knew everybody at the company really well who really took me under her wing,” he said. “She literally moved my desk so I sat in the middle of the engineers, product managers and designers and took me into every meeting she went into. By necessity that experience made me listen.” Embedded in the Business In-house teams have long been organized by disciplines—IP, employment, commercial contracts and litigation. While legal departments need that specialized expertise, they also need lawyers to advise companies on the products and services they offer, said Adrienne Go, former associate general counsel at eBay. “While we absolutely have to have that expertise, at the same time, the real question is, 'Who is looking after the goods and services?' That's what the company is built on. That's what their brand is built on. It's not necessarily built on that great lawsuit that they just won. It really is built on providing excellent products, things that make people happy,” Go said. “With our rapid product life cycles in the past 20 years, businesses are being led more and more by their products. And it’s not just a just a brand campaign; it really is how much they are delivering value to their customers," Go added. "And that's where the product counsel comes in—someone who ... really knew the product, cradle to grave and who could actually sit down with the folks who are building these products.” The product could be anything from an insurance policy to a rideshare service. “And if the product lawyer is there at the right time, we have the ability to really influence that as it's being developed during the product life cycle, and it puts us in a very good place to be able to advise on something as it's being developed, before it's being launched and not after it's a problem,” Go said. Olga Mack, the co-founder of Product Law Hub, came to product counseling early in her career at VISA, where she was the first lawyer dedicated to its debit processing services. She said the job prepared her for later general counsel roles. “This idea of advising and guiding products from idea to launch to growth to scale to sunset, became something that sort of helped me become a general counsel and become closer to the business,” Mack said. “It is a very proactive role. It's not just waiting for issues to arise. It's embedded in the product teams and technology and marketing and sales and ensuring that everything from sort of functionality to compliance is aligned with business goals.” Later, Mack would go on to other executive roles like vice president of strategy at security auditing blockchain platform Quantstamp Inc. and eventually start her own company Parley Pro, which she sold to LexisNexis in 2022. “People ask me a lot about what area of law prepared me for business roles," she said. It's those same skills.” The role has matured over the last 20 years at large tech firms like Amazon, Airbnb, Google, Facebook and eBay, but “now you also now see smaller companies, part time or full time, hiring a product counsel to fulfill the role of bringing something to market and guiding it throughout the life cycle,” Mack said. “The idea is to see ahead, be preventative, simplify complex ideas, and help companies to navigate issues that may or may not be yet regulated.” A Framework for the Future Most of what Mack learned about product counseling was self-taught. "There was no class in law school at the time,” Mack said, adding that she learned on the job and through talking to peers from big and small companies across the tech industry. She would also field questions from aspiring product lawyers. “People would reach out to me, usually with questions like, ‘How do I become one? How do I build a product legal department?' I had a few law schools reach out to me to ask if I had a syllabus,” Mack said. That’s when she decided it it was time to write a book. Her collaboration with Go led to a formal product law framework laid out in their book, "Product Counsel, Advise, Innovate and Inspire." They also created a modular syllabus that’s open-sourced under Creative Commons and available for download at Product Law Hub. A proposed survey course, titled "Navigating Legal Challenges in Tech Innovation," is designed so that law schools can offer one- to three-unit classes covering topics such as product development, tech regulation, data privacy principles, ethics in tech innovation and smart risk-taking, “You are free to cut and paste. You are free to monetize it. You can do whatever you want," Mack said. "We know there's a lot of product lawyers who are not teaching, because they don't have a textbook and a syllabus. Now they have a textbook and a syllabus and, if you have experience, our hope is that they take it to their law schools or law schools nearby and offer it.” Other product lawyers had a hand in drafting the syllabus, including Didday and Linsey Krolik, a former in-house lawyer at PayPal and an assistant clinical professor at Santa Clara University School of Law’s Entrepreneurs’ Law Clinic. Krolik said the idea is to show students that you must be able to take smart risks as a product lawyer. Krolik, who now practices privacy law at her own firm, said she had always worked in-house, where knowing the business and its goals was essential to being able to issue-spot. But practical training is somewhat lacking in law school, and most on-the-job instruction happens in law firms. "That is why you see students and junior attorneys going to law firms, because law firms are built financially on the model that they're going to invest money in training this person, and actually that they're going to make money off the backs of that person," Krolik said. "And they know that they won't stay forever, necessarily, unless they're going the partner route," Krolik added. "So many people do leave and go in-house, especially in Silicon Valley.” But as more students opt to go in-house right out of law school, they'll need to know how legal departments operate, Krolik said. Krolik’s course forces students to think on their feet and problem-solve with limited information. One product counsel simulation gives students a problem to solve and 30 minutes to come up with a presentation. It’s never perfect, but “that's exactly what you experience as a new lawyer in-house," Krolik said. "You don't have all the information. You've got to go from meeting to meeting. You've got to pull something together. You’ve got maybe 80%, and you've got to move. And you've got to also know when you do need more time. But students start to get more comfortable by the end of the semester.” At UC Law San Francisco, Didday introduces his students to product counseling by bringing in different department experts to field questions about how they work. This semester, his class was visited by a cybersecurity professional, an engineer and a product designer. “The student sees there exists a design department and gets to know what the design department is thinking about," Didday said. "So when you encounter that person on the job you can have a conversation with them and when they ask something of you, you can answer.” Being curious about what your client does is invaluable, he added, often more so than any given law or legal analysis. “When you go to law school it feels like this is the entire universe and it’s so important what Justice Kagan said in her dissent in footnote 16,” Didday said. “This is trying to get them to realize, just so you know, not only is this case not the center of the universe, lawyers aren't the center of the universe in companies, generally.”

The truism that law school doesn’t prepare you to be an in-house lawyer in tech is quickly changing. Veteran product attorneys are translating their years of experience in the trenches of Silicon Valley into practical lessons that will equip the next generation of in-house counsel with the skills to navigate the fast-paced world of tech.

“Part of it is coming into law school wanting to give information to students that I didn't necessarily see when I went to law school and had to figure out myself,” said adjunct UC Law San Francisco professor John Didday, who just wrapped his inaugural semester teaching “Product Counseling: Actionable Legal Advice for Tech Companies.”

The basic idea is to “introduce people to the realities of tech companies,” Didday said, something he learned on the fly as a young product and technology counsel.

Didday, an associate general counsel of product and privacy at Zendesk, grew up in the Bay Area and was familiar with the boom-and-bust cycle of tech. But it wasn’t until he went in-house at cloud-based electronic health record company Practice Fusion after four years in Big Law that he got a crash course in how those companies actually operate, and what being an “effective and helpful” in-house lawyer really means.

“Listening to how the business operates and advising on how they can comply with the law is the core definition of what it is to be a lawyer.” Didday said.

The product counsel's job is to figure out what the company is planning to do and ensure that the path to that goal from idea to launch is legal, he added.

Didday said lawyers tend to think of the world as “two sided”: There are plaintiffs and defendants, winners and losers; someone is right and someone is wrong.

“A tech company is more complex," he added. "It's not my job to say finance is right and engineering is wrong. It's more like, 'What are all those departments, and what are they trying to do as a company?' That skill set of learning about and being curious about and communicating with those departments is the crux of the skill that I realized was going to be so important.”

Fortunately, Didday had a mentor early on “who knew everybody at the company really well who really took me under her wing,” he said. “She literally moved my desk so I sat in the middle of the engineers, product managers and designers and took me into every meeting she went into. By necessity that experience made me listen.”

In-house teams have long been organized by disciplines—IP, employment, commercial contracts and litigation. While legal departments need that specialized expertise, they also need lawyers to advise companies on the products and services they offer, said Adrienne Go, former associate general counsel at eBay.

“While we absolutely have to have that expertise, at the same time, the real question is, 'Who is looking after the goods and services?' That's what the company is built on. That's what their brand is built on. It's not necessarily built on that great lawsuit that they just won. It really is built on providing excellent products, things that make people happy,” Go said.

“With our rapid product life cycles in the past 20 years, businesses are being led more and more by their products. And it’s not just a just a brand campaign; it really is how much they are delivering value to their customers," Go added. "And that's where the product counsel comes in—someone who ... really knew the product, cradle to grave and who could actually sit down with the folks who are building these products.”

The product could be anything from an insurance policy to a rideshare service.

“And if the product lawyer is there at the right time, we have the ability to really influence that as it's being developed during the product life cycle, and it puts us in a very good place to be able to advise on something as it's being developed, before it's being launched and not after it's a problem,” Go said.

Olga Mack, the co-founder of Product Law Hub, came to product counseling early in her career at VISA, where she was the first lawyer dedicated to its debit processing services. She said the job prepared her for later general counsel roles.

“This idea of advising and guiding products from idea to launch to growth to scale to sunset, became something that sort of helped me become a general counsel and become closer to the business,” Mack said. “It is a very proactive role. It's not just waiting for issues to arise. It's embedded in the product teams and technology and marketing and sales and ensuring that everything from sort of functionality to compliance is aligned with business goals.”

Later, Mack would go on to other executive roles like vice president of strategy at security auditing blockchain platform Quantstamp Inc. and eventually start her own company Parley Pro, which she sold to LexisNexis in 2022.

“People ask me a lot about what area of law prepared me for business roles," she said. "It’s, hands down, product law. It's not contracts. I'm a former litigator, and it's not litigation. It is product law. It's those same skills.”

The role has matured over the last 20 years at large tech firms like Amazon, Airbnb, Google, Facebook and eBay, but “now you also now see smaller companies, part time or full time, hiring a product counsel to fulfill the role of bringing something to market and guiding it throughout the life cycle,” Mack said. “The idea is to see ahead, be preventative, simplify complex ideas, and help companies to navigate issues that may or may not be yet regulated.”

A Framework for the Future

Most of what Mack learned about product counseling was self-taught.

"There was no class in law school at the time,” Mack said, adding that she learned on the job and through talking to peers from big and small companies across the tech industry.

She would also field questions from aspiring product lawyers.

article.title: Legal Chief of Retailer Beyond Exiting at Tumultuous Time
article.description: The company recently said that its deal to invest $40 million in the ailing Container Store chain is on the rocks.
article.text: Beyond Inc., the housewares giant formerly known as Overstock, is losing its legal chief on Dec. 31, according to a late Friday securities filing. E. Glen Nickle joined the company as associate general counsel in 2016 and became chief legal officer in 2021. The filing comes just days after Midvale, Utah-based Beyond announced that its $40 million investment in the Container Store was on the rocks due because of The Container Store's inability to “secure adequate financing to support the business going forward." One analyst recently said Container Store is in a "freefall." Beyond is struggling as well, having not received the financial boost it expected from buying Bed Bath & Beyond out of bankruptcy for $21.5 million last year. In the second quarter, the most recent available, Beyond lost $42.6 million on revenue of $399.1 million, down 6% from a year earlier. In October, Beyond, which started the year with 830 employees, laid off 20% of its workforce, including Chief Product Officer Carlisha Robinson. The company did not respond to a request for comment from Law.com on Nickle’s departure. Nickle, who earned $1.3 million in 2023, will be entitled to severance, according to Friday's filing, which did not disclose the amount. A May securities filing had said he would be entitled to $606,398 in severance in the event of his termination. After Nickle steps down at year-end, he will transition to an advisory role, the filing said. It did not indicate whether the company had found a successor or initiated a search for one. Nickle has spent his entire career in-house. After receiving his law degree from Brigham Young University, he was an associate general counsel at exercise equipment maker HealthRider, then served as general counsel at NordicTrack, a subsidiary of ICON Health & Fitness. He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on his departure.

article.title: Porsche's Luxembourg-Based Venture Capital Arm Hires General Counsel From Clifford Chance
article.description: Early-career attorney Lynn Nussbaum is taking the legal reins of Porsche Ventures as it hits the gas on its next phase of growth.
article.text: Porsche Ventures, the Luxembourg-based venture capital arm of the luxury car maker Porsche AG, has hired Clifford Chance lawyer Lynn Nussbaum as general counsel, according to a LinkedIn announcement from Nussbaum. Nussbaum did not respond to a message from Law.com seeking comment on the move, and a Porsche spokesperson said the company "does not"comment on personnel matters at this level." The role marks the first in-house job for the young lawyer, who joined Clifford Chance in 2020 after short stints as a legal intern at Luxembourg-based law firms Kleyr Grasso SCS, Trialys and Elvinger Hoss Prussen. Porsche Ventures has been on an investing tear since launching in 2016, pumping funds into startups in such areas as mobility, e-commerce, battery technology and virtual reality. From launch through 2022, Porsche Ventures invested in 39 startups and provided financing to 13 others through Forward 31, a separate Porsche building its own portfolio of startups. Porsche Deputy Chairman Lutz Meschke called that 2016-2022 time frame "the first generation" of Porsche Ventures. In that span, it invested repeatedly in Croatian electric sports car maker Rimac, pumping in a a total of more than $100 million and building its stake to 20%. It also made big bets on WayRay, a Swiss company that makes holographic augmented-reality head-up display technologies for vehicles, Anagog, an Israeli startup specializing in artificial intelligence for mobile phones, and iMaker, a Chinese company that creates virtual influencers and digital ecosystems. In 2023, Porsche Ventures announced it was “shifting into high gear” and had earmarked €250 million (U.S. $263 million) for investments in new companies and its existing portfolio of about 60 startups. Last year, Stuttgart, Germany-based Porsche moved the headquarters of Porsche Ventures to Luxembourg. The VC arm also has offices in Berlin, Shanghai, as well as in Palo Alto, California. So far this year, Porsche Ventures has invested in companies producing technology for lithium-ion batteries, self-driving cars and semiconductors.

article.title: Corporate Bans of AI Tools Come With Their Own Risks
article.description: "You can ban it on company equipment but you can't ban it on other devices that employees might be using. It would be like banning email, or Google search, or a reticence to using the Google enterprise suite of products," said Nithya Das, former chie
article.text: Worries about generative artificial intelligence tools and chatbots show no sign of abating, including the potential for inadvertent leaks of confidential information. A string of companies, including Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase, has restricted or barred the use of AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google's Bard on work devices, fearing employees might inadvertently share source code or business secrets with these platforms. "I think it's shortsighted," said Nithya Das, former chief operating officer and chief legal officer at Olo, a software company that sells online ordering and delivery programs to restaurants. "You can ban it on company equipment but you can't ban it on other devices that employees might be using. It would be like banning email, or Google search, or a reticence to using the Google enterprise suite of products. These are tools that are going to become part of the way people work." Das said she uses ChatGPT for routine queries and contract language, and the results have been a huge time-saver. "I just used it to give me a first draft of some terms of service for a generative AI tool. It wasn't perfect, but it was a good starting point. It saved me a few hours of work and from having to start from scratch," she said. "A lot of colleagues use it for things like that—terms of service, nondisclosure agreements, privacy policies, and using it to give summaries of routine concepts they want to explain to others." Banning new technology is at best a temporary solution to a decadeslong problem around data leaks and intellectual property protection, experts said, especially when employees are already either experimenting with generative AI applications on their own time, or are using them for substantive work. "In a sense, the horse is already somewhat out of the barn. The odds are that employees already are making use of these latest AI tools and have failed to consider the enormous risks involved," said global AI expert and Forbes columnist Lance Eliot. "One thing that is unlikely to work and that can entirely backfire consists of outright banning the use of generative AI. Firms that do this are forsaking the benefits of generative AI. They are also hamstringing the employees that want to save the company time and money by leveraging generative AI. A ban simply says that the top leaders, including the general counsel, are out of touch." Tim Pham, general counsel of Patented.ai, said legal chiefs have long grappled with how to safeguard trade secrets and company knowledge. "I think a lot of the tech companies, in my view, are like the Black Pearl in 'Pirates of the Caribbean,'" Pham said. "Those wooden ships always have leaks. In terms of IP, there's a front door through which you should normally send IP outside, but there are always back doors and side doors; employees leaving, or sending out emails by mistake." AI tools, he said, "have opened up a new category of leaks. And I think the problem is huge." Pham, formerly deputy general counsel and head of IP at Twitter and head of patent prosecution at Google, said that even with training and guidance from security teams, employees can still struggle with identifying and distinguishing confidential company information. "At least with one of the companies I worked at, there was a lot of training and we had a pretty robust InfoSec team. We said what you can and can't do with confidential information and we even labeled certain things as confidential," he said. "But at a tech company you're generating so many documents. And especially if the culture of the company is to share information as much as possible, it is extremely difficult for the average employee to know what is confidential information." Security software designed to prevent users from entering sensitive information and proprietary source code into chatbots offers one solution. Patented.ai created a plug-in called LLM Shield, named after the large language models that serve as the foundational technology behind AI chatbots, to recognize key words and warn users if they're about to inadvertently enter something confidential. "If you are a developer or sales or marketing person and you don't know what's confidential, this provides that co-pilot," Pham said. "It trains itself on all the information that you tell it is confidential. It sees that and can flag it for you." Pham said that for companies such software tools "may help move the risk needle to something that is more acceptable." He added, "I look at the risk needle in terms of IP leaks and sensitive information. The introduction of LLMs have just changed this. The entropy provided by that is just crazy, just moved the needle way up, and I think there are certain things we can do to move it back." OpenAI, which released its public version of ChatGPT in November, is also trying to move the needle back, rolling out new privacy features that allow users to delete their chat history and opt out of sharing their data for training purposes. Companies who use OpenAI's app programming interface can opt in to sharing their data to train the tool's algorithm. Deputy General Counsel Che Chang said the plan is to bring that feature to an enterprise-worthy version of ChatGPT, called ChatGPT Business. "I think the No. 1 request is how GCs can get comfortable with their employees putting information into ChatGPT," Chang said. "They want to allow the use of our technology in a productive way, but they want to understand how to develop a safe policy that protects their company," he said. "Recently, we announced ChatGPT Business, which we think will be a good middle ground and can address these concerns. We plan to make ChatGPT Business available in the coming months." Das said legal chiefs should make sure whatever technology vendor they use has the right security guardrails in place. "Part of this is making sure that as a company you're using either the right paid model, like ChatGPT or Google's Bard product, and educating employees about the risks of using a free tool or a plug-in that may not have the same security provisions," she said. Educating employees on how to use these tools safely can be a challenge, Das said, "but it's always one that can be overcome. If we rewind in time just 10 years ago, employees weren't as familiar with the concept of phishing or not clicking on links. Education increases as the tech becomes more prevalent." She said tech law firms, along with networking groups such as Tech GC and the Women's General Counsel Network, are starting to dig into how legal chiefs can advise their companies on adopting generative AI tools while mitigating risk. While a ban can be an easy legal fix, it's unsustainable as a business strategy, she said, because if a company doesn't embrace this technology, their competitors surely will. "As an executive, I would wonder what the impact on innovation, engagement and talent is if I'm at a company that takes such a firm position instead of treating employees like adults," Das said. "The really strong GCs will figure out how to use this technology in a safe and responsible manner to increase growth." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. "A lot of colleagues use it for things like that—terms of service, nondisclosure agreements, privacy policies, and using it to give summaries of routine concepts they want to explain to others."

Banning new technology is at best a temporary solution to a decadeslong problem around data leaks and intellectual property protection, experts said, especially when employees are already either experimenting with generative AI applications on their own time, or are using them for substantive work.

"In a sense, the horse is already somewhat out of the barn. The odds are that employees already are making use of these latest AI tools and have failed to consider the enormous risks involved," said global AI expert and Forbes columnist Lance Eliot.

"One thing that is unlikely to work and that can entirely backfire consists of outright banning the use of generative AI. Firms that do this are forsaking the benefits of generative AI. They are also hamstringing the employees that want to save the company time and money by leveraging generative AI. A ban simply says that the top leaders, including the general counsel, are out of touch."

Tim Pham, general counsel of Patented.ai, said legal chiefs have long grappled with how to safeguard trade secrets and company knowledge.

"I think a lot of the tech companies, in my view, are like the Black Pearl in 'Pirates of the Caribbean,'" Pham said. "Those wooden ships always have leaks. In terms of IP, there's a front door through which you should normally send IP outside, but there are always back doors and side doors; employees leaving, or sending out emails by mistake."

AI tools, he said, "have opened up a new category of leaks. And I think the problem is huge."

Pham, formerly deputy general counsel and head of IP at Twitter and head of patent prosecution at Google, said that even with training and guidance from security teams, employees can still struggle with identifying and distinguishing confidential company information.

"At least with one of the companies I worked at, there was a lot of training and we had a pretty robust InfoSec team. We said what you can and can't do with confidential information and we even labeled certain things as confidential," he said. "But at a tech company you're generating so many documents. And especially if the culture of the company is to share information as much as possible, it is extremely difficult for the average employee to know what is confidential information."

Security software designed to prevent users from entering sensitive information and proprietary source code into chatbots offers one solution. Patented.ai created a plug-in called LLM Shield, named after the large language models that serve as the foundational technology behind AI chatbots, to recognize key words and warn users if they're about to inadvertently enter something confidential.

"If you are a developer or sales or marketing person and you don't know what's confidential, this provides that co-pilot," Pham said. "It trains itself on all the information that you tell it is confidential. It sees that and can flag it for you."

Pham said that for companies such software tools "may help move the risk needle to something that is more acceptable."

He added, "I look at the risk needle in terms of IP leaks and sensitive information. The introduction of LLMs have just changed this. The entropy provided by that is just crazy, just moved the needle way up, and I think there are certain things we can do to move it back."

OpenAI, which released its public version of ChatGPT in November, is also trying to move the needle back, rolling out new privacy features that allow users to delete their chat history and opt out of sharing their data for training purposes.

Companies who use OpenAI's app programming interface can opt in to sharing their data to train the tool's algorithm. Deputy General Counsel Che Chang said the plan is to bring that feature to an enterprise-worthy version of ChatGPT, called ChatGPT Business.

"I think the No. 1 request is how GCs can get comfortable with their employees putting information into ChatGPT," Chang said.

"They want to allow the use of our technology in a productive way, but they want to understand how to develop a safe policy that protects their company," he said. "Recently, we announced ChatGPT Business, which we think will be a good middle ground and can address these concerns. We plan to make ChatGPT Business available in the coming months."

Das said legal chiefs should make sure whatever technology vendor they use has the right security guardrails in place.

"Part of this is making sure that as a company you're using either the right paid model, like ChatGPT or Google's Bard product, and educating employees about the risks of using a free tool or a plug-in that may not have the same security provisions," she said.

Educating employees on how to use these tools safely can be a challenge, Das said, "but it's always one that can be overcome. If we rewind in time just 10 years ago, employees weren't as familiar with the concept of phishing or not clicking on links. Education increases as the tech becomes more prevalent."

She said tech law firms, along with networking groups such as Tech GC and the Women's General Counsel Network, are starting to dig into how legal chiefs can advise their companies on adopting generative AI tools while mitigating risk.

While a ban can be an easy legal fix, it's unsustainable as a business strategy, she said, because if a company doesn't embrace this technology, their competitors surely will.

"As an executive, I would wonder what the impact on innovation, engagement and talent is if I'm at a company that takes such a firm position instead of treating employees like adults," Das said. "The really strong GCs will figure out how to use this technology in a safe and responsible manner to increase growth."
