article.title: Antitrust Blitzkrieg Against Google Tests Company on Myriad Fronts
article.description: Google's long-held dominance in digital advertising is threatened by intensifying legal woes, including a fresh spate of lawsuits that seek to break up its lucrative advertising business.
article.text: Google's long-held dominance in digital advertising is threatened by intensifying legal woes, including a fresh spate of lawsuits that seek to break up its lucrative advertising business. The Mountain View, California-based company is girding for battle on multiple fronts, as the U.S. Department of Justice, major news publishers and 17 state attorneys general have coalesced around allegations that its stranglehold on the technology behind digital advertising represents an abusive monopoly and allows it to undercut rivals and siphon away advertising dollars from website publishers. The advertising battle is the latest flash point in a long-standing assault on the tech giant by regulators alleging it has illegally used its massive scale to gain competitive advantage. Among the highest-stakes legal battles is a 2020 Department of Justice lawsuit alleging Google gained an illegal lock on the internet search business. The case is scheduled for trial later this year. All the scrutiny could make Google reluctant to strike back at competitive threats as aggressively as it otherwise would have, legal scholars and tech analysts say. Similarly, it could distract leadership, putting it a step behind rivals in the quest to innovate. That's what happened to Microsoft after the federal government in the late 1990s brought its landmark antitrust case against the company alleging it abused its stronghold on the personal computer operating system market, said John Lopatka, an antitrust scholar and Penn State law professor. Microsoft lost the case, but the biggest loss was a loss of focus, Lopatka said. Bill Gates later acknowledged that defending the company diverted his attention from what the company should have been working on at the time—an operating system for mobile phones. "The biggest loss for Microsoft wasn't the effect of the judgment; it was that they weren't paying attention to the marketplace and the technology," Lopatka said. The latest potential distraction is the escalating ad-tech litigation claiming Google controls every layer of the process between advertisers and the webpages that display their ads, beginning with the ad servers that inventory the available space for digital ads, and the auctions through which brands compete over that space. When someone opens a webpage, the ad server flags when a slot is available and puts it up for sale, soliciting bids on ad exchanges where brands compete to win the ability to display their ad to users. Advertisers also use buying tools to specify what demographics they want to target and to set the price they are willing to pay for an ad slot. In a lawsuit filed last month, newspaper publisher Gannett contends that Google bought rather than built its way into ad-tech supremacy, starting with its 2008 purchase of leading ad server DoubleClick. The acquisition led to subsequent purchases of other ad server firms, allowing Google to control the tool publishers use to manage their inventory of available slots for digital ads. Google controls 90% of the publisher-ad-server market via its acquisition of DoubleClick, and the auction side through its ad exchange AdX, which controls 60% of the exchange market. Lopatka said the complexity of the ad market will factor into Google's defense. "It's usually pretty clear when an action could have some benefits for consumers and when it isn't really going to have a benefit," he said. "But this is a complicated market and the technology is complicated. The question is if there is some benefit Google can point to. That's what they're going to have to show." Lopatka said Google will also argue that the government has too narrowly defined the markets at issue. "They're going to begin by saying, 'We don't have any monopoly power. You can't define a market for publisher ad servers; it's broader than that,'" he said. Google is also fending off an antitrust probe from across the Atlantic, as the European Commission informed the tech giant in June that it believes it abused its market position by favoring its own ad-tech services. "Google is present at almost all levels of the so-called adtech supply chain," Europe's antitrust chief Margrethe Vestager said in a statement. "Our preliminary concern is that Google may have used its market position to favor its own intermediation services." The commission said past behavioral remedies have been ineffective and that "only the mandatory divestment by Google of part of its services would address its competition concerns." Google has vehemently defended itself in several withering blog posts, asserting that its ad-tech tools work with competitors' products, and noting that the Justice Department investigated and cleared its two major ad-tech acquisition more than a decade ago. "We make it easy for partners to choose the products and services they want to use across more than 80 rival platforms for publishers and over 700 rival platforms for advertisers," Dan Taylor, Google's vice president for global ads, wrote. Antitrust experts believe divestiture, an extraordinary remedy in both the United States and Europe, poses a bigger, more existential threat to Google's ad machine than a hefty fine. "The normal sanction in Europe is a fine. They've done that in three cases against Google, which is still standing. Forcing them to divest certain things may be a whole different story," Harry First, an antitrust specialist and professor at NYU School of Law, said. "Money is money, but if they have to change the way they do business, it's much more long-standing and much more harmful to their business," he said. He noted that display ads on third-party websites generated just 12% of parent company Alphabet's $32.8 billion in revenue last year. "This may not be the most profitable part of their empire, but they are defending it very vigorously," First said. "They're in many ways an ad company and their revenues run on ads. They would be legitimately worried about anything that strikes at the way they've put together this machine." Experts also say that divestiture, seen by most courts as a drastic measure, would be tough to pull off. "Google is going to say, 'We're an integrated business. All of this flows together and you can't just break things off,'" Lopatka said. "If we get to that stage where the court finds a violation, remedies will be another stage of litigation." Regulators in the U.S., European Union and around the world have been scrutinizing Google for antitrust violations as far back as 2010, but they've turned up the heat this decade. The Justice Department's 2020 lawsuit took direct aim at Google's dominion over search and search advertising, claiming it "used anticompetitive tactics to maintain and extend its monopolies in the markets for general search services, search advertising, and general search text advertising—the cornerstones of its empire." The suit also targets Google's agreements with phone manufacturers such as Apple, Samsung and LG that favor Google over other search engines. At least 11 states have since signed on to the federal lawsuit, which is scheduled to go to trial later this year after a judge rejected Google's bid to have it dismissed. In another sharply worded response, Google's president of global affairs, Kent Walker, called the DOJ's search ad complaint "dubious" and "deeply flawed." He wrote in a blog post, "People use Google because they choose to, not because they're forced to, or because they can't find alternatives." The lawsuit, he added, would do nothing for consumers. "To the contrary, it would artificially prop up lower-quality search alternatives, raise phone prices, and make it harder for people to get the search services they want to use." Google's search ad business gushes cash. It generated $163 billion in revenue last year, 57% of Alphabet's total revenue. Joseph Teasdale, head of tech at the research firm Enders Analysis, said some pro-competitive interventions by regulators, such as curtailing its ability to make its search engine the default, could threaten Google's position in search. "Google controls various surfaces—things like Chrome, Android, Google Assistant—and in the past the ability to make Google the default or only search engine on those surfaces helped maintain its dominance. This tying of Google search to other Google surfaces has been a focus for regulators," he said. But Teasdale said he doesn't believe these interventions ultimately would have much of an effect on its search market share. "At this point Google search is genuinely preferred by users," he said. However, the fact that Google already faces intense antitrust scrutiny could make it harder for the company to strike back when competitors try to encroach on its territory. "In the old days, if Bing added a hot new feature like AI chat, Google could respond by making it difficult or impossible to switch the default search on Android and Chrome," Teasdale said. "That degree of tying is no longer an option, which makes Google's position a bit more vulnerable in theory." He said Microsoft's Bing also could deal a blow to Google if it was able to persuade Apple to make Bing the default search engine on iPhones. But even more worrisome is the potential for the lawsuits to impede Google's ability to use its existing might to help launch new products, Teasdale said. "Although Google search doesn't need a boost from being tied to other Google services, any new products would really benefit from that kind of help," he said. "But Google will be very wary about wielding its full power, and competition regulators will be watching like hawks for any abuse of dominance. This leaves Google hamstrung when competing in the new areas that promise to drive the growth of the tech sector for the next decade: AI, gaming, cloud, VR/AR, and video." He said Google's massive scale and interconnectedness already hinders its ability to be nimble. "So if there's a risk, it's that Google has to run its plans by three or more competition authorities every time it tries to enter a new market or update a product, while competitors don't have to manage that kind of obligation," he said. article.title: 'The Show Must Go On': Solo-GC-of-Year Kevin Colby Pulls Off Perpetual Juggling Act
article.description: "Unless there’s something where they really need a specialist, I pretty much can do it. And they have enjoyed this ability. Not to mention that I can negotiate things in Spanish and Portuguese," said Colby, general counsel of GOWell International Inc
article.text: Kevin Colby is a busy man. As the only in-house lawyer at global energy technology company GOWell International Inc. he has to be flexible. “Sometimes, I have meetings at 7 a.m. and other meetings at 9:30 p.m. It depends on what has to be done,” he said. "For what I'm doing, there's no way this would be a 9-to-5 job. For a GC, you've just got to do what you've got to do.” Colby, winner of Corporate Counsel's 2024 Solo GC of the Year Award, has been a one-man legal department for more than a decade, since joining GOWell from Camara & Sibley, a boutique firm in Houston. But the company, which was founded in China before expanding to open research and development centers in Houston and Dubai, originally had a very different approach to doing legal work. “It was more Chinese thinking at that point. It's now much more global thinking. We still have some cultural issues—you know, in China, lawyers are just seen as administrators, not really part of the whole process. But this is not how the company operates,” Colby said. When he came on board, Colby immediately realized that GOWell needed a serious overhaul of its contracting process. “When there was a document, they would have utter trust in the other side. They would sign these things that were just completely like, ‘Why did you sign this?’” Part of that had to do with the culture, he said. Contracts in China contain very little legal language. Colby had to teach the company it couldn’t just rubber-stamp the other party’s four-page contract, trusting that the other side would be fair, without any terms and conditions. “That was the first thing to attack and create, pretty much out of nothing,” he chuckled. “It was challenging but fun, too.” He also helped institute a strong compliance framework for its many global transactions and robust compliance training for employees, a necessity when your global footprint includes Azerbaijan, Egypt, Indonesia, Mexico, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia. Scott Maberry, a partner at Sheppard Mullin who works closely with Colby on Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other international compliance issues, said the legal terrain Colby navigates has land mines in every direction. "This is a company with operations in a lot of geographies. That includes not just sales in different companies but R&D labs and software engineers all over the place. They’re kind of far-flung. There's a lot of international trade law risk in any company like that," he said. “Of my clients, he’s in the top tier of compliance. He’s really good at that, and it’s a critical general counsel skill. Culturally speaking, if I was hiring a GC for a business I was trying to run, that's the No. 1 thing I’d look for: someone who really understands compliance and gets ahead of problems,” Maberry said. Colby is also particularly adept at issue spotting, Maberry said. “He may not know what the rules are or what the U.S. sanctions on a given country are as of today. But if he knows there’s a big sanctions regime and if they're going to start doing business with that country and they have an R&D lab in that country, he asks the right questions. Then he can go to the business unit and say, ‘This is easy, go ahead’ or ‘We have to expend some resources to make sure this can be done,’" he said. The word “no” isn’t really part of Colby’s lexicon. “Never say no," he said. "There are law departments in many companies that just say, ‘No, you can't do that.’ 'No, you shouldn't do this because of the risk.' But this company does take risks. They're more comfortable with risk, much, much more than other companies.” Maberry said Colby’s success comes in part from his entrepreneurial mindset. “He really understands the goals of the business and its different units and is good at communicating those to me, too," he said. "He’s really proactive with me, saying, 'This is where we have zero risk tolerance and need to be careful,' by contrast with ‘Here’s an area where we want to see what the possibilities are and are willing to take some regulatory risk.’ That’s a difficult skill. I just started to understand it when I was in my 50s and 60s. I don’t know of a lot of young GCs who are good at this yet.” He’s also an integral part of the business. “That was very important to make it that way,” Colby said. “You know, it's not like going to the other building where the legal department is. I'm part of a very organic group that has grown, and me with it.” GOWell Chief Technology Officer Marvin Rourke also appreciates how indispensable Colby has been as the company has expanded its reach throughout the world. “We're juggling lots of different things, whether it's contracts, whether it's negotiations, investors, all of this falls under Kevin’s remit, particularly around … working with different cultures, working with different time zones, different languages," Rourke said. "He doesn’t have a team of people behind him that speaks different languages or is familiar with how things are done in Azerbaijan or Indonesia or Malaysia." And yet, Rourke said, he's worked effectively with local legal counsel and stakeholders of all sizes and interests. "It's always a pleasure to be in a meeting with him," he said. For Colby, who was born and raised in Brazil with an American father and Brazilian mother and speaks English, Spanish and Portuguese, it’s second nature to him to navigate multiple cultures. “I’m a foreigner myself, “ he joked. “Well, not a foreigner, but I grew up with both cultures, Brazilian and American. So this concept of how to explain American concepts to foreigners is not something completely new to me.” In addition to his international background, Colby also came up in the theater. While his work is quite a departure from his first career as a playwright in New York, Colby said his resilience comes in part from that experience. “I think there's a little bit of that theater thing where the show must go on," he said. "You do anything. You do the scenery. You do etc. And I think I have applied that into lawyering. Unless there’s something where they really need a specialist, I pretty much can do it. And they have enjoyed this ability. Not to mention that I can negotiate things in Spanish and Portuguese.” And he does it all with a sense of humor. “Sometimes I have to answer the phone and say, ‘Yes, just a second, Mr. Colby will be right with you,’” he joked. Colby, winner of Corporate Counsel's 2024 Solo GC of the Year Award, has been a one-man legal department for more than a decade, since joining GOWell from Camara & Sibley, a boutique firm in Houston. But the company, which was founded in China before expanding to open research and development centers in Houston and Dubai, originally had a very different approach to doing legal work.

“It was more Chinese thinking at that point. It's now much more global thinking. We still have some cultural issues—you know, in China, lawyers are just seen as administrators, not really part of the whole process. But this is not how the company operates,” Colby said.

When he came on board, Colby immediately realized that GOWell needed a serious overhaul of its contracting process. “When there was a document, they would have utter trust in the other side. They would sign these things that were just completely like, ‘Why did you sign this?’”

Part of that had to do with the culture, he said. Contracts in China contain very little legal language. Colby had to teach the company it couldn’t just rubber-stamp the other party’s four-page contract, trusting that the other side would be fair, without any terms and conditions.

“That was the first thing to attack and create, pretty much out of nothing,” he chuckled. “It was challenging but fun, too.”

He also helped institute a strong compliance framework for its many global transactions and robust compliance training for employees, a necessity when your global footprint includes Azerbaijan, Egypt, Indonesia, Mexico, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia.

Scott Maberry, a partner at Sheppard Mullin who works closely with Colby on Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other international compliance issues, said the legal terrain Colby navigates has land mines in every direction.

"This is a company with operations in a lot of geographies. That includes not just sales in different companies but R&D labs and software engineers all over the place. They’re kind of far-flung. There's a lot of international trade law risk in any company like that," he said.

“Of my clients, he’s in the top tier of compliance. He’s really good at that, and it’s a critical general counsel skill. Culturally speaking, if I was hiring a GC for a business I was trying to run, that's the No. 1 thing I’d look for: someone who really understands compliance and gets ahead of problems,” Maberry said.

Colby is also particularly adept at issue spotting, Maberry said. “He may not know what the rules are or what the U.S. sanctions on a given country are as of today. But if he knows there’s a big sanctions regime and if they're going to start doing business with that country and they have an R&D lab in that country, he asks the right questions. Then he can go to the business unit and say, ‘This is easy, go ahead’ or ‘We have to expend some resources to make sure this can be done,’" he said.

The word “no” isn’t really part of Colby’s lexicon. “Never say no," he said. "There are law departments in many companies that just say, ‘No, you can't do that.’ 'No, you shouldn't do this because of the risk.' But this company does take risks. They're more comfortable with risk, much, much more than other companies.”

Maberry said Colby’s success comes in part from his entrepreneurial mindset.

“He really understands the goals of the business and its different units and is good at communicating those to me, too," he said. "He’s really proactive with me, saying, 'This is where we have zero risk tolerance and need to be careful,' by contrast with ‘Here’s an area where we want to see what the possibilities are and are willing to take some regulatory risk.’ That’s a difficult skill. I just started to understand it when I was in my 50s and 60s. I don’t know of a lot of young GCs who are good at this yet.”

He’s also an integral part of the business. “That was very important to make it that way,” Colby said. “You know, it's not like going to the other building where the legal department is. I'm part of a very organic group that has grown, and me with it.”

GOWell Chief Technology Officer Marvin Rourke also appreciates how indispensable Colby has been as the company has expanded its reach throughout the world.

“We're juggling lots of different things, whether it's contracts, whether it's negotiations, investors, all of this falls under Kevin’s remit, particularly around … working with different cultures, working with different time zones, different languages," Rourke said. "He doesn’t have a team of people behind him that speaks different languages or is familiar with how things are done in Azerbaijan or Indonesia or Malaysia." And yet, Rourke said, he's worked effectively with local legal counsel and stakeholders of all sizes and interests. "It's always a pleasure to be in a meeting with him," he said.

For Colby, who was born and raised in Brazil with an American father and Brazilian mother and speaks English, Spanish and Portuguese, it’s second nature to him to navigate multiple cultures. “I’m a foreigner myself, “ he joked. “Well, not a foreigner, but I grew up with both cultures, Brazilian and American. So this concept of how to explain American concepts to foreigners is not something completely new to me.”

In addition to his international background, Colby also came up in the theater. While his work is quite a departure from his first career as a playwright in New York, Colby said his resilience comes in part from that experience.

“I think there's a little bit of that theater thing where the show must go on," he said. "You do anything. You do the scenery. You do etc. And I think I have applied that into lawyering. Unless there’s something where they really need a specialist, I pretty much can do it. And they have enjoyed this ability. Not to mention that I can negotiate things in Spanish and Portuguese.”

And he does it all with a sense of humor. “Sometimes I have to answer the phone and say, ‘Yes, just a second, Mr. Colby will be right with you,’” he joked.

article.title: Companies' Dirty Little Secret: Those Privacy Opt-Out Requests Usually Aren't Honored
article.description: “Ignoring privacy requests in states where they are legally obligatory creates a huge legal risk. Most companies that do so usually don't have evil intentions but haven't properly configured their consent-management tools," said Jules Polonetsky,
article.text: Global privacy control lets computer users set privacy preferences in their browsers, automatically sharing those choices whenever users go to a site. It's supposed to give individuals more control over their personal data, allowing them to opt in or out of cookie usage, data sharing, data selling and targeted advertising. But they only work if companies honor them. And in most instances, they don't. Research from two major privacy compliance firms found that the vast majority of the most-visited websites in the United States and Europe do not honor GPC and opt-out preference signals. “It's not that they don't want compliance or they don't want to honor; it's just somehow it's broken,” said Vaibhav Antil, CEO of privacy software company Privado, whose State of Website Privacy Report 2024 found 76 of the top 100 websites in the United States do not honor opt-out consent signals, as the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 requires. More than 80% of those sites were in the media, e-commerce and lifestyle industries, which rely heavily on ads to drive and monetize website traffic. The United Kingdom fared no better, with 74 of the 100 most-visited sites not honoring the opt-in preferences required under the Data Protection Act 2018, which mirrors the provisions of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation of 2016. “In Europe, there is no signal. You have to interact with the banner. So, in our test, we actually interacted with the banner. We would go in, reject all cookies and see if still calls are being made or trackers are being fired or cookies are being stored,” Antil said. They were. And if these websites are not honoring GPC signals, it’s fair to assume that they are not honoring simple “do not sell/share” opt-out clicks. “We didn't explore it, but it should be similar because the thing is these are misconfigurations,” he said. Privado’s findings track with similar data from consent management platform DataGrail in its 2024 Data Privacy Trends Report. DataGrail audited more than 5,000 websites and found 75% of them do not comply with GPC requests. This comes as consumers are increasingly interested in protecting their privacy. DataGrail found more than a 200% increase in data subject access requests from 2021 to 2023. “When you actually engage with the cookie banner, and you're hopefully trying to address your preferences, you actually hope they work. Sorry to tell you they probably don't,” DataGrail CEO Daniel Barber said at his firm’s annual privacy summit in June. Why is that? It’s complicated, said Jules Polonetsky, internet privacy expert and CEO of the Future of Privacy Forum. “When you visit a website, a kaleidoscope of cascading things occurs. The second you request a webpage, your browser is requesting cookies from a website. Milliseconds later, the servers that have just been pinged are pinging companies and other companies and networks and multiple third-party plug-ins are loading,” he said. “Ignoring privacy requests in states where they are legally obligatory creates a huge legal risk. Most companies that do so usually don't have evil intentions but haven't properly configured their consent-management tools. Getting these tools to work properly can be hugely complicated, and we see even sophisticated companies dropping the ball, or shall I say, dropping the cookie,” he said. The nebulousness of an internet protocol address makes it more difficult to identify who is making the opt-out request. “An IP address could be you and your laptop at home or at a Wi-Fi on a university campus, and that's one IP address for the whole college,” said Ryan O'Leary, research director at International Data Corp. “It's hard to manage the consent, and after you leave that website, it's almost like you weren't there. When you have a known relationship with a brand—let’s say you log into your Apple ID or Target account—you're a known person" and have to manage the consent there," he said. "But it's virtually impossible to marry that ID to the IP address that clicked ‘do not track.’ If you're just bumping around from channel to channel or website to website, they don't have a duty to honor your choices.” GPC has some 50 million users worldwide. Currently, just three states—California, Colorado and Connecticut—require companies to comply with GPC signals. But laws requiring opt-out signals kick in in Delaware and Montana on Jan. 1, and in Oregon and Texas one year later. And while New York doesn't have a consumer data protection law, its attorney general, Letitia James, argued in guidance released this summer that data laws on the books bar websites from making false or misleading statements, which she said means that any privacy controls a site claims to offer must work as described. Justin Yedor, a Baker & Hostetler partner who specializes in California privacy laws, said that many consumers who have set up GPC signals live in states without a privacy law requiring websites to honor them. “So just the fact that the GPC is not being recognized, I don't think implies there's necessarily any non-compliance,” he said. But the legal risks from failing to honor opt-out signals are real. “Sale/sharing opt-out has been the most enforced issue under the [California Consumer Privacy Act] from the very beginning of the CCPA enforcement. It's a big issue for both the California [attorney general] and the California Privacy Protection Agency, who are dual enforcers. Both of them are highly interested in this issue. In terms of top compliance issues from a regulator standpoint under the CCPA I think it's really difficult to conclude that there's any other issue that comes first before that one,” Yedor said. And beyond the regulatory realm, plaintiffs lawyers are lurking, Yedor said. “If you right click in Chrome, you can inspect the site and see what cookies are loading. You can see when certain scripts are firing. You can review the data packets that are within a cookie. There's really a lot that you can see without any sophisticated tools. If you take the extra steps to look, you can see it. And that's what plaintiffs counsel are doing," he said. "It's important for businesses that are working to comply with these laws to make sure that they're checking, as well, because they don't want to be the only one in the dark. You don’t want plaintiffs counsel intensely scrutinizing your site and you haven't taken a look at it,” he added. Polonetsky said that while there are "the crappy lawyers sending copy-and-paste lawsuits to thousands of companies offering to settle and go away, the more sophisticated ones run real forensic tools and do a lot of research." For instance, he said, the plaintiffs firm Edelson operates technical labs and does in-depth forensic work. State attorneys general also are on the prowl for violations, relying on technology built by computer scientists, including Ashkan Soltani, a former chief technologist for the Federal Trade Commission who's now executive director of the California Privacy Protection Agency. At the federal level Polonetsky said, the FTC is focusing on websites related to health care and mental health. “We've seen actions, particularly in areas where data might be particularly sensitive,” he said. So how do companies avoid all of this scrutiny? By making sure consent management settings are properly configured. “Putting up a consent banner is not enough. You need to actually test if it is working or not,” Antil said. That's trickier than it sounds. Antil said websites are so dynamic that it’s hard to keep up, especially as companies add more third-party integrations. “So literally you add a line of code, and you suddenly have Google Analytics as part of your website, Meta Ads. Now, it has moved to a point where you literally have platforms where you just insert one integration of a tag manager, and then that is owned by a marketing team. And from there you can actually switch on and switch off third parties just by a click of button,” he said. “As you've democratized adding more and more third parties and made it easier for that integration to happen on the website, I think that's one of the main reasons why these consent issues pop up. There is a real possibility that you have a 100-person marketing department, and they might not know the consequences of switching on a new pixel," he said. O’Leary added: "The challenge is this is not the main business for folks. It's an additional kind of workflow you need to do, and it's not bringing in any revenue." At the same time, the consequences of missteps can be substantial, ranging from costly settlements or judgments to reputational damage and an erosion of consumer trust. “The whole impetus behind these regulations is to give people the ability to opt out,” O’Leary said, noting that awareness is growing among consumers of the harms that can result from being tracked without their knowledge. “There's a lot of scary stuff that could happen," O'Leary said. "There are certainly people that would not want to be tracked and have a lot to lose.” NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. article.title: Climate Change Will Up Pressure on Tech Over Energy-Hungry Data Centers
article.description: Data centers, the giant facilities that form the backbone of the internet, soon will fall under more scrutiny as climate risk disclosure rules and investor expectations put more pressure on tech to reduce its environmental footprint.
article.text: Data centers, the giant facilities that form the backbone of the internet, soon will fall under more scrutiny as climate risk disclosure rules and investor expectations put more pressure on tech to reduce its environmental footprint. With the rise of social media, video streaming, self-driving vehicles and generative artificial intelligence tools, the amount of digital data being created, replicated and processed every year is escalating, and with it the global demand for storage. The market research firm International Data Corp. estimates that the "datasphere" will grow to 175 zettabytes by 2025, likening the world's entire data collection to a stack of DVDs that could circle the Earth 222 times. And the buildings that house the servers on which most of this data sits consume a great deal of energy, accounting for nearly 2% of the electricity use in the U.S., according to the U.S. Department of Energy. They also account for roughly 2% of worldwide greenhouse gas emissions and 3% of the world's electricity supply, twice as much as 10 years ago, according to the Association of Computing Machinery. Data centers also require a tremendous amount of water. A Virginia Tech study says data centers consume water both directly to prevent overheating and indirectly to generate electricity, drawing from 90% of U.S. watersheds. Making matters worse, they disproportionately rely on increasingly scarce water supplies. The researchers noted that "many of the water-sheds in the Western U.S. exhibit high levels of water stress, which is exacerbated by data centers direct and indirect water demands." Communities in both Europe and the western United States have pushed back on new data center construction, even those that purport to use renewable energy. In 2021, a Dutch farming community challenged Meta's plans to build a hyper-scale data center with more than 5,000 servers, culminating in the social media giant's pulling the plug last year. Environmental advocacy groups have also expressed concern over Google's efforts to expand its data center footprint in The Dalles, Oregon. "We have set goals to replenish more water than we consume by 2030 and to support water security in communities where we operate," the company said in its latest 10-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. "We are focused on three areas: enhancing our stewardship of water resources across Google offices and data centers; replenishing our water use and improving watershed health and ecosystems in water-stressed communities; and sharing technology and tools that help everyone predict, prevent, and recover from water stress," the company said. This all comes at a time when regulators, shareholders and consumers are demanding more action from the tech sector on climate change. Beginning in 2024, close to 10,000 American companies with more than $162 million (€150 million) in annual revenue that operate in Europe will have to report how their businesses affect the environment and verify their sustainability efforts under the EU's new climate sustainability reporting directive. The SEC also has a rule in the works that will require companies to detail climate-related risks and emissions data, including any reduction plans or targets. Former SEC Assistant Director Emily Pierce, now an associate general counsel and chief global policy officer at Persefoni, a software firm that helps companies manage climate disclosure requirements, said the pressure will be ramping up. "That pressure is both from existing market forces, as well as market forces that will be accelerated by upcoming regulatory expectations or requirements," she said. "It's sort of like a little infinity loop. You get all this market pressure growing, and now the regulators are stepping in to get more consistent, reliable, comparable disclosures about emissions information, which is just going to further the market pressures on companies to manage their emissions better." Data centers, she said, will be one more crucial element of the broader fight to mitigate the effects of climate change. "There is a lot of energy use associated with data centers. It's going to be an important factor among many factors that a company has to consider when thinking about what data center to use," Pierce said. "Tech is such a fundamental part of our economy. It's one of those things that it has to happen, but can we find ways to do it in a more efficient way? And I think there's absolutely going to be both market pressure and regulatory pressure to try to find ways to do it differently." The highly anticipated SEC climate rule is expected to be released in late summer or early fall. While it doesn't mandate that companies take steps to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, it will draw more attention on how their operations effect the planet. "To the extent to which tech companies will have to disclose greenhouse gas emissions or other metrics related to data centers is a little bit of a question mark, but it certainly will put more of a spotlight on energy usage and greenhouse gas emissions by data centers and put pressure on them to either take additional substantive steps to reduce those emissions and energy usage or at least disclose their plans to do so," said Michael Littenberg, a Ropes & Gray partner who heads its environmental, social and governance, corporate social responsibility, and business and human rights practice. Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer, said he believes the SEC rules are still a "long way off from becoming final" and "will be much watered down" as it faces inevitable legal challenges. Regardless, companies "will have to respond to investor demands and what investors want in terms of climate disclosure, Rosen said. He said that SEC Chair Gary Gensler proposed the rule last year on the premise that "investors are demanding consistent and verifiable climate disclosure." In the meantime, he said companies shouldn't discount California, where the Legislature is pushing two aggressive bills, the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act and the Climate-Related Financial Risk Act. They would apply to both private and public companies that do business in California. Public companies are already required to make disclosures about climate risks that are material to their business, and many are already voluntarily going further than that. Microsoft's annual report outlines both its progress and difficulties in achieving "carbon negative" goal by 2030, noting that its scope 3 emissions have increased in 2021 "due in substantial part to significant global datacenter expansions and growth in Xbox sales and usage as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic," adding, "We have learned the impact of our work will not all be felt immediately, and our experience highlights how progress won't always be linear." Some industry groups see the problem as ever more urgent. "The energy demands and carbon output of computing and the entire ICT [information communication technology] sector must be dramatically moderated if climate change is to be slowed in time to avoid catastrophic environmental damage. The scale of the challenge is great and growing fast," the Association of Computing Machinery's Tech Policy Council said in a 2021 brief. The brief says that company pledges to adopt 100% renewable energy are important, though on their own will not eliminate their climate impacts. While a switch to 100% renewable energy could reduce ICT emissions by more than 80%, the brief says, "this should not be seen as license for continued growth in data center energy demand, nor computing energy demand in general." Rosen noted that there have been some positive developments that can help companies lessen the imprint of data centers on the climate. In May, the Environmental Protection Agency, with input from data center operators Equinix and Iron Mountain, put out best practices to help customers of shared data centers mitigate their carbon footprint. "So there are steps that can be taken; things like replacing the old, inefficient hardware, setting up more efficient infrastructure, addressing airflow management, optimal operating temperatures, proper cabling, separation of the hot and cold aisles, server efficiency," he said. This all comes at a time when regulators, shareholders and consumers are demanding more action from the tech sector on climate change. Beginning in 2024, close to 10,000 American companies with more than $162 million (€150 million) in annual revenue that operate in Europe will have to report how their businesses affect the environment and verify their sustainability efforts under the EU's new climate sustainability reporting directive.

The SEC also has a rule in the works that will require companies to detail climate-related risks and emissions data, including any reduction plans or targets.

Former SEC Assistant Director Emily Pierce, now an associate general counsel and chief global policy officer at Persefoni, a software firm that helps companies manage climate disclosure requirements, said the pressure will be ramping up.

"That pressure is both from existing market forces, as well as market forces that will be accelerated by upcoming regulatory expectations or requirements," she said. "It's sort of like a little infinity loop. You get all this market pressure growing, and now the regulators are stepping in to get more consistent, reliable, comparable disclosures about emissions information, which is just going to further the market pressures on companies to manage their emissions better."

Data centers, she said, will be one more crucial element of the broader fight to mitigate the effects of climate change.

"There is a lot of energy use associated with data centers. It's going to be an important factor among many factors that a company has to consider when thinking about what data center to use," Pierce said.

"Tech is such a fundamental part of our economy. It's one of those things that it has to happen, but can we find ways to do it in a more efficient way? And I think there's absolutely going to be both market pressure and regulatory pressure to try to find ways to do it differently."

The highly anticipated SEC climate rule is expected to be released in late summer or early fall. While it doesn't mandate that companies take steps to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, it will draw more attention on how their operations effect the planet.

"To the extent to which tech companies will have to disclose greenhouse gas emissions or other metrics related to data centers is a little bit of a question mark, but it certainly will put more of a spotlight on energy usage and greenhouse gas emissions by data centers and put pressure on them to either take additional substantive steps to reduce those emissions and energy usage or at least disclose their plans to do so," said Michael Littenberg, a Ropes & Gray partner who heads its environmental, social and governance, corporate social responsibility, and business and human rights practice.

Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer, said he believes the SEC rules are still a "long way off from becoming final" and "will be much watered down" as it faces inevitable legal challenges.

Regardless, companies "will have to respond to investor demands and what investors want in terms of climate disclosure, Rosen said. He said that SEC Chair Gary Gensler proposed the rule last year on the premise that "investors are demanding consistent and verifiable climate disclosure."

In the meantime, he said companies shouldn't discount California, where the Legislature is pushing two aggressive bills, the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act and the Climate-Related Financial Risk Act. They would apply to both private and public companies that do business in California.

Public companies are already required to make disclosures about climate risks that are material to their business, and many are already voluntarily going further than that. Microsoft's annual report outlines both its progress and difficulties in achieving "carbon negative" goal by 2030, noting that its scope 3 emissions have increased in 2021 "due in substantial part to significant global datacenter expansions and growth in Xbox sales and usage as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic," adding, "We have learned the impact of our work will not all be felt immediately, and our experience highlights how progress won't always be linear."

Some industry groups see the problem as ever more urgent. "The energy demands and carbon output of computing and the entire ICT [information communication technology] sector must be dramatically moderated if climate change is to be slowed in time to avoid catastrophic environmental damage. The scale of the challenge is great and growing fast," the Association of Computing Machinery's Tech Policy Council said in a 2021 brief.

The brief says that company pledges to adopt 100% renewable energy are important, though on their own will not eliminate their climate impacts. While a switch to 100% renewable energy could reduce ICT emissions by more than 80%, the brief says, "this should not be seen as license for continued growth in data center energy demand, nor computing energy demand in general."

Rosen noted that there have been some positive developments that can help companies lessen the imprint of data centers on the climate.

In May, the Environmental Protection Agency, with input from data center operators Equinix and Iron Mountain, put out best practices to help customers of shared data centers mitigate their carbon footprint.

"So there are steps that can be taken; things like replacing the old, inefficient hardware, setting up more efficient infrastructure, addressing airflow management, optimal operating temperatures, proper cabling, separation of the hot and cold aisles, server efficiency," he said.

article.title: More Aspiring GCs Finding Fulfillment in Wild and Woolly Realm of Private Equity | Corporate Counsel
article.description: “You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that,” said Sarah Tinsley, general counsel of Culture Amp.
article.text: "You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that," said Sarah Tinsley, general counsel of Culture Amp. July 22, 2024 at 10:39 AM 8 minute read By Maria Dinzeo In-house lawyers eyeing the general counsel seat will find a limited number of options in the Fortune 500. But a growing number of aspiring GCs are finding opportunities abound in the sometimes-overlooked realm of private equity portfolio companies. While the number of public companies has waned since the late 1990s, the private equity industry has boomed, creating in-house opportunities at private equity-owned companies and companies backed by venture capital. The sector needs legal leaders with business savvy, a healthy appetite for risk and the ability to see the job as a long-term investment, said John Gilmore, co-founder and managing partner of the recruiting firm BarkerGilmore. Gilmore said his firm just finished six candidate searches for private equity clients. Portfolio companies see the general counsel role as a "mission critical hire," Gilmore said. With a base salary at around $300,000 and bonuses at 60%, compensation comes mostly in the form of equity, which can deter those seeking guaranteed higher upfront remuneration, Gilmore said. "You're not going to see the cash award windfall immediately, but more important than the cash is that you wind up with the title of enterprise general counsel and you can use that as a launching pad for your career," he said. "It's not about the money, it's about the opportunity to do something." That spirit of adventure is what led Sarah Tinsley in 2019 to become general counsel of the Australian human resource and employee feedback platform Culture Amp. After a decade working in-house, Tinsley said she was looking to step out of her comfort zone as a lawyer and "learn something completely new and different." The founders at Culture Amp "caught me at a moment where I was really contemplating what is my next move. I've been doing this for a while. Where's my next growth opportunity coming from?" Tinsley said. The job gave her the chance to be more hands-on in the business and manage projects that fell outside the legal scope. "You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that," Tinsley said. "I've done stuff that is very much outside of the conventional legal lane. So for my own growth and development, that's been incredible. And as a GC, every time I do something like that, I'm learning more about the business. So it makes me more effective because I really understand what's going on. And that is always powerful knowledge to get as a GC," she said. Learning on the Fly Gilmore said companies owned by private equity tend to hire their first general counsel to shift work away from outside lawyers. Others hire to replace a retiring outside counsel and may upgrade the position and responsibilities as the company grows. He said his clients are looking for lawyers with high emotional intelligence who deal well with pressure. "They want the lawyer who the first thing they do isn't call outside counsel. They want someone who can figure things out first—the person who can master things quickly," he said. Tech investor David Cheng, a partner at San Francisco-based venture capital firm DCM, said his portfolio companies tend to look for a general counsel once they start to run into bottlenecks, such as unreasonable delays in closing sales as contracts wait to be reviewed or employment issues going unaddressed because the HR team is too overwhelmed. "A lot of times, our series A companies will hire someone who isn't a GC and give them a broader title that encompasses more of the business side, something to do with strategy and operations, and it also encompasses legal because there isn't enough legal work to do," he said. "When I'm interviewing GCs, I pitch it as an opportunity to expand your purview beyond legal. It allows them to increase the breadth of their work." Charlotte Morgan was a law firm lawyer and an entrepreneur before she joined the New York City-based lingerie and swimwear brand Adore Me as chief legal officer in 2016, a job that she says has stretched her in ways she didn't expect. The company had launched five years earlier, and Morgan was its only lawyer. "And when you are the one and only lawyer in the room, you are expected to do everything legal, and things that are not part of the legal function as well," she said. Morgan said the job has given her a crash course in areas where she had little or no experience, such as real estate, employment and intellectual property law. When Adore Me received a demand letter on a patent, for instance, Morgan found herself learning how patents apply to bras and to the curvature of the padding inserted into their cups. "You're always learning something new. But it's just doing the best you can to learn everything, relying on outside counsel where you exceed the scope of your expertise, and integrating it for the next adventure," she said. "I think that somebody who's going to do really well in the GC role … is really someone who likes to roll their sleeves up and get their hands dirty. The way you learn in any business is really by doing," she said. Morgan has since taken on the additional role of chief administrative officer. "I run both the people and the legal function. I don't think lawyers are generally known to be people masters. So that is a skill set that I've had to develop on the fly," she said. 'Is It Going to Overwhelm You?' When Tinsley jumped aboard Culture Amp in 2019, eight years after its founding, she was its third lawyer. It has since had as many as 10 in-house counsel based in Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom. Lawyers wanting to be the GC of a startup "really have to be comfortable in a less structured environment than most lawyers are used to working in. I find that incredibly stimulating and fun. It's not for everyone," Tinsley said. "One of the challenges when you're looking at your next move is to be really honest with yourself about that. Is that intensity and speed something that you are going to get energy from? Or is it going to overwhelm you?" Tinsley said she thoroughly researched how the company was run "because I needed to know that there was a really solid basis behind this company, and certainly the founders were very good with me in giving me lots of information to make that decision. But there was a little bit of a leap of faith when it comes to salary. The equity piece is never a guarantee in the startup space and in the private company space. So you do need to be aware of that." Morgan agreed that GCs of portfolio companies need to have "a bit more risk tolerance than your average lawyer, if for no other reason that the salary is not as good or as steady as at law firms." "Once you leave law firm life, you are no longer guaranteed 'lifetime employment.' But of course, that's an overstatement, but it is riskier. You're joining a business with ups and downs and you need to perform or there are consequences for the lack of performance. Often times you negotiate a stake of equity, and you need to be comfortable with that risk and comfortable that that long-term investment will pay off," Morgan said. Gilmore said his biggest challenge in filling portfolio company GC roles is finding "entrepreneurial, highly qualified lawyers who are not focused on short-term cash compensation." "These lawyers are highly vested with the success of the business through sizable equity grants and motivated by the long-term potential. I have witnessed several general counsel managing multiple transactions with the same company who achieved greater wealth than most public company peers," he said. But it doesn't always work out, Cheng cautioned. "I've joined companies that went bankrupt and my stock options ended up being worthless, so I lost money," he said. "That's always the risk. You're taking a pay cut in terms of cash assuming the stock equity is going to be worth something." Tinsley said that as much as she "would love for a great outcome for everyone in the company, particularly the founders," she doesn't want to obsess over it. "In the meantime, my focus is on having a great journey by enjoying what I do, making sure that I'm learning, building a great team, doing really good work and growing," she said. "And hopefully being remunerated well along the way. But I think if you focus too much on the end goal, it will skew your perspective." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. After a decade working in-house, Tinsley said she was looking to step out of her comfort zone as a lawyer and "learn something completely new and different."

The founders at Culture Amp "caught me at a moment where I was really contemplating what is my next move. I've been doing this for a while. Where's my next growth opportunity coming from?" Tinsley said.

The job gave her the chance to be more hands-on in the business and manage projects that fell outside the legal scope.

"You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that," Tinsley said.

"I've done stuff that is very much outside of the conventional legal lane. So for my own growth and development, that's been incredible. And as a GC, every time I do something like that, I'm learning more about the business. So it makes me more effective because I really understand what's going on. And that is always powerful knowledge to get as a GC," she said.

Learning on the Fly

Gilmore said companies owned by private equity tend to hire their first general counsel to shift work away from outside lawyers. Others hire to replace a retiring outside counsel and may upgrade the position and responsibilities as the company grows.

He said his clients are looking for lawyers with high emotional intelligence who deal well with pressure.

Tech investor David Cheng, a partner at San Francisco-based venture capital firm DCM, said his portfolio companies tend to look for a general counsel once they start to run into bottlenecks, such as unreasonable delays in closing sales as contracts wait to be reviewed or employment issues going unaddressed because the HR team is too overwhelmed.

"A lot of times, our series A companies will hire someone who isn't a GC and give them a broader title that encompasses more of the business side, something to do with strategy and operations, and it also encompasses legal because there isn't enough legal work to do," he said. "When I'm interviewing GCs, I pitch it as an opportunity to expand your purview beyond legal. It allows them to increase the breadth of their work."


Charlotte Morgan was a law firm lawyer and an entrepreneur before she joined the New York City-based lingerie and swimwear brand Adore Me as chief legal officer in 2016, a job that she says has stretched her in ways she didn't expect.

The company had launched five years earlier, and Morgan was its only lawyer. "And when you are the one and only lawyer in the room, you are expected to do everything legal, and things that are not part of the legal function as well," she said.

Morgan said the job has given her a crash course in areas where she had little or no experience, such as real estate, employment and intellectual property law. When Adore Me received a demand letter on a patent, for instance, Morgan found herself learning how patents apply to bras and to the curvature of the padding inserted into their cups.

"You're always learning something new. But it's just doing the best you can to learn everything, relying on outside counsel where you exceed the scope of your expertise, and integrating it for the next adventure," she said.

"I think that somebody who's going to do really well in the GC role … is really someone who likes to roll their sleeves up and get their hands dirty. The way you learn in any business is really by doing," she said.

Morgan has since taken on the additional role of chief administrative officer. "I run both the people and the legal function. I don't think lawyers are generally known to be people masters. So that is a skill set that I've had to develop on the fly," she said.

'Is It Going to Overwhelm You?'

When Tinsley jumped aboard Culture Amp in 2019, eight years after its founding, she was its third lawyer. It has since had as many as 10 in-house counsel based in Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom.

Lawyers wanting to be the GC of a startup "really have to be comfortable in a less structured environment than most lawyers are used to working in. I find that incredibly stimulating and fun. It's not for everyone," Tinsley said. "One of the challenges when you're looking at your next move is to be really honest with yourself about that. Is that intensity and speed something that you are going to get energy from? Or is it going to overwhelm you?"

Tinsley said she thoroughly researched how the company was run "because I needed to know that there was a really solid basis behind this company, and certainly the founders were very good with me in giving me lots of information to make that decision. But there was a little bit of a leap of faith when it comes to salary. The equity piece is never a guarantee in the startup space and in the private company space. So you do need to be aware of that."

Morgan agreed that GCs of portfolio companies need to have "a bit more risk tolerance than your average lawyer, if for no other reason that the salary is not as good or as steady as at law firms."

"Once you leave law firm life, you are no longer guaranteed 'lifetime employment.' But of course, that's an overstatement, but it is riskier. You're joining a business with ups and downs and you need to perform or there are consequences for the lack of performance. Often times you negotiate a stake of equity, and you need to be comfortable with that risk and comfortable that that long-term investment will pay off," Morgan said.

Gilmore said his biggest challenge in filling portfolio company GC roles is finding "entrepreneurial, highly qualified lawyers who are not focused on short-term cash compensation."

But it doesn't always work out, Cheng cautioned. "I've joined companies that went bankrupt and my stock options ended up being worthless, so I lost money," he said. "That's always the risk. You're taking a pay cut in terms of cash assuming the stock equity is going to be worth something."

article.title: 'It Was a Bunch of Spooked Wildebeests': How Tech GCs Survived the SVB Panic
article.description: "This bank was very helpful to the tech community. Dealing with mainstream traditional banks for early stage startups is going to be way more burdensome," said Manuel Martinez-Herrera, GC of BetterCloud.
article.text: Silicon Valley Bank's astonishingly rapid meltdown tested tech's top in-house lawyers, who flew into emergency response mode to help steer their companies through the chaos. Greg Raiten, co-founder of the general counsel network and platform TechGC, said the upheaval wrought by SVB's collapse within the tech in-house community was on par only with the COVID-19 pandemic. "We saw four or five waves just like this," he said, referring to the early days of the coronavirus. "First, the conversation was about closing offices, transitioning to remote work, impact to business models. Then came layoffs and PPP loans. Then came vaccine mandates and whether/how to go back to office. There were all these spikes of tough and unprecedented questions that the community was navigating together." Raiten said he started closely monitoring SVB on March 9, the day before federal banking regulators took it over, after seeing chatter about the institution's troubles on social media. By the next day, it was clear that circumstances had deteriorated, as murmurs about a possible bank run began to reverberate across Twitter and industry group chats. Raiten started reaching out to the tech and venture fund GCs that comprise TechGC's nearly 4,000 members. His business partner Kiran Lingam, a former GC at equity crowd-funder SeedInvest, rallied industry chief financial officers for an emergency clubhouse session on March 10 through TechGC's sister platform, The F Suite. Raiten said about 250 CFOs participated. Midway through the call, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. announced it had taken control of the bank. Hungry for clarity and guidance, hundreds of finance and legal chiefs logged on over the weekend to share information. "It was partially group therapy—a lot of this is being with your peers, venting and sharing fear—but it was mostly just how do we figure this out. Everyone wanted to know what everyone else was doing and what they were hearing," Raiten said. TechGC global chair Danielle Sheer added: "When something happens, and nobody knows how to solve it, it's the general counsel that the question lands on. No matter the topic, no matter if it's truly legal in nature, when there's a problem that nobody knows how to solve, the general counsel is at the center of that storm." Even compared with the 2008 financial crisis, the panic that followed SVB's sudden demise was striking. "It was the eight craziest days of my professional career," said Sheer, the chief legal and compliance officer of the privacy software company Commvault. About 300 GCs from across the tech industry convened for a March 11 forum led by Sheer and Manuel Martinez-Herrera, GC of BetterCloud. "It was very hectic for the whole community," Martinez-Herrera said. "Payroll was No. 1 top-of-mind issue over [that] weekend for many members of the community. Then it morphed into, 'Are my customers going to be OK, I need bank accounts at other places, and are my clients going to think I'm in trouble because we were banking at SVB?'" Sheer said GCs worried about the legal ramifications around missing upcoming payroll deadlines, whether wires they'd initiated on Friday would go through, and whether they would have to furlough employees. "There were calls all weekend long for the companies in the greatest amount of pain and stress," Sheer said. "The community rallied to help with thinking through different options, and helping them get creative on inbound financing to keep them afloat." Templates were shared for bridge financing and short-term loan agreements. On March 12, the community hosted an employment webinar with partners from Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati. Sheer said her company had $1 million at SVB, but did most of its banking at JPMorgan Chase. "I wasn't worried that the lights were going to go out, but I was an SVB customer, so I was going through everything that the rest of the GCs were going through," she said. "And a lot of our GCs had all of their money in Silicon Valley Bank because their lead venture capitalist who gave them that money as an investment insisted that it be held at Silicon Valley Bank." Such was the situation at venture-backed retailer Camp, which had most of its cash in SVB. Sheer said it held a 50% off sale to raise emergency capital, but was left scrambling to find a new bank to process payments. "There was a lot of discussion about how fast it was to open accounts at banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America versus going to other regional banks," she said. Meanwhile, venture fund GCs were grappling with their own unique set of issues, including the regulatory implications of making bridge loans to portfolio companies. TechGC ended up hosting a separate venture fund GC webinar with a corporate partner from Gunderson Dettmer, which specializes in venture-backed companies and investors. Raiten said some executives raised concerns about the potential for other bank failures. First Republic Bank, which ended up receiving a $30 billion lifeline from a consortium of bigger institutions on March 16, was at the center of the discussion, as GCs debated in TechGC forums whether they should pull out their funds, a move they acknowledged would worsen First Republic's problems. "There were a lot of people calling this type of behavior out, saying, 'This was what caused the problem, let's not do that again.' But it was also a tough situation; everyone generally acknowledged that viewpoint in theory, but you also can't take that type of a core business risk based on a principled stance without considering reality," Raiten said. "Everyone was struggling with that. We had several members who were making big statements that we should not do this, and others said, 'I agree, but at the same time, we have to protect our business,'" he added. Even with the federal government's decision on March 12 to guarantee uninsured deposits at SVB, GCs still face uncertainty about the weeks and months ahead. "Things weren't quite working just yet," said Rene Paula, general counsel at biotech company Vaxxinity. Paula, who worked on the receivership for San Juan-based Eurobank after it was shuttered in 2010, said that despite assurances from regulators, some companies still had trouble accessing their money. "People couldn't still quite get their wire transfers processed, and there were questions about how sweep accounts were going to be treated," he said. SVB's collapse was a major blow for the tech industry, Martinez-Herrera said, leaving many to wonder how startups will be affected in the years to come by the loss of a longtime banking partner. "This bank was very helpful to the tech community. Dealing with mainstream traditional banks for early stage startups is going to be way more burdensome," he said. "Silicon Valley Bank filled a niche need in the tech industry: to provide lines of credit and a great banking service to the tech industry. And their terms were great," Sheer said. "When you're negotiating a deal with JPMorgan versus Silicon Valley Bank, there are differences in the terms," she said. "What does that mean for companies going forward, and for the future of investing in startups?" She added that the tech industry remains anxious about what the future holds. "How do we make sure to future-proof keeping our business up and running in light of a banking crisis, which can happen very fast," she said. "It was like a stampede, that's what it was. It was just a stampede. It was a bunch of spooked wildebeests." In the short term, tech industry leaders are focused on liquidity, and trying to insulate their companies from future financial disasters. "What a lot of people are saying now is that you need to have multiple banking relationships, at least one of which should be with an SIB," Raiten said, referring to systemically important banks. "And you should have enough liquid capital to cover payroll from more than one account in case any one gets frozen like this. The next layer people are thinking about is their cash management and investment strategies of their 'excess' cash." GCs also talked about moving funds back to Silicon Valley Bridge Bank, the newly created entity in charge of what remains of SVB. "Some venture funds have been publicly encouraging portfolio companies to stay there with some portion of their cash," Raiten said, citing a petition circulating on LinkedIn. TechGC has moved to support the new bank, replenishing its account with the $250,000 it had stored there. "We moved it out when we could, and then moved it back to support the SVBB after we saw the announcements they made," he said. "But it's not what we need for payroll." Sheer said that going forward startups probably will have to shoulder more of the burden of ensuring their own financial stability. "Given what we just lived through, it is the company's responsibility to make sure that they can survive any number of events. And I think a lot of companies will think twice about banking with just one bank," she said. "I think the pendulum will swing to the companies to implement the right capital deposit strategy versus the VCs who are telling them where they want their money held," she added. Sheer said SVB's failure opened a whole new realm of risk exposure for companies. "Our boards are starting to talk about this as a key enterprise risk, because a bunch of companies were going to come to an absolute standstill," she said. "That didn't happen, thank God, but how can we be prepared for this in the future, and are we capitalized correctly to make it through a three- or six-month period of chaos? Because it's not over yet." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. All other uses, submit a request to [email protected]. "It was very hectic for the whole community," Martinez-Herrera said. "Payroll was No. 1 top-of-mind issue over [that] weekend for many members of the community. Then it morphed into, 'Are my customers going to be OK, I need bank accounts at other places, and are my clients going to think I'm in trouble because we were banking at SVB?'"

Sheer said GCs worried about the legal ramifications around missing upcoming payroll deadlines, whether wires they'd initiated on Friday would go through, and whether they would have to furlough employees.

"There were calls all weekend long for the companies in the greatest amount of pain and stress," Sheer said. "The community rallied to help with thinking through different options, and helping them get creative on inbound financing to keep them afloat."

Templates were shared for bridge financing and short-term loan agreements. On March 12, the community hosted an employment webinar with partners from Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati.

Sheer said her company had $1 million at SVB, but did most of its banking at JPMorgan Chase.

"I wasn't worried that the lights were going to go out, but I was an SVB customer, so I was going through everything that the rest of the GCs were going through," she said. "And a lot of our GCs had all of their money in Silicon Valley Bank because their lead venture capitalist who gave them that money as an investment insisted that it be held at Silicon Valley Bank."

Such was the situation at venture-backed retailer Camp, which had most of its cash in SVB. Sheer said it held a 50% off sale to raise emergency capital, but was left scrambling to find a new bank to process payments.

"There was a lot of discussion about how fast it was to open accounts at banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America versus going to other regional banks," she said.

Meanwhile, venture fund GCs were grappling with their own unique set of issues, including the regulatory implications of making bridge loans to portfolio companies. TechGC ended up hosting a separate venture fund GC webinar with a corporate partner from Gunderson Dettmer, which specializes in venture-backed companies and investors.

Raiten said some executives raised concerns about the potential for other bank failures. First Republic Bank, which ended up receiving a $30 billion lifeline from a consortium of bigger institutions on March 16, was at the center of the discussion, as GCs debated in TechGC forums whether they should pull out their funds, a move they acknowledged would worsen First Republic's problems.

"There were a lot of people calling this type of behavior out, saying, 'This was what caused the problem, let's not do that again.' But it was also a tough situation; everyone generally acknowledged that viewpoint in theory, but you also can't take that type of a core business risk based on a principled stance without considering reality," Raiten said.

"Everyone was struggling with that. We had several members who were making big statements that we should not do this, and others said, 'I agree, but at the same time, we have to protect our business,'" he added.

Even with the federal government's decision on March 12 to guarantee uninsured deposits at SVB, GCs still face uncertainty about the weeks and months ahead.

"Things weren't quite working just yet," said Rene Paula, general counsel at biotech company Vaxxinity. Paula, who worked on the receivership for San Juan-based Eurobank after it was shuttered in 2010, said that despite assurances from regulators, some companies still had trouble accessing their money.

"People couldn't still quite get their wire transfers processed, and there were questions about how sweep accounts were going to be treated," he said.

SVB's collapse was a major blow for the tech industry, Martinez-Herrera said, leaving many to wonder how startups will be affected in the years to come by the loss of a longtime banking partner.

"This bank was very helpful to the tech community. Dealing with mainstream traditional banks for early stage startups is going to be way more burdensome," he said.

"Silicon Valley Bank filled a niche need in the tech industry: to provide lines of credit and a great banking service to the tech industry. And their terms were great," Sheer said.

"When you're negotiating a deal with JPMorgan versus Silicon Valley Bank, there are differences in the terms," she said. "What does that mean for companies going forward, and for the future of investing in startups?"

She added that the tech industry remains anxious about what the future holds. "How do we make sure to future-proof keeping our business up and running in light of a banking crisis, which can happen very fast," she said. "It was like a stampede, that's what it was. It was just a stampede. It was a bunch of spooked wildebeests."

In the short term, tech industry leaders are focused on liquidity, and trying to insulate their companies from future financial disasters.

"What a lot of people are saying now is that you need to have multiple banking relationships, at least one of which should be with an SIB," Raiten said, referring to systemically important banks. "And you should have enough liquid capital to cover payroll from more than one account in case any one gets frozen like this. The next layer people are thinking about is their cash management and investment strategies of their 'excess' cash."

GCs also talked about moving funds back to Silicon Valley Bridge Bank, the newly created entity in charge of what remains of SVB. "Some venture funds have been publicly encouraging portfolio companies to stay there with some portion of their cash," Raiten said, citing a petition circulating on LinkedIn.

TechGC has moved to support the new bank, replenishing its account with the $250,000 it had stored there. "We moved it out when we could, and then moved it back to support the SVBB after we saw the announcements they made," he said. "But it's not what we need for payroll."

Sheer said that going forward startups probably will have to shoulder more of the burden of ensuring their own financial stability.

"Given what we just lived through, it is the company's responsibility to make sure that they can survive any number of events. And I think a lot of companies will think twice about banking with just one bank," she said.

"I think the pendulum will swing to the companies to implement the right capital deposit strategy versus the VCs who are telling them where they want their money held," she added.

Sheer said SVB's failure opened a whole new realm of risk exposure for companies.

"Our boards are starting to talk about this as a key enterprise risk, because a bunch of companies were going to come to an absolute standstill," she said. "That didn't happen, thank God, but how can we be prepared for this in the future, and are we capitalized correctly to make it through a three- or six-month period of chaos? Because it's not over yet."
