article.title: As SVB's Risks Skyrocketed, Bank Let Chief Risk Officer Post Sit Vacant for Months
article.description: "It's like having an airplane without a pilot or a ship without a captain. It will move, but to what direction?" said Charles Elson, a retired professor of corporate governance at the University of Delaware.
article.text: The abrupt collapse of venture capital darling Silicon Valley Bank has exposed several glaring governance and risk management lapses, including that it parted ways with its chief risk officer in April 2022 and appears to have operated without a full-time replacement for nearly the remainder of the year. In its 2023 proxy statement filed March 3, SVB revealed that it initiated talks with chief risk officer Laura Izurieta to leave her job in early 2022. Pursuant to a separation agreement, Izurieta stepped down April 29, 2022, and moved into a "non-executive role focused on certain transition-related duties," which looked to be mostly an advisory role that included helping to find her replacement. The filing did not explain what drove the departure of Izurieta, who'd joined SVB in 2016 after 16 years at Capital One, where she'd risen to executive vice president. She did not respond to a request for comment by ALM. "Given the significance of the position of the Chief Risk Officer, it was important to the Company that the transition be facilitated in a manner that supported continuity and retention within the Risk organization as we searched for a new Chief," SVB wrote in its filing. The filing noted that the new CRO, Kim Olson, started on Dec. 27, 2022. Olson came from Japan-based Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp., where she was chief risk officer for the Americas. The CRO's job is to manage the company's risk-valuation process, said Charles Elson, a retired professor of corporate governance at the University of Delaware. "Someone should be there to steward the operation and evaluate how the group is functioning. Without that, it's like having an airplane without a pilot or a ship without a captain. It will move, but to what direction? That's the concern," he said. For a CRO role to sit unfilled for eight months isn't entirely unwonted. Clifford Rossi, a former chief risk officer for Citigroup's Consumer Lending Group, said his role also had been open for eight months before he joined Citigroup in 2007. But the position is so technically complex that such a vacancy can be problematic. "It makes it difficult that risk is being properly managed across the enterprise," Rossi said. Rossi, who is an executive-in-residence at the University of Maryland's Robert H. Smith School of Business, said he also was struck by the apparent lack of risk management expertise among board members on SVB's risk committee, to which the CRO directly reports. Rossi said SVB's board, which represents shareholders, had a responsibility to ensure that management wasn't engaging in risky activities that could lead to a situation as dire and unprecedented as the $42 billion bank run that caused the institution to fail last week. "You need people who can effectively challenge management on those decisions. I have personally been at those meetings at places like Countrywide, Citigroup, and Washington Mutual, where I was managing liaison," he said. At SVB, Rossi said, "few had any level of knowledge around risk management to push back and ask the right questions. If the board can't ask the right questions, how can they represent shareholders?" According to its 2023 proxy statement, SVB's risk committee members consisted of board chair and former Ernst & Young partner Beverly Kay Matthews, former U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Mary Miller, retired Kaiser Permanente chief information officer Richard Daniels, consulting firm owner Joel Friedman, and venture capitalists and investors Éric Benhamou, Kate Mitchell and Garen Staglin. Noah Barsky, a professor in executive and graduate business programs at Villanova University School of Business, noted the absence of SVB board member Thomas King, a former Barclays investment banking CEO, from this group. "He ostensibly has far greater substantive financial services experience than the committee comprised of a Napa vineyard owner, a retired healthcare CIO, a former U.S. Treasury undersecretary, venture capital partners and consulting firm heads," Barsky wrote in an analysis for Forbes. Rossi posited that the absence of a CRO might have created a risk management vacuum that gave individuals on the business side who push for riskier investments "much more of a voice in risk committee meetings than they should have had. At least a chief risk officer is there to provide the credible challenge against the other voice. Otherwise, the [committee members] have no way of telling that what they hear isn't right." SVB's investment strategy, which included pouring billions of dollars into U.S. Treasuries and government-backed mortgage securities, has fallen under heavy scrutiny. The securities, which the bank had intended to hold to maturity, lost value as the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates. As worried customers withdrew deposits, the bank on March 8 sold a $21 billion portfolio at a $1.8 billion loss to shore up liquidity. "We'd been living in a declining interest rate environment, so people didn't have to worry about managing interest rate risks, but when interest rates spiked and a bank sits on top of fixed income assets, people are going to get hurt," Rossi said. Morris Pearl, a former managing director at investment firm BlackRock, put it even more bluntly. "I think the bank management writ large screwed up in a major way," Pearl said, noting that of the $212 billion in assets SVB reported for the fourth quarter of 2022, "at least $68 billion of this was mortgages with a high degree of interest rate risk." SVB's 10-K filed Feb. 24 said $57 billion of those mortgages were government-sponsored enterprises such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. A little more than $10 billion were fixed-rate collateralized mortgage obligations. "They also had this huge unrealized loss of $11 billion" from those mortgage-backed securities, Pearl said. Pearl, who was part of a team that helped the federal government assess the cost of Citibank's bailout during the 2008 financial crisis, said SVB was using short-term money to fund long-term investments, and appears to have miscalculated that interest rates weren't going to continue to rise. "A risk officer's job would be to think about these things at least," Pearl said, adding that ultimately the bank's failure belongs to the whole of its management. The risk committee's unusually high number of meetings—18 in 2022, according to its proxy statement—suggests the committee suspected something was afoot. The prior year, the committee met just seven times. "It's unusual to have that many meetings. That tells me there was panic," Rossi said. "Every risk committee has to have minutes. I'd love to see the minutes of those." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. article.title: SVB's Implosion Has Tech Companies Reeling. Here's What They Should Do
article.description: "The board, the c-suite, are all going to be looking at the lawyers and my guess is this is a once in a lifetime crisis, so you want to make sure you have people you can count on on your legal team," said three-time general counsel Sterling Miller.
article.text: The demise of startup financing cornerstone Silicon Valley Bank on Friday sent tech corporate executives and legal department chiefs scrambling to find other sources of financing and immediate solutions. With New York-based Signature Bank becoming the next financial institution to fall, the Federal Reserve moved swiftly over the weekend to stem the fallout. The Fed's measures, announced late Sunday, underscored the potential for the contagion to spread. In the days and weeks ahead, observers said, corporate leaders and in-house legal teams will be racing to identify financial and payroll risks. Some affected companies may want to extend payment terms with vendors, review insurance options as well as lean on outside counsel, they said, with general counsel immediately taking on a mountain of new responsibilities to help their companies regain footing in a shaky financial ecosystem. Companies that had the bulk of their funds deposited with SVB were in a particularly tight spot as the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. (FDIC) only insures up to $250,000 in deposits, offering a receivership certificate for the rest. "This is an apocalyptic moment for companies," said Foster Sayers, general counsel for software company Pramata on Friday. He said Pramata was able to pull money out of the bank and transfer it to another institution where it had an account just in time. The wire cleared Thursday afternoon. "It was not a moment too soon," he said. Others weren't so fortunate. Streaming company Roku disclosed in an 8-k filing on Friday that 26%, or roughly $487 million of its cash, is currently in uninsured deposits at SVB. "At this time, the company does not know to what extent the company will be able to recover its cash on deposit at SVB." It added that it believes it will be able to meet its obligations with the rest of its $1.4 billion in cash. Biotech company Wave Life Sciences reported that it has $1.5 million in cash at SVB, which is $1.25 million over the FDIC-insured amount, while Oncorus, another biotech company, disclosed that SVB has approximately $10 million, or 23% of its total cash. It also has a standby letter of credit with SVB of about $3.4 million to meet its lease obligations for its Innovation Park offices. By Friday afternoon, SVB's collapse was official, and for many companies, meeting payroll immediately became a top concern, as it wasn't yet certain whether they would be able to access their uninsured deposits on Monday. "The best thing you can do to keep people focused on their work is not having them worried about if they are going to get paid," Sayers said, adding that companies should "figure out and immediately confront any spend that will be going out the door in the next weeks relative to payroll and figure out how they can adjust." He also said that companies left in dire financial straits should temporarily freeze any money going out the door. "You want to talk with anyone in finance, and everyone in procurement, and everyone in legal. Look at contracts to understand what is coming up for renewal and what invoices are coming in so you can put everything on freeze," he said. "A lot of tech companies don't want to deal with invoices and looking at payments, so you want to make sure you lock everything down and immediately communicate with your vendors, especially the ones whose payments are going to be impacted and say, 'I need extended payment terms.'" Sterling Miller, former General Counsel at Travelocity and now CEO and senior counsel at Hilgers Graben, said companies should also be looking for any alternative funding sources to fill their immediate cash needs. "Do I have a line of credit with anyone else? Can I call on private equity to bridge any temporary cash needs I might have? And on the flip side of that, I'm looking at what can I not pay. If I'm in conserve cash flow mode, what are the bills that have to be paid, like payroll, and what can I push out?" Miller also recommended that companies review their insurance policies to see what their coverage options are. "You never know about something that's covered until you pick up the phone and call your broker," he said, adding that companies should also review their contracts for force majeure clauses. "After the pandemic, a lot of companies changed how they define force majeure in ways that are broader than they were before. It's both a shield and a sword." Stephen Mar, general counsel at Odeko, said his company was fortunate not to have been directly impacted by SVB's failure, but for those that were, general counsel will be under a lot of pressure to make decisions quickly with limited information. He said legal chiefs and their executive teams should be prepared to act, but shouldn't panic. "Equally important is understanding what decisions are not time-critical and could benefit from further deliberation," Mar said in an email to Law.com. He said companies should identify and address their primary risk areas first. "For example, here, general counsel should work with their CFOs to understand all institutions where the company's assets are held, the amounts that are insured versus uninsured, and what (if any) immediate actions should be taken," he said. Lawrence Cunningham, a corporate advisor and law professor at George Washington University, said bringing in outside help will be critical, and firms with expertise in banking, regulations and insolvency will be in high demand. "I'm sure the first thing most of these general counsel are doing is asking what outside law firm can they get to help. General counsel can do some work on their own, but will need reinforcements," Cunningham said. Mar echoed this point. "This is one of those times where it helps to have strong relationships with outside counsel who will pick up your call immediately." Miller, a three-time general counsel, said that while outside counsel can help explain the new financial landscape, it's important for legal chiefs to have the backing of a strong in-house team. "The board, the c-suite, are all going to be looking at the lawyers. And my guess is this is a once-in-a-lifetime crisis, so you want to make sure you have people you can count on on your legal team," he said. It's also an opportunity for general counsel to shine. "This is an opportunity to provide value. Embrace it, run to the fire," Miller said. "This is what you've trained for." Benjamin Rhode, a partner in Ropes & Gray's business restructuring group, said Friday that he'd been in client calls all day. "The biggest concern is there are a lot of unknowns. This is obviously evolving very quickly," he said. "The key thing they should be doing is looking for alternative sources for immediate term financing, whether that's a private company or your sponsor, or whether that's getting a bridge loan from a financing institution to shore up near term liquidity needs. Rhode said he was aware of at least one situation where a company had essentially all of its cash in SVB. "They had a line on potential bridge financing to get them through the next couple of weeks while they're going to figure out what's going to happen with the receivership," he said. For some, SVB's failure recalled the 2008 financial crisis— and the accompanying fear and panic that caused markets to freeze. "That caused enormous pain and loss and threatened the entire global economy. The only solution was to find capital to flood the markets," Cunningham said. "I don't think we're in that extreme, but a collapse can freeze a part of the economy, and if you trying to unfreeze that, you need to flood it with capital." Rhode said the coming week will reveal whether a "healthy bank" steps up to assume all of SVB's deposit obligations. "People are going to have to live day to day for the near term until we get more clarity on how this process is going to play out," Rhode said. The demise of SVB, Cunningham said, represents a tragic case study in risk and corporate governance, as well as a lesson in the cascade effect sparked by the collapse of the bank and crytpo-focused Silvergate Capital Corp. on March 9. "The macro environment behind the failures are not isolated, and there are significant systemic risks. But the FDIC is supposed to be there for this. It's whole function is it's there to stabilize, to provide support, and to protect depositors up to certain limits while trying to distribute the pain fairly. It's cold comfort, but nevertheless, we do have a mechanism for addressing this." Cunningham said, adding that it's up to the regulators "to exercise their powers in a way that restores confidence and prevents the systemic fallout." Miller, a three-time general counsel, said that while outside counsel can help explain the new financial landscape, it's important for legal chiefs to have the backing of a strong in-house team.

"The board, the c-suite, are all going to be looking at the lawyers. And my guess is this is a once-in-a-lifetime crisis, so you want to make sure you have people you can count on on your legal team," he said.

It's also an opportunity for general counsel to shine. "This is an opportunity to provide value. Embrace it, run to the fire," Miller said. "This is what you've trained for."

Benjamin Rhode, a partner in Ropes & Gray's business restructuring group, said Friday that he'd been in client calls all day. "The biggest concern is there are a lot of unknowns. This is obviously evolving very quickly," he said. "The key thing they should be doing is looking for alternative sources for immediate term financing, whether that's a private company or your sponsor, or whether that's getting a bridge loan from a financing institution to shore up near term liquidity needs.

Rhode said he was aware of at least one situation where a company had essentially all of its cash in SVB. "They had a line on potential bridge financing to get them through the next couple of weeks while they're going to figure out what's going to happen with the receivership," he said.

For some, SVB's failure recalled the 2008 financial crisis— and the accompanying fear and panic that caused markets to freeze.

"That caused enormous pain and loss and threatened the entire global economy. The only solution was to find capital to flood the markets," Cunningham said. "I don't think we're in that extreme, but a collapse can freeze a part of the economy, and if you trying to unfreeze that, you need to flood it with capital."

Rhode said the coming week will reveal whether a "healthy bank" steps up to assume all of SVB's deposit obligations. "People are going to have to live day to day for the near term until we get more clarity on how this process is going to play out," Rhode said.

The demise of SVB, Cunningham said, represents a tragic case study in risk and corporate governance, as well as a lesson in the cascade effect sparked by the collapse of the bank and crytpo-focused Silvergate Capital Corp. on March 9.

"The macro environment behind the failures are not isolated, and there are significant systemic risks. But the FDIC is supposed to be there for this. It's whole function is it's there to stabilize, to provide support, and to protect depositors up to certain limits while trying to distribute the pain fairly. It's cold comfort, but nevertheless, we do have a mechanism for addressing this." Cunningham said, adding that it's up to the regulators "to exercise their powers in a way that restores confidence and prevents the systemic fallout."

article.html:
ANALYSIS

Bell Tolls on Mandatory Retirement for Exxon Mobil GC

Exxon Mobil's mandatory retirement age of 65 forced the oil giant's prior two general counsel into retirement. Will current GC Craig Morford be next when he turns 65 on Feb. 10?

Corporate Governance

Chris O'Malley
  • Many large companies still have mandatory retirement ages for executives, though firms sometimes make exceptions.
  • Some governance experts question their usefulness in an era of extended life spans.
  • Exxon Mobil isn't commenting on how it will handle General Counsel Craig Morford's turning 65.

Feb. 10 could be bittersweet for Exxon Mobil General Counsel Craig Morford.

Craig Morford joined Exxon Mobil as deputy GC in 2019 and become GC a year later. Courtesy photo

Morford will celebrate his 65th birthday. But unless the energy giant makes an exception to its mandatory retirement policy, or has quietly jettisoned it, it also will be his last official day on the job.

article.title: No Crystal Ball Needed: Predicting Litigation Outcomes Through Data Analytics
article.description: Advancements in technology and AI have led to data analytics becoming an indispensable part of most services and industries. The legal industry has not been untouched by this, and law firms, governments and alternative legal service providers have…
article.text: Advancements in technology and AI have led to data analytics becoming an indispensable part of most services and industries. The legal industry has not been untouched by this, and law firms, governments and alternative legal service providers have also started utilizing data analytics to predict outcomes with remarkable results. In litigation, analytics is able to provide deep insights not previously possible during initial phases. Machine learning and AI are able to mitigate the challenges of information volume and unstructured data as they process and learn from masses of data in fractions of seconds and equip attorneys with the desired details needed to proceed. There are many e-discovery providers that have adopted AI and infused it into their offerings. Their products process and consume terabytes of data on a day-to-day basis, which gives them a head start in data analytics and allows them to provide precise insights from the data with predictive categorization, sentiment analysis, personal information analysis and more. Data consultants and ALSPs are adept at leveraging these tools to assess data and provide lawyers with actionable insights at all stages of the litigation lifecycle. Litigation data analytics covers a variety of techniques designed to analyze information to unlock deep insights from unstructured data using a variety of techniques: Predictive Modeling: This method utilizes historical data, such as for personal injury litigation or commercial litigation, to predict future outcomes, helping lawyers assess the likelihood of success in similar cases. By incorporating diverse case data points, legal professionals can leverage the versatility of predictive modeling across various legal scenarios. Sentiment Analysis: The emotions conveyed in written documents, such as witness statements or jury decisions, can be analyzed to gauge underlying biases or perceptions that may impact case outcomes. However, it’s important to be mindful of the ethical implications of sentiment analysis, ensuring fairness and transparency in legal proceedings. Case Law Analysis: Past judgments can be used to identify patterns that might influence the direction of current cases. Analysis can also be helpful in understanding how different jurisdictions interpret legal precedents and frame litigation strategies. Witness Credibility Assessments: Data can be used to determine the reliability of witness testimony by comparing it against known data points. Discussing challenges such as data quality and the need for human oversight in witness credibility assessment is also required to interpret nuances, context and sentiments which data analytics may overlook. Jury Selection Optimization: Predictive models can assist in selecting jurors who are more likely to sympathize with the case arguments based on demographics and past behavior. However, it’s crucial to balance data-driven jury selection with legal and ethical considerations to ensure fairness. Case Outcome Predictions: By aggregating outcomes from similar cases, lawyers can better prepare for potential challenges and adjust their strategies accordingly. Future trends in data analytics, such as the integration of blockchain technology for data integrity, could further enhance the accuracy of case outcome predictions. Here are some real-world examples of how these techniques have been used: A major law firm applied predictive analytics to determine the most favorable jurisdiction for filing a patent infringement case, leading to a successful outcome that aligned closely with predictive insights. AI was fed all the older cases related to patent infringement claims involving similar technologies, and analysis revealed a judge known for patent rights stands and awarding damages in infringement cases. The law firm filed the case in the identified jurisdiction and got a good result. Data analysis can also be a game-changer in personal injury cases. By looking at past cases with similar injuries, medical records and settlements, lawyers can get a better idea of what kind of compensation clients might receive. This helps with negotiation strategies and building a strong case. Data was used to assist a software company in a copyright case where a competitor used a piece of code in an application and released it on the market. Leveraging technology and AI, the original code and alleged copied code were compared and assessed along with data from metadata fields and error reports, and these were employed to help the client win the case. The use of data analytics in legal processes is no longer optional, but crucial as it advances. With these tools at their disposal, lawyers can approach litigation with a data-driven strategy, rather than relying just on luck and hours of manual review. Streamlining the litigation process and improving the accuracy and timeliness of court decisions save time and money for all parties concerned. Lawyers who are keen to apply this strategy need to begin by collaborating with data consultants or ALSPs adept at data science and employing the best-suited data analytics techniques based on case requirements to develop a winning strategy. In the longer term, to effectively incorporate these technologies into their legal practice and maintain their competitive edge, lawyers will also need to make significant investments in training and development. currently serves as portfolio manager, litigation & investigation services at Proxiio Global Solutions. With more than eight years of experience in the e-discovery and forensics industry, Garg has successfully led and delivered complex projects that involved data collection, processing, review, and production. He can be reached at [email protected].

  • Sentiment Analysis: The emotions conveyed in written documents, such as witness statements or jury decisions, can be analyzed to gauge underlying biases or perceptions that may impact case outcomes. However, it’s important to be mindful of the ethical implications of sentiment analysis, ensuring fairness and transparency in legal proceedings.
  • Case Law Analysis: Past judgments can be used to identify patterns that might influence the direction of current cases. Analysis can also be helpful in understanding how different jurisdictions interpret legal precedents and frame litigation strategies.
  • Witness Credibility Assessments: Data can be used to determine the reliability of witness testimony by comparing it against known data points.   • Jury Selection Optimization: Predictive models can assist in selecting jurors who are more likely to sympathize with the case arguments based on demographics and past behavior. However, it’s crucial to balance data-driven jury selection with legal and ethical considerations to ensure fairness.

Future trends in data analytics, such as the integration of blockchain technology for data integrity, could further enhance the accuracy of case outcome predictions.

Here are some real-world examples of how these techniques have been used:

A major law firm applied predictive analytics to determine the most favorable jurisdiction for filing a patent infringement case, leading to a successful outcome that aligned closely with predictive insights. Lawyers who are keen to apply this strategy need to begin by collaborating with data consultants or ALSPs adept at data science and employing the best-suited data analytics techniques based on case requirements to develop a winning strategy. In the longer term, to effectively incorporate these technologies into their legal practice and maintain their competitive edge, lawyers will also need to make significant investments in training and development.

article.title: 'This Worries Me Gravely': Regulators Struggle to Set Ground Rules for AI Decision-Making Tools
article.description: Creating rules around how businesses can use consumers’ personal information is proving to be easier said than done, as privacy regulators wrestle with how to rein in artificial intelligence and automated decision-making tools, or ADMT. Regulations…
article.text: Creating rules around how businesses can use consumers’ personal information is proving to be easier said than done, as privacy regulators wrestle with how to rein in artificial intelligence and automated decision-making tools, or ADMT. Regulations intended to protect consumers from having significant decisions made about them by machines are a sticking point for the California Privacy Protection Agency, whose board met Tuesday to hammer out details on draft regulations around ADMT. One of those rules would require businesses to submit risk assessments to the CPPA detailing how they use and protect personal information and what the consequences and benefits might be to consumers.
article.html:
Creating rules around how businesses can use consumers’ personal information is proving to be easier said than done, as privacy regulators wrestle with how to rein in artificial intelligence and automated decision-making tools, or ADMT.

Regulations intended to protect consumers from having significant decisions made about them by machines are a sticking point for the California Privacy Protection Agency, whose board met Tuesday to hammer out details on draft regulations around ADMT. One of those rules would require businesses to submit risk assessments to the CPPA detailing how they use and protect personal information and what the consequences and benefits might be to consumers.

article.title: Tech Giants Have Halted Their Legal 'Hiring Frenzy,' but Specialists Will Still Be in Demand
article.description: What You Need to Know Companies face an increasingly risky regulatory landscape.They'll continue to need specialized expertise in areas like antitrust and privacy.Indiscriminate legal cuts would be short-sighted, legal observers say. In-house legal…
article.text: What You Need to Know Companies face an increasingly risky regulatory landscape.They'll continue to need specialized expertise in areas like antitrust and privacy.Indiscriminate legal cuts would be short-sighted, legal observers say. In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory road ahead. “The tech industry experienced unprecedented growth over the last couple of years, which is the reason for the incredible volume of hiring,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The current layoffs in the industry have been more of a market correction given the hiring frenzy over the last couple of years.” That rapid expansion includes e-commerce giant Amazon, whose legal team grew from 800 in 2017 to a LinkedIn directory listing more than 1,800 people employed in some corporate counsel capacity. Facebook parent Meta Platforms also went on a hiring spree last year in the face of tightening privacy regulations. Now both companies have moved to cut staffing levels amid a business slump. “In the last year and a half, all the big tech companies—Facebook, Twitter, Google, Apple, Netflix—they’ve all grown explosively. Now no one is growing,” observed one Bay Area recruiter who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “There’s no ‘we need to hire lawyers to keep up with the growing demand of business.’ Any hiring is very strategic.” Guo with Major, Lindsey & Africa also said in-house hiring has fallen off, but there’s still a demand for attorneys with specialized expertise. “We have seen a slowdown in terms of legal hiring, but we are still having companies and clients coming to us looking for skilled attorneys. We haven’t seen a huge slash in legal departments. That’s not to say lawyers aren’t being laid off, but, at the end of the day, any company that’s looking to grow or pivot is going to need great lawyers.” Guo said attorneys with privacy, compliance or transactional experience will have more favorable prospects. “Privacy attorneys are still very much in demand, and attorneys with specific transaction experience will continue to be fine, even if they have been laid off, given that skills set its very marketable,” she said. “Also attorneys with general corporate and securities experience. Although not as many companies are going public, at the end of the day, if you’re a public company or private company looking to go public, having corporate securities experience is valuable.” As regulators continue to bear down on tech companies over privacy, antitrust and corporate governance, cuts to in-house legal teams may be shortsighted, legal observers say. “I would think it would be at least pretty risky,” said Joshua Davis, a research professor at UC Hastings College of the Law and an expert in antitrust litigation. “There was a perfect storm where Republicans perceived many of these companies as anti-Republican, and Democrats are concerned with market power. And that means really big companies like Facebook and Amazon and Apple—the true monsters—they’ve been really vulnerable. I don’t think that’s changed. It’s quite possible we will see new antitrust legislation passed, which we haven’t seen in 100 years, and that’s going to mean there’s some formidable challenges.” Karen Woody, an associate professor at the Washington and Lee University School of Law, said issues like privacy and cybersecurity aren’t going away simply simply because companies have pared back. “The downturn in the economy and tech industry is unfortunate but not indicative that those issues are going anywhere. They’ll just have less budget to deal with those issues,” she said. “The irony and unfortunate reality is, if you have fewer compliance people, you might have more compliance work to do.” While Amazon confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that it is making cuts to its devices division, which includes Kindle, voice assistant Alexa and speaker Echo, in-house attorneys who support those units could be vulnerable. But Guo said product counsel may be able to pivot to support other areas of the business. News reports say managers are telling many affected employees that they have two months to find another job internally or accept severance. “Really strong product attorneys are not necessarily wedded to one type of product. They understand the different legal issues in relation to the product—be it privacy matters or commercial product launches. Those all are skills that are transitional to other products,” Guo said. “If an attorney at a brand name tech company is laid off but they have strong translational experience, they are marketable.” Former Airbnb general counsel and chief ethics officer Rob Chesnut said companies would be wise not to just slash numbers indiscriminately. “Intelligent companies are looking around corners a little better and they’re not just cutting numbers, but understanding that if you’re cutting an entire business unit and a lawyer was supporting that business unit, you can cut that lawyer because you don’t need them anymore. But the business units that you do operate need certain types of support and they may involve regulatory concerns and privacy concerns,” he said. “Smart companies aren’t just cutting privacy and compliance lawyers. They recognize the value.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Companies face an increasingly risky regulatory landscape.
  • They'll continue to need specialized expertise in areas like antitrust and privacy.
  • Indiscriminate legal cuts would be short-sighted, legal observers say.

In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory road ahead.

“The tech industry experienced unprecedented growth over the last couple of years, which is the reason for the incredible volume of hiring,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The current layoffs in the industry have been more of a market correction given the hiring frenzy over the last couple of years.”

That rapid expansion includes e-commerce giant Amazon, whose legal team grew from 800 in 2017 to a LinkedIn directory listing more than 1,800 people employed in some corporate counsel capacity. Facebook parent Meta Platforms also went on a hiring spree last year in the face of tightening privacy regulations. Now both companies have moved to cut staffing levels amid a business slump.

“In the last year and a half, all the big tech companies—Facebook, Twitter, Google, Apple, Netflix—they’ve all grown explosively. Now no one is growing,” observed one Bay Area recruiter who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “There’s no ‘we need to hire lawyers to keep up with the growing demand of business.’ Any hiring is very strategic.”

Guo with Major, Lindsey & Africa also said in-house hiring has fallen off, but there’s still a demand for attorneys with specialized expertise. “We have seen a slowdown in terms of legal hiring, but we are still having companies and clients coming to us looking for skilled attorneys. We haven’t seen a huge slash in legal departments. That’s not to say lawyers aren’t being laid off, but, at the end of the day, any company that’s looking to grow or pivot is going to need great lawyers.”

Guo said attorneys with privacy, compliance or transactional experience will have more favorable prospects.

“Privacy attorneys are still very much in demand, and attorneys with specific transaction experience will continue to be fine, even if they have been laid off, given that skills set its very marketable,” she said. “Also attorneys with general corporate and securities experience. Although not as many companies are going public, at the end of the day, if you’re a public company or private company looking to go public, having corporate securities experience is valuable.”

As regulators continue to bear down on tech companies over privacy, antitrust and corporate governance, cuts to in-house legal teams may be shortsighted, legal observers say.

“I would think it would be at least pretty risky,” said Joshua Davis, a research professor at UC Hastings College of the Law and an expert in antitrust litigation. “There was a perfect storm where Republicans perceived many of these companies as anti-Republican, and Democrats are concerned with market power. And that means really big companies like Facebook and Amazon and Apple—the true monsters—they’ve been really vulnerable. I don’t think that’s changed. It’s quite possible we will see new antitrust legislation passed, which we haven’t seen in 100 years, and that’s going to mean there’s some formidable challenges.”

Karen Woody, an associate professor at the Washington and Lee University School of Law, said issues like privacy and cybersecurity aren’t going away simply simply because companies have pared back.

“The downturn in the economy and tech industry is unfortunate but not indicative that those issues are going anywhere. They’ll just have less budget to deal with those issues,” she said. “The irony and unfortunate reality is, if you have fewer compliance people, you might have more compliance work to do.”

While Amazon confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that it is making cuts to its devices division, which includes Kindle, voice assistant Alexa and speaker Echo, in-house attorneys who support those units could be vulnerable. But Guo said product counsel may be able to pivot to support other areas of the business. News reports say managers are telling many affected employees that they have two months to find another job internally or accept severance.

“Really strong product attorneys are not necessarily wedded to one type of product. They understand the different legal issues in relation to the product—be it privacy matters or commercial product launches. Those all are skills that are transitional to other products,” Guo said. “If an attorney at a brand name tech company is laid off but they have strong translational experience, they are marketable.”

Former Airbnb general counsel and chief ethics officer Rob Chesnut said companies would be wise not to just slash numbers indiscriminately.

“Intelligent companies are looking around corners a little better and they’re not just cutting numbers, but understanding that if you’re cutting an entire business unit and a lawyer was supporting that business unit, you can cut that lawyer because you don’t need them anymore. But the business units that you do operate need certain types of support and they may involve regulatory concerns and privacy concerns,” he said.

“Smart companies aren’t just cutting privacy and compliance lawyers. They recognize the value.”

article.title: The Morning Minute: Latest Big Law Layoffs Illustrate Inconsistency in Market
article.description: TOO MUCH, TOO FAST - Despite impressive gains at the top of the Am Law 200 charts and a mindset geared more toward growth, layoffs and cuts continue to rattle the industry. Productivity and utilization remain a problem, observers and analysts have…
article.text: TOO MUCH, TOO FAST - Despite impressive gains at the top of the Am Law 200 charts and a mindset geared more toward growth, layoffs and cuts continue to rattle the industry. Productivity and utilization remain a problem, observers and analysts have told Law.com’s Andrew Maloney , as some firms expect deal work to improve only ”incrementally” and the tech sector in particular just hasn’t shown enough resilience. Those assessments come as Fenwick & West told employees on Tuesday that it was laying off “just under” 10% of its professionals, including attorneys and staff. The firm cited a surge in demand from 2020 through early 2022 that caused Fenwick & West to hire “quite aggressively,” said Richard Dickson, the firm’s chair, in a memo viewed by Law.com. “It felt necessary at the time. But, with the benefit of hindsight, it represented a deviation from our core principle of managing for the long-term,” Dickson said. LEGAL ORGANIZATION - From the casinos on the Las Vegas Strip to Hollywood’s writing rooms, workers are turning to their unions to seek protections against the risks that emerging technologies like genAI may pose to their jobs. Could a growing movement by employees to prepare for the impact of generative AI spread to an industry that hasn’t traditionally been prone to unionization, like legal? As Law.com’s Cassandre Coyer reports , in many ways, the legal industry is now at an inflection point. Stuck between the prospect of roles being transformed, if not entirely threatened, by the technology, an ongoing push toward business-oriented structural changes, and questions around the longevity of the billable hour, some believe this could be the industry’s first real opportunity to meaningfully consider collective bargaining.

article.title: Companies Flummoxed by Regulatory Chaos Around Cybersecurity
article.description: The American Bar Association hosted a panel Thursday on the fragmented cybersecurity regime. Some companies feel second-guessed instead of supported. The newly created White House Office of the National Cyber Director has promised to bring harmony to…
article.text: The American Bar Association hosted a panel Thursday on the fragmented cybersecurity regime. Some companies feel second-guessed instead of supported. The newly created White House Office of the National Cyber Director has promised to bring harmony to the landscape. Companies are facing an increasingly unpredictable, burdensome and fragmented regulatory regime when it comes to cybersecurity. Such was the prevailing message Thursday at a virtual panel on cybersecurity law and policy hosted by the American Bar Association’s Homeland Security Law Institute. Megan Leef Brown, a partner with Wiley Rein, said the private sector is struggling to handle multiple reporting obligations regarding data breaches or ransomware attacks. “I’m seeing major shifts in the regulatory landscape, some of which I really find quite troubling. It’s daunting for the private sector. I perceive a real dissonance and fragmentation in how some of the agencies are approaching this,” she said. This content has been archived. It is available through our partners, LexisNexis® and Bloomberg Law. LexisNexis® and Bloomberg Law customers are able to access and use ALM's content, including content from the National Law Journal, The American Lawyer, Legaltech News, The New York Law Journal, and Corporate Counsel, as well as other sources of legal information.
article.html:
• The American Bar Association hosted a panel Thursday on the fragmented cybersecurity regime.
  • Some companies feel second-guessed instead of supported.
  • The newly created White House Office of the National Cyber Director has promised to bring harmony to the landscape.

Companies are facing an increasingly unpredictable, burdensome and fragmented regulatory regime when it comes to cybersecurity. Such was the prevailing message Thursday at a virtual panel on cybersecurity law and policy hosted by the American Bar Association’s Homeland Security Law Institute.

Megan Leef Brown, a partner with Wiley Rein, said the private sector is struggling to handle multiple reporting obligations regarding data breaches or ransomware attacks. “I’m seeing major shifts in the regulatory landscape, some of which I really find quite troubling. It’s daunting for the private sector. I perceive a real dissonance and fragmentation in how some of the agencies are approaching this,” she said.

article.title: BlackBerry’s Randall Cook Ignites Change While Facing Novel Challenges
article.description: Smartphone revolutionizer BlackBerry Inc. had been struggling to find new entry points into the technology market, but in Randall Cook’s first year he’s helped the company pivot its overall business. Joining BlackBerry in August 2018 as chief legal…
article.text: Smartphone revolutionizer BlackBerry Inc. had been struggling to find new entry points into the technology market, but in Randall Cook’s first year he’s helped the company pivot its overall business. Joining BlackBerry in August 2018 as chief legal officer and corporate secretary, Cook oversaw the process of the company providing security software that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning in multiple areas from cybersecurity to crisis communication, which according to the company is being used by over 70% of the U.S. government. Customers include other global governments, financial services institutions, major automotive manufacturers, aerospace and defense companies, health care companies and media companies. Cook oversaw BlackBerry’s $1.4 billion acquisition of Cylance, an artificial intelligence and cybersecurity company that was completed in February 2019. It’s the largest deal in the company’s history. Adding more business meant winding down other lines of business to transition from a handset company to one focused on security software, especially when it can dominate the market with more than $1 billion in revenue. What made BlackBerry a recognizable name has evolved with Cook’s legal department finalizing the exit of the last licensed phone manufacturer for the legacy smartphone business. Cook assisted the company in keeping the encrypted messaging platform business under a global licensing agreement worth over $100 million.

article.title: Former Deputy GC at EV Company Canoo Among Execs Accused of Corporate Espionage
article.description: What You Need to Know Canoo alleges former deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow played a key role in a corporate espionage scheme. The suit says Fielkow and others stole intellectual property and poached employees to start Harbinger Motors.…
article.text: What You Need to Know Canoo alleges former deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow played a key role in a corporate espionage scheme. The suit says Fielkow and others stole intellectual property and poached employees to start Harbinger Motors. Harbinger calls the allegations baseless. Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which is known for its distinctive egg-shaped auto design, filed a federal lawsuit on Dec. 22 accusing former Canoo CEO John Harris, chief technology officer Phillip Weicker, chief operating officer William Eberts, vice president Alexi Charbonneau and Fielkow of swiping Canoo’s proprietary technology and poaching its employees to create Harbinger Motors in 2021. Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology.

Canoo, which is known for its distinctive egg-shaped auto design, filed a federal lawsuit on Dec. 22 accusing former Canoo CEO John Harris, chief technology officer Phillip Weicker, chief operating officer William Eberts, vice president Alexi Charbonneau and Fielkow of swiping Canoo’s proprietary technology and poaching its employees to create Harbinger Motors in 2021.

article.title: Congressional Probes Often Catch Companies Off Guard. Is Your Company Ready?
article.description: "Regardless of the political landscape, there's bipartisan interest in scrutinizing companies, especially larger ones with more perceived influence in the economy," said Kimberly Hamm, a partner at Mayer Brown. Congressional investigations of…
article.text: "Regardless of the political landscape, there's bipartisan interest in scrutinizing companies, especially larger ones with more perceived influence in the economy," said Kimberly Hamm, a partner at Mayer Brown. Congressional investigations of companies are becoming more common, and they pose numerous, unique challenges, said Kimberly Hamm, who joined the Washington, D.C., office of Mayer Brown as partner in January after spending most of the last decade in key government legal roles. She said congressional inquiries often are complicated by political divisions, lack of precedents and the potential that multiple committees will be conducting separate but overlapping inquiries at the same time. Hamm was immersed in the process herself as chief counsel to House Speaker Kevin McCarthy before his ouster last October. Before that, she was chief counsel for investigations in the U.S. Senate. Other roles included chief counsel to Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Jay Clayton during the Trump administration and associate general counsel of the House. She started her legal career at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, where she spent 11 years. In a conversation with Corporate Counsel, Hamm discussed how her years in government will inform the advice she’ll give clients. She also talked about what sets congressional probes apart from inquiries from other arms of government. The conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length. Corporate Counsel: You have served as chief counsel to an SEC chairman and a House speaker and in the House General Counsel’s Office. How have those experiences impacted the way you advise clients and approach your work? Kimberly Hamm: In all of my jobs, my role was to take a difficult set of facts or a difficult regulatory issue and create the best advocacy for them. Across my previous positions, I played a significant role in institutional issues, including determining the best approach for congressional investigations and protecting congressional interests and tools. Also, taking into account all these divergent viewpoints. So in all cases, it was a combination of advocacy, listening and being able to hear different perspectives. In the House, in particular, people have different ideas about how to do things. The focus has to be on what’s the right thing for the committee and the institution, because protecting congressional prerogatives was a big part of what I did. CC: What are some of the potential changes in congressional investigations under a new administration that companies or GCs should be aware of? KH: It’s really hard to predict that. If there’s a Republican president next year, much will depend on whether the Republican Party also controls the House and Senate. Should that be the case, oversight and investigations may focus on the private sector and scrutinize programs implemented during the Biden administration. However, if there’s a split with a Democratic House or Senate, attention may shift toward oversight of the executive branch’s actions, including how they’re implementing laws and spending money. There will still be a really big focus on the private sector, as we’ve seen this Congress. Regardless of the political landscape, there’s bipartisan interest in scrutinizing companies, especially larger ones with more perceived influence in the economy. So even if there’s a different president, you’ll see private sector scrutiny. In the House, the majority party determines the direction of investigations. Unlike in the Senate, if a House committee wants to issue a subpoena to either a government entity or private sector entity to get documents or testimony, that can be done unilaterally by the chair—they do not need the minority party’s consent. There doesn’t have to be a vote of the committee. There doesn’t have to be a vote in the House. The chairmen can do that themselves. So whoever controls the majority in the House really controls the direction of investigations. CC: What are some of the things that companies should be aware of when it comes to ESG investigations? And what should their initial response be should they be faced with an ESG investigation? KH: One fascinating aspect to consider is the broadening of the ESG debate within congressional investigations. Previously, ESG issues primarily fell under the purview of specific committees, such as the House Financial Services Committee. However, now we’re witnessing ESG-related investigations spanning multiple committees, including the House Ways and Means Committee, the House Oversight and Accountability Committee and the House Judiciary Committee. This poses unique challenges for companies, particularly those in the financial sector, as they navigate interactions with various committees, each with its own jurisdiction and focus. What began as a narrow discussion on ESG investing has evolved into a multifaceted debate touching on diverse environmental, social and governance matters. Dealing with multiple committees concurrently, albeit investigating similar themes, adds layers of complexity. Hence, it’s essential to engage legal counsel well-versed across all relevant committees. What attracted me to Mayer Brown is its long and established history of expertise and relationships across committees. That’s really important, because you’re seeing increasingly where multiple committees are getting involved in a single issue at the same time. CC: What is something that sets you apart as a lawyer in your practice area? KH: I have a very unique perspective on congressional investigations because of my extensive experience across various committees. During my time at the House General Counsel’s Office, I had the opportunity to advise numerous committees on their investigations, which allowed me to witness firsthand how different committees approach investigations and the tools they use. If there’s litigation, it’s the House Office of General Counsel that goes to court to enforce subpoenas. So, I have that experience. Working in the speaker’s office provided me with a unique leadership perspective, overseeing committee activities and offering strategic guidance. This dual vantage point—combining litigation expertise with leadership insights—is somewhat rare in the legal field. Few individuals have engaged in litigating congressional subpoena cases, and while litigation is not the desired outcome, understanding the relevant rules, case law and precedents is crucial. So I think that’s a great asset for companies that are finding themselves under scrutiny. CC: How can corporate legal departments prepare when the government comes knocking? What are some best practices? KH: Well, the first step is acknowledging that sometimes you won’t have advance notice of an impending investigation. However, in cases like ESG, where companies could anticipate scrutiny if the House shifted to Republican control, early preparation is key. This involves assembling a cross-functional team comprising legal, compliance, government affairs and external public relations and regulatory experts. You want to make sure that your team is assembled and ready to act quickly and that you have at least some of the messaging and the responses ready. That said, when it comes to congressional investigations, often it’s very event-specific and can move rapidly, catching companies off guard, because there could be an accident or a whistleblower that you weren’t aware of. In that case, it’s really important that you assemble your team quickly and that you make sure that team includes all of the right people, and that team needs to be able to work seamlessly together. It’s also important to understand how congressional investigations are different from other government investigations. For example, sometimes they can move much more quickly than a regulatory investigation. Another example is when congressional investigators tell you that attorney-client privilege does not apply, meaning companies will have to potentially produce documents that are privileged. Now, there’s some recent cases that call that into question. But if you have experienced counsel who understands how to navigate that with the committee, it’s really important, because committees can choose to allow those privilege assertions to be made, and they often do, but you really need somebody who knows how to navigate that. Companies need to be aware that committees can often release confidential documents, and so, when you’re providing information to Congress, you really need somebody to help you navigate that to protect you as much as possible, if you end up providing information. It’s also important to keep an eye on everything. One aspect that we’re seeing increasingly with investigations is that companies are facing different kinds of investigations on broadly the same topic at one time. It could be a congressional investigation. It might be a federal such as regulatory investigation, it might be a DOJ investigation. There might also be a state attorney general action or a civil litigation. Maybe your shareholders are starting to make demands and all of these things are happening at one time. Having the right internal and external experts in place who can work together to navigate these risks is very important. CC: What are some other trends you are seeing, or expect to see, in congressional investigations? How might they impact corporate legal departments?? KH: There are several notable trends emerging. Firstly, an increasing number of multinational corporations are finding themselves embroiled in U.S. congressional investigations. This trend is not entirely new but has intensified as more companies expand their operations beyond U.S. borders or as foreign companies establish a presence in the United States. As companies engage in cross-border activities, there are heightened risks related to offshore document storage and compliance with local privacy and country laws, which can hinder information disclosure to congressional investigators. Unlike federal court litigation, congressional proceedings lack clear legal precedents, making navigation challenging. Moreover, bipartisan interest in supply chain risks is growing among congressional investigators. Companies face scrutiny if they source products from regions with human rights concerns or potential national security issues. Because of that, supply chain investigations are becoming more frequent and are likely to persist across different political administrations. Also, the dynamics of divided government can become very challenging for corporations. With a Democratic administration and a Republican-controlled House, corporate executives can find themselves navigating contentious political issues with divergent expectations from different parties. Companies risk facing increased scrutiny if they are perceived to align more closely with one political party over another. So there are complexities of divided government that companies will have to navigate.

This dual vantage point—combining litigation expertise with leadership insights—is somewhat rare in the legal field. Few individuals have engaged in litigating congressional subpoena cases, and while litigation is not the desired outcome, understanding the relevant rules, case law and precedents is crucial. So I think that’s a great asset for companies that are finding themselves under scrutiny.

CC: How can corporate legal departments prepare when the government comes knocking? What are some best practices?

KH: Well, the first step is acknowledging that sometimes you won’t have advance notice of an impending investigation. However, in cases like ESG, where companies could anticipate scrutiny if the House shifted to Republican control, early preparation is key. This involves assembling a cross-functional team comprising legal, compliance, government affairs and external public relations and regulatory experts. You want to make sure that your team is assembled and ready to act quickly and that you have at least some of the messaging and the responses ready.

That said, when it comes to congressional investigations, often it’s very event-specific and can move rapidly, catching companies off guard, because there could be an accident or a whistleblower that you weren’t aware of. In that case, it’s really important that you assemble your team quickly and that you make sure that team includes all of the right people, and that team needs to be able to work seamlessly together.

It’s also important to understand how congressional investigations are different from other government investigations. For example, sometimes they can move much more quickly than a regulatory investigation.

Another example is when congressional investigators tell you that attorney-client privilege does not apply, meaning companies will have to potentially produce documents that are privileged. Now, there’s some recent cases that call that into question. But if you have experienced counsel who understands how to navigate that with the committee, it’s really important, because committees can choose to allow those privilege assertions to be made, and they often do, but you really need somebody who knows how to navigate that.

Companies need to be aware that committees can often release confidential documents, and so, when you’re providing information to Congress, you really need somebody to help you navigate that to protect you as much as possible, if you end up providing information.

It’s also important to keep an eye on everything. One aspect that we’re seeing increasingly with investigations is that companies are facing different kinds of investigations on broadly the same topic at one time.

It could be a congressional investigation. It might be a federal such as regulatory investigation, it might be a DOJ investigation. There might also be a state attorney general action or a civil litigation. Maybe your shareholders are starting to make demands and all of these things are happening at one time. Having the right internal and external experts in place who can work together to navigate these risks is very important.

CC: What are some other trends you are seeing, or expect to see, in congressional investigations? How might they impact corporate legal departments??

KH: There are several notable trends emerging. Firstly, an increasing number of multinational corporations are finding themselves embroiled in U.S. congressional investigations. This trend is not entirely new but has intensified as more companies expand their operations beyond U.S. borders or as foreign companies establish a presence in the United States.

As companies engage in cross-border activities, there are heightened risks related to offshore document storage and compliance with local privacy and country laws, which can hinder information disclosure to congressional investigators. Unlike federal court litigation, congressional proceedings lack clear legal precedents, making navigation challenging.

Moreover, bipartisan interest in supply chain risks is growing among congressional investigators. Companies face scrutiny if they source products from regions with human rights concerns or potential national security issues. Because of that, supply chain investigations are becoming more frequent and are likely to persist across different political administrations.

Also, the dynamics of divided government can become very challenging for corporations. With a Democratic administration and a Republican-controlled House, corporate executives can find themselves navigating contentious political issues with divergent expectations from different parties. Companies risk facing increased scrutiny if they are perceived to align more closely with one political party over another. So there are complexities of divided government that companies will have to navigate.

article.title: Kraft Heinz Promotes Legal Chief After Year in Which Her Pay Declined
article.description: Longtime Kraft Heinz General Counsel Rashida La Lande was promoted to chief legal and corporate affairs officer at the end of last year, the company disclosed in its newly filed proxy statement. The filing also noted that her compensation fell by 22%…
article.text: Longtime Kraft Heinz General Counsel Rashida La Lande was promoted to chief legal and corporate affairs officer at the end of last year, the company disclosed in its newly filed proxy statement. The filing also noted that her compensation fell by 22% last year, as she received a significantly smaller stock award; $3 million in 2023 compared with $4.3 million the year before. Her total compensation was $5.2 million last year, down from about $6.4 million in 2022.

article.title: Renee Meisel, GC of UnitedLex, on Understanding and Growing the Business
article.description: While many women have made significant strides and are now better represented in the legal field, there remains room for improvement, particularly in attaining more representative leadership roles, UnitedLex’s general counsel, Renee Meisel, said.…
article.text: While many women have made significant strides and are now better represented in the legal field, there remains room for improvement, particularly in attaining more representative leadership roles, UnitedLex’s general counsel, Renee Meisel, said. “Recently, I came across a list of newly appointed GCS, and what struck me was that amidst a long list dominated by male names, there were only about two or three female names. Seeing this compiled on a list made me realize the lack of female representation in upward mobility within companies. It made me question whether women are adequately represented in promotion decisions or if they need to seek opportunities outside their current organizations.”
article.html:
While many women have made significant strides and are now better represented in the legal field, there remains room for improvement, particularly in attaining more representative leadership roles, UnitedLex’s general counsel, Renee Meisel, said.

“Recently, I came across a list of newly appointed GCS, and what struck me was that amidst a long list dominated by male names, there were only about two or three female names. Seeing this compiled on a list made me realize the lack of female representation in upward mobility within companies. It made me question whether women are adequately represented in promotion decisions or if they need to seek opportunities outside their current organizations.”

article.title: Collision-Repair Giant's Executive Overhaul Includes Hiring PE Veteran as CLO
article.description: After 25 years in lodging, Mark Chloupek said he is excited to transition from an industry that measures its success by "heads in beds" to one that does so by "cars in bays." Lewisville, Texas-based Caliber Collision, the nation’s largest collision…
article.text: After 25 years in lodging, Mark Chloupek said he is excited to transition from an industry that measures its success by "heads in beds" to one that does so by "cars in bays." Lewisville, Texas-based Caliber Collision, the nation’s largest collision repair chain, has hired Mark Chloupek as chief legal officer. Chloupek comes to Caliber Collision, which has more than 1,750 stores across 41 states, from Plano, Texas-based Aimbridge Hospitality, which manages more than 1,500 hotels in 23 countries. The properties operate under a litany of brands, from Hilton and Hyatt to Westin and Wyndham. Until now, Chloupek had spent his entire in-house career in the lodging industry. He was chief counsel at Wyndham International before becoming general counsel at La Quinta Holdings and then CorePoint Lodging. He’d been CLO of Aimbridge since July 2022. He’s also a veteran of the private equity industry. During his tenure at Wyndham, private equity investors bought the company for $3 billion, and during his tenure at CorePoint, private equity investors bought it for $1.5 billion. Soon thereafter, he joined Aimbridge, which also is private equity-owned, as is Caliber. Chloupek is jumping aboard 27-year-old Caliber at a pivotal moment in its history. The firm, which unleashed a blizzard of acquisitions over a quarter-century to consolidate the mom-and-pop body shop industry, began its executive refresh in January by appointing Mark Sanders as CEO. Sanders succeeded Steve Grimshaw, who has transitioned into a full-time executive chairman role after more than a decade leading the business. In a statement, Chloupek said, “After 25 years in hospitality, I am excited to transition from ‘heads in beds’ to ‘cars in bays.’”
article.html:
After 25 years in lodging, Mark Chloupek said he is excited to transition from an industry that measures its success by "heads in beds" to one that does so by "cars in bays."

Lewisville, Texas-based Caliber Collision, the nation’s largest collision repair chain, has hired Mark Chloupek as chief legal officer.

Chloupek comes to Caliber Collision, which has more than 1,750 stores across 41 states, from Plano, Texas-based Aimbridge Hospitality, which manages more than 1,500 hotels in 23 countries. The properties operate under a litany of brands, from Hilton and Hyatt to Westin and Wyndham.

Until now, Chloupek had spent his entire in-house career in the lodging industry. He was chief counsel at Wyndham International before becoming general counsel at La Quinta Holdings and then CorePoint Lodging. He’d been CLO of Aimbridge since July 2022.

He’s also a veteran of the private equity industry. During his tenure at Wyndham, private equity investors bought the company for $3 billion, and during his tenure at CorePoint, private equity investors bought it for $1.5 billion. Soon thereafter, he joined Aimbridge, which also is private equity-owned, as is Caliber.

Chloupek is jumping aboard 27-year-old Caliber at a pivotal moment in its history. The firm, which unleashed a blizzard of acquisitions over a quarter-century to consolidate the mom-and-pop body shop industry, began its executive refresh in January by appointing Mark Sanders as CEO.

Sanders succeeded Steve Grimshaw, who has transitioned into a full-time executive chairman role after more than a decade leading the business.

In a statement, Chloupek said, “After 25 years in hospitality, I am excited to transition from ‘heads in beds’ to ‘cars in bays.’”

article.title: I Got Royalties, Babe: L.A. Federal Court Sides With Cher On Income from Sonny's Song Interests
article.description: After Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, Mary Bono agreed to a confirmation of Cher’s continued rights under a 1978 marital settlement agreement. In 2016, Mary sent termination notices to music publishers to which Sonny had assigned his…
article.text: After Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, Mary Bono agreed to a confirmation of Cher’s continued rights under a 1978 marital settlement agreement. In 2016, Mary sent termination notices to music publishers to which Sonny had assigned his copyright interests. Cher argued that Mary has undone her ownership of her royalties from the songs and recordings that she and Sonny made famous during their marriage, and deprived her of long-established rights under the 1978 agreement. After Beach Boy Brian Wilson’s ex-wife Marilyn filed a request in Los Angeles Superior Court for an accounting and for payment, under the couple’s 1981 divorce judgment, of 50% of the monies Brian received from his 2021 sale of his song rights to Universal Music, Brian’s counsel had the case removed to Los Angeles federal court citing federal question jurisdiction. This was because the songs sale occurred after Brian had recaptured his copyrights under the 17 U.S.C. §304(c) copyright-assignment termination provision of the U.S. Copyright Act. Wilson v. Rutherford, 2:22-cv-01982 (C.D.Calif. 2022). But Central District of California federal Judge Josephine L. Staton decided in Wilson that federal copyright law didn’t preempt Marilyn’s state law claim, then remanded the case back to the state superior court. In doing so, District Judge Staton noted, “Marilyn does not assert that she has a right to terminate any grants of copyrights in the [songs] ….” Judge Staton added: “Section 304(c) provides that ‘[t]ermination of a grant under this subsection affects only those rights covered by the grant that arise under this title, and in no way affects rights arising under’ state law.”
article.html:
• After Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, Mary Bono agreed to a confirmation of Cher’s continued rights under a 1978 marital settlement agreement.
  • In 2016, Mary sent termination notices to music publishers to which Sonny had assigned his copyright interests.
  • Cher argued that Mary has undone her ownership of her royalties from the songs and recordings that she and Sonny made famous during their marriage, and deprived her of long-established rights under the 1978 agreement.

After Beach Boy Brian Wilson’s ex-wife Marilyn filed a request in Los Angeles Superior Court for an accounting and for payment, under the couple’s 1981 divorce judgment, of 50% of the monies Brian received from his 2021 sale of his song rights to Universal Music, Brian’s counsel had the case removed to Los Angeles federal court citing federal question jurisdiction. This was because the songs sale occurred after Brian had recaptured his copyrights under the 17 U.S.C. §304(c) copyright-assignment termination provision of the U.S. Copyright Act. Wilson v. Rutherford, 2:22-cv-01982 (C.D.Calif. 2022).

But Central District of California federal Judge Josephine L. Staton decided in Wilson that federal copyright law didn’t preempt Marilyn’s state law claim, then remanded the case back to the state superior court. In doing so, District Judge Staton noted, “Marilyn does not assert that she has a right to terminate any grants of copyrights in the [songs] ….” Judge Staton added: “Section 304(c) provides that ‘[t]ermination of a grant under this subsection affects only those rights covered by the grant that arise under this title, and in no way affects rights arising under’ state law.”

article.title: GM General Counsel, Kirkland Attorneys Leveraged US Corruption Probe to Sue Fiat Chrysler
article.description: On Wednesday the GM lawyers filed a federal racketeering lawsuit against Fiat Chrysler, accusing Fiat of “a systemic and near decade-long conspiracy to bribe senior union officials to corrupt the collective bargaining process and labor relations” to…
article.text: On Wednesday the GM lawyers filed a federal racketeering lawsuit against Fiat Chrysler, accusing Fiat of “a systemic and near decade-long conspiracy to bribe senior union officials to corrupt the collective bargaining process and labor relations” to GM’s detriment. Carefully tracking a yearslong U.S. attorney’s probe into corruption at the United Auto Workers, General Motors Co. general counsel Craig Glidden and his outside counsel at Kirkland & Ellis began to see a pattern emerging. On Wednesday the GM lawyers revealed what they saw in a federal racketeering lawsuit filed against Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV. The suit accuses Fiat Chrysler of “a systemic and near decade-long conspiracy to bribe senior union officials to corrupt the collective bargaining process and labor relations,” to GM’s detriment.

article.title: 'Surprised, Angry, Dismayed': Legal Departments Vow to Fight Law Firms' Rate-Hike Plans
article.description: Law firms want to raise rates an average of 7% to 8% in 2023, according to the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group. A consultant said strategies differ dramatically from firm to firm, from no increase to a 45% hike. Legal departments say they're in a…
article.text: Law firms want to raise rates an average of 7% to 8% in 2023, according to the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group. A consultant said strategies differ dramatically from firm to firm, from no increase to a 45% hike. Legal departments say they're in a financial squeeze and can't absorb big increases. The in-house legal community is expressing outrage that law firms will be pressing for aggressive rate hikes in 2023, even though they know that legal departments are under extraordinary pressure as the economic outlook sours. “Law firms are claiming to raise rates due to inflation, but anyone who’s ever taken an economics class knows that the real reason they’re raising rates is because they think no one will notice under the guise of inflation,” said Stephanie Corey, a former legal ops leader at HP and VMware who now leads the consulting firm UpLevel Ops.
article.html:
• Law firms want to raise rates an average of 7% to 8% in 2023, according to the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group.
  • A consultant said strategies differ dramatically from firm to firm, from no increase to a 45% hike.
  • Legal departments say they're in a financial squeeze and can't absorb big increases.

The in-house legal community is expressing outrage that law firms will be pressing for aggressive rate hikes in 2023, even though they know that legal departments are under extraordinary pressure as the economic outlook sours.

“Law firms are claiming to raise rates due to inflation, but anyone who’s ever taken an economics class knows that the real reason they’re raising rates is because they think no one will notice under the guise of inflation,” said Stephanie Corey, a former legal ops leader at HP and VMware who now leads the consulting firm UpLevel Ops.
