article.title: Cyberattacks Are Accelerating With AI's Help
article.description: What You Need to Know Large language models enable even novices to develop malicious code. That vastly increases the number of potential cybercriminals. Companies will need to train employees to be on the lookout for scams. Cybercriminals are…
article.text: What You Need to Know Large language models enable even novices to develop malicious code. That vastly increases the number of potential cybercriminals. Companies will need to train employees to be on the lookout for scams. Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they’ve only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence’s threat-acceleration potential. At last month’s RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. “We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models,” he said. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Large language models enable even novices to develop malicious code.
  • That vastly increases the number of potential cybercriminals.
  • Companies will need to train employees to be on the lookout for scams.

Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they’ve only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence’s threat-acceleration potential.

At last month’s RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. “We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models,” he said.

article.title: Google, HP Alum Hired as GC of Startup Bringing AI to Classrooms
article.description: Former Google and HP lawyer Scott Pojunas is joining Merlyn Mind, a startup that makes AI products for the classroom. Pojunas is a patent, IP specialist who most recently helped launch Google Cloud's first generative AI products. Merlyn Mind recently…
article.text: Former Google and HP lawyer Scott Pojunas is joining Merlyn Mind, a startup that makes AI products for the classroom. Pojunas is a patent, IP specialist who most recently helped launch Google Cloud's first generative AI products. Merlyn Mind recently announced a partnership with Google Cloud to support its AI infrastructure. Meryln Mind, New York-based maker of AI-powered digital assistants for teachers, has found its first general counsel in Google in-house lawyer Scott Pojunas. Pojunas announced the news Wednesday on LinkedIn. He was previously senior patent counsel at Google, but in the last year he’s taken on a more AI-focused role as senior product counsel for Google Cloud’s artificial intelligence arm, where according to his LinkedIn profile he helped launch Google Cloud’s first generative AI products and advised on emerging issues related to regulations and standards and “responsible AI.”
article.html:
• Former Google and HP lawyer Scott Pojunas is joining Merlyn Mind, a startup that makes AI products for the classroom.
  • Pojunas is a patent, IP specialist who most recently helped launch Google Cloud's first generative AI products.
  • Merlyn Mind recently announced a partnership with Google Cloud to support its AI infrastructure.

Meryln Mind, New York-based maker of AI-powered digital assistants for teachers, has found its first general counsel in Google in-house lawyer Scott Pojunas.

Pojunas announced the news Wednesday on LinkedIn. He was previously senior patent counsel at Google, but in the last year he’s taken on a more AI-focused role as senior product counsel for Google Cloud’s artificial intelligence arm, where according to his LinkedIn profile he helped launch Google Cloud’s first generative AI products and advised on emerging issues related to regulations and standards and “responsible AI.”

article.title: Ransomware Gangs Are Increasingly Going After Smaller, Easier Targets
article.description: Ransomware gangs favor smaller companies, as they're more likely to have a smaller IT budget and less cybersecurity expertise. Threat actors are changing their tactics and launching smaller-scale attacks with more frequency. Ransomware attacks have…
article.text: Ransomware gangs favor smaller companies, as they're more likely to have a smaller IT budget and less cybersecurity expertise. Threat actors are changing their tactics and launching smaller-scale attacks with more frequency. Ransomware attacks have decreased this year compared with the latter half of 2022, but many companies have delayed reporting, and the number of reported attacks is expected to rise in the second half of the year. Small companies beware: You’re more likely to be a victim of a ransomware attack. A new report on the 2023 ransomware threat landscape from cyber-risk quantification platform Kovrr found ransomware actors tend to favor companies with revenue in the $10 million to $50 million range. “Smaller companies have a smaller IT budget and less security expertise. So it makes them easier targets, for sure,” said Guy Propper, head of data for Kovrr. Threat actors are also choosing to forgo larger extortion payments from high-revenue companies in favor of easier and more plentiful targets. “They’re willing to have the smaller ransoms for having easier attacks, and being able to perform more attacks because some of these companies use the same cloud services, the same programs,” Propper said. Preying on smaller companies also minimizes risk as larger targets are more likely to draw swift action from law enforcement, Kovrr’s report says, citing the 2021 attack on Colonial Pipeline. “Attacking smaller companies, while possibly promising lower rewards, also poses a lower risk for ransomware groups, as they are less likely to be prosecuted due to a single attack,” the report says. Propper said the leaked internal communications of one notorious ransomware gang called Conti also warned members to be careful when attacking large companies for this reason. The services sector was the hardest-hit industry, particularly business services, as they make the best targets for extortion, Kovrr’s report says. One reason is because they provide services to other companies, so they are more likely to want to avoid as much downtime as possible. They also rely more on third-party services, such as cloud hosting. And perhaps most important, Propper said, they collect vast amounts of consumer data. Ransomware has developed into a cottage industry in recent years, as threat actors grow more sophisticated and adaptive. Gone are the days of the lone hacker sitting in his mother’s basement. Now ransomware attacks are more likely to be executed by organized groups of individuals each working within their own specialty, whether it’s running the ransomware itself, finding the right target or handling the negotiations. In this way, they operate like small companies themselves, Propper said. Ransomware gangs are also using artificial intelligence tools to perform some of the more laborious work involved in cyber extortion. For example, hackers can use large language models to write ransomware code or hunt for new targets. “It can help you in finding information that might be relevant for your scans,” Propper said. “For example, they could start with a simple question, ‘What are the top 100 health care companies with the most customers, and what are their domains?’ And then they could ask, ‘Which of these domains uses specific technology?’ And then from there, it just saves them a lot of time.” Kovrr found that ransomware attacks dropped by 32% in the first half of 2023, though the firm suspects that this may be caused by delayed reporting by victim companies. Reported attacks may still increase in the second half of the year, following trends over the last two years. “In the previous two years, more attacks have been reported, or have occurred, in the second half of the year compared to the first half,” Kovrr’s report says. Blockchain data analysis firm Chainalysis also reported an uptick in ransomware payments in 2023. “In fact, ransomware attackers are on pace for their second-biggest year ever, having extorted at least $449.1 million through June,” the company says in its midyear crypto crime update. Chainalysis attributes this increase to a rise in both “big-game hunting,” where hackers target deep-pocketed organizations, as well as a rise in successful smaller attacks. “[W]e’re seeing growth in ransomware payments at both ends of the spectrum,” Chainalysis reports. Kovrr looked at data from multiple sources for its study, including data breach notifications from victim companies, news reports of ransomware attacks, and from sites on the dark web, where attackers publish their exploits. Kovrr gathered its data on ransomware leaks from the research project Double Extortion, as well as its own proprietary sources and methods. Kovrr’s study found that most of the attacks that occurred this year were carried out by a handful of ransomware gangs, a proverbial “top 10” of the most active groups, all of which directed their attacks at firms with under $50 million in revenue. Those groups accounted for 87% of attacks during the first half of 2023. The top three most active groups, Lockbit 3.0, BlackCat and Clop, took credit for 53% of the attacks. “They’re willing to have the smaller ransoms for having easier attacks, and being able to perform more attacks because some of these companies use the same cloud services, the same programs,” Propper said.

Preying on smaller companies also minimizes risk as larger targets are more likely to draw swift action from law enforcement, Kovrr’s report says, citing the 2021 attack on Colonial Pipeline. “Attacking smaller companies, while possibly promising lower rewards, also poses a lower risk for ransomware groups, as they are less likely to be prosecuted due to a single attack,” the report says.

Propper said the leaked internal communications of one notorious ransomware gang called Conti also warned members to be careful when attacking large companies for this reason.

The services sector was the hardest-hit industry, particularly business services, as they make the best targets for extortion, Kovrr’s report says. One reason is because they provide services to other companies, so they are more likely to want to avoid as much downtime as possible. They also rely more on third-party services, such as cloud hosting. And perhaps most important, Propper said, they collect vast amounts of consumer data.

Ransomware has developed into a cottage industry in recent years, as threat actors grow more sophisticated and adaptive. Gone are the days of the lone hacker sitting in his mother’s basement. Now ransomware attacks are more likely to be executed by organized groups of individuals each working within their own specialty, whether it’s running the ransomware itself, finding the right target or handling the negotiations. In this way, they operate like small companies themselves, Propper said.

Ransomware gangs are also using artificial intelligence tools to perform some of the more laborious work involved in cyber extortion. For example, hackers can use large language models to write ransomware code or hunt for new targets.

“It can help you in finding information that might be relevant for your scans,” Propper said. “For example, they could start with a simple question, ‘What are the top 100 health care companies with the most customers, and what are their domains?’ And then they could ask, ‘Which of these domains uses specific technology?’ And then from there, it just saves them a lot of time.”

Kovrr found that ransomware attacks dropped by 32% in the first half of 2023, though the firm suspects that this may be caused by delayed reporting by victim companies. Reported attacks may still increase in the second half of the year, following trends over the last two years.

“In the previous two years, more attacks have been reported, or have occurred, in the second half of the year compared to the first half,” Kovrr’s report says.

Blockchain data analysis firm Chainalysis also reported an uptick in ransomware payments in 2023. “In fact, ransomware attackers are on pace for their second-biggest year ever, having extorted at least $449.1 million through June,” the company says in its midyear crypto crime update.

Chainalysis attributes this increase to a rise in both “big-game hunting,” where hackers target deep-pocketed organizations, as well as a rise in successful smaller attacks. “[W]e’re seeing growth in ransomware payments at both ends of the spectrum,” Chainalysis reports.

Kovrr looked at data from multiple sources for its study, including data breach notifications from victim companies, news reports of ransomware attacks, and from sites on the dark web, where attackers publish their exploits. Kovrr gathered its data on ransomware leaks from the research project Double Extortion, as well as its own proprietary sources and methods.

Kovrr’s study found that most of the attacks that occurred this year were carried out by a handful of ransomware gangs, a proverbial “top 10” of the most active groups, all of which directed their attacks at firms with under $50 million in revenue. Those groups accounted for 87% of attacks during the first half of 2023. The top three most active groups, Lockbit 3.0, BlackCat and Clop, took credit for 53% of the attacks.

article.title: Solo-GC-of-Year Helped Provider of VR-Based Pain Therapy Overcome Novel Challenges
article.description: "I've built my career on being a solutions-oriented, practical business partner," said Deitzah Raby, general counsel of AppliedVR from July 2022 to September 2023. "These were big wins, and it was exciting to be part of that." Tech startups often…
article.text: "I've built my career on being a solutions-oriented, practical business partner," said Deitzah Raby, general counsel of AppliedVR from July 2022 to September 2023. "These were big wins, and it was exciting to be part of that." Tech startups often must juggle complex legal issues, involving everything from IP to regulation, with at most one in-house attorney and often none, instead relying on outside counsel. The challenges are even more daunting for startups in highly regulated industries, such as health care. The first in-house attorney often comes aboard to help usher a product through regulatory approval and commercial launch.

article.text: More than a half-century ago, Emanuel Bronner would hand out soaps as freebies to attendees of his lectures espousing unity across religious and ethnic divides. Today, they are available in mass-market retailers such as Target and Walgreens and in some 40 countries. Diana Cohen has joined the Vista, California-based company as general counsel. Dr. Bronner's embraces environmental and social causes and caps its executive pay at five times that of its lowest-paid workers.

article.title: Evidence Fight Breaks Out as Bribery Trial Nears for Ex-Cognizant Legal Chief | Corporate Counsel
article.description: Jones Day partner James Loonam, lead defense attorney in the government's corruption case against former Cognizant executives, says the prosecution's star witness is pointing the finger at ex-legal chief Steven Schwartz and his co-defendant, former president Gordon Coburn, to cover up his own misconduct.
article.text: Former Cognizant legal chief Steven Schwartz is fighting to get evidence admitted that his defense says will show that he and his co-defendant did not violate the anti-bribery provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Schwartz and former Cognizant President Gordon Coburn are charged with authorizing a $2 million bribe to Indian officials. The two are set to go on trial in May. Former Cognizant Chief Legal Officer Steven Schwartz and former Cognizant President Gordon Coburn are battling with prosecutors over whether a federal judge should admit evidence that the executives claim would help prove they are innocent of the bribery allegations they face. The fight broke out in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey in recent weeks as the parties prepare for a May trial. It's the latest twist in the drama-filled case. The trial was to occur last October but was delayed because the government was unable to persuade Indian officials to allow its key witness, Srimanikadan Ramamoorthy, the former Cognizant vice president of administration, to travel to the United States. Cognizant, based in Teaneck, New Jersey, is an information technology consulting and services behemoth, with $19 billion in annual revenue, a stock market value of $39 billion and 355,000 employees, most based in India. article.title: Regulatory Upheaval Is Coming. How Businesses Prepare and Respond Will Separate Winners and Losers
article.description: “Every regulation is going to be questioned. ... And that'll be a better environment for many businesses once the regulations are wiped away. But they're going to have to adapt their businesses to exploit that," said Sean West, co-founder of Hence Technologies.
article.text: The only constant is change, the adage goes. And it was particularly salient at Berkeley Law’s Fall Forum on Corporate Governance this week, where business and legal leaders convened to hear what they can expect in the year ahead, and how to navigate an ever-shifting regulatory environment. Angeli Patel, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business, which hosted the event along with Cooley, said change management could be deemed the loose theme of Tuesday’s program. Attendees were treated to a slate of panel discussions on how to manage volatility and risk in areas such as artificial intelligence, climate and environmental, social and governance, and the incoming Trump administration. Here are highlights from Tuesday’s sessions: | The State of AI Regulation If change and uncertainty are the closest descriptors for the current state of corporate governance, “safety” is the buzzword most closely associated with regulating AI. But federal efforts to put up legislative guardrails have largely fallen flat. More than 120 AI bills have been introduced in Congress, but not one has passed. “Congress has deeply struggled for many years to regulate the tech sector,” California state Sen. Scott Weiner, D-San Francisco, noted at a panel on regulatory developments in AI. President-elect Donald Trump has vowed to repeal President Joe Biden’s sweeping executive order on AI, and members of the U.S. House of Representatives have expressed an interest in defunding the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Weiner said. “California more than ever has not just a role, but a responsibility to act,” he said. But California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, recently vetoed SB 1047, an ambitious bill written by Weiner that required testing of large and expensive “frontier” AI models and held AI developers liable for catastrophic harms those models may cause. It also mandated a “kill switch” that could shut down AI models if they started to do anything “problematic.” “I think there were some in the opposition to SB 1047 who, I thought, were in a very flippant way dismissing any idea of regulating anything at the model level,” Weiner said. “They would refer to it as ‘regulating math.’ OK, sure. But it's math that has incredible power, and the power is at the model level. The model level is what allows those applications to happen.” Weiner said there’s no way to remove any chance of risk or force companies to certify that their AI models will cause no harm. “All we were asking is, 'Hey, can you please do a basic safety evaluation of your model to determine if there is a risk of catastrophic bargain? And if you do identify that risk, can you please take reasonable steps not to eliminate the risk, but to reduce the risk?'" Gerard de Graaf, the European Union's digital envoy to the United States, took a similar tack. “The keyword is safety here," he said. "You step into an airplane, you believe it's safe. If you buy a car seat for your kids, you believe it's safe. Because it's regulated. And AI has tremendous potential. It's a fantastic technology. But there are safety issues. If you look at some of the automated decision-making systems, many of them are like black boxes or are biased in a way.” The EU passed its AI Act in March and will be phasing it in incrementally, starting in February 2025. By 2027, the law will apply to AI embedded in products. "It is something to get used to," de Graaf said. "If you're a social media company, you haven't been regulated for a very long time, and suddenly you're regulated. But that's the way life has changed. In the EU, you're regulated.” As for the United States, substantive AI regulation will fall to the states. “You will continue to see not much being done around tech policy on AI, especially with the Trump administration,” said Irene Liu, founder of Hypergrowth GC and an AI adviser for the California Senate. She noted that nearly 700 AI bills have been introduced in 45 states this year, with topics ranging from deepfakes and restrictions of digital replicas to the government's use of AI. Liu anticipates more collaboration between tech and government, and even more lobbying around the issue. “Companies are investing a lot in advocacy so that they can try to help governments understand the technology so that it's not stifling their innovation,” she said. “And what you'll continue to see is that continued collaboration and, if anything, more advocacy and more investment in advocacy and lobbying teams. You'll hear louder voices, particularly from Big Tech, that are asking for particular regulations, particularly at the output level versus the input level, or regulating at the application level versus the model level.” | Board Oversight of Climate Risk The incoming president has made it pretty clear that climate change regulatory rollbacks are on the way. But investors still will expect companies to plan for and disclose their climate risks. Boards, which are entrusted with thinking about longer-term risk, will have a critical role in this, said Kristina Wyatt, a former senior counsel for climate and ESG at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. “Whether we're talking about climate risk, or other financial risk, they need to be able to look around the corner and project out where that risk is going to manifest over the short, medium and long term," said Wyatt, now the deputy general counsel and chief sustainability officer at the carbon accounting firm Persefoni. Wyatt, who helped write the SEC’s climate change disclosure rule, said that despite the regulation’s uncertain future, boards that comply with existing climate reporting frameworks, such as Europe’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and California’s recently enacted law requiring some companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related financial risk, will be better prepared to respond to investor pressure. “It seems much less likely that there will be an SEC rule, but it almost doesn't really matter because of the pressure put on companies from the CSRD and California,” Wyatt said. Cooley partner Beth Sasfai said boards should focus more on compliance and data, rather than the granularity of reporting. “Boards should be asking for data. If you don't understand what your company's carbon footprint is, you can't really understand what kinds of climate goals may or may not be appropriate. You can't understand what your risks may be,” she said. “Just like in every other area in connection with board oversight, you need to understand your business, your strategy, your operations and how those are affected by climate considerations. So just the act of gathering the data, making sure that it's good data, understanding where it's coming from and processing that is important.” Sasfai said ESG started as a voluntary exercise. Environmental and social governance plans were more aspirational in nature, and boards may not have even known about them. What has changed in the last 10 years is that boards are starting to ask about climate goals. "We see loads asking very tough questions about what is the line of sight to our goals. Do we need to adjust our business strategy or operations in any way? Are there assumptions that we made at the time we set these goals that today aren't holding true, such that we need to reconsider and reevaluate? And then all of that translates into thinking about your disclosure. Are you talking about these challenges in meeting your targets? And sometimes that's very, very hard for companies and boards to get their arms around.” | 'There's Volatility Everywhere' Corporate leaders are viewing Trump’s reclaiming of the White House with a mix of consternation and anticipation. Some look forward to a more business-friendly climate and easing of burdensome regulation. Others are concerned that the ever-pugnacious and vindictive incoming commander in chief will single out political enemies for retribution. Expect no sacred cows, said Sean West, co-founder of tech company Hence Technologies, whose AI software helps law firms and corporate legal departments forecast geopolitical events and translate them into risk. “Every regulation is going to be questioned," he said. "We're going to start to see a reduction in the sheer amount of regulation. And that'll be a better environment for many businesses once the regulations are wiped away. But they're going to have to adapt their businesses to exploit that. That's a lot of work. And figuring out how to do that is challenging.” Trying to game out AI regulation, for example, will be particularly challenging for legal departments. “We don't have settled law about what you can do with respect to using technology, but if you wait competitors are going to speed ahead of you,” West said. “Businesses are going to win in the market because they're going to get so far ahead of companies that are cautious. But that's a really tough position for legal departments to take. I think that's where the money is going to be made for businesses, and that's where legal departments will either be enablers of change or will be brakes on that.” As companies prepare themselves for pullback in regulation, they’ll also need to brace for implementation of the incoming president's immigration agenda, including mass deportations. “Look, the world is an unruly place right now. There's volatility everywhere,” West said. “Trump is a force for more of that change, which is probably good news for the private practice folks in the room—you've got a lot of work to do. But for the corporate legal teams here, increasingly these political questions wash up to your desks." John Christiansen, a partner at the consultancy FGS Global, said workers are seeking guidance from their employers on whether they should avoid going back to their home countries during the holidays because of the risk they won't be allowed to reenter the United States. “We don't have these answers," he said. "For the most part, companies don't. So what I think is key at this moment in time is to be very thoughtful about showing empathy with employees, being very factual to the extent we can, and having the right managers trained appropriately so that companies don't say things that they later regret to employees in an environment where we just don't know.” State Sen. Nancy Skinner, D-Berkeley, projected that Trump's immigration policies will have a negative impact on segments of the state's economy heavily reliant on migrant labor, such as construction and agriculture. On the other hand, she predicted that businesses, particularly large corporations, will be very influential with the new administration. Though Trump vowed to go after his enemies, including California, he is a savvy politician and recognizes that large companies won’t stand for drastic measures, such as punishing tariffs. “Trump is going to be responsive to business, and Trump is going to be responsive to prices. So I think the business community can have a significant say in moderating—in effect, influencing—the policies,” Skinner said. “There will still be some dramatic performative policies—there will be. But ones that really get at the core of hurting certain business sectors, maybe not. But that will be up to how businesses themselves unite and communicate to that administration.” NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. The only constant is change, the adage goes. And it was particularly salient at Berkeley Law’s Fall Forum on Corporate Governance this week, where business and legal leaders convened to hear what they can expect in the year ahead, and how to navigate an ever-shifting regulatory environment.

Angeli Patel, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business, which hosted the event along with Cooley, said change management could be deemed the loose theme of Tuesday’s program. Attendees were treated to a slate of panel discussions on how to manage volatility and risk in areas such as artificial intelligence, climate and environmental, social and governance, and the incoming Trump administration.

Here are highlights from Tuesday’s sessions:
|

The State of AI Regulation

If change and uncertainty are the closest descriptors for the current state of corporate governance, “safety” is the buzzword most closely associated with regulating AI. But federal efforts to put up legislative guardrails have largely fallen flat. More than 120 AI bills have been introduced in Congress, but not one has passed.

“Congress has deeply struggled for many years to regulate the tech sector,” California state Sen. Scott Weiner, D-San Francisco, noted at a panel on regulatory developments in AI.

President-elect Donald Trump has vowed to repeal President Joe Biden’s sweeping executive order on AI, and members of the U.S. House of Representatives have expressed an interest in defunding the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Weiner said. “California more than ever has not just a role, but a responsibility to act,” he said.

But California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, recently vetoed SB 1047, an ambitious bill written by Weiner that required testing of large and expensive “frontier” AI models and held AI developers liable for catastrophic harms those models may cause. It also mandated a “kill switch” that could shut down AI models if they started to do anything “problematic.”

“I think there were some in the opposition to SB 1047 who, I thought, were in a very flippant way dismissing any idea of regulating anything at the model level,” Weiner said. “They would refer to it as ‘regulating math.’ OK, sure. But it's math that has incredible power, and the power is at the model level. The model level is what allows those applications to happen.”

Weiner said there’s no way to remove any chance of risk or force companies to certify that their AI models will cause no harm. “All we were asking is, 'Hey, can you please do a basic safety evaluation of your model to determine if there is a risk of catastrophic bargain? And if you do identify that risk, can you please take reasonable steps not to eliminate the risk, but to reduce the risk?'"

Gerard de Graaf, the European Union's digital envoy to the United States, took a similar tack. “The keyword is safety here," he said. "You step into an airplane, you believe it's safe. If you buy a car seat for your kids, you believe it's safe. Because it's regulated. And AI has tremendous potential. It's a fantastic technology. But there are safety issues. If you look at some of the automated decision-making systems, many of them are like black boxes or are biased in a way.”

The EU passed its AI Act in March and will be phasing it in incrementally, starting in February 2025. By 2027, the law will apply to AI embedded in products.

"It is something to get used to," de Graaf said. "If you're a social media company, you haven't been regulated for a very long time, and suddenly you're regulated. But that's the way life has changed. In the EU, you're regulated.”

As for the United States, substantive AI regulation will fall to the states. “You will continue to see not much being done around tech policy on AI, especially with the Trump administration,” said Irene Liu, founder of Hypergrowth GC and an AI adviser for the California Senate. She noted that nearly 700 AI bills have been introduced in 45 states this year, with topics ranging from deepfakes and restrictions of digital replicas to the government's use of AI.

Liu anticipates more collaboration between tech and government, and even more lobbying around the issue.

“Companies are investing a lot in advocacy so that they can try to help governments understand the technology so that it's not stifling their innovation,” she said. “And what you'll continue to see is that continued collaboration and, if anything, more advocacy and more investment in advocacy and lobbying teams. You'll hear louder voices, particularly from Big Tech, that are asking for particular regulations, particularly at the output level versus the input level, or regulating at the application level versus the model level.”
|

Board Oversight of Climate Risk

The incoming president has made it pretty clear that climate change regulatory rollbacks are on the way. But investors still will expect companies to plan for and disclose their climate risks.

Boards, which are entrusted with thinking about longer-term risk, will have a critical role in this, said Kristina Wyatt, a former senior counsel for climate and ESG at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. “Whether we're talking about climate risk, or other financial risk, they need to be able to look around the corner and project out where that risk is going to manifest over the short, medium and long term," said Wyatt, now the deputy general counsel and chief sustainability officer at the carbon accounting firm Persefoni.

Wyatt, who helped write the SEC’s climate change disclosure rule, said that despite the regulation’s uncertain future, boards that comply with existing climate reporting frameworks, such as Europe’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and California’s recently enacted law requiring some companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related financial risk, will be better prepared to respond to investor pressure. “It seems much less likely that there will be an SEC rule, but it almost doesn't really matter because of the pressure put on companies from the CSRD and California,” Wyatt said.

Cooley partner Beth Sasfai said boards should focus more on compliance and data, rather than the granularity of reporting. “Boards should be asking for data. If you don't understand what your company's carbon footprint is, you can't really understand what kinds of climate goals may or may not be appropriate. You can't understand what your risks may be,” she said.

“Just like in every other area in connection with board oversight, you need to understand your business, your strategy, your operations and how those are affected by climate considerations. So just the act of gathering the data, making sure that it's good data, understanding where it's coming from and processing that is important.”

Sasfai said ESG started as a voluntary exercise. Environmental and social governance plans were more aspirational in nature, and boards may not have even known about them. What has changed in the last 10 years is that boards are starting to ask about climate goals.

"We see loads asking very tough questions about what is the line of sight to our goals. Do we need to adjust our business strategy or operations in any way? Are there assumptions that we made at the time we set these goals that today aren't holding true, such that we need to reconsider and reevaluate? And then all of that translates into thinking about your disclosure. Are you talking about these challenges in meeting your targets? And sometimes that's very, very hard for companies and boards to get their arms around.”
|

'There's Volatility Everywhere'

Corporate leaders are viewing Trump’s reclaiming of the White House with a mix of consternation and anticipation. Some look forward to a more business-friendly climate and easing of burdensome regulation. Others are concerned that the ever-pugnacious and vindictive incoming commander in chief will single out political enemies for retribution.

Expect no sacred cows, said Sean West, co-founder of tech company Hence Technologies, whose AI software helps law firms and corporate legal departments forecast geopolitical events and translate them into risk. “Every regulation is going to be questioned," he said. "We're going to start to see a reduction in the sheer amount of regulation. And that'll be a better environment for many businesses once the regulations are wiped away. But they're going to have to adapt their businesses to exploit that. That's a lot of work. And figuring out how to do that is challenging.”

Trying to game out AI regulation, for example, will be particularly challenging for legal departments. “We don't have settled law about what you can do with respect to using technology, but if you wait competitors are going to speed ahead of you,” West said. “Businesses are going to win in the market because they're going to get so far ahead of companies that are cautious. But that's a really tough position for legal departments to take. I think that's where the money is going to be made for businesses, and that's where legal departments will either be enablers of change or will be brakes on that.”

As companies prepare themselves for pullback in regulation, they’ll also need to brace for implementation of the incoming president's immigration agenda, including mass deportations.

“Look, the world is an unruly place right now. There's volatility everywhere,” West said. “Trump is a force for more of that change, which is probably good news for the private practice folks in the room—you've got a lot of work to do. But for the corporate legal teams here, increasingly these political questions wash up to your desks."

John Christiansen, a partner at the consultancy FGS Global, said workers are seeking guidance from their employers on whether they should avoid going back to their home countries during the holidays because of the risk they won't be allowed to reenter the United States.

“We don't have these answers," he said. "For the most part, companies don't. So what I think is key at this moment in time is to be very thoughtful about showing empathy with employees, being very factual to the extent we can, and having the right managers trained appropriately so that companies don't say things that they later regret to employees in an environment where we just don't know.”

State Sen. Nancy Skinner, D-Berkeley, projected that Trump's immigration policies will have a negative impact on segments of the state's economy heavily reliant on migrant labor, such as construction and agriculture. On the other hand, she predicted that businesses, particularly large corporations, will be very influential with the new administration.

Though Trump vowed to go after his enemies, including California, he is a savvy politician and recognizes that large companies won’t stand for drastic measures, such as punishing tariffs. “Trump is going to be responsive to business, and Trump is going to be responsive to prices. So I think the business community can have a significant say in moderating—in effect, influencing—the policies,” Skinner said. “There will still be some dramatic performative policies—there will be. But ones that really get at the core of hurting certain business sectors, maybe not. But that will be up to how businesses themselves unite and communicate to that administration.”

article.title: AI Insurance, Governance and Responsibility: Overheard at 2024 AI Expo
article.description: Rhythmed by demos of next-generation drones, VR headsets and in-device artificial intelligence, the AI Expo for National Competitiveness unfolded in Washington, D.C., on May 7. The two-day conference hosted by the Special Competitive Studies Project…
article.text: Rhythmed by demos of next-generation drones, VR headsets and in-device artificial intelligence, the AI Expo for National Competitiveness unfolded in Washington, D.C., on May 7. The two-day conference hosted by the Special Competitive Studies Project assessed the state of AI advancements across industries and invited stakeholders to weigh in on what’s ahead, from AI-generated threats and election interference to new regulations. Below, Legaltech News gathered some quotes from the conference that were particularly telling of the current state of the AI market and of what’s to come. “By far the most prevalent things we’re seeing are the generation of artificial child sexual abuse material, and artificial non-consensual intimate imagery of women and girls—the overwhelming majority of activity has happened using open-source models.” David Willner, Fellow, Stanford Program on the Governance of Emerging Technologies The proliferation of criminal content is not always happening because of open-source developers’ malicious motives, but instead because of the technical limitations, which don’t allow these models to be as “robust” against misuse, Willner explained. He added, “As someone who more generally does think open-source is good as a broader movement, I worry about this. … We need better solutions there to make those models more robust against misuse—because currently they’re not.” “If you’re looking for who’s responsible for the challenges of AI and the challenges of content on the internet, it’s you and me. It’s not the companies. It’s not the government.” Jamil Jaffer, Venture Partner and Strategic Adviser, Paladin Capital Group Governments and companies do have their own roles to play in framing appropriate AI governance, either by intervening to set standards or by being the ones identifying and mitigating risks, respectively. But Jaffer emphasized the importance of bringing consumers and investors in the conversation to shape and mitigate AI risks. “It is not simply sufficient for investors to stand by and say it’s fine, we’re just investing purely for return. And in fact, we led a group of nine investors … to commit to voluntary standards on trust, safety and security, including investing in American and Ally technologies and investing in capabilities that are consistent with the values of free open societies,” he said. “These are words you don’t typically hear investors use or investors talk about.” “It’s antithetical to many aspects of the legal process to put the onus on consumers to protect themselves.” Belle Torek, Senior Fellow for AI & Tech Advocacy, Human Rights Campaign Torek pushed back on the argument that consumers’ buying power is enough to influence companies’ approach to safe AI. In fact, there are already several legal frameworks in place that are specifically designed to ensure that consumers have a reasonable expectation of safety and viability when they purchase a product, she noted. But, at a time where both disinformation and misinformation are proliferating, especially on social media, consumers’ ability to keep up with companies’ privacy practices and their approach to AI is growing more limited. “It shouldn’t be incumbent, necessarily, on consumers to go through the intense media literacy process of determining what is and isn’t real,” she said. “Government procurement is a big lever. … Short of hard law, that’s a pretty effective way of creating behavioral change.” Var Shankar, Executive Director, Responsible AI Institute In the weeks following the release of the Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, many rushed to assess the impact that the order could eventually have on the AI market. Months into 2024, it’s becoming more clear that the order’s impact is less direct, and will instead trickle down through agencies’ own approaches to leveraging the technology, Shankar explained. Ani Gevorkian, director for Responsible AI Public Policy at Microsoft, echoed this analysis, noting, “That executive order has teeth in that it required the White House Office of Management and Budget (OBM) to put out these requirements that federal agencies must abide by, and those are requirements passed down to vendors, to suppliers, to AI companies who want to offer their systems and services to federal governments and federal agencies. And we’ve seen this system happen before. Oftentimes federal procurement is sort of the first push in developing a set of best practices and standardizing practices.” “Eligibility for insurance products for AI is going to be an incredible incentive for good governance.” Phillip Dawson, Head of AI Policy, Armilla AI Dawson noted Armilla AI is currently working to develop new insurance products specifically for AI risks. “Part of our process for determining eligibility is assessing enterprises against the very frameworks we’ve been discussing today: How mature are your risk management processes? Have you tested the models? What types of performance and vulnerabilities do we see? All feeding into an underwriting model to price coverage for AI risk. So there’s going to be an incredible market-based incentive for companies,” he said. Today, many organizations are relying on “silent coverage”—either existing cybersecurity or errors and omissions policies, which offer some extent of coverage. But that could soon change. “The insurance community is looking at carving much of this out and creating bespoke products,” Dawson added. “We’re in a battle for what it means to have trust and security in this ecosystem. It is not a battle between random parties. It’s not a battle of economics. It is a battle of values.” Jamil Jaffer, Venture Partner and Strategic Adviser, Paladin Capital Group As organizations across the globe are attempting to issue best practices, these will ultimately be shaped by their jurisdictions’ values and priorities, Jaffer noted. “There are our values, western values, values in the United States or allies, and there are other countries that have different values. … If we want to maintain that lead, we’ve got to embed trust, safety and security in our capabilities, we’ve got to build [AI products] around our values.” “There are existing domains to leverage insights from as we move forward with this new technology.” Angela McKay, Director, T&S Research & Partnerships, Google McKay emphasized the idea that most organizations can and should leverage existing frameworks to inform their approach to AI governance. “Whether it is the insurance market, whether it is the continual learning of standards, whether it is the idea that there is some safety and security that is a public good and not something that is competitive,” she provided as examples. “We don’t have the time with AI to iterate incessantly for the next 10 years.” Philip Reiner, Chief Executive Officer, Institute for Security and Technology Not everyone believes that existing frameworks may be enough to craft solid AI standards. In fact, Reiner noted that some of the standards being created “won’t be changeable later,” leaving organizations with unworkable frameworks. “We’ve experienced this in cybersecurity in a very, very painful way,” he noted. Reiner added, “We need to be very frank with ourselves when thinking about frameworks for evaluation, for investment, etc. We’re going to learn a little from the past, but at the end of the day we have to come up with brand news ways of thinking about this problem and we need to do it way faster.”

Rhythmed by demos of next-generation drones, VR headsets and in-device artificial intelligence, the AI Expo for National Competitiveness unfolded in Washington, D.C., on May 7.

The two-day conference hosted by the Special Competitive Studies Project assessed the state of AI advancements across industries and invited stakeholders to weigh in on what’s ahead, from AI-generated threats and election interference to new regulations.

Below, Legaltech News gathered some quotes from the conference that were particularly telling of the current state of the AI market and of what’s to come.

“By far the most prevalent things we’re seeing are the generation of artificial child sexual abuse material, and artificial non-consensual intimate imagery of women and girls—the overwhelming majority of activity has happened using open-source models.” David Willner, Fellow, Stanford Program on the Governance of Emerging Technologies

The proliferation of criminal content is not always happening because of open-source developers’ malicious motives, but instead because of the technical limitations, which don’t allow these models to be as “robust” against misuse, Willner explained. He added, “As someone who more generally does think open-source is good as a broader movement, I worry about this. … We need better solutions there to make those models more robust against misuse—because currently they’re not.”

“If you’re looking for who’s responsible for the challenges of AI and the challenges of content on the internet, it’s you and me. It’s not the companies. It’s not the government.” Jamil Jaffer, Venture Partner and Strategic Adviser, Paladin Capital Group

Governments and companies do have their own roles to play in framing appropriate AI governance, either by intervening to set standards or by being the ones identifying and mitigating risks, respectively. But Jaffer emphasized the importance of bringing consumers and investors in the conversation to shape and mitigate AI risks.

“It is not simply sufficient for investors to stand by and say it’s fine, we’re just investing purely for return. And in fact, we led a group of nine investors … to commit to voluntary standards on trust, safety and security, including investing in American and Ally technologies and investing in capabilities that are consistent with the values of free open societies,” he said. “These are words you don’t typically hear investors use or investors talk about.”

“It’s antithetical to many aspects of the legal process to put the onus on consumers to protect themselves.” Belle Torek, Senior Fellow for AI & Tech Advocacy, Human Rights Campaign

Torek pushed back on the argument that consumers’ buying power is enough to influence companies’ approach to safe AI. In fact, there are already several legal frameworks in place that are specifically designed to ensure that consumers have a reasonable expectation of safety and viability when they purchase a product, she noted.

But, at a time where both disinformation and misinformation are proliferating, especially on social media, consumers’ ability to keep up with companies’ privacy practices and their approach to AI is growing more limited. “It shouldn’t be incumbent, necessarily, on consumers to go through the intense media literacy process of determining what is and isn’t real,” she said.

“Government procurement is a big lever. … Short of hard law, that’s a pretty effective way of creating behavioral change.” Var Shankar, Executive Director,  Responsible AI Institute

In the weeks following the release of the Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, many rushed to assess the impact that the order could eventually have on the AI market. Months into 2024, it’s becoming more clear that the order’s impact is less direct, and will instead trickle down through agencies’ own approaches to leveraging the technology, Shankar explained.

Ani Gevorkian, director for Responsible AI Public Policy at Microsoft, echoed this analysis, noting, “That executive order has teeth in that it required the White House Office of Management and Budget (OBM) to put out these requirements that federal agencies must abide by, and those are requirements passed down to vendors, to suppliers, to AI companies who want to offer their systems and services to federal governments and federal agencies. And we’ve seen this system happen before. Oftentimes federal procurement is sort of the first push in developing a set of best practices and standardizing practices.”

“Eligibility for insurance products for AI is going to be an incredible incentive for good governance.” Phillip Dawson, Head of AI Policy, Armilla AI

Dawson noted Armilla AI is currently working to develop new insurance products specifically for AI risks.

“Part of our process for determining eligibility is assessing enterprises against the very frameworks we’ve been discussing today: How mature are your risk management processes? Have you tested the models? What types of performance and vulnerabilities do we see? All feeding into an underwriting model to price coverage for AI risk. So there’s going to be an incredible market-based incentive for companies,” he said.

Today, many organizations are relying on “silent coverage”—either existing cybersecurity or errors and omissions policies, which offer some extent of coverage. But that could soon change. “The insurance community is looking at carving much of this out and creating bespoke products,” Dawson added.

“We’re in a battle for what it means to have trust and security in this ecosystem. It is not a battle between random parties. It’s not a battle of economics. It is a battle of values.” Jamil Jaffer, Venture Partner and Strategic Adviser, Paladin Capital Group

As organizations across the globe are attempting to issue best practices, these will ultimately be shaped by their jurisdictions’ values and priorities, Jaffer noted.

“There are our values, western values, values in the United States or allies, and there are other countries that have different values. … If we want to maintain that lead, we’ve got to embed trust, safety and security in our capabilities, we’ve got to build [AI products] around our values.”

“There are existing domains to leverage insights from as we move forward with this new technology.” Angela McKay, Director, T&S Research & Partnerships, Google

McKay emphasized the idea that most organizations can and should leverage existing frameworks to inform their approach to AI governance.

“Whether it is the insurance market, whether it is the continual learning of standards, whether it is the idea that there is some safety and security that is a public good and not something that is competitive,” she provided as examples.

“We don’t have the time with AI to iterate incessantly for the next 10 years.” Philip Reiner, Chief Executive Officer, Institute for Security and Technology

Not everyone believes that existing frameworks may be enough to craft solid AI standards. In fact, Reiner noted that some of the standards being created “won’t be changeable later,” leaving organizations with unworkable frameworks. “We’ve experienced this in cybersecurity in a very, very painful way,” he noted.

Reiner added, “We need to be very frank with ourselves when thinking about frameworks for evaluation, for investment, etc. We’re going to learn a little from the past, but at the end of the day we have to come up with brand news ways of thinking about this problem and we need to do it way faster.”

article.title: How a Latham Team Helped Shut Down the Inductors Antitrust Litigation in the Face of Panasonic’s Leniency Application
article.description: An all-women team from Latham & Watkins helped power down the remaining action in a flurry of antitrust litigation against Japanese manufacturers of electric circuit components. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila of the Northern District of California…
article.text: An all-women team from Latham & Watkins helped power down the remaining action in a flurry of antitrust litigation against Japanese manufacturers of electric circuit components. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila of the Northern District of California last week dismissed with prejudice allegations that manufacturers Panasonic Corp., Sagami Elec Co. and Sumida Corp. were involved in a market-wide conspiracy to stabilize the prices of inductors between 2003 and 2014.

article.title: 'Deeply Troubling': Tesla Sued Over 'Racially Hostile Work Environment' Amid Surge of Racial Discrimination Litigation
article.description: Tesla was sued for alleged racial discrimination toward employees at two of its California factories just three months after settling another race harassment lawsuit. The complaint argues that Tesla supervisors and colleagues repeatedly harassed and…
article.text: Tesla was sued for alleged racial discrimination toward employees at two of its California factories just three months after settling another race harassment lawsuit. The complaint argues that Tesla supervisors and colleagues repeatedly harassed and discriminated against African American, Hispanic and Latinx employees, who were ignored or punished by management for reporting racist incidents. Tesla is currently the target of a proposed employee class action alleging racist behavior at California EV manufacturing facilities. Tesla was hit with another complaint alleging racial discrimination on Monday in Alameda County Superior Court just three months after settling a separate race harassment lawsuit. The plaintiffs, represented by Arias Sanguinetti Wang & Team and Law Brothers – Injury Attorneys (named as Lalezary Law Firm in the complaint), include both current and former Tesla employees who worked at Tesla’s electric vehicle manufacturing facilities in Fremont and Lathrop, California. They allege that supervisors and colleagues at these factories created a “racially hostile work environment” by routinely harassing African American, Hispanic and Latinx Tesla employees.

• Tesla was sued for alleged racial discrimination toward employees at two of its California factories just three months after settling another race harassment lawsuit.

  • Tesla is currently the target of a proposed employee class action alleging racist behavior at California EV manufacturing facilities.

article.title: Biden Picks Former Obama Lawyer for White House Counsel | Corporate Counsel
article.description: During his first stint at the White House, Ed Siskel helped fend off attacks on the Affordable Care Act. He also spearheaded the response to congressional inquiries into the 2012 Benghazi attack that resulted in the killing of the U.S. ambassador to Libya.
article.text: Trending Michael G. Bongiorno, Andrew Scott Dulberg and Elizabeth E. Driscoll from Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr have stepped in to represent Symbotic Inc., an A.I.-enabled technology platform that focuses on increasing supply chain efficiency, and other defendants in a pending shareholder derivative lawsuit. The case, filed Oct. 2 in Massachusetts District Court by the Brown Law Firm on behalf of Stephen Austen, accuses certain officers and directors of misleading investors in regard to Symbotic's potential for margin growth by failing to disclose that the company was not equipped to timely deploy its systems or manage expenses through project delays. The case, assigned to U.S. District Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, is 1:24-cv-12522, Austen v. Cohen et al. Read More Edmund Polubinski and Marie Killmond of Davis Polk & Wardwell have entered appearances for data platform software development company MongoDB and other defendants in a pending shareholder derivative lawsuit.
