article.title: Executives in Crosshairs as FTC Bears Down on Companies Over Data Breaches
article.description: "I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, 'If it doesn't work it's your fault,’” said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman. November 22,…
article.text: "I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, 'If it doesn't work it's your fault,’” said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman. November 22, 2022 at 07:04 AM 6 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know In two recent cases, the FTC held a senior leader accountable for a company's lax data security.A recent action against the CEO of Drizly would follow him to other employers.A debate is raging within the FTC on the approach. The Federal Trade Commission is taking a tougher stance on companies that fail to safeguard consumer data—and is even going so far as to hold individuals personally accountable for those failings. Two recent cases demonstrate the agency’s willingness to go after individuals. In early October, a federal jury convicted former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan of concealing a 2016 data breach from law enforcement and obstructing an investigation by the FTC into Uber’s security practices. A federal judge will hear his motion for acquittal next month. The FTC late last month penalized alcohol delivery platform Drizly and its CEO, James Cory Rellas, for a data breach that exposed the personal information of 2.5 million customers. The order personally applies to Rellas. Should he go to another company that collects consumer information, he’d have to follow additional data-security requirements. “CEOs who take shortcuts on security should take note,” Samuel Levine, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, warned in a statement. “I think there is a gradually developing trend to hold senior officials personally accountable,” said former FTC chairman William Kovacic, now a professor at the George Washington University School of Law. “The source of the trend comes foremost from the concern that the traditional approach, which has emphasized institutional accountability, fails to create incentives for effective compliance.” He said the movement has been accelerated in part by the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the commission imposed a hefty $5 billion fine and other restrictions on Facebook for collecting and selling users’ personal data. While the FTC did not name CEO Mark Zuckerberg, it required him to periodically certify the company’s compliance with the privacy reforms outlined in its order or face civil and criminal penalties. “I think as we carry this ahead, when the government imposes remedies and accepts settlements though negotiation, these kinds of provisions that require the CEO to sign … are going to be more common,” Kovacic said. The FTC’s order against Drizly carried no fines but threatened Rellas and the company with financial sanctions if they fail to destroy unnecessary customer data or fail to limit data collection and protect against future data breaches. In his statement, the FTC’s Levine said the agency’s action “ensures the CEO faces consequences for the company’s carelessness.” RECOMMENDED FOR YOU Book Internet and Online Law This authoritative work describes the nature and growth of the law of the Internet and explains the legal obligations, opportunities, rights, and risks inherent in this c... View This Book The fact the order would follow Rellas to other employers sends a powerful signal to executives, legal observers said. “The issue here generally is what happens if the guy who runs Drizly leaves for somewhere else and runs another company that has very lax security,” said David Vladeck, director of Georgetown Law’s Center on Privacy and Technology. “You want that person to be responsible, even if he is no longer with the company that got into trouble. That is one reason why there have been, in what the FTC thinks are egregious cases, good reasons to put a CEO or senior official under an order.” Vladek said the internal debate on whether to hold CEOs personally liable isn’t settled. In the Drizly case, Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented from the part of the settlement that applies to Rellas, writing, “CEOs have hundreds of issues and numerous regulatory obligations to navigate. Companies, not federal regulators, are better positioned to evaluate what risks require the regular attention of a CEO.” Chair Lina Khan responded, “Overseeing a big company is not an excuse to subordinate legal duties in favor of other priorities. The FTC has a role to play in making sure a company’s legal obligations are weighed in the boardroom.” She added that the order and settlement “sends a very clear message: Protecting Americans’ data is not discretionary. It must be a priority for any chief executive. If anything, it only grows more important as a firm grows.” Kovacic said naming an individual puts an immediate spotlight on the human beings behind the corporation. “It’s called naming and shaming,” he said. “It says, this didn’t just happen. It happened because you failed. This is your fault, and any sanctions that may be imposed may fall on you personally.” But Vladeck says the commission is still debating the issue. “If you put an individual under order, what’s really the point? Yes, you’ve embarrassed this person, but the question is, ‘Is this adding to deterrence?’ There is a legitimate disagreement in the commission on that issue.” Vladeck said when he served as the director of the commission’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, “there were a few cases where there was a robust discussion on the commission about whether that adds to deterrence and whether conduct by the CEO was concerning enough to have an order that explicitly put the CEO in the crosshairs. “It’s a very public debate. I don’t think the FTC has landed on a position that has yielded unanimity. But there will be more attention paid to making senior corporate officials respondents in FTC consent orders.” He noted that lax security had been a persistent problem for Drizly. “There were weaknesses they were well aware of and they didn’t do anything to forestall a breach,” Vladeck said, adding that companies who fail to adequately fund cybersecurity will draw the most attention from regulators. “It may be cheaper for a company to endure a data breach than to have more robust security. Most of the cases the FTC pursues they are companies not investing in data security at all.” While executives may be tempted to hand off the data security and compliance issues to subordinates, they could still be blamed if anything goes wrong. “The job of senior leadership is to put in place incentives and structures to make sure people obey the law,” Kovacic said, raising the analogy of admiral Hyman G. Rickover, who oversaw the development of naval nuclear propulsion and, to lead by example, made a point of being aboard during test dives of every nuclear submarine under construction. “The best way is to single out senior leaders and say, ‘This is your job.’” “I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, ‘If it doesn’t work it’s your fault,’” he said. Legal chiefs also could be targets for censure if companies shirk their compliance responsibilities. “Anybody in a position of leadership who creates and builds the human and organizational structures that ensure compliance, it’s your job to make sure it works,” Kovacic said. He said it’s not enough for a general counsel to say, “‘the headstrong CEO wouldn’t listen to me.’ If you’re as smart as you say you are, find a way to get your message across. One thing that does help lawyers in-house to be effective is having powerful examples of what happened to somebody else.”
article.html:
"I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, 'If it doesn't work it's your fault,’” said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman.

November 22, 2022 at 07:04 AM

6 minute read

Risk and Compliance

Maria Dinzeo




What You Need to Know

  • In two recent cases, the FTC held a senior leader accountable for a company's lax data security.
  • A recent action against the CEO of Drizly would follow him to other employers.
  • A debate is raging within the FTC on the approach.

The Federal Trade Commission is taking a tougher stance on companies that fail to safeguard consumer data—and is even going so far as to hold individuals personally accountable for those failings.

Two recent cases demonstrate the agency’s willingness to go after individuals. In early October, a federal jury convicted former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan of concealing a 2016 data breach from law enforcement and obstructing an investigation by the FTC into Uber’s security practices. A federal judge will hear his motion for acquittal next month.

The FTC late last month penalized alcohol delivery platform Drizly and its CEO, James Cory Rellas, for a data breach that exposed the personal information of 2.5 million customers. The order personally applies to Rellas. Should he go to another company that collects consumer information, he’d have to follow additional data-security requirements. “CEOs who take shortcuts on security should take note,” Samuel Levine, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, warned in a statement.

“I think there is a gradually developing trend to hold senior officials personally accountable,” said former FTC chairman William Kovacic, now a professor at the George Washington University School of Law. “The source of the trend comes foremost from the concern that the traditional approach, which has emphasized institutional accountability, fails to create incentives for effective compliance.”

He said the movement has been accelerated in part by the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the commission imposed a hefty $5 billion fine and other restrictions on Facebook for collecting and selling users’ personal data. While the FTC did not name CEO Mark Zuckerberg, it required him to periodically certify the company’s compliance with the privacy reforms outlined in its order or face civil and criminal penalties.

“I think as we carry this ahead, when the government imposes remedies and accepts settlements though negotiation, these kinds of provisions that require the CEO to sign … are going to be more common,” Kovacic said.

The FTC’s order against Drizly carried no fines but threatened Rellas and the company with financial sanctions if they fail to destroy unnecessary customer data or fail to limit data collection and protect against future data breaches. In his statement, the FTC’s Levine said the agency’s action “ensures the CEO faces consequences for the company’s carelessness.”

RECOMMENDED FOR YOU


Book

Internet and Online Law

This authoritative work describes the nature and growth of the law of the Internet and explains the legal obligations, opportunities, rights, and risks inherent in this c...

View This Book


The fact the order would follow Rellas to other employers sends a powerful signal to executives, legal observers said.

“The issue here generally is what happens if the guy who runs Drizly leaves for somewhere else and runs another company that has very lax security,” said David Vladeck, director of Georgetown Law’s Center on Privacy and Technology.

“You want that person to be responsible, even if he is no longer with the company that got into trouble. That is one reason why there have been, in what the FTC thinks are egregious cases, good reasons to put a CEO or senior official under an order.”

Vladek said the internal debate on whether to hold CEOs personally liable isn’t settled. In the Drizly case, Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented from the part of the settlement that applies to Rellas, writing, “CEOs have hundreds of issues and numerous regulatory obligations to navigate. Companies, not federal regulators, are better positioned to evaluate what risks require the regular attention of a CEO.”

Chair Lina Khan responded, “Overseeing a big company is not an excuse to subordinate legal duties in favor of other priorities. The FTC has a role to play in making sure a company’s legal obligations are weighed in the boardroom.” She added that the order and settlement “sends a very clear message: Protecting Americans’ data is not discretionary. It must be a priority for any chief executive. If anything, it only grows more important as a firm grows.”

Kovacic said naming an individual puts an immediate spotlight on the human beings behind the corporation. “It’s called naming and shaming,” he said. “It says, this didn’t just happen. It happened because you failed. This is your fault, and any sanctions that may be imposed may fall on you personally.”

But Vladeck says the commission is still debating the issue.

“If you put an individual under order, what’s really the point? Yes, you’ve embarrassed this person, but the question is, ‘Is this adding to deterrence?’ There is a legitimate disagreement in the commission on that issue.”

Vladeck said when he served as the director of the commission’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, “there were a few cases where there was a robust discussion on the commission about whether that adds to deterrence and whether conduct by the CEO was concerning enough to have an order that explicitly put the CEO in the crosshairs.

“It’s a very public debate. I don’t think the FTC has landed on a position that has yielded unanimity. But there will be more attention paid to making senior corporate officials respondents in FTC consent orders.”

He noted that lax security had been a persistent problem for Drizly. “There were weaknesses they were well aware of and they didn’t do anything to forestall a breach,” Vladeck said, adding that companies who fail to adequately fund cybersecurity will draw the most attention from regulators.

“It may be cheaper for a company to endure a data breach than to have more robust security. Most of the cases the FTC pursues they are companies not investing in data security at all.”

While executives may be tempted to hand off the data security and compliance issues to subordinates, they could still be blamed if anything goes wrong.

“The job of senior leadership is to put in place incentives and structures to make sure people obey the law,” Kovacic said, raising the analogy of admiral Hyman G. Rickover, who oversaw the development of naval nuclear propulsion and, to lead by example, made a point of being aboard during test dives of every nuclear submarine under construction. “The best way is to single out senior leaders and say, ‘This is your job.’”

“I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, ‘If it doesn’t work it’s your fault,’” he said.

Legal chiefs also could be targets for censure if companies shirk their compliance responsibilities.

“Anybody in a position of leadership who creates and builds the human and organizational structures that ensure compliance, it’s your job to make sure it works,” Kovacic said.

He said it’s not enough for a general counsel to say, “‘the headstrong CEO wouldn’t listen to me.’ If you’re as smart as you say you are, find a way to get your message across. One thing that does help lawyers in-house to be effective is having powerful examples of what happened to somebody else.”

article.title: Former Facebook Security Chief Sounds Off on the Case that Rocked the Cybersecurity World
article.description: The government's recent prosecution of a former Uber executive for failing to disclose a data breach to law enforcement has company executives, and security chiefs in particular, anxious that they might be next.
article.text: Companies of all sizes are under assault from sophisticated ransomware groups, and the government's recent prosecution of a former Uber executive for failing to disclose a data breach to law enforcement has company executives, and security chiefs in particular, anxious that they might be next. Alex Stamos, former chief security officer at Facebook and now director at the Stanford Internet Observatory, said Tuesday that the unprecedented criminal case against ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan, the first of its kind against a company executive, is problematic on several fronts. "Being breached, paying the attackers, and then not notifying law enforcement is something that happens dozens, or perhaps hundreds, of times a day in the United States," Stamos told Berkeley Law's Irene Liu at a webinar it hosted as part of its executive education program. "Because of the ransomware crisis we're living through, companies of all sizes are being targeted by ransomware groups, they're being breached, and if you're a CEO and one of these hackers comes to you and says, 'For $5 million this problem just goes way,' it is completely in their economic interest and shareholder interest to do so." Stamos said companies will sometimes notify law enforcement about data breaches, but in many cases they do not. Sullivan was found guilty of one count of obstructing the Federal Trade Commission ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices, and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. Stamos, who is friends with Sullivan and took over his job as security chief at Facebook when Sullivan left for Uber, said the latter charge was the most unsettling. "Joe is being punished for something that actually happens all the time, and for which we don't have good legal guidance," he said. Stamos said he supports a federal standard for reporting breaches to law enforcement, but right now no such law exists at the federal level. "We should not have U.S. attorneys and judges just inventing this really important and impactful precedent on their own with the prosecution of one person." Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Prosecutors say the breach looked terrible for Sullivan, who was brought on to help the company beef up its cybersecurity after a similar breach in 2014 in which a hacker accessed unencrypted customer data housed in Uber's Amazon data store using a key Uber engineers had left sitting exposed in GitHub. After one of the hackers reached out to Sullivan's personal email address and demanded a six-figure payment, Sullivan and his security team decided to treat the incident as a routine bug bounty and funneled a $100,000 bitcoin ransom through HackerOne. Sullivan's storied past as one of the nation's first cybercrime prosecutors may have made him an easy target, Stamos said. His law degree, and his career as a high-level in-house lawyer at a number of big tech companies, also made it harder for the jury to swallow his defense that he was following the advice of Uber's in-house counsel when he failed to notify the FTC or law enforcement about the breach. Salle Yoo, who was Uber's general counsel at the time, testified that she was kept in the dark about the hack, while Craig Clark, an in-house lawyer at Uber who worked under Sullivan and was given immunity for his testimony, said Sullivan had asked him to figure out whether the breach could be classified as a bug bounty. Stamos had his own theory of the case, which was that Sullivan, who also kept mum at the behest of former CEO Travis Kalanick, was the sacrificial lamb in a power play between his old boss and Dara Khosrowshahi, who took over after Kalanick left the company under a cloud of scandal. "Uber got a new CEO, the new CEO Travis Kalanick was still on the board and the new CEO wanted him off the board. You had new management come in and look through the history of the company for bad things that happened to try to pin on Travis," Stamos said. "This was a war between millionaires and billionaires, and unfortunately the U.S. attorney's office in Northern California allowed themselves to be used as a weapon in a corporate boardroom war. And they decided to go after Joe as a way to get to Travis Kalanick, and in the end, they didn't get Travis. He's walked away scot-free from this." Ultimately, a lack of communication between Uber's security and legal teams proved to be a fatal weakness. "One of the failures here was that Uber didn't have a crisis management team," Stamos said. "What I recommend is that companies should predefine what their cybersecurity crisis team looks like, and that always has the general counsel or an assistant general counsel who works on cybersecurity issues, the CEO, the CFO, and probably somebody like a chief marketing officer to represent the customers." The security chief should be briefing the group regularly so the company can plan an appropriate response should a data breach occur. Companies should also keep outside counsel on retainer in the event of a crisis—ideally a firm that has strong cyber-practice expertise. "In one of those situations where you're trying to say what is our legal obligation under 30 something state laws, you want to have a firm that's done that work over and over again," Stamos said. Sullivan is set to be sentenced on May 4 after a federal judge declined to overturn his conviction. Stamos said he expects his sentencing will be "the number one topic over drinks" at the upcoming RSA conference in San Francisco, as Sullivan is facing significant time in federal prison— the same place where he sent dozens of child predators through is work at the Justice Department. "At a minimum, I hope if he has to actually be incarcerated that they're thinking about his safety," Stamos said. "Because he's a guy who has a decent number of enemies out there." Stamos said he supports a federal standard for reporting breaches to law enforcement, but right now no such law exists at the federal level. "We should not have U.S. attorneys and judges just inventing this really important and impactful precedent on their own with the prosecution of one person."

Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers.

Prosecutors say the breach looked terrible for Sullivan, who was brought on to help the company beef up its cybersecurity after a similar breach in 2014 in which a hacker accessed unencrypted customer data housed in Uber's Amazon data store using a key Uber engineers had left sitting exposed in GitHub.

After one of the hackers reached out to Sullivan's personal email address and demanded a six-figure payment, Sullivan and his security team decided to treat the incident as a routine bug bounty and funneled a $100,000 bitcoin ransom through HackerOne.

Sullivan's storied past as one of the nation's first cybercrime prosecutors may have made him an easy target, Stamos said.

His law degree, and his career as a high-level in-house lawyer at a number of big tech companies, also made it harder for the jury to swallow his defense that he was following the advice of Uber's in-house counsel when he failed to notify the FTC or law enforcement about the breach.

Salle Yoo, who was Uber's general counsel at the time, testified that she was kept in the dark about the hack, while Craig Clark, an in-house lawyer at Uber who worked under Sullivan and was given immunity for his testimony, said Sullivan had asked him to figure out whether the breach could be classified as a bug bounty.

Stamos had his own theory of the case, which was that Sullivan, who also kept mum at the behest of former CEO Travis Kalanick, was the sacrificial lamb in a power play between his old boss and Dara Khosrowshahi, who took over after Kalanick left the company under a cloud of scandal.

"Uber got a new CEO, the new CEO Travis Kalanick was still on the board and the new CEO wanted him off the board. You had new management come in and look through the history of the company for bad things that happened to try to pin on Travis," Stamos said.

"This was a war between millionaires and billionaires, and unfortunately the U.S. attorney's office in Northern California allowed themselves to be used as a weapon in a corporate boardroom war. And they decided to go after Joe as a way to get to Travis Kalanick, and in the end, they didn't get Travis. He's walked away scot-free from this."

Ultimately, a lack of communication between Uber's security and legal teams proved to be a fatal weakness.

"One of the failures here was that Uber didn't have a crisis management team," Stamos said. "What I recommend is that companies should predefine what their cybersecurity crisis team looks like, and that always has the general counsel or an assistant general counsel who works on cybersecurity issues, the CEO, the CFO, and probably somebody like a chief marketing officer to represent the customers."

The security chief should be briefing the group regularly so the company can plan an appropriate response should a data breach occur. Companies should also keep outside counsel on retainer in the event of a crisis—ideally a firm that has strong cyber-practice expertise. "In one of those situations where you're trying to say what is our legal obligation under 30 something state laws, you want to have a firm that's done that work over and over again," Stamos said.

Sullivan is set to be sentenced on May 4 after a federal judge declined to overturn his conviction. Stamos said he expects his sentencing will be "the number one topic over drinks" at the upcoming RSA conference in San Francisco, as Sullivan is facing significant time in federal prison— the same place where he sent dozens of child predators through is work at the Justice Department.

"At a minimum, I hope if he has to actually be incarcerated that they're thinking about his safety," Stamos said. "Because he's a guy who has a decent number of enemies out there."

article.title: Ex-Uber Security Chief's Impending Sentencing Exposes Divide in Cybersecurity Community
article.description: "I recognize the costs the case has had on so many—and I believe they all could have been avoided if I had acted differently back in 2016," Joe Sullivan wrote in a letter to the court.
article.text: A federal judge on Thursday will sentence former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for his role in covering up a 2016 data breach that exposed the personal information of 57 million riders and drivers. His October 2022 conviction, considered the first criminal case brought against a tech executive over a data breach, has divided the cybersecurity community, where Sullivan was a highly respected fixture. Some security experts decry Sullivan's decision to pay two hackers $100,000 through a recently created Uber bug bounty program as a selfish act designed to protect his own reputation and avoid more scrutiny from regulators. Uber already was under investigation by the Federal Trade Commission over lax data security practices that resulted in a similar cyberattack two years earlier. Just 10 days before the hackers contacted him by email to demand a six-figure payment, Sullivan gave a lengthy deposition to the FTC on Uber's progress in tightening security after the 2014 breach. But Sullivan also has a multitude of supporters, many of them security chiefs themselves, who have argued that Sullivan's actions are fairly commonplace, and that a prison sentence would only serve to scare people away from a profession that often requires its leaders to make difficult judgment calls. "We have been closely following Joe Sullivan's trial, the resulting verdict, and the upcoming sentencing. While the trial and the verdict have already had a considerable (and sometimes troubling) impact on our industry, we are particularly concerned about Joe's sentence in this case," says a letter filed by 63 current and former security chiefs. "The CISO job is already hard enough that many professionals do not choose it as their career path, or leave these positions for other professional roles. We are concerned that a prison sentence for Joe will further discourage people from taking these necessary jobs. With the threat of increasing liability, we already see candidates shying away from the role." But given the unique facts of the case, their fears of other security chiefs getting prosecuted might be overblown. Peter Swire, a professor of law and ethics at the Georgia Institute of Technology's Scheller College of Business, said Sullivan's sworn testimony before the FTC about Uber's efforts to beef up security after the 2014 breach and his failure to alert the commission after learning about the much larger breach just days after giving that testimony, were aggravating factors that led to his prosecution. "This new breach was enormous. It was far larger than the previous Uber breach and Uber clearly knew by that time that it was under a legal obligation to report a data breach," he said. "Security chiefs ought to know already that they shouldn't submit sworn testimony that is untrue or seriously misleading. Here we have a combination of a large breach, clear notice to the company of the government's concerns about breaches and a lack of accuracy in the sworn testimony." Swire, a cyberlaw scholar who advised presidents Clinton and Obama on privacy and technology, also emphasized that the breach was not disclosed to the FTC until 2017, when new CEO Dara Khosrowshahi took over the company and fired Sullivan. "A year delay in reporting a massive data breach is egregious behavior," Swire said. Sullivan faces up to eight years in prison. Prosecutors favor a sentence of 15 months, while Sullivan's defense team has asked for leniency, arguing that probation would be appropriate "to promote respect for the law, reflect the seriousness of the offense, and afford adequate deterrence." Sullivan, for his part, says he deeply regrets how he handled things. In a letter to U.S. District Judge William Orrick, Sullivan said not a day has gone by since he was fired in 2017 that he hasn't agonized over the decisions that led up to his prosecution. "I recognize the costs the case has had on so many—and I believe they all could have been avoided if I had acted differently back in 2016," Sullivan wrote. He also said he knew it "would have been embarrassing to Uber" if the details of the incident were made public, which was why he "helped pursue what I was told was an 'aggressive' legal strategy of putting them into Uber's bug bounty program," which "provided the company with a plausible basis to resolve the incident internally, and quietly, without having to treat the incident as a 'data breach' necessitating disclosures to the authorities." Sullivan said he should have "seen to it that authorities were notified of the incident. He added that "good cyber governance should involve transparency, clear lines of accountability, and erring on the side of disclosure rather than looking for ways to avoid it. My actions in 2016 fell short of these ideals." More than 185 people submitted letters of support ahead of Sullivan's sentencing, his defense lawyers say, including longtime friend and colleague Rob Chesnut, former senior vice president of global trust and safety at eBay. "[S]ome might believe that a jail sentence is important here to send a message to others in the cyber security field. I disagree," wrote Chesnut, who worked with Sullivan at the e-commerce platform in the early 2000s. Chesnut wrote that many of the security professionals he's spoken with since Sullivan's trial are distressed by its outcome. "The fact that a criminal case was brought against Joe, and that he was convicted, has shaken many within the industry who understand that cyber events are a way of life in this field," he wrote. "Some security executives expressed deep concern over taking any C level security position at a top company, and questioned whether they needed to get their own independent outside counsel to advise them on breaches." He said that on a positive note, the case has spurred changes to the way companies handle data breaches, leading to better internal communication and more clarity around who in a company holds the ultimate decision-making authority to report a breach to law enforcement and regulators. "One security officer recently told me that he would report a breach even if his company explicitly decided not to do it, all because of this case," he wrote. "If prosecutors were hoping to get the security industry's attention with this prosecution, they have already succeeded." Since his conviction, Sullivan has been keeping busy with charity work. According to his LinkedIn profile, he left his job as Cloudflare's security chief and took over as the CEO of a nonprofit providing humanitarian aid to Ukraine. "I now oversee programs ensuring there are enough first-aid kits distributed across Ukraine to deal with all the traumatic injuries caused by the war, and providing laptops and other support to the over 1.5 million children in Ukraine stuck doing remote education," Sullivan wrote to Judge Orrick, highlighting a recent trip to Ukraine. "I was fortunate enough to recently spend 2 weeks in Ukraine, traveling to Kyiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv, and Lviv, where I met incredible people who are resilient in the face of war. I can't wait to go back and want to do all I can to help them until their crisis is over." In the government's sentencing memo, U.S. Attorney Stephanie Hinds urged Orrick not to show leniency, arguing that Sullivan's humanitarian work only serves to "whitewash his criminal record." The letters of support submitted on Sullivan's behalf, she wrote, underscore his "extraordinarily privileged position" and "mainly demonstrate that defendant is a wealthy, powerful man, with a strong network of family and friends that has benefited him throughout his life." She likened Sullivan to another tech executive, Anthony Levandowski, whom U.S. District Judge William Alsup sentenced in 2020 to 18 months in prison for stealing Google's trade secrets for self-driving cars. "Defendant Sullivan, like Anthony Levandowski before him, has a spotless history. He is respected in his community. He is an innovator in his field. He is loyal to his friends and has supported those less fortunate. But, when given the opportunity to choose between himself and adherence to the law, he chose himself," she wrote. "Worse than that, Defendant Sullivan prioritized his and Uber's interests over those of the tens of millions of Uber users and riders who trusted their personal information to the company." Hinds said tech companies have long thrived on their willingness to take risks, "But prison is a risk too far." She said a prison sentence in Sullivan's case "will communicate to others in the industry that the willful interference with government investigations, even when they are uncomfortable or costly, is not amenable to a cost-benefit analysis because the sanction—incarceration—is unacceptable." article.title: Former Deputy GC at EV Company Canoo Among Execs Accused of Corporate Espionage
article.description: Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which…
article.text: Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which is known for its distinctive egg-shaped auto design, filed a federal lawsuit on Dec. 22 accusing former Canoo CEO John Harris, chief technology officer Phillip Weicker, chief operating officer William Eberts, vice president Alexi Charbonneau and Fielkow of swiping Canoo’s proprietary technology and poaching its employees to create Harbinger Motors in 2021. Canoo’s complaint, first reported by Business Insider, describes the band of higher-ups as a “group of serial grifters” hellbent on owning and controlling their own EV company at any cost. Torrance, California-based Canoo also is suing Gardena, California-based Harbinger’s investors, who the company alleges ”were willing to turn a blind eye to such misconduct to enjoy a shortcut to success.” Harris, Weicker, Eberts and Charbonneau formerly worked together at another EV startup, Los Angeles-based Faraday Future, where Canoo claims the nefarious plot took shape. “Canoo believes it was at Faraday where Harris, Weicker, Eberts, and Charbonneau honed their trade craft of stealing intellectual property for personal financial gain. In lieu of starting an EV company using their own independent work, the four decided that it would be far more expeditious and inexpensive to do so by stealing privileged information and intellectual property while learning what works and doesn’t work—all at the employer’s expense,” its complaint says. Canoo, which launched in 2018, accuses the former executives of pilfering its patented EV technology; a driving platform it calls a “skateboard” that can convert gas-powered vehicles to electric at a minimal cost. The suit also alleges the executives sabotaged Canoo’s deal with step-delivery van maker Morgan Olson to integrate skateboard into that company’s existing fleet. Canoo says Harbinger suspiciously made its own deal with Morgan Olson in 2022. Reached for comment by Law.com, a spokesman for Harbinger dismissed the allegations against Fielkow and the other defendants as “baseless.” The statement said, “Harbinger and its co-founders have always operated with the utmost integrity and have never engaged in any actions that would give rise to this meritless lawsuit.” In the lawsuit, Canoo calls out Fielkow’s conduct as deserving “particular scrutiny” given that he served as Canoo’s deputy general counsel for three years. He rose to vice president of corporate legal, securities and global strategies, leaving the company in March 2022 to become Harbinger’s general counsel. Fielkow oversaw a wide-ranging scope of in-house matters at Canoo, including its “strategic transactions and investments, corporate governance, board advisory, product development, intellectual property and technology licensing, IP litigation, regulatory compliance, securities law, data privacy, and commercial contracts with suppliers and partners,” the lawsuit says. Fielkow also was part of Canoo’s business development team, the complaint notes, “where he assisted in setting and developing plans for business and revenue growth, researching and planning new market initiatives, and meeting with business partners.” This would mean Fielkow had intimate knowledge of Canoo’s business strategy, including its planned partnership with Morgan Olson. Canoo says Filekow and his colleagues “undoubtedly” used confidential information they gleaned from Canoo’s year-and-a-half-long negotiations with Morgan Olson to form the Harbinger-Morgan Olson venture. “Canoo trusted Fielkow to provide counsel free of fraud, theft, and divided loyalty. Fielkow grossly abused that trust, stealing untold amounts of Canoo’s privileged documents and communications, intellectual property, and even misrepresenting on several occasions that he would not join a competitor,” Canoo’s complaint says. It adds, “Unfortunately for Canoo, its trust in Fielkow was misplaced. Fielkow grossly abused his fiduciary position, stealing untold amounts of Canoo’s intellectual property, and even misrepresenting on several occasions that he would not join a competitor. Fielkow knew (or should have known) of the devastating impacts often caused by an attorney violating his ethical and professional responsibilities—yet he intentionally casted them aside.” Reached by Law.com, Fielkow referred questions to the Harbinger spokesman, who would not comment beyond the written statement. According to Canoo, the former executives’ scheme unraveled around March 2022, when Canoo mistakenly received an email from outside counsel referencing three patent applications that listed Harris, Eberts and Weicker as the inventors. “Harbinger had engaged Canoo’s own outside patent counsel for patent work—privileged information that Fielkow (as Canoo’s Deputy General Counsel) would have known,” Canoo says. “It is particularly telling that Fielkow left Canoo for Harbinger on March 11, 2022, just six days before the patent applications were sent by mistake to Canoo.” Canoo notes that the lengthy patent application drafting process meant it was going on “through at least the latter months of Fielkow’s tenure at Canoo.” Canoo says that by working for Harbinger while still a Canoo employee, Fielkow “flagrantly disregarded” his ethical duty to Canoo. Canoo says it believes that because Ebert and Weicker developed the underlying technology while they were employed by Canoo, Harbinger’s patent applications involved technology “potentially derivable from Canoo’s technology,” and that under the terms of the confidentiality agreement the former executives signed, that technology could possibly be assignable to Canoo. “Fielkow, an attorney, knew that,” Canoo says. Responding to questions from Law.com on Fielkow’s specific role in the alleged scheme, a Canoo spokesperson said, “Fielkow was involved in all aspects of the company, including the patent filing process.” Attorneys from Los Angeles law firm Munck Wilson and Mandela, which represents Canoo, declined to comment, but managing partner William Munck said in a statement that “our client has a clear case and the lawsuit speaks for itself.”

article.title: Cyberattacks Are Accelerating With AI's Help
article.description: Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential.
article.text: Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential. At last month's RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. "We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models," he said. In an interview with Information Security Media Group, Hyppönen recounted an email he received from a malware writer boasting that he'd created a "completely new virus" using OpenAI's GPT that can create computer code from instructions written in English. "It's the first malware we've ever seen which uses ChatGPT to rewrite its code," Hyppönen told Information Security's Matthew Schwartz. "It calls GPT to write the code for it, which means every time it's different, and it will be trivial to modify to write it in any other language." Although ChatGPT can blacklist malicious users, Hyppönen said eventually developers might be able to create malware with their own LLMs built in. Though less sophisticated than malware created by human beings, LLMs have expanded the pool of would-be cybercriminals by enabling even novices to develop malicious code, some experts say. Sergey Shykevich, lead ChatGPT researcher at cybersecurity company Check Point, said he's seen hackers bragging in dark web forums about creating malware and ransomware using ChatGPT. "What's important is that ChatGPT allows everyone, even those with zero experience in coding, to develop that skill. Maybe in six months or something, it will be able to also create completely sophisticated malware that we've never before seen," he said. "Now, it mostly allows people who are not software developers to create malware. That makes the threat higher because at the end of the day there will be more malware criminals in the wild and more malware criminals will try and attack corporations." LLMs also can streamline phishing attacks by composing convincing emails impersonating trusted institutions such as a bank or the Internal Revenue Service. "Take, for example, Russian cybercriminals, because most of them don't speak English or their English levels are extremely low. Up until now they used what are called external vendors. They went to graduates of English literature at Russian colleges who wrote them phishing emails in English," Shykevich said. "Now ChatGPT allows them to make their operations much more cost-effective. They just write in ChatGPT, or other similar tools, 'please write an email that looks like it comes from Chase Bank or any other bank' and asks the recipient to provide their bank account information or Social Security number. The chatbot can then generate the email in perfect English," he said. Scott Giordano, general counsel of data loss protection company Spirion, said AI's greatest strength is its ability to quickly pore over mountains of code to find and exploit weaknesses in a company's network before a defender can fix it. "That's the sharpest point that AI has right now. If you're a bad guy and you're not using ChatGPT or other LLMs to go and find vulnerabilities, you're probably not doing your job as a bad guy," Giordano said. "And the converse is true for the good guys. This is an arms race and both sides need to understand how to use this technology for their side," he said. The bad guys, Giordano said, currently have the advantage. "They only have to be right once. They only have to trick you once to start exploiting your network," he said. But companies can combat this by adding AI to their directory of enterprise risks, moving to a zero-trust architecture and training their employees to flag phishing scams or anything else that looks suspicious, Giordano said. "The best cybersecurity measure ever invented is an alert employee," he said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential.

At last month's RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. "We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models," he said.

In an interview with Information Security Media Group, Hyppönen recounted an email he received from a malware writer boasting that he'd created a "completely new virus" using OpenAI's GPT that can create computer code from instructions written in English.

"It's the first malware we've ever seen which uses ChatGPT to rewrite its code," Hyppönen told Information Security's Matthew Schwartz. "It calls GPT to write the code for it, which means every time it's different, and it will be trivial to modify to write it in any other language."

Although ChatGPT can blacklist malicious users, Hyppönen said eventually developers might be able to create malware with their own LLMs built in.

Though less sophisticated than malware created by human beings, LLMs have expanded the pool of would-be cybercriminals by enabling even novices to develop malicious code, some experts say.

Sergey Shykevich, lead ChatGPT researcher at cybersecurity company Check Point, said he's seen hackers bragging in dark web forums about creating malware and ransomware using ChatGPT.

"What's important is that ChatGPT allows everyone, even those with zero experience in coding, to develop that skill. Maybe in six months or something, it will be able to also create completely sophisticated malware that we've never before seen," he said.

"Now, it mostly allows people who are not software developers to create malware. That makes the threat higher because at the end of the day there will be more malware criminals in the wild and more malware criminals will try and attack corporations."

LLMs also can streamline phishing attacks by composing convincing emails impersonating trusted institutions such as a bank or the Internal Revenue Service.

"Take, for example, Russian cybercriminals, because most of them don't speak English or their English levels are extremely low. Up until now they used what are called external vendors. They went to graduates of English literature at Russian colleges who wrote them phishing emails in English," Shykevich said.

"Now ChatGPT allows them to make their operations much more cost-effective. They just write in ChatGPT, or other similar tools, 'please write an email that looks like it comes from Chase Bank or any other bank' and asks the recipient to provide their bank account information or Social Security number. The chatbot can then generate the email in perfect English," he said.

Scott Giordano, general counsel of data loss protection company Spirion, said AI's greatest strength is its ability to quickly pore over mountains of code to find and exploit weaknesses in a company's network before a defender can fix it.

"That's the sharpest point that AI has right now. If you're a bad guy and you're not using ChatGPT or other LLMs to go and find vulnerabilities, you're probably not doing your job as a bad guy," Giordano said.

"And the converse is true for the good guys. This is an arms race and both sides need to understand how to use this technology for their side," he said.

The bad guys, Giordano said, currently have the advantage. "They only have to be right once. They only have to trick you once to start exploiting your network," he said.

But companies can combat this by adding AI to their directory of enterprise risks, moving to a zero-trust architecture and training their employees to flag phishing scams or anything else that looks suspicious, Giordano said.

"The best cybersecurity measure ever invented is an alert employee," he said.

article.title: Disney's Impending Restructuring Presents a Test for Its Star General Counsel
article.description: “Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around?" said Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University. November 23, 2022 at 07:41 AM 6 minute read Corporate Governance Maria…
article.text: “Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around?" said Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University. November 23, 2022 at 07:41 AM 6 minute read Corporate Governance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page. Horacio Gutierrez landed one of the top legal jobs in the world last December—general counsel of The Walt Disney Co. But just months into the job, the board has fired Bob Chapek—the man who hired him—a sudden shift that presents the first big test for the former Spotify chief legal officer. Legal observers say the big question is whether Gutierrez can conform to new CEO Bob Iger’s vision as he undos some changes by Chapek, whom the board dismissed Sunday after nearly three years at the helm. The change-out occurred after the company reported terrible fiscal fourth-quarter results on Nov. 8, and Chapek was widely criticized for nonetheless striking an upbeat tone during a conference call with analysts later that day. While Iger hasn’t revealed specifics, he said in a staff memo that he will be instituting “organizational and operating changes,” adding, “It is my intention to restructure things in a way that honors and respects creativity as the heart and soul of who we are,” with more control shifting to content-creating teams. Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said Iger will assess whether Gutierrez fits into his new vision of the company. “Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around? A lot of times when you have CEO changes, the CEO likes to ensure their direct reports and executive management team are all in alignment and can work well together, especially in a situation where you are trying to right the ship,” he said. “The reality of it is, when you’re steering a large ship like this, the executive team needs to be a well-oiled machine and all be on the same page on where the company is going to go and how it’s going to get there. If that’s not the case, the strategy is sort of doomed to failure.” Randy Milch, a former executive vice president and general counsel of Verizon, said Gutierrez has the chops to weather the changes. Gutierrez has more than 35 years of legal experience. He joined Spotify in 2016, starting out as vice president of business and legal affairs. Three years later, the company promoted him to head of global affairs and chief legal officer. He came to Spotify from Microsoft, where he’d spent 17 years, rising to general counsel. This is Iger’s second go-round as Disney CEO. He spent 15 years at the helm of the Burbank, California-based company, a period when it prospered, before retiring in 2020. He remained on the board until stepping down as executive chairman at the end of last year, nine days after the company announced the hiring of Gutierrez as senior executive vice president and general counsel. “Gutierrez has been a senior lawyer at a bunch of companies for quite a long time. I think he’s as well positioned as anyone to understand what happens in the corporate structure when the CEO changes,” Milch said. “The thing that is a little bit different here is that Iger was the CEO for a very long time, very successfully. He had a structure in place and his successor changed that structure, and Iger seems to be saying more or less that he’s going to change the structure back to the way it was.” Gutierrez succeeded Alan Braverman, who retired after nearly two decades as general counsel. Braverman regularly ranked among the highest-paid GCs in the country. In 2021, he received total compensation of $16.6 million. That included $8.8 million in cash—more than any other legal chief. Gutierrez has a rich pay package, as well. His employment agreement shows he could earn more than $22 million in his first year, including an initial stock grant of $10 million and a $2 million signing bonus. Gutierrez, who could not be reached for comment for this story, started his new job in February. He is one of the newer faces on Disney’s leadership roster, which includes longtime executives Alan Bergman, Rebecca Campbell, James Pitaro and Christine McCarthy. Milch, the former Verizon general counsel, said Chapek’s ouster fundamentally changes Gutierrez’s job. “When you’re a new general counsel, you come in and you have a CEO who has not been there very long who is remolding the place. That means there’s time to bond with that new CEO and become an effective executor of that vision he has. And that vision is now going to be changed,” Milch said. “And [Iger] had the benefit of working with Braverman for a very long time.” Gutierrez’s Spotify background should serve him well as the company tries to wring profitably out of its streaming platform, an area Iger made a priority when he unveiled Disney+ in 2019. “My prediction is not that there’s going to be further turmoil, but there is going to be a successful effort to work together,” Milch said. Foehl—who spent nearly a decade in-house at Target, including serving as its first director of corporate compliance and ethics—said one of Gutierrez’s biggest challenges will be ensuring the company meets its compliance obligations as it restructures and resets priorities. “You have a company who is reporting concerning financial numbers, and you have changes that are happening and more that are to come. The opportunities tend to be increased a bit in maybe taking ethical or compliance shortcuts,” he said. “They need to makes sure they are on guard. When the seas are stormy and everyone’s eyes are on ‘what’s going to happen to me’ and that sort of thing, it’s important that companies have a heightened vigilance when it comes to ethical and compliance issues.” Disney’s in-house team also will have to see the company through any plans for asset sales or purchases. Some investors have suggested the company sell ESPN or accelerate the purchase of the one-third of Hulu it doesn’t already own. The stake is held by Comcast. Under the existing agreement between the two companies, Disney has the right to buy it starting in 2024. “Whatever the new strategy is will have to be navigated from a legal perspective,” Foehl said. “Change can be concerning and it can be anxiety inducing. But the flip side for that is change can be exciting and incredibly fulfilling from a professional perspective.”

“Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around?" said Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University.

November 23, 2022 at 07:41 AM

6 minute read

Corporate Governance

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.
  • The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.
  • Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page.

Horacio Gutierrez landed one of the top legal jobs in the world last December—general counsel of The Walt Disney Co. But just months into the job, the board has fired Bob Chapek—the man who hired him—a sudden shift that presents the first big test for the former Spotify chief legal officer. Legal observers say the big question is whether Gutierrez can conform to new CEO Bob Iger’s vision as he undos some changes by Chapek, whom the board dismissed Sunday after nearly three years at the helm. The change-out occurred after the company reported terrible fiscal fourth-quarter results on Nov. 8, and Chapek was widely criticized for nonetheless striking an upbeat tone during a conference call with analysts later that day.

While Iger hasn’t revealed specifics, he said in a staff memo that he will be instituting “organizational and operating changes,” adding, “It is my intention to restructure things in a way that honors and respects creativity as the heart and soul of who we are,” with more control shifting to content-creating teams.

Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said Iger will assess whether Gutierrez fits into his new vision of the company.

“Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around? A lot of times when you have CEO changes, the CEO likes to ensure their direct reports and executive management team are all in alignment and can work well together, especially in a situation where you are trying to right the ship,” he said.

“The reality of it is, when you’re steering a large ship like this, the executive team needs to be a well-oiled machine and all be on the same page on where the company is going to go and how it’s going to get there. If that’s not the case, the strategy is sort of doomed to failure.”

Randy Milch, a former executive vice president and general counsel of Verizon, said Gutierrez has the chops to weather the changes.

Gutierrez has more than 35 years of legal experience. He joined Spotify in 2016, starting out as vice president of business and legal affairs. Three years later, the company promoted him to head of global affairs and chief legal officer. He came to Spotify from Microsoft, where he’d spent 17 years, rising to general counsel.

This is Iger’s second go-round as Disney CEO. He spent 15 years at the helm of the Burbank, California-based company, a period when it prospered, before retiring in 2020. He remained on the board until stepping down as executive chairman at the end of last year, nine days after the company announced the hiring of Gutierrez as senior executive vice president and general counsel.

“Gutierrez has been a senior lawyer at a bunch of companies for quite a long time. I think he’s as well positioned as anyone to understand what happens in the corporate structure when the CEO changes,” Milch said.

“The thing that is a little bit different here is that Iger was the CEO for a very long time, very successfully. He had a structure in place and his successor changed that structure, and Iger seems to be saying more or less that he’s going to change the structure back to the way it was.”

Gutierrez succeeded Alan Braverman, who retired after nearly two decades as general counsel. Braverman regularly ranked among the highest-paid GCs in the country. In 2021, he received total compensation of $16.6 million. That included $8.8 million in cash—more than any other legal chief.

Gutierrez has a rich pay package, as well. His employment agreement shows he could earn more than $22 million in his first year, including an initial stock grant of $10 million and a $2 million signing bonus.

Gutierrez, who could not be reached for comment for this story, started his new job in February.

He is one of the newer faces on Disney’s leadership roster, which includes longtime executives Alan Bergman, Rebecca Campbell, James Pitaro and Christine McCarthy.

Milch, the former Verizon general counsel, said Chapek’s ouster fundamentally changes Gutierrez’s job.

“When you’re a new general counsel, you come in and you have a CEO who has not been there very long who is remolding the place. That means there’s time to bond with that new CEO and become an effective executor of that vision he has. And that vision is now going to be changed,” Milch said. “And [Iger] had the benefit of working with Braverman for a very long time.”

Gutierrez’s Spotify background should serve him well as the company tries to wring profitably out of its streaming platform, an area Iger made a priority when he unveiled Disney+ in 2019.

“My prediction is not that there’s going to be further turmoil, but there is going to be a successful effort to work together,” Milch said.

Foehl—who spent nearly a decade in-house at Target, including serving as its first director of corporate compliance and ethics—said one of Gutierrez’s biggest challenges will be ensuring the company meets its compliance obligations as it restructures and resets priorities.

“You have a company who is reporting concerning financial numbers, and you have changes that are happening and more that are to come. The opportunities tend to be increased a bit in maybe taking ethical or compliance shortcuts,” he said.

“They need to makes sure they are on guard. When the seas are stormy and everyone’s eyes are on ‘what’s going to happen to me’ and that sort of thing, it’s important that companies have a heightened vigilance when it comes to ethical and compliance issues.”

Disney’s in-house team also will have to see the company through any plans for asset sales or purchases. Some investors have suggested the company sell ESPN or accelerate the purchase of the one-third of Hulu it doesn’t already own. The stake is held by Comcast. Under the existing agreement between the two companies, Disney has the right to buy it starting in 2024.

“Whatever the new strategy is will have to be navigated from a legal perspective,” Foehl said. “Change can be concerning and it can be anxiety inducing. But the flip side for that is change can be exciting and incredibly fulfilling from a professional perspective.”

article.title: Why Progress on Law Firm Diversity Is 'Minimal at Best'
article.description: Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity.
article.text: Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity. "Do in-house departments still care about improving diversity in the legal profession? The answer is yes, they do. They absolutely do. I don't think this has ever been a question of people not caring," said Akshay Verma, a former legal-ops chief at Meta and Coinbase. "But not much has changed. Everyone talks a big game, and nothing has happened." Legal observers and DEI advocates attribute the disappointing results to many factors and say there's plenty of blame to go around. For starters, just 21% of legal departments are asking their law firms to report diversity data, a June Association of Corporate Counsel study found, and an even smaller percentage are demanding that firms staff matters with attorneys from underrepresented groups. And, while law firms do hire associates from underrepresented groups, they too often keep them in the background. One legal industry expert said there simply aren't enough diverse attorneys to go around, underscoring the need to expand the pipeline. The percentage of women and minority associates inched up in 2022, reaching an all-time high, according to data released last month from the National Association for Law Placement. Yet NALP, which has been tracking the data for 33 years, calls the progress "excruciatingly slow" and "minimal at best." Over the past decade, NALP data shows, the percentage of partners who are people of color has increased from 7% to 12%, and the percentage of partners who are women of color rose from 2% to 4%. One point of tension is whether legal departments should use a "stick" approach, punishing firms that fail to show meaningful progress on diversifying their ranks, or should instead take a "carrot approach," rewarding diversity gains with the opportunity to land more work. One cautionary tale for "stick" advocates is Bradley Gayton, who became general counsel of The Coca-Cola Co. in September 2020 after a nearly 30-year in-house career at Ford. The following January, he announced stringent new diversity guidelines for the beverage giant's outside firms, writing that diversity scorecards, summits and committees that were meant to drive meaningful change "are not working." Under his plan, 15% of a law firm's lawyers working on Coca-Cola's matters had to be Black, and at least another 15% had to be diverse. Firms that failed to meet the requirements would face reduced fees and could ultimately lose Coca-Cola as a client. The backlash was intense, and by April Gayton had resigned, with Coca-Cola putting the new system on hold and eventually scrapping it. 'Legally Thorny' Last year's U.S. Supreme Court ruling striking down affirmative action in higher education, as well as conservative groups' subsequent challenges to corporate diversity programs, caused some companies and law firms to pull back on DEI or at least reframe those efforts. A much-cited Littler Mendelson survey released in January found organizations are still committed to diversity, with 55% saying they're promoting more diverse employees to leadership roles. But the report also said they've been "slower to implement legally thorny" inclusion, equity and diversity goals. For example, only 34% of the 320 respondents said they were defining benchmarks and metrics to assess progress, "While executives are largely maintaining or increasing their IE&D commitments, more than one in three (35%) do not agree that their organizations have clear plans and goals in place related to IE&D," the report said. It noted that just 23% of companies are providing incentives to executives to advance diversity priorities. Diversity progress for both legal departments and law firms has been slow, acknowledged Jim Chosy, general counsel of U.S. Bancorp. "We have a lot more work to do as a broader profession," he said. "We've had a lot of organizations, whether they be diversity-focused organizations, law firms or corporate legal departments, just kind of doing their own thing. There's still just a bit of sort of us-them—we're doing this and they're doing that—and they don't always come together in the way that they should." Keeping Quiet Many law firms are reluctant to discuss what they're doing on the diversity front—perhaps spooked by conservative groups' assertion that the efforts often amount to reverse discrimination. Several law firms last year modified their diversity fellowships after activist Edward Blum filed lawsuits challenging their legality. Of the dozen or so law firms Law.com reached out to for this story, only a handful would go on the record, and some outright declined to discuss DEI matters. Jennifer Martinez, chief diversity, equity and inclusion officer at the San Francisco, California-based law firm Hanson Bridgett, said many of the firm's clients share that reticence. "My sense is that a lot of clients are maybe toning down public messaging," said Martinez, a Hanson Bridgett partner. "In-house lawyers will say, 'Can we avoid talking about this?' My gut is that they are not necessarily backing off the actual actions, but they don't want to be in the public media about what they are doing." Martinez said a minority of Hanson Bridgett's clients require her firm to report diversity metrics, and nearly half require it to report the demographics of the attorneys submitting bills. "It's not always clear to me what they do with that information. … A small number [pay] a success bonus," she said. 'Little Movement' Last June's Association of Corporate Counsel report showed little change in recent years in legal departments' use of metrics to measure outside counsel diversity. The 21% of departments gathering diversity data in the latest survey was unchanged from 2022 and up 3 percentage points from 2021. The 2023 study, based on an online survey of 449 legal departments, found that just 28% of legal departments had their own internal diversity metrics and targets. That was down from the 29% reported in 2022 and 2021. "There has been little movement in these numbers over the past three years despite the increased attention and desire to establish a more inclusive and equitable environment within the legal profession," the report said. Verma, the former Meta and Coinbase legal-ops chief, finds those numbers exasperating. "I truly believe that data is a way for you to understand how your systems work. Impact and improvement of diversity in our profession is a systems issue. You have to change the way that you do things, not just measure and say, 'Hey, we need to do better,'" said Verma, now chief operating officer at legal tech firm SpotDraft. When he was head of legal ops at Meta, Verma co-led an initiative to survey and track diversity metrics with its top 40 law firms, an effort he chronicled in an article for Black In-House Network's 2022 annual report. "We wanted to know who was working on our matters, so we did a baseline for our top 40 firms in year one " he said. "We knew it wasn't going to be overnight, but we really felt like we had a shot to change it with our top 40 firms, which are the top 40 firms on the planet, by the way. And the idea was, if we know what the bottom rung looks like, we can impact the next rung, which will then impact the next rung." Verma said the data led Meta to tell some law firms, "It's not good enough. Here's where we think it should be, and here's where you need to get to." He added; "Some of them were uncomfortable conversations. That's what I think it takes in order for us to have true progress. You can't just blame people. … You have to be willing to tell them, 'You have to change the systems within which you are currently working in order for this to have true impact.'" Taking the Lead Chosy of U.S Bancorp said law firms want their clients to provide direction on diversity measures. He said his legal team is willing to provide guidance, but "we'd rather work together and collaborate and try to drive diversity for the benefit of the broader profession." Stephen Mar, chief legal and administrative officer of the software firm Odeko, said he wishes law firms were more proactive. "There are of course exceptions, but I do think that the burden is often on clients to request or demand firms' commitment to diversity," he said. "I wish it weren't that way, but we in-house counsel need to continue to demand a commitment to diversity from our law firms and other vendors until it becomes more normalized." So what will it take to move the needle? "A firm is made up of lawyers," Mar said, "and so a firm will be committed to diversity if its own members—especially its partners—demand it." He said in an email that firms adopt diversity measures "when it makes good business sense," adding, "That doesn't just mean more money or clients in the short term, however. A firm could (and in my view, should) believe that it is in the firm's long-term business interest to have a diverse firm from top to bottom." Alan York, a partner at Reed Smith and global chair of its committee on diversity and inclusion, said his firm has taken that approach. "It's not an effort to set specific goals. It's more of an effort to make sure this is in our consciousness and awareness on a regular basis—fielding diverse teams is a business imperative," he said. Even with the Supreme Court's affirmative action ruling, York said the firm has received "a stream of requests for reporting on how we staff their matters to provide diverse teams." He said he's not seen any indication clients are pulling back. But other firms say they've seen the opposite. "We serve the middle market, and that's not anything we've seen pushed," said Kyle Ferguson, CEO of Dallas-based Ferguson Braswell Fraser Kubasta. He said that, while his firm wants to diversify its bench, the talent pool is small. "There are still not a lot of diverse candidates graduating law school," Ferguson said. Aviva Will, the co-chief operating officer of the litigation finance firm Burford Capital, said that even as legal departments say they want their outside law firms to be more diverse, they're uncomfortable putting an unfamiliar team of lawyers on high-stakes matters. "People trust who they trust, and trust who they know and who they have experience with. The most sure-fire way we know how to reduce the risk of that lawsuit is to continue with somebody who has shown through experience that they can get the results we need. And that's not an irrational thing to do," she said. "When you're playing with company money, and you're responsible for that lawsuit, it's a natural thing to want to be as careful as you can about how you use your company's budget and ensure the best results that you can." That comfort with the familiar helps perpetuate the diversity problem, according to a recent survey of 66 general counsel, heads of litigation and other senior lawyers at companies in the U.S., Europe, Asia and Australia, "Much of it is pattern and practice. People like to hire and work with people that they know and trust, so it is harder for diverse professionals to break into that inner circle," an energy company general counsel interviewed for the survey said. Diverse lawyers need the opportunity to work on important cases in order to build the relationships that will put them on other important cases, But landing that first important case often is a daunting hurdle, attorneys and legal observers say. "How do I find that person, and how do I get comfortable that I should take a risk with somebody new that I don't have any experience with?" Will said. "Those are probably the two most commonly heard obstacles I hear. And I think they're both real and valid." Power of the Purse Mar said that, while he hasn't switched firms mid-matter over a lack of diversity, he has moved work away from firms that fall short in showing a "true commitment" to diversity, such as failing to staff matters with diverse attorneys or not promoting diverse attorneys to partners. Diversity also has played a significant role in how he chooses outside counsel for follow-on work and when he issues RFPs for legal services. "I have also had law firms pitch me with a nondiverse group of lawyers, and I have declined to move forward with engagement because it showed me that the firm either did not care or did not understand that diversity was important to me," Mar said. "It's important to note, however, that this can be a positive tool. If a firm is consistently displaying a commitment to diversity, and otherwise providing excellent legal service, I am more likely to engage them or (once engaged) want to give them work." One of the most powerful ways legal departments can advance diversity is by stressing in RFPs that it will be a key criteria in deciding who gets the work, said Danielle Carr, chief officer of inclusion at Lowenstein Sandler. "What I've seen that I think is effective is when in-house legal departments are looking for new counsel, in their RFPs, they say, 'This 'is a core value. This is important. We want to see this.' And guess what? The teams that are presented are diverse. And if they truly emphasize it in the RFP they get it." Carr said she's also seen legal departments ask how firms award origination credits on matters. "One of the partners here recently completed an RFP that was similar to this, and it was like the United Nations team," she said. "Maybe it would have looked like that without those questions being asked. Maybe it wouldn't. But it's definitely going to get people thinking." Adtalem Global Education, the largest health-care educator in the country, embraces that direct approach, said Doug Beck, its general counsel since 2021. He said the company asks for diversity information from law firms and tells them it is a significant factor in the selection process. "Many of the law firms we have approached have been receptive to our request, which we appreciate because it demonstrates that the firm aligns with Adtalem's values, specifically around fostering a diverse and inclusive workforce," he said. Verma said that even small companies lacking the financial clout of a corporate giant should seek to hold their outside counsel to a higher standard—and without worrying whether broaching the subject ruffle firm leaders. "I think what gets in the way is fear. If you're going to advance an interest like diversity in our profession, you have to have some courage," he said.
