article.html:
Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity.

"Do in-house departments still care about improving diversity in the legal profession? The answer is yes, they do. They absolutely do. I don't think this has ever been a question of people not caring," said Akshay Verma, a former legal-ops chief at Meta and Coinbase. "But not much has changed. Everyone talks a big game, and nothing has happened."

Legal observers and DEI advocates attribute the disappointing results to many factors and say there's plenty of blame to go around.

For starters, just 21% of legal departments are asking their law firms to report diversity data, a June Association of Corporate Counsel study found, and an even smaller percentage are demanding that firms staff matters with attorneys from underrepresented groups.

And, while law firms do hire associates from underrepresented groups, they too often keep them in the background. One legal industry expert said there simply aren't enough diverse attorneys to go around, underscoring the need to expand the pipeline.

The percentage of women and minority associates inched up in 2022, reaching an all-time high, according to data released last month from the National Association for Law Placement. Yet NALP, which has been tracking the data for 33 years, calls the progress "excruciatingly slow" and "minimal at best."

Over the past decade, NALP data shows, the percentage of partners who are people of color has increased from 7% to 12%, and the percentage of partners who are women of color rose from 2% to 4%.

One point of tension is whether legal departments should use a "stick" approach, punishing firms that fail to show meaningful progress on diversifying their ranks, or should instead take a "carrot approach," rewarding diversity gains with the opportunity to land more work.

One cautionary tale for "stick" advocates is Bradley Gayton, who became general counsel of The Coca-Cola Co. in September 2020 after a nearly 30-year in-house career at Ford. The following January, he announced stringent new diversity guidelines for the beverage giant's outside firms, writing that diversity scorecards, summits and committees that were meant to drive meaningful change "are not working."

Under his plan, 15% of a law firm's lawyers working on Coca-Cola's matters had to be Black, and at least another 15% had to be diverse. Firms that failed to meet the requirements would face reduced fees and could ultimately lose Coca-Cola as a client.

The backlash was intense, and by April Gayton had resigned, with Coca-Cola putting the new system on hold and eventually scrapping it.

'Legally Thorny'

Last year's U.S. Supreme Court ruling striking down affirmative action in higher education, as well as conservative groups' subsequent challenges to corporate diversity programs, caused some companies and law firms to pull back on DEI or at least reframe those efforts.

A much-cited Littler Mendelson survey released in January found organizations are still committed to diversity, with 55% saying they're promoting more diverse employees to leadership roles. But the report also said they've been "slower to implement legally thorny" inclusion, equity and diversity goals. For example, only 34% of the 320 respondents said they were defining benchmarks and metrics to assess progress,

"While executives are largely maintaining or increasing their IE&D commitments, more than one in three (35%) do not agree that their organizations have clear plans and goals in place related to IE&D," the report said. It noted that just 23% of companies are providing incentives to executives to advance diversity priorities.

Diversity progress for both legal departments and law firms has been slow, acknowledged Jim Chosy, general counsel of U.S. Bancorp.

"We have a lot more work to do as a broader profession," he said. "We've had a lot of organizations, whether they be diversity-focused organizations, law firms or corporate legal departments, just kind of doing their own thing. There's still just a bit of sort of us-them—we're doing this and they're doing that—and they don't always come together in the way that they should."

Keeping Quiet

Many law firms are reluctant to discuss what they're doing on the diversity front—perhaps spooked by conservative groups' assertion that the efforts often amount to reverse discrimination. Several law firms last year modified their diversity fellowships after activist Edward Blum filed lawsuits challenging their legality.

Of the dozen or so law firms Law.com reached out to for this story, only a handful would go on the record, and some outright declined to discuss DEI matters.

Jennifer Martinez, chief diversity, equity and inclusion officer at the San Francisco, California-based law firm Hanson Bridgett, said many of the firm's clients share that reticence.

"My sense is that a lot of clients are maybe toning down public messaging," said Martinez, a Hanson Bridgett partner. "In-house lawyers will say, 'Can we avoid talking about this?' My gut is that they are not necessarily backing off the actual actions, but they don't want to be in the public media about what they are doing."

Martinez said a minority of Hanson Bridgett's clients require her firm to report diversity metrics, and nearly half require it to report the demographics of the attorneys submitting bills.

"It's not always clear to me what they do with that information. … A small number [pay] a success bonus," she said.

'Little Movement'

Last June's Association of Corporate Counsel report showed little change in recent years in legal departments' use of metrics to measure outside counsel diversity. The 21% of departments gathering diversity data in the latest survey was unchanged from 2022 and up 3 percentage points from 2021.

The 2023 study, based on an online survey of 449 legal departments, found that just 28% of legal departments had their own internal diversity metrics and targets. That was down from the 29% reported in 2022 and 2021.

"There has been little movement in these numbers over the past three years despite the increased attention and desire to establish a more inclusive and equitable environment within the legal profession," the report said.

Verma, the former Meta and Coinbase legal-ops chief, finds those numbers exasperating.

"I truly believe that data is a way for you to understand how your systems work. Impact and improvement of diversity in our profession is a systems issue. You have to change the way that you do things, not just measure and say, 'Hey, we need to do better,'" said Verma, now chief operating officer at legal tech firm SpotDraft.

When he was head of legal ops at Meta, Verma co-led an initiative to survey and track diversity metrics with its top 40 law firms, an effort he chronicled in an article for Black In-House Network's 2022 annual report.

"We wanted to know who was working on our matters, so we did a baseline for our top 40 firms in year one " he said. "We knew it wasn't going to be overnight, but we really felt like we had a shot to change it with our top 40 firms, which are the top 40 firms on the planet, by the way. And the idea was, if we know what the bottom rung looks like, we can impact the next rung, which will then impact the next rung."

Verma said the data led Meta to tell some law firms, "It's not good enough. Here's where we think it should be, and here's where you need to get to."

He added; "Some of them were uncomfortable conversations. That's what I think it takes in order for us to have true progress. You can't just blame people. … You have to be willing to tell them, 'You have to change the systems within which you are currently working in order for this to have true impact.'"

Taking the Lead

Chosy of U.S Bancorp said law firms want their clients to provide direction on diversity measures. He said his legal team is willing to provide guidance, but "we'd rather work together and collaborate and try to drive diversity for the benefit of the broader profession."

Stephen Mar, chief legal and administrative officer of the software firm Odeko, said he wishes law firms were more proactive.

"There are of course exceptions, but I do think that the burden is often on clients to request or demand firms' commitment to diversity," he said. "I wish it weren't that way, but we in-house counsel need to continue to demand a commitment to diversity from our law firms and other vendors until it becomes more normalized."

So what will it take to move the needle? "A firm is made up of lawyers," Mar said, "and so a firm will be committed to diversity if its own members—especially its partners—demand it."

He said in an email that firms adopt diversity measures "when it makes good business sense," adding, "That doesn't just mean more money or clients in the short term, however. A firm could (and in my view, should) believe that it is in the firm's long-term business interest to have a diverse firm from top to bottom."

Alan York, a partner at Reed Smith and global chair of its committee on diversity and inclusion, said his firm has taken that approach.

"It's not an effort to set specific goals. It's more of an effort to make sure this is in our consciousness and awareness on a regular basis—fielding diverse teams is a business imperative," he said.

Even with the Supreme Court's affirmative action ruling, York said the firm has received "a stream of requests for reporting on how we staff their matters to provide diverse teams." He said he's not seen any indication clients are pulling back.

But other firms say they've seen the opposite.

"We serve the middle market, and that's not anything we've seen pushed," said Kyle Ferguson, CEO of Dallas-based Ferguson Braswell Fraser Kubasta. He said that, while his firm wants to diversify its bench, the talent pool is small. "There are still not a lot of diverse candidates graduating law school," Ferguson said.

Aviva Will, the co-chief operating officer of the litigation finance firm Burford Capital, said that even as legal departments say they want their outside law firms to be more diverse, they're uncomfortable putting an unfamiliar team of lawyers on high-stakes matters.

"People trust who they trust, and trust who they know and who they have experience with. The most sure-fire way we know how to reduce the risk of that lawsuit is to continue with somebody who has shown through experience that they can get the results we need. And that's not an irrational thing to do," she said.

"When you're playing with company money, and you're responsible for that lawsuit, it's a natural thing to want to be as careful as you can about how you use your company's budget and ensure the best results that you can."

That comfort with the familiar helps perpetuate the diversity problem, according to a recent survey of 66 general counsel, heads of litigation and other senior lawyers at companies in the U.S., Europe, Asia and Australia,

"Much of it is pattern and practice. People like to hire and work with people that they know and trust, so it is harder for diverse professionals to break into that inner circle," an energy company general counsel interviewed for the survey said.

Diverse lawyers need the opportunity to work on important cases in order to build the relationships that will put them on other important cases, But landing that first important case often is a daunting hurdle, attorneys and legal observers say.

"How do I find that person, and how do I get comfortable that I should take a risk with somebody new that I don't have any experience with?" Will said. "Those are probably the two most commonly heard obstacles I hear. And I think they're both real and valid."

Power of the Purse

Mar said that, while he hasn't switched firms mid-matter over a lack of diversity, he has moved work away from firms that fall short in showing a "true commitment" to diversity, such as failing to staff matters with diverse attorneys or not promoting diverse attorneys to partners.

Diversity also has played a significant role in how he chooses outside counsel for follow-on work and when he issues RFPs for legal services.

"I have also had law firms pitch me with a nondiverse group of lawyers, and I have declined to move forward with engagement because it showed me that the firm either did not care or did not understand that diversity was important to me," Mar said.

"It's important to note, however, that this can be a positive tool. If a firm is consistently displaying a commitment to diversity, and otherwise providing excellent legal service, I am more likely to engage them or (once engaged) want to give them work."

One of the most powerful ways legal departments can advance diversity is by stressing in RFPs that it will be a key criteria in deciding who gets the work, said Danielle Carr, chief officer of inclusion at Lowenstein Sandler.

"What I've seen that I think is effective is when in-house legal departments are looking for new counsel, in their RFPs, they say, 'This 'is a core value. This is important. We want to see this.' And guess what? The teams that are presented are diverse. And if they truly emphasize it in the RFP they get it."

Carr said she's also seen legal departments ask how firms award origination credits on matters. "One of the partners here recently completed an RFP that was similar to this, and it was like the United Nations team," she said. "Maybe it would have looked like that without those questions being asked. Maybe it wouldn't. But it's definitely going to get people thinking."

Adtalem Global Education, the largest health-care educator in the country, embraces that direct approach, said Doug Beck, its general counsel since 2021. He said the company asks for diversity information from law firms and tells them it is a significant factor in the selection process.

"Many of the law firms we have approached have been receptive to our request, which we appreciate because it demonstrates that the firm aligns with Adtalem's values, specifically around fostering a diverse and inclusive workforce," he said.

Verma said that even small companies lacking the financial clout of a corporate giant should seek to hold their outside counsel to a higher standard—and without worrying whether broaching the subject ruffle firm leaders.

"I think what gets in the way is fear. If you're going to advance an interest like diversity in our profession, you have to have some courage," he said.

article.title: The AI Revolution Is Here. Who Will Be the Winners and Losers in Legal Services?
article.description: AI is a disruptive force in the legal services market. Legal tech vendors, alternative service providers and law firms are all vying for in-house counsel's attention, and the winners in the legal field will be those who figure out how to put it
article.text: Law firms, alternative legal service providers and legal tech companies are racing to attract in-house counsel dollars amid the generative AI explosion. AI promises to move a lot of previously outsourced work in-house, so firms will have to change out they provide services to clients. Some lawyers predict that AI will force firms to combine their specialized expertise and AI to solve the most complex client-specific problems. The explosion of generative AI has triggered endless speculation about the extent to which technology threatens the law firm business model. Empowered by the ability to automate more routine work, corporate legal departments could do more in-house and depend less on outside counsel. Legal teams would also have more choices, working directly with tech vendors to subscribe directly to AI tools that can help inform their decisions on everything from litigation strategy to changes in employment law. But legal industry experts say AI isn't a threat to firms. If anything, it's giving them more to do, and changing their value proposition for in-house clients. However, AI is still a disruptive force in the legal services market. Legal tech vendors, alternative service providers and law firms are all vying for in-house counsel's attention, and the winners in the legal field will be those who figure out how to put it to the best use for those clients. "This technology is going to be a game changer, and we're just in at the ground floor," said Stephanie Corey, co-founder of the legal ops consulting firm UpLevel Ops. In-Sourcing AI Most in-house teams are in the early stages of AI adoption, but some legal departments are starting to realize that much of the work they used to farm out to firms can be done internally. Ed Sohn, head of global insights for legal services provider Factor, said a groundswell has been building for years in legal departments toward "in-sourcing," mostly through the advent of legal operations and the adoption of legal tech tools. "When I've spoken to people throughout the years in working closely with in-house legal departments, I've heard people say, 'There are definitely times when we're paying a law firm to use tech on our behalf.' And that's crazy. We believe there is both opportunity and ability for in-house legal departments to take advantage of a transformative technological wave," Sohn said. While legal teams have generally struggled with using enterprise tools, generative AI is different. "It's crashing into everyone's tech stack," Sohn said. "In-house lawyers can tap into it and adapt it easily if they can just pull together the necessary commitment and collaboration that's required." Some large companies are already experimenting with AI internally. Earlier this year, Intel, DXC Technology, Microsoft, Adobe, Crowdstrike, Ford and Anglo American got together with Factor to form the Sense Collective, billed as "a collaborative community" for sharing knowledge about how to speed up generative AI adoption in the corporate legal realm. Sohn said the collective's members are generally larger organizations with a strong tech culture and high expectations around leading in AI. "They are also companies that have significant critical mass in terms of legal workloads," he said. "We do have departments that are a little smaller and where AI isn't as high as a priority, but they have leaders who are trying to innovate. They're not equipped or empowered to go on huge shopping sprees, but they have a tool entering their environment that can amplify or expand their scale." Foundational AI tools like Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT are popular with those smaller teams, Sohn said. "Legal functions are looking at general-purpose AI tools first because they portend great capability," he said. "This is something that behaves like a virtual teammate. They know how to ask for work from members of their team in very prescriptive ways." While a lot of in-house lawyers are busy with the day-to-day work of answering legal questions and reviewing contracts, Corey said legal teams are facing growing pressure to shift their focus to advising on business strategy, so it's inevitable that a lot of routine legal work will be automated. "Teams are expected to be more strategic and add more value and not just churn," she said. "And general counsel are getting a lot of pressure from CFOs. They can't just spend willy-nilly. And now with this technology, I think it's going to be an accelerator." With tightening budgets and more big-picture demands on legal, Corey with UpLevel Ops said legal tech partners and alternative legal service providers will shoulder much of the daily legal workload, freeing up clients "to do exactly what they've been complaining that they don't have time to do right now, which is be more client-advisory." Corey went on to say that she expects to see a lot of alternative service providers "winning" in this arena, adding, "They embrace technology already, they're willing to experiment, their model is not based on hours so they're not locked into a certain kind of compensation model that the law firms are very locked into. They have every incentive to be more efficient." Bracing for Impact Am Law 200 firm leaders appear to accept the fact that generative AI may shift some work away from their firms and toward in-house counsel. "We think we would be foolish not to assume that it will, quite frankly," said Chris Balch, management committee chair of Mountain West Am Law 200 firm Holland & Hart. Balch said he doesn't expect the shift to happen in the near future, but said he could imagine clients such as private equity firms or acquisitive corporations taking due diligence work in-house with the help of generative AI. Holland & Hart's role could shift from doing said work to advising legal departments on how to use the technology. "I definitely think there are areas where in-house counsel is going to deploy it, or we license the tech and let our clients know we are employing this kind of technology as a service we provide. Maybe there's a third element where we buy, build or let in-house counsel use our own tools that may displace the kinds of services we provide," he said. "I spend every day trying to keep educated on these tools. I'm talking to our AI committee about the tools that are coming that have the potential, and are very likely to be, disruptive. We would be foolish not to remain educated and be thoughtful about the ways we can help clients using technology." In the intellectual property realm, Fish & Richardson President and CEO John Adkisson said clients are taking a cautious approach to generative AI due to the precision required for the legal work. But even when the technology becomes more precise, Adkisson believes clients will still see the value in hiring skilled attorneys. "I think IP clients hire Fish because of a depth of technical knowledge and specialization, and I think that AI as it exists today isn't particularly well-equipped to provide the same depth that our people are," Adkisson said. Stephen Zubiago, managing partner of Am Law 100 firm Nixon Peabody, echoed similar sentiments, noting, "There's a range of things we do for clients, and the things we do best and the things clients value most and pay a premium for is our judgment, our experience and our advice. Obviously, things that can be routinized and automated are less high-value, and certainly AI may be able to take over some of those tasks." While the traditional law firm won't disappear entirely, Corey predicts that firms will have to change the way they do things to survive. "You'll see firms who are insisting on doing things on flat rates and offering technology and knowledge management programs to their clients," she said. Some will splinter into offshoots, building entirely new law firms that specialize in tech. "Maybe what you'll see is the techie firm kind of growing and the old-school traditional firm kind of shrinking. And there will be losers. I think you're going to see some firms folding into each other and going away." Plus, there will always be legal departments that can't or won't deploy their own internal AI systems, Corey said. "The CFO is less likely to question law firms, so it's easier for the general counsel to spend money with a law firm than it is with a tech vendor. So I think that there is a play to be made there now, though maybe not for the bigger companies. For the bigger companies, it does make sense for them to deploy their own technology, usually," she said. Corey suggested law firms may have to move to flat rates or subscription models where they charge one price to do large volumes of work. "If they figure out how to incorporate this technology into their comp model, then they'll be the winners," Corey said. "It is not a threat to firms if they embrace it, and figure out how it can best serve their clients." AI-Enabled Judgment Some firms, perhaps seeing the writing on the wall, have been at it for years. At a recent event hosted by LegalTech Hub on AI for in-house lawyers, Danielle Benecke, founder and global head of Baker McKenzie's machine learning practice, said firms can offer their clients value by using their own expertise combined with AI to solve very singular high-stakes problems, what she calls "AI-enabled judgment as a service." "We're going to see more multidisciplinary teams pop up within the firms that are laser-focused on working on really specific problems," she said. "What is very useful is when you take that reading comprehension capability [of AI] and pair that with playbooks and really helpful use cases and expertise." In a few years, Benecke said, the real value will be in solving client problems that cannot be solved now, perhaps created by the technology itself. "That's the true opportunity here. If you think about law as a static profession where the types of problems we're solving don't change, that's not true," she said. "I think we have a technology that is advancing in tandem with the problem. The problem for our clients is increasing legal complexity driven by increasing social and political complexity." Clients are also looking to firms to experiment with AI on their behalf. Ari Kaplan, a principal at Ari Kaplan Advisors, said he recently asked general counsel about the types of tasks for which they are most comfortable using AI as part of an annual white paper released by FTI Consulting and legal tech firm Relativity. "Areas that require more human judgment, like internal investigations for example, were areas where they were still reluctant. But many of them said, 'we are going to rely on our law firms to assume certain risks of using technology,'" Kaplan told Law.com. He sees the interplay between companies, law firms and tech vendors as less like the Wild West, and more of a combined team effort. "I really see this interesting interdependence of intelligence," Kaplan said. "We're definitely not at a point where a piece of a piece of technology, even a very advanced piece of technology, is replacing legal counsel." Clients are also looking to firms to experiment with AI on their behalf. Ari Kaplan, a principal at Ari Kaplan Advisors, said he recently asked general counsel about the types of tasks for which they are most comfortable using AI as part of an annual white paper released by FTI Consulting and legal tech firm Relativity.

"Areas that require more human judgment, like internal investigations for example, were areas where they were still reluctant. But many of them said, 'we are going to rely on our law firms to assume certain risks of using technology,'" Kaplan told Law.com.

He sees the interplay between companies, law firms and tech vendors as less like the Wild West, and more of a combined team effort.

"I really see this interesting interdependence of intelligence," Kaplan said. "We're definitely not at a point where a piece of a piece of technology, even a very advanced piece of technology, is replacing legal counsel."

article.title: Think Gen AI Is Mind-Blowing Today? Next Decade's Advancements Will Be 'Momentous
article.description: The legal industry's ambivalence about generative artificial intelligence is on the wane. And if it isn't, it should be.
article.text: The legal industry's ambivalence about generative artificial intelligence is on the wane. And if it isn't, it should be. That was the central message Thursday from Suffolk University Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who provided the closing keynote for this year's CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas. He said the conversation has moved beyond the associated risks and pitfalls surrounding generative AI to how lawyers should be exploring it for their practice. The greatest risk, Perlman said, is in getting left behind. "I could say it will not be too long before we move away from concerns that the use of generative AI is incompetent to concluding that failing to use generative AI is incompetent," Perlman told an audience of several hundred legal professionals. He said people who compose legal documents using today's prevailing methods might be viewed in the future just as anachronistically as someone today who does so using a typewriter. "In the future, I believe anyone who opens up a blank screen and starts to type or goes to an old version of a document, saves it as a new one and does a 'find and a replace' will be similarly viewed as incompetent," Perlman said. OpenAI's chatbot is already capable of drafting a personal-injury complaint based on a slip and fall outside someone's home after a snowstorm with great precision. Perlman said he was surprised to see ChatGPT cite a Philadelphia code provision that imposes a duty on homeowners to keep their sidewalks clear after a snowstorm within a certain number of hours. At first, he thought it was hallucinating. But, sure enough, the provision exists. The GPT model was also capable of composing interrogatories, including one that asked the plaintiff to describe the footwear worn at the time the fall occurred. "It knew enough that it was a personal injury, slip-and-fall case, and that it should ask about the footwear of the plaintiff," he said. Perlman then asked it to "attack its own work" by drafting a brief in support of a motion to dismiss the complaint, and it gave him three decent arguments in response. "Now to be very, very clear, would I file this in court without looking at it? Not if I want to continue to be licensed in Massachusetts. Nor would I recommend that any lawyer do that. But can this give us guidance and a first draft of what we might use in the future? I think the answer is most certainly yes," Perlman said. ChatGPT and similar tools also can draft terms and conditions of a merger agreement between companies based in different countries. It can give suggestions on how to improve policy documents, suggesting edits or new language for a legal department to consider, while showing its reasoning for doing so. Perlman said he expects this will be the new way of working. There are still kinks to work out, such as algorithmic bias and hallucination. It also can try to get users to believe things they know to be untrue. "It is the best gaslighter you have ever met," he said. "It is a serious problem that we are going to have to consider in the future." But there is a plethora of customer solutions, dozens of which were featured at the CLOC conference this week, and the technology is only going to improve in the years ahead. Perlman said he's been talking to law firms, in-house counsel and bar associations, and across the board they agree that no one has figured it out yet. "At the same time, I'm a big fan of this quote from Bill Gates: 'We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next few years and underestimate the next 10.' "I think that describes generative AI and legal services perfectly. If I came back here two years from now, we'll see some changes, to be sure. But will they be dramatic? Will they be industry-changing developments? I think the answer is no. But if you come back 10 years from now, I think the changes are going to be momentous. In light of that. I think even though there's a lot of uncertainty, don't use it as an excuse to do nothing." Perlman urged audience members to experiment. "You can just ask generative AI to help you strategize what your plan should be inside of your legal department. I recently did that, and it can be an excellent road map. "And … it suggested some ways in which you might communicate your steps to the C-suite in your company. It even drafted an email for me along those lines," he said. "These are the ways in which we can use it, and they are nonthreatening and helpful. They enable us to think in new ways about the nature of the work that we do." While ChatGPT and its competitors have drawn comparisons to the advent of the internet and search engines, Perlman said this is bigger. "I believe it is going to be the most significant technology ever created for the legal industry and many others," he said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. article.title: Old Laws, New Tricks: Lawyers Using Patchwork of Creative Legal Theories to Target New Tech
article.description: The web-tracking litigation landscape is growing ever more frightening amid an onslaught of lawsuits targeting anyone with a website.
article.text: The web-tracking litigation landscape is growing ever more frightening amid an onslaught of lawsuits targeting anyone with a website. With no single statute governing website tracking, crafty plaintiffs' lawyers are haunting modern digital practices with a zombie horde of old laws, including ones aimed at videorecording, wiretapping and false advertising. "Most of the litigation to date is novel, and a win in one court doesn't necessarily scare away the plaintiff's counsel from trying over and over again, or from flooding every website that their clients come in contact with and sending a demand letter," said Bethany Lukitsch, co-leader of BakerHostetler's class action defense practice. "So we see new lawsuits and new theories that are being developed throughout the year. Almost monthly, we come into contact with some new theory. Lukitsch made this observation at a recent Halloween-themed webinar hosted by the firm on website tracking litigation trends. Lukitsch said she would never have expected three years ago to see such a proliferation of website tracking litigation, particularly in California, where she practices. "Who would have thought that wiretapping would become such a big trend with website tracking?" Lukitsch said. "These are decades-old laws that were written to protect against spying or listening in on telephone conversations. They have now morphed into trying to be applicable to internet activity, and not just conversations like we think of in any sort of email communication or web chat or an actual textual communication, but literally any application of any website tracking technology to a website is subject to one of these wiretapping claims." Wiretapping claims started exploding in 2022 with Javier v. Assurance IQ, where the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that California's wiretapping law, the California Invasion of Privacy Act applies to Internet technologies. Lukitsch said these lawsuits argue that "when consumers come to your website, their actions on your web button clicks, whether they be chat, whether they be just visiting and browsing, constitute a communication for purposes of these wiretapping statutes." She noted that, just last month, the Massachusetts Supreme Court shot down a lawsuit brought under Massachusetts's state wiretapping law, a development she termed a bit of "good news" for corporate defendants, though certainly not a magic bullet. Lukitsch said a lot of the complaints she sees aren't alleging a single cause of action. "The plaintiff will throw in whatever they could possibly throw in in terms of legal theories," she said, adding, "I think one of the reasons that we're seeing all of these creative theories is because of a lack of private right of action in many of these different state privacy statutes." The federal Video Privacy Protection Act is another popular example of an old law being repurposed for a new legal theory. "If you're a retailer or somebody that has an occasional video on your website, you're probably in decent shape of escaping one of these or defending against one of these claims, but if you do have video content or streaming service as part of your customer contract, I think it's going to be potentially more difficult to evade these cases at an early motion stage," Lukitsch said. Marketers may love "session replay" technology for its ability to track how consumers interact with websites, but they have also become a major pitfall. Lukitsch recommended that companies delay recording a screen until a banner or notification secures user consent, or record sessions intermittently, providing only a random sample of user interactions. "So still helpful for your marketing team, but no one particular user is going to be able to say, 'Aha, this session was recorded when I was visiting,'" she said. She also counsels clients to avoid collecting sensitive data—such as names, addresses or chat content—or to mask such information in session replays. Every website tracking tool carries some risk, but some are necessary to make sure your website, and its opt-out mechanism, function properly. The term "necessary" hasn't yet been litigated. "What is absolutely required and where you need to provide opt-outs is a little bit squishy. So you don't have to provide some sort of opt-out right for every single type of technology," Lukitsch said, though she's not sure if that gets companies around the wiretapping claim absent some type of advance notice and consent. "This is the area that is being hotly litigated and tested," she said. Justin Yedor, a BakerHostetler partner who specializes in California privacy laws, said companies should focus on disclosure and consent as a way to push back. "Sometimes it is sufficient to deter plaintiff's counsel—it sort of depends on the nature of the claim that they're attempting to make," he said. "It is definitely not a panacea, but it can be really helpful." The language of cookie banners should also be as clear and specific as possible. "It's very important to be careful to make sure that when you are crafting the language for that banner, you're doing it not only in a way that is sufficient to obtain consent if that's your goal, but also that it is not misleading," Yedor said. How cookies are classified or labeled can have a big impact, Yedor said. Even something as simple as labeling them as "targeting" vs "functional" is important. If it's not done correctly, it can undermine the user's ability to actually control the tracking technologies on the site, even if you have a cookie banner or preference center that suggests they can. "From the outside and just at a casual glance at the website, it may appear that everything is working properly. There's a button. The user clicks it. The interface displays that targeting cookies are turned off. But if that one cookie is not classified correctly, then of course it's still going to fire and you still have risk," he said. While there isn't a single authoritative source on how to classify cookies properly, there are many tools out there that can scan a website and help companies understand their cookies better, such as OneTrust, Evidon or Ghostery. Yedor said another safe bet is for companies to minimize the data they're collecting, and weigh the benefit of tracking users on websites with the risks. "I always encourage thinking about what you truly need on your website," he said. "Because in the risk-benefit balance for these technologies, there's certainly plenty of risk." article.title: Ex-Twitter Exec Sues for $20M, Says Musk Fired Her as 'Petty Retribution'
article.description: Leslie Berland was chief marketing officer until October 2022, when a meeting with advertisers went off the rails, leaving Musk embarrassed and looking for someone to blame, she says.
article.text: Another former Twitter executive has joined the chorus of fired employees suing Elon Musk alleging unpaid severance. This time, it's ex-chief marketing officer Leslie Berland, who says she was fired so that Musk could avoid paying her $20 million in severance and benefits. Berland, who until October 2022 was Twitter's chief marketing officer, said Musk fired her in an act of "petty retribution" after a meeting with advertisers went off the rails, and also to "rid himself of her large compensation package." The fateful meeting happened on Oct. 31, just days after he completed his $44 billion takeover of the San Francisco-based social media company, now called X Corp. Its purpose was to preserve the platform's relationships with legacy advertisers. Because chief commercial officer Sarah Personette had just resigned, Berland recommended Musk connect with her successor, head of global sales Jean-Philippe Maheu. But Musk went "off-script," Berland says, suggesting in front of the advertisers that "he ought to send a Tweet teasing the reinstatement of Donald Trump's then-suspended Twitter account." Maheu suggested Musk not do this, which prompted an "embarrassed and angry" Musk to text Berland "JP is not going to work out. Bad recommendation," according to the suit. Musk ended up firing them both. The suit alleges that Musk blamed Berland for personally vouching for Maheu and terminated her "for cause" to get out of paying her the roughly $20 million in severance she would be owed for her nearly seven years at the company. Her lawsuit claims her firing was a "jarring reversal" from Musk's attitude the week prior to the meeting. At one point Musk's chief of staff, Jehn Balajadia, confided to Berland that she was "the only one here [at Twitter] that Elon trusts," the suit alleges. Berland says in the suit that Musk had a human resources employee call her to tell her that her computer access had been shut off and that security was outside her office door, ready to escort her out of the building. Confused as to why, Berland says she texted Musk, saying she was "rooting" for him and asking to talk about the situation. He did not respond, and the two never spoke again, according to her complaint. When Berland appealed the for-cause termination and denial of benefits, she was met with a host of reasons for denial, including that she violated Twitter's travel policy by taking chartered flights in her last week of employment that cost the company "approximately $200,000." Berland says the flights were a pretext, and that she had to fly to San Francisco at the last minute to assist Musk and his team. A commercial flight would not have gotten her there in time, her lawsuit claims. In addition to an undisclosed amount in cash severance, Berland says she was denied accelerated equity vesting and payment of COBRA premiums to cover health insurance for herself and two children. "Musk's belated characterization of Ms. Berland's termination as 'for cause' was done for the unlawful purpose of denying Ms. Berland these benefits. This is consistent with Musk's long pattern of not paying his bills," her lawsuit says. After leaving Twitter, Berland spent a year at Peloton before becoming Verizon's chief marketing officer in January, according to her LinkedIn profile. Musk's legal team did not respond to requests for comment on her case. The company did not respond to an inquiry sent to its reestablished press inbox. The billionaire is currently fending off a slew of lawsuits filed by ex-employees claiming they were cheated out of severance, including one brought by former CEO Parag Agrawal, CFO Ned Segal, CLO Vijaya Gadde and General Counsel Sean Edgett. On Nov. 1, U.S. District Judge Maxine Chesney denied Musk's motion to dismiss the case, rejecting Musk's argument that he was acting in his capacity as an employer, not as a fiduciary, when he terminated the foursome. Musk racked up a win, however, in another severance case brought on behalf of about 6,000 employees terminated following Musk's takeover. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. article.title: AI Isn't Meeting Legal's Expectations, New Research Finds
article.description: Amid the initial burst of excitement around generative AI, companies invested vast sums into the technology. But now many say the results are falling short of expectations. And the biggest disappointment of all is in legal
article.text: After investing vast sums into generative AI, many companies are disappointed with the results, a Bain Research report says. Among all parts of companies, the dissatisfaction is greatest in legal, Bain found. Industry experts say that while some of the early products aren't good enough, companies may have had unrealistic expectations or be using the wrong tools. Amid the initial burst of excitement around generative AI, companies invested vast sums into the technology. But now many say the results are falling short of expectations, according to a quarterly survey by Bain Research. And the biggest disappointment of all is in legal, where satisfaction with AI's performance declined sharply in just a five-month span. Industry experts say the dismal survey results indicate that users may have skewed expectations of how generative AI should perform and that, in all likelihood, survey respondents have yet to tap into the best use cases that unlock its true potential. "I'm certainly not disregarding Bain's survey results, but it does clash with other trends and data I'm seeing, both empirical and anecdotal," said startup founder and legal tech investor Zach Abramowitz. "It's also hard to know which use cases lawyers we're talking about because 'legal' is fairly broad," he added. "That being said, sufficiency and accuracy of outputs are the two biggest reasons people listed for their expectations not being met, both of which are critical in legal, an already conservative profession." A mere 53% of respondents surveyed by Bain in early 2024 said generative AI use cases "met or exceeded expectations," representing an 18-point drop in satisfaction since October. Forty-three percent of those disappointed respondents said generative AI "could not perform the necessary task with sufficient performance," and 42% cited "poor output quality." Thirty-eight percent said they couldn't understand how to use generative AI tools, and 29% attributed their disappointment to the "low quality" of the vendor and its product. Sales, software development, marketing and customer service fared much better, with all of these business units reporting increased satisfaction with AI over the five months. "The thrust of the study lines up with my instincts of what's going on—that legal is high potential but is very slow to realize that potential," said Jason Winmill, managing partner of the Boston-based legal department consultancy Argopoint. He said the reasons for legal professionals' disappointment are varied. "Legal is not particularly agile with technology compared to other parts of the company. And they don't like to admit that, but it's true," Winmill said. "Second, they often lack expertise to implement new technologies. And there is often a standards problem and things need to be absolutely perfect or legal will use that as an excuse to resist change. Yes, work submitted to the court needs to meet high standards, but the majority of work going on in a legal department is not being submitted to courts." He drew the analogy to revolutionary technologies of the past that still haven't achieved perfect results. "If we're sitting around waiting for perfect cell reception in 100% of the country 100% of the time before we use mobile phones for work, then we're going to be sitting around for a long time." The survey comes as investment in AI is surging. Bain found that companies are spending an average of about $5 million annually on generative AI, with an average of 100 employees dedicating at least some of their time to working with the technology. About 20% of large companies are investing up to $50 million per year. "Overall, the results of our quarterly survey show that across industries, companies have high expectations for the value that generative AI can add to their businesses, and they are investing appropriately in talent and other resources," Bain said. "Some use cases are already showing more promise than others, and we expect executive teams to adjust their expectations (and their funding) as they learn more," the Bain report says, noting that tech companies "are further along in their development of generative AI use cases, and they may already have more realistic expectations." Mary O'Carroll, chief community officer at the contract management platform Ironclad, said she wasn't shocked by the findings, given that her company was founded by a former lawyer who was dissatisfied with the legal software on the market. "Lawyers have a high bar," she said. "I strongly believe that there's an amazing use case for AI here, and the bar hasn't been met by the crop of early stage startups that are trying to solve this." O'Carroll said while AI models are getting better, user expectations are rising at an even faster rate. "Sure, hallucinations have gotten better, but many people thought things would have changed faster than they have. We're in year two now. Year one was about convincing people that this is real and worth experimenting with. Year two is about looking for more use cases, demonstrative impact, and moving the usage up the value chain. We're very close to being there, but squarely still in the experimental mode." Bain's findings stand in sharp contrast with a widely touted Goldman Sachs study from last year that predicted AI could end up automating 44% of legal tasks in the United States. That led some observers to assume the technology eventually would replace lawyers altogether. That turned out not to be true, of course, and the consensus has become that generative AI will both automate routine tasks and help lawyers work more efficiently on complex matters. Goldman Sachs has since delved deeper into the subject, finding in a June 2024 report that AI investment has yielded little in the way of tangible results. "The promise of generative AI technology to transform companies, industries, and societies continues to be touted, leading tech giants, other companies, and utilities to spend an estimated—$1tn on capex in coming years, including significant investments in data centers, chips, other AI infrastructure and the power grid. But this spending has little to show for it so far beyond reports of efficiency gains among developers," the report says. Jim Covello, head of equity research at Goldman Sachs, said in the report that AI is too expensive to justify its cost. "AI bulls seem to just trust that use cases will proliferate as the technology evolves. But eighteen months after the introduction of generative AI to the world, not one truly transformative—let alone cost-effective—application has been found," he said. Covello said people generally overestimate the technology's capabilities. "In our experience, even basic summarization tasks often yield illegible and nonsensical results. This is not a matter of just some tweaks being required here and there; despite its expensive price tag, the technology is nowhere near where it needs to be in order to be useful for even such basic tasks," he said. Experts on the technology told Law.com that users could be setting themselves up for disappointment if they expect AI to deliver 100% hallucination-free results after less than two years on the market," "People overestimate what happens in one year and underestimate what can happen in 10 years. And I think we're right in the middle of that," he said. Even the technology's biggest advocates say users could be setting themselves up for disappointment if they expect AI to deliver 100% hallucination-free results after less than two years on the market. "People overestimate what happens in one year and underestimate what can happen in 10 years. And I think we're right in the middle of that," said Eddie Nasser, an attorney and head of legal product at legal research startup Paxton AI. Nasser said the Bain survey, conducted between October 2023 and February 2024, represents a "snapshot in time," one that reflects a growing awareness that any AI-driven transformation in the legal profession won't happen overnight. "I think it's natural to overestimate and expect right now a huge change that is very possibly going to come not in 18 months but more in the latter half of the decade," he said. Contacted by Law.com, a Bain spokesperson said the firm would not be able to answer further about the survey results or the makeup of the respondent pool. It's hard to analyze the Bain survey without knowing more about the methodology, but Nasser said it's likely that the results were drawn from Bain's client base. "It's important to note that in all likelihood their clients are going to be the biggest law firms, the biggest, most sophisticated legal departments doing the most complex, difficult, challenging, cutting-edge work. So it kind of makes sense where in those use cases where there is no right answer, where there is tremendous amounts of judgment involved, it might be more difficult to get high-level satisfaction among their users," Nasser said. Tanguy Chau, co-founder and CEO of Paxton AI, said he was surprised by the sentiments expressed in the Bain survey because they differ sharply from what his clients are saying. He said some of the dissatisfaction expressed in the survey may trace back to users turning to the wrong AI tools. "If you're limiting yourself to a generalized model, to something like Microsoft Copilot, it's not well designed to support legal use cases," he said. "What we're observing here is the transformation comes from new entrants, new players that are AI-native companies that are rethinking the entire stack, and are not just saying, 'Hey, we're going to put AI on top of our existing content.'" Fear of inaccurate outputs also looms large for many lawyers, including those surveyed by Bain, Abramowitz said. "I'm willing to bet their opinion is mostly formed about the story of the lawyer who was sanctioned for writing a brief using ChatGPT. I know many lawyers and every single one of them knows that story," he said. He said lawyers focusing too much on current outputs are missing the bigger picture. "My takeaway is that lawyers are likely being too monolithic in thinking about use cases like contract review and drafting instead of realizing that AI is incredibly powerful as a general purpose learning tool," Abramowitz said. "Lawyers might see their expectations met better by replacing Google with ChatGPT than replacing Microsoft Word with a gen AI legal tool. At the moment, there is increasing gulf between lawyers who are diving deeper into AI and those who are sitting on the sidelines, hoping this is all just a bunch of hype." article.title: An In-House Revolution: Early Adopters of AI Reduce 'Rote Tasks,' Spend More Time on Strategy
article.description: Early generative AI adopters have reached an epiphany: It's going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days.
article.text: Generative artificial intelligence is triggering a range of emotions in legal departments—from anxiety to exhilaration—but early adopters already have reached an epiphany: It's going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days. Whether they're the only lawyer at their company or part of a department of 1,000, in-house counsel are putting tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Bard to use for more than just drafting contracts and legal memos. They're using them to comb through vast repositories of data, summarize long, complicated legal documents and find opportunities to advance business. "I have AI going out there and looking for new revenue development possibilities," said Kelly Slavitt, general counsel and head of corporate development at Sikka.ai, a cloud platform that makes applications for the health care industry. "There are some of us who are using it to control costs and save time, but I believe there is also a way to drive revenue. … It takes away some of those rote tasks, so you can use your business and legal teams to push for revenue-driving strategies and find new space where you can innovate." In interviews with more than a dozen in-house attorneys and other legal and technology experts, Law.com found legal departments in a broad range of company sizes and industries have moved beyond experimenting with the technology to integrating it into their day-to-day processes. At startups, for instance, legal chiefs are using tools like ChatGPT to beef up their negotiation skills and spot potential snags in business deals and contracts. Large legal departments like Ford Motor Co.'s are finding generative AI tools boost productivity and reduce the time attorneys spend tracking down answers to questions. "We jokingly say, 'It's like having a really solid first-year sitting next to you working on things with you,'" said Darth Vaughn, litigation counsel and managing director of legal ops for the automaker. Vaughn added: "We haven't seen a practice area where we don't think this is applicable yet," Slavitt said she uses public AI tools like Claude and Bard to study business trends, research competitors and find potential business partners. "I can look into companies that we want to go into business with. I can go out there and say, 'Hey we have this new partnership with Wells Fargo. What else can we be doing to match their needs? What initiatives do they have going on? How can we partner with them? Getting AI to go out there and do that research is very useful." AI also has helped Sikka.ai's privacy officer and head of IT better protect customer data, Slavitt said. "It can go out and find publicly filed data breach notifications, and it aggregates it and saves me the research time," she said. "The value-add for me is helping me with my compliance program. I use it to see if there are any trends or mistakes that were made that are now being publicly reported. It can save me the time in going out there and finding what data breach notifications that were filed. AI can go out there and find that information for me and bring it back to me." Legal and technology experts say in-house attorneys who seize on the benefits of AI are making themselves more valuable, paving the way for advancement opportunities at their current employer or to stand out in applications for plum jobs elsewhere. "Once you learn as a general counsel or in-house lawyer how to leverage AI in the work you do day to day, you're putting yourself in the position to identify opportunities in the business itself," said Laura Safdie, general counsel at Casetext, whose AI tool Co-Counsel was built using OpenAI's platform. "We have several large companies we've worked with closely, and we saw a general counsel or an associate general counsel take this path where they're like, 'Here's a huge business problem, and I understand how to leverage this technology.' And it's putting them in a position to advise the business in a way that's more powerful and more value-creating than what they were able to do before." Safdie recently spoke with a general counsel who sends 100,000 contracts every year to India, where lawyers create a structured database by reading each one in full then tagging it. "He came to me and said, 'I don't need to do that anymore, do I?'' and I said, 'No you don't.'" AI-Driven Insights Because AI actually can reason and understand what users want to learn from large databases of content, "the amount of information and knowledge you can glean from these huge databases of unstructured data is so much higher than it ever was," Safdie said. "People used to rely on these very manual, resource-intensive approaches … and they're finding they don't need to do that." Generative AI—AI capable of generating text, images or other media—is a subset of AI that's been under development almost since the start of AI research in the 1950s. Despite those many decades of research, generative AI did not fully make its way into the public consciousness until San Francisco-based OpenAI dazzled the world by releasing ChatGPT in November 2022. Colin Levy, head of legal at contract-lifecycle-management firm Malbek, said that while he's been interested in artificial intelligence for a long time, advancements that make it practical for business leaders to use it to improve decision-making are relatively recent. He said he uses AI's ability to analyze and summarize data in a range of ways, "whether it be drafting brief and making it more likely probability-wise to succeed in court based on past cases and perhaps the judge who heard the case, or looking at prior case law and what have been effective arguments against what you were trying to argue for." He also uses AI to spot, outline and brainstorm ideas. For transactions, AI can look for problematic language in agreements or suggest language that can lead to a quicker negotiation. When he doesn't have time to read through an article, he just feeds it into the AI mode and it pulls out key points. For external tools, Levy said he's "a big fan" of Anthropic's Claude but sometimes uses ChatGPT, or Microsoft's Bing AI. "I pretty much use all of them for different purposes. Some are better than others with respect to certain tasks, but in general they're all on par with one another." Levy said some tools, including ChatGPT, "are more verbose and don't necessarily give you what you're looking for. Claude is more specific and restrained, and that's on purpose because it is supposed to be attuned to what you're looking for. That's an important consideration." Caution Reigns A recent study of 165 in-house lawyers by Lowenstein Sandler and the Association of Corporate Counsel found widespread enthusiasm for generative AI, with 62% of respondents seeing potential for increased productivity. Yet the findings also reflected a wariness, seemingly driven by a lack of knowledge. Just 36% of respondents have used generative AI for legal tasks, and 54% were aware of anyone in their legal department who had. Only 25% of respondents said they've received any training related to AI, and more than half said they don't have plans for such training. Given the scarcity of training, it is perhaps not surprising that 43% reported either no confidence or slight confidence in their understanding of the principles and mechanisms underlying generative AI models. Yaron Dori, a Covington & Burling partner who represents companies in technology, media and other industries, said many legal departments express trepidation as they approach him for guidance. "If I could characterize them broadly, they're approaching AI tools with some caution and asking for advice as to the best way to approach them," he said. "Typically, we offer a couple of key points that they need to understand: privacy and disclosure concerns, and concerns regarding the reliability of outputs. Because AI models have been built in large part on publicly accessible information, they have a flaw in that they sometimes can hallucinate, so the outputs aren't always reliable. For these reasons, most people with whom we speak are exercising caution." Mary Hildebrand, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler and chair of its privacy and cybersecurity practice, said she's seen an "enormous amount of caution" around generative AI since this summer, when a New York lawyer landed in headlines around the globe for submitting a ChatGPT-written brief that contained fake case citations. Lowenstein Sandler's survey ranked potential for inaccuracy highest among risks associated with generative AI (44%), That was followed by confidentiality/data breach concerns (32%) and lack of human understanding and context (10%). In-house attorneys using generative AI don't dismiss those concerns but say they aren't cause to avoid generative AI entirely. "I'm always concerned and thinking about the risks and ethics involved with using any type of technology solution but especially generative AI," said Levy, the head of legal at Malbek. "I already take the approach that, if I'm providing it with data, it's data I know is not confidential and wouldn't have a problem sharing on Twitter or LinkedIn or anywhere public at all. That allows me to use these tools more comfortably because I'm not putting myself or my company at risk." Slavitt said lawyers are researchers by trade and need to apply those skills—including ensuring they're asking the right questions and evaluating the credibility of their sources—when using generative AI. "To me the free version of these AI platforms is the same thing as Google—it's a place to start.," she said. Starting Small Hildebrand said some legal departments are potentially being held back by having to make the case to company leadership that generative AI tools are worth the investment, a restriction law firms may not have. "It's imperative for outside law firms, in terms of enhancing productivity and doing things more efficiently. To some extent, clients will expect us to adopt it," she said. The findings of an August LexisNexis study of 7,950 lawyers, law students and others in the U.S. and three other countries squares with that perception. Sixty percent of respondents agreed that they expect law firms to use cutting-edge technology like generative AI. Only 10% disagreed. Brandi Pack, an AI consultant with the legal ops advisory firm UpLevel Ops, said she saw hesitancy among corporate clients at the beginning of the year but has seen more interest the past four months. "We recommend that people start with gateway tools—general administrative and content-generation tools that are inexpensive and widely available and reside in programs like Microsoft Copilot, Firefly's meeting assistant and ChatGPT," she said. "These are things companies can use now without making a big legal tech investment." Despite growing interest, Pack said she thinks it will be a while before legal departments incorporate generative AI en masse. "We're making progress, but we're a year or two out from mass adoption," she said. "We're not seeing a lot of desire for adoption; we're seeing a desire for information right now." 'Get Your Hands Dirty' For Slavitt, who works for a tech startup, AI is second nature. "Sikka Software Corporation is an AI-driven company, and so using AI in the legal department is something we do regularly." It's even more valuable for a legal department of one. "We're a small startup and I'm probably using it more because we have such a lack of resources. Small companies are turning to it out of necessity," Slavitt said. Some big legal departments are counting on significant benefits from AI adoption, too. Meta chief legal officer Jennifer Newstead said the tech giant is partnering with AI legal tech firms on pilots to study how it can use AI more broadly in its operations. "We are thinking about it very actively. I want our department to be on the cutting edge of how the profession adapts to AI," she said. "I do think there is an expectation in the sector that we will find and gain efficiencies in our operations from AI." Newstead said Meta also is asking outside counsel about their plans to use AI, "not because we expect anything immediately to change but because we think they're all thinking about it and we can learn from them and they can see how we are using it." Ford's legal department has been tracking the return on investment for generative AI across all of its practice areas since September. Whitney Stefko Dover, associate director and senior counsel for legal operations, said the automaker has found generative AI most valuable for summarizing documents. "For any use case that has … voluminous amounts of documentation, we have been able to use large language models to go in and summarize that documentation and remove a significant amount of human time in that particular task," she said. Ford also has found strong ROI from using generative AI to review and analyze documents. Stefko Dover said the legal department hopes to "see the most evolution" in generative AI's ability to compare and spot differences between documents and reference materials—though it's seeing some benefits from applying the technology in that way. "It's the basic tasks that seem to scale across our different practice areas," Ford's Vaughn said of generative AI's potential. "If you're a commercial transactions attorney, you're analyzing documents and drafting and summarizing. If you're an intellectual property attorney, you're doing something similar." But AI adoption hasn't been hitch-free, Vaughn said. While some in-house counsel believe generative AI has transformed their professional lives, others "have struggled to figure out how it will improve what they're doing," he said. In some cases, he said, the problem is a gap in training. "Just like with everything else, there are people that are distrustful of the technology, and more cautious, and we certainly understand all of that. At the end of the day it's just another tool. And people need to be taught how to use tools and when it's appropriate to use certain tools for certain things." Vaughn advises in-house counsel to play around with the tools on their own, to get a sense of how they work. "In order to do the analysis, you have to be familiar enough with the technology. You're not going to know unless you start to get your hands dirty with it and understand what it can do, the benefits and the risks," he said. "If you simply wait, you may just be further behind."
