Vaughn added: "We haven't seen a practice area where we don't think this is applicable yet,"

Slavitt said she uses public AI tools like Claude and Bard to study business trends, research competitors and find potential business partners.

"I can look into companies that we want to go into business with. I can go out there and say, 'Hey we have this new partnership with Wells Fargo. What else can we be doing to match their needs? What initiatives do they have going on? How can we partner with them? Getting AI to go out there and do that research is very useful."

AI also has helped Sikka.ai's privacy officer and head of IT better protect customer data, Slavitt said. "It can go out and find publicly filed data breach notifications, and it aggregates it and saves me the research time," she said.

"The value-add for me is helping me with my compliance program. I use it to see if there are any trends or mistakes that were made that are now being publicly reported. It can save me the time in going out there and finding what data breach notifications that were filed. AI can go out there and find that information for me and bring it back to me."

Legal and technology experts say in-house attorneys who seize on the benefits of AI are making themselves more valuable, paving the way for advancement opportunities at their current employer or to stand out in applications for plum jobs elsewhere.

"Once you learn as a general counsel or in-house lawyer how to leverage AI in the work you do day to day, you're putting yourself in the position to identify opportunities in the business itself," said Laura Safdie, general counsel at Casetext, whose AI tool Co-Counsel was built using OpenAI's platform.

"We have several large companies we've worked with closely, and we saw a general counsel or an associate general counsel take this path where they're like, 'Here's a huge business problem, and I understand how to leverage this technology.' And it's putting them in a position to advise the business in a way that's more powerful and more value-creating than what they were able to do before."

Safdie recently spoke with a general counsel who sends 100,000 contracts every year to India, where lawyers create a structured database by reading each one in full then tagging it. "He came to me and said, 'I don't need to do that anymore, do I?'' and I said, 'No you don't.'"

AI-Driven Insights

Because AI actually can reason and understand what users want to learn from large databases of content, "the amount of information and knowledge you can glean from these huge databases of unstructured data is so much higher than it ever was," Safdie said. "People used to rely on these very manual, resource-intensive approaches … and they're finding they don't need to do that."

Generative AI—AI capable of generating text, images or other media—is a subset of AI that's been under development almost since the start of AI research in the 1950s. Despite those many decades of research, generative AI did not fully make its way into the public consciousness until San Francisco-based OpenAI dazzled the world by releasing ChatGPT in November 2022.

Colin Levy, head of legal at contract-lifecycle-management firm Malbek, said that while he's been interested in artificial intelligence for a long time, advancements that make it practical for business leaders to use it to improve decision-making are relatively recent.

He said he uses AI's ability to analyze and summarize data in a range of ways, "whether it be drafting brief and making it more likely probability-wise to succeed in court based on past cases and perhaps the judge who heard the case, or looking at prior case law and what have been effective arguments against what you were trying to argue for."

He also uses AI to spot, outline and brainstorm ideas. For transactions, AI can look for problematic language in agreements or suggest language that can lead to a quicker negotiation. When he doesn't have time to read through an article, he just feeds it into the AI mode and it pulls out key points.

For external tools, Levy said he's "a big fan" of Anthropic's Claude but sometimes uses ChatGPT, or Microsoft's Bing AI.

"I pretty much use all of them for different purposes. Some are better than others with respect to certain tasks, but in general they're all on par with one another."

Levy said some tools, including ChatGPT, "are more verbose and don't necessarily give you what you're looking for. Claude is more specific and restrained, and that's on purpose because it is supposed to be attuned to what you're looking for. That's an important consideration."

Caution Reigns

A recent study of 165 in-house lawyers by Lowenstein Sandler and the Association of Corporate Counsel found widespread enthusiasm for generative AI, with 62% of respondents seeing potential for increased productivity.

Yet the findings also reflected a wariness, seemingly driven by a lack of knowledge.

Just 36% of respondents have used generative AI for legal tasks, and 54% were aware of anyone in their legal department who had.

Only 25% of respondents said they've received any training related to AI, and more than half said they don't have plans for such training.

Given the scarcity of training, it is perhaps not surprising that 43% reported either no confidence or slight confidence in their understanding of the principles and mechanisms underlying generative AI models.

Yaron Dori, a Covington & Burling partner who represents companies in technology, media and other industries, said many legal departments express trepidation as they approach him for guidance.

"If I could characterize them broadly, they're approaching AI tools with some caution and asking for advice as to the best way to approach them," he said.

"Typically, we offer a couple of key points that they need to understand: privacy and disclosure concerns, and concerns regarding the reliability of outputs. Because AI models have been built in large part on publicly accessible information, they have a flaw in that they sometimes can hallucinate, so the outputs aren't always reliable. For these reasons, most people with whom we speak are exercising caution."

Mary Hildebrand, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler and chair of its privacy and cybersecurity practice, said she's seen an "enormous amount of caution" around generative AI since this summer, when a New York lawyer landed in headlines around the globe for submitting a ChatGPT-written brief that contained fake case citations.

Lowenstein Sandler's survey ranked potential for inaccuracy highest among risks associated with generative AI (44%), That was followed by confidentiality/data breach concerns (32%) and lack of human understanding and context (10%).

In-house attorneys using generative AI don't dismiss those concerns but say they aren't cause to avoid generative AI entirely.

"I'm always concerned and thinking about the risks and ethics involved with using any type of technology solution but especially generative AI," said Levy, the head of legal at Malbek.

"I already take the approach that, if I'm providing it with data, it's data I know is not confidential and wouldn't have a problem sharing on Twitter or LinkedIn or anywhere public at all. That allows me to use these tools more comfortably because I'm not putting myself or my company at risk."

Slavitt said lawyers are researchers by trade and need to apply those skills—including ensuring they're asking the right questions and evaluating the credibility of their sources—when using generative AI.

"To me the free version of these AI platforms is the same thing as Google—it's a place to start.," she said.

Starting Small

Hildebrand said some legal departments are potentially being held back by having to make the case to company leadership that generative AI tools are worth the investment, a restriction law firms may not have.

"It's imperative for outside law firms, in terms of enhancing productivity and doing things more efficiently. To some extent, clients will expect us to adopt it," she said.

The findings of an August LexisNexis study of 7,950 lawyers, law students and others in the U.S. and three other countries squares with that perception. Sixty percent of respondents agreed that they expect law firms to use cutting-edge technology like generative AI. Only 10% disagreed.

Brandi Pack, an AI consultant with the legal ops advisory firm UpLevel Ops, said she saw hesitancy among corporate clients at the beginning of the year but has seen more interest the past four months.

"We recommend that people start with gateway tools—general administrative and content-generation tools that are inexpensive and widely available and reside in programs like Microsoft Copilot, Firefly's meeting assistant and ChatGPT," she said. "These are things companies can use now without making a big legal tech investment."

Despite growing interest, Pack said she thinks it will be a while before legal departments incorporate generative AI en masse. "We're making progress, but we're a year or two out from mass adoption," she said. "We're not seeing a lot of desire for adoption; we're seeing a desire for information right now."

'Get Your Hands Dirty'

For Slavitt, who works for a tech startup, AI is second nature. "Sikka Software Corporation is an AI-driven company, and so using AI in the legal department is something we do regularly."

It's even more valuable for a legal department of one. "We're a small startup and I'm probably using it more because we have such a lack of resources. Small companies are turning to it out of necessity," Slavitt said.

Some big legal departments are counting on significant benefits from AI adoption, too.

Meta chief legal officer Jennifer Newstead said the tech giant is partnering with AI legal tech firms on pilots to study how it can use AI more broadly in its operations.

"We are thinking about it very actively. I want our department to be on the cutting edge of how the profession adapts to AI," she said. "I do think there is an expectation in the sector that we will find and gain efficiencies in our operations from AI."

Newstead said Meta also is asking outside counsel about their plans to use AI, "not because we expect anything immediately to change but because we think they're all thinking about it and we can learn from them and they can see how we are using it."

Ford's legal department has been tracking the return on investment for generative AI across all of its practice areas since September.

Whitney Stefko Dover, associate director and senior counsel for legal operations, said the automaker has found generative AI most valuable for summarizing documents.

"For any use case that has … voluminous amounts of documentation, we have been able to use large language models to go in and summarize that documentation and remove a significant amount of human time in that particular task," she said.

Ford also has found strong ROI from using generative AI to review and analyze documents. Stefko Dover said the legal department hopes to "see the most evolution" in generative AI's ability to compare and spot differences between documents and reference materials—though it's seeing some benefits from applying the technology in that way.

"It's the basic tasks that seem to scale across our different practice areas," Ford's Vaughn said of generative AI's potential. "If you're a commercial transactions attorney, you're analyzing documents and drafting and summarizing. If you're an intellectual property attorney, you're doing something similar."

But AI adoption hasn't been hitch-free, Vaughn said.

While some in-house counsel believe generative AI has transformed their professional lives, others "have struggled to figure out how it will improve what they're doing," he said.

In some cases, he said, the problem is a gap in training. "Just like with everything else, there are people that are distrustful of the technology, and more cautious, and we certainly understand all of that. At the end of the day it's just another tool. And people need to be taught how to use tools and when it's appropriate to use certain tools for certain things."

Vaughn advises in-house counsel to play around with the tools on their own, to get a sense of how they work.

"In order to do the analysis, you have to be familiar enough with the technology. You're not going to know unless you start to get your hands dirty with it and understand what it can do, the benefits and the risks," he said. "If you simply wait, you may just be further behind."

article.title: Quantum Computing Company to Part With General Counsel
article.description: Rick Danis joined Rigetti in 2019 after a little more than a year at satellite antenna company Kymeta.
article.text: Rigetti Computing, a Berkeley, California-based designer and maker of quantum computers, is saying goodbye to Rick Danis, its general counsel of five years. Danis informed the company last week that he plans to resign on Nov. 30, Rigetti announced in a securities filing. Danis joined Rigetti in 2019 after a little more than a year at satellite antenna company Kymeta. He also held leading in-house roles at Nokia, Yahoo, media company Leaf Group, and domain name provider Rightside Group, which he helped sell to the domain name registry Donuts for $213 million in 2017. Rigetti did not respond to an inquiry from Law.com about the reasoning behind his resignation. In a LinkedIn message, Danis said he is "moving on to another great opportunity," adding, "I have nothing but good things to say about Rigetti and will be a strong supporter of the company going forward." The company’s 8-K Securities and Exchange Commission filing says he will act as a consultant for the company through March 31, 2025. Founded in 2013 by a former IBM physicist, Rigetti Computing specializes in building quantum processors and the software necessary to harness quantum computing, an advanced area of computing that uses quantum mechanics to solve complex problems beyond the capacity of classical computers. It specializes in developing quantum processors and the software necessary to harness quantum computing for practical applications, helping scientists and engineers work on issues like climate change, drug development and discovery and artificial intelligence. Last year, it released its first commercially available quantum processing unit called Novera, designed to provide researchers and developers with hands-on access to advanced quantum computing technology. It also offers a cloud services platform that allows users to integrate Rigetti's quantum machines into any cloud environment. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. article.title: SEC Under Trump 2.0 Likely to Take More 'Measured' Enforcement Approach, Observers Say
article.description: "While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates.
article.text: "While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates. 5 minute read Financial Services and Banking The original version of this story was published on Corporate Counsel Donald Trump's reclaiming of the White House could spell the end of one of the most aggressive SEC rulemaking and enforcement regimes in history. Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority and more concerned with issues affecting Main Street and everyday retail investors. "We've already seen what the SEC in a Trump 1.0 administration looked like, where the SEC focused on bread-and-butter cases focused on addressing harm to retail investors, such as offering frauds, Ponzi schemes and excessive fees charged by investment advisory firms," said Jennifer Lee, a Jenner & Block partner who formerly spent 12 years with the SEC, rising to assistant regional director of its enforcement division. By contrast, the SEC under current Chair Gary Gensler has been more willing to bring individual compliance cases against public companies and investment firms it regulates, even if there is no investor harm," she said. In his three years as chair, Gensler has steered the commission into uncharted territory, pushing initiatives on climate change disclosure, environmental, social and governance investing and corporate greenwashing. Preemptive compliance measures were at the center of Gensler's ambitious regulatory agenda. Observers said he wanted to get ahead of issues that, if left unchecked, could lead to greater fraud or investor harm down the road. To that end, the commission expanded its authority into policing data-security incidents and cyber-risk disclosures, greenhouse gas emission reporting and regulating the use of AI and other types of predictive analytics by broker-dealers and investment advisers. "The SEC under Chair Gensler has been aggressive in terms of really putting in prospective requirements in emerging substance areas like cybersecurity, ESG and also AI," Lee said. She expects that, under the Trump administration, the SEC will likely pull back on rulemaking and adopt a less stringent stance on enforcement, particularly when it comes to pushing the bounds of existing rules. Trump already has vowed to fire Gensler "on day one" and appoint a replacement. One credible successor is Robinhood Chief Legal, Compliance and Corporate Affairs Officer Dan Gallagher, who was an SEC commissioner from 2011 to 2015, according to people familiar with the discussions, Also well-respected in the legal community and a potential to successor are Hester Pierce, who has been a Republican GOP commissioner since 2017 and is known for her incisive dissents, and Chris Giancarlo, a former chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, who is now a partner at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Legal observers say that, under a new chair, the SEC likely will abandon ESG rulemaking and will stop trying to implement its new rule requiring public companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions. That rule is on holding amid challenges by industry groups and Republican-run states. Novel legal theories also likely will be out, including its controversial push to apply internal accounting controls to cybersecurity, legal observers said. In July, a federal judge sided with software firm SolarWinds on the question of whether the provisions of the the Securities Exchange Act that give the SEC authority to regulate accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls. The judge "resoundingly rejected" that premise, finding that the SEC was overreaching. Aravind Swaminathan, a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, told Law.com at the time. Lee said the SEC under its next chair will be less likely to test its legal boundaries. "There will be more of a hewing to tried and true legal theories," she said. "The SEC under Trump will generally be more skeptical of novel theories in enforcement actions. The posture will also matter—the SEC may be more open to novel theories that will be litigated before a court or tried in front of a jury, versus theories that companies may feel they have to settle just to move on from an issue." She also anticipates that the SEC will be less exacting in its demands around cyber-incident disclosures and will shy away from bringing enforcement actions in instances where regulatory violations may have occurred but there is no evidence of consumers being harmed. Last month, the commission fined four companies that it said downplayed intrusions into their systems and misled investors about their cybersecurity risks, an action that brought a strong dissent from Pierce and fellow GOP commissioner Mark Uyeda. Lee said that, in the future, the SEC might not require minute details like the identity of a threat actor or the percentage of data exfiltrated from a company's systems, issues that came into play in its enforcement action against the four companies. Instead, she and other attorneys expect the SEC's focus to shift back to staple issues like retail fraud, calculation of fees and conflicts of interest associated with financial incentives, as well as ensuring that firms aren't misrepresenting themselves to consumers. "While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates and member of its asset management and investment funds practice. "Ultimately what the SEC's priorities are is going to depend on the new chair, but I would expect that their approach to rulemaking and enforcement would be more consistent with what we saw during the first Trump administration." article.html:
"While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates.

5 minute read

Financial Services and Banking

The original version of this story was published on Corporate Counsel


Donald Trump's reclaiming of the White House could spell the end of one of the most aggressive SEC rulemaking and enforcement regimes in history.

Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority and more concerned with issues affecting Main Street and everyday retail investors.

"We've already seen what the SEC in a Trump 1.0 administration looked like, where the SEC focused on bread-and-butter cases focused on addressing harm to retail investors, such as offering frauds, Ponzi schemes and excessive fees charged by investment advisory firms," said Jennifer Lee, a Jenner & Block partner who formerly spent 12 years with the SEC, rising to assistant regional director of its enforcement division.

By contrast, the SEC under current Chair Gary Gensler has been more willing to bring individual compliance cases against public companies and investment firms it regulates, even if there is no investor harm," she said.

In his three years as chair, Gensler has steered the commission into uncharted territory, pushing initiatives on climate change disclosure, environmental, social and governance investing and corporate greenwashing.

Preemptive compliance measures were at the center of Gensler's ambitious regulatory agenda. Observers said he wanted to get ahead of issues that, if left unchecked, could lead to greater fraud or investor harm down the road.

To that end, the commission expanded its authority into policing data-security incidents and cyber-risk disclosures, greenhouse gas emission reporting and regulating the use of AI and other types of predictive analytics by broker-dealers and investment advisers.

"The SEC under Chair Gensler has been aggressive in terms of really putting in prospective requirements in emerging substance areas like cybersecurity, ESG and also AI," Lee said. She expects that, under the Trump administration, the SEC will likely pull back on rulemaking and adopt a less stringent stance on enforcement, particularly when it comes to pushing the bounds of existing rules.

Trump already has vowed to fire Gensler "on day one" and appoint a replacement. One credible successor is Robinhood Chief Legal, Compliance and Corporate Affairs Officer Dan Gallagher, who was an SEC commissioner from 2011 to 2015, according to people familiar with the discussions,

Also well-respected in the legal community and a potential to successor are Hester Pierce, who has been a Republican GOP commissioner since 2017 and is known for her incisive dissents, and Chris Giancarlo, a former chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, who is now a partner at Willkie Farr & Gallagher.

Legal observers say that, under a new chair, the SEC likely will abandon ESG rulemaking and will stop trying to implement its new rule requiring public companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions. That rule is on holding amid challenges by industry groups and Republican-run states.

Novel legal theories also likely will be out, including its controversial push to apply internal accounting controls to cybersecurity, legal observers said.

In July, a federal judge sided with software firm SolarWinds on the question of whether the provisions of the the Securities Exchange Act that give the SEC authority to regulate accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls. The judge "resoundingly rejected" that premise, finding that the SEC was overreaching. Aravind Swaminathan, a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, told Law.com at the time.

Lee said the SEC under its next chair will be less likely to test its legal boundaries.

"There will be more of a hewing to tried and true legal theories," she said. "The SEC under Trump will generally be more skeptical of novel theories in enforcement actions. The posture will also matter—the SEC may be more open to novel theories that will be litigated before a court or tried in front of a jury, versus theories that companies may feel they have to settle just to move on from an issue."

She also anticipates that the SEC will be less exacting in its demands around cyber-incident disclosures and will shy away from bringing enforcement actions in instances where regulatory violations may have occurred but there is no evidence of consumers being harmed.

Last month, the commission fined four companies that it said downplayed intrusions into their systems and misled investors about their cybersecurity risks, an action that brought a strong dissent from Pierce and fellow GOP commissioner Mark Uyeda.

Lee said that, in the future, the SEC might not require minute details like the identity of a threat actor or the percentage of data exfiltrated from a company's systems, issues that came into play in its enforcement action against the four companies.

Instead, she and other attorneys expect the SEC's focus to shift back to staple issues like retail fraud, calculation of fees and conflicts of interest associated with financial incentives, as well as ensuring that firms aren't misrepresenting themselves to consumers.

"While the issues of what's in the best interest of an investor will continue to be important, we won't see as much energy put behind trying to expand those obligations beyond the regulatory frameworks that already exist," said Jennifer Klass, a partner at K&L Gates and member of its asset management and investment funds practice.

"Ultimately what the SEC's priorities are is going to depend on the new chair, but I would expect that their approach to rulemaking and enforcement would be more consistent with what we saw during the first Trump administration."

article.title: Microsoft's Banner Year Pushed Brad Smith's Pay Sharply Higher
article.description: The company racked up lots of wins in the fiscal year that ended June 30, including completing its largest acquisition ever, the $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard—a deal Smith pushed across the finish line in October.
article.text: Who Got The Work Michael G. Bongiorno, Andrew Scott Dulberg and Elizabeth E. Driscoll from Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr have stepped in to represent Symbotic Inc., an A.I.-enabled technology platform that focuses on increasing supply chain efficiency, and other defendants in a pending shareholder derivative lawsuit. The case, filed Oct. 2 in Massachusetts District Court by the Brown Law Firm on behalf of Stephen Austen, accuses certain officers and directors of misleading investors in regard to Symbotic's potential for margin growth by failing to disclose that the company was not equipped to timely deploy its systems or manage expenses through project delays. The case, assigned to U.S. District Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, is 1:24-cv-12522, Austen v. Cohen et al. Read More Who Got The Work Edmund Polubinski and Marie Killmond of Davis Polk & Wardwell have entered appearances for data platform software development company MongoDB and other defendants in a pending shareholder derivative lawsuit. The action, filed Oct. 7 in New York Southern District Court by the Brown Law Firm, accuses the company's directors and/or officers of falsely expressing confidence in the company’s restructuring of its sales incentive plan and downplaying the severity of decreases in its upfront commitments. The case is 1:24-cv-07594, Roy v. Ittycheria et al. Read More Who Got The Work Amy O. Bruchs and Kurt F. Ellison of Michael Best & Friedrich have entered appearances for Epic Systems Corp. in a pending employment discrimination lawsuit. The suit was filed Sept. 7 in Wisconsin Western District Court by Levine Eisberner LLC and Siri & Glimstad on behalf of a project manager who claims that he was wrongfully terminated after applying for a religious exemption to the defendant's COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The case, assigned to U.S. Magistrate Judge Anita Marie Boor, is 3:24-cv-00630, Secker, Nathan v. Epic Systems Corporation. Read More Who Got The Work David X. Sullivan, Thomas J. Finn and Gregory A. Hall from McCarter & English have entered appearances for Sunrun Installation Services in a pending civil rights lawsuit. The complaint was filed Sept. 4 in Connecticut District Court by attorney Robert M. Berke on behalf of former employee George Edward Steins, who was arrested and charged with employing an unregistered home improvement salesperson. The complaint alleges that had Sunrun informed the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection that the plaintiff's employment had ended in 2017 and that he no longer held Sunrun's home improvement contractor license, he would not have been hit with charges, which were dismissed in May 2024. The case, assigned to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey A. Meyer, is 3:24-cv-01423, Steins v. Sunrun, Inc. et al. Read More Who Got The Work Greenberg Traurig shareholder Joshua L. Raskin has entered an appearance for boohoo.com UK Ltd. in a pending patent infringement lawsuit. The suit, filed Sept. 3 in Texas Eastern District Court by Rozier Hardt McDonough on behalf of Alto Dynamics, asserts five patents related to an online shopping platform. The case, assigned to U.S. District Judge Rodney Gilstrap, is 2:24-cv-00719, Alto Dynamics, LLC v. boohoo.com UK Limited.

article.title: GCs Face Peril as Foreign Bribery Probes Second-Guess 'Routine' Advice
article.description: Federal enforcement agencies are prowling for instances of bribery and corruption around the world—scrutiny that can put general counsel in peril, even those who believe they've stayed on the right side of the law as they navigate the inevitable gray…
article.text: Federal enforcement agencies are prowling for instances of bribery and corruption around the world—scrutiny that can put general counsel in peril, even those who believe they've stayed on the right side of the law as they navigate the inevitable gray zones that come along. October 10, 2024 at 03:26 PM 12 minute read Foreign Corrupt Practices Act By Maria Dinzeo Federal enforcement agencies are prowling for instances of bribery and corruption around the world—scrutiny that can put general counsel in peril, even those who believe they've stayed on the right side of the law as they navigate the inevitable gray zones that come along. Many countries where American companies do business have an array of business practices and customs that might be frowned upon in this country, but whether they cross the sometimes-blurry lines of legality isn't always clear. The club enforcers wield is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, a 1977 law that bars companies from providing anything of value to foreign officials to gain a business advantage. "The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act is a tricky issue because it's omnipresent and business practices are different in different areas," said Laura Schumacher, the former chief legal officer at Abbvie. But it is the general counsel's duty to ensure that their company is operating responsibly, even in jurisdictions where payments to foreign officials might be expected. Executives are also navigating a landscape fraught with personal risk as the Justice Department steps up its whistleblower and self-reporting incentives. Legal chiefs in particular could find themselves facing unexpected scrutiny over what may seem like routine advice, and they could become potential targets of federal enforcement agencies bent on holding individuals accountable for misconduct. The high-profile prosecution of an ousted legal chief at a large tech company highlights the growing risk of personal liability over legal and business advice given years after the fact. For the last five years, Steven Schwartz has been awaiting trial on charges of violating FCPA, conspiracy, falsifying books and records, and circumventing and failing to implement internal accounting controls. He stands accused of authorizing a contractor to bribe foreign government officials in India. If convicted, he faces 180 years in prison. His indictment dates back to 2019, but the facts of the case go back even further. Schwartz was chief legal officer at Cognizant, a giant tech firm headquartered in New Jersey but with significant operations in India, including half of its 250,000 global workforce. One of its specialties is building call centers, and in 2014, Cognizant had a major project in the works in Chennai. The company had hired an Indian multinational construction firm, Larsen and Toubro, to build the 2.7-million-square-foot campus, a job that included securing the necessary permits. In April 2014, Schwartz was pulled into two videoconference calls with his co-defendant, former Cognizant president Gordon Coburn. It was on those calls, the government claims, that the pair authorized L&T to pay $2 million to an Indian government official who had demanded payment in exchange for a planning permit that would help keep the project on track. L&T allegedly asked to be reimbursed the money, and Coburn and Schwartz "agreed that cognizant would reimburse the construction company for the bribe payment through a change order request at the end of the project." According to the indictment, Schwartz agreed that this approach was acceptable "but cautioned that the reimbursement payment should not stand out in the change order request." The government was turned on to the allegations after Cognizant self-reported the incident following an internal investigation led by DLA Piper in 2016. The company ended up paying a total of $28 million in disgorgement and penalties to the DOJ and Securities & Exchange Commission in 2019 but received a nonprosecution agreement in exchange for its cooperation. The trial has been delayed multiple times due to difficulties in getting India to cooperate with the defense's effort to depose L&T executives, including CEO Sekharipuram Narayanan Subrahmanyan, who at the time was head of L&T's real estate division, was involved in the Chennai project and is under investigation in India for corruption. A new trial date has been set for March 2025, to "preserve the integrity of the truth seeking process," says an order by U.S. District Judge Michael Farbiarz, who took over the case from retiring U.S. District Judge Kevin McNulty in October 2023. It's difficult to speculate without more specifics about how the call went down, in-house and outside counsel experts say. But while a general counsel can be pulled into calls and asked for quick legal advice on a contract they've not seen before, it's rare for a general counsel to be asked to make a quick judgment call on the fly about approving payments to foreign officials through intermediaries and even more rare for a general counsel to agree to answer such a question on the spot. In short, there's no such thing as "routine" legal advice when it comes to the FCPA. "My antenna is instantly going up," said Sterling Miller, three-time general counsel turned CEO and senior counsel at Hilgers Graben. "Assuming it was presented like, 'Hey we need to authorize a payment to an official to get a permit,' the first thing I'd be asking is, 'Why are you looping in the legal department on paying for a permit?' I'd be thinking, 'Why am I being asked to weigh in on this?"' Schumacher, who spent decades at the legal helm of heavily regulated global companies, said every issue depends on facts, circumstances and context. "Being called in at the last minute to give an opinion is not an uncommon thing, but what is uncommon is giving an opinion without understanding the facts and circumstances," she said. "What the GC would do is say, 'I need to speak with the businesspeople on the ground and understand what that contract is and what that payment is.' To give advice on the fly when you're dealing with international issues and FCPA, the ramifications are so significant for the individual and the organization just saying ok would not be an appropriate response." Any payment demand from an overseas official could be a potential FCPA issue. Former FCPA prosecutor Eric Beste, now a partner at Barnes & Thornburg in San Diego, said it's best to check in with multiple sources on the ground, and preferably someone who doesn't have a stake in the business deal. "As a general counsel or a chief compliance officer in the U.S., the key is you really want to look for as many facts as you can get from the local jurisdiction as possible and not just rely on one person's characterization," he said. "There are 150 countries and 150 different systems. Sometimes it's broken down by province or region and there are an infinite number of permutations around this. Rely on people on the ground that you trust in that jurisdiction or multiple sources of information so you can check what you're being told," Beste said. General counsel and compliance officers at global companies to be keenly aware of the risk factors in the countries where they operate and to stay alert in high-risk jurisdictions. India remains a fairly high-risk region for compliance under the FCPA, particularly due to ongoing issues with corruption, bureaucracy, and reliance on third-party intermediaries. Trace International gives it a score of 55 putting it at 122 out of 194 countries for bribery risk. In contrast, the United States ranks at number 12, while North Korea is at 194. The least risky country? Norway with a score of 5. Snežana Gebauer, a partner at the consulting and investigations firm StoneTurn, said legal chiefs should be especially cautious around things like facilitation and commissions. "They are two of the most common types of bribery payments, along with consulting fees for generalized consulting services. While facilitation payments are allowed in certain countries, in many others they are illegal. It's not always easy to identify a questionable payment or to decide whether a questionable payment is a bribe," she said. Gebauer, who has a long history of leading complicated cross-border investigations into corruption, fraud, embezzlement and misconduct, said she has seen several instances where payments are approved without being sufficiently scrutinized. "In one case a compliance officer questioned the business unit that requested a payment, and was provided with a facially sufficient justification. Because the compliance officer was satisfied with the explanation, they approved the payment," she said. "Later, an investigation by the authorities questioned the payment as a kickback." Gebauer said the compliance officer failed to conduct appropriate due diligence on the third party recipient of the payment, which would have surfaced recent information about their integrity. One can never be too cautious when working with third-parties, she warned. "Fortunately, there are different controls that can be implemented to detect and prevent fraudulent payments. Companies operating in high-risk markets should have a well-developed anti-bribery and corruption framework. Conducting thorough due diligence on third parties, intermediaries and business partners is critically important," Gebauer said. "Very often, companies don't even realize that they are interacting with state-owned entities or third-party intermediaries with links to local government. In these situations, a company may be paying a commission to an individual that is actually a government official," she says. Miller said companies need to "have a fairly rigorous process" for vetting their third-party vendors. "Most embassies in these foreign countries that deal with business relationships on the ground for American companies will tell you what you think they could be helpful to you." Gebauer said the GC's role has changed in recent years. "They're increasingly acting as trusted advisers to their CEOs who bring them into meetings and want their seal of approval, verbal or otherwise. Accordingly, they need to be cautious and not rush into decisions. It's easy to say yes if you don't have enough facts, so it's really important to take a step back and say, 'I need some time to vet this. I'll get back to you after a proper review.'" Schwartz's defense is expected to argue that, as the legal chief of a giant tech and consulting firm, he didn't regularly manage the minutiae of real estate deals. He was brought on the call to provide textbook legal advice about a "turnkey" contract where L&T was responsible for everything, including navigating local laws and regulations. He certainly didn't condone bribery. L&T, for its part, has flatly denied bribing anyone, or soliciting reimbursement of a bribe from Cognizant. Miller said that a turnkey contract in the U.S. "wouldn't concern me, but if I'm in a foreign country that is potentially problematic. What I need to make sure of is what agreements do we have in place with these intermediaries because you are on the hook for anything the intermediary does on your behalf." The DOJ has been encouraging companies for years to self-disclose instances of foreign corruption and bribery. Since 2016, the DOJ has increasingly pushed for self-disclosure and full cooperation, giving companies credit and leniency in return, and in fact, Cognizant had asked through its attorneys to be included in the agency's newly launched FCPA pilot program back in 2016. The DOJ announced in 2019 that it declined to prosecute Cognizant for FCPA violations in part because it had self-disclosed and cooperated fully with the government. In a ruling last year, McNulty found Cognizant "made an independent decision to conduct an internal investigation," and while it desired leniency under the FCPA pilot program it "did not act at the government's direction." Beste, whose practice focuses on white collar criminal defense, compliance and internal investigations, said the government generally wants companies to self-report because it lacks the resources to investigate every possible instance of wrongdoing. "They're just trying to incentivize companies to have a culture where we just don't do this kind of stuff," he said. Deciding whether to self-disclose can be a fraught process. "In general companies are rightly concerned about self disclosure and is it really worth it," Beste said. "Very often a company will tell the department [DOJ], "'Here is one payment to one third-party consultant,' and you can pretty much guarantee that, in response, the government is going to say, 'What is your compliance structure around payments to all third-party consultants, and do you actually follow that procedure?'" "So all of a sudden what was one payment then turns into all payments to all third-party consultants. The company as an entity is then worse off than if it just handled it. But on the flip side, if you can fix it on your own, great, but the risk you run is that someone in the organization is going to go to the DOJ and then you're stuck and you don't get full credit for not self-disclosing, and you lose the ability to craft the message to the department." With the caveat that he is not commenting on the Schwartz case and doesn't know what evidence will be prevented at trial, Beste said the DOJ has generally made a lot of statements about wanting to empower chief compliance officers and general counsel. "When they prosecute GCs and CCOs for corrupt payments it could send the contrary message. But the DOJ looks at every case on its own facts. They would push back on the concept that every GC is potentially at risk." Schumacher said a good chief legal officer wouldn't be too worried about his or her own personal liability. "A good chief legal officer should always be doing the right thing for the company and not worry necessarily about their personal liability, because at the end of the day they will insulate themselves from personal liability" by doing the right thing. "Approaching a decision-making set by only thinking about your own personal profile or liability is not thinking about your client first."

article.title: When Law Firms Get Hacked, Are Their Corporate Clients on the Hook?
article.description: Analysis "Law firms are being heavily targeted now because they have a lot of sensitive information and they need to operate," said Brian Levine, managing director of Ernst & Young's cybersecurity and data privacy practice. 8 minute read…
article.text: October 15, 2024 at 03:37 PM 8 minute read Cybersecurity By Maria Dinzeo Cyber criminals are giving corporate litigation departments yet another reason to worry—that organizations could be on the hook for their law firms' data breaches. Global snack food conglomerate Mondelez found this out the hard way when it was sued over a data breach suffered by its law firm, Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, in 2023. The plaintiffs, a proposed class of 1,100 current and former Mondelez employees, argued that the company had not properly protected their sensitive data by ensuring that Bryan Cave had "reasonable cybersecurity procedures" in place when intruders accessed its systems in February 2023, "including an area it used to store certain customer files." During the intrusion, which ran through March 1, 2023, hackers made off with a host of personal and financial data from Mondelez employees, including names, addresses, birthdates and Social Security numbers, as well as employment identification numbers and retirement plan information. Mondelez initially fought to have the case dismissed, arguing that it didn't have a duty to make sure that its law firm had adequate security, and it shouldn't be held accountable for a breach that didn't involve its own systems. U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso of the Northern District of Illinois summed it up nicely: "Bryan Cave's information systems, not Mondelez's, were hacked, and Mondelez argues that there are no plausible allegations to support the claim that Mondelez should be held responsible for a breach not of its own systems, but Bryan Cave's." Alonso noted that neither side pointed to any previous cases where judges have directly tackled this theory in a similar situation, let alone decided for or against it. But rather than dismiss the claim, Alonso adopted a "let's see where this goes" approach, ruling, "To the extent that there is little precedent to guide the parties and the court as to plaintiffs' precise legal theory, there is all the more reason to develop the facts first, rather than to hastily proceed to a dispositive ruling." But that wasn't to be. Mondelez quickly settled with the plaintiffs a few months later for $750,000. This comes at a time of skyrocketing data breaches targeting the world's most prominent law firms. Brian Levine, managing director of Ernst & Young's cybersecurity and data privacy practice, said firms are attractive targets for breaches because they are a central repository of lucrative, non-public information. Their bill-by-the-hour revenue model also opens them up to ransomware gangs looking to exploit any shutdown in operations. "Law firms are being heavily targeted now because they have a lot of sensitive information and they need to operate. So from a ransomware perspective, law firms work on the billable hour. If their employees can't do their job and if their attorneys can't do their job, they're not earning revenue. But even more importantly, a high percentage of their documents are attorney-client privileged or confidential. They may contain trade secrets that are pre-patent. They may contain merger plans, acquisition plans, strategic plans that bad guys have actually taken—not to do ransomware or hurt the firm—but to trade on," he said. Law firms are also not specifically attuned to implementing sophisticated cybersecurity policies, procedures, and controls. "One sort of universal vulnerability that I would say probably applies to law firms different from other industry verticals, it probably has to be a sort of relative lack of security governance maturity," said Jack Freund, chief risk officer for cyber-risk-quantification platform Kovrr. Even with great security, attackers will always look for the easiest method of intrusion. Reused passwords, phishing emails, "very basic, stupid ways," Freund said. Hackers are also looking to exploit security flaws in software and products that "are in the wild" exist but haven't been fixed yet. "You can have very sophisticated security controls, but if you're leaving the back door open, well I'll just walk right in. And that tends to be the way a lot of security hackers tend to target," he said. And the amount of vulnerable is growing with the use of AI. "It's going to encourage organizations to record more, to save more. And then we come back to that data retention issue again," Freund said. "So when the pile of potentially explosive information becomes more interesting and larger, then you're going to see more attackers going after it." But why should a law firm's data retention policies be their client's problem? Because if that data gets out, they're going after the entity they entrusted it to in the first place. "If you do business with a company and you give them your personal identifying information, and the information gets out there, you don't really care as the consumer who did business with the company, whether the company lost it itself, or whether they gave it to a third party and that third party lost it," Levine said. While there are legitimate reasons for sharing personally identifiable information with law firms, companies are ultimately responsible for what happens to it. "You can't outsource duty of care," said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio. "The fact that they're sharing that information with their law firm does not in any way, shape or form obviate that duty. Worst-case situation, if the law firm goes kaput, even if the enterprise didn't do anything wrong, they're still on the hook." But even while experts say perfect security does not exist, there are still affirmative steps companies can take to put them on more secure footing with their firms. "First of all, what you don't do is assume that this is an internationally recognized law firm that deals with the most sensitive information so I don't have to even ask the question, because they must have great security," Levine said, something he hears all the time in his job evaluating the security of organizations. "One of the things I always ask is about their third-party risk management, and quite frequently their answer is, 'We only do business with vendors like Microsoft and AWS and very large companies that surely have good programs, so we don't need to look into it.' Well, we all know what happens when you assume." What you should assume is that something will probably go wrong at some point. "Nothing's perfect, and no organization is impenetrable. You have to assume that somebody that you're going to give data to is going to have an event at some point," Kannry said. "That doesn't mean that there aren't things that can't be done in terms of contractual indemnifications and limitations of liability. That enterprise ought to make sure that If that happens, they have indemnity protections from the law firm, meaning that the law firm minimally pays the bills or the costs associated with the event. It could mean that the enterprise takes extra steps to ensure that if the law firm can't fulfill that indemnity or that responsibility, that the enterprise's insurance provider would still pay those costs." Data minimization is equally important. Levine said in-house should figure out what employee information their outside counsel specifically needs, and just provide that. "They need to talk to the attorney about what information they need about each of these people? Do you actually need their Social Security number? Do you actually need their date of birth? "You know, do you need their home address, or do you just need their name and title? And then you have to make it clear to your IT person or whoever is going to actually send over the information that they just need their name and title." "Please don't send everything else over as well. Because it's always going to be easier for someone to send over the file as it currently exists, which probably has everything in it, then to create another file, delete all the unused data and just send that over in a protected form," Levine said, noting that it may involve an extra step, but it's an important one. And finally, heavily scrutinize your outside counsel's data security practices. "There is a burgeoning industry of security ratings companies out there," Freund said. It can also mean having a tough conversation with your firm about their cybersecurity, Levine said, but don't let that intimidate you. "You can't let the awkwardness of the potential question prevent you from asking it," he said. This doesn't mean sitting down with the litigation partner handling your matters. "Any large organization, law firm or otherwise, is going to have somebody who's in charge of just handling those inquiries, and they will have all their security information that the company is comfortable sharing. They're going to have all the evidence," Levine said. "What you're asking is not, 'Mr. Partner of the law firm who focuses on tax, can you tell me about your security?' You're really asking, 'Can you get me a conversation with the person who demonstrates security for your organization so that I can connect them with my security person?' When it comes to third-party risk management, law firms can get left off the list because in-house counsel don't put them in the same category as vendors. "Maybe it's because of the close, confidential relationship where they feel more like they're part of the team. Maybe it feels like they're just giving advice, which is super valuable," Levine said. "But whoever is thinking about third-party risk management for the organization should be including law firms in that program."
article.html:
October 15, 2024 at 03:37 PM


8 minute read

Cybersecurity


By Maria Dinzeo



Cyber criminals are giving corporate litigation departments yet another reason to worry—that organizations could be on the hook for their law firms' data breaches.

Global snack food conglomerate Mondelez found this out the hard way when it was sued over a data breach suffered by its law firm, Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, in 2023. The plaintiffs, a proposed class of 1,100 current and former Mondelez employees, argued that the company had not properly protected their sensitive data by ensuring that Bryan Cave had "reasonable cybersecurity procedures" in place when intruders accessed its systems in February 2023, "including an area it used to store certain customer files."

During the intrusion, which ran through March 1, 2023, hackers made off with a host of personal and financial data from Mondelez employees, including names, addresses, birthdates and Social Security numbers, as well as employment identification numbers and retirement plan information.

Mondelez initially fought to have the case dismissed, arguing that it didn't have a duty to make sure that its law firm had adequate security, and it shouldn't be held accountable for a breach that didn't involve its own systems.

U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso of the Northern District of Illinois summed it up nicely: "Bryan Cave's information systems, not Mondelez's, were hacked, and Mondelez argues that there are no plausible allegations to support the claim that Mondelez should be held responsible for a breach not of its own systems, but Bryan Cave's."

Alonso noted that neither side pointed to any previous cases where judges have directly tackled this theory in a similar situation, let alone decided for or against it. But rather than dismiss the claim, Alonso adopted a "let's see where this goes" approach, ruling, "To the extent that there is little precedent to guide the parties and the court as to plaintiffs' precise legal theory, there is all the more reason to develop the facts first, rather than to hastily proceed to a dispositive ruling."

But that wasn't to be. Mondelez quickly settled with the plaintiffs a few months later for $750,000.

This comes at a time of skyrocketing data breaches targeting the world's most prominent law firms. Brian Levine, managing director of Ernst & Young's cybersecurity and data privacy practice, said firms are attractive targets for breaches because they are a central repository of lucrative, non-public information. Their bill-by-the-hour revenue model also opens them up to ransomware gangs looking to exploit any shutdown in operations.

"Law firms are being heavily targeted now because they have a lot of sensitive information and they need to operate. So from a ransomware perspective, law firms work on the billable hour. If their employees can't do their job and if their attorneys can't do their job, they're not earning revenue. But even more importantly, a high percentage of their documents are attorney-client privileged or confidential. They may contain trade secrets that are pre-patent. They may contain merger plans, acquisition plans, strategic plans that bad guys have actually taken—not to do ransomware or hurt the firm—but to trade on," he said.

Law firms are also not specifically attuned to implementing sophisticated cybersecurity policies, procedures, and controls. "One sort of universal vulnerability that I would say probably applies to law firms different from other industry verticals, it probably has to be a sort of relative lack of security governance maturity," said Jack Freund, chief risk officer for cyber-risk-quantification platform Kovrr. Even with great security, attackers will always look for the easiest method of intrusion. Reused passwords, phishing emails, "very basic, stupid ways," Freund said.

Hackers are also looking to exploit security flaws in software and products that "are in the wild" exist but haven't been fixed yet. "You can have very sophisticated security controls, but if you're leaving the back door open, well I'll just walk right in. And that tends to be the way a lot of security hackers tend to target," he said.

And the amount of vulnerable is growing with the use of AI. "It's going to encourage organizations to record more, to save more. And then we come back to that data retention issue again," Freund said. "So when the pile of potentially explosive information becomes more interesting and larger, then you're going to see more attackers going after it."

But why should a law firm's data retention policies be their client's problem? Because if that data gets out, they're going after the entity they entrusted it to in the first place.

"If you do business with a company and you give them your personal identifying information, and the information gets out there, you don't really care as the consumer who did business with the company, whether the company lost it itself, or whether they gave it to a third party and that third party lost it," Levine said.

While there are legitimate reasons for sharing personally identifiable information with law firms, companies are ultimately responsible for what happens to it.

"You can't outsource duty of care," said Scott Kannry, CEO of cyber risk management firm Axio. "The fact that they're sharing that information with their law firm does not in any way, shape or form obviate that duty. Worst-case situation, if the law firm goes kaput, even if the enterprise didn't do anything wrong, they're still on the hook."

But even while experts say perfect security does not exist, there are still affirmative steps companies can take to put them on more secure footing with their firms.

"First of all, what you don't do is assume that this is an internationally recognized law firm that deals with the most sensitive information so I don't have to even ask the question, because they must have great security," Levine said, something he hears all the time in his job evaluating the security of organizations.

"One of the things I always ask is about their third-party risk management, and quite frequently their answer is, 'We only do business with vendors like Microsoft and AWS and very large companies that surely have good programs, so we don't need to look into it.' Well, we all know what happens when you assume."

What you should assume is that something will probably go wrong at some point. "Nothing's perfect, and no organization is impenetrable. You have to assume that somebody that you're going to give data to is going to have an event at some point," Kannry said.

"That doesn't mean that there aren't things that can't be done in terms of contractual indemnifications and limitations of liability. That enterprise ought to make sure that If that happens, they have indemnity protections from the law firm, meaning that the law firm minimally pays the bills or the costs associated with the event. It could mean that the enterprise takes extra steps to ensure that if the law firm can't fulfill that indemnity or that responsibility, that the enterprise's insurance provider would still pay those costs."

Data minimization is equally important. Levine said in-house should figure out what employee information their outside counsel specifically needs, and just provide that.

"They need to talk to the attorney about what information they need about each of these people? Do you actually need their Social Security number? Do you actually need their date of birth?

"You know, do you need their home address, or do you just need their name and title? And then you have to make it clear to your IT person or whoever is going to actually send over the information that they just need their name and title."

"Please don't send everything else over as well. Because it's always going to be easier for someone to send over the file as it currently exists, which probably has everything in it, then to create another file, delete all the unused data and just send that over in a protected form," Levine said, noting that it may involve an extra step, but it's an important one.

And finally, heavily scrutinize your outside counsel's data security practices. "There is a burgeoning industry of security ratings companies out there," Freund said.

It can also mean having a tough conversation with your firm about their cybersecurity, Levine said, but don't let that intimidate you. "You can't let the awkwardness of the potential question prevent you from asking it," he said.

This doesn't mean sitting down with the litigation partner handling your matters. "Any large organization, law firm or otherwise, is going to have somebody who's in charge of just handling those inquiries, and they will have all their security information that the company is comfortable sharing. They're going to have all the evidence," Levine said.

"What you're asking is not, 'Mr. Partner of the law firm who focuses on tax, can you tell me about your security?' You're really asking, 'Can you get me a conversation with the person who demonstrates security for your organization so that I can connect them with my security person?'

When it comes to third-party risk management, law firms can get left off the list because in-house counsel don't put them in the same category as vendors.

"Maybe it's because of the close, confidential relationship where they feel more like they're part of the team. Maybe it feels like they're just giving advice, which is super valuable," Levine said. "But whoever is thinking about third-party risk management for the organization should be including law firms in that program."

article.title: At DataGrail Summit, Legal Leaders Call for Transparency in the Age of AI
article.description: Kirsten Daru had a revelation after landing her first general counsel role. She had spent the previous 11 years as chief privacy officer at Electronic Arts, where she was the first privacy lawyer at the company. She joined in 2008 just as privacy was…
article.text: Kirsten Daru had a revelation after landing her first general counsel role. She had spent the previous 11 years as chief privacy officer at Electronic Arts, where she was the first privacy lawyer at the company. She joined in 2008 just as privacy was blowing up, and built its program from the ground up. But even as she had much more on her plate as a GC—contracts, financing deals and partnerships, IP prosecution, patent litigation, employment and antitrust matters—she realized something that never occurred to her in those 11 years at EA. Privacy was still by far the most challenging legal discipline in existence. And now with AI exploding on the scene, it’s even more complicated. Kirsten Daru, general counsel and chief privacy officer Netgear. Courtesy of DataGrail

article.title: SEC Probing Companies Victimized by Massive MOVEit Cyberattack
article.description: The agency has dispatched dozens of sweep letters to companies affected by the hack, which compromised the private information of 2,770 organizations and more than 94 million individuals. April 26, 2024 at 06:57 AM Maria Dinzeo Securities and…
article.text: The agency has dispatched dozens of sweep letters to companies affected by the hack, which compromised the private information of 2,770 organizations and more than 94 million individuals. April 26, 2024 at 06:57 AM Maria Dinzeo Securities and Exchange Commission investigators are sending sweep letters to companies that fell prey to last year’s MOVEit cyberattack, Law.com has learned. The commission is examining the material impact of the May 2023 hack, which compromised the private information of 2,770 organizations and more than 94 million individuals worldwide, according to a running tally by anti-virus software firm Emisisoft. The victims include banks, insurance companies, hotels, airlines, hospitals and multiple federal agencies. To pull it off, the ransomware gang C10p exploited a vulnerability in Progress Software’s secure file encryption and transfer tool MOVEit, making off with a trove of social security numbers, birthdates, driver’s license numbers, tax identification numbers and health records. Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & Gray’s data, privacy and cybersecurity practice, said more downstream victims are still emerging. “The MOVEit hack itself impacted several large professional services firms such as lawyers and auditors, and this has led to a very complicated situation where fourth parties and fifth parties are learning of it and the SEC is continuing to figure out how to grapple with oversight of the supply chain risk because of its complexity,” he said. The letters went to dozens of companies and cover such topics as the timeline and content of notification from Burlington, Massachusetts-based Progress, whether that notice triggered other notices to clients and ransom requests or payments, as well as cybersecurity governance and external communications about cyber incidents. The SEC’s targeted exams are part of an information-gathering process commonly known as a sweep. Amy Jane Longo, a former SEC trial lawyer and partner in Ropes & Gray’s litigation and enforcement practice, confirmed that the SEC “has issued letters asking for information on a voluntary basis about the impact of the hack.” The existence of the sweep letters has not been previously reported. Longo said the letters could have a dual purpose: to investigate the circumstances related to the hack and to “look into registrants’ response to the hack in light of any obligations the SEC imposes on the registrants like investment advisers, broker dealers and public companies.” She said the latter piece “could be focused on how registrants responded to the hack and compliance with policies and procedures they may have, and whether they were obligated to make disclosures.” Longo and McNicholas said they were unable to discuss specifics about the letters or reveal which companies received them. This isn’t the first time the SEC has used this investigative tool in connection with a cyberattack. In 2021, the SEC issued sweep letters as part of its probe into the massive 2020 SolarWinds hack, which was perpetrated by a Russia-backed hacker group Cozy Bear. The group committed what’s known as a supply-chain attack, injecting malicious code into SolarWinds’ software platform Orion that created a backdoor through which it could access customers’ files undetected. Routine software updates infected with the code allowed the malware to proliferate. The SEC’s investigation of the hack led the commission in October to bring civil fraud charges against SolarWinds and its chief information security officer, Timothy Brown. The suit, filed in federal court in New York, accuses SolarWinds and Brown of overstating SolarWinds’ cybersecurity practices and understating or failing to disclose known risks. The company and Brown deny the allegations. “SolarWinds was a nation-state attack focused on espionage, whereas MOVEit, because of the nature of the software, had a much broader impact across sectors,” said McNicholas, who represents former SolarWinds CEO Kevin Thompson. “We saw it impact health care, financial services or anyone who wanted to send files securely.” McNicholas said the SEC is examining “the timing of notice of the MOVEit breach and how long it took information to get to particular entities,” along with ransom demands and payments. The SEC, which has not made the sweep or its targets public, did not respond respond to a request for comment from Law.com. A company’s receipt of a sweep letter does not signal the firm is under investigation, though the agency could later use information gathered in the sweep to bring enforcement actions, or to support its case for more stringent regulation. Progress Software disclosed in an August SEC filing that the agency had subpoenaed the company as part of a formal fact-finding inquiry into the breach. “To the extent that staff is investigating Progress, it’s likely casting the letters quite widely to try to develop information of the extent of the impact,” Longo said. “My expectation is they are trying to get information very broadly to assess whether there are any potential violations they want to pursue.” The inquiry comes amid the SEC’s growing interest in protecting investors from cyberthreats. In July, the agency adopted new disclosure rules requiring companies to report breaches that materially impact their business within four days of making that determination. Longo said she doesn’t think the SEC’s sweep letters are directly related to the new rules, because it’s “looking mainly at activity before they came into effect.” But “one could imagine that once the new rule has been in place for a longer time, there may be more public information routinely disclosed around cyber incidents that could be responsive,” she said. “The new rules spell out to public companies what disclosures are required in those circumstances, So certainly depending on their analysis of the impact of such an event, they may have to make some kind of disclosure about it. The SEC rule is very proscriptive about these disclosures.” The SEC’s interest in the MOVEit hack seems broader, covering both how it impacted public companies and registered investment advisers. The commission has also proposed new cybersecurity risk management rules for registered investment advisers, and last year announced plans to amend Regulation S-P to require that broker-dealers, investment companies, registered investment advisers and transfer agents “provide notice to individuals affected by certain types of data breaches that may put them at risk of identity theft or other harm.” SEC Chair Gary Gensler said in a statement a year ago that requiring firms covered under the revised rule to notify customers about breaches will “close the gap” in current regulations around cybersecurity. “I believe that these amendments, if adopted, would help customers maintain their privacy and protect themselves,” he said. Longo said the SEC has been transparent about its belief that cybersecurity risk affects every participant in the financial system. “An incident like the MOVEit hack, because it targeted particularly confidential information, likely raises heightened concerns for the SEC about client and customer information that financial institutions like investment advisers and broker dealers have, and whether the security of such information was affected,” she said.
