article.title: Pay for Autodesk Legal Chief Jumped 37% in Latest Year
article.description: Ruth Ann Keene, who was an Autodesk attorney for 11 years earlier in her career and boomeranged back to become the company’s chief legal officer in January 2022, received compensation of $3.97 million in the fiscal year ended Jan. 31. Keene’s fiscal…
article.text: Ruth Ann Keene, who was an Autodesk attorney for 11 years earlier in her career and boomeranged back to become the company’s chief legal officer in January 2022, received compensation of $3.97 million in the fiscal year ended Jan. 31. Keene’s fiscal 2024 pay, revealed in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing Thursday, represented a 37% jump from the $2.92 million she earned in her first full year with the company, which makes design software for such industries as architecture and construction.
article.html:
Ruth Ann Keene, who was an Autodesk attorney for 11 years earlier in her career and boomeranged back to become the company’s chief legal officer in January 2022, received compensation of $3.97 million in the fiscal year ended Jan. 31.

Keene’s fiscal 2024 pay, revealed in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing Thursday, represented a 37% jump from the $2.92 million she earned in her first full year with the company, which makes design software for such industries as architecture and construction.

article.title: 'Walk a Fine Line': Managing Hyperpolarized Environment Zooms Up Employers' List of Worries
article.description: Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears. Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler…
article.text: Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears. Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler Mendelson 12th Annual Employer Survey said they were moderately concerned or very concerned about managing divisive political or social beliefs in the leadup to the 2024 election. Another 38% expressed slight concern, leaving just 13% of respondents who were “not at all concerned.” That’s a big shift from the start of the year, when 27% of respondents to Littler’s Inclusion, Equity and Diversity C-Suite Survey Report said they were ”not at all challenged” by managing divisive political beliefs among employees The employer survey, released last week, found anxiety levels were especially high among large employers, with just 6% saying they are not at all worried about the topic. Littler, which bills itself as the world’s largest management-side employment law firm, advised companies to “walk a fine line,” noting that those inclined to restrict politically toxic conversations face a legal minefield. It noted that the National Labor Relations Board—whose authority extends to most private-sector employers—has been interpreting the National Labor Relations Act in ways that expand the rights of workers to speak out. A September 2023 ruling, for instance, came down on the side of an employee who’d been fired after creating a brouhaha in the workplace advocating that her organization rehire a non-U.S. citizen it had earlier let go when her work authorization had expired. In February, the NLRB ruled a former Home Depot worker who’d resigned in protest after the retailer ordered him to remove “BLM” from his apron had been within his rights to display it. Meanwhile, some states also are expanding protections for political speech. In March, for instance, the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment bulked up protections for public employees. “Given the ramifications of the election’s outcome on employment law, as well as the labor-related statements offered by both candidates, employers attempting to limit contentious political conversations should be careful not to run afoul of the recently expanded interpretations of the NLRA and state laws, Littler’s report says. Political and social tensions already have boiled over at some workplaces. In April, Google fired 50 workers who held protests at the company’s New York and Sunnyvale, California, offices protesting the company’s cloud-computing contract with the Israeli government. Southwest Airlines’ yearslong legal battle over its 2017 firing of flight attendant Charlene Carter serves as a cautionary tale for other employers trying to manage discord in the workplace. The airline had said it fired Carter for violating a civility policy after she expressed her opposition to abortion by sending graphic videos and images of an aborted fetus to her union president. A jury in 2022, however, deemed her dismissal unlawful, finding that her opposition to abortion was rooted in her religious beliefs and that she was a victim of religious discrimination. The jury awarded her $5.1 million in punitive damages, though a judge later reduced the award to $800,000, citing federal limits on punitive damages. In 2020, both Basecamp and Coinbase grabbed headlines—and spurred dozens of employees to quit—by imposing outright bans on political speech. Other firms have taken a middle ground. Intuit, for instance, moderates company channels, flagging language “that could be hurtful or exclude.” In April, the DEI consultant Seramount issued an eight-page guide for employers titled “Managing Politics in the Workplace.” It recommends a proactive approach in which employers arrange discussions conducted in a respectful tone. Seramount noted that failing to engage on the topic can itself fan discord, noting that employees and other stakeholders increasingly expect their employers to engage on social and political topics. “It is important to allow employees the time and space to share their stories and perceptions in both formal and informal ways. Despite political differences, we can almost always find common ground and discover ways in which we are similar and share certain values and experiences,” the report says.
article.html:
Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears.

Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler Mendelson 12th Annual Employer Survey said they were moderately concerned or very concerned about managing divisive political or social beliefs in the leadup to the 2024 election.

Another 38% expressed slight concern, leaving just 13% of respondents who were “not at all concerned.” That’s a big shift from the start of the year, when 27% of respondents to Littler’s Inclusion, Equity and Diversity C-Suite Survey Report said they were ”not at all challenged” by managing divisive political beliefs among employees

The employer survey, released last week, found anxiety levels were especially high among large employers, with just 6% saying they are not at all worried about the topic.

Littler, which bills itself as the world’s largest management-side employment law firm, advised companies to “walk a fine line,” noting that those inclined to restrict politically toxic conversations face a legal minefield.

It noted that the National Labor Relations Board—whose authority extends to most private-sector employers—has been interpreting the National Labor Relations Act in ways that expand the rights of workers to speak out.

A September 2023 ruling, for instance, came down on the side of an employee who’d been fired after creating a brouhaha in the workplace advocating that her organization rehire a non-U.S. citizen it had earlier let go when her work authorization had expired. In February, the NLRB ruled a former Home Depot worker who’d resigned in protest after the retailer ordered him to remove “BLM” from his apron had been within his rights to display it.

Meanwhile, some states also are expanding protections for political speech. In March, for instance, the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment bulked up protections for public employees.

“Given the ramifications of the election’s outcome on employment law, as well as the labor-related statements offered by both candidates, employers attempting to limit contentious political conversations should be careful not to run afoul of the recently expanded interpretations of the NLRA and state laws, Littler’s report says.

Political and social tensions already have boiled over at some workplaces. In April, Google fired 50 workers who held protests at the company’s New York and Sunnyvale, California, offices protesting  the company’s cloud-computing contract with the Israeli government.

Southwest Airlines’ yearslong legal battle over its 2017 firing of flight attendant Charlene Carter serves as a cautionary tale for other employers trying to manage discord in the workplace. The airline had said it fired Carter for violating a civility policy after she expressed her opposition to abortion by sending graphic videos and images of an aborted fetus to her union president.

A jury in 2022, however, deemed her dismissal unlawful, finding that her opposition to abortion was rooted in her religious beliefs and that she was a victim of religious discrimination. The jury awarded her $5.1 million in punitive damages, though a judge later reduced the award to $800,000, citing federal limits on punitive damages.

In 2020, both Basecamp and Coinbase grabbed headlines—and spurred dozens of employees to quit—by imposing outright bans on political speech. Other firms have taken a middle ground. Intuit, for instance, moderates company channels, flagging language “that could be hurtful or exclude.”

In April, the DEI consultant Seramount issued an eight-page guide for employers titled “Managing Politics in the Workplace.” It recommends a proactive approach in which employers arrange discussions conducted in a respectful tone.

Seramount noted that failing to engage on the topic can itself fan discord, noting that employees and other stakeholders increasingly expect their employers to engage on social and political topics.

“It is important to allow employees the time and space to share their stories and perceptions in both formal and informal ways. Despite political differences, we can almost always find common ground and discover ways in which we are similar and share certain values and experiences,” the report says.

article.title: Southwest Calls 'Religious Liberty' Training Ideological, Judge's Order Mandating It 'Unprecedented'
article.description: Southwest wants a federal judge to stay his order for religious liberty training for three senior in-house attorneys. The judge sanctioned Southwest after finding it failed to comply with an earlier order in the case, which was brought by a flight…
article.text: Southwest wants a federal judge to stay his order for religious liberty training for three senior in-house attorneys. The judge sanctioned Southwest after finding it failed to comply with an earlier order in the case, which was brought by a flight attendant who alleged religious discrimination and won a jury trial last year. Southwest says the flight attendant is conflating religious freedom with Title VII's employment discrimination protections. Southwest Airlines say a judge’s civil contempt order mandating that three of its senior attorneys attend “religious liberty” training violates the airline’s First Amendment right to disagree with the outcome of a flight attendant’s lawsuit asserting she was fired for expressing anti-abortion views. The judge’s Aug. 7 order follow a 2022 jury verdict in favor of flight attendant Charlene Carter. The airline says it fired her for violating the airline’s employee civility policy by texting her co-worker a picture of an aborted fetus along with a hostile message disparaging their views.
article.html:
• Southwest wants a federal judge to stay his order for religious liberty training for three senior in-house attorneys.
  • The judge sanctioned Southwest after finding it failed to comply with an earlier order in the case, which was brought by a flight attendant who alleged religious discrimination and won a jury trial last year.
  • Southwest says the flight attendant is conflating religious freedom with Title VII's employment discrimination protections.

Southwest Airlines say a judge’s civil contempt order mandating that three of its senior attorneys attend “religious liberty” training violates the airline’s First Amendment right to disagree with the outcome of a flight attendant’s lawsuit asserting she was fired for expressing anti-abortion views.

The judge’s Aug. 7 order follow a 2022 jury verdict in favor of flight attendant Charlene Carter. The airline says it fired her for violating the airline’s employee civility policy by texting her co-worker a picture of an aborted fetus along with a hostile message disparaging their views.

article.title: Founding GC of Animal Health Giant Zoetis Steps Down
article.description: Zoetis, the world's largest maker of animal vaccines and medicine, is looking for a new general counsel. Founding General Counsel Heidi Chen has stepped down and will officially depart on July 16. Chen joined Zoetis from Pfizer in 2012, just before…
article.text: Zoetis, the world's largest maker of animal vaccines and medicine, is looking for a new general counsel. Founding General Counsel Heidi Chen has stepped down and will officially depart on July 16. Chen joined Zoetis from Pfizer in 2012, just before the former Pfizer subsidiary spun off into a separate company following its IPO in 2013. The world’s largest animal health company has disclosed that its founding general counsel, Heidi Chen, is stepping down from the role she’s held for more than a decade. The company disclosed her impending departure in a securities filing. Chen had been at the helm of Zoetis’ legal department since 2012. She joined Zoetis as founding general counsel from Pfizer, where she had been an assistant general counsel for 13 years.

article.text: Levi Strauss & Co. has promoted David Jedrzejek to general counsel. Jedrzejek joined Levi's in 2015 and most recently ran its commercial legal department. Jedrzejek will succeed Seth Jaffe, who will retire as chief legal officer on June 2. Levi Strauss & Co.’s legal chief Seth Jaffe is retiring this summer after 26 years at the iconic San Francisco-based clothier, and deputy general counsel David Jedrzejek will step into his shoes on June 2. Jedrzejek has been in-house at the company for seven years, most recently running its commercial legal department. article.title: As Cyberattacks Rise, Firms Face 'Significantly Broadened' Duty to Protect Worker Data
article.description: What You Need to Know There's no generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures. Even so, employers should be reducing their vulnerability by encrypting data and changing passwords regularly. They also should be…
article.text: What You Need to Know There's no generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures. Even so, employers should be reducing their vulnerability by encrypting data and changing passwords regularly. They also should be purging no-longer-needed data, especially for former employees.
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • There's no generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures.
  • Even so, employers should be reducing their vulnerability by encrypting data and changing passwords regularly.
  • They also should be purging no-longer-needed data, especially for former employees.

article.title: Paul Weiss’ Trio of Kirkland Hires Could Each Score $20M Yearly
article.description: Paul Weiss-bound partners Neel Sachdev, Roger Johnson and Eric Wedel could each make $20 million annually at their new firm. Pay for the transactional trio depends on a number of factors, including how much client business they bring from Kirkland,…
article.text: Paul Weiss-bound partners Neel Sachdev, Roger Johnson and Eric Wedel could each make $20 million annually at their new firm. Pay for the transactional trio depends on a number of factors, including how much client business they bring from Kirkland, their status in Paul Weiss' equity system and the firm's profitability. At some Am Law 25 firms, a handful of partners have comp in excess of $25 million. Three of the Kirkland & Ellis partners heading to Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison could each earn $20 million in annual compensation at their new firm, according to people with knowledge of the partners’ moves. Overall, annual pay for transactional partners Neel Sachdev and Roger Johnson in the U.K. and Eric Wedel in the U.S. could be more or less than $20 million, depending on how much client business they bring from Kirkland, their status in the firm’s share system, and Paul Weiss’ profitability, the people said.
article.html:
• Paul Weiss-bound partners Neel Sachdev, Roger Johnson and Eric Wedel could each make $20 million annually at their new firm.
  • Pay for the transactional trio depends on a number of factors, including how much client business they bring from Kirkland, their status in Paul Weiss' equity system and the firm's profitability.
  • At some Am Law 25 firms, a handful of partners have comp in excess of $25 million.

Three of the Kirkland & Ellis partners heading to Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison could each earn $20 million in annual compensation at their new firm, according to people with knowledge of the partners’ moves.

Overall, annual pay for transactional partners Neel Sachdev and Roger Johnson in the U.K. and Eric Wedel in the U.S. could be more or less than $20 million, depending on how much client business they bring from Kirkland, their status in the firm’s share system, and Paul Weiss’ profitability, the people said.

article.title: As SVB's Risks Skyrocketed, Bank Let Chief Risk Officer Post Sit Vacant for Months
article.description: Silicon Valley Bank was without a chief risk officer from April 29 to Dec. 27, 2022. Meanwhile, the board's risk committee was thin on risk expertise, experts say. The risk committee met 18 times in 2022, a sign it realized trouble was afoot. The…
article.text: Silicon Valley Bank was without a chief risk officer from April 29 to Dec. 27, 2022. Meanwhile, the board's risk committee was thin on risk expertise, experts say. The risk committee met 18 times in 2022, a sign it realized trouble was afoot. The abrupt collapse of venture capital darling Silicon Valley Bank has exposed several glaring governance and risk management lapses, including that it parted ways with its chief risk officer in April 2022 and appears to have operated without a full-time replacement for nearly the remainder of the year. In its 2023 proxy statement filed March 3, SVB revealed that it initiated talks with chief risk officer Laura Izurieta to leave her job in early 2022. Pursuant to a separation agreement, Izurieta stepped down April 29, 2022, and moved into a “non-executive role focused on certain transition-related duties,” which looked to be mostly an advisory role that included helping to find her replacement. The abrupt collapse of venture capital darling Silicon Valley Bank has exposed several glaring governance and risk management lapses, including that it parted ways with its chief risk officer in April 2022 and appears to have operated without a full-time replacement for nearly the remainder of the year.

In its 2023 proxy statement filed March 3, SVB revealed that it initiated talks with chief risk officer Laura Izurieta to leave her job in early 2022. Pursuant to a separation agreement, Izurieta stepped down April 29, 2022, and moved into a “non-executive role focused on certain transition-related duties,” which looked to be mostly an advisory role that included helping to find her replacement.

article.title: Corporate Bans of AI Tools Come With Their Own Risks
article.description: Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase have restricted or barred AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google’s Bard on work devices. AI experts say the move is shortsighted and may put those companies at a competitive disadvantage. Educating employees is a…
article.text: Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase have restricted or barred AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google’s Bard on work devices. AI experts say the move is shortsighted and may put those companies at a competitive disadvantage. Educating employees is a better route to reducing the risk of confidential information leaking. Worries about generative artificial intelligence tools and chatbots show no sign of abating, including the potential for inadvertent leaks of confidential information. A string of companies, including Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase, has restricted or barred the use of AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google’s Bard on work devices, fearing employees might inadvertently share source code or business secrets with these platforms. article.title: FTC Strikes Back at MGM for Fighting Its Probe of Massive Cyberattack
article.description: In one line of attack, MGM is seeking to disqualify FTC Chair Lina Khan, who was staying at the company's Las Vegas hotel when the hackers struck and, because of the disruption, was asked by a front desk clerk to write her credit card number on a…
article.text: In one line of attack, MGM is seeking to disqualify FTC Chair Lina Khan, who was staying at the company's Las Vegas hotel when the hackers struck and, because of the disruption, was asked by a front desk clerk to write her credit card number on a piece of paper. The Federal Trade Commission is asking a federal court to force MGM Resorts International to comply with its investigative demands regarding a crippling cyberattack in September that exposed the personal information of 1.5 million MGM guests and brought down the hotel and casino operator’s systems for more than a week. “To date, MGM has failed to provide any documents or responses to interrogatories. Respondents’ failure to comply with the CID [civil investigative demand] has materially impeded the Commission’s ongoing investigation,” the FTC says in a petition filed in the District of Nevada on Friday.
article.html:
In one line of attack, MGM is seeking to disqualify FTC Chair Lina Khan, who was staying at the company's Las Vegas hotel when the hackers struck and, because of the disruption, was asked by a front desk clerk to write her credit card number on a piece of paper.

The Federal Trade Commission is asking a federal court to force MGM Resorts International to comply with its investigative demands regarding a crippling cyberattack in September that exposed the personal information of 1.5 million MGM guests and brought down the hotel and casino operator’s systems for more than a week.

“To date, MGM has failed to provide any documents or responses to interrogatories. Respondents’ failure to comply with the CID [civil investigative demand] has materially impeded the Commission’s ongoing investigation,” the FTC says in a petition filed in the District of Nevada on Friday.

U.S. District Judge Sara L. Ellis for the Northern District of Illinois granted a motion for summary judgment filed by plaintiff Grainger as to its request for recoupment against the company’s former vice president of total rewards, Scott Witz, for $1.38 million in equity-based awards and approximately $295,782 in cash incentive payments pursuant to Grainger’s management incentive program. The plan and award agreements provide for recoupment in the event an employee engages in misconduct, including criminal activity or violations of company policy, according to the May 13 opinion. However, Ellis rejected Grainger’s request for summary judgment on its claims that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the company. Grainger claimed Witz owed a duty of care and loyalty to the company as a corporate officer but placed Grainger in danger of potential liability through his illegal conduct. After Witz left the company in July 2021, Grainger received a request from law enforcement for Witz’s Grainger-issued laptop. It was later revealed that Witz stored the illegal content on his company-issued laptop. Witz pleaded guilty to one count of possession of child pornography, the opinion said. Grainger’s board determined that Witz’s conduct triggered the recoupment provisions in the award agreements and passed a resolution authorizing recoupment of certain incentive compensation of Witz’s. After notifying Witz of its intent to recoup the compensation, Witz’s counsel told Grainger that he would not agree to repay the compensation, resulting in Grainger initiating the action. Grainger argued that it was undisputed that the company was entitled to recoup the award agreements, while Witz argued against recovery because the compensation committee of the board of directors allegedly abused its discretion in seeking to take back the incentive compensation. Ellis concluded that the court didn’t need to definitively resolve the recoupment matter as to whether the covenant of good faith applied to the board’s decision. “Even assuming that the covenant of good faith limited the Board’s discretion, Witz has not created a question of fact as to whether the board violated the covenant,” Ellis wrote. “Because the award agreements provided that the board could authorize recoupment of Witz’s incentive compensation based on the board’s determination of whether Witz complied with applicable laws and Grainger policies, the parties expressly contemplated the situation at hand, an attempt at recoupment based on Witz’s violation of the acceptable use policy. In other words, Grainger did not act in bad faith when it exercised its discretion to recoup Witz’s incentive compensation for violating a company policy.” The court also rejected Witz’s argument because he violated Grainger’s acceptable use policy relating to the use of its technology and devices. “The parties agreed in the award agreements that the board had sole discretion in determining the extent to which it would seek recovery for any incentive compensation, meaning Witz cannot argue he did not contemplate the board pursuing recoupment if he violated a policy, regardless of its allegedly selective enforcement of the provision,” Ellis said. In regard to Grainger’s remaining claims, the court concluded that the company failed to set forth elements to support its argument that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the organization. Should Grainger pursue these claims, it may renew its request for summary judgment at the close of discovery, Ellis said. Witz also filed a counterclaim alleging that Grainger violated Section 2-103 of the Illinois Human Rights Act, failed to pay him certain compensation, and violated wage laws. Neither party sought summary judgment on those claims. A status hearing was set for Aug. 7. Grainger’s attorney, Ryan Hamilton Vann of Cooley in Chicago, declined to comment. Witz’s attorney, Dennis Ray Favaro of Favaro & Gorman in Lakewood, Illinois, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
article.html:
A federal judge in Chicago this week granted the industrial supply company W.W. Grainger’s attempt to recoup more than $1.5 million in incentive compensation from a former executive who was convicted of possessing child pornography on his work-issued laptop.

U.S. District Judge Sara L. Ellis for the Northern District of Illinois granted a motion for summary judgment filed by plaintiff Grainger as to its request for recoupment against the company’s former vice president of total rewards, Scott Witz, for $1.38 million in equity-based awards and approximately $295,782 in cash incentive payments pursuant to Grainger’s management incentive program. The plan and award agreements provide for recoupment in the event an employee engages in misconduct, including criminal activity or violations of company policy, according to the May 13 opinion. 

However, Ellis rejected Grainger’s request for summary judgment on its claims that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the company. Grainger claimed Witz owed a duty of care and loyalty to the company as a corporate officer but placed Grainger in danger of potential liability through his illegal conduct.

After Witz left the company in July 2021, Grainger received a request from law enforcement for Witz’s Grainger-issued laptop. It was later revealed that Witz stored the illegal content on his company-issued laptop. Witz pleaded guilty to one count of possession of child pornography, the opinion said.

Grainger’s board determined that Witz’s conduct triggered the recoupment provisions in the award agreements and passed a resolution authorizing recoupment of certain incentive compensation of Witz’s. After notifying Witz of its intent to recoup the compensation, Witz’s counsel told Grainger that he would not agree to repay the compensation, resulting in Grainger initiating the action.

Grainger argued that it was undisputed that the company was entitled to recoup the award agreements, while Witz argued against recovery because the compensation committee of the board of directors allegedly abused its discretion in seeking to take back the incentive compensation.

Ellis concluded that the court didn’t need to definitively resolve the recoupment matter as to whether the covenant of good faith applied to the board’s decision.

“Even assuming that the covenant of good faith limited the Board’s discretion, Witz has not created a question of fact as to whether the board violated the covenant,” Ellis wrote. “Because the award agreements provided that the board could authorize recoupment of Witz’s incentive compensation based on the board’s determination of whether Witz complied with applicable laws and Grainger policies, the parties expressly contemplated the situation at hand, an attempt at recoupment based on Witz’s violation of the acceptable use policy. In other words, Grainger did not act in bad faith when it exercised its discretion to recoup Witz’s incentive compensation for violating a company policy.”

The court also rejected Witz’s argument because he violated Grainger’s acceptable use policy relating to the use of its technology and devices.

“The parties agreed in the award agreements that the board had sole discretion in determining the extent to which it would seek recovery for any incentive compensation, meaning Witz cannot argue he did not contemplate the board pursuing recoupment if he violated a policy, regardless of its allegedly selective enforcement of the provision,” Ellis said.

In regard to Grainger’s remaining claims, the court concluded that the company failed to set forth elements to support its argument that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the organization. Should Grainger pursue these claims, it may renew its request for summary judgment at the close of discovery, Ellis said.

Witz also filed a counterclaim alleging that Grainger violated Section 2-103 of the Illinois Human Rights Act, failed to pay him certain compensation, and violated wage laws. Neither party sought summary judgment on those claims.

A status hearing was set for Aug. 7.

Grainger’s attorney, Ryan Hamilton Vann of Cooley in Chicago, declined to comment.

Witz’s attorney, Dennis Ray Favaro of Favaro & Gorman in Lakewood, Illinois, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

article.title: Blockchain Domains: New Developments for Brand Owners
article.description: Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification. Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising…
article.text: Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification. Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising enhanced security, privacy and censorship resistance. However, these benefits come with significant challenges, particularly for brand owners seeking to protect their trademarks in these new digital spaces. Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification. One of its latest frontiers relates to the domain name system (DNS). Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising enhanced security, privacy and censorship resistance. However, these benefits come with significant challenges, particularly for brand owners seeking to protect their trademarks in these new digital spaces. This article explores the issues associated with trademark protection in blockchain domain names and examines new steps and policies that blockchain domain registrars should implement to safeguard brand owners. Traditional Domain Name Registration and Protections Traditional DNS operates under a hierarchical structure managed by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN). This centralized authority oversees domain name registrations and resolves disputes through established policies such as the Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP). Developed more than 20 years ago, the UDRP was ICANN’s first consensus policy and was intended to address cybersquatting in the DNS. Cybersquatting involves the registration of domain names that are identical or confusingly similar to trademarks with the intent of registering and using those names in bad faith.
article.html:
• Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification.
  • Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising enhanced security, privacy and censorship resistance.
  • However, these benefits come with significant challenges, particularly for brand owners seeking to protect their trademarks in these new digital spaces.

article.title: Morning Minute
article.description: Welcome to Friday, You made it! If you feel worn to the bone, it’s perhaps because a fortuitous string of federal holidays has softened you up, eliminating one work day three of the last seven weeks. We better rebuild our stamina—the next holiday…
article.text: Welcome to Friday, You made it! If you feel worn to the bone, it’s perhaps because a fortuitous string of federal holidays has softened you up, eliminating one work day three of the last seven weeks. We better rebuild our stamina—the next holiday isn’t until Labor Day, Sept. 2. In today’s edition, we look at the ever-rising pay for the nation’s most elite law firm partners. Not long ago, $10 million was difficult to fathom. Now, the top range is $25 million to $30 million. Are the ever-higher payouts sustainable? Also, after going ga-ga for generative AI over the past two years, corporate America is experiencing something of a reality check. New research shows many companies say the results of their hefty AI investments are disappointing. We examine what went wrong.

article.title: Becoming a Trusted Adviser in the Age of Disruption
article.description: There are many conversations about how the legal industry has adapted—or failed to adapt—to the various challenges and disruptions it faces. Lawyers’ own adaptations have been explored considerably less, as has the topic of how well firms have…
article.text: There are many conversations about how the legal industry has adapted—or failed to adapt—to the various challenges and disruptions it faces. Lawyers’ own adaptations have been explored considerably less, as has the topic of how well firms have prepared them to adapt. There are at least a few fascinating but under-explored questions in this area that deserve far more attention: What does a lawyer need to understand to be a trusted adviser to corporate clients surfing the waves of change in an age of disruption? How does the very nature of the legal profession—smart, well-educated, experienced professionals managing known risks based on precedent and experience—sync with a world where the businesses they are counseling are rapidly shapeshifting or disappearing? Where does expertise of any sort fit in a completely new world emerging from technological advances as varied as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, Big Data, machine learning, space-age materials, robotics, 3-D printing, and every other fantastical advance that is going to utterly reshape our world?
article.html:
There are many conversations about how the legal industry has adapted—or failed to adapt—to the various challenges and disruptions it faces. Lawyers’ own adaptations have been explored considerably less, as has the topic of how well firms have prepared them to adapt. There are at least a few fascinating but under-explored questions in this area that deserve far more attention:

  • What does a lawyer need to understand to be a trusted adviser to corporate clients surfing the waves of change in an age of disruption?
  • How does the very nature of the legal profession—smart, well-educated, experienced professionals managing known risks based on precedent and experience—sync with a world where the businesses they are counseling are rapidly shapeshifting or disappearing?
  • Where does expertise of any sort fit in a completely new world emerging from technological advances as varied as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, Big Data, machine learning, space-age materials, robotics, 3-D printing, and every other fantastical advance that is going to utterly reshape our world?

article.title: Zynga Hit With Class Action Lawsuit Over Data Breach
article.description: Social game developer Zynga Inc., the company behind popular mobile games including Words with Friends, has been hit with a class action lawsuit stemming from a data breach that reportedly resulted in hundreds of millions of user accounts being…
article.text: Social game developer Zynga Inc., the company behind popular mobile games including Words with Friends, has been hit with a class action lawsuit stemming from a data breach that reportedly resulted in hundreds of millions of user accounts being hacked. Lawyers at Cotchett, Pitre & McCarthy; Foulston Siefkin; and The Miller Law Firm filed suit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on behalf of a nationwide class of Zynga account holders whose personally identifiable information was stolen in the breach disclosed on the company’s website in September.
article.html:
Social game developer Zynga Inc., the company behind popular mobile games including Words with Friends, has been hit with a class action lawsuit stemming from a data breach that reportedly resulted in hundreds of millions of user accounts being hacked. 

Lawyers at Cotchett, Pitre & McCarthy; Foulston Siefkin; and The Miller Law Firm filed suit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on behalf of a nationwide class of Zynga account holders whose personally identifiable information was stolen in the breach disclosed on the company’s website in September.

article.description: Do in-house leaders truly care about diversity? Sure, they’ve signed letters and joined initiatives to encourage law firms and legal departments to hire and promote more diverse lawyers. But has much of it been a show? From where Donald Prophete…
article.text: Do in-house leaders truly care about diversity? Sure, they’ve signed letters and joined initiatives to encourage law firms and legal departments to hire and promote more diverse lawyers. But has much of it been a show? article.title: FTC Defends Ethics Chief Who Issued Meta Opinion While Owning Meta Stock
article.description: The FTC's three commissioners called Lorielle Pankey a dedicated and honest career civil servant who complies with ethics rules. Meta had asked FTC Chair Lina Khan to recuse herself from the FTC's investigation of its $400 million Within acquisition.…
article.text: The FTC's three commissioners called Lorielle Pankey a dedicated and honest career civil servant who complies with ethics rules. Meta had asked FTC Chair Lina Khan to recuse herself from the FTC's investigation of its $400 million Within acquisition. Khan declined the request, despite Pankey's concern that Khan's past criticisms of Meta could affect her ability to appear impartial. The Federal Trade Commission is defending its ethics chief following a Wall Street Journal report Friday highlighting that she owned stock in Meta when she recommended that FTC Chair Lina Khan recuse herself from a case involving the company. Hours after the report’s publication, Khan and the agency’s other two commissioners, all Democrats, issued a statement standing by Lorielle Pankey, a Harvard law grad who serves as the agency’s associate general counsel for ethics.
article.html:

article.title: In-House Hiring Gains Strength Despite Recession Threat
article.description: “One of the things we saw [from 2008 to 2010] is that when the economy takes a hit, corporations will move to hire in-house attorneys because it can be a cost-saver,” Alice Rafalko, a senior legal consultant at Beacon Hill Legal in Philadelphia,…
article.text: “One of the things we saw [from 2008 to 2010] is that when the economy takes a hit, corporations will move to hire in-house attorneys because it can be a cost-saver,” Alice Rafalko, a senior legal consultant at Beacon Hill Legal in Philadelphia, said. In-house legal hiring went up in May and stayed in line with the Bureau of Labor Statistics report, which showed more legal jobs were added to the economy last month despite the threat of a looming recession, according to recruiters who spoke to Corporate Counsel on Wednesday. “One of the things we saw [from 2008 to 2010] is that when the economy takes a hit, corporations will move to hire in-house attorneys because it can be a cost-saver,” Alice Rafalko, a senior legal consultant at Beacon Hill Legal in Philadelphia, said.
article.html:
“One of the things we saw [from 2008 to 2010] is that when the economy takes a hit, corporations will move to hire in-house attorneys because it can be a cost-saver,” Alice Rafalko, a senior legal consultant at Beacon Hill Legal in Philadelphia, said.

In-house legal hiring went up in May and stayed in line with the Bureau of Labor Statistics report, which showed more legal jobs were added to the economy last month despite the threat of a looming recession, according to recruiters who spoke to Corporate Counsel on Wednesday.

“One of the things we saw [from 2008 to 2010] is that when the economy takes a hit, corporations will move to hire in-house attorneys because it can be a cost-saver,” Alice Rafalko, a senior legal consultant at Beacon Hill Legal in Philadelphia, said.

article.html:
Compensation is creeping up again for general counsel and other senior in-house lawyers, according to a new in-house compensation report from executive search firm BarkerGilmore.

Median compensation for in-house counsel rose 4.4% more in 2024 compared with a year earlier, the report says, with managing counsel seeing the largest increase (3.8%), followed by general counsel (3.2%) and senior counsel (2.9%).

article.title: Former Deputy GC at EV Company Canoo Among Execs Accused of Corporate Espionage
article.description: Canoo alleges former deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow played a key role in a corporate espionage scheme. The suit says Fielkow and others stole intellectual property and poached employees to start Harbinger Motors. Harbinger calls the…
article.text: Canoo alleges former deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow played a key role in a corporate espionage scheme. The suit says Fielkow and others stole intellectual property and poached employees to start Harbinger Motors. Harbinger calls the allegations baseless. Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which is known for its distinctive egg-shaped auto design, filed a federal lawsuit on Dec. 22 accusing former Canoo CEO John Harris, chief technology officer Phillip Weicker, chief operating officer William Eberts, vice president Alexi Charbonneau and Fielkow of swiping Canoo’s proprietary technology and poaching its employees to create Harbinger Motors in 2021. article.title: Tupperware's CLO Resigning as Company Fights to Stay Afloat
article.description: Karen Sheehan, a fixture at Tupperware during a period of rapid change and sales struggles, is resigning as chief legal officer. The company said her exit does not stem from a disagreement with management or the board over policies or practices.…
article.text: Karen Sheehan, a fixture at Tupperware during a period of rapid change and sales struggles, is resigning as chief legal officer. The company said her exit does not stem from a disagreement with management or the board over policies or practices. Tupperware is trying to find new sales channels to replace its reliance on independent dealers who pitched products at home parties. The longtime legal chief of Tupperware is stepping down as the once-iconic company, best-known for its plastic, air-tight containers, fights for survival. Karen Sheehan joined Tupperware as deputy general counsel in December 2014 and took the legal reins two years later. The Orlando, Florida-based company said in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing that she will leave Sept. 30, but did not provide a reason.
article.html:
• Karen Sheehan, a fixture at Tupperware during a period of rapid change and sales struggles, is resigning as chief legal officer.
  • The company said her exit does not stem from a disagreement with management or the board over policies or practices.
  • Tupperware is trying to find new sales channels to replace its reliance on independent dealers who pitched products at home parties.

The longtime legal chief of Tupperware is stepping down as the once-iconic company, best-known for its plastic, air-tight containers, fights for survival.

Karen Sheehan joined Tupperware as deputy general counsel in December 2014 and took the legal reins two years later. The Orlando, Florida-based company said in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing that she will leave Sept. 30, but did not provide a reason.

article.title: Ten Lessons About Great Outside Counsel from My Time In House
article.description: A decade ago, I moved from private practice to BP p.l.c. after the company’s accident in the Gulf of Mexico. My reasons were twofold: I am drawn to helping clients through their most difficult challenges, and I believed that going in house would help…
article.text: A decade ago, I moved from private practice to BP p.l.c. after the company’s accident in the Gulf of Mexico. My reasons were twofold: I am drawn to helping clients through their most difficult challenges, and I believed that going in house would help me become a better lawyer. I returned to private practice with ten observations about what makes the most effective outside counsel. I share them for the benefit of outside lawyers who continuously seek to improve client relationships, and in-house counsel who recognize that success requires identifying the behaviors that they value in the lawyers they hire. Win. Win the lawsuit, close the deal, end the investigation. While this seems obvious, law firms sometimes lose sight of their main purpose. Corporate clients have many metrics and priorities, but those things do not matter unless you win. No one will applaud you for being 5% under budget while losing the bet-the-company case. Understand how your client defines a true “win” and deliver it. Understand your client’s business and how you fit into their objectives and challenges. Executives and in-house counsel are managing a vast spectrum of issues, of which your matter is one small part. Effective lawyers understand their place in the big picture. For example, a client under investigation wants it over, but concurrently needs to grow, secure financing, maintain relationships, and the like. Lawyers who focus on the whole, not just their part, add far more value. They also connect with smaller gestures, such as avoiding nonurgent calls just before quarterly results, or not wandering into a meeting oblivious to a major corporate announcement or share price drop. Constantly seek to add value as a trusted advisor and partner. Great lawyers do not simply chuck advice over the fence to their clients. They pick up a shovel alongside clients and figure out how to implement it in a way that adds value to the business. “This is what the law requires” may be accurate, but “here is how to make this work in a way that promotes your objectives” is much better. These lawyers earn a seat at the table through relentless focus on adding value to their clients’ businesses. Offer your opinion on what to do, not just options to pick. Many lawyers present their clients with options and leave them with the hard decision of picking one. Give them your judgment on what you would do. Your client may disagree, and that is ok; you will still help them reach a better decision by taking a reasoned view. Be resourceful in achieving business objectives. Some lawyers default to “no” when a client asks if something challenging is possible. But as J.P. Morgan reportedly observed long ago, “I [do not] want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do,” but “to tell how to do what I want to do.” Great lawyers exhaust all options before they get to “no,” looking creatively for ways to achieve the client’s goals. Clients are more willing to accept a rare “no” from these lawyers because they know it comes from diligence. Focus on material risks and have courage to say what is not. Lawyers are trained to highlight even remote risks. The best lawyers do this while focusing the client on what is really important. It takes judgment to separate the likely from the possible. Understanding a law’s real-world application to a business and the likelihood and impact of its enforcement will help clients prioritize resources. A useful test is: “If I owned this company and every dollar spent was mine, would I focus on this?” Be a paragon of discretion. Lawyers help clients at highly sensitive points in their careers and lives. One of the greatest privileges of a lawyer is to be entrusted with a client’s confidences, and few things are more damaging to a lawyer’s reputation than inappropriately disclosing them, whether by loud calls in an airport, carelessly discarded files, or indiscreet war stories after drinks. Insist on feedback. Great lawyers get actionable client feedback on how they can improve. They go beyond passively asking “how are things going” or surfacing only issues that have boiled to dissatisfaction. Rather, they press for specific feedback on what could be better. They do not avoid known issues, but raise them proactively with a proposed solution. Partner with in-house counsel. In-house counsel are not just there to review invoices and serve as a mailbox between law firms and the company. They have unique insights on the client’s business and are an invaluable partner. Great lawyers purposefully involve them in ways that lead to better outcomes, and are responsive to their communications, requests, and ideas. Communicate succinctly. Brevity takes effort but is critical. Executives often make billion-dollar decisions that chart the course of companies on the basis of a brief memo. Sometimes clients need a long exegesis, but more often they are looking for a succinct, practical answer. What should they do, and what are the costs and risks if they do not? In my experience in house, the most effective outside counsel consistently demonstrated these ten behaviors regardless of their practice area, location, or background. I encourage outside and in-house counsel to talk openly with each other about what behaviors are on the latter’s list. All of us aspire to be capable lawyers who serve our clients well, and a shared understanding about what in-house counsel value and outside counsel are delivering is necessary for both to represent their client effectively.
article.html:
A decade ago, I moved from private practice to BP p.l.c. after the company’s accident in the Gulf of Mexico.  My reasons were twofold: I am drawn to helping clients through their most difficult challenges, and I believed that going in house would help me become a better lawyer.  I returned to private practice with ten observations about what makes the most effective outside counsel.  I share them for the benefit of outside lawyers who continuously seek to improve client relationships, and in-house counsel who recognize that success requires identifying the behaviors that they value in the lawyers they hire.

  1. Win. Win the lawsuit, close the deal, end the investigation. While this seems obvious, law firms sometimes lose sight of their main purpose.  Corporate clients have many metrics and priorities, but those things do not matter unless you win.  No one will applaud you for being 5% under budget while losing the bet-the-company case.  Understand how your client defines a true “win” and deliver it.
  2. Understand your client’s business and how you fit into their objectives and challenges. Executives and in-house counsel are managing a vast spectrum of issues, of which your matter is one small part. Effective lawyers understand their place in the big picture.  For example, a client under investigation wants it over, but concurrently needs to grow, secure financing, maintain relationships, and the like.  Lawyers who focus on the whole, not just their part, add far more value.  They also connect with smaller gestures, such as avoiding nonurgent calls just before quarterly results, or not wandering into a meeting oblivious to a major corporate announcement or share price drop.
  3. Constantly seek to add value as a trusted advisor and partner. Great lawyers do not simply chuck advice over the fence to their clients. They pick up a shovel alongside clients and figure out how to implement it in a way that adds value to the business.  “This is what the law requires” may be accurate, but “here is how to make this work in a way that promotes your objectives” is much better.  These lawyers earn a seat at the table through relentless focus on adding value to their clients’ businesses.
  4. Offer your opinion on what to do, not just options to pick. Many lawyers present their clients with options and leave them with the hard decision of picking one. Give them your judgment on what you would do.  Your client may disagree, and that is ok; you will still help them reach a better decision by taking a reasoned view.
  5. Be resourceful in achieving business objectives. Some lawyers default to “no” when a client asks if something challenging is possible. But as J.P. Morgan reportedly observed long ago, “I [do not] want a lawyer to tell me what I cannot do,” but “to tell how to do what I want to do.”  Great lawyers exhaust all options before they get to “no,” looking creatively for ways to achieve the client’s goals.  Clients are more willing to accept a rare “no” from these lawyers because they know it comes from diligence.
  6. Focus on material risks and have courage to say what is not. Lawyers are trained to highlight even remote risks. The best lawyers do this while focusing the client on what is really important.  It takes judgment to separate the likely from the possible.  Understanding a law’s real-world application to a business and the likelihood and impact of its enforcement will help clients prioritize resources.  A useful test is: “If I owned this company and every dollar spent was mine, would I focus on this?”
  7. Be a paragon of discretion. Lawyers help clients at highly sensitive points in their careers and lives. One of the greatest privileges of a lawyer is to be entrusted with a client’s confidences, and few things are more damaging to a lawyer’s reputation than inappropriately disclosing them, whether by loud calls in an airport, carelessly discarded files, or indiscreet war stories after drinks.
  8. Insist on feedback. Great lawyers get actionable client feedback on how they can improve. They go beyond passively asking “how are things going” or surfacing only issues that have boiled to dissatisfaction.  Rather, they press for specific feedback on what could be better.  They do not avoid known issues, but raise them proactively with a proposed solution.
  9. Partner with in-house counsel. In-house counsel are not just there to review invoices and serve as a mailbox between law firms and the company. They have unique insights on the client’s business and are an invaluable partner.  Great lawyers purposefully involve them in ways that lead to better outcomes, and are responsive to their communications, requests, and ideas.
  10. Communicate succinctly. Brevity takes effort but is critical. Executives often make billion-dollar decisions that chart the course of companies on the basis of a brief memo.  Sometimes clients need a long exegesis, but more often they are looking for a succinct, practical answer.  What should they do, and what are the costs and risks if they do not?

In my experience in house, the most effective outside counsel consistently demonstrated these ten behaviors regardless of their practice area, location, or background.  I encourage outside and in-house counsel to talk openly with each other about what behaviors are on the latter’s list.  All of us aspire to be capable lawyers who serve our clients well, and a shared understanding about what in-house counsel value and outside counsel are delivering is necessary for both to represent their client effectively.

article.title: Fresh Off $1.2 Billion IPO, AI Company Hires Ex-Expedia Exec as CLO
article.description: SentinelOne software company headquarters in Silicon Valley, California. Credit: Michael Vi/Shutterstock SentinelOne, a cybersecurity firm, said it was drawn to Keenan Conder's experience at high-growth companies. Conder formerly was general counsel…
article.text: SentinelOne software company headquarters in Silicon Valley, California. Credit: Michael Vi/Shutterstock SentinelOne, a cybersecurity firm, said it was drawn to Keenan Conder's experience at high-growth companies. Conder formerly was general counsel at both Expedia and Travelocity. SentinelOne is poised for continued growth after raising $1.2 billion in an IPO. Cybersecurity platform SentinelOne, which uses artificial intelligence to monitor personal computers and devices, announced Wednesday that it has appointed Keenan Conder as chief legal officer. Conder, most recently general counsel at Tableau Software and former GC at both Expedia and Travelocity, is joining the company just a few months after an IPO that raised $1.2 billion. Called the “largest cybersecurity IPO of all time” by Forbes, the offering is just the latest move in what Chief Operating Officer Nicholas Warner calls an explosive growth strategy.

article.title: 'Are You Respecting Their Dignity?': Employee-Surveillance Trend Deeply Splits Employers
article.description: What You Need to Know More than 500 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals weighed in on employee monitories in a new Littler Mendelson survey. The survey found 45% of companies were using employee surveillance and 41% were not and…
article.text: What You Need to Know More than 500 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals weighed in on employee monitories in a new Littler Mendelson survey. The survey found 45% of companies were using employee surveillance and 41% were not and weren't considering doing so. Surveillance was most prevalent at companies with more than 10,000 employees. From keystroke loggers to screenshot-capturing software and webcam eye-trackers, employee-monitoring tools have been on the rise since the COVID-19 pandemic drove white collar workers out of their cubicles and into home offices. But a new survey from Littler Mendelson found a deep divide among employers on whether the technologies are a good idea. The survey of 515 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals in the U.S. found 45% of companies are using them, but 41% are not and aren’t considering doing so. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • More than 500 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals weighed in on employee monitories in a new Littler Mendelson survey.
  • The survey found 45% of companies were using employee surveillance and 41% were not and weren't considering doing so.
  • Surveillance was most prevalent at companies with more than 10,000 employees.

From keystroke loggers to screenshot-capturing software and webcam eye-trackers, employee-monitoring tools have been on the rise since the COVID-19 pandemic drove white collar workers out of their cubicles and into home offices.

But a new survey from Littler Mendelson found a deep divide among employers on whether the technologies are a good idea. The survey of 515 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals in the U.S. found 45% of companies are using them, but 41% are not and aren’t considering doing so. Twelve percent are considering adoption, and 1% have made the decision to adopt but haven’t yet done so.

article.title: China Finalizes New Regulations to Relax Personal Data Exports
article.description: On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations. The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment.…
article.text: On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations. The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment. We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China. Nearly six months after the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) was first introduced for public consultation, with its draft regulations proposing to ease outbound data transfers from China (Draft Regulations) (see our article “China Releases Draft Regulation to Significantly Ease Cross-border Data Transfers,” Privacy World), the much-awaited final rules on Regulating and Facilitating Cross-border Data Flows were published and came into effect on March 22, 2024 (New Regulations). The New Regulations largely repeat the Draft Regulations, but now have further relaxed personal data exports from China. Exceptions to Signing Standard Contracts and Easing of Government Security Assessment Thresholds The New Regulations largely implement exceptions set forth in the Draft Regulations, permitting certain cross-border transfers of personal data from China without the need to sign or file a standard contract (SC) or file a personal information privacy impact assessment (PIPIA) with the CAC. However, as compared to the Draft Regulations, the New Regulations further lessen export obligations requiring SCs and PIPIA filings by increasing the threshold from 10,000 individuals to 100,000 individuals for non-sensitive data. The New Regulations also make important clarifications that are commonly of concern to multinational companies and businesses: Business/marketing/scientific data (other than personal data and important data) can be freely transferred.The specific list or catalogue of “important data” will be provided by the government, either through public announcement or notice to specific entities. Accordingly, businesses will not need to make a self-judgement as to whether they possess or process important data.Exports of personal data originally collected and generated outside of China, and then transferred into China for processing is exempted from a government security assessment, as well as the signing and filing of a standard contract, provided that no domestic personal data or important data is introduced during the processing.The validity period for a government security assessment is extended from two years to three years, with the possibility of extending the validity period for another three years.Free trade zones may establish whitelists to further relax data flows among applicable jurisdictions therein. The New Regulations took effect immediately upon their publication, i.e., March 24, 2024. We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China, including the categories and quantities of data transferred in each scenario described above to evaluate their compliance with New Regulations. Companies should also keep in mind that even if they are exempted from having to pass a government security assessment or sign and file a standard contract, they are still required to fulfill their ongoing statutory obligations of providing the requisite notifications to and obtaining individuals’ relevant consents, as well as conducting PIPIAs for their data transfer activities. We would advise that these compliance measures be properly documented to demonstrate accountability with the PIPL and New Regulations.
article.html:
• On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations.
  • The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment.
  • We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China.

Nearly six months after the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) was first introduced for public consultation, with its draft regulations proposing to ease outbound data transfers from China (Draft Regulations) (see our article “China Releases Draft Regulation to Significantly Ease Cross-border Data Transfers,” Privacy World), the much-awaited final rules on Regulating and Facilitating Cross-border Data Flows were published and came into effect on March 22, 2024 (New Regulations). The New Regulations largely repeat the Draft Regulations, but now have further relaxed personal data exports from China.

Exceptions to Signing Standard Contracts and Easing of Government Security Assessment Thresholds

The New Regulations largely implement exceptions set forth in the Draft Regulations, permitting certain cross-border transfers of personal data from China without the need to sign or file a standard contract (SC) or file a personal information privacy impact assessment (PIPIA) with the CAC. However, as compared to the Draft Regulations, the New Regulations further lessen export obligations requiring SCs and PIPIA filings by increasing the threshold from 10,000 individuals to 100,000 individuals for non-sensitive data.

The New Regulations also make important clarifications that are commonly of concern to multinational companies and businesses:

  • Business/marketing/scientific data (other than personal data and important data) can be freely transferred.
  • The specific list or catalogue of “important data” will be provided by the government, either through public announcement or notice to specific entities. Accordingly, businesses will not need to make a self-judgement as to whether they possess or process important data.
  • Exports of personal data originally collected and generated outside of China, and then transferred into China for processing is exempted from a government security assessment, as well as the signing and filing of a standard contract, provided that no domestic personal data or important data is introduced during the processing.
  • The validity period for a government security assessment is extended from two years to three years, with the possibility of extending the validity period for another three years.
  • Free trade zones may establish whitelists to further relax data flows among applicable jurisdictions therein.

The New Regulations took effect immediately upon their publication, i.e., March 24, 2024. We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China, including the categories and quantities of data transferred in each scenario described above to evaluate their compliance with New Regulations. Companies should also keep in mind that even if they are exempted from having to pass a government security assessment or sign and file a standard contract, they are still required to fulfill their ongoing statutory obligations of providing the requisite notifications to and obtaining individuals’ relevant consents, as well as conducting PIPIAs for their data transfer activities. We would advise that these compliance measures be properly documented to demonstrate accountability with the PIPL and New Regulations.

article.title: An In-House Revolution: Early Adopters of AI Reduce 'Rote Tasks,' Spend More Time on Strategy
article.description: Small and large legal departments are using generative AI in a broad range of ways, from summarizing documents to finding potential new sources of revenue. But so far those departments are in the minority; many are leery of embracing the technology.…
article.text: Small and large legal departments are using generative AI in a broad range of ways, from summarizing documents to finding potential new sources of revenue. But so far those departments are in the minority; many are leery of embracing the technology. Advocates of generative AI say the risk is manageable—and that those who remain on the sidelines risk falling behind. Generative artificial intelligence is triggering a range of emotions in legal departments—from anxiety to exhilaration—but early adopters already have reached an epiphany: It’s going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days. Whether they’re the only lawyer at their company or part of a department of 1,000, in-house counsel are putting tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Bard to use for more than just drafting contracts and legal memos. They’re using them to comb through vast repositories of data, summarize long, complicated legal documents and find opportunities to advance business.
article.html:
• Small and large legal departments are using generative AI in a broad range of ways, from summarizing documents to finding potential new sources of revenue.
  • But so far those departments are in the minority; many are leery of embracing the technology.
  • Advocates of generative AI say the risk is manageable—and that those who remain on the sidelines risk falling behind.

Generative artificial intelligence is triggering a range of emotions in legal departments—from anxiety to exhilaration—but early adopters already have reached an epiphany: It’s going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days.

Whether they’re the only lawyer at their company or part of a department of 1,000, in-house counsel are putting tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Bard to use for more than just drafting contracts and legal memos. They’re using them to comb through vast repositories of data, summarize long, complicated legal documents and find opportunities to advance business.

article.title: Teva CLO David Stark Moving On After Two Rough-and-Tumble Decades
article.description: David Stark, who spent his entire 21-year in-house career at Teva Pharmaceuticals, is stepping down as legal chief. Stark made the announcement on LinkedIn, saying he was ready after steering the company through several major settlements. Teva did…
article.text: David Stark, who spent his entire 21-year in-house career at Teva Pharmaceuticals, is stepping down as legal chief. Stark made the announcement on LinkedIn, saying he was ready after steering the company through several major settlements. Teva did not respond to a request for comment. Longtime Teva Pharmaceuticals legal chief David Stark is stepping down after 21 years at the Israeli drugmaker, the last seven of them at the helm of its global legal department as the company grappled with an onslaught of opioid litigation and criminal charges that it fixed the price of generic drugs. In a LinkedIn post, Stark said he has decided to part from Teva having resolved “extremely challenging matters.”
article.html:
• David Stark, who spent his entire 21-year in-house career at Teva Pharmaceuticals, is stepping down as legal chief.
  • Stark made the announcement on LinkedIn, saying he was ready after steering the company through several major settlements.
  • Teva did not respond to a request for comment.

Longtime Teva Pharmaceuticals legal chief David Stark is stepping down after 21 years at the Israeli drugmaker, the last seven of them at the helm of its global legal department as the company grappled with an onslaught of opioid litigation and criminal charges that it fixed the price of generic drugs.

In a LinkedIn post, Stark said he has decided to part from Teva having resolved “extremely challenging matters.”

article.title: Big Law Has 'False Sense of Security' as Clients Depart for Midsized Firms
article.description: Since the financial crisis of 2007-2008, "market power shifted decisively from law firms to the clients, rapidly moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market for legal services," a new report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law says. Thomson…
article.text: Since the financial crisis of 2007-2008, "market power shifted decisively from law firms to the clients, rapidly moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market for legal services," a new report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law says. Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law have released their 2024 legal market report. It notes that clients often don't inform Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred firms when they choose cheaper firms for new matters. That, plus the M&A boom that sustained Big Law for years, has obscured the extent of clients' move down market. Legal departments are aggressively shifting work from the Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred to less expensive law firms, a new study found, a trend that began to take root during the 2007-2008 financial crisis but was partly masked by a decadelong boom in transactional work. With M&A activity down sharply the past two years, the extent of the shift is only now coming into full focus, according to a new legal market report by Thomson Reuters and the Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession at Georgetown Law.
article.html:
Since the financial crisis of 2007-2008, "market power shifted decisively from law firms to the clients, rapidly moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market for legal services," a new report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law says.

  • Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law have released their 2024 legal market report.
  • It notes that clients often don't inform Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred firms when they choose cheaper firms for new matters.
  • That, plus the M&A boom that sustained Big Law for years, has obscured the extent of clients' move down market.

Legal departments are aggressively shifting work from the Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred to less expensive law firms, a new study found, a trend that began to take root during the 2007-2008 financial crisis but was partly masked by a decadelong boom in transactional work.

With M&A activity down sharply the past two years, the extent of the shift is only now coming into full focus, according to a new legal market report by Thomson Reuters and the Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession at Georgetown Law.

article.description: Rena Reiss joined Marriott International as general counsel in 2017. Since her arrival, Marriott has weathered the pandemic, massive data breaches, the death of a CEO and a $100 million defamation lawsuit. Before joining Marriott, Reiss was legal…
article.text: Rena Reiss joined Marriott International as general counsel in 2017. Since her arrival, Marriott has weathered the pandemic, massive data breaches, the death of a CEO and a $100 million defamation lawsuit. Before joining Marriott, Reiss was legal chief at Hyatt Hotels. With 12 years of general counsel experience under her belt, Rena Reiss is no stranger to crisis. In her five years as executive vice president and general counsel of Bethesda, Maryland-based Marriott International, where she leads a legal team of 120, Reiss has weathered a global pandemic, labor shortages, the death of a CEO, and a series of high-profile data breaches that exposed the personal information of some 500 million guests worldwide. article.title: What Every General Counsel Should Know Before Doing a Spin-Off
article.description: Spin-offs are an attractive option for a public company looking to rationalize its portfolio and unlock shareholder value. At the same time, they are monster transactions that play out over a long timeline, all under strict tax rules that impact…
article.text: Spin-offs are an attractive option for a public company looking to rationalize its portfolio and unlock shareholder value. At the same time, they are monster transactions that play out over a long timeline, all under strict tax rules that impact every step of the process. This article addresses what every GC should know when their Board starts talking about a spin-off. Spin-offs are an attractive option for a public company looking to rationalize its portfolio and unlock shareholder value. They are tax-efficient, do not depend on a pool of willing buyers or a strong IPO market, and allow a high degree of flexibility in defining the scope and terms of the separation. At the same time, they are monster transactions that play out over a long timeline, all under strict tax rules that impact every step of the process. Here is what every general counsel should know when their Board starts talking about a spin-off.

article.title: Factor, Top GCs Form Sense Collective to Create ‘Recipe Book’ for Corporate Gen AI Success
article.description: Earlier this month, integrated law company Factor joined forces with the general counsels of several global corporations to create The Sense Collective, a “collaboration community aimed at accelerating the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) in the…
article.text: Earlier this month, integrated law company Factor joined forces with the general counsels of several global corporations to create The Sense Collective, a “collaboration community aimed at accelerating the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) in the corporate legal realm,” according to a press release. The founding members of The Sense Collective, who have been vocal in leading the charge to bolster legal innovation through the use of generative AI, are Intel, DXC Technology, Microsoft, Adobe, Crowdstrike, Ford and Anglo American, while Factor is “facilitating and hosting” the collective. The goal of the collaboration, according to the release, is to “address common challenges across corporate legal teams,” given the “torrential speed” with which generative AI is transforming knowledge work and the “mounting expectations” for the technology across the legal industry.
