article.title: Former Political Refugee Exits Discover for Top Legal Post at Cantaloupe
article.description: What You Need to Know Payments company Cantaloupe has hired Anna Novoseletsky as chief legal and compliance officer. The company is rapidly expanding deployment of cashless self-service payment systems, including overseas. CEO Ravi Venkatesan says…
article.text: What You Need to Know Payments company Cantaloupe has hired Anna Novoseletsky as chief legal and compliance officer. The company is rapidly expanding deployment of cashless self-service payment systems, including overseas. CEO Ravi Venkatesan says Novoseletsky will help accelerate the international push. Fresh off a $41 million purchase of the self-checkout company Three Square Market, the cashless payments firm Cantaloupe just made another big acquisition: hiring veteran Discover Financial Services attorney Anna Novoseletsky as chief legal and compliance officer. Novoseletsky, who announced the move on LinkedIn on Tuesday, had been with Discover for 11 years. She started as head of the payment services legal advisory group before ascending the in-house ranks to become vice president and associate general counsel last year. At Discover, she advised senior executives on the risks surrounding its global business plans and helped set strategy in the payments business. article.text: On the stand at his fraud trial Wednesday, former Autonomy CEO Mike Lynch dismissed email evidence that presented a gloomy picture of his company’s finances leading up to its $11 billion sale to Hewlett-Packard in 2011. The emails, largely from finance chief Sushovan Hussain, offered a glimpse into the mad end-of-quarter rush to close deals, hit sales targets and realize revenue, a process that grew increasingly stressful between 2009 and 2011.

article.title: Ex-GC of Autonomy Says Accounting Turned Odd Before $11B Sale to HP
article.description: It was around 2007 when Joel Scott, then general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, started to get concerned about some of the business tactics being pushed by his employers. There were fishy transactions. For example,…
article.text: It was around 2007 when Joel Scott, then general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, started to get concerned about some of the business tactics being pushed by his employers. There were fishy transactions. For example, Autonomy held itself out as an enterprise software firm but had started covertly selling hardware. It also entered into transactions with resellers that didn’t quite make sense. Resellers would purchase Autonomy’s software without paying for it fully or selling to an end user, but Autonomy would record the deal as revenue.
article.html:
It was around 2007 when Joel Scott, then general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, started to get concerned about some of the business tactics being pushed by his employers.

It also entered into transactions with resellers that didn’t quite make sense. Resellers would purchase Autonomy’s software without paying for it fully or selling to an end user, but Autonomy would record the deal as revenue.

article.title: U.S. Senate Confirms Eumi Lee to California's Northern District Bench
article.description: A sharply divided U.S. Senate on Wednesday confirmed Eumi Lee to the U.S. District Court for Northern California, ending an eight-month process that required President Joe Biden to re-nominate the Alameda County trial judge. Lee was confirmed on a…
article.text: A sharply divided U.S. Senate on Wednesday confirmed Eumi Lee to the U.S. District Court for Northern California, ending an eight-month process that required President Joe Biden to re-nominate the Alameda County trial judge. Lee was confirmed on a largely partisan 50-49 vote. Sen. Joe Manchin, D-West Virginia, joined Republicans in voting no, and Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Oklahoma, did not vote. The former white-collar defense attorney and law school teacher is Biden’s 144th confirmed U.S. district court judge.
article.html:
A sharply divided U.S. Senate on Wednesday confirmed Eumi Lee to the U.S. District Court for Northern California, ending an eight-month process that required President Joe Biden to re-nominate the Alameda County trial judge.

Lee was confirmed on a largely partisan 50-49 vote. Sen. Joe Manchin, D-West Virginia, joined Republicans in voting no, and Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Oklahoma, did not vote. The former white-collar defense attorney and law school teacher is Biden’s 144th confirmed U.S. district court judge.

article.title: Startup Using Tech to Disrupt Health Care Fills Long-Vacant GC Post
article.description: Solera Health, a technology platform that matches patients with chronic health conditions to nonmedical wellness and disease-prevention programs, hired Zachary McBride as its general counsel. McBride was most recently associate general counsel at…
article.text: Solera Health, a technology platform that matches patients with chronic health conditions to nonmedical wellness and disease-prevention programs, hired Zachary McBride as its general counsel. McBride was most recently associate general counsel at Galileo, a venture capital-backed telehealth startup founded by doctors and focused on providing 24/7 mobile access to medical consultations and prescription services for common medical issues. He also spent nearly a decade in-house with the Boston-based health care nonprofit Commonwealth Care Alliance, where he was vice president and senior associate general counsel.

article.title: For In-House Lawyers Trying to Keep Up on AI Regulation, States Are Ground Zero
article.description: Federal artificial intelligence policy has seen a dizzying array of developments in recent months, from President Joe Biden’s executive order on AI safety signed last fall to Senate Majority Leader Chuck’s Schumer’s framework for AI regulation…
article.text: Federal artificial intelligence policy has seen a dizzying array of developments in recent months, from President Joe Biden’s executive order on AI safety signed last fall to Senate Majority Leader Chuck’s Schumer’s framework for AI regulation released this week. It can be overwhelming for in-house counsel trying to advise the business on the most-pressing twists and turns. In an online discussion on AI regulation hosted by In-House Connect Thursday, panelists said that, while in-house counsel need to monitor federal AI activity, they should keep a closer eye in the short term on the growing number of narrowly tailored state laws and how they might apply to specific company-use cases.

article.title: In Unredacted Filing, Former Twitter CLO Alleges Musk Bullied Board Ahead of Sale
article.description: A federal judge recently ordered the unsealing of previously redacted portions of a lawsuit filed in March by four former Twitter executives who claim Elon Musk bilked them out of severance. The unredacted complaint alleges that Musk, who wanted to…
article.text: A federal judge recently ordered the unsealing of previously redacted portions of a lawsuit filed in March by four former Twitter executives who claim Elon Musk bilked them out of severance. The unredacted complaint alleges that Musk, who wanted to back out of the deal, used his lawyers to intimidate the board into lowering the price for Twitter. Musk also allegedly wanted to fire every Twitter in-house lawyer who worked to enforce the deal. Incensed that he couldn’t back out of his agreement to buy Twitter, Elon Musk allegedly sought to fire every in-house lawyer who worked on the lawsuit to force him to close the deal and tried to intimidate the board of directors into lowering the purchase price, according to a newly unredacted complaint filed by lawyers representing its former legal chief, general counsel, CEO and CFO in a severance dispute. The new filing follows a May 31 order by U.S. District Senior Judge Maxine Chesney of the Northern District of California to unseal portions of the complaint that Musk and Twitter, now known as X Corp., had tried to keep private. Chesney found the majority of the redacted information was not confidential.
article.html:
• A federal judge recently ordered the unsealing of previously redacted portions of a lawsuit filed in March by four former Twitter executives who claim Elon Musk bilked them out of severance.
  • The unredacted complaint alleges that Musk, who wanted to back out of the deal, used his lawyers to intimidate the board into lowering the price for Twitter.
  • Musk also allegedly wanted to fire every Twitter in-house lawyer who worked to enforce the deal.

Incensed that he couldn’t back out of his agreement to buy Twitter, Elon Musk allegedly sought to fire every in-house lawyer who worked on the lawsuit to force him to close the deal and tried to intimidate the board of directors into lowering the purchase price, according to a newly unredacted complaint filed by lawyers representing its former legal chief, general counsel, CEO and CFO in a severance dispute.

The new filing follows a May 31 order by U.S. District Senior Judge Maxine Chesney of the Northern District of California to unseal portions of the complaint that Musk and Twitter, now known as X Corp., had tried to keep private. Chesney found the majority of the redacted information was not confidential.

article.title: Hiring From a Law Firm for an In-House Position? Use Caution
article.description: Within my niche practice of recruiting attorneys exclusively for companies, 90% of the lawyers my search firm has placed in the past four years came with current or previous in-house experience. Our mix of placement backgrounds was closer to 60/40…
article.text: Within my niche practice of recruiting attorneys exclusively for companies, 90% of the lawyers my search firm has placed in the past four years came with current or previous in-house experience. Our mix of placement backgrounds was closer to 60/40 just ten years ago, meaning almost half of our placements were lawyers moving into their first in-house position. I think this is a meaningful observation that speaks to change that has occurred on a boarder scale. Specifically, law firm career paths and in-house career paths are increasingly viewed as two divergent roads. It used to be much easier for a law firm Partner to move in-house as, to stay with the metaphor, the transition was viewed more as just changing lanes.
article.html:
Within my niche practice of recruiting attorneys exclusively for companies, 90% of the lawyers my search firm has placed in the past four years came with current or previous in-house experience.  Our mix of placement backgrounds was closer to 60/40 just ten years ago, meaning almost half of our placements were lawyers moving into their first in-house position.

I think this is a meaningful observation that speaks to change that has occurred on a boarder scale.  Specifically, law firm career paths and in-house career paths are increasingly viewed as two divergent roads.  It used to be much easier for a law firm Partner to move in-house as, to stay with the metaphor, the transition was viewed more as just changing lanes.

article.title: 'This Is Your Time': AI Gives In-House Counsel Unprecedented Leverage
article.description: Generative AI is giving in-house teams more leverage than ever before with outside counsel as the technology promises to allow them to insource even more work. In-house counsel spoke Wednesday at a legal tech conference in San Francisco about how…
article.text: Generative AI is giving in-house teams more leverage than ever before with outside counsel as the technology promises to allow them to insource even more work. In-house counsel spoke Wednesday at a legal tech conference in San Francisco about how they are using generative AI in everyday work. But the technology still has problems with accuracy, necessitating human review of its output. Startup founder and tech investor Zach Abramowitz has been hearing some version of the same story over the past few months: A law firm has a great relationship with a long-standing client, one that’s sent a steady stream of work to the firm for years. But now it has an artificial intelligence tool, and the amount of work sent to the firm has been cut in half. “At first I was a little bit skeptical. But I keep hearing it over and over again,” Abramowitz told a room full of in-house counsel and legal tech vendors at the Contemporary Jewish Museum in downtown San Francisco.
article.html:
• Generative AI is giving in-house teams more leverage than ever before with outside counsel as the technology promises to allow them to insource even more work.
  • In-house counsel spoke Wednesday at a legal tech conference in San Francisco about how they are using generative AI in everyday work.
  • But the technology still has problems with accuracy, necessitating human review of its output.

Startup founder and tech investor Zach Abramowitz has been hearing some version of the same story over the past few months: A law firm has a great relationship with a long-standing client, one that’s sent a steady stream of work to the firm for years. But now it has an artificial intelligence tool, and the amount of work sent to the firm has been cut in half.

“At first I was a little bit skeptical. But I keep hearing it over and over again,” Abramowitz told a room full of in-house counsel and legal tech vendors at the Contemporary Jewish Museum in downtown San Francisco.

article.title: ‘Perfection Is Highly Impractical': How Neiman Marcus' CLO Leads
article.description: "At the end of the day, no matter what the organizational goals are, no matter what my professional goals are, I have to live with myself. I have to look back on who I am as a person and be comfortable with that person," Neiman Marcus legal chief Tom…
article.text: "At the end of the day, no matter what the organizational goals are, no matter what my professional goals are, I have to live with myself. I have to look back on who I am as a person and be comfortable with that person," Neiman Marcus legal chief Tom Mattei said. Tom Mattei is the chief legal officer of Neiman Marcus. Mattei has been with Neiman Marcus for over four years. He wants his legacy to be consistent with what Tracy Preston and Hannah Kim built at Neiman Marcus. “Part of being a good leader is taking things that seem like really complex situations and distilling them and making them as simple as possible,” Neiman Marcus Chief Legal Officer Tom Mattei said. He said that, as a leader, he tries to bring the scale, acumen and skill of the legal department to help the company figure out the answers to questions.
article.html:
"At the end of the day, no matter what the organizational goals are, no matter what my professional goals are, I have to live with myself. I have to look back on who I am as a person and be comfortable with that person," Neiman Marcus legal chief Tom Mattei said.

  • Mattei has been with Neiman Marcus for over four years.
  • He wants his legacy to be consistent with what Tracy Preston and Hannah Kim built at Neiman Marcus.

article.title: Former Gartner GC Jules Kaufman's Exit Package Topped $1 Million
article.description: Gartner announced in July that Jules Kaufman would cease to be its general counsel on Sept. 1, though he served in an on-call capacity until his last official day of employment on Feb. 15, 2023 Kaufman was given an exit package of a little more than…
article.text: Gartner announced in July that Jules Kaufman would cease to be its general counsel on Sept. 1, though he served in an on-call capacity until his last official day of employment on Feb. 15, 2023 Kaufman was given an exit package of a little more than $1 million. Kaufman's replacement Thomas Kim took the legal reins on April 17. Former Gartner general counsel Jules Kaufman was paid a little over $1 million when he left the firm in February, the management consultancy’s latest proxy statement reveals. His exit package included 52 weeks of salary totaling $535,600, a pro-rated target bonus of $365,360, and $51,500 in unused vacation days totaling $1,001,465. The payout, on top of his regular salary and $1,475,729 in stock awards, brought his total compensation for 2022 to $3.6 million. This content has been archived. The Federal Trade Commission is taking a tougher stance on companies that fail to safeguard consumer data—and is even going so far as to hold individuals personally accountable for those failings. Two recent cases demonstrate the agency’s willingness to go after individuals. In early October, a federal jury convicted former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan of concealing a 2016 data breach from law enforcement and obstructing an investigation by the FTC into Uber’s security practices. A federal judge will hear his motion for acquittal next month. The FTC late last month penalized alcohol delivery platform Drizly and its CEO, James Cory Rellas, for a data breach that exposed the personal information of 2.5 million customers. The order personally applies to Rellas. Should he go to another company that collects consumer information, he’d have to follow additional data-security requirements. “CEOs who take shortcuts on security should take note,” Samuel Levine, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, warned in a statement. “I think there is a gradually developing trend to hold senior officials personally accountable,” said former FTC chairman William Kovacic, now a professor at the George Washington University School of Law. “The source of the trend comes foremost from the concern that the traditional approach, which has emphasized institutional accountability, fails to create incentives for effective compliance.” He said the movement has been accelerated in part by the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the commission imposed a hefty $5 billion fine and other restrictions on Facebook for collecting and selling users’ personal data. While the FTC did not name CEO Mark Zuckerberg, it required him to periodically certify the company’s compliance with the privacy reforms outlined in its order or face civil and criminal penalties. “I think as we carry this ahead, when the government imposes remedies and accepts settlements though negotiation, these kinds of provisions that require the CEO to sign … are going to be more common,” Kovacic said. The FTC’s order against Drizly carried no fines but threatened Rellas and the company with financial sanctions if they fail to destroy unnecessary customer data or fail to limit data collection and protect against future data breaches. In his statement, the FTC’s Levine said the agency’s action “ensures the CEO faces consequences for the company’s carelessness.” RECOMMENDED FOR YOU Book Corporate Privileges and Confidential Information Corporate Privileges and Confidential Information is designed to assist inside and outside counsel in negotiating obstacles to maintaining corporate secrecy. View This Book The fact the order would follow Rellas to other employers sends a powerful signal to executives, legal observers said. “The issue here generally is what happens if the guy who runs Drizly leaves for somewhere else and runs another company that has very lax security,” said David Vladeck, director of Georgetown Law’s Center on Privacy and Technology. “You want that person to be responsible, even if he is no longer with the company that got into trouble. That is one reason why there have been, in what the FTC thinks are egregious cases, good reasons to put a CEO or senior official under an order.” Vladek said the internal debate on whether to hold CEOs personally liable isn’t settled. In the Drizly case, Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented from the part of the settlement that applies to Rellas, writing, “CEOs have hundreds of issues and numerous regulatory obligations to navigate. Companies, not federal regulators, are better positioned to evaluate what risks require the regular attention of a CEO.” Chair Lina Khan responded, “Overseeing a big company is not an excuse to subordinate legal duties in favor of other priorities. The FTC has a role to play in making sure a company’s legal obligations are weighed in the boardroom.” She added that the order and settlement “sends a very clear message: Protecting Americans’ data is not discretionary. It must be a priority for any chief executive. If anything, it only grows more important as a firm grows.” Kovacic said naming an individual puts an immediate spotlight on the human beings behind the corporation. “It’s called naming and shaming,” he said. “It says, this didn’t just happen. It happened because you failed. This is your fault, and any sanctions that may be imposed may fall on you personally.” But Vladeck says the commission is still debating the issue. “If you put an individual under order, what’s really the point? Yes, you’ve embarrassed this person, but the question is, ‘Is this adding to deterrence?’ There is a legitimate disagreement in the commission on that issue.” Vladeck said when he served as the director of the commission’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, “there were a few cases where there was a robust discussion on the commission about whether that adds to deterrence and whether conduct by the CEO was concerning enough to have an order that explicitly put the CEO in the crosshairs. “It’s a very public debate. I don’t think the FTC has landed on a position that has yielded unanimity. But there will be more attention paid to making senior corporate officials respondents in FTC consent orders.” He noted that lax security had been a persistent problem for Drizly. “There were weaknesses they were well aware of and they didn’t do anything to forestall a breach,” Vladeck said, adding that companies who fail to adequately fund cybersecurity will draw the most attention from regulators. “It may be cheaper for a company to endure a data breach than to have more robust security. Most of the cases the FTC pursues they are companies not investing in data security at all.” While executives may be tempted to hand off the data security and compliance issues to subordinates, they could still be blamed if anything goes wrong. “The job of senior leadership is to put in place incentives and structures to make sure people obey the law,” Kovacic said, raising the analogy of admiral Hyman G. Rickover, who oversaw the development of naval nuclear propulsion and, to lead by example, made a point of being aboard during test dives of every nuclear submarine under construction. “The best way is to single out senior leaders and say, ‘This is your job.’” “I think the majority of the commission believes that the only way you’re going to get adequate senior leadership’s attention to these issues is to say, ‘If it doesn’t work it’s your fault,’” he said. Legal chiefs also could be targets for censure if companies shirk their compliance responsibilities. “Anybody in a position of leadership who creates and builds the human and organizational structures that ensure compliance, it’s your job to make sure it works,” Kovacic said. He said it’s not enough for a general counsel to say, “‘the headstrong CEO wouldn’t listen to me.’ If you’re as smart as you say you are, find a way to get your message across. One thing that does help lawyers in-house to be effective is having powerful examples of what happened to somebody else.”

What You Need to Know

  • In two recent cases, the FTC held a senior leader accountable for a company's lax data security.
  • A recent action against the CEO of Drizly would follow him to other employers.
  • A debate is raging within the FTC on the approach.

The Federal Trade Commission is taking a tougher stance on companies that fail to safeguard consumer data—and is even going so far as to hold individuals personally accountable for those failings.

Two recent cases demonstrate the agency’s willingness to go after individuals. In early October, a federal jury convicted former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan of concealing a 2016 data breach from law enforcement and obstructing an investigation by the FTC into Uber’s security practices. A federal judge will hear his motion for acquittal next month.

The FTC late last month penalized alcohol delivery platform Drizly and its CEO, James Cory Rellas, for a data breach that exposed the personal information of 2.5 million customers. The order personally applies to Rellas. Should he go to another company that collects consumer information, he’d have to follow additional data-security requirements. “CEOs who take shortcuts on security should take note,” Samuel Levine, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, warned in a statement.

“I think there is a gradually developing trend to hold senior officials personally accountable,” said former FTC chairman William Kovacic, now a professor at the George Washington University School of Law. “The source of the trend comes foremost from the concern that the traditional approach, which has emphasized institutional accountability, fails to create incentives for effective compliance.”

He said the movement has been accelerated in part by the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the commission imposed a hefty $5 billion fine and other restrictions on Facebook for collecting and selling users’ personal data. While the FTC did not name CEO Mark Zuckerberg, it required him to periodically certify the company’s compliance with the privacy reforms outlined in its order or face civil and criminal penalties.

“I think as we carry this ahead, when the government imposes remedies and accepts settlements though negotiation, these kinds of provisions that require the CEO to sign … are going to be more common,” Kovacic said.

The FTC’s order against Drizly carried no fines but threatened Rellas and the company with financial sanctions if they fail to destroy unnecessary customer data or fail to limit data collection and protect against future data breaches. In his statement, the FTC’s Levine said the agency’s action “ensures the CEO faces consequences for the company’s carelessness.”

The fact the order would follow Rellas to other employers sends a powerful signal to executives, legal observers said. “The issue here generally is what happens if the guy who runs Drizly leaves for somewhere else and runs another company that has very lax security,” said David Vladeck, director of Georgetown Law’s Center on Privacy and Technology. “You want that person to be responsible, even if he is no longer with the company that got into trouble. That is one reason why there have been, in what the FTC thinks are egregious cases, good reasons to put a CEO or senior official under an order.” Vladek said the internal debate on whether to hold CEOs personally liable isn’t settled. In the Drizly case, Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented from the part of the settlement that applies to Rellas, writing, “CEOs have hundreds of issues and numerous regulatory obligations to navigate. Companies, not federal regulators, are better positioned to evaluate what risks require the regular attention of a CEO.” Chair Lina Khan responded, “Overseeing a big company is not an excuse to subordinate legal duties in favor of other priorities. The FTC has a role to play in making sure a company’s legal obligations are weighed in the boardroom.” She added that the order and settlement “sends a very clear message: Protecting Americans’ data is not discretionary. It must be a priority for any chief executive. If anything, it only grows more important as a firm grows.” Kovacic said naming an individual puts an immediate spotlight on the human beings behind the corporation. “It’s called naming and shaming,” he said. “It says, this didn’t just happen. It happened because you failed. This is your fault, and any sanctions that may be imposed may fall on you personally.” But Vladeck says the commission is still debating the issue. “If you put an individual under order, what’s really the point? Yes, you’ve embarrassed this person, but the question is, ‘Is this adding to deterrence?’ There is a legitimate disagreement in the commission on that issue.” Vladeck said when he served as the director of the commission’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, “there were a few cases where there was a robust discussion on the commission about whether that adds to deterrence and whether conduct by the CEO was concerning enough to have an order that explicitly put the CEO in the crosshairs. “It’s a very public debate. I don’t think the FTC has landed on a position that has yielded unanimity. But there will be more attention paid to making senior corporate officials respondents in FTC consent orders.” He noted that lax security had been a persistent problem for Drizly. “There were weaknesses they were well aware of and they didn’t do anything to forestall a breach,” Vladeck said, adding that companies who fail to adequately fund cybersecurity will draw the most attention from regulators. “It may be cheaper for a company to endure a data breach than to have more robust security. Most of the cases the FTC pursues they are companies not investing in data security at all.” While executives may be tempted to hand off the data security and compliance issues to subordinates, they could still be blamed if anything goes wrong. “The job of senior leadership is to put in place incentives and structures to make sure people obey the law,” Kovacic said, raising the analogy of admiral Hyman G. Legal chiefs also could be targets for censure if companies shirk their compliance responsibilities. “Anybody in a position of leadership who creates and builds the human and organizational structures that ensure compliance, it’s your job to make sure it works,” Kovacic said. He said it’s not enough for a general counsel to say, “‘the headstrong CEO wouldn’t listen to me.’ If you’re as smart as you say you are, find a way to get your message across. One thing that does help lawyers in-house to be effective is having powerful examples of what happened to somebody else.”

article.title: 'A Huge Shift': Job-Hunting Attorneys Turn to Stable Companies, Cash Over Stock Options
article.description: What You Need to Know Sexy startups have lost some of their allure.Candidates worry they'll be out of a job if funding dries up.Some in-house attorneys are considering going back to law firms. Top in-house lawyers in the job market are ratcheting…
article.text: What You Need to Know Sexy startups have lost some of their allure.Candidates worry they'll be out of a job if funding dries up.Some in-house attorneys are considering going back to law firms. Top in-house lawyers in the job market are ratcheting down their appetite for risk, favoring stable, less flashy companies as economic headwinds buffet the tech industry and venture-backed startups. Recruiters say candidates also are seeking more of their compensation in cash instead of stock options. Options can soar if a company hits it big. But many recent grants have slid underwater, amid falling tech stock prices and declining valuations at startups. “Those fly-by-night, Series A companies people would quit their law firm jobs for—no one is quitting for them now,” said Sean Burke, founding partner of the boutique legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. “There’s definitely right now a huge shift toward prioritizing security and maybe going with a resume builder that has a higher base salary or stock at an actual public company, and not options,” he said. The tech industry has long made equity a significant part of compensation packages, an approach that often makes attorneys, many of them risk-averse by nature, uneasy even in brighter economic environments. That anxiety is even higher these days, recruiters say. “Stock is certainly something candidates think about and worry about as they think about an opportunity. If the company sounds promising and they aren’t as competitive on the cash, sometimes candidates are willing to take a risk on the equity. But given what the current market is, candidates have been a little more hesitant,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “Especially at private companies, candidates are going to be doing as much due diligence as possible every step of the way because it is a real concern that they may be out of the job if there’s not a lot of funding,” Guo said. Mike Evers, president of Evers Legal Search, said job candidates continue to find tech jobs alluring. But the last year has been sobering, amid a deluge of job cuts. Layoffs.fyi tallies that 898 tech companies have laid off 142,942 employees this year. “Nothing has changed with the startup culture, but they are risky and your equity might end up being worthless and you might end up out of a job. The last 12 months have told us that risk is real, and a lot of lawyers have hunkered down into the mindset of risk aversion,” he said. Evers said he recently received a call from an attorney at the e-scooter startup Bird, famous for achieving unicorn status when its valuation hit $1 billion in 2018. But its meteoric rise preceded a swift decent. After going public last year through a special purpose acquisition company merger, its stock has fallen from $8.40 to 23 cents. Evers said positions at startups such as Bird that offered employees a chunk of equity have lost much of their luster. “One of the attorneys who left a major law firm to take one of those sexy, highly competitive jobs just made a change to go work in the legal department at United Airlines. You can’t get more opposite than that,” he said. “We’re now seeing that not every startup situation is a golden job,” he added. “The desire to take those sexy jobs hasn’t changed, but we’re in a period where there are less of them, and there are some lawyers who are proactively looking for exit strategies from startups.” Burke said the challenging environment for tech companies also is spurring lawyers who earlier jumped from law firms to in-house to consider returning to law firms. “Right now there’s more than one IP transaction or SAS licensing attorney who is saying to themselves, ‘I’m working 60-80 hours a week, I’m making less than at a law firm, and now I have stock options that are worth nothing,” he said. “Law firms are steady money, it’s guaranteed, there’s more of a safety net,” he said. “And law firms with tech clients love a lawyer that used to work for a startup, because it shows they are a problem solver—a Wild West lawyer who has handled all kinds of different things. That in-house experience is proof that you’re a bad ass.”

  • Candidates worry they'll be out of a job if funding dries up.
  • Some in-house attorneys are considering going back to law firms.

Recruiters say candidates also are seeking more of their compensation in cash instead of stock options. Options can soar if a company hits it big. But many recent grants have slid underwater, amid falling tech stock prices and declining valuations at startups.

“Those fly-by-night, Series A companies people would quit their law firm jobs for—no one is quitting for them now,” said Sean Burke, founding partner of the boutique legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners.

The tech industry has long made equity a significant part of compensation packages, an approach that often makes attorneys, many of them risk-averse by nature, uneasy even in brighter economic environments.

That anxiety is even higher these days, recruiters say.

“Stock is certainly something candidates think about and worry about as they think about an opportunity. If the company sounds promising and they aren’t as competitive on the cash, sometimes candidates are willing to take a risk on the equity. But given what the current market is, candidates have been a little more hesitant,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco.

“Especially at private companies, candidates are going to be doing as much due diligence as possible every step of the way because it is a real concern that they may be out of the job if there’s not a lot of funding,” Guo said.

Mike Evers, president of Evers Legal Search, said job candidates continue to find tech jobs alluring. But the last year has been sobering, amid a deluge of job cuts. Layoffs.fyi tallies that 898 tech companies have laid off 142,942 employees this year.

article.title: Law Firms Risk Bad Optics With Lavish Year-End Bonuses
article.description: What You Need to Know Major law firm bonus announcements may strike their in-house clients as tone-deaf.In-house counsel say associates may deserve bonuses, but firms should be aware of the optics amid rate hikes.Firms should remain client-centric in…
article.text: What You Need to Know Major law firm bonus announcements may strike their in-house clients as tone-deaf.In-house counsel say associates may deserve bonuses, but firms should be aware of the optics amid rate hikes.Firms should remain client-centric in their business decisions, one expert says. In-house legal chiefs already bristling at outside counsel rate hikes may find themselves chafing at Big Law’s rollout of year-end bonuses, many in the six-figure range for eighth year associates. While these events are hardly unexpected, they are also playing out amid widespread tech industry layoffs and an undercurrent of economic precarity that lends an air of insouciance to this year’s parade of bonus announcements. “Law firms face serious pressures to attract and retain talent that is of appropriate quality, and they’re certainly entitled to compensate their professionals appropriately. No one is going to debate that fact. The bigger issue is the context. Many in-house counsel are struggling to retain their teams and they’re only allowed to give out meager pay increases and modest bonuses, so it strikes many reasonable people as just not fair,” said Jason Winmill, managing partner at Argopoint, a consulting firm that advises Fortune 500 legal departments. Shrinking budgets already have legal departments on edge, especially as general counsel are being asked to take on more responsibilities without commensurate pay raises. Frederick Paulmann, a former senior attorney at Pfizer Inc. and founder of The Counsel Management Group, said associate bonuses could be regarded as a questionable decision, given both the general economic climate and reports of law firm and tech industry layoffs. “Against this backdrop, it is by no means clear that associate bonus decisions will sit well with clients,” he said. It could also leave in-house clients wondering whether they’re footing the bill. “A key related question that often occurs but doesn’t always get asked is how are the bonuses funded – from partners’ pockets or on the backs of clients? If law firms choose to issue bonuses, and at the same time are committing to no rate increases into next year, then that’s a much different story. This is especially true if they have found other ways to save, whether it be shrinking their real estate footprint or using technology more effectively. But if law firms seek to grant these bonuses, and at the same time are planning on significant rate increases to fund compensation, then that would not sit as well,” Paulmann said. Some legal chiefs said they didn’t mind the bonuses so much, but noted that excessive base pay for junior associates is often a main driver of high legal bills, particularly when in-house lawyers with years of experience usually make less than lower-level associates. Generous bonus awards have the dual function of retaining top legal talent while signaling a firm’s success and prestige. In-house counsel with outside law firm experience said they understood that the publicity around year-end bonuses can be an incentive for associates who work long hours on high-risk matters. “The announcement of year-end bonuses doesn’t concern me. I come from Big Law myself, so I understand that publishing year-end bonuses is a part of associate talent attraction and retention. I also think that associates that work hard should be rewarded,” said Stephen Mar, general counsel of software startup Odeko. “At the same time, I do think that law firms should be aware of the optics—and potential collateral consequences—of raising rates at the same time they are announcing lofty bonuses and record profits.” Mar said alternative fee agreements are one way outside counsel can maintain good relationships with in-house clients and help them manage costs. “In-house counsel are being asked to take a hard look at their outside counsel budgets, and so increasing rates may have the unintended effect of general counsels bringing more work in-house and sending less of it to firms. One potential solution, and one I recommend every chance I get, is for firms to be more proactive about working with their in-house counterparts on alternative fee arrangements. Done correctly, AFAs can account for clients’ cost sensitivities and ultimately lead to win-win solutions for firms and their clients,” he said. Paulmann, whose data analytics firm helps companies reduce their legal fees, said law firms should consider the long term reverberations of both rate increases and bonus announcements noting that the best-managed companies remain client-focused when making internal business decisions. “As their challenges mount and clients are forced to make tougher spending decisions, the optics of associate bonuses now may not hold up well under scrutiny. Some firms may respond—but clients continue to pay, and they still call. But again, just because they have done so up to now does not mean they will continue to do so in the future,” he said. “It’s important to think carefully about these bonuses and rate increases, because decisions that clients view as tone deaf can come back to bite.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Major law firm bonus announcements may strike their in-house clients as tone-deaf.
  • In-house counsel say associates may deserve bonuses, but firms should be aware of the optics amid rate hikes.
  • Firms should remain client-centric in their business decisions, one expert says.

In-house legal chiefs already bristling at outside counsel rate hikes may find themselves chafing at Big Law’s rollout of year-end bonuses, many in the six-figure range for eighth year associates. While these events are hardly unexpected, they are also playing out amid widespread tech industry layoffs and an undercurrent of economic precarity that lends an air of insouciance to this year’s parade of bonus announcements.

“Law firms face serious pressures to attract and retain talent that is of appropriate quality, and they’re certainly entitled to compensate their professionals appropriately. No one is going to debate that fact. The bigger issue is the context. Many in-house counsel are struggling to retain their teams and they’re only allowed to give out meager pay increases and modest bonuses, so it strikes many reasonable people as just not fair,” said Jason Winmill, managing partner at Argopoint, a consulting firm that advises Fortune 500 legal departments.

Shrinking budgets already have legal departments on edge, especially as general counsel are being asked to take on more responsibilities without commensurate pay raises.

Frederick Paulmann, a former senior attorney at Pfizer Inc. and founder of The Counsel Management Group, said associate bonuses could be regarded as a questionable decision, given both the general economic climate and reports of law firm and tech industry layoffs.

“Against this backdrop, it is by no means clear that associate bonus decisions will sit well with clients,” he said.

It could also leave in-house clients wondering whether they’re footing the bill.

“A key related question that often occurs but doesn’t always get asked is how are the bonuses funded – from partners’ pockets or on the backs of clients? If law firms choose to issue bonuses, and at the same time are committing to no rate increases into next year, then that’s a much different story. This is especially true if they have found other ways to save, whether it be shrinking their real estate footprint or using technology more effectively. But if law firms seek to grant these bonuses, and at the same time are planning on significant rate increases to fund compensation, then that would not sit as well,” Paulmann said.

Some legal chiefs said they didn’t mind the bonuses so much, but noted that excessive base pay for junior associates is often a main driver of high legal bills, particularly when in-house lawyers with years of experience usually make less than lower-level associates.

Generous bonus awards have the dual function of retaining top legal talent while signaling a firm’s success and prestige. In-house counsel with outside law firm experience said they understood that the publicity around year-end bonuses can be an incentive for associates who work long hours on high-risk matters.

“The announcement of year-end bonuses doesn’t concern me. I come from Big Law myself, so I understand that publishing year-end bonuses is a part of associate talent attraction and retention. I also think that associates that work hard should be rewarded,” said Stephen Mar, general counsel of software startup Odeko. “At the same time, I do think that law firms should be aware of the optics—and potential collateral consequences—of raising rates at the same time they are announcing lofty bonuses and record profits.”

Mar said alternative fee agreements are one way outside counsel can maintain good relationships with in-house clients and help them manage costs.

“In-house counsel are being asked to take a hard look at their outside counsel budgets, and so increasing rates may have the unintended effect of general counsels bringing more work in-house and sending less of it to firms. One potential solution, and one I recommend every chance I get, is for firms to be more proactive about working with their in-house counterparts on alternative fee arrangements. Done correctly, AFAs can account for clients’ cost sensitivities and ultimately lead to win-win solutions for firms and their clients,” he said.

Paulmann, whose data analytics firm helps companies reduce their legal fees, said law firms should consider the long term reverberations of both rate increases and bonus announcements noting that the best-managed companies remain client-focused when making internal business decisions.

“As their challenges mount and clients are forced to make tougher spending decisions, the optics of associate bonuses now may not hold up well under scrutiny. Some firms may respond—but clients continue to pay, and they still call. But again, just because they have done so up to now does not mean they will continue to do so in the future,” he said. “It’s important to think carefully about these bonuses and rate increases, because decisions that clients view as tone deaf can come back to bite.”

article.title: US Judge Disinclined to Overturn Former Uber Security Chief's Conviction in Data Breach Case
article.description: "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in…
article.text: "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in 2016. What You Need to Know A jury found former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan guilty of covering up a 2016 data breach.Sullivan is seeking acquittal or a new trial, and his attorneys argue he had no duty to report the breach to regulators investigating the company's security practices.Sullivan's prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach. A federal judge said Wednesday that he’s inclined to uphold a jury verdict finding former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan guilty of trying to cover up a 2016 data breach, a conviction that rocked the cybersecurity community in October. Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber’s Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver’s license numbers. Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Dawson said Sullivan orchestrated the cover-up and hid it from both his employers and the Federal Trade Commission, which was investigating Uber’s data security practices in the wake of a different data breach in 2014. Sullivan met with Federal Trade Commission regulators investigating Uber’s security practices in 2016, assuring them that Uber had addressed the security vulnerabilities that led up to the 2014 breach, such as reusing passwords and storing data access keys on a public GitHub page. Just 10 days later, hackers breached Uber’s AWS servers a second time in a similar fashion. Dawson said that knowing the second hack would “play very badly” with regulators, Sullivan bought the two hackers off with a payment of $100,000 and funneled it through Uber’s bug-bounty program. “Sullivan knew exactly what he had done. He covered up a data breach, he covered up a crime and he obstructed the FTC’s effort to safeguard user data,” Dawson told the jury, describing Sullivan’s actions as “comprehensive and calculated.” Sullivan also signed off on a letter proposing that the FTC close its two-year investigation and enter into a settlement agreement. “Joe was supportive of proceeding with the recommendation to settle,” former in-house attorney Sabrina Ross testified at the trial. Sullivan was fired in 2017, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at trial. In 2020 the ex-security chief was charged with one count of obstructing the FTC’s investigation and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. His prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach. Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts specializing in cybersecurity and incident response, said it is rare for the government to charge someone with taking affirmative steps to conceal a felony, but prosecutors could feel emboldened by Sullivan’s conviction. “The fact that it was used here—and used successfully—should make any in-house counsel for any company perk their ears up,” Baker told ALM. “There’s a very interesting legal precedent that will create ripples from a compliance perspective.” At a hearing Wednesday on Sullivan’s motion for acquittal or a new trial, his attorney John Cline argued that the government failed to show Sullivan had a duty to disclose the breach, and that prosecutors made only a general contention that Uber’s in-house counsel relied on Sullivan and his team to keep them updated on any significant security developments that would require disclosure. U.S. District Judge William Orrick, who presided over the nearly monthlong jury trial in September, was unconvinced. “I think there was more than sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction,” he said. Dawson said there was much more to Sullivan’s obstructive actions than mere omission. “There’s misrepresentation, there’s concealment, there’s hush money, there’s a variety of obstructive acts and the Ninth Circuit has recognized the variety with which obstruction can be accomplished,” he said. “I would urge the court not to get caught up in just the omission slice. There was a more comprehensive strategy rather than sitting in a corner and staying silent.” Cline said he plans to appeal the conviction and will likely rely on the Ninth Circuit’s recent ruling in United States v. Kirst to support the argument that Sullivan did not make affirmative misrepresentations to the FTC, and that simply failing to inform authorities of the breach is not enough to support a conviction. “We’re flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal,” he told Orrick. The judge replied, “well-flexed,” and took the arguments under submission.
article.html:
"We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in 2016.

What You Need to Know

  • A jury found former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan guilty of covering up a 2016 data breach.
  • Sullivan is seeking acquittal or a new trial, and his attorneys argue he had no duty to report the breach to regulators investigating the company's security practices.
  • Sullivan's prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach.

A federal judge said Wednesday that he’s inclined to uphold a jury verdict finding former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan guilty of trying to cover up a 2016 data breach, a conviction that rocked the cybersecurity community in October.

Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber’s Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver’s license numbers.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Dawson said Sullivan orchestrated the cover-up and hid it from both his employers and the Federal Trade Commission, which was investigating Uber’s data security practices in the wake of a different data breach in 2014.

Sullivan met with Federal Trade Commission regulators investigating Uber’s security practices in 2016, assuring them that Uber had addressed the security vulnerabilities that led up to the 2014 breach, such as reusing passwords and storing data access keys on a public GitHub page.

Just 10 days later, hackers breached Uber’s AWS servers a second time in a similar fashion.

Dawson said that knowing the second hack would “play very badly” with regulators, Sullivan bought the two hackers off with a payment of $100,000 and funneled it through Uber’s bug-bounty program. “Sullivan knew exactly what he had done. He covered up a data breach, he covered up a crime and he obstructed the FTC’s effort to safeguard user data,” Dawson told the jury, describing Sullivan’s actions as “comprehensive and calculated.” Sullivan also signed off on a letter proposing that the FTC close its two-year investigation and enter into a settlement agreement. “Joe was supportive of proceeding with the recommendation to settle,” former in-house attorney Sabrina Ross testified at the trial.

Sullivan was fired in 2017, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at trial. In 2020 the ex-security chief was charged with one count of obstructing the FTC’s investigation and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. His prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach.

Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts specializing in cybersecurity and incident response, said it is rare for the government to charge someone with taking affirmative steps to conceal a felony, but prosecutors could feel emboldened by Sullivan’s conviction.

“The fact that it was used here—and used successfully—should make any in-house counsel for any company perk their ears up,” Baker told ALM. “There’s a very interesting legal precedent that will create ripples from a compliance perspective.”

At a hearing Wednesday on Sullivan’s motion for acquittal or a new trial, his attorney John Cline argued that the government failed to show Sullivan had a duty to disclose the breach, and that prosecutors made only a general contention that Uber’s in-house counsel relied on Sullivan and his team to keep them updated on any significant security developments that would require disclosure.

U.S. District Judge William Orrick, who presided over the nearly monthlong jury trial in September, was unconvinced. “I think there was more than sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction,” he said.

Dawson said there was much more to Sullivan’s obstructive actions than mere omission. “There’s misrepresentation, there’s concealment, there’s hush money, there’s a variety of obstructive acts and the Ninth Circuit has recognized the variety with which obstruction can be accomplished,” he said. “I would urge the court not to get caught up in just the omission slice. There was a more comprehensive strategy rather than sitting in a corner and staying silent.”

Cline said he plans to appeal the conviction and will likely rely on the Ninth Circuit’s recent ruling in United States v. Kirst to support the argument that Sullivan did not make affirmative misrepresentations to the FTC, and that simply failing to inform authorities of the breach is not enough to support a conviction.

“We’re flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal,” he told Orrick.

The judge replied, “well-flexed,” and took the arguments under submission.

article.title: In-House Counsel Expect Diversity From Law Firms. New Research Says They Aren't Getting It
article.description: “We’re expecting firms to find a way to get out there and find, groom and support diverse and inclusive talent. Companies are definitely watching," Ginny Johnson, chief legal officer of Aspen Aerogels, said. A new Burford Capital survey says legal…
article.text: “We’re expecting firms to find a way to get out there and find, groom and support diverse and inclusive talent. Companies are definitely watching," Ginny Johnson, chief legal officer of Aspen Aerogels, said. A new Burford Capital survey says legal departments want diversity in their outside attorneys but are inconsistent in setting expectations. In-house lawyers want law firms to provide diverse associates more opportunities to interact with clients in low-pressure settings. Law firms giving short shrift to nurturing diverse talent risk losing business. When Ericsson’s legal department needed outside counsel to conduct an investigation, it hired a law firm that touted its bilingual capabilities and claimed to have partners who could conduct interviews in Spanish. But when the interview took place, Ericsson’s in-house team was shocked to see it led entirely in English by a white partner while a Spanish-speaking associate sat silent. Such was the story relayed at a panel discussion on in-house and outside counsel relationships last month at the Women, Influence & Power in Law conference in New Orleans, where in-house lawyers spoke candidly about how law firms are often all words and no substance on diversity.

article.title: Shein Loses U.S. General Counsel as It Fights Flurry of Litigation, Preps for IPO
article.description: Valerie Ho, the top U.S. lawyer for online fast-fashion giant Shein has left the company, a spokesperson confirmed to Law.com Tuesday. Ho had been with Singapore-based company since 2021 and worked on crafting its global legal and compliance…
article.text: Valerie Ho, the top U.S. lawyer for online fast-fashion giant Shein has left the company, a spokesperson confirmed to Law.com Tuesday. Ho had been with Singapore-based company since 2021 and worked on crafting its global legal and compliance structure. She previously was a shareholder at Greenberg Traurig, where she advised on IP issues and represented clients in copyright, patent and trademark disputes, according to a biography provided by Stanford Law School when Ho spoke at a conference there last year. The biography noted that Ho, who is based in Los Angeles, was Shein’s primary outside counsel before she became its U.S. general counsel.

article.title: As Litigation Demand Soared, DC Boutiques Saw Strong Business Year
article.description: Firm leaders at Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll, Zuckerman Spaeder, and Hollingsworth reported 2023 as a solid year. D.C.-based litigation boutiques represented clients such as CVS, Amgen and Microsoft in matters last year. Demand in the litigation…
article.text: Firm leaders at Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll, Zuckerman Spaeder, and Hollingsworth reported 2023 as a solid year. D.C.-based litigation boutiques represented clients such as CVS, Amgen and Microsoft in matters last year. Demand in the litigation practice was up 3.2% last year, according to the latest report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law. Leaders of several Washington, D.C.-based litigation boutiques said they had a solid year in business in 2023, buoyed by strong demand for disputes work. Some even said it was one of their best financial years and that they are expecting more demand growth in 2024. Indeed, litigation was a big driver for law firm growth in 2023, in particular among smaller and midsize firms outside Big Law. Midsize law firms saw their biggest counter-cyclical gain in litigation hours, according to a recent legal market report by Thomson Reuters and the Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession at Georgetown Law. Overall, litigation was the biggest driver of demand growth for the legal industry in 2023, expanding by a 15-year high of 3.2%, according to the report.

article.title: Legal Research, Drafting Startup Alexi Raises $11 Million in Series A Funding
article.description: On Monday, Canadian legal tech startup Alexi, which offers generative artificial intelligence-powered legal research and drafting tools, announced that it raised $11 million ($15 million CAD) in a series A funding round led by venture capital firm…
article.text: On Monday, Canadian legal tech startup Alexi, which offers generative artificial intelligence-powered legal research and drafting tools, announced that it raised $11 million ($15 million CAD) in a series A funding round led by venture capital firm Drive Capital and including existing investor Draper Associates. Founded in 2017, Alexi, formerly known as Alexsei, leverages generative AI models, including OpenAI’s GPT models, to help legal professionals automate a number of tasks. While the startup first focused on drafting research memos for users based on their questions, it has since expanded to offer an AI-powered litigation assistant called Alexi Chat and a tool that uses AI to help lawyers brainstorm legal arguments for desired outcomes called “Arguments.”

article.title: In-House Lesson No. 1 From FTX Calamity: Don't 'Put Your Head in the Sand'
article.description: What You Need to Know General counsel need to develop a relationship of trust with business leaders to get ahead of problems.Lack of transparency can be a red flag.Ignorance is not a good defense strategy, a former compliance officer said. The…
article.text: What You Need to Know General counsel need to develop a relationship of trust with business leaders to get ahead of problems.Lack of transparency can be a red flag.Ignorance is not a good defense strategy, a former compliance officer said. The staggering degree of mismanagement and laxity called out in a court filing by new FTX CEO John Ray sent shockwaves through the legal community, raising the question of what level of culpability, if any, may rest with the platform’s legal division. “Never in my career have I seen such a complete failure of corporate controls and such a complete absence of trustworthy financial information as occurred here,” wrote the new CEO, who past experience includes supervising Enron’s notorious bankruptcy. “From compromised systems integrity and faulty regulatory oversight abroad, to the concentration of control in the hands of a very small group of inexperienced, unsophisticated and potentially compromised individuals, this situation is unprecedented.” While the extent of the implosion underway at FTX may be unprecedented, the chaos serves as a cautionary tale for in-house attorneys on how to avoid a similar crisis. “If you are a general counsel or an in-house lawyer—you don’t have to be in crypto trading—anybody in these roles can be thinking, ‘Could I be in this situation where management is engaged in doing something inappropriate, and what is my responsibility, based on what I directly knew or the red flags that should have led me to ask questions, to have detected that?” Baker Botts partner Michael Ward said. “And if I was aware or didn’t ask reasonable questions, what is my personal liability?’ ” said Ward, a former federal prosecutor who also worked for years as a chief compliance officer at companies like Adobe, Cisco and Juniper Networks. Ward added: “The best strategy is not to put your head in the sand but to be diligent and proactive to identify problems and solve them. You wouldn’t want to rely on a lack of knowledge as a strategy. Be attentive to red flags and follow up on them.” Little is known publicly so far about what went on behind the scenes with FTX’s legal team, other than the bulk of its compliance and legal staff quit earlier this week, including General Counsel Can Sun, whose LinkedIn page shows him now working at a stealth mode blockchain startup. Ryne Miller, general counsel for FTX’s U.S. subsidiary, is still with the company, and in a Slack message reviewed by the Wall Street Journal, he bemoaned the opacity of its top brass. “I have very limited transparency, and more is not possible without full cooperation from the founders,” he wrote. “I thought of that as a takeaway,” Jennifer Judge, former in-house attorney and general counsel who co-hosts the Lawyers Behaving Badly podcast, said of Miller’s admission. Neither Miller nor Sun responded to messages from Law.com. Lack of transparency from the top is a major headache for in-house counsel. For Judge, it’s a red flag. “I would be really wary of working with a business team where you felt like you didn’t have the full picture, especially when it comes to financials and holding other people’s money,” she said. “You hope when you’re hired, especially as a general counsel, you are hired on not to just provide legal advice but as a strategic spot leader. If the CEO clearly doesn’t want your legal advice or strategic judgment, there’s only so far you can go in terms of being at that company.” Foster Sayers, the general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, echoed that point. “Attorneys need to be as involved as they can be to be successful as in-house counsel,” he said. “If you want to be an effective in-house counsel, then you make yourself a seat at the table.” Sayers said it’s problematic when a general counsel is in the dark about business decisions. “It’s in those meetings where you hear the things that come up, when you can be proactive. Often we are too reactive. They come to us when things go sideways. But if we are a partner at the business, then that paradigm shifts and we can get out in front of the issues.” Ward, the Baker Botts partner, said increased regulatory and law enforcement scrutiny in recent years sometimes has resulted in an adversarial relationship between in-house lawyers and company management. “Lawyers and gatekeepers need to fulfill their responsibilities, but they can best do that if there’s a relationship of trust, and if you create this relationship of distrust, the amount of information flow is reduced,” he said. Botts said that, in the past, it was virtually unheard of for regulatory bodies and law enforcement to probe the actions of compliance officers or general counsel, let alone hold them criminally liable for the actions of their companies. But now it’s a realistic threat, as the government has started examining the effectiveness of compliance programs for companies under investigation, and holding legal and compliance teams accountable. “In-house counsel should operate with the assumption that their communications with management will not remain confidential forever, and privilege may someday be waived by the company. You should be planning for transparency and keeping as little as possible under attorney-client privilege,” he said. “What you want to do is make a contemporaneous record to demonstrate to regulators or law enforcement officials your diligence in trying to get it right.” As a former general counsel, Judge said she also would be worried about criminal or civil liability from corporate wrongdoing. “That’s always something you have to keep in the back of your mind. There’s also just general fraud allegations—where, if your company defrauds enough people, you might find yourself as a defendant in some sort of class action. It’s something you have to keep in mind when you’re at a company where you suspect something like this may be going on.” At FTX, she said, “I’m not sure that ethos permeated the corporate culture there.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • General counsel need to develop a relationship of trust with business leaders to get ahead of problems.
  • Lack of transparency can be a red flag.
  • Ignorance is not a good defense strategy, a former compliance officer said.

The staggering degree of mismanagement and laxity called out in a court filing by new FTX CEO John Ray sent shockwaves through the legal community, raising the question of what level of culpability, if any, may rest with the platform’s legal division.

“Never in my career have I seen such a complete failure of corporate controls and such a complete absence of trustworthy financial information as occurred here,” wrote the new CEO, who past experience includes supervising Enron’s notorious bankruptcy. “From compromised systems integrity and faulty regulatory oversight abroad, to the concentration of control in the hands of a very small group of inexperienced, unsophisticated and potentially compromised individuals, this situation is unprecedented.”

While the extent of the implosion underway at FTX may be unprecedented, the chaos serves as a cautionary tale for in-house attorneys on how to avoid a similar crisis.

“If you are a general counsel or an in-house lawyer—you don’t have to be in crypto trading—anybody in these roles can be thinking, ‘Could I be in this situation where management is engaged in doing something inappropriate, and what is my responsibility, based on what I directly knew or the red flags that should have led me to ask questions, to have detected that?” Baker Botts partner Michael Ward said.

“And if I was aware or didn’t ask reasonable questions, what is my personal liability?’ ” said Ward, a former federal prosecutor who also worked for years as a chief compliance officer at companies like Adobe, Cisco and Juniper Networks.

Ward added: “The best strategy is not to put your head in the sand but to be diligent and proactive to identify problems and solve them. You wouldn’t want to rely on a lack of knowledge as a strategy. Be attentive to red flags and follow up on them.”

Little is known publicly so far about what went on behind the scenes with FTX’s legal team, other than the bulk of its compliance and legal staff quit earlier this week, including General Counsel Can Sun, whose LinkedIn page shows him now working at a stealth mode blockchain startup.

Ryne Miller, general counsel for FTX’s U.S. subsidiary, is still with the company, and in a Slack message reviewed by the Wall Street Journal, he bemoaned the opacity of its top brass.

“I have very limited transparency, and more is not possible without full cooperation from the founders,” he wrote.

“I thought of that as a takeaway,” Jennifer Judge, former in-house attorney and general counsel who co-hosts the Lawyers Behaving Badly podcast, said of Miller’s admission.

Neither Miller nor Sun responded to messages from Law.com.

Lack of transparency from the top is a major headache for in-house counsel. For Judge, it’s a red flag.

“I would be really wary of working with a business team where you felt like you didn’t have the full picture, especially when it comes to financials and holding other people’s money,” she said.

“You hope when you’re hired, especially as a general counsel, you are hired on not to just provide legal advice but as a strategic spot leader. If the CEO clearly doesn’t want your legal advice or strategic judgment, there’s only so far you can go in terms of being at that company.”

Foster Sayers, the general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, echoed that point. “Attorneys need to be as involved as they can be to be successful as in-house counsel,” he said. “If you want to be an effective in-house counsel, then you make yourself a seat at the table.”

Sayers said it’s problematic when a general counsel is in the dark about business decisions. “It’s in those meetings where you hear the things that come up, when you can be proactive. Often we are too reactive. They come to us when things go sideways. But if we are a partner at the business, then that paradigm shifts and we can get out in front of the issues.”

Ward, the Baker Botts partner, said increased regulatory and law enforcement scrutiny in recent years sometimes has resulted in an adversarial relationship between in-house lawyers and company management.

“Lawyers and gatekeepers need to fulfill their responsibilities, but they can best do that if there’s a relationship of trust, and if you create this relationship of distrust, the amount of information flow is reduced,” he said.

Botts said that, in the past, it was virtually unheard of for regulatory bodies and law enforcement to probe the actions of compliance officers or general counsel, let alone hold them criminally liable for the actions of their companies. But now it’s a realistic threat, as the government has started examining the effectiveness of compliance programs for companies under investigation, and holding legal and compliance teams accountable.

“In-house counsel should operate with the assumption that their communications with management will not remain confidential forever, and privilege may someday be waived by the company. You should be planning for transparency and keeping as little as possible under attorney-client privilege,” he said. “What you want to do is make a contemporaneous record to demonstrate to regulators or law enforcement officials your diligence in trying to get it right.”

As a former general counsel, Judge said she also would be worried about criminal or civil liability from corporate wrongdoing.

“That’s always something you have to keep in the back of your mind. There’s also just general fraud allegations—where, if your company defrauds enough people, you might find yourself as a defendant in some sort of class action. It’s something you have to keep in mind when you’re at a company where you suspect something like this may be going on.”

At FTX, she said, “I’m not sure that ethos permeated the corporate culture there.”

article.text: Thirteen state attorneys general sent a letter late last week to the nation’s largest employers warning them that they’ll “face serious legal consequences” if they use racial preferences in recruiting, hiring and contracting decisions. The letter to Fortune 100 firms is the latest evidence that, while the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision last month striking down affirmative action in college admissions applies only to the education sector, it is emboldening critics of companies’ increasingly aggressive programs to bolster workplace diversity. Thirteen state attorneys general sent a letter late last week to the nation’s largest employers warning them that they’ll “face serious legal consequences” if they use racial preferences in recruiting, hiring and contracting decisions.

The letter to Fortune 100 firms is the latest evidence that, while the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision last month striking down affirmative action in college admissions applies only to the education sector, it is emboldening critics of companies’ increasingly aggressive programs to bolster workplace diversity.

article.description: What You Need to Know The EEOC says AMTCR turned a blind eye to sexual harassment of young employees. AMTCR owns 18 McDonald's in California, Arizona and Nevada. The company and one of its attorneys did not respond to requests for comment. The owner…
article.text: What You Need to Know The EEOC says AMTCR turned a blind eye to sexual harassment of young employees. AMTCR owns 18 McDonald's in California, Arizona and Nevada. The company and one of its attorneys did not respond to requests for comment. The owner of 18 McDonald’s franchises in California, Arizona and Nevada will pay roughly $2 million to settle allegations that it allowed sexual harassment against teenage employees to continue unabated, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced Friday. The EEOC alleged in a lawsuit filed last year that AMTCR Inc. knew that supervisors, managers and coworkers were harassing the teens at various McDonald’s restaurants since at least 2017 but failed to address the problem. article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • The EEOC says AMTCR turned a blind eye to sexual harassment of young employees.
  • AMTCR owns 18 McDonald's in California, Arizona and Nevada.
  • The company and one of its attorneys did not respond to requests for comment.

The owner of 18 McDonald’s franchises in California, Arizona and Nevada will pay roughly $2 million to settle allegations that it allowed sexual harassment against teenage employees to continue unabated, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced Friday.

The EEOC alleged in a lawsuit filed last year that AMTCR Inc. knew that supervisors, managers and coworkers were harassing the teens at various McDonald’s restaurants since at least 2017 but failed to address the problem. Nearly all quit because working conditions became intolerable, the agency alleged.
