article.title: SEC Fines Parent of NYSE $10M, Says It Failed to Immediately Disclose Cyber Incident
article.description: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission slapped the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange with a $10 million penalty Wednesday, saying it failed to comply with a rule requiring securities exchanges to immediately notify the agency of…
article.text: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission slapped the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange with a $10 million penalty Wednesday, saying it failed to comply with a rule requiring securities exchanges to immediately notify the agency of cyber intrusions. Receiving immediate notification is critical because of the potential that the SEC would need to step in to protect markets, Gurbir Grewal, director of the agency’s division of enforcement, said in a statement.
article.html:
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission slapped the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange with a $10 million penalty Wednesday, saying it failed to comply with a rule requiring securities exchanges to immediately notify the agency of cyber intrusions.

Receiving immediate notification is critical because of the potential that the SEC would need to step in to protect markets, Gurbir Grewal, director of the agency’s division of enforcement, said in a statement.

article.title: CLOC 2024 Takeaways: Gen AI Is Changing Everything, and 'Data Is the New Gold'
article.description: "The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president. More than 1,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas…
article.text: "The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president. More than 1,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas last week for the 2024 CLOC Global Institute, with generative artificial intelligence taking center stage. Legal industry professionals are shedding their initial fears that the burgeoning technology will come for everyone’s jobs. Now, the conversation has shifted to how legal ops and in-house counsel can put it to use to automate rote tasks and solve complicated business problems. A few of the panels featured practical discussions on how legal departments have experimented with generative AI in the past year, and what they envision for the future. Law firms also will be challenged to think more deeply about the value they bring to their client relationships, as the technology displaces some of the services outside lawyers currently provide. Below are some observations and takeaways: Legal Ops 3.0 The Corporate Legal Operations Consortium appointed Jenn McCarron as president in January, making this the first CGI where she ran the show. McCarron used the platform to showcase her vision to move the profession beyond being simply a support function for legal with “sharply defined limits” into becoming a true strategic business adviser. In her opening keynote, McCarron said legal ops pros “have spent too much time on questions like ‘what is the right contract life cycle management solution for my team?” instead of on the bigger picture. “We need to take control of the technology and innovation agenda. We can’t solely rely on our product teams anymore. All this transformation we’re talking about, it goes through the technology. So if we aren’t pushing the software development life cycle, then we aren’t creating the impact that we need fast enough,” she said. McCarron went into more detail in a conversation with Law.com. Legal has always touched every aspect of the business, but is still siloed, she explained. McCarron said those who can use their positions effectively can deliver value beyond legal and grab the attention of the C-suite. “If some of us are doing this right, and I’m starting to see this now, with some real senior thought leaders in our industry, your role will transcend legal. You’ll be pulled up into a C-suite, advising, strategic, focused capacity, because you are driving an impact that is hundreds of millions of dollars or whatever it equates to in big numbers for your business,” she said. She pointed to Allison Silver, former head of legal ops at Zoom. Silver is now global head of operations and strategy and reports to Chief Operating Officer Aparna Bawa, who was herself chief legal officer before being promoted. Legal Ops 3.0 is still in the nascent stage, and many CLOC goers are still puzzled over what it means in practice. One attendee predicted a backlash from general counsel, who have been fighting for years for that same C-suite attention. Another was too focused on the day-to-day job—taking on more legal work with fewer resource—to fixate on other ambitions. And that’s OK, McCarron said, noting that for a while there was a lot of buzz in legal ops around the chief of staff role. “I’m all of that, but that’s not for me. That’s not my archetype and I would not do well in that role,” she said. “But I love doing the technologist work inside of the legal department. What are the other endpoints? So stay in legal if that makes sense, if that’s where your role starts, and that’s where you are for the foreseeable future. And it’s OK if it transcends in time,” she said. ‘The Future Is Written in Data’ Executive aspirations notwithstanding, everyone was talking about how to better use data. “Data is the new gold,” McCarron told the CLOC audience in her keynote. “It’s the entire point of all this technology we spend our lives deploying. The future is written in data. There’s no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don’t become masters of collecting and exploiting it.” Many of CLOC’s panels focused on how legal can make the most of the swaths of data companies interact with every day. One blockbuster launch was the Legal Data Intelligence framework, a tool developed by a group of volunteers from companies such as Google, Moderna, Walgreens, Marsh McLennan and Edward Jones. It outlines how legal departments can identify and use data to complete legal tasks and solve business problems around disputes and investigations, contract review, data protection and privacy, and outside counsel management. Jeremiah Weasenforth, assistant general counsel and ​​legal analytics director at Edward Jones, said the LDI model, with its step-by-step guidelines, can help legal teams put that underlying data to work. At its core, it separates the sensitive, useful and necessary data from the redundant, obsolete and trivial, and transforms it into “answers, insights and advice.” He gave the example of litigation, where everyone has had the motion that never gets granted. Weasenforth said legal data intelligence can help in-house teams figure out whether that motion is even worth filing. “You have your own internal data intelligence that you’ve done on the same question. You have law firm data of intelligence, you have opposing counsel data intelligence. So you could make an actual decision around ‘do we push this motion forward? Do we file it?’ That is a question that you could answer with the legal data intelligence model,” he said. The most important use case, he said, may be in the business of law. “Every challenge that we solve as legal operations professionals has a data intelligence component. If you want to make a business case for a new technology, a new resource, a new anything, how are you getting funding for that? You’re using data, you’re initiating, you’re investigating, and you’re implementing a data intelligence model to get that resource,” he said. “If you want to save money on outside counsel invoices, you’re following the same process. You’re using data intelligence to say, actually, I know this is litigation in Alabama, but historically it has not cost what we’re expecting it to cost. Is there a reason or a nuance about this case that we can use in negotiations with outside counsel or with local counsel?” It can also help in-house counsel transcend legal and act as true business advisers. “You can think about a new product, a new service, a new offering that’s coming in. And you understand from your data intelligence the common factors that have led to customer attrition, that have led to customer complaints, and that have ultimately led to litigation,” Weasenforth said. “And as you mature, you can start to develop models around the work that you’re doing to start to predict where those issues are going to come up. It will give you opportunities to place guardrails around products that you may not have seen coming without that data intelligence background in the tool,” he said. Disrupting Client-Law Firm Relationships In addition to harnessing the power of data, legal teams are looking to use generative AI in their everyday work. While it hasn’t obviated the need for outside counsel, clients are starting to question why they would pay upward of $800 an hour for tasks that take minutes. One attendee predicted that firms will be enlisted to sign off on work done in-house using generative AI-powered assistants, and they can charge a similar amount for the value of assuming the risk on behalf of their clients. Law firms that rely heavily on high-volume litigation for revenue will be in trouble. “Technology and generative AI is testing the traditional relationship of client and outside counsel,” a former law partner said. Firms need to start assuming now that anything that can be automated currently with generative AI, will be. At a Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI, one in-house leader said corporate clients will no longer put up with the status quo from their firms. Another said in-house requests for proposal ask outside counsel how they are using generative AI and large language models, and that firms that do not have a satisfactory answer will lose business. Experiment, Experiment, Experiment Experimentation was a recurring theme, as in-house counsel were urged to play around with generative AI tools before making any big changes to their workflows. McCarron told Law.com that she advises against going out and buying any off-the-shelf tech without doing proof of concept. “Pick one, do an RFP formally, or do what I do—call my ‘five five’ in legal ops. And I go, ‘what do you see who’s on the cutting edge right now with the new product that wants to innovate with us?’ And I’ll do a proof of concept with them, a small use case, one use case, usually for a small amount of money.” Or as one in-house lawyer at the Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI put it, “Figure out what you want to do and find the tool that will get you there.” Getting Buy-In Some legal ops leaders said they’ve encountered little resistance to generative AI on their teams. “I think people are just so interested in freeing up time that they’re willing to try it out,” said Jen Lenander, director of legal operations at enterprise search company Elastic. For others who need a bit more convincing, Suffolk Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who gave the closing keynote, said in-house teams should “consider pilots.” It’s hard to change an entire law department culture, he said, “but I can tell you from my own experience, even inside the law school, which traditionally law schools are considered very conservative when it comes to change, pilots make an enormous difference.” Hire Continual Learners One in-house leader said his generative AI is not threatening jobs on his legal team, but the type of lawyers in-house teams are hiring is changing. The new priority is lawyers who have a “growth mindset” and are willing to adapt to new technology. “You cannot rely on what you learned a year ago,” he said. “You have to keep changing your skill set.” One law firm partner said his firm is hiring more associates, not fewer, “but it will affect the kind of people we hire.” The complexity of the laws and state and federal AI regulations are actually producing more work than the firm can handle. But the firms want to see adaptability from candidates. “I want to see you embrace the revolution,” he said.

"The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president.

More than 1,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas last week for the 2024 CLOC Global Institute, with generative artificial intelligence taking center stage.

Legal industry professionals are shedding their initial fears that the burgeoning technology will come for everyone’s jobs. Now, the conversation has shifted to how legal ops and in-house counsel can put it to use to automate rote tasks and solve complicated business problems.

A few of the panels featured practical discussions on how legal departments have experimented with generative AI in the past year, and what they envision for the future. Law firms also will be challenged to think more deeply about the value they bring to their client relationships, as the technology displaces some of the services outside lawyers currently provide.

Below are some observations and takeaways:

Legal Ops 3.0

The Corporate Legal Operations Consortium appointed Jenn McCarron as president in January, making this the first CGI where she ran the show. McCarron used the platform to showcase her vision to move the profession beyond being simply a support function for legal with “sharply defined limits” into becoming a true strategic business adviser.

In her opening keynote, McCarron said legal ops pros “have spent too much time on questions like ‘what is the right contract life cycle management solution for my team?” instead of on the bigger picture.

“We need to take control of the technology and innovation agenda. We can’t solely rely on our product teams anymore. All this transformation we’re talking about, it goes through the technology. So if we aren’t pushing the software development life cycle, then we aren’t creating the impact that we need fast enough,” she said.

McCarron went into more detail in a conversation with Law.com. Legal has always touched every aspect of the business, but is still siloed, she explained. McCarron said those who can use their positions effectively can deliver value beyond legal and grab the attention of the C-suite.

“If some of us are doing this right, and I’m starting to see this now, with some real senior thought leaders in our industry, your role will transcend legal. You’ll be pulled up into a C-suite, advising, strategic, focused capacity, because you are driving an impact that is hundreds of millions of dollars or whatever it equates to in big numbers for your business,” she said.

She pointed to Allison Silver, former head of legal ops at Zoom. Silver is now global head of operations and strategy and reports to Chief Operating Officer Aparna Bawa, who was herself chief legal officer before being promoted.

Legal Ops 3.0 is still in the nascent stage, and many CLOC goers are still puzzled over what it means in practice. One attendee predicted a backlash from general counsel, who have been fighting for years for that same C-suite attention. Another was too focused on the day-to-day job—taking on more legal work with fewer resource—to fixate on other ambitions.

And that’s OK, McCarron said, noting that for a while there was a lot of buzz in legal ops around the chief of staff role. “I’m all of that, but that’s not for me. That’s not my archetype and I would not do well in that role,” she said.

“But I love doing the technologist work inside of the legal department. What are the other endpoints? So stay in legal if that makes sense, if that’s where your role starts, and that’s where you are for the foreseeable future. And it’s OK if it transcends in time,” she said.

‘The Future Is Written in Data’

Executive aspirations notwithstanding, everyone was talking about how to better use data.

“Data is the new gold,” McCarron told the CLOC audience in her keynote. “It’s the entire point of all this technology we spend our lives deploying. The future is written in data. There’s no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don’t become masters of collecting and exploiting it.”

Many of CLOC’s panels focused on how legal can make the most of the swaths of data companies interact with every day. One blockbuster launch was the Legal Data Intelligence framework, a tool developed by a group of volunteers from companies such as Google, Moderna, Walgreens, Marsh McLennan and Edward Jones. It outlines how legal departments can identify and use data to complete legal tasks and solve business problems around disputes and investigations, contract review, data protection and privacy, and outside counsel management.

Jeremiah Weasenforth, assistant general counsel and ​​legal analytics director at Edward Jones, said the LDI model, with its step-by-step guidelines, can help legal teams put that underlying data to work.

At its core, it separates the sensitive, useful and necessary data from the redundant, obsolete and trivial, and transforms it into “answers, insights and advice.”

He gave the example of litigation, where everyone has had the motion that never gets granted.

Weasenforth said legal data intelligence can help in-house teams figure out whether that motion is even worth filing. “You have your own internal data intelligence that you’ve done on the same question. You have law firm data of intelligence, you have opposing counsel data intelligence. So you could make an actual decision around ‘do we push this motion forward? Do we file it?’ That is a question that you could answer with the legal data intelligence model,” he said.

The most important use case, he said, may be in the business of law. “Every challenge that we solve as legal operations professionals has a data intelligence component. If you want to make a business case for a new technology, a new resource, a new anything, how are you getting funding for that? You’re using data, you’re initiating, you’re investigating, and you’re implementing a data intelligence model to get that resource,” he said.

“If you want to save money on outside counsel invoices, you’re following the same process. You’re using data intelligence to say, actually, I know this is litigation in Alabama, but historically it has not cost what we’re expecting it to cost. Is there a reason or a nuance about this case that we can use in negotiations with outside counsel or with local counsel?”

It can also help in-house counsel transcend legal and act as true business advisers.

“You can think about a new product, a new service, a new offering that’s coming in. And you understand from your data intelligence the common factors that have led to customer attrition, that have led to customer complaints, and that have ultimately led to litigation,” Weasenforth said.

“And as you mature, you can start to develop models around the work that you’re doing to start to predict where those issues are going to come up. It will give you opportunities to place guardrails around products that you may not have seen coming without that data intelligence background in the tool,” he said.

Disrupting Client-Law Firm Relationships

In addition to harnessing the power of data, legal teams are looking to use generative AI in their everyday work.

While it hasn’t obviated the need for outside counsel, clients are starting to question why they would pay upward of $800 an hour for tasks that take minutes. One attendee predicted that firms will be enlisted to sign off on work done in-house using generative AI-powered assistants, and they can charge a similar amount for the value of assuming the risk on behalf of their clients.

Law firms that rely heavily on high-volume litigation for revenue will be in trouble. “Technology and generative AI is testing the traditional relationship of client and outside counsel,” a former law partner said. Firms need to start assuming now that anything that can be automated currently with generative AI, will be.

At a Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI, one in-house leader said corporate clients will no longer put up with the status quo from their firms. Another said in-house requests for proposal ask outside counsel how they are using generative AI and large language models, and that firms that do not have a satisfactory answer will lose business.

Experiment, Experiment, Experiment

Experimentation was a recurring theme, as in-house counsel were urged to play around with generative AI tools before making any big changes to their workflows.

McCarron told Law.com that she advises against going out and buying any off-the-shelf tech without doing proof of concept. “Pick one, do an RFP formally, or do what I do—call my ‘five five’ in legal ops. And I go, ‘what do you see who’s on the cutting edge right now with the new product that wants to innovate with us?’ And I’ll do a proof of concept with them, a small use case, one use case, usually for a small amount of money.”

Or as one in-house lawyer at the Chatham House rules roundtable on generative AI put it, “Figure out what you want to do and find the tool that will get you there.”

Getting Buy-In

Some legal ops leaders said they’ve encountered little resistance to generative AI on their teams. “I think people are just so interested in freeing up time that they’re willing to try it out,” said Jen Lenander, director of legal operations at enterprise search company Elastic.

For others who need a bit more convincing, Suffolk Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who gave the closing keynote, said in-house teams should “consider pilots.”

It’s hard to change an entire law department culture, he said, “but I can tell you from my own experience, even inside the law school, which traditionally law schools are considered very conservative when it comes to change, pilots make an enormous difference.”

Hire Continual Learners

One in-house leader said his generative AI is not threatening jobs on his legal team, but the type of lawyers in-house teams are hiring is changing. The new priority is lawyers who have a “growth mindset” and are willing to adapt to new technology. “You cannot rely on what you learned a year ago,” he said. “You have to keep changing your skill set.”

One law firm partner said his firm is hiring more associates, not fewer, “but it will affect the kind of people we hire.”

The complexity of the laws and state and federal AI regulations are actually producing more work than the firm can handle. But the firms want to see adaptability from candidates. “I want to see you embrace the revolution,” he said.

article.title: No Clear Winner in Faceoff Over Outside Counsel Fees
article.description: What You Need to Know Law firm clients are experiencing 2023 rate increases that generally fall between 5% to 15%.But some hikes are topping 30%.Legal departments are pushing back harder, but many lack a sophisticated rate-review process. Legal…
article.text: What You Need to Know Law firm clients are experiencing 2023 rate increases that generally fall between 5% to 15%.But some hikes are topping 30%.Legal departments are pushing back harder, but many lack a sophisticated rate-review process. Legal departments expressed outrage and girded for battle last fall when their outside law firms rolled out plans for aggressive rate increases for 2023. Yet the showdown that seemed sure to come never really materialized. Legal observers say that while some law departments pushed back on increases more than they had in recent years, and some won larger-than-typical concessions, many departments are ending up with substantial hikes, sometimes more than 15%. And few departments are exercising the nuclear option of firing firms over higher rates. Jason Winmill, a managing partner at the in-house consulting firm Argopoint, said rates have shot upward in 2023, in contrast to the gradual increases of the recent past. “Prior years tended toward 4-6%—with gains accumulating via consistent year-over-year bump-ups vs. single year spikes,” he said. However, 2022 saw increases around 5-7%, and 2023 increases are even loftier, with high-end firms commanding more than 30%. “2023 rate hikes are 7-8% for many. But even steeper hikes are coming from the premium band, where it’s all over the place: sometimes 12% but also sometimes 32%,” he said. “While cracks may be emerging here and there, it’s been a very good time to be outside counsel.” Law firms saw average billing rate increases of 5.8% in 2022, according to Wells Fargo Private Bank Legal Specialty Group. By comparison, firms raised rates by an average of 6.7% in 2021 and 5.9% in 2020. Winmill said the steeper increases could be attributed to demand outstripping supply for the high-end legal services on which Fortune 500 clients depend. “Outside counsel has capitalized on that by ratcheting rates up a few more clicks on top of the normal increases,” he said. The trend was borne out in the yearly letters in-house received from firms. “This year was an avalanche,” said Aarash Darroodi, executive vice president and general counsel of the guitar-maker Fender. “I don’t know if outside counsel couldn’t afford eggs or milk or something. On the receiving end, it’s kind of comedic for us. It’s like, ‘Here it is—the lawyers trying to milk more from us.’” Consulting a price sheet he’d recently received from a firm, Darroodi noticed a marked increase in one associate’s hourly rates. “This one seems to have gone up by about $30 an hour,” he said. During negotiations aimed at ratcheting down proposed law firm increases, “some firms were incredibly flexible … while others drew a hard line,” said Jessica Vander Ploeg, vice president of legal operations for software provider Micro Focus. Vander Ploeg also said she and legal ops executives at other companies have been comparing notes. “More than half saw rate increases of 30% from some of their law firms, and most saw double-digit increases,” she said. “That was their starting point, though; they all negotiated down from that 30%, or most did. It’s not unusual though, to see double-digit increases.” ‘Many Reasons Firms Increase Rates’ Law firms usually begin sending out the dreaded rate-increase notices at the end of the year in the hopes of locking in a new rate as close to Jan. 1 as they can. it’s not unusual for rate negotiations to extend into the first quarter. Vander Ploeg said Micro Focus negotiates rates every two years and when old rates expired at the end of December, her company continued to pay at that level until it reached new agreements. For her company, the average rate increase across all its law firms was 16%. On the low end was a 3% increase, and the high end was 32%, based on attorneys’ roles, recent promotions and the geography they were covering, Vander Ploeg said. The firms’ justifications for increases, she said, ran the gamut—from economic pressures to singular expertise. “I’ve heard inflation, cost-of-living changes, ‘the work we’re doing is specialized,’” she said. “There are many reasons firms increase rates. The key is to evaluate if the increases are reasonable—which is subjective for each in-house department and competitive within the marketplace.” Darroodi noticed the same thing. “Sometimes the increases are justified, like when a senior associate becomes a partner because you’re getting a different level of advice,” he said. “But if they’re just doing it because of inflation, I wonder what sort of inflationary pressures law firms are having. If you’re going to raise the fee, why don’t you improve the way you serve the in-house counsel first?” ‘Trying to Make the Right Moves’ Law firms say they’re genuinely pinched by inflation, which rose 6.5% in 2022, according to the U,.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. “What keeps me up at night or what I’m worried about is the inflationary environment,” Chase Simmons, CEO of the law firm Polsinelli, said in an interview earlier this month, noting its effect on billing rates and attorney compensation. “Getting that mix right [between rising associate pay and billing rates]—that’s moving so fast and is so dynamic. Just trying to make the right moves is something we spend a lot of time on,” Simmons said. Associate pay rose 9.3% in 2021 and 9.4% last year, according to Thomson Reuters’ latest State of the Market Report. Given the “skyrocketing” compensation increases, legal industry analysts have warned that if firms can’t secure significant billing rate increases, they’ll face “increasingly difficult decisions” this year,” such as significant layoffs. “Law firms actually have to raise rates because they have raised incoming associate salaries so much that they have to raise rates to maintain their margins,” said Nathan Cemenska, director of legal operations and industry insights at Wolters Kluwer ELM Solutions. Owen Burman, segment manager for Wells Fargo Private Bank Legal Specialty Group, said that while he doesn’t yet have data on 2023 rate increases, he expects them to end up averaging 7% to 8%. He said firms might introduce hikes gradually to make them more palatable. ‘Throwing Spaghetti Up Against the Wall’ Winmill said law firms don’t appear to be have a common approach to pricing this year, and as a result they “were all over the board” with rate increases. “What I saw felt like many firms were just throwing spaghetti up against the wall to see what would stick,” he said. “My conclusion is that this year—more than any prior—there was a lack of consensus view regarding pricing on the part of outside counsel.” Winmill said most legal departments could stomach a 3-6% increase, and while many were falling within that range there were outliers. “Many of the firms who came in well above that range had experienced a banner 2022—and were using 2023 prices to signal their confidence and market power,” Winmill said. Law firm leaders consider practice area, industry and geographic location to determine rate increases, analysts said. Cemenska noted that the largest firms have the greatest ability to secure significant increases. Their actions often also create a ripple effect through the industry. Larger firms have “broken clients into the idea of accepting big increases,” he said. He said practice areas such as finance and securities, commercial transactions and corporate/M&A are among those with the greatest pricing power. “Even though M&A work is drying up, demand is very inelastic and companies are afraid to use any but the largest firms for important transactions,” Cemenska said, noting that less exclusive practices such as labor and employment and real estate likely will see smaller increases. He said law firms in the Am Law 200 Second Hundred historically been less aggressive in rate negotiations. Even so, Cemenska, they’re likely to see an average increase in 2023 exceeding the 6.2% they saw in 2022. Meanwhile, he said, unranked firms should be able to achieve an average increase of about 5% “simply by asking” because it will look so reasonable compared to what some large firms are doing. Geographic location also will continue to factor into rate increases, analysts said, with companies on the coasts, where the Am Law 50 are strongest, likely seeing more aggressive increases than those in the central part of the country. ‘A Crazy Quilt of Spreadsheets and Emails’ Cemenska said many legal departments hurt themselves in the negotiating process by not being as sophisticated as they should be. For example, most don’t use external benchmarking. If legal departments instead rely on internal benchmarking, which assesses only the rates they are paying their various firms, data shows many end up paying 20% or more than their peers for the exact same attorneys, Cemenska said. Benchmarking “against those inflated rates is just setting yourself up for failure,” he said. Additionally, many legal departments manage and negotiate rates through “a crazy-quilt of spreadsheets and emails” among dozens of people, Cemenska said. On top of all that, “many of them also have stacked the game against themselves by putting “friendly” rate negotiators—typically in-house attorneys from the alumni network of the very firms they are now supposed to negotiate against—in charge of negotiations,” he said. Argopoint’s Winmill said legal departments are getting better. While many roll over, “increasingly in-house departments are challenging outside counsel. Higher rate hikes will engender a response from departments like, ‘We want to review these.’” Tighter legal budgets also are driving in-house counsel to give outside counsel bills more scrutiny, said Aaron Kornblum, global general counsel at online learning platform BYJU’S Learning. “Every general counsel should be monitoring and tracking their outside counsel spend month over month and working with finance in looking for deviations from the norm,” he said. “The worst thing you can do is simply pay the bill without reading or analyzing it.” Another taboo is to accept a rate increase without even trying to negotiate it down, in-house counsel say. “There’s almost never an instance where you cannot negotiate,” said Vander Ploeg, the Micro Focus legal ops leader. “The worst they can say is ‘no.’ Even firms that appeared most unwilling to negotiate reduced rates to some degree.” Vander Ploeg added: “It’s important for everyone within the legal community to remember this is a relationship business. Building inroads and communicating what we expect impacts how rate increases and negotiations happen.” Those relationships are one reason why Kornblum said his rates have held steady. “We didn’t receive any letters about end-of-year rate increases because we’ve had a healthy relationship with our firms. Having that healthy conversation has helped to ensure that our rates remained constant into 2023,” he said. “If you’re waiting for rate increase letters, you’re already behind.” Another strategy is to request a flat fee, or alternative fee arrangement, for a particular matter. “People are keen on the idea of putting together a key agreement for a specific matter so rates don’t come into play,” Vander Ploeg said. While switching firms is also an option, Vander Ploeg said outside counsel partnerships don’t hinge on rates alone. “I think moving firms is often based on several factors, not just rates. This is a relationship business, and choosing to move firms over rate increases would often mean there are other underlying issues and rate increases were the final straw,” she said. “In-house teams are less likely to move when they have a long-term partner working on strategic matters.” But legal departments should be prepared to walk away if a relationship sours, Kornblum said. “It’s important to have those calls with outside counsel in a frank and routine way if the work no longer justifies an outside counsel arrangement,” he said. “Not making a change and not ending a relationship is a decision in itself. Sometimes it’s hard to say goodbye, but sometimes that’s the right way to go.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Law firm clients are experiencing 2023 rate increases that generally fall between 5% to 15%.
  • But some hikes are topping 30%.
  • Legal departments are pushing back harder, but many lack a sophisticated rate-review process.

Legal departments expressed outrage and girded for battle last fall when their outside law firms rolled out plans for aggressive rate increases for 2023. Yet the showdown that seemed sure to come never really materialized.

Legal observers say that while some law departments pushed back on increases more than they had in recent years, and some won larger-than-typical concessions, many departments are ending up with substantial hikes, sometimes more than 15%. And few departments are exercising the nuclear option of firing firms over higher rates.

Jason Winmill, a managing partner at the in-house consulting firm Argopoint, said rates have shot upward in 2023, in contrast to the gradual increases of the recent past. “Prior years tended toward 4-6%—with gains accumulating via consistent year-over-year bump-ups vs. single year spikes,” he said.

However, 2022 saw increases around 5-7%, and 2023 increases are even loftier, with high-end firms commanding more than 30%. “2023 rate hikes are 7-8% for many. But even steeper hikes are coming from the premium band, where it’s all over the place: sometimes 12% but also sometimes 32%,” he said.

“While cracks may be emerging here and there, it’s been a very good time to be outside counsel.”

Law firms saw average billing rate increases of 5.8% in 2022, according to Wells Fargo Private Bank Legal Specialty Group. By comparison, firms raised rates by an average of 6.7% in 2021 and 5.9% in 2020.

Winmill said the steeper increases could be attributed to demand outstripping supply for the high-end legal services on which Fortune 500 clients depend. “Outside counsel has capitalized on that by ratcheting rates up a few more clicks on top of the normal increases,” he said.

The trend was borne out in the yearly letters in-house received from firms. “This year was an avalanche,” said Aarash Darroodi, executive vice president and general counsel of the guitar-maker Fender.

“I don’t know if outside counsel couldn’t afford eggs or milk or something. On the receiving end, it’s kind of comedic for us. It’s like, ‘Here it is—the lawyers trying to milk more from us.’”

Consulting a price sheet he’d recently received from a firm, Darroodi noticed a marked increase in one associate’s hourly rates. “This one seems to have gone up by about $30 an hour,” he said.

During negotiations aimed at ratcheting down proposed law firm increases, “some firms were incredibly flexible … while others drew a hard line,” said Jessica Vander Ploeg, vice president of legal operations for software provider Micro Focus.

Vander Ploeg also said she and legal ops executives at other companies have been comparing notes. “More than half saw rate increases of 30% from some of their law firms, and most saw double-digit increases,” she said. “That was their starting point, though; they all negotiated down from that 30%, or most did. It’s not unusual though, to see double-digit increases.”

‘Many Reasons Firms Increase Rates’

Law firms usually begin sending out the dreaded rate-increase notices at the end of the year in the hopes of locking in a new rate as close to Jan. 1 as they can. it’s not unusual for rate negotiations to extend into the first quarter.

Vander Ploeg said Micro Focus negotiates rates every two years and when old rates expired at the end of December, her company continued to pay at that level until it reached new agreements.

For her company, the average rate increase across all its law firms was 16%. On the low end was a 3% increase, and the high end was 32%, based on attorneys’ roles, recent promotions and the geography they were covering, Vander Ploeg said.

The firms’ justifications for increases, she said, ran the gamut—from economic pressures to singular expertise.

“I’ve heard inflation, cost-of-living changes, ‘the work we’re doing is specialized,’” she said. “There are many reasons firms increase rates. The key is to evaluate if the increases are reasonable—which is subjective for each in-house department and competitive within the marketplace.”

Darroodi noticed the same thing.

“Sometimes the increases are justified, like when a senior associate becomes a partner because you’re getting a different level of advice,” he said. “But if they’re just doing it because of inflation, I wonder what sort of inflationary pressures law firms are having. If you’re going to raise the fee, why don’t you improve the way you serve the in-house counsel first?”

‘Trying to Make the Right Moves’

Law firms say they’re genuinely pinched by inflation, which rose 6.5% in 2022, according to the U,.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“What keeps me up at night or what I’m worried about is the inflationary environment,” Chase Simmons, CEO of the law firm Polsinelli, said in an interview earlier this month, noting its effect on billing rates and attorney compensation.

“Getting that mix right [between rising associate pay and billing rates]—that’s moving so fast and is so dynamic. Just trying to make the right moves is something we spend a lot of time on,” Simmons said.

Associate pay rose 9.3% in 2021 and 9.4% last year, according to Thomson Reuters’ latest State of the Market Report. Given the “skyrocketing” compensation increases, legal industry analysts have warned that if firms can’t secure significant billing rate increases, they’ll face “increasingly difficult decisions” this year,” such as significant layoffs.

“Law firms actually have to raise rates because they have raised incoming associate salaries so much that they have to raise rates to maintain their margins,” said Nathan Cemenska, director of legal operations and industry insights at Wolters Kluwer ELM Solutions.

Owen Burman, segment manager for Wells Fargo Private Bank Legal Specialty Group, said that while he doesn’t yet have data on 2023 rate increases, he expects them to end up averaging 7% to 8%. He said firms might introduce hikes gradually to make them more palatable.

‘Throwing Spaghetti Up Against the Wall’

Winmill said law firms don’t appear to be have a common approach to pricing this year, and as a result they “were all over the board” with rate increases.

“What I saw felt like many firms were just throwing spaghetti up against the wall to see what would stick,” he said. “My conclusion is that this year—more than any prior—there was a lack of consensus view regarding pricing on the part of outside counsel.”

Winmill said most legal departments could stomach a 3-6% increase, and while many were falling within that range there were outliers. “Many of the firms who came in well above that range had experienced a banner 2022—and were using 2023 prices to signal their confidence and market power,” Winmill said.

Law firm leaders consider practice area, industry and geographic location to determine rate increases, analysts said. Cemenska noted that the largest firms have the greatest ability to secure significant increases. Their actions often also create a ripple effect through the industry.

Larger firms have “broken clients into the idea of accepting big increases,” he said.

He said practice areas such as finance and securities, commercial transactions and corporate/M&A are among those with the greatest pricing power.

“Even though M&A work is drying up, demand is very inelastic and companies are afraid to use any but the largest firms for important transactions,” Cemenska said, noting that less exclusive practices such as labor and employment and real estate likely will see smaller increases.

He said law firms in the Am Law 200 Second Hundred historically been less aggressive in rate negotiations. Even so, Cemenska, they’re likely to see an average increase in 2023 exceeding the 6.2% they saw in 2022.

Meanwhile, he said, unranked firms should be able to achieve an average increase of about 5% “simply by asking” because it will look so reasonable compared to what some large firms are doing.

Geographic location also will continue to factor into rate increases, analysts said, with companies on the coasts, where the Am Law 50 are strongest, likely seeing more aggressive increases than those in the central part of the country.

‘A Crazy Quilt of Spreadsheets and Emails’

Cemenska said many legal departments hurt themselves in the negotiating process by not being as sophisticated as they should be.

For example, most don’t use external benchmarking. If legal departments instead rely on internal benchmarking, which assesses only the rates they are paying their various firms, data shows many end up paying 20% or more than their peers for the exact same attorneys, Cemenska said.

Benchmarking “against those inflated rates is just setting yourself up for failure,” he said.

Additionally, many legal departments manage and negotiate rates through “a crazy-quilt of spreadsheets and emails” among dozens of people, Cemenska said.

On top of all that, “many of them also have stacked the game against themselves by putting “friendly” rate negotiators—typically in-house attorneys from the alumni network of the very firms they are now supposed to negotiate against—in charge of negotiations,” he said.

Argopoint’s Winmill said legal departments are getting better. While many roll over, “increasingly in-house departments are challenging outside counsel. Higher rate hikes will engender a response from departments like, ‘We want to review these.’”

Tighter legal budgets also are driving in-house counsel to give outside counsel bills more scrutiny, said Aaron Kornblum, global general counsel at online learning platform BYJU’S Learning.

“Every general counsel should be monitoring and tracking their outside counsel spend month over month and working with finance in looking for deviations from the norm,” he said. “The worst thing you can do is simply pay the bill without reading or analyzing it.”

Another taboo is to accept a rate increase without even trying to negotiate it down, in-house counsel say.

“There’s almost never an instance where you cannot negotiate,” said Vander Ploeg, the Micro Focus legal ops leader. “The worst they can say is ‘no.’ Even firms that appeared most unwilling to negotiate reduced rates to some degree.”

Vander Ploeg added: “It’s important for everyone within the legal community to remember this is a relationship business. Building inroads and communicating what we expect impacts how rate increases and negotiations happen.”

Those relationships are one reason why Kornblum said his rates have held steady.

“We didn’t receive any letters about end-of-year rate increases because we’ve had a healthy relationship with our firms. Having that healthy conversation has helped to ensure that our rates remained constant into 2023,” he said. “If you’re waiting for rate increase letters, you’re already behind.”

Another strategy is to request a flat fee, or alternative fee arrangement, for a particular matter. “People are keen on the idea of putting together a key agreement for a specific matter so rates don’t come into play,” Vander Ploeg said.

While switching firms is also an option, Vander Ploeg said outside counsel partnerships don’t hinge on rates alone.

“I think moving firms is often based on several factors, not just rates. This is a relationship business, and choosing to move firms over rate increases would often mean there are other underlying issues and rate increases were the final straw,” she said.

“In-house teams are less likely to move when they have a long-term partner working on strategic matters.”

But legal departments should be prepared to walk away if a relationship sours, Kornblum said.

“It’s important to have those calls with outside counsel in a frank and routine way if the work no longer justifies an outside counsel arrangement,” he said.

“Not making a change and not ending a relationship is a decision in itself. Sometimes it’s hard to say goodbye, but sometimes that’s the right way to go.”

article.title: CEO Favors Building Rapport With Regulators, Rather Than Waiting for Their Call
article.description: Checkr CEO Daniel Yanisse said his company reached out to regulators—over the objection of his outside counsel. He said it's important for founders to educate themselves on how their industry is regulated. He spoke on a Berkeley Law webinar on…
article.text: Checkr CEO Daniel Yanisse said his company reached out to regulators—over the objection of his outside counsel. He said it's important for founders to educate themselves on how their industry is regulated. He spoke on a Berkeley Law webinar on Tuesday. Companies generally try to avoid attracting the attention of regulators, especially when they’re in a heavily scrutinized industry. So when Daniel Yanisse, co-founder and CEO of the background-check platform Checkr, decided to ask for a meeting with the Federal Trade Commission, his outside counsel was less than thrilled. “Our outside counsel took me aside and told me I was crazy to proactively go to regulators, because it’s a dangerous thing to do and businesses don’t do it. They come to you, and you don’t want to be on their radar,” he said. “Initially, she was not very excited about my idea to connect with the regulators and explain what we do to them.” This content has been archived. article.html:
• Checkr CEO Daniel Yanisse said his company reached out to regulators—over the objection of his outside counsel.
  • He said it's important for founders to educate themselves on how their industry is regulated.
  • He spoke on a Berkeley Law webinar on Tuesday.

Companies generally try to avoid attracting the attention of regulators, especially when they’re in a heavily scrutinized industry. So when Daniel Yanisse, co-founder and CEO of the background-check platform Checkr, decided to ask for a meeting with the Federal Trade Commission, his outside counsel was less than thrilled.

“Our outside counsel took me aside and told me I was crazy to proactively go to regulators, because it’s a dangerous thing to do and businesses don’t do it. They come to you, and you don’t want to be on their radar,” he said. “Initially, she was not very excited about my idea to connect with the regulators and explain what we do to them.”

article.title: 'Risk Management Is a Team Sport': What GCs Should Learn From Uber Cybersecurity Verdict
article.description: What You Need to Know A jury in October found a former Uber security chief criminally liable in a 2016 data breach.Participants in a panel discussion said Sullivan's conduct was especially egregious and that the government is unlikely to pursue…
article.text: What You Need to Know A jury in October found a former Uber security chief criminally liable in a 2016 data breach.Participants in a panel discussion said Sullivan's conduct was especially egregious and that the government is unlikely to pursue personal liability regularly.Even so, the case underscores the importance of strong lines of communication between legal departments and CISOs. The October conviction of former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for concealing a 2016 data breach from government regulators sent ripples of anxiety through the C-suite over the prospect of more executives being held personally liable after a hack. At a recent panel on what the verdict means for corporate security and legal teams, the consensus was that Sullivan’s prosecution was unusual, and his actions egregious. But while companies shouldn’t panic, general counsel and security chiefs should band together to tackle cybersecurity incidents with transparency and open communication. “Cyber and privacy is a companywide concern, and that includes the board of directors, all the way down the line,” said Cari Robinson, a cybersecurity expert and former Revlon general counsel. “Teamwork is critical. If I don’t have a collaborative, transparent and open relationship with my CIO, my CISO, I’m not going to be able to give advice to the company or ultimately to the board of directors.” The panel, hosted by the woman-led market network Fourth Floor and moderated by founder Breen Sullivan, also included virtual chief security officer and data privacy risk adviser Donna Gallaher and ClearOPS founder Caroline McCaffery. Robinson, who also headed cybersecurity investigations as an assistant general counsel at IBM, said general counsel should have an “open and collaborative” relationship with security chiefs so that they can fully understand the incident and how to best advise the CEO on what the company’s response should be. Sullivan’s conviction may have shaken the cybersecurity community, but Robinson said the government is unlikely to turn its sights on executives who act in good faith. Where Sullivan and Uber went wrong, she said, was in confining their handling of the breach to just a handful of top executives, including then-CEO Travis Kalanick, while keeping the general counsel and Uber’s legal department in the dark. “It was an easy situation for the government to make an example of,” Robinson said. Gallaher said she was struck by the apparent communication gap between Sullivan and Uber’s general counsel at the time, Sally Yoo. Rather than keep Yoo in the loop, Sullivan decided, after consulting with another Uber in-house lawyer, that the hack was not disclosable. That lawyer, Craig Clark, also kept the breach from the general counsel and was given immunity for testifying against Sullivan. “Risk management is a team sport,” Gallaher said. “And as much as the attorney is playing chess while the CISOs are playing checkers when it comes to navigating the legal processes and how to maneuver the legal system, the CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is.” She said general counsel should cultivate a strong relationship with their company’s security chief as a hedge against risk. “Some people might be looking at the Uber case as a general counsel and seeing the CISO got a criminal conviction and thinking, ‘That kind of sucks for him.’ Well, it’s going to suck for you if you end up having to have to do battle with the CISO, who has more technical expertise than you do,” Gallaher said. “So just get ahead of that now. Make that person your friend.” Legal and security chiefs may speak different languages, but should work together to understand the facts of an incident, Robinson said. “If you told me, ‘There’s an intrusion in the system and we’re in trouble because they have access to all of our stuff,’ I’d have to ask you a million questions about what happened, how did it happen, can it be stopped, et cetera. So if you’re not having those discussions, then you’re not going to be able to make a good decision for the company.” Uber was criticized back in 2016 for a lax culture around security that led to two similar data breaches within two years. As cyberattacks grow in sophistication and frequency, Robinson said executives will need to speak up when they spot issues, or walk away from a toxic company culture. “If you find yourself as a CISO or general counsel in an environment that is so toxic that you raise an issue and you’re just told to go away and be quiet, and if you don’t feel like you can change that culture by opening up the lines of communication, you know what? Free legal advice: Leave,” she said.
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • A jury in October found a former Uber security chief criminally liable in a 2016 data breach.
  • Participants in a panel discussion said Sullivan's conduct was especially egregious and that the government is unlikely to pursue personal liability regularly.
  • Even so, the case underscores the importance of strong lines of communication between legal departments and CISOs.

The October conviction of former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for concealing a 2016 data breach from government regulators sent ripples of anxiety through the C-suite over the prospect of more executives being held personally liable after a hack.

At a recent panel on what the verdict means for corporate security and legal teams, the consensus was that Sullivan’s prosecution was unusual, and his actions egregious. But while companies shouldn’t panic, general counsel and security chiefs should band together to tackle cybersecurity incidents with transparency and open communication.

“Cyber and privacy is a companywide concern, and that includes the board of directors, all the way down the line,” said Cari Robinson, a cybersecurity expert and former Revlon general counsel. “Teamwork is critical. If I don’t have a collaborative, transparent and open relationship with my CIO, my CISO, I’m not going to be able to give advice to the company or ultimately to the board of directors.”

The panel, hosted by the woman-led market network Fourth Floor and moderated by founder Breen Sullivan, also included virtual chief security officer and data privacy risk adviser Donna Gallaher and ClearOPS founder Caroline McCaffery.

Robinson, who also headed cybersecurity investigations as an assistant general counsel at IBM, said general counsel should have an “open and collaborative” relationship with security chiefs so that they can fully understand the incident and how to best advise the CEO on what the company’s response should be.

Sullivan’s conviction may have shaken the cybersecurity community, but Robinson said the government is unlikely to turn its sights on executives who act in good faith.

Where Sullivan and Uber went wrong, she said, was in confining their handling of the breach to just a handful of top executives, including then-CEO Travis Kalanick, while keeping the general counsel and Uber’s legal department in the dark.

“It was an easy situation for the government to make an example of,” Robinson said.

Gallaher said she was struck by the apparent communication gap between Sullivan and Uber’s general counsel at the time, Sally Yoo. Rather than keep Yoo in the loop, Sullivan decided, after consulting with another Uber in-house lawyer, that the hack was not disclosable.

That lawyer, Craig Clark, also kept the breach from the general counsel and was given immunity for testifying against Sullivan.

“Risk management is a team sport,” Gallaher said. “And as much as the attorney is playing chess while the CISOs are playing checkers when it comes to navigating the legal processes and how to maneuver the legal system, the CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is.”

She said general counsel should cultivate a strong relationship with their company’s security chief as a hedge against risk.

“Some people might be looking at the Uber case as a general counsel and seeing the CISO got a criminal conviction and thinking, ‘That kind of sucks for him.’ Well, it’s going to suck for you if you end up having to have to do battle with the CISO, who has more technical expertise than you do,” Gallaher said. “So just get ahead of that now. Make that person your friend.”

Legal and security chiefs may speak different languages, but should work together to understand the facts of an incident, Robinson said.

“If you told me, ‘There’s an intrusion in the system and we’re in trouble because they have access to all of our stuff,’ I’d have to ask you a million questions about what happened, how did it happen, can it be stopped, et cetera. So if you’re not having those discussions, then you’re not going to be able to make a good decision for the company.”

Uber was criticized back in 2016 for a lax culture around security that led to two similar data breaches within two years.

As cyberattacks grow in sophistication and frequency, Robinson said executives will need to speak up when they spot issues, or walk away from a toxic company culture.

“If you find yourself as a CISO or general counsel in an environment that is so toxic that you raise an issue and you’re just told to go away and be quiet, and if you don’t feel like you can change that culture by opening up the lines of communication, you know what? Free legal advice: Leave,” she said.

article.title: IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger
article.description: NEWS IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger Glen Weinstein will help stabilize iRobot now that it is retaining its independence. Resistance from European antitrust regulators scuttled Amazon's plan to buy it for $1.7 billion.…
article.text: NEWS IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger Glen Weinstein will help stabilize iRobot now that it is retaining its independence. Resistance from European antitrust regulators scuttled Amazon's plan to buy it for $1.7 billion. Technology Media and Telecom Maria Dinzeo Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon. The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works since August 2022, amid strong resistance from antitrust regulators in the European Union. In November, the EU’s competition authority said it was concerned that the acquisition, which would have added the Roomba to Amazon’s range of devices, would unfairly restrict competition in the market for robot vacuums. Amazon said it will pay iRobot a $94 million termination fee for walking way from the deal. NEWS

IRobot's Top Lawyer Takes CEO Reins After Failed Amazon Merger

Glen Weinstein will help stabilize iRobot now that it is retaining its independence. Resistance from European antitrust regulators scuttled Amazon's plan to buy it for $1.7 billion.

Technology Media and Telecom

Maria Dinzeo

Glen Weinstein, longtime iRobot legal chief, will be taking over as interim CEO at the Roomba maker in the wake of its failed sale to Amazon.

The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works since August 2022, amid strong resistance from antitrust regulators in the European Union. In November, the EU’s competition authority said it was concerned that the acquisition, which would have added the Roomba to Amazon’s range of devices, would unfairly restrict competition in the market for robot vacuums. Amazon said it will pay iRobot a $94 million termination fee for walking way from the deal.

article.title: The Indispensable Role of Litigation Analytics in Modern Class Action Practice
article.description: The legal profession is on the cusp of a new era, where data-driven insights become as integral to legal strategy as legal knowledge. Litigation analytics in class action practice offers a wealth of benefits, from strategic planning and risk…
article.text: The legal profession is on the cusp of a new era, where data-driven insights become as integral to legal strategy as legal knowledge. Litigation analytics in class action practice offers a wealth of benefits, from strategic planning and risk mitigation to client acquisition and case management. Embracing the power of data and analytics is a commitment to excellence in an ever-evolving legal landscape. As an in-house counsel at a company specializing in litigation analytics, I’ve had a front-row seat to the transformative impact that data-driven decision-making can have in the legal field, particularly in the realm of class action litigation. The world of law, often perceived as steeped in tradition and precedent, is undergoing a quiet revolution. The rise of big data and advanced analytics has ushered in a new era. The need for precise, accurate, and comprehensive data analysis is paramount in class action litigation, where the stakes are high and the complexities manifold. At the heart of this change is the rising tide of litigation analytics — a tool that is reshaping how legal professionals approach, strategize, and ultimately win class action cases. The Evolving Landscape of Class Action Litigation Class action litigation presents unique challenges and opportunities. These cases often involve large groups of individuals, significant financial stakes, and complex legal issues. While invaluable, traditional legal approaches can benefit immensely from integrating data-driven insights. This is where litigation analytics comes into play, offering a new lens through which to view the legal landscape. The Power of Data In Strategy and Decision-Making

article.title: 'Things Have Changed a Fair Bit': Latest Tech Layoffs Have Begun to Cut Into Legal Departments
article.description: Larger tech companies have been more willing to cut legal jobs than smaller players. Still, there hasn't been a surge in laid-off in-house attorneys. Those out of work might need to broaden their job searches. Legal departments are staying mostly…
article.text: Larger tech companies have been more willing to cut legal jobs than smaller players. Still, there hasn't been a surge in laid-off in-house attorneys. Those out of work might need to broaden their job searches. Legal departments are staying mostly intact as layoffs continue to batter the tech industry, though recruiters say in-house teams at larger companies are starting to feel the pinch. “A lot of GCs I’ve talked to have been able to hold onto their teams,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The really large tech companies have been pretty indiscriminate when it comes to layoffs, and there’s a certain percentage of folks getting cut at companies that have a lot of lawyers. Small to midsize companies have maybe lost a couple. But the legal teams weren’t necessarily bloated to begin with.” This content has been archived. article.title: Dominion Says Fox Legal Chief Should Have Blocked Airing of False Claims
article.description: Dominion Voting Systems charges Fox Corp. legal chief Viet Dinh is obscuring his role by hiding behind attorney-client privilege. In a deposition, Dinh said he didn't make editorial decisions. Dominion's lawsuit accuses Fox News of pushing falsehoods…
article.text: Dominion Voting Systems charges Fox Corp. legal chief Viet Dinh is obscuring his role by hiding behind attorney-client privilege. In a deposition, Dinh said he didn't make editorial decisions. Dominion's lawsuit accuses Fox News of pushing falsehoods about voter fraud to appease viewers. A Dominion Voting Systems court filing on Wednesday argues that Fox Corp. chief legal and policy officer Viet Dinh should have prevented Fox News from airing false claims that Dominion’s voting machines were rigged. The filing, a reply brief to Fox’s motion for summary judgment, accuses Dinh of shirking his legal obligations while hiding behind attorney-client privilege. It’s the latest effort by Denver-based Dominion to cast Dinh, a Harvard-educated lawyer and Kirkland & Ellis alum who’s held the legal reins since 2018, as a central figure in the network’s trashing of Dominion in the wake of Donald Trump’s defeat in the 2020 presidential election. article.title: Everyone Talks About Their Law Firm’s ‘Culture,’ But Is It Possible to Measure It?
article.description: Cultural inventories have taken a new level of importance at law firms since shifting to remote work and facing recruitment pressures. Another factor driving the importance of culture is the growth of business administrative staff at firms. Legal…
article.text: Cultural inventories have taken a new level of importance at law firms since shifting to remote work and facing recruitment pressures. Another factor driving the importance of culture is the growth of business administrative staff at firms. Legal consultant Marcie Borgal Shunk became certified to use a proprietary tool to measure business culture a decade ago. But it wasn’t until last year that a law firm hired her to measure its culture using the Chicago-based cultural inventory tool developer Human Synergistics. Cultural inventories have been more of a staple in Fortune 500 companies than the legal industry. In law firms, similar survey-based analyses had the limited purpose of assessing merger prospects or associate retention. But in 2022, Borgal Shunk had three clients—a global law firm, a midsize regional firm and a plaintiffs firm—ask her to assess what it was like for employees to work there. article.title: 'I'm Aghast': Viral Paul Hastings Presentation Garners Strong In-House Reaction
article.description: A slide prepared by a senior Paul Hastings associate listing nonnegotiable expectations for junior colleagues touched a nerve in the legal community. Some in-house attorneys said it exposed a deep misunderstanding of what clients actually want. Some…
article.text: A slide prepared by a senior Paul Hastings associate listing nonnegotiable expectations for junior colleagues touched a nerve in the legal community. Some in-house attorneys said it exposed a deep misunderstanding of what clients actually want. Some called the expectations appalling; others said that young lawyers tend to be coddled and need reminding that the client comes first. A presentation by a senior Paul Hastings associate with a demanding list of “nonnegotiable expectations” for junior colleagues is sparking a broad range of reactions in the in-house community, from a shrug to outrage. The debate reverberated across social media in recent days, with the outcry on Twitter especially spirited. “Definite big time Glengarry Glen Ross energy coming through on this one,” one commenter tweeted. “Reason 6,540,329 I am so glad I had nothing to do with these firms,” said another. article.title: Former Twitter Legal Chief, General Counsel and Other Executives Sue Elon Musk for Severance
article.description: Four former Twitter executives say they are owed more than $128 million in contractual severance. All four were fired right after Musk bought Twitter in 2022. The complaint cites Walter Isaacson's biography of Musk, saying he timed the firing to…
article.text: Four former Twitter executives say they are owed more than $128 million in contractual severance. All four were fired right after Musk bought Twitter in 2022. The complaint cites Walter Isaacson's biography of Musk, saying he timed the firing to avoid paying the severance. Four of the most senior members of Twitter’s past C-suite are suing Elon Musk for more than $128.6 million, claiming the new owner of the social media giant schemed to bilk them out of their contractual severance to save $200 million after buying the site back in 2022. “Because Musk decided he didn’t want to pay plaintiffs’ severance benefits, he simply fired them without reason, then made up fake cause and appointed employees of his various companies to uphold his decision,” their complaint said. A federal complaint filed Monday in San Francisco by Sidley Austin lawyers says Musk had it out for Twitter’s former Chief Executive Officer Parag Agrawal, Chief Financial Officer Ned Segal, Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde, and General Counsel Sean Edgett, and told his biographer Walter Isaacson that he would fire them “for cause” before their stock options could vest. Apparently Musk was furious that he had to go through with purchasing the company, and allegedly said he would “hunt every single one of” Twitter’s executives and directors “till the day they die.”

article.title: California's Latest Trailblazing Privacy Rules Getting Criticized From Every Direction
article.description: Business, labor and consumer interests expressed sharply differing views at a public forum Wednesday over proposed California rules that would govern how companies use customers’ personal information for anything from hiring decisions to advertising.…
article.text: Business, labor and consumer interests expressed sharply differing views at a public forum Wednesday over proposed California rules that would govern how companies use customers’ personal information for anything from hiring decisions to advertising. The California Privacy Protection Agency rules, in the works since the latter half of 2023, require companies that use automated decision-making technology to provide consumers with notice, a way to opt out, and a way to find out how the business uses ADMT to make decisions about them.
article.html:
