article.title: ChatGPT Might Simplify Life for In-House Counsel—While Also Creating New Risks
article.description: What You Need to Know ChatGPT can help automate routine communication, but legal experts say it isn't ready for prime time.In-house counsel need to learn how nonlegal employees are using ChatGPT, as they could exposing confidential information.…
article.text: What You Need to Know ChatGPT can help automate routine communication, but legal experts say it isn't ready for prime time.In-house counsel need to learn how nonlegal employees are using ChatGPT, as they could exposing confidential information. Analysts and academics are already theorizing about how Open AI’s ChatGPT will transform the legal field, with the more bullish of them seeing the AI-powered chatbot as automating routine tasks so that lawyers are freed up to work on more important matters. The discussion is part of a blizzard of debate fueled by the public debut of Open AI’s ChatGPT in November. The powerful tool has sparked speculation and angst, raising questions across industries about its ability to revolutionize communication and potential to lay waste to entire professions. “The reason people are paying so much attention to ChatGPT is it reveals the promise of these types of tools for law practice and what it might be capable of doing in not too long,” said Andrew Perlman, dean of the Suffolk University Law School. “But it’s not ready for prime time in terms of using it for anything important. Open AI’s CEO said that himself, and my own experience using it reveals how imperfect the tool can be,” he said. Perlman said he can envision ChatGPT as a system for answering common, repetitive questions on certain subjects. “It could also be used as a triage tool that could engage people back and forth and get them to the right resources, reducing the demands on the time of in-house lawyers and staff,” he said. “ChatGPT presents us with a way to streamline and make more efficient those kinds of routine communications.” ChatGPT is built on a large language model called text-davincci-003, or GPT-3.5, as it’s colloquially known, that can generate natural-sounding text fit for drafting simple content like an employee handbook, internal corporate policies or anything that requires a standard format. It also can be useful for converting complex legal terminology into plain English. But there are still kinks in the system. Joshua Lenon, a lawyer in residence at the legal software company Clio, said his compliance team recently put ChatGPT to the test, asking it to create a chart of how various state data-breach notification laws define the term “personally identifiable information.” “They are very specific in their drafting, but each state might not be exactly the same. We said, ‘Hey, why not see if ChatGPT could do this chart?’ Well, it couldn’t,” he said. “It wrote back that each state has different definitions but didn’t say what they were.” Lenon, who specializes in compliance, privacy and data security issues, said the experience helped delineate ChatGPT’s abilities and limitations. “It’s good way to transform clear data you already have but not a good way to go out and find data—certainly not to the degree that would be required in a legal environment.” Even for drafting contracts or other documents, Lenon said, ChatGPT requires a sharp human eye to look out for knowledge gaps. “You still have to put in a lot of work. It’s good for marketing and ad copy, but when it looks at legal it might get the format right but not the substance. That’s where it might be tripping for in-house counsel,” he said. Martin Gomez, a partner with Goodwin Procter specializing in intellectual property and tech issues, cautioned against putting blind trust in a generative-AI tool. “For in-house counsel, being able to focus on more high-value tasks or frankly being able to do their job faster, that has value. But we shouldn’t forget that lawyers have a fiduciary duty to their clients—so, for in-house, that’s the company. “They have a duty to get it right. One of the risky things about AI is even the people who make the AI don’t necessarily know where the answers came from. Having an overall understanding that it might get it wrong or could get it wrong and what sort of tasks are appropriate to outsource to an AI and what sort of things should never be trusted to an AI engine, that is something in-house will have to grapple with,” Gomez said. He said ChatGPT can be useful for questions for which there are black-and-white answers, but in-house counsel are often faced with the opposite. “So much of being a lawyer is operating in the gray and making judgment calls,” he said. Technologists note that ChatGPT is only as good as the data on which it is trained, a precept known among programmers as “garbage in, garbage out.” And, for that reason, corporate legal departments shouldn’t rely on the public version of ChatGPT. OpenAI is already at work on a professional variant of the tool. Perlman said he can see a custom version of ChatGPT, trained on a company’s knowledge base, being used effectively for research purposes. “One could imagine a situation where you put a query into a proprietary chatbot, asking it to create the first draft of a document that involves XYZ issues, and get a first draft using the department’s existing library and knowledge that’s already been created within the company But it would be a first draft. It would not be something you could rely on.” Lawyers also should be wary of company employees using ChatGPT for work matters. Perlman noted a recent instance where Amazon asked its employees not to feed customer AWS support questions into ChatGPT, even though it made their jobs much easier. According to the news website Insider, an Amazon lawyer also warned coders not to share confidential code with the chatbot. “This is important because your inputs may be used as training data for a further iteration of ChatGPT, and we wouldn’t want its output to include or resemble our confidential information (and I’ve already seen instances where its output closely matches existing material),” according to the lawyer’s memo to employees. “Confidentiality is a significant potential risk,” Perlman said. “It could be that a company can purchase a proprietary instance of an AI tool and they can hive it off in a way that protects the information, but I don’t think that at least in its current form, lawyers should be putting anything sensitive into these chatbots.” Lenon echoed this concern. “If in-house counsel should have any worries, it should be: How is this tool being used within my company already? Are my marketing people writing emails for the company using ChatGPT? Is it generating information that puts the company at risk, and are my external counsel relying upon it? “You’re probably breaking confidentiality by bringing in this outside party that is not your vendor, because you’re their product.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • ChatGPT can help automate routine communication, but legal experts say it isn't ready for prime time.
  • In-house counsel need to learn how nonlegal employees are using ChatGPT, as they could exposing confidential information.

Analysts and academics are already theorizing about how Open AI’s ChatGPT will transform the legal field, with the more bullish of them seeing the AI-powered chatbot as automating routine tasks so that lawyers are freed up to work on more important matters.

The discussion is part of a blizzard of debate fueled by the public debut of Open AI’s ChatGPT in November. The powerful tool has sparked speculation and angst, raising questions across industries about its ability to revolutionize communication and potential to lay waste to entire professions.

“The reason people are paying so much attention to ChatGPT is it reveals the promise of these types of tools for law practice and what it might be capable of doing in not too long,” said Andrew Perlman, dean of the Suffolk University Law School.

“But it’s not ready for prime time in terms of using it for anything important. Open AI’s CEO said that himself, and my own experience using it reveals how imperfect the tool can be,” he said.

Perlman said he can envision ChatGPT as a system for answering common, repetitive questions on certain subjects. “It could also be used as a triage tool that could engage people back and forth and get them to the right resources, reducing the demands on the time of in-house lawyers and staff,” he said. “ChatGPT presents us with a way to streamline and make more efficient those kinds of routine communications.”

ChatGPT is built on a large language model called text-davincci-003, or GPT-3.5, as it’s colloquially known, that can generate natural-sounding text fit for drafting simple content like an employee handbook, internal corporate policies or anything that requires a standard format. It also can be useful for converting complex legal terminology into plain English.

But there are still kinks in the system.

Joshua Lenon, a lawyer in residence at the legal software company Clio, said his compliance team recently put ChatGPT to the test, asking it to create a chart of how various state data-breach notification laws define the term “personally identifiable information.”

“They are very specific in their drafting, but each state might not be exactly the same. We said, ‘Hey, why not see if ChatGPT could do this chart?’ Well, it couldn’t,” he said. “It wrote back that each state has different definitions but didn’t say what they were.”

Lenon, who specializes in compliance, privacy and data security issues, said the experience helped delineate ChatGPT’s abilities and limitations. “It’s good way to transform clear data you already have but not a good way to go out and find data—certainly not to the degree that would be required in a legal environment.”

Even for drafting contracts or other documents, Lenon said, ChatGPT requires a sharp human eye to look out for knowledge gaps. “You still have to put in a lot of work. It’s good for marketing and ad copy, but when it looks at legal it might get the format right but not the substance. That’s where it might be tripping for in-house counsel,” he said.

Martin Gomez, a partner with Goodwin Procter specializing in intellectual property and tech issues, cautioned against putting blind trust in a generative-AI tool.

“For in-house counsel, being able to focus on more high-value tasks or frankly being able to do their job faster, that has value. But we shouldn’t forget that lawyers have a fiduciary duty to their clients—so, for in-house, that’s the company.

“They have a duty to get it right. One of the risky things about AI is even the people who make the AI don’t necessarily know where the answers came from. Having an overall understanding that it might get it wrong or could get it wrong and what sort of tasks are appropriate to outsource to an AI and what sort of things should never be trusted to an AI engine, that is something in-house will have to grapple with,” Gomez said.

He said ChatGPT can be useful for questions for which there are black-and-white answers, but in-house counsel are often faced with the opposite.

“So much of being a lawyer is operating in the gray and making judgment calls,” he said.

Technologists note that ChatGPT is only as good as the data on which it is trained, a precept known among programmers as “garbage in, garbage out.” And, for that reason, corporate legal departments shouldn’t rely on the public version of ChatGPT.

OpenAI is already at work on a professional variant of the tool. Perlman said he can see a custom version of ChatGPT, trained on a company’s knowledge base, being used effectively for research purposes.

“One could imagine a situation where you put a query into a proprietary chatbot, asking it to create the first draft of a document that involves XYZ issues, and get a first draft using the department’s existing library and knowledge that’s already been created within the company But it would be a first draft. It would not be something you could rely on.”

Lawyers also should be wary of company employees using ChatGPT for work matters. Perlman noted a recent instance where Amazon asked its employees not to feed customer AWS support questions into ChatGPT, even though it made their jobs much easier.

According to the news website Insider, an Amazon lawyer also warned coders not to share confidential code with the chatbot. “This is important because your inputs may be used as training data for a further iteration of ChatGPT, and we wouldn’t want its output to include or resemble our confidential information (and I’ve already seen instances where its output closely matches existing material),” according to the lawyer’s memo to employees.

“Confidentiality is a significant potential risk,” Perlman said. “It could be that a company can purchase a proprietary instance of an AI tool and they can hive it off in a way that protects the information, but I don’t think that at least in its current form, lawyers should be putting anything sensitive into these chatbots.”

Lenon echoed this concern.

“If in-house counsel should have any worries, it should be: How is this tool being used within my company already? Are my marketing people writing emails for the company using ChatGPT? Is it generating information that puts the company at risk, and are my external counsel relying upon it?

“You’re probably breaking confidentiality by bringing in this outside party that is not your vendor, because you’re their product.”

article.text: In-house counsel believe that the scope and scale of risks are growing and that they feel less prepared to deal with them than ever. That was among the stark findings of “The General Counsel Report 2024,” issued Wednesday by FTI Consulting and the legal tech firm Relativity. It was based on interviews and surveys conducted with 60 chief legal officers and general counsel in North America, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Australia.
article.html:
In-house counsel believe that the scope and scale of risks are growing and that they feel less prepared to deal with them than ever.

That was among the stark findings of “The General Counsel Report 2024,” issued Wednesday by FTI Consulting and the legal tech firm Relativity. It was based on interviews and surveys conducted with 60 chief legal officers and general counsel in North America, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Australia.

article.text: Struggling outdoor recreation and sporting goods company Vista Outdoor has brought in veteran in-house lawyer Jung Choi to help it spin off of its outdoor products business into a separate public company. Choi will serve as co-general counsel of Anoka, Minnesota-based Vista until the split. Then she will head up the legal department at Revelyst, a new company that will be headquartered in Bozeman, Montana, and will employ 2,900. article.title: 2 Extremes of AI's Copyright Fight: Permit IP Theft on Colossal Scale or Hinder Advancements in Human Expression
article.description: While many artists fixate on the potential for generative artificial intelligence to imitate their work and infringe their copyrights, some advocates for the technology say those fears obscure the technology’s potential to unlock new forms of…
article.text: While many artists fixate on the potential for generative artificial intelligence to imitate their work and infringe their copyrights, some advocates for the technology say those fears obscure the technology’s potential to unlock new forms of artistic expression and new pathways for human communication. Those two extremes served as the foundation for a lively debate Thursday at Stanford Law School’s CodeX FutureLaw 2024.
article.html:
While many artists fixate on the potential for generative artificial intelligence to imitate their work and infringe their copyrights, some advocates for the technology say those fears obscure the technology’s potential to unlock new forms of artistic expression and new pathways for human communication.

Those two extremes served as the foundation for a lively debate Thursday at Stanford Law School’s CodeX FutureLaw 2024.

article.title: 'Just Does Not Want to Pay': Attorneys for Ex-Twitter CLO Call Out Elon Musk in $1.1M Billing Dispute
article.description: In the latest in the ongoing saga over former Twitter legal chief Vijaya Gadde’s unpaid legal bills, her attorneys hit back at the social media platform—and its new owner—for refusing to pony up $1.1 million for fees she incurred in preparing to…
article.text: In the latest in the ongoing saga over former Twitter legal chief Vijaya Gadde’s unpaid legal bills, her attorneys hit back at the social media platform—and its new owner—for refusing to pony up $1.1 million for fees she incurred in preparing to testify before Congress earlier this year, saying in a court filing this week that Twitter “just does not want to pay.” Gadde and two other former Twitter executives sued the San Francisco-based company in the Delaware Court of Chancery in April seeking reimbursement for legal fees they’d racked up on Twitter-related matters, including lawsuits and investigations, since Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the company in October and immediately fired them. article.html:
In the latest in the ongoing saga over former Twitter legal chief Vijaya Gadde’s unpaid legal bills, her attorneys hit back at the social media platform—and its new owner—for refusing to pony up $1.1 million for fees she incurred in preparing to testify before Congress earlier this year, saying in a court filing this week that Twitter “just does not want to pay.”

Gadde and two other former Twitter executives sued the San Francisco-based company in the Delaware Court of Chancery in April seeking reimbursement for legal fees they’d racked up on Twitter-related matters, including lawsuits and investigations, since Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the company in October and immediately fired them.

article.title: AI Might Kill Off the Billable Hour Someday, But It Will Be a Slow Death
article.description: "The people who regulate the profession are the profession. They are judges and members of the bar. So what incentive do they have to give away that control to the machine?" said Foster Sayers, vice president of legal ops at health tech company…
article.text: "The people who regulate the profession are the profession. They are judges and members of the bar. So what incentive do they have to give away that control to the machine?" said Foster Sayers, vice president of legal ops at health tech company symplr. A new report from Lex Mundi has reinvigorated the debate over the fate of the billable hour. It was based on insights gleaned from general counsel who attended the law firm network's summit in Milan in October. Attendees said generative AI will make legal departments less reliant on law firms for basic advice. The legal industry’s deeply entrenched pricing model—the billable hour—isn’t going away any time soon, though generative artificial intelligence may chip away at its dominance for certain types of work, in-house counsel and legal industry experts say.
article.html:
"The people who regulate the profession are the profession. They are judges and members of the bar. So what incentive do they have to give away that control to the machine?" said Foster Sayers, vice president of legal ops at health tech company symplr.

  • A new report from Lex Mundi has reinvigorated the debate over the fate of the billable hour.
  • It was based on insights gleaned from general counsel who attended the law firm network's summit in Milan in October.
  • Attendees said generative AI will make legal departments less reliant on law firms for basic advice.

The legal industry’s deeply entrenched pricing model—the billable hour—isn’t going away any time soon, though generative artificial intelligence may chip away at its dominance for certain types of work, in-house counsel and legal industry experts say.

article.title: Anheuser-Busch Litigation Head Joins Lab-Grown Meat Pioneer as CLO
article.description: Marc Shelley has joined Israel-based Believer Meats after six years at the brewing giant. Believer Meats expanded into the U.S. in 2022, breaking ground on what it calls the largest cultivated meat production plant in the world. It raised $347…
article.text: Marc Shelley has joined Israel-based Believer Meats after six years at the brewing giant. Believer Meats expanded into the U.S. in 2022, breaking ground on what it calls the largest cultivated meat production plant in the world. It raised $347 million in Series B funding last year led by Tyson Foods' venture capital arm. Anheuser-Busch global litigation head Marc Shelley started this week as chief legal officer at Believer Meats, an Israeli cultivated-meat startup that broke ground on its first U.S. commercial-scale facility in December. Shelley was at Anheuser-Busch for six years, starting out as director of global litigation. He most recently took on the additional role as head of the brewer’s IP, employment law and crisis management strategy, according to his LinkedIn profile. He was also a partner for 13 years at Kansas City, Missouri-based Shook, Hardy & Bacon, where as a member of the products liability team he advised multinational manufacturers on consumer protection claims.
article.html:
• Marc Shelley has joined Israel-based Believer Meats after six years at the brewing giant.
  • Believer Meats expanded into the U.S. in 2022, breaking ground on what it calls the largest cultivated meat production plant in the world.
  • It raised $347 million in Series B funding last year led by Tyson Foods' venture capital arm.

Anheuser-Busch global litigation head Marc Shelley started this week as chief legal officer at Believer Meats, an Israeli cultivated-meat startup that broke ground on its first U.S. commercial-scale facility in December.

Shelley was at Anheuser-Busch for six years, starting out as director of global litigation. He most recently took on the additional role as head of the brewer’s IP, employment law and crisis management strategy, according to his LinkedIn profile. He was also a partner for 13 years at Kansas City, Missouri-based Shook, Hardy & Bacon, where as a member of the products liability team he advised multinational manufacturers on consumer protection claims.

article.title: Feds Jump Into Algorithmic Pricing Suit, Say Collusion Can Occur Without Humans Uttering a Word
article.description: A class-action lawsuit filed last year alleged that Atlantic City hotels engaged in price fixing by knowingly adopting the same algorithmic pricing platform. The defendants want the suit dismissed, saying plaintiffs failed to meet their burden of…
article.text: A class-action lawsuit filed last year alleged that Atlantic City hotels engaged in price fixing by knowingly adopting the same algorithmic pricing platform. The defendants want the suit dismissed, saying plaintiffs failed to meet their burden of showing when or how conspirators arranged their scheme. The DOJ and FTC say the defendants have no such burden and can prevail without showing the hotels even communicated. Federal antitrust enforcers say competing casino hotels illegally colluded to set room rates by knowingly adopting the same algorithmic pricing platform, a tacit agreement that amounts to an antitrust violation, even if the hotels never communicated directly. The Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice filed a statement of interest late Thursday in Cornish-Adebiyi v. Caesars Entertainment, where a class of New Jersey hotel guests claim they paid “supracompetitive” prices for rooms at Caesars Atlantic City Hotel & Casino and the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Atlantic City. The suit, filed in May 2023, says the prices were driven by an algorithmic pricing platform called Rainmaker that analyzes real-time data about market supply and demand to generate “optimal” room rates.
article.html:
• A class-action lawsuit filed last year alleged that Atlantic City hotels engaged in price fixing by knowingly adopting the same algorithmic pricing platform.
  • The defendants want the suit dismissed, saying plaintiffs failed to meet their burden of showing when or how conspirators arranged their scheme.
  • The DOJ and FTC say the defendants have no such burden and can prevail without showing the hotels even communicated.

Federal antitrust enforcers say competing casino hotels illegally colluded to set room rates by knowingly adopting the same algorithmic pricing platform, a tacit agreement that amounts to an antitrust violation, even if the hotels never communicated directly.

The Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice filed a statement of interest late Thursday in Cornish-Adebiyi v. Caesars Entertainment, where a class of New Jersey hotel guests claim they paid “supracompetitive” prices for rooms at Caesars Atlantic City Hotel & Casino and the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Atlantic City. The suit, filed in May 2023, says the prices were driven by an algorithmic pricing platform called Rainmaker that analyzes real-time data about market supply and demand to generate “optimal” room rates.

During a panel discussion Tuesday at the CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas, a diverse group of general counsel and legal operations leaders shared how they are making use of generative AI and how they got started.
article.html:
No legal department wants to get left behind on generative AI. But corporate legal departments are in various stages of readiness to adopt this rapidly evolving technology, and legal leaders are still figuring out how to unlock its potential while mitigating risk.

During a panel discussion Tuesday at the CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas, a diverse group of general counsel and legal operations leaders shared how they are making use of generative AI and how they got started.

article.title: Orrick's Data Breach Was Bigger Than Previously Reported
article.description: Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe, 400 Howard St., San Francisco, CA. Photo: Jason Doiy/ALM An additional 176,000 people were added to the affected cohort, while several other firms reported new data breaches at the end of 2023. The original version of…
article.text: Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe, 400 Howard St., San Francisco, CA. Photo: Jason Doiy/ALM An additional 176,000 people were added to the affected cohort, while several other firms reported new data breaches at the end of 2023. The original version of this story was published on The American Lawyer Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe revised a data breach report in late December to include more than 630,000 affected individuals. Orrick settled four class action lawsuits regarding the breach in December. A class action lawsuit against Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner over a 2023 data breach is ongoing. Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe’s data breach last year involved more people than previously reported, according to a late December update the firm filed with the offices of multiple state attorneys general. Meanwhile, several other firms also reported data breaches around the end of 2023.
article.html:
Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe, 400 Howard St., San Francisco, CA. Photo: Jason Doiy/ALM

An additional 176,000 people were added to the affected cohort, while several other firms reported new data breaches at the end of 2023.

The original version of this story was published on The American Lawyer

  • Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe revised a data breach report in late December to include more than 630,000 affected individuals.
  • Orrick settled four class action lawsuits regarding the breach in December.
  • A class action lawsuit against Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner over a 2023 data breach is ongoing.

Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe’s data breach last year involved more people than previously reported, according to a late December update the firm filed with the offices of multiple state attorneys general.

Meanwhile, several other firms also reported data breaches around the end of 2023.

article.title: Growing Geopolitical Threats Expand Role of GC
article.description: 01/23/2024 Daily Report TO: ALL MEMBERS OF THE BAR AND ALL CITIZENS OF THE CITY OF ATLANTA The Atlanta Judicial Commission is now accepting nominations for the position of Municipal Court Judge for the City of Atlanta Municipal Court. Members of the…
article.text: 01/23/2024 Daily Report TO: ALL MEMBERS OF THE BAR AND ALL CITIZENS OF THE CITY OF ATLANTA The Atlanta Judicial Commission is now accepting nominations for the position of Municipal Court Judge for the City of Atlanta Municipal Court. Members of the bar may nominate themselves or others, and the public is invited to submit nominations. DuBose, Esq. 75 14th Street, NE, Suite 2110, Atlanta, GA 30309 A nominee must be at least 25 years of age, a resident of the City of Atlanta for one year prior to appointment and shall have been admitted to practice law in the State of Georgia for at least five years. article.title: All the News That's Fit to Pinch: NYT v. OpenAI
article.description: The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new…
article.text: The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new technology. Perhaps the most troublesome of all so far is the new complaint filed by The New York Times alleging that OpenAI, Microsoft and others committed copyright infringement in training its GPT systems and wrongfully attributing false information to The Times. Whatever effects ultimately are wrought, there are several key legal precedents to assess how such a new and potentially transformative technology aligns with the dictates of copyright law. Courts have said time and again that the fair use doctrine may be “‘the most troublesome in the whole law of copyright.’” See, e.g., Oracle Am., Inc. v. Google Inc., 886 F.3d 1179, 1191 (Fed. Cir. 2018) [internal citations omitted], rev’d on other grounds, 141 S. Ct. 1183 (2021). The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new technology. Several such cases to date have received considerable publicity, including two class actions by Michael Chabon, Ta-Nehisi Coates and others, Chabon v. OpenAI Inc., No. 3:23-cv-04625 (N.D.Cal.) and Chabon v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 3:23-cv-04663, (N.D.Cal.); another class action involving several best-selling authors, Authors Guild v. OpenAI Inc., No. 1:23-cv-08292 (S.D.N.Y.), and another class action including Sarah Silverman, Kadrey v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D.Cal). Perhaps the most troublesome of all so far is the new complaint filed by The New York Times alleging that OpenAI, Microsoft and others committed copyright infringement in training its Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT) systems and wrongfully attributing false information to The Times via the output from systems such as ChatGPT and Bing Chat. The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft Corp., No. 1:23-cv-11195 (S.D.N.Y.) The Times asserts claims for direct as well as vicarious and contributory copyright infringement, unfair competition, trademark dilution, and violation of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act — Removal of Copyright Measurement Information (17 U.S.C. §1202). Among other things, the complaint alleges that GPT not only copied published articles verbatim but could be prompted to offer up content that is normally protected by The Times‘ paywall. The complaint cites several such examples of nearly verbatim copying of large sections of articles and includes screenshots of GPT delivering up the first paragraphs of articles as well as ensuing paragraphs when prompted to do so. The complaint alleges that the “training” of the program included storing encoded copies of the works in computer memory and repeatedly reproducing copies of the training dataset, such that millions of The Times works were “copied and ingested — multiple times — for the purpose of ‘training” Defendants’ GPT models.” The Times further alleges that when OpenAI’s chatbots are not revealing verbatim copying, they instead (when actual content is not available) entirely fabricate “hallucinations” — inventing and misattributing to The Times content that it did not publish.
article.html:
• The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new technology.
  • Perhaps the most troublesome of all so far is the new complaint filed by The New York Times alleging that OpenAI, Microsoft and others committed copyright infringement in training its GPT systems and wrongfully attributing false information to The Times.
  • Whatever effects ultimately are wrought, there are several key legal precedents to assess how such a new and potentially transformative technology aligns with the dictates of copyright law.

Courts have said time and again that the fair use doctrine may be “‘the most troublesome in the whole law of copyright.’” See, e.g., Oracle Am., Inc. v. Google Inc., 886 F.3d 1179, 1191 (Fed. Cir. 2018) [internal citations omitted], rev’d on other grounds, 141 S. Ct. 1183 (2021). OpenAI Inc., No. 1:23-cv-08292 (S.D.N.Y.), and another class action including Sarah Silverman, Kadrey v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D.Cal).

Perhaps the most troublesome of all so far is the new complaint filed by The New York Times alleging that OpenAI, Microsoft and others committed copyright infringement in training its Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT) systems and wrongfully attributing false information to The Times via the output from systems such as ChatGPT and Bing Chat. article.title: FTC Scrutinizing Volume Discounts in Pharma, Using Dormant Law It Could Apply to Other Industries
article.description: "Sellers in every industry should monitor these developments to see how the agency's enforcement priorities evolve and are treated by the courts, so they can calibrate their compliance policies accordingly," said Mary Kaiser, a Morrison & Foerster…
article.text: "Sellers in every industry should monitor these developments to see how the agency's enforcement priorities evolve and are treated by the courts, so they can calibrate their compliance policies accordingly," said Mary Kaiser, a Morrison & Foerster partner. The Federal Trade Commission is invoking the Robinson-Patman Act of 1936 as it investigates drug pricing. The law had been unused for decades before the agency last year used it to investigate the alcoholic beverage industry. Its original purpose was to protect mom-and-pop grocery stores from price discrimination during the Depression.
article.html:
"Sellers in every industry should monitor these developments to see how the agency's enforcement priorities evolve and are treated by the courts, so they can calibrate their compliance policies accordingly," said Mary Kaiser, a Morrison & Foerster partner.

  • Its original purpose was to protect mom-and-pop grocery stores from price discrimination during the Depression.

article.title: Senior Boeing Attorney Steps In to HR Chief Role as Contentious Labor Talks Loom
article.description: NEWS Senior Boeing Attorney Steps In to HR Chief Role as Contentious Labor Talks Loom Uma Amuluru's move to human resources "is great training to someday sit in the GC seat," legal recruiter Deborah Ben-Canaan said. In House Moves Maria Dinzeo Uma…
article.text: NEWS Senior Boeing Attorney Steps In to HR Chief Role as Contentious Labor Talks Loom Uma Amuluru's move to human resources "is great training to someday sit in the GC seat," legal recruiter Deborah Ben-Canaan said. In House Moves Maria Dinzeo Uma Amuluru, who has rapidly climbed the leadership rungs in Boeing's legal department, will become chief human resources officer. She'll replace Michael D'Ambrose, who is retiring. Boeing in March will kick off contract talks with its largest union. Uma Amuluru, general counsel for Boeing Co.’s defense and aerospace division, is headed for the C-suite this spring. She’ll replace current HR chief Michael D’Ambrose when her job starts on April 1, Boeing said. D’Ambrose said he plans to retire in July, capping a career extending back to the 1970s that included senior leadership roles at Ingersoll Rand, The Travelers, Citigroup, Toys R Us and ADM. Senior Boeing Attorney Steps In to HR Chief Role as Contentious Labor Talks Loom

Uma Amuluru's move to human resources "is great training to someday sit in the GC seat," legal recruiter Deborah Ben-Canaan said.

In House Moves

Maria Dinzeo
  • Uma Amuluru, who has rapidly climbed the leadership rungs in Boeing's legal department, will become chief human resources officer.
  • She'll replace Michael D'Ambrose, who is retiring.
  • Boeing in March will kick off contract talks with its largest union.

Uma Amuluru, general counsel for Boeing Co.’s defense and aerospace division, is headed for the C-suite this spring.

She’ll replace current HR chief Michael D’Ambrose when her job starts on April 1, Boeing said. D’Ambrose said he plans to retire in July, capping a career extending back to the 1970s that included senior leadership roles at Ingersoll Rand, The Travelers, Citigroup, Toys R Us and ADM.

article.title: Early Impact of the CHIPS Act
article.description: The CHIPS Act was driven in part by concerns among U.S. policymakers that the U.S. semiconductor industry had fallen behind other modern manufacturing hubs abroad. The Act provides for a total of $52.7 billion in appropriations from 2023 through…
article.text: The CHIPS Act was driven in part by concerns among U.S. policymakers that the U.S. semiconductor industry had fallen behind other modern manufacturing hubs abroad. The Act provides for a total of $52.7 billion in appropriations from 2023 through 2027. This year and beyond look to be a critical period for the semiconductor industry, both in the United States and worldwide. The Creating Helpful Incentives to Protect Semiconductors Act (the CHIPS Act or the Act) was signed into law in August 2022, providing for a total of $52.7 billion in appropriations from 2023 through 2027. This article describes certain key developments in the period from passage of the CHIPS Act through the present day, including a summary of commitments by semiconductor companies to increase capital investment in the United States (possibly reflecting incentives created by the legislation). We also provide a brief survey of key grantmaking and investment activity by U.S. government agencies since passage of the Act. Finally, we discuss the Act’s likely future, as well as analogous policy developments in critical East Asian manufacturing centers. The CHIPS Act was driven in part by concerns among U.S. policymakers that the U.S. semiconductor industry had fallen behind other modern manufacturing hubs, primarily in East Asia (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and, to some extent, China). See, id. at 2. In light of these concerns and others, the Act was structured in large part to provide incentives and financial resources to companies who wished to expand or develop semiconductor manufacturing operations in the United States. See, id. at 6 – 10. To this end, the Act earmarked up to $38.22 billion to provide financial incentives to build, expand, and equip U.S.-based semiconductor fabrication plants, as well as other manufacturing facilities, necessary for the overall supply and value chain (e.g., packaging). See, id. at 14, 16. You Might Like May 14, 2024 May 10, 2024 Government Should Reconsider Law Firm Obligations on Russia Sanctions, Says Law Society February 06, 2024

article.title: Orthofix Replaces Legal Chief Fired for 'Offensive Conduct'
article.description: Andres Cedron has taken the legal reins at Orthofix after 14 years at Stryker Corp. Orthofix fired its top executives last year, including its legal chief, for offensive conduct. The firings were made by the board after an investigation conducted by…
article.text: Andres Cedron has taken the legal reins at Orthofix after 14 years at Stryker Corp. Orthofix fired its top executives last year, including its legal chief, for offensive conduct. The firings were made by the board after an investigation conducted by independent outside counsel, which cost the company $10 million. After firing its previous legal chief for offensive misconduct last year, medical device company Orthofix has replaced him with Andres Cedron, a former in-house leader at Stryker Corp. “With a broad breadth of experience in the medical device industry and legal transactions, Andres is the perfect fit for this important leadership role,” Orthofix President and CEO Massimo Calafiore said in a news release announcing the hire Tuesday. “His extensive understanding of our business and the overall market will be an asset in helping the company drive profitability and growth as we continue to power Orthofix’s transformation.”
article.html:
• Andres Cedron has taken the legal reins at Orthofix after 14 years at Stryker Corp.
  • Orthofix fired its top executives last year, including its legal chief, for offensive conduct.
  • The firings were made by the board after an investigation conducted by independent outside counsel, which cost the company $10 million.

After firing its previous legal chief for offensive misconduct last year, medical device company Orthofix has replaced him with Andres Cedron, a former in-house leader at Stryker Corp.

“With a broad breadth of experience in the medical device industry and legal transactions, Andres is the perfect fit for this important leadership role,” Orthofix President and CEO Massimo Calafiore said in a news release announcing the hire Tuesday. “His extensive understanding of our business and the overall market will be an asset in helping the company drive profitability and growth as we continue to power Orthofix’s transformation.”

article.title: Ex-GC of Autonomy Says Accounting Turned Odd Before $11B Sale to HP
article.description: NEWS Ex-GC of Autonomy Says Accounting Turned Odd Before $11B Sale to HP Joel Scott, the former general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, took the stand Thursday in the fraud trial of former Autonomy CEO Mike Lynch,…
article.text: NEWS Ex-GC of Autonomy Says Accounting Turned Odd Before $11B Sale to HP Joel Scott, the former general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, took the stand Thursday in the fraud trial of former Autonomy CEO Mike Lynch, accused of padding his company’s revenue to dupe HP into the purchase. April 19, 2024 at 12:09 PM 10 minute read Criminal Law Maria Dinzeo It was around 2007 when Joel Scott, then general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, started to get concerned about some of the business tactics being pushed by his employers. There were fishy transactions. For example, Autonomy held itself out as an enterprise software firm but had started covertly selling hardware. It also entered into transactions with resellers that didn’t quite make sense. Resellers would purchase the Autonomy’s software without paying for it fully or selling to an end user, but Autonomy would record the deal as revenue. NEWS

Ex-GC of Autonomy Says Accounting Turned Odd Before $11B Sale to HP

Joel Scott, the former general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, took the stand Thursday in the fraud trial of former Autonomy CEO Mike Lynch, accused of padding his company’s revenue to dupe HP into the purchase.

April 19, 2024 at 12:09 PM

10 minute read

Criminal Law

Maria Dinzeo

It was around 2007 when Joel Scott, then general counsel of the U.K.-based tech company Autonomy’s U.S. division, started to get concerned about some of the business tactics being pushed by his employers.

There were fishy transactions. For example, Autonomy held itself out as an enterprise software firm but had started covertly selling hardware. It also entered into transactions with resellers that didn’t quite make sense. Resellers would purchase the Autonomy’s software without paying for it fully or selling to an end user, but Autonomy would record the deal as revenue.

article.title: 3 Orthofix Execs Fired for 'Offensive Conduct' Claim Wrongful Termination, Demand Severance
article.description: NEWS 3 Orthofix Execs Fired for 'Offensive Conduct' Claim Wrongful Termination, Demand Severance Ex-Chief Legal Officer Patrick Keran, ex-CEO Keith Valentine and ex-Chief Financial Officer John Bostjancic are fighting back, asserting the company has…
article.text: NEWS 3 Orthofix Execs Fired for 'Offensive Conduct' Claim Wrongful Termination, Demand Severance Ex-Chief Legal Officer Patrick Keran, ex-CEO Keith Valentine and ex-Chief Financial Officer John Bostjancic are fighting back, asserting the company has defamed them. General Counsel and In House Counsel Maria Dinzeo Three former Orthofix executives fired last September over “offensive conduct” have filed arbitration claims against the medical device company alleging wrongful termination, Orthofix disclosed in its latest proxy statement. Chief Legal Officer Patrick Keran, CEO Keith Valentine and Chief Financial Officer John Bostjancic contend that the Lewisville, Texas-based company fired them for cause even though their conduct did not meet the contractually applicable definition of the term. article.title: Legal Industry Experts Launch 'Legal Data Intelligence' With Help From Relativity
article.description: The framework, meant to help legal departments harness data in a smarter way, was founded by legal tech veteran Omar Haroun, who was joined by nearly 20 other industry experts. The venture has received resources from e-discovery company Relativity.…
article.text: The framework, meant to help legal departments harness data in a smarter way, was founded by legal tech veteran Omar Haroun, who was joined by nearly 20 other industry experts. The venture has received resources from e-discovery company Relativity. Omar Haroun, who led AI strategy for e-discovery provider Relativity, left the company in 2023 with hints of a stealth project in the works. On Thursday, he announced the launch of the Legal Data Intelligence. Haroun is the CEO of Cicero, a technology startup in stealth mode, and one of the framework’s several founders. Legal Data Intelligence is categorized as a “framework” or “model” outlining step-by-step guidelines for how a legal department might identify and use data to complete legal tasks in a more efficient way, Haroun told Legaltech News. For Haroun, who has been discussing this framework with industry experts since 2022, the key pain point the model aims to solve is the silos in which not just legal data exists, but also those charged with handling the data, he said. “There’s no shortage of data scientists, engineering teams who are prioritizing AI for the business and even maybe the back office functions [in legal departments],” he explained. “But I think where there’s a massive disconnect and risk is that if you’re not really mindful of all of the nuances that only apply to legal, then you’re taking on a lot of risk [by] not handling [data] the right way.” The project is supported by Relativity, though not in terms of direct funding. Rather, with resources like web designers who worked on the Legal Data Intelligence website, which was unveiled at the Corporate Legal Operations Consortium (CLOC) Global Institute 2024 conference in Las Vegas on Wednesday. “Some of the creative resources have been provided by Relativity. And that’s really been a huge benefit, because we wouldn’t be able to visually necessarily do all this,” Haroun said. But for the most part, the e-discovery company has “kept a distance” from the venture, acknowledging that its findings “may not always benefit them,” since some of the “use cases” listed by the framework do not yet reflect the products available within Relativity, he added. In an emailed statement, Relativity noted that its “goal is to work with these founding members and other innovators in our market to share this approach throughout our industry so more people in our community can benefit from it.” The website identifies the venture’s goal as empowering “the legal industry with a vocabulary, framework, and best practices to manage legal data, and ultimately accelerat[ing] the dispensation of legal advice and the pursuit of justice.” Currently, Legal Data Intelligence consists of around twenty voluntary founding members from corporate legal departments and law firms, including Haroun. Those listed by the framework document include: Briordy Meyers, discovery counsel at Google; Adam Rouse, senior counsel and director of e-discovery operations at Walgreens; Jeff Salling, chief of staff and senior director of legal operations at Moderna; Ashley Christakis, senior manager of e-discovery and legal operations at CrowdStrike; Jeremiah Weasenforth, legal analytics director at Edward Jones; Farrah Pepper, chief legal innovation counsel (CLIC) at Marsh McLennan; Bobby Malhotra, litigation partner at Winston & Strawn; Josh Kreamer, chief strategy officer and general counsel at Fileread ; Scott Milner, global practice group leader of eData practice group at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius; and Geof Vance, litigation partner and firmwide chair of e-discovery services & strategy practice at Perkins Coie. Currently, the model covers use cases under four umbrellas: Disputes and Investigations: Litigation, Regulatory Requests, Third-party Subpoenas, Internal InvestigationsCorporate: Contract Reviews, Contract Lifecycle Management, DiverstituresData Protection Compliance: FOIA Requests, DSARs, Data Breach Response, Personal Data Identification and AnonymizationBusiness of Law: Invoice Review, Operational Efficiency However, Haroun said that as more within the legal industry explore and understand the framework, it is likely to grow in both use cases and number of members. The group is not directly funded, and all work done is on a voluntary-basis. “I think there’s kind of a decision among the twenty-ish of us that this was just better to be kind of a skunkworks project that was all done on our own respective nights and weekends, so to speak, and truly came out of passion for what we are doing… for the good of the industry,” he said.
article.html:
The framework, meant to help legal departments harness data in a smarter way, was founded by legal tech veteran Omar Haroun, who was joined by nearly 20 other industry experts. The venture has received resources from e-discovery company Relativity.

Omar Haroun, who led AI strategy for e-discovery provider Relativity, left the company in 2023 with hints of a stealth project in the works. On Thursday,  he announced the launch of the Legal Data Intelligence.

Haroun is the CEO of Cicero, a technology startup in stealth mode, and one of the framework’s several founders.

Legal Data Intelligence is categorized as a “framework” or “model” outlining step-by-step guidelines for how a legal department might identify and use data to complete legal tasks in a more efficient way, Haroun told Legaltech News.

For Haroun, who has been discussing this framework with industry experts since 2022, the key pain point the model aims to solve is the silos in which not just legal data exists, but also those charged with handling the data, he said.

“There’s no shortage of data scientists, engineering teams who are prioritizing AI for the business and even maybe the back office functions [in legal departments],” he explained. “But I think where there’s a massive disconnect and risk is that if you’re not really mindful of all of the nuances that only apply to legal, then you’re taking on a lot of risk [by] not handling [data] the right way.”

The project is supported by Relativity, though not in terms of direct funding. Rather, with resources like web designers who worked on the Legal Data Intelligence website, which was unveiled at the Corporate Legal Operations Consortium (CLOC) Global Institute 2024 conference in Las Vegas on Wednesday.

“Some of the creative resources have been provided by Relativity. And that’s really been a huge benefit, because we wouldn’t be able to visually necessarily do all this,” Haroun said. But for the most part, the e-discovery company has “kept a distance” from the venture, acknowledging that its findings “may not always benefit them,” since some of the “use cases” listed by the framework do not yet reflect the products available within Relativity, he added.

In an emailed statement, Relativity noted that its “goal is to work with these founding members and other innovators in our market to share this approach throughout our industry so more people in our community can benefit from it.”

The website identifies the venture’s goal as empowering “the legal industry with a vocabulary, framework, and best practices to manage legal data, and ultimately accelerat[ing] the dispensation of legal advice and the pursuit of justice.”

Currently, Legal Data Intelligence consists of around twenty voluntary founding members from corporate legal departments and law firms, including Haroun. Those listed by the framework document include: Briordy Meyers, discovery counsel at Google; Adam Rouse, senior counsel and director of e-discovery operations at Walgreens; Jeff Salling, chief of staff and senior director of legal operations at Moderna; Ashley Christakis, senior manager of e-discovery and legal operations at CrowdStrike; Jeremiah Weasenforth, legal analytics director at Edward Jones; Farrah Pepper, chief legal innovation counsel (CLIC) at Marsh McLennan; Bobby Malhotra, litigation partner at Winston & Strawn; Josh Kreamer, chief strategy officer and general counsel at Fileread ; Scott Milner, global practice group leader of eData practice group at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius; and Geof Vance, litigation partner and firmwide chair of e-discovery services & strategy practice at Perkins Coie.

Currently, the model covers use cases under four umbrellas:

  1. Disputes and Investigations: Litigation, Regulatory Requests, Third-party Subpoenas, Internal Investigations
  2. Corporate: Contract Reviews, Contract Lifecycle Management, Diverstitures
  3. Data Protection Compliance: FOIA Requests, DSARs, Data Breach Response, Personal Data Identification and Anonymization
  4. Business of Law: Invoice Review, Operational Efficiency

However, Haroun said that as more within the legal industry explore and understand the framework, it is likely to grow in both use cases and number of members.

The group is not directly funded, and all work done is on a voluntary-basis.

“I think there’s kind of a decision among the twenty-ish of us that this was just better to be kind of a skunkworks project that was all done on our own respective nights and weekends, so to speak, and truly came out of passion for what we are doing… for the good of the industry,” he said.

article.title: Why the DOJ and FTC Are Wrong on Algorithms and Antitrust
article.description: Algorithms Don’t Violate the Sherman Antitrust Act contend that the company (and the property managers who utilize it) are in violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, which condemns “[a]ny combination which tampers with price structures,” because such…
article.text: Algorithms Don’t Violate the Sherman Antitrust Act contend that the company (and the property managers who utilize it) are in violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, which condemns “[a]ny combination which tampers with price structures,” because such a combination “directly interfer[es] with the free play of market forces.” However, the DOJ and FTC appear to be forgetting one crucial fact: proving “collusion” requires demonstrating the parties in question entered into an agreement or understanding to price fix. In other words, the government needs to establish an intent to engage in an illegal activity. Property managers do not collude when utilizing RealPage; they do not even communicate with one another. Nor do most of the other actors who use algorithms across a wide range of economic sectors. Business owners use algorithmic services because they are efficient, just like how most good real estate agents reference comparable past closings on the MLS before listing their clients’ properties. They do not depend on their pricing recommendations or follow it blindly; they just use it as a tool to ensure their pricing remains dynamic and competitive. Multiple entities using the same software is hardly proof of a general intent to price fix—it is not even proof of any two entities colluding together—so it cannot be a violation of the Sherman Act. The property managers’ actions are nothing but a classic example of conscious parallelism, which is perfectly legal. DOJ and FTC’s Case Law ‘Evidence’ Doesn’t Hold Up First, the DOJ and FTC cited Plymouth Dealers’ Association, which dealt with competing dealers agreeing on a “fixed uniform list price” for Plymouth cars. Plymouth may very well be an example of a Sherman Act violation as the Supreme Court found (lower courts disagreed), but still, this case involved companies banding together in a coordinated fashion. RealPage does not, nor do most of the other algorithms that other sectors utilize today engage in any sort of coordinated fashion based on some sort of mutual understanding or agreement. “The plaintiffs presented evidence that the defendants had excess production capacity, yet they still bought HFCS from one another and resold it to customers. Additionally, the defendants’ market share remained stable even as output grew. The plaintiffs presented noneconomic evidence in the form of statements from the defendants suggesting a conspiracy, including references to ‘an understanding within the industry not to undercut each other’s prices’ and to new entrants having to ‘play by the rules.’ The district court held there was not enough evidence for a reasonable jury to find the existence of a price-fixing conspiracy and granted summary judgment to the defendants. The plaintiffs appealed.” Again, the DOJ and FTC do not have such evidence for RealPage or other algorithms, so the comparison proves disingenuous. Conclusion The DOJ and FTC’s misguided suit against RealPage is not supported by antitrust jurisprudence, and $7 trillion in economic growth is on the line. No court should allow this precedent against algorithmic use moving forward. The actions against RealPage by the government should be dismissed before it is too late. The continued progression of the U.S. digital economy depends on it. professor of law, Florida International University, is a national legal scholar specializing in a host of fields, including corporate law, constitutional law, administrative law, immigrational policy and civil rights.
article.html:
Algorithms Don’t Violate the Sherman Antitrust Act 

contend that the company (and the property managers who utilize it) are in violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, which condemns “[a]ny combination which tampers with price structures,” because such a combination “directly interfer[es] with the free play of market forces.” However, the DOJ and FTC appear to be forgetting one crucial fact: proving “collusion” requires demonstrating the parties in question entered into an agreement or understanding to price fix. In other words, the government needs to establish an intent to engage in an illegal activity. 

Property managers do not collude when utilizing RealPage; they do not even communicate with one another. Nor do most of the other actors who use algorithms across a wide range of economic sectors. Business owners use algorithmic services because they are efficient, just like how most good real estate agents reference comparable past closings on the MLS before listing their clients’ properties. They do not depend on their pricing recommendations or follow it blindly; they just use it as a tool to ensure their pricing remains dynamic and competitive. Multiple entities using the same software is hardly proof of a general intent to price fix—it is not even proof of any two entities colluding together—so it cannot be a violation of the Sherman Act.

The property managers’ actions are nothing but a classic example of conscious parallelism, which is perfectly legal. 

DOJ and FTC’s Case Law ‘Evidence’ Doesn’t Hold Up 

First, the DOJ and FTC cited Plymouth Dealers’ Association, which dealt with competing dealers agreeing on a “fixed uniform list price” for Plymouth cars. Plymouth may very well be an example of a Sherman Act violation as the Supreme Court found (lower courts disagreed), but still, this case involved companies banding together in a coordinated fashion. RealPage does not, nor do most of the other algorithms that other sectors utilize today engage in any sort of coordinated fashion based on some sort of mutual understanding or agreement. 

“The plaintiffs presented evidence that the defendants had excess production capacity, yet they still bought HFCS from one another and resold it to customers. Additionally, the defendants’ market share remained stable even as output grew. The plaintiffs presented noneconomic evidence in the form of statements from the defendants suggesting a conspiracy, including references to ‘an understanding within the industry not to undercut each other’s prices’ and to new entrants having to ‘play by the rules.’ The district court held there was not enough evidence for a reasonable jury to find the existence of a price-fixing conspiracy and granted summary judgment to the defendants. The plaintiffs appealed.”

Again, the DOJ and FTC do not have such evidence for RealPage or other algorithms, so the comparison proves disingenuous.

Conclusion 

The DOJ and FTC’s misguided suit against RealPage is not supported by antitrust jurisprudence, and $7 trillion in economic growth is on the line. No court should allow this precedent against algorithmic use moving forward. The actions against RealPage by the government should be dismissed before it is too late. The continued progression of the U.S. digital economy depends on it.
