article.title: A Controversial Regulation: How the FTC Noncompete Ban Might Affect the Legal Industry
article.description: The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the…
article.text: The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the legal industry from across the Law.com Newsroom. In House In a hearing Tuesday, agency staffers provided reassurance to rattled businesses, noting that other tools remain at their disposal to protect IP and investments in training. “Nonsolicitation agreements will be that much more important, that much more of a prevalent part of how private entities regulate … or manage the market for employment and employment mobility,” said John Siegal, a Baker & Hostetler partner. “If you take this to its natural extension, the FTC is invalidating hundreds and hundreds of years of a common law, of statutes being implemented on this topic,” Jason Tremblay, a partner with Saul Ewing, said. Regulatory “You’re going to still see enforcement by some states for time, space and scope-type noncompete roles,” said Gwendolyn Lindsay Coole, Wisconsin’s antitrust chief. “First, in my mind, the plain text of the FTC Act clearly gives the agency the authority to promulgate rules addressing unfair methods of competition,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said. Not everyone agrees. The Federal Trade Commission is scheduled to vote Tuesday on its rule that would prohibit noncompetes. The FTC said it would sue as early as Wednesday. “The freedom to change jobs is core to economic liberty and to a competitive, thriving economy,” Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said. Business of Law “If it did go into effect, certainly it’s going to create a demand for people to make sure their nonsolicitation provisions are tightly drafted,” said Ogletree partner Christine Bestor Townsend. Headhunting firms have used covenants to prevent their employees from leaving. Now these firms could become more vulnerable to poaching. Gibson Dunn, Sullivan & Cromwell Tapped to Challenge FTC’s Noncompete Ban Gibson Dunn’s Eugene Scalia, the former U.S. labor secretary, is representing tax services firm Ryan LLC. Sullivan & Cromwell is representing the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Legal Technology Many in legal tech are split on if the FTC’s ban on noncompetes will bring massive changes in hiring and talent acquisition, or come up short. “I’m a defense lawyer primarily, but at the end of the day, noncompete agreements were not meant to be a tool to prevent your midlevel workers from going from Company A to Company B,” employment attorney Michael Elkins said.
article.html:
The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the legal industry from across the Law.com Newsroom.

In House

In a hearing Tuesday, agency staffers provided reassurance to rattled businesses, noting that other tools remain at their disposal to protect IP and investments in training.

“Nonsolicitation agreements will be that much more important, that much more of a prevalent part of how private entities regulate … or manage the market for employment and employment mobility,” said John Siegal, a Baker & Hostetler partner.

“If you take this to its natural extension, the FTC is invalidating hundreds and hundreds of years of a common law, of statutes being implemented on this topic,” Jason Tremblay, a partner with Saul Ewing, said.

Regulatory

“You’re going to still see enforcement by some states for time, space and scope-type noncompete roles,” said Gwendolyn Lindsay Coole, Wisconsin’s antitrust chief.

“First, in my mind, the plain text of the FTC Act clearly gives the agency the authority to promulgate rules addressing unfair methods of competition,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said. Not everyone agrees.

The Federal Trade Commission is scheduled to vote Tuesday on its rule that would prohibit noncompetes. The FTC said it would sue as early as Wednesday.

“The freedom to change jobs is core to economic liberty and to a competitive, thriving economy,” Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said.

Business of Law

“If it did go into effect, certainly it’s going to create a demand for people to make sure their nonsolicitation provisions are tightly drafted,” said Ogletree partner Christine Bestor Townsend.

Headhunting firms have used covenants to prevent their employees from leaving. Now these firms could become more vulnerable to poaching.

Gibson Dunn, Sullivan & Cromwell Tapped to Challenge FTC’s Noncompete Ban

Gibson Dunn’s Eugene Scalia, the former U.S. labor secretary, is representing tax services firm Ryan LLC. Sullivan & Cromwell is representing the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

Legal Technology

Many in legal tech are split on if the FTC’s ban on noncompetes will bring massive changes in hiring and talent acquisition, or come up short.

“I’m a defense lawyer primarily, but at the end of the day, noncompete agreements were not meant to be a tool to prevent your midlevel workers from going from Company A to Company B,” employment attorney Michael Elkins said.

article.title: Are You Doing 'Deep Fake' Marketing? Consider Using a Scorecard
article.description: Generative artificial intelligence is dynamically revolutionizing the ways we develop new audio and video content for marketing initiatives and advertising campaigns. For those in-house counsel tasked with reviewing and approving these initiatives,…
article.text: Generative artificial intelligence is dynamically revolutionizing the ways we develop new audio and video content for marketing initiatives and advertising campaigns. For those in-house counsel tasked with reviewing and approving these initiatives, understanding the potential legal risks, and assessing those risks efficiently, is increasingly becoming a business imperative. One of those new areas involves “deep fake” marketing. By “deep fake,” we refer to a combination of “deep learning” and replicating technology that leverages machine learning algorithms to create realistic—but “fake”—video and audio content of both actual or synthetic individuals. Two forms make up the bulk of the deep fake use cases: deep faces and deep voices. Deep faces replaces the faces of real people with virtual faces, or even creates an entirely synthetic face. Deep voices alters or mimics voices to make a real person appear to have said something they did not say. Thanks to the continuous evolution of AI-powered deep fake technology, we now have more sophisticated and convincing results that can be obtained in a matter of minutes for minimal cost. AI’s deep learning capabilities enable the computerized study and re-creation of human features that blur the line between fiction and reality. This evolutionary progress raises legal and ethical questions about the responsible use of AI when creating “deep fake” or synthetic marketing campaigns. When done lawfully and ethically, however, most marketing officers agree that synthetic marketing presents brands with untapped opportunities to lower campaign costs, produce better quality content, and engage with audiences in unprecedented ways through highly individualized storytelling experiences. These experiences include, for example, interacting with a synthetic version of a living or deceased iconic figure. Fashion brands can showcase products on models with innumerable skin tones, heights, and body types presenting consumers with a more inclusive and relatable experience. In a global context, finding a local actor or model fluent in a language or dialect no longer needs to be a barrier to market entry. The same globally recognized artist can appear to speak hundreds of languages using deep voice overlays. In this context, how can in-house counsel swiftly and competently assess legal risks for newly minted AI-driven campaigns? The answer lies in striking a balance of acceptable levels of legal risk, as defined within your organization, that conform with applicable industry standards, and guided by broader ethical considerations specific to your use case. With this in mind, assemble a scorecard with the following factors included to weigh the likelihood and severity associated with any deep fake marketing campaign. 1. Content-Driven AI Considerations Visual vs. audio. Is the content video or audio? While it is important to understand the copyright, right of publicity, intellectual property, licensing, and other legal restrictions for any content included in a marketing campaign, video content may pose additional legal risks.Still vs. video. Is the visual content a still or video? Does the still image qualify as artwork? Video presents more legal risk than a still image, as most marketing videos incorporate numerous individual images and personas, as well as audio. Understanding potentially applicable copyright protections, intellectual property, and other legal restrictions is important.Music. Does audio content qualify as music? Again, music likely presents additional legal risk since copyright protections may apply for both a particular sound recording as well as the underlying musical composition. Some lawyers argue that the biggest unresolved legal issue is whether artists, record labels, and publishers can claim infringement as AI learns from copyrighted works, even if the output bears little relation to the original compositions or lyrics.Real people likeness or voices of actual persons. Is content taken from the likeness of an actual living or deceased individual? Or is it the synthesized image and voice of a fictional character? Consent or other legal basis to use content may apply, including SAG-AFTRA union contract compliance obligations in the U.S., as well as endorsement rules.Endorsements. Marketing materials using AI actors/voices that include an endorsement present significant risk, even if a disclosure is provided such as “fictionalization using an AI-generated actor.” It could be inherently and incurably deceptive to use an endorsement purporting to be spoken by a real human, about a personal experience that never happened, when, in fact, the person and experience do not exist. See the Federal Trade Commission’s “Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising.”Kids. Do any of the synthetic voice or visuals resemble or target children? Children are always afforded greater protections under the law, and will naturally present higher legal risk if prominently featured in a deep fake marketing campaign. In this regard, proceed with caution.Outside the U.S. Will the visual or audio content be used outside the U.S.? If so, consider potential local market restrictions beyond those set out above. 2. Legal and Litigation Landscape U.S. Landscape. The use of AI in any context remains new and quickly evolving under U.S. law. Many federal and state legislative proposals are being considered and enacted that would require the disclosure—and potentially limit the use—of AI in certain marketing contexts. It is important, therefore, to continually monitor the fast-moving legislative developments in this area.Global Landscape. If your content is being used outside the U.S., monitor legislative developments such as the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act and other similar proposals.Industry Landscape. Numerous industries are also imposing specific guidance or other binding codes of conduct that may apply to the use of AI-driven marketing. One example is the SAG-AFTRA labor agreement covering the use of AI to digitally simulate the voice or likeness of a union member to create a new performance.Contractual Landscape. Risk allocation remains an unpredictable component in assessing legal risk. Advertisers, agencies, and others have yet to settle on industry standards for the use and deployment of AI-driven marketing. The same is true for insurers. Defining a clear company posture on risk tolerances in advance of a new AI-driven initiative will help your review proceed efficiently.Litigation Landscape. Courts are just now beginning to grapple with the broad use of AI in the marketplace, and have shown a reluctance to disturb the rights of individuals and organic human invention in the context of AI. For example, a district court recently found that works of art created by AI without any human input cannot be copyrighted under U.S. law. Only works with human authors can receive copyrights. Still, leveraging AI may infringe rights of human authors if the AI-generated material is substantially similar to an existing work that was used to train the AI platform. 3. Data Privacy and Security Privacy and data protection. The use of AI in any context remains new and unfamiliar; thus any AI-driven marketing campaign could provoke questions about the scope of consumer targeting, personalization, and tracking. Use of deep-fake technology to create and customize marketing content for different market segments could benefit from transparency to address privacy and data protection considerations. Above all, assess AI-driven marketing content for potential unethical marketing practices that capture personal information or make undisclosed and overbroad inferences about individuals. The impact of any unlawful campaigns could draw unwanted regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. and abroad.Cybersecurity. Security is always a top concern. With every AI-driven marketing campaign, assess the risk that the same content and technology can be used to create unauthorized deep fakes that can inflict both reputational and financial harm to your brand. Be ready to swiftly respond to unlawful visual or audio content.Bias and discrimination. Depending on the underlying training model, technology, or platform, inherent biases based on the data training set can lead to discriminatory outcomes, determinations, or predictions. As part of your legal review, be sure to assess how the risk of bias and unlawful discrimination was addressed technically, especially in culturally sensitive campaigns. 4. Organizational Measures Pilot projects. Start small before going big. Build a suitable framework that is adequate for your company size, industry vertical, and company culture. Involve a broad group of stakeholders in developing that framework, and test it in controlled environments before wide-scale deployment.Board-level buy-in. Legal is not the only risk to consider, but it is certainly an important one. Establish acceptable levels of risk within the Board of Directors or other senior management. Going first certainly presents the potential for big payoffs, but also comes with technical and regulatory risk.Education and training. Once buy-in and risk tolerances are properly assessed, reduce those to policy and standards, and train against those with your creative teams. Set the expectations about how far you are willing to go in deep fake marketing in the near future, and how you will periodically reassess your posture in light of the legal and regulatory landscape.Insurance. Insurance is a risk mitigation tool. Understanding the role insurance plays in your AI-driven marketing strategy (self-insured vs. covered event), however, is also important. Involve your risk officer, broker, or carrier in evaluating whether your current coverages would cover any claims in the context of deep fake marketing. Again, this area is still poorly understood, and events that result in potential liability remain open to broad and unpredictable interpretation.Explainability. At every turn, promote transparency in your practices. Within the contract or within the content, avoid deception or dark patterns that could result in legal liability or regulatory scrutiny. In sum, deep fakes offer advertisers countless opportunities to re-create iconic moments, reuse or enhance existing content, or create entirely fictional characters that result in viral and memorable deep fake campaigns. As deep fake technology continues to advance, however, the need for guardrails, countermeasures, and security controls becomes crucial. From technological solutions that can detect unauthorized deep fakes to legal frameworks that deter malicious use, a proactive approach to potential legal risks is necessary. Developing an overall understanding of the potential severity for a flawed deployment, as well as the likelihood of those consequences being applied to your specific situation, are the key elements to balancing your scorecard. For now, balancing these new marketplace developments against long-established legal principles will forge a path forward for us in AI-enabled synthetic marketing.
article.html:
Generative artificial intelligence is dynamically revolutionizing the ways we develop new audio and video content for marketing initiatives and advertising campaigns. For those in-house counsel tasked with reviewing and approving these initiatives, understanding the potential legal risks, and assessing those risks efficiently, is increasingly becoming a business imperative. One of those new areas involves “deep fake” marketing.

By “deep fake,” we refer to a combination of “deep learning” and replicating technology that leverages machine learning algorithms to create realistic—but “fake”—video and audio content of both actual or synthetic individuals. Two forms make up the bulk of the deep fake use cases: deep faces and deep voices. Deep faces replaces the faces of real people with virtual faces, or even creates an entirely synthetic face. Deep voices alters or mimics voices to make a real person appear to have said something they did not say. Thanks to the continuous evolution of AI-powered deep fake technology, we now have more sophisticated and convincing results that can be obtained in a matter of minutes for minimal cost.

AI’s deep learning capabilities enable the computerized study and re-creation of human features that blur the line between fiction and reality. This evolutionary progress raises legal and ethical questions about the responsible use of AI when creating “deep fake” or synthetic marketing campaigns. When done lawfully and ethically, however, most marketing officers agree that synthetic marketing presents brands with untapped opportunities to lower campaign costs, produce better quality content, and engage with audiences in unprecedented ways through highly individualized storytelling experiences.

These experiences include, for example, interacting with a synthetic version of a living or deceased iconic figure. Fashion brands can showcase products on models with innumerable skin tones, heights, and body types presenting consumers with a more inclusive and relatable experience. In a global context, finding a local actor or model fluent in a language or dialect no longer needs to be a barrier to market entry. The same globally recognized artist can appear to speak hundreds of languages using deep voice overlays.

In this context, how can in-house counsel swiftly and competently assess legal risks for newly minted AI-driven campaigns? The answer lies in striking a balance of acceptable levels of legal risk, as defined within your organization, that conform with applicable industry standards, and guided by broader ethical considerations specific to your use case. With this in mind, assemble a scorecard with the following factors included to weigh the likelihood and severity associated with any deep fake marketing campaign.

1. Content-Driven AI Considerations

  • Visual vs. audio. Is the content video or audio? While it is important to understand the copyright, right of publicity, intellectual property, licensing, and other legal restrictions for any content included in a marketing campaign, video content may pose additional legal risks.
  • Still vs. video. Is the visual content a still or video? Does the still image qualify as artwork? Video presents more legal risk than a still image, as most marketing videos incorporate numerous individual images and personas, as well as audio. Understanding potentially applicable copyright protections, intellectual property, and other legal restrictions is important.
  • Music. Does audio content qualify as music? Again, music likely presents additional legal risk since copyright protections may apply for both a particular sound recording as well as the underlying musical composition. Some lawyers argue that the biggest unresolved legal issue is whether artists, record labels, and publishers can claim infringement as AI learns from copyrighted works, even if the output bears little relation to the original compositions or lyrics.
  • Real people likeness or voices of actual persons. Is content taken from the likeness of an actual living or deceased individual? Or is it the synthesized image and voice of a fictional character? Consent or other legal basis to use content may apply, including SAG-AFTRA union contract compliance obligations in the U.S., as well as endorsement rules.
  • Endorsements. Marketing materials using AI actors/voices that include an endorsement present significant risk, even if a disclosure is provided such as “fictionalization using an AI-generated actor.” It could be inherently and incurably deceptive to use an endorsement purporting to be spoken by a real human, about a personal experience that never happened, when, in fact, the person and experience do not exist. See the Federal Trade Commission’s “Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising.”
  • Kids. Do any of the synthetic voice or visuals resemble or target children? Children are always afforded greater protections under the law, and will naturally present higher legal risk if prominently featured in a deep fake marketing campaign. In this regard, proceed with caution.
  • Outside the U.S. Will the visual or audio content be used outside the U.S.? If so, consider potential local market restrictions beyond those set out above.

2. Legal and Litigation Landscape

  • U.S. Landscape. The use of AI in any context remains new and quickly evolving under U.S. law. Many federal and state legislative proposals are being considered and enacted that would require the disclosure—and potentially limit the use—of AI in certain marketing contexts. It is important, therefore, to continually monitor the fast-moving legislative developments in this area.
  • Global Landscape. If your content is being used outside the U.S., monitor legislative developments such as the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act and other similar proposals.
  • Industry Landscape. Numerous industries are also imposing specific guidance or other binding codes of conduct that may apply to the use of AI-driven marketing. One example is the SAG-AFTRA labor agreement covering the use of AI to digitally simulate the voice or likeness of a union member to create a new performance.
  • Contractual Landscape. Risk allocation remains an unpredictable component in assessing legal risk. Advertisers, agencies, and others have yet to settle on industry standards for the use and deployment of AI-driven marketing. The same is true for insurers. Defining a clear company posture on risk tolerances in advance of a new AI-driven initiative will help your review proceed efficiently.
  • Litigation Landscape. Courts are just now beginning to grapple with the broad use of AI in the marketplace, and have shown a reluctance to disturb the rights of individuals and organic human invention in the context of AI. For example, a district court recently found that works of art created by AI without any human input cannot be copyrighted under U.S. law. Only works with human authors can receive copyrights. Still, leveraging AI may infringe rights of human authors if the AI-generated material is substantially similar to an existing work that was used to train the AI platform.

3. Data Privacy and Security

  • Privacy and data protection. The use of AI in any context remains new and unfamiliar; thus any AI-driven marketing campaign could provoke questions about the scope of consumer targeting, personalization, and tracking. Use of deep-fake technology to create and customize marketing content for different market segments could benefit from transparency to address privacy and data protection considerations. Above all, assess AI-driven marketing content for potential unethical marketing practices that capture personal information or make undisclosed and overbroad inferences about individuals. The impact of any unlawful campaigns could draw unwanted regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. and abroad.
  • Cybersecurity. Security is always a top concern. With every AI-driven marketing campaign, assess the risk that the same content and technology can be used to create unauthorized deep fakes that can inflict both reputational and financial harm to your brand. Be ready to swiftly respond to unlawful visual or audio content.
  • Bias and discrimination. Depending on the underlying training model, technology, or platform, inherent biases based on the data training set can lead to discriminatory outcomes, determinations, or predictions. As part of your legal review, be sure to assess how the risk of bias and unlawful discrimination was addressed technically, especially in culturally sensitive campaigns.

4. Organizational Measures

  • Pilot projects. Start small before going big. Build a suitable framework that is adequate for your company size, industry vertical, and company culture. Involve a broad group of stakeholders in developing that framework, and test it in controlled environments before wide-scale deployment.
  • Board-level buy-in. Legal is not the only risk to consider, but it is certainly an important one. Establish acceptable levels of risk within the Board of Directors or other senior management. Going first certainly presents the potential for big payoffs, but also comes with technical and regulatory risk.
  • Education and training. Once buy-in and risk tolerances are properly assessed, reduce those to policy and standards, and train against those with your creative teams. Set the expectations about how far you are willing to go in deep fake marketing in the near future, and how you will periodically reassess your posture in light of the legal and regulatory landscape.
  • Insurance. Insurance is a risk mitigation tool. Understanding the role insurance plays in your AI-driven marketing strategy (self-insured vs. covered event), however, is also important. Involve your risk officer, broker, or carrier in evaluating whether your current coverages would cover any claims in the context of deep fake marketing. Again, this area is still poorly understood, and events that result in potential liability remain open to broad and unpredictable interpretation.
  • Explainability. At every turn, promote transparency in your practices. Within the contract or within the content, avoid deception or dark patterns that could result in legal liability or regulatory scrutiny.

In sum, deep fakes offer advertisers countless opportunities to re-create iconic moments, reuse or enhance existing content, or create entirely fictional characters that result in viral and memorable deep fake campaigns. As deep fake technology continues to advance, however, the need for guardrails, countermeasures, and security controls becomes crucial. From technological solutions that can detect unauthorized deep fakes to legal frameworks that deter malicious use, a proactive approach to potential legal risks is necessary. Developing an overall understanding of the potential severity for a flawed deployment, as well as the likelihood of those consequences being applied to your specific situation, are the key elements to balancing your scorecard.

For now, balancing these new marketplace developments against long-established legal principles will forge a path forward for us in AI-enabled synthetic marketing.

article.title: Everlaw Offers Free Gen AI Access Through 'Everlaw for Good' Program
article.description: The latest to do so is Everlaw, which announced on May 9 that it expanded its Everlaw for Good program to include its generative AI features, in a move to increase the number of cases supported by the program by 60% before the end of the year. “If…
article.text: The latest to do so is Everlaw, which announced on May 9 that it expanded its Everlaw for Good program to include its generative AI features, in a move to increase the number of cases supported by the program by 60% before the end of the year. “If you think about all the ways you could try to address the [justice] gap, there are many ways that we can’t control as a company,” AJ Shankar, founder and CEO at Everlaw, told Legaltech News. “There are systemic issues, and it’s super complicated, but we can build the technology that can help facilitate some of this. And I think it’s actually really important to think about technology as a tool. Because you can imagine a world where, if it’s hard to access critical technology, then it can widen the access-the-justice gap.” The program provides unlimited access to the Everlaw platform, including, now, its generative AI offering Everlaw AI Assistant, which is currently available in beta for select paying customers and is slated to be released for general availability some time this year. All tools accessed through the Everlaw for Good program are offered free of charge up to “a monthly cap,” with discounted rates for larger matters. Everlaw for Good is open to eligible 501(c)(3) organizations, pro bono practices and investigative journalists focused on access-to-justice issues. “We have made our eligibility very, very open. So if you’re a 501(c)(3) in good standing that operates in the legal space and has a use case for e-discovery, we have (six) broad program categories,” explained social impact expert Joanne Sprague, who joined Everlaw last October as the first-ever director of the program. In fact, Everlaw for Good seeks to support matters in the following categories: low-income populations, civil rights, civil liberties, human rights, public rights and environmental rights. The use cases between those different types of matters and organizations vary, but the overall needs often align. “Fundamentally in our field there’s two jobs: one, you have to go from a huge haystack of evidence to find a small handful of needles, and then two, you’ve got to take those needles and build a compelling narrative,” Shankar explained. “And in the corporate or the private-sector world, you solve those problems with a lot of human power. … When you’re a legal aid entity, you don’t have those resources.” The program has been running since 2017. In that time, Everlaw estimates it contributed approximately $2.75 million in platform services and served more than 125 organizations. While generative AI has sometimes been received with a bit of a sticker shock by the legal industry, Shankar noted that Everlaw was able to expand its beta program to nonprofit purposes for multiple reasons. On one side, the profitability of the rest of the organization is key to the sustainability of the program. “I want to emphasize that this program can only exist because we exist as a commercial entity, a for-profit entity that is allowed to invest in technology to serve lots of people. And so I think they go really hand-in-hand,” he said. But he also noted that once the technology is developed, expanding it to more users requires few additional resources. “We build software, and software is scalable in a way that human services aren’t quite scalable. I mean, you write some code once and you can run it many, many times. … So fundamentally, I think when you think about the benefits of technology, one of those benefits is scale,” Shankar added.

article.title: CLOC Legal Tech Rundown: Ironclad Custom AI, New Lexis Tool and More
article.description: ContractPodAi: On Monday, contract lifecycle management (CLM) provider ContractPodAi announced the general availability of Leah Helpdesk, its generative AI-powered application. The application will expand to provide legal support through Leah Draft—a…
article.text: ContractPodAi: On Monday, contract lifecycle management (CLM) provider ContractPodAi announced the general availability of Leah Helpdesk, its generative AI-powered application. The application will expand to provide legal support through Leah Draft—a generative AI-powered chatbot meant help structure and cleanly format legal documents. The expansion will automate contract drafting processes throughout the Leah tools. “In-house legal teams are increasingly taking on more work, and we’re excited that we can provide immediate relief to our customers, through Leah,” said Gabriel Buigas, EVP of legal and compliance solutions at Integreon. “With Leah’s new offerings and updates, customers can immediately take advantage, and reap the benefits, of GenAI services. These will enhance our ability to drive true transformation for our customers, at scale.” Evisort + Icertis: On Tuesday, CLM and intelligence software provider Icertis announced a new alliance with CLM company Evisort. This strategic partnership platform will enable new and existing Icertis customers to leverage Evisort’s contract-specific AI engine, accelerating the ingestion and analysis of contract data to deliver insights and optimize workflows, according to the press release. Since Icertis works to transform the key contents of a contract into “strategic assets,” the ability to use software to extract the critical information contained in contracts, structuring it into a common data model, and connecting it with operational systems like ERP, SCM, CRM and HCM is key, the release stated. Indeed, Evisort’s contract-specific AI engine will work in concert with Icertis Discover Copilot to do just that. ”By integrating our contract-specific AI engine with the Icertis Contract Intelligence platform, we can enable joint customers to rapidly ingest and analyze both legacy and new agreements, accelerating insights that drive business performance. Our collaboration with Icertis will set new standards for how contracts are managed and executed, and deliver exceptional outcomes to our joint customers,” said Jerry Ting, CEO of Evisort, in the release. Ironclad: On Thursday, CLM software provider Ironclad announced the launch of Custom AI, defined as a set of features that allows users to improve the quality of their AI results and expand the model’s ability to absorb data, domain knowledge and context, according to the press release. Currently, Ironclad’s AI suite, including Ironclad Smart Import, AI Playbooks and AI Assist, can detect 175 clauses and 19 fields, collectively called “AI contract data points,” out of the box. The added-on layer of Custom AI will enable users to train Ironclad AI on clauses that sit outside of that box and are unique to their use cases and business requirements, leveraging the concept of “fine-tuning,” according to the release. The specific capabilities of the new offering include Custom Clauses, consolidated data management across the AI suite, out-of-the-box clause training, the ability to restrict user permissions and the ability to hide or limit which data points are available depending on their relevance and the priorities of the business, as per the release. LexisNexis: On Tuesday, LexisNexis announced the launch of CounselLink+, a legal solution meant to integrate matters with its combined Enterprise Legal Management (ELM) and CLM platforms. article.title: NJ Attorney General Announces New Antitrust Section, Pledges to Pursue Actions Against 'Unchecked Monopolies'
article.description: “There is a pressing need in New Jersey for dedicated resources and specialized expertise for antitrust issues, which are becoming increasingly complex,” Attorney General Matthew J. Platkin said. “As the attorney general, I have the critical…
article.text: “There is a pressing need in New Jersey for dedicated resources and specialized expertise for antitrust issues, which are becoming increasingly complex,” Attorney General Matthew J. Platkin said. “As the attorney general, I have the critical obligation to protect consumers and workers from the problems that result from unchecked monopolies and oligopolies." With New Jersey becoming more actively involved in litigation against major players across various industries over the past few years, New Jersey Attorney General Matthew J. Platkin has announced the establishment of a new antitrust section within the Division of Law aimed at better protecting consumers in the marketplace. Platkin said his office created the Antitrust Litigation and Competition Enforcement Section to safeguard the interests of New Jersey residents and foster a fair and competitive marketplace. In 2022, Gov. Phil Murphy signed S-901 into law, which amended the state’s antitrust statute and allows the attorney general to pursue bad actors and obtain restitution at all levels of the supply chain, according to a statement from Platkin’s office.
article.html:
“There is a pressing need in New Jersey for dedicated resources and specialized expertise for antitrust issues, which are becoming increasingly complex,” Attorney General Matthew J. Platkin said. “As the attorney general, I have the critical obligation to protect consumers and workers from the problems that result from unchecked monopolies and oligopolies."

Platkin said his office created the Antitrust Litigation and Competition Enforcement Section to safeguard the interests of New Jersey residents and foster a fair and competitive marketplace. In 2022, Gov. Phil Murphy signed S-901 into law, which amended the state’s antitrust statute and allows the attorney general to pursue bad actors and obtain restitution at all levels of the supply chain, according to a statement from Platkin’s office.

article.title: Audible Sued for Alleged Streaming Technology Patent Infringement
article.description: The plaintiff contends Audible had notice that it was infringing on its patents more than 10 years ago. Audio Pod IP has filed three patent infringement suits against Amazon, AWS and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia. The plaintiffs allege…
article.text: The plaintiff contends Audible had notice that it was infringing on its patents more than 10 years ago. Audio Pod IP has filed three patent infringement suits against Amazon, AWS and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia. The plaintiffs allege that after a meeting to discuss sharing Audio Pod's technology with Audible went nowhere, the company started using their innovations without permission. So far defense counsel has only appeared in one case and has moved for either a full dismissal, a partial dismissal or a transfer to New Jersey. An audiobook company represented by Chandran Iyer, Ronald Daignault and Kevin Sprenger of intellectual property firm Daignault Iyer recently filed three patent infringement lawsuits against Amazon, Amazon Web Services and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia. The company, Audio Pod IP, alleges in one complaint that it invented “several key media streaming technologies” after it was founded in 2005, including segmenting and sequencing streaming files to work around long download times for large files, bookmarking digital content so it can be paused and played at a later time and a subscriber-paid streaming service launched in 2006. The complaint cited a January 2008 front-page article in the Ottawa Citizen to document its early trajectory.
article.html:
The plaintiff contends Audible had notice that it was infringing on its patents more than 10 years ago.

  • Audio Pod IP has filed three patent infringement suits against Amazon, AWS and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia.
  • The plaintiffs allege that after a meeting to discuss sharing Audio Pod's technology with Audible went nowhere, the company started using their innovations without permission.
  • So far defense counsel has only appeared in one case and has moved for either a full dismissal, a partial dismissal or a transfer to New Jersey.

An audiobook company represented by Chandran Iyer, Ronald Daignault and Kevin Sprenger of intellectual property firm Daignault Iyer recently filed three patent infringement lawsuits against Amazon, Amazon Web Services and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia.

The company, Audio Pod IP, alleges in one complaint that it invented “several key media streaming technologies” after it was founded in 2005, including segmenting and sequencing streaming files to work around long download times for large files, bookmarking digital content so it can be paused and played at a later time and a subscriber-paid streaming service launched in 2006. The complaint cited a January 2008 front-page article in the Ottawa Citizen to document its early trajectory.

article.title: Ex-Uber Security Chief Appeals Conviction That Shook Cybersecurity World
article.description: A judge in May sentenced Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan to three years of probation for obstruction of justice and covering up a felony after a 2016 data breach. Though Sullivan avoided prison, his attorneys say his conviction jeopardizes bug…
article.text: A judge in May sentenced Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan to three years of probation for obstruction of justice and covering up a felony after a 2016 data breach. Though Sullivan avoided prison, his attorneys say his conviction jeopardizes bug bounty programs on which security chiefs rely to keep data secure. Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan is appealing his conviction for covering up a 2016 data breach and obstructing a regulator’s investigation into Uber’s security practices. Sullivan was sentenced in May to three years of probation following a nearly monthlong jury trial in 2022. He faced up to eight years in prison for obstructing the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing investigation into Uber’s security practices and misprision of a felony, a rare charge that involves taking active steps to conceal a crime. article.title: Va. Supreme Court Rejects 4th Amendment Exclusionary Rule in Warrantless Civil Search
article.description: The Virginia Supreme Court reversed the state appeals court in a warrantless search dispute involving a church home office. The state high court ruled the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule does not apply in civil cases. Fairfax County argued…
article.text: The Virginia Supreme Court reversed the state appeals court in a warrantless search dispute involving a church home office. The state high court ruled the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule does not apply in civil cases. Fairfax County argued successfully that it did not need to examine the constitutionality of the warrantless civil search. The Virginia Supreme Court resolved a major Fourth Amendment dispute this month, ruling that a zoning official’s search of a church-friendly home did not require the Fairfax County Board of Zoning Appeals to examine the constitutionality of the search. Reversing the judgment of the Virginia Court of Appeals, the state Supreme Court ruled that the Fourth Amendment’s exclusionary rule does not apply in civil cases and found that the New World Church of the Christ President Rita M. Leach-Lewis operated home offices in violation of local zoning regulations.

article.title: Venus Williams to Speak at WIPL on Acing Self-Empowerment and Inspiring Change
article.description: Come join us at WIPL to be part of an intimate conversation with Venus Williams as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality. I am excited to announce that headlining day two of this year’s…
article.text: Come join us at WIPL to be part of an intimate conversation with Venus Williams as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality. I am excited to announce that headlining day two of this year’s Women, Influence & Power in Law conference will be tennis champion and New York Times best-selling author Venus Williams! With seven Grand Slam titles, including five Wimbledon championships, and four Olympic gold medals, Venus is one of the most accomplished and inspiring women in the history of sports. Beyond her accomplishments on the court, Venus has also been a steadfast advocate for equality throughout her career. In 2006, UNESCO, the United Nations’ cultural organization, titled her as the first “Promoter of Gender Equality.” In 2007, it was her unwavering fight which led Wimbledon to award women players the same pay as their male counterparts. Most recently, she launched an awareness initiative called the #PrivilegeTax to bring attention to wage inequality and unveiled a platform of resources for young women to get inspired and address the issue on a grassroots level. Register today to be part of this intimate conversation with Venus as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality. Whether it’s overcoming self-doubt or providing tools to navigate a male-dominated industry, Venus’ unique insights will sure to inspire our WIPL community to not only discover that inner champion but unleash its full potential! We are also excited that this year’s WIPL conference will be held in Chicago at the Hyatt Regency McCormick Place. I hope to see you there!
article.html:
Come join us at WIPL to be part of an intimate conversation with Venus Williams as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality.

I am excited to announce that headlining day two of this year’s Women, Influence & Power in Law conference will be tennis champion and New York Times best-selling author Venus Williams!

With seven Grand Slam titles, including five Wimbledon championships, and four Olympic gold medals, Venus is one of the most accomplished and inspiring women in the history of sports.

Beyond her accomplishments on the court, Venus has also been a steadfast advocate for equality throughout her career.

In 2006, UNESCO, the United Nations’ cultural organization, titled her as the first “Promoter of Gender Equality.” In 2007, it was her unwavering fight which led Wimbledon to award women players the same pay as their male counterparts.

Most recently, she launched an awareness initiative called the #PrivilegeTax to bring attention to wage inequality and unveiled a platform of resources for young women to get inspired and address the issue on a grassroots level.

Register today to be part of this intimate conversation with Venus as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality. Whether it’s overcoming self-doubt or providing tools to navigate a male-dominated industry, Venus’ unique insights will sure to inspire our WIPL community to not only discover that inner champion but unleash its full potential!

We are also excited that this year’s WIPL conference will be held in Chicago at the Hyatt Regency McCormick Place.

I hope to see you there!

article.title: Suits Flooding Courts Seize on Decades-Old Wiretapping Laws to Allege Data Breaches
article.description: What You Need to Know Companies have fended off cases so far, but largely on procedural grounds. The suits target so-called session-replay software, which tracks consumers' keystrokes and mouse movements. Attorneys advise companies to make sure they…
article.text: What You Need to Know Companies have fended off cases so far, but largely on procedural grounds. The suits target so-called session-replay software, which tracks consumers' keystrokes and mouse movements. Attorneys advise companies to make sure they understand how their ad-tech tools work and that they have a strong disclosure and consent policy. Data privacy class actions focused on “session replay” software and other ad tech tools that track how users interact with websites are piling up by the day, unabated by a spate of rulings favoring defendants. Legal observers say the hitch in those defendant victories is that they have largely been on procedural or statute-of-limitation grounds, keeping alive plaintiffs’ attorneys hopes that their legal strategy eventually will strike gold. article.title: Supreme Court Ruling 'Clarifying' Workplace Religious Accommodation Standard Does Anything But
article.description: What You Need to Know The high court found employers should approve religious accommodation requests unless doing so would impose a substantial cost on the organization. That will make it tougher for employers to deny requests than it was in the…
article.text: What You Need to Know The high court found employers should approve religious accommodation requests unless doing so would impose a substantial cost on the organization. That will make it tougher for employers to deny requests than it was in the past. But the ruling doesn't define what would meet the definition of substantial cost. The U.S. Supreme Court’s recent ruling reviving the debate on religious accommodations in the workplace sent a glaring message to employers: They had better have a good reason for denying an employee’s request. But what constitutes a good reason? Experts say the ruling makes that harder to determine, though it does set the bar higher for employers to show that an accommodation would be an “undue hardship.” The high court on June 29 sided with Gerald Groff, an evangelical Christian mail carrier who claimed the postal service discriminated against him by disciplining him when he refused to deliver packages on Sundays. While the justices declined to rule on the merits of his claims, they overturned an appeals court’s dismissal of the case that found Groff’s objection to Sunday work “imposed on his coworkers, disrupted the workplace and workflow, and diminished employee morale.” Since 1977, courts have hewed to the standard set in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison that defines an undue hardship as anything that would require an employer to “bear more than a di minimis cost.” Berkeley Law Dean Erwin Chemerinsky said the di minimis standard “made it very difficult for employees to be able to prevail, so it led to some litigation, but not much.” That could be about to change. In a unanimous opinion, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an employer now must show “that the burden of granting an accommodation would result in substantial increased costs in relation to the conduct of its particular business.” Chemerinsky said this heightened burden “dramatically changes the legal standard” for when an employer can deny a religious accommodation. “It used to be from 1977 until the end of June that an employer would not have to bear more than a minimal cost to accommodate an employees’ religious beliefs. Now an employer would have to do it unless it poses a substantial cost,” Chemerinsky said, adding that the ruling “very much favors employees making requests for religious accommodations.” Event Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards (WIPLA) 2023 Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards honors women lawyers who have made a remarkable difference in the legal profession. Get More Information The decision also undoes decades of legal precedent, said Debbie Kaminer a law professor at Baruch College at the City University of New York. “It totally changed the law and pretended it didn’t. Undue hardship has always meant de minimis. No one knows what ‘substantial cost’ means; no one has a clue.” While the ruling largely flew under the radar, overshadowed by the Supreme Court’s monumental decisions on affirmative action and student loan forgiveness, Kaminer said the Groff decision will have an outsized impact in the workplace. “This is a case that is going to be have enormous impact because it affects every workplace with more than 15 employees,” she said. “It’s a huge, huge number.” The court’s opinion gives employers little to go on when trying to assess substantial costs to their businesses. Alioto said the issue will have to be decided by the courts, and each case will be “context-specific.” He wrote, “[C]ourts should resolve whether a hardship would be substantial in the context of an employer’s business in the commonsense manner that it would use in applying any such test.” Chemerinsky said this ambiguity will likely lead to a spike in religious accommodation requests, and more litigation for employers. “Justice Alito’s opinion doesn’t offer a standard for a substantial cost—that in itself is an invitation for requests and litigation,” he said. “I think it’s going to lead to a great deal of litigation and will take a lot of time to clarify the standard.” Employers long have looked to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for guidance on whether to grant an employee’s request for religious accommodation. The Supreme Court’s ruling declines to adopt the EEOC’s past interpretations of undue hardship, though it does say it may prompt “little to no change” in the agency’s guidance. A spokesman for the agency said it is in the process of updating that guidance. Phileda Tennant, counsel with Vinson & Elkins’ employment, labor & OSHA practice, said employers will need to keep watch out for that response. She said that, as with cases of reasonable accommodation for a disability, they likely will want to pull in outside counsel to help them understand the new standard. The Supreme Court ruling comes on the heels of a historic surge in filings of religion-based discrimination charges with the EEOC. In the fiscal year that ended in September 2022, the EEOC received 13,814, up from 2,111—a spike the agency says may be related to COVID-19 vaccine mandates. The expected increase in religious accommodation requests might have disproportionate effect on the retail and hospitality industries that rely on weekend labor. Matthew Roberts, an employment law counsel with the California Chamber of Commerce, said he recently spoke with a small business owner on the chamber’s labor law helpline who had received three separate requests for Sundays off. “They are a retail yogurt shop. They have to provide this time off but can’t cover the work they’re losing,” Roberts said. This puts the business owner in the tough position of having to either foist Sunday shifts on other employees or hiring someone to work only on Sundays, a solution Roberts said is highly impracticable. “It’s another avenue to make business more difficult here,” Roberts said. Small businesses have been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic to hire and retain staff, Roberts said. Requests for time off on weekends just adds to the burden, particularly given that California already has high standards for denying religious accommodation requests. “It’s difficult in California, because you go through the whole recruitment process and you can’t ask scheduling questions that might reveal someone’s religious beliefs. So you hire this person and the first day they say, ‘I need Sunday off,’ and the employer is blindsided,” Roberts said. “What happens is other existing employees have to take on those shifts, leading to burnout, and that exacerbates the recruiting and retaining problem.” Tennant said the ruling also could complicate matters for employers who are contractually obligated to honor seniority rights when they schedule shifts. “Particularly among unionized workforces, scheduling is a function to some extent of seniority. And so the idea that a religious accommodation would interfere with that is something that the court suggests might constitute an undue hardship,” Tennant said. “So it seems that example pushes the definition of undue hardship away from a particular dollar value, and more toward consideration of a contractual right. I think that we’re just going to have to see what exactly is the sort of undue hardship that the court has intended in the context of the employers business.” Courts will also have to sort out whether an accommodation’s effect on an employee’s co-workers counts as undue hardship, Tennant said, noting that in her concurrence, Justice Sonia Sotomayor writes that “some hardships, such as the labor costs of coordinating voluntary shift swaps, are not ‘undue’ because they are too insubstantial.” Kaminer said the ruling is murky on the subject, long considered settled by a string of earlier cases holding that an accommodation that causes more than a de minimis impact on coworkers creates an undue hardship. “It’s not clear if a burden on co-workers is even going to matter anymore,” she said. It also raises thorny questions on how far an employer must go to accommodate a religious employee when it might mean demeaning someone else—sparking new conflict over religious rights vs. the right to a discrimination-free workplace. She cited one instance where an HP employee who objected to his employer’s diversity posters put up Bible verses around his cubicle condemning homosexuality. While the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that HP did not have to accommodate the employee’s religious expression if it meant discriminating against his co-workers, Kaminer said the Groff decision could trigger more cases of this sort. “There will be more of a sort of testing of the waters, particularly with certain people trying to figure out how far they can go with this,” she said. He wrote, “[C]ourts should resolve whether a hardship would be substantial in the context of an employer’s business in the commonsense manner that it would use in applying any such test.”

Chemerinsky said this ambiguity will likely lead to a spike in religious accommodation requests, and more litigation for employers. “Justice Alito’s opinion doesn’t offer a standard for a substantial cost—that in itself is an invitation for requests and litigation,” he said. “I think it’s going to lead to a great deal of litigation and will take a lot of time to clarify the standard.”

Employers long have looked to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for guidance on whether to grant an employee’s request for religious accommodation. The Supreme Court’s ruling declines to adopt the EEOC’s past interpretations of undue hardship, though it does say it may prompt “little to no change” in the agency’s guidance.

A spokesman for the agency said it is in the process of updating that guidance.

Phileda Tennant, counsel with Vinson & Elkins’ employment, labor & OSHA practice, said employers will need to keep watch out for that response. She said that, as with cases of reasonable accommodation for a disability, they likely will want to pull in outside counsel to help them understand the new standard.

The Supreme Court ruling comes on the heels of a historic surge in filings of religion-based discrimination charges with the EEOC. In the fiscal year that ended in September 2022, the EEOC received 13,814, up from 2,111—a spike the agency says may be related to COVID-19 vaccine mandates.

The expected increase in religious accommodation requests might have disproportionate effect on the retail and hospitality industries that rely on weekend labor. Matthew Roberts, an employment law counsel with the California Chamber of Commerce, said he recently spoke with a small business owner on the chamber’s labor law helpline who had received three separate requests for Sundays off.

“They are a retail yogurt shop. They have to provide this time off but can’t cover the work they’re losing,” Roberts said. This puts the business owner in the tough position of having to either foist Sunday shifts on other employees or hiring someone to work only on Sundays, a solution Roberts said is highly impracticable. “It’s another avenue to make business more difficult here,” Roberts said.

Small businesses have been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic to hire and retain staff, Roberts said. Requests for time off on weekends just adds to the burden, particularly given that California already has high standards for denying religious accommodation requests.

“It’s difficult in California, because you go through the whole recruitment process and you can’t ask scheduling questions that might reveal someone’s religious beliefs. So you hire this person and the first day they say, ‘I need Sunday off,’ and the employer is blindsided,” Roberts said. “What happens is other existing employees have to take on those shifts, leading to burnout, and that exacerbates the recruiting and retaining problem.”

Tennant said the ruling also could complicate matters for employers who are contractually obligated to honor seniority rights when they schedule shifts.

“Particularly among unionized workforces, scheduling is a function to some extent of seniority. And so the idea that a religious accommodation would interfere with that is something that the court suggests might constitute an undue hardship,” Tennant said.

“So it seems that example pushes the definition of undue hardship away from a particular dollar value, and more toward consideration of a contractual right. I think that we’re just going to have to see what exactly is the sort of undue hardship that the court has intended in the context of the employers business.”

Courts will also have to sort out whether an accommodation’s effect on an employee’s co-workers counts as undue hardship, Tennant said, noting that in her concurrence, Justice Sonia Sotomayor writes that “some hardships, such as the labor costs of coordinating voluntary shift swaps, are not ‘undue’ because they are too insubstantial.”

Kaminer said the ruling is murky on the subject, long considered settled by a string of earlier cases holding that an accommodation that causes more than a de minimis impact on coworkers creates an undue hardship. “It’s not clear if a burden on co-workers is even going to matter anymore,” she said.

It also raises thorny questions on how far an employer must go to accommodate a religious employee when it might mean demeaning someone else—sparking new conflict over religious rights vs. the right to a discrimination-free workplace.

She cited one instance where an HP employee who objected to his employer’s diversity posters put up Bible verses around his cubicle condemning homosexuality. While the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that HP did not have to accommodate the employee’s religious expression if it meant discriminating against his co-workers, Kaminer said the Groff decision could trigger more cases of this sort. “There will be more of a sort of testing of the waters, particularly with certain people trying to figure out how far they can go with this,” she said.

article.title: Women Lawyers Want Far More Support for Menopause Care, Other Hush-Hush Health Issues
article.description: More employers are including menopause coverage in benefits packages. But they're far from the majority, in part because benefits decisions often are made by male-dominated leadership teams. Panelists urged employees to band together to create…
article.text: More employers are including menopause coverage in benefits packages. But they're far from the majority, in part because benefits decisions often are made by male-dominated leadership teams. Panelists urged employees to band together to create transparency around health challenges women face, and to advocate for better benefits. A recent panel on women’s health, part of ALM Global’s Women, Influence & Power in Law conference in New Orleans, dove into how women can combat the stigma of menopause and advocate for what they need from their employers. It was a groundbreaking discussion, given that the topic has long been taboo to discuss in the workplace, despite that more than 30 million American workers are going through menopause at any given time. article.description: Former Molson Coors general counsel Anne-Marie D'Angelo has become legal chief for hospitality giant Hilton. D'Angelo stepped down at Molson Coors earlier this year for personal reasons. She succeeds Kristin Campbell, who retired in December after 12…
article.text: Former Molson Coors general counsel Anne-Marie D'Angelo has become legal chief for hospitality giant Hilton. D'Angelo stepped down at Molson Coors earlier this year for personal reasons. She succeeds Kristin Campbell, who retired in December after 12 years as Hilton's legal chief. Anne-Marie D’Angelo, who resigned earlier this year as legal chief at Molson Coors for personal reasons, has returned as executive vice president and general counsel at Tysons, Virginia-based Hilton Hotels. “I am honored to be joining Hilton, a company I have long respected for its history, innovation and award-winning workplace culture,” D’Angelo said in a statement sent to Law.com Monday. “Hilton’s global presence and powerful franchise model has a positive impact on businesses and travelers around the world, and I look forward to helping strengthen Hilton’s already strong reputation.” Want to continue reading?Become an ALM Digital Reader for Free!   • D'Angelo stepped down at Molson Coors earlier this year for personal reasons.
  • She succeeds Kristin Campbell, who retired in December after 12 years as Hilton's legal chief.

Anne-Marie D’Angelo, who resigned earlier this year as legal chief at Molson Coors for personal reasons, has returned as executive vice president and general counsel at Tysons, Virginia-based Hilton Hotels.

“I am honored to be joining Hilton, a company I have long respected for its history, innovation and award-winning workplace culture,” D’Angelo said in a statement sent to Law.com Monday. “Hilton’s global presence and powerful franchise model has a positive impact on businesses and travelers around the world, and I look forward to helping strengthen Hilton’s already strong reputation.”

article.title: Risks Abound With Twitter In-House Gutting
article.description: A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts. A legal team that once stood at 150…
article.text: A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts. A legal team that once stood at 150 employees is now closer to 10 to 20, according to a source familiar with the situation, though that figure could not be independently verified. Nearly all of Twitter’s senior legal leadership has resigned or been fired, leaving the company to face heightened regulatory scrutiny and a raft of federal employment litigation with presumably little guidance from the top. The departure of Twitter’s last remaining deputy general counsel Regina Lima, first reported by Bloomberg, marks the latest in the mass exodus of senior in-house lawyers. Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde was among the first to be axed when Musk took over, along with General Counsel Sean Edgett. Musk dismissed Deputy General Counsel James Baker last week over his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter. Musk brought in his personal lawyer Alex Spiro to help fill the leadership void, though the New York Times reported this week that Spiro has since decamped. The draining of legal talent has also forced the embattled CEO to draw on senior in-house counsel from his other companies, Tesla and SpaceX. The in-house upheaval has some observers wondering whether the company can live up to the terms of a consent decree it entered into with the Federal Trade Commission after the regulator fined it $150 million this year for continuing to mislead users about privacy protections. Though the FTC doesn’t comment on its investigations, a spokesperson said in November that it’s keeping a close watch on developments at Twitter. Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said a small in-house department isn’t necessarily a liability, but it becomes concerning in a situation such as Twitter’s, where a legal department shrinks in such an abrupt fashion. “The concerning thing is how rapidly this appears to have happened,” he said. “It raises the risk that things are going to fall through the cracks.” Foehl, who also served as general counsel at ACA International and has a long history of working with regulatory bodies, said the FTC has no patience for companies and executive who fail to follow its orders. “I have a lot of experience sitting across the table with regulators, and one of the things that really makes their skin crawl is when their consent orders are not complied with,” he said. “You’re sending the message that you’re not taking the regulator seriously and that’s a big problem because the regulator is much more likely to bring its full enforcement power to bear.” In the last five months, all of the executives on Twitter’s Data Governance Committee responsible for sending quarterly updates to the FTC were fired or left the company, said a source familiar with the committee’s operations. The departures, borne out in media reports, include chief compliance officer Marianne Fogarty, chief information security officer Lea Kissner, and revenue product head Bruce Falck. Former Airbnb general counsel and chief ethics officer Rob Chesnut said Twitter’s regulatory vulnerability bears some similarity to the case of Joseph Sullivan, the former security chief at Uber who is currently fighting his conviction for concealing a 2016 data security breach from authorities and obstructing an FTC investigation of Uber’s security practices. “There are factors in that case that are also present here,” Chesnut said. “Uber had a track record of being close to the edge, in the grey, and even beyond it when it had to deal with regulators. If you have a company like that, you don’t get a break. And if a prosecutor gets a chance to take a shot and there’s any violation of law, you have problem.” Chesnut said the stakes are high for Twitter, whose new owner has a history of contempt for regulators. “Anybody involved in this area at the company has to do everything they can to ensure the FTC order is complied with, and if not, they need to make sure everyone high up at the company is aware of the problem,” he said. Foehl said Musk’s shaky history with regulators, combined with the revolving door of general counsels, is worrisome. “Those two things in combination are really what’s causing the concern here, and the expressed concern from the FTC,” he said.
article.html:

A legal team that once stood at 150 employees is now closer to 10 to 20, according to a source familiar with the situation, though that figure could not be independently verified.

Nearly all of Twitter’s senior legal leadership has resigned or been fired, leaving the company to face heightened regulatory scrutiny and a raft of federal employment litigation with presumably little guidance from the top. The departure of Twitter’s last remaining deputy general counsel Regina Lima, first reported by Bloomberg, marks the latest in the mass exodus of senior in-house lawyers.

Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde was among the first to be axed when Musk took over, along with General Counsel Sean Edgett. Musk dismissed Deputy General Counsel James Baker last week over his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter.

Musk brought in his personal lawyer Alex Spiro to help fill the leadership void, though the New York Times reported this week that Spiro has since decamped. The draining of legal talent has also forced the embattled CEO to draw on senior in-house counsel from his other companies, Tesla and SpaceX.

The in-house upheaval has some observers wondering whether the company can live up to the terms of a consent decree it entered into with the Federal Trade Commission after the regulator fined it $150 million this year for continuing to mislead users about privacy protections. Though the FTC doesn’t comment on its investigations, a spokesperson said in November that it’s keeping a close watch on developments at Twitter.

Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said a small in-house department isn’t necessarily a liability, but it becomes concerning in a situation such as Twitter’s, where a legal department shrinks in such an abrupt fashion. “The concerning thing is how rapidly this appears to have happened,” he said. “It raises the risk that things are going to fall through the cracks.”

Foehl, who also served as general counsel at ACA International and has a long history of working with regulatory bodies, said the FTC has no patience for companies and executive who fail to follow its orders.

“I have a lot of experience sitting across the table with regulators, and one of the things that really makes their skin crawl is when their consent orders are not complied with,” he said. “You’re sending the message that you’re not taking the regulator seriously and that’s a big problem because the regulator is much more likely to bring its full enforcement power to bear.”

In the last five months, all of the executives on Twitter’s Data Governance Committee responsible for sending quarterly updates to the FTC were fired or left the company, said a source familiar with the committee’s operations.

The departures, borne out in media reports, include chief compliance officer Marianne Fogarty, chief information security officer Lea Kissner, and revenue product head Bruce Falck.

Former Airbnb general counsel and chief ethics officer Rob Chesnut said Twitter’s regulatory vulnerability bears some similarity to the case of Joseph Sullivan, the former security chief at Uber who is currently fighting his conviction for concealing a 2016 data security breach from authorities and obstructing an FTC investigation of Uber’s security practices.

“There are factors in that case that are also present here,” Chesnut said. “Uber had a track record of being close to the edge, in the grey, and even beyond it when it had to deal with regulators. If you have a company like that, you don’t get a break. And if a prosecutor gets a chance to take a shot and there’s any violation of law, you have problem.”

Chesnut said the stakes are high for Twitter, whose new owner has a history of contempt for regulators.

“Anybody involved in this area at the company has to do everything they can to ensure the FTC order is complied with, and if not, they need to make sure everyone high up at the company is aware of the problem,” he said.

Foehl said Musk’s shaky history with regulators, combined with the revolving door of general counsels, is worrisome.

“Those two things in combination are really what’s causing the concern here, and the expressed concern from the FTC,” he said.

article.title: Women's General Counsel Network Founder Joins Climate Consultancy as It Expands Globally

article.text: Fast-growing climate consultancy 3Degrees Group hired Jan Kang, a veteran in-house leader and founder of the Women’s General Counsel Network, as general counsel. Kang was previously chief operating officer and general counsel at cybersecurity startup Stairwell, where she was also a board member. After leaving the GC role in October, she was an adviser until her official departure in January.
