article.title: Companies Must Tread Carefully as Regulators Step Up Enforcement Actions
article.description: ANALYSIS “These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself— but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a…
article.text: ANALYSIS “These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself— but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner," said Jonathan Direnfeld, an Orrick, Herrington and Sutcliffe partner. January 20, 2023 at 05:36 AM 4 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Enforcement actions have increased under the Biden administration.That trend likely will accelerate this year, as the Biden administration enters its third year.Some of the tactics investigators have been targeting have been accepted industry practices. Companies are facing immense pressure from regulators over how they market their services and engage with consumers. Experts say enforcement actions will increase this year, as government agencies zero in on businesses that use deceitful tactics to try to separate consumers from their money or data. “One thing we’ve seen increase in over the last two years is partnerships between the FTC and state attorneys general in bringing actions” said Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe partner Jonathan Direnfeld at a recent webinar on regulatory trends jointly hosted by Orrick and the consulting firm Kroll. Direnfeld attributed this shift to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in AMG Capital Management, LLC v. FTC, which limited the agency’s ability to seek monetary relief, specifically consumer restitution. This has led the FTC to lean on the broad civil penalty authority enjoyed by state attorneys general. Direnfeld said regulators are becoming more aggressive, pursuing more actions and seeking more money from companies that run afoul of consumer protection rules. He pointed to two large FTC settlements announced last year. In one, internet phone service provider Vonage agreed to pay $100 million in restitution over automatic subscription renewals. It also exacted a whopping $520 million settlement from Fortnite maker Epic Games after alleging it violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and misled players into making in-game purchases. The Epic Games settlement in particular, Direnfeld said, signals the FTC’s priorities for this year. “First and foremost there’s going to be an increased focused on all things children-directed." This means any kind of marketing aimed at children, be it direct targeted advertising or ads dressed up as entertainment. The FTC also has considered changing its rules around “stealth advertising”—digital media that softens the line between marketing and content by embedding ads in social media, online games and video-sharing platforms. Direnfeld observed that the last two big FTC settlements used the term “dark patterns” to describe tactics that make it easier for unwitting consumers to make purchases. In a post-webinar interview, Direnfeld said the challenge for companies is that some of the things the FTC would classify as a “dark pattern” like automatic renewals and certain user interface designs, have long been commonplace and accepted industry practices. “It poses a lot of challenges to companies—to be able to make decisions on how to potentially modify user flows or sales processes to try to reduce risk while not materially impacting business operations,” he said. Direnfeld, who defends tech and data-driven companies against regulatory enforcement actions, said such decision-making will require general counsel to “go after it with a scalpel, not a cleaver.” "Find the highest-risk pieces to reduce your overall risk profile, particularly if you’re in an industry where where everyone else is doing it,” he said. Should a company find itself the subject of a regulatory investigation, Direnfeld said in-house counsel should immediately start preserving documents. Beyond that, reach out to experienced outside counsel. One thing companies shouldn’t do is try to handle everything in-house, he said. “These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself—but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner, Direnfeld said. “Companies that do not find way to effectively navigate through this could easily find themselves out of business.” He said the heat is only to get more intense. “The scrutiny and work going on at these agencies is only continuing to ramp up. We’re only at about the halfway mark of the Biden administration, and their teams have only been in place for about a year and a half. So in some ways they’re only just starting to pick up steam.”
article.html:
ANALYSIS

“These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself— but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner," said Jonathan Direnfeld, an Orrick, Herrington and Sutcliffe partner.

January 20, 2023 at 05:36 AM

4 minute read

Risk and Compliance

Maria Dinzeo




What You Need to Know

  • Enforcement actions have increased under the Biden administration.
  • That trend likely will accelerate this year, as the Biden administration enters its third year.
  • Some of the tactics investigators have been targeting have been accepted industry practices.

Companies are facing immense pressure from regulators over how they market their services and engage with consumers. Experts say enforcement actions will increase this year, as government agencies zero in on businesses that use deceitful tactics to try to separate consumers from their money or data.

“One thing we’ve seen increase in over the last two years is partnerships between the FTC and state attorneys general in bringing actions” said Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe partner Jonathan Direnfeld at a recent webinar on regulatory trends jointly hosted by Orrick and the consulting firm Kroll.

Direnfeld attributed this shift to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in AMG Capital Management, LLC v. FTC, which limited the agency’s ability to seek monetary relief, specifically consumer restitution. This has led the FTC to lean on the broad civil penalty authority enjoyed by state attorneys general.

Direnfeld said regulators are becoming more aggressive, pursuing more actions and seeking more money from companies that run afoul of consumer protection rules. He pointed to two large FTC settlements announced last year. In one, internet phone service provider Vonage agreed to pay $100 million in restitution over automatic subscription renewals. It also exacted a whopping $520 million settlement from Fortnite maker Epic Games after alleging it violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and misled players into making in-game purchases.

The Epic Games settlement in particular, Direnfeld said, signals the FTC’s priorities for this year. “First and foremost there’s going to be an increased focused on all things children-directed."

This means any kind of marketing aimed at children, be it direct targeted advertising or ads dressed up as entertainment. The FTC also has considered changing its rules around “stealth advertising”—digital media that softens the line between marketing and content by embedding ads in social media, online games and video-sharing platforms.

Direnfeld observed that the last two big FTC settlements used the term “dark patterns” to describe tactics that make it easier for unwitting consumers to make purchases.

In a post-webinar interview, Direnfeld said the challenge for companies is that some of the things the FTC would classify as a “dark pattern” like automatic renewals and certain user interface designs, have long been commonplace and accepted industry practices.

“It poses a lot of challenges to companies—to be able to make decisions on how to potentially modify user flows or sales processes to try to reduce risk while not materially impacting business operations,” he said.

Direnfeld, who defends tech and data-driven companies against regulatory enforcement actions, said such decision-making will require general counsel to “go after it with a scalpel, not a cleaver.”

"Find the highest-risk pieces to reduce your overall risk profile, particularly if you’re in an industry where where everyone else is doing it,” he said.

Should a company find itself the subject of a regulatory investigation, Direnfeld said in-house counsel should immediately start preserving documents. Beyond that, reach out to experienced outside counsel.

One thing companies shouldn’t do is try to handle everything in-house, he said. “These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself—but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner, Direnfeld said.

“Companies that do not find way to effectively navigate through this could easily find themselves out of business.”

He said the heat is only to get more intense. “The scrutiny and work going on at these agencies is only continuing to ramp up. We’re only at about the halfway mark of the Biden administration, and their teams have only been in place for about a year and a half. So in some ways they’re only just starting to pick up steam.”

article.title: SEC's New Insider Trading Rules Could Have Some Unintended Consequences
article.description: ANALYSIS “When you put up barriers to use of 10b5-1 plans, I think you set up scenarios that might create some more urgent circumstances for trading, and those are the ones that are harder for general counsel to make a call on," said Daniel O'Connor,…
article.text: ANALYSIS “When you put up barriers to use of 10b5-1 plans, I think you set up scenarios that might create some more urgent circumstances for trading, and those are the ones that are harder for general counsel to make a call on," said Daniel O'Connor, a partner with Ropes and Gray. January 20, 2023 at 04:48 AM 5 minute read Corporate Governance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Tougher SEC rules on insider trading may result in fewer Rule 10b5-1 plans, experts say.Instead, executives might engage in more open-market transactions.General counsel will have to decide what constitutes material, nonpublic information. General counsel may find themselves pulled into difficult conversations with top executives as the Securities and Exchange Commission tightens its rules on company insiders looking to dump their stock. Insider trading has long been an SEC bugbear. But the steady drumbeat of outrage over high-level executives trading on information ahead of the public has ramped up over the last two decades, said securities law expert Karen Woody, a professor at Washington and Lee University. Suspicion that trades were becoming too well-timed led to unanimous agreement at the SEC that it was time to update its longstanding rule under which corporate insiders are allowed to schedule trades in advance. “There are some old-school theories about why some people are against regulating insider trading—one argument is that insider trading is an employment perk. It’s part of your executive compensation,” Woody said. “But this rule is truly the opposite. It says, ‘We’re not going to let you game the system just because you happen to be working there.’” The misuse of these Rule 10b5-1 plans mostly involved executives trying to take advantage of its flexibility, said former SEC trial attorney Daniel O’Connor, who now co-leads Ropes & Gray’s securities and futures enforcement practice. “Some of the abuses that the staff was talking about have to do with people putting in place multiple plans on either side of a good or bad event—canceling one and then revising another while potentially possessing MNPI [material non-public information],” he said. Now Rule 10b5-1 will only allow one trade plan a year and imposes a 90-to-120 day “cooling off” period for officers and directors between the adoption of the plan and the first trade. Everyone else must adhere to a 30-day waiting period. “That extended cooling off period will help general counsel advise executives on whether certain information is material non-public information,” O’Connor said. The updated rule eliminates Rule 10b5-1 as an affirmative defense against insider trading, and requires directors and officers to certify that their trading plans were made in good faith and that they are not trading on material, nonpublic information. Daniel Taylor, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business who co-authored an influential study on potential 10b5-1 abuses, said one pressing area of concern will be the rule’s prohibition on executives delaying public disclosure of bad news until after they’ve sold off their shares. “Most people view 10b5-1 as altering the timing of the trades, but there’s also evidence that executives move the timing of the disclosure. Let’s say I learn the company lost a major contract. I may be tempted to delay disclosure of that bad news until after my scheduled sale is complete. The SEC clarified that would be a violation of the good-faith requirement,” Taylor said. He said the new restrictions may lead to less use of 10b5-1 plans. “I do think we will see the use and abuse of these plans decline, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing.” Woody with Washington and Lee said the SEC’s tougher stance also may rectify the perception of executives exploiting loopholes in the existing rules. “Hopefully it will dial down the impression of some funny business around trades,” she said. O’Connor with Ropes & Gray said the revised rule may lead to more executives engaging in open-market transactions, which have their own headaches. “My worry is that the rule makes it less likely people will use 10b5-1 plans and more likely to engage in market transactions where they get pre-clearance, or go ahead and trade without a prior plan. In my experience, that’s the type of trading where things can get more challenging,” he said. “It’s a lot easier to become comfortable about whether a situation is material or not knowing the trade is going to be 90 days off. But if you have to make that decision today about a trade that might happen tomorrow, I think those conversations can be more challenging and make it less likely that the general counsel will want to provide clearance for a trade.” O’Connor said 10b5-1 plans allow for more careful consideration around trades. The alternative could lead to general counsel being called on for trade advice more often, and more pressure to get calls right. “When you put up barriers to use of 10b5-1 plans, I think you set up scenarios that might create some more urgent circumstances for trading, and those are the ones that are harder for general counsel to make a call on,” he said. “By making it more difficult to set up plan trading via 10b5-1 plans, there’s going to be an increased focus on the need to get calls right in connection with market transactions.”
article.html:
ANALYSIS

“When you put up barriers to use of 10b5-1 plans, I think you set up scenarios that might create some more urgent circumstances for trading, and those are the ones that are harder for general counsel to make a call on," said Daniel O'Connor, a partner with Ropes and Gray.

January 20, 2023 at 04:48 AM

5 minute read

Corporate Governance

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • Tougher SEC rules on insider trading may result in fewer Rule 10b5-1 plans, experts say.
  • Instead, executives might engage in more open-market transactions.
  • General counsel will have to decide what constitutes material, nonpublic information.

General counsel may find themselves pulled into difficult conversations with top executives as the Securities and Exchange Commission tightens its rules on company insiders looking to dump their stock. Insider trading has long been an SEC bugbear. But the steady drumbeat of outrage over high-level executives trading on information ahead of the public has ramped up over the last two decades, said securities law expert Karen Woody, a professor at Washington and Lee University. Suspicion that trades were becoming too well-timed led to unanimous agreement at the SEC that it was time to update its longstanding rule under which corporate insiders are allowed to schedule trades in advance. “There are some old-school theories about why some people are against regulating insider trading—one argument is that insider trading is an employment perk. It’s part of your executive compensation,” Woody said. “But this rule is truly the opposite. It says, ‘We’re not going to let you game the system just because you happen to be working there.’” The misuse of these Rule 10b5-1 plans mostly involved executives trying to take advantage of its flexibility, said former SEC trial attorney Daniel O’Connor, who now co-leads Ropes & Gray’s securities and futures enforcement practice. “Some of the abuses that the staff was talking about have to do with people putting in place multiple plans on either side of a good or bad event—canceling one and then revising another while potentially possessing MNPI [material non-public information],” he said. Now Rule 10b5-1 will only allow one trade plan a year and imposes a 90-to-120 day “cooling off” period for officers and directors between the adoption of the plan and the first trade. Everyone else must adhere to a 30-day waiting period. “That extended cooling off period will help general counsel advise executives on whether certain information is material non-public information,” O’Connor said. The updated rule eliminates Rule 10b5-1 as an affirmative defense against insider trading, and requires directors and officers to certify that their trading plans were made in good faith and that they are not trading on material, nonpublic information. Daniel Taylor, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business who co-authored an influential study on potential 10b5-1 abuses, said one pressing area of concern will be the rule’s prohibition on executives delaying public disclosure of bad news until after they’ve sold off their shares.

“Most people view 10b5-1 as altering the timing of the trades, but there’s also evidence that executives move the timing of the disclosure. Let’s say I learn the company lost a major contract. I may be tempted to delay disclosure of that bad news until after my scheduled sale is complete. The SEC clarified that would be a violation of the good-faith requirement,” Taylor said.

He said the new restrictions may lead to less use of 10b5-1 plans. “I do think we will see the use and abuse of these plans decline, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing.”

Woody with Washington and Lee said the SEC’s tougher stance also may rectify the perception of executives exploiting loopholes in the existing rules. “Hopefully it will dial down the impression of some funny business around trades,” she said.

O’Connor with Ropes & Gray said the revised rule may lead to more executives engaging in open-market transactions, which have their own headaches.

“My worry is that the rule makes it less likely people will use 10b5-1 plans and more likely to engage in market transactions where they get pre-clearance, or go ahead and trade without a prior plan. In my experience, that’s the type of trading where things can get more challenging,” he said.

“It’s a lot easier to become comfortable about whether a situation is material or not knowing the trade is going to be 90 days off. But if you have to make that decision today about a trade that might happen tomorrow, I think those conversations can be more challenging and make it less likely that the general counsel will want to provide clearance for a trade.”

O’Connor said 10b5-1 plans allow for more careful consideration around trades. The alternative could lead to general counsel being called on for trade advice more often, and more pressure to get calls right.

“When you put up barriers to use of 10b5-1 plans, I think you set up scenarios that might create some more urgent circumstances for trading, and those are the ones that are harder for general counsel to make a call on,” he said. “By making it more difficult to set up plan trading via 10b5-1 plans, there’s going to be an increased focus on the need to get calls right in connection with market transactions.”

article.title: Litigators' Advice to Companies on FTC Non-Compete Ban
article.description: What You Need to Know Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance.Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential.FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes with…
article.text: What You Need to Know Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance.Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential.FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes with low-wage workers. With the Federal Trade Commission poised to sharply curtail non-compete clauses, litigation experts say now is the time for companies to take stock of their employment agreements. “You want to have a clear message when the FTC or anyone else comes calling and asks, ‘Why do you have these agreements?’” said John Barry, who heads Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ employment litigation practice and co-authored a recent client_briefing on the issue. Barry said companies should audit their agreements to ensure they’re justifiable and reasonable in scope. Legitimate business reasons like protecting trade secrets or preserving customer goodwill can be a shield against antitrust scrutiny. Adding another complication, the FTC’s rule proposes to ban any employment contract language that the FTC views as a “de facto” non-compete clause. Customer non-solicitation agreements, non-disclosure agreements and equity forfeiture provisions could all be interpreted to function as such. “There’s a threshold question about this proposed rule as to whether it would apply to incentive compensation arrangements that contain non-competes,” Barry said. “There’s a possibility that non-competes in connection with equity might still be OK. That’s what we who advise businesses are trying to figure out; are forfeiture for non-competition provisions at risk? If that ability to incentivize talent to come to companies goes away, that’s going to be every problematic for companies, particularly the startups.” Prohibitions on non-compete agreements already are familiar territory to Silicon Valley tech companies, as California already deems them unenforceable. Their disallowance is part of the reason why the Northern District of California is home to the largest docket of trade secret cases in the country. For those outside of California, non-competes are a handy tool to protect against trade secret and intellectual property theft. “If these rules are passed, which is a big if, the companies will certainly have to rely on and follow the California approach,” Barry said, “which is to make sure they’ve identified their trade secrets so if someone does go to work for another company and starts producing a similar product, they’ll be in a better place to enforce and bring an action to try to protect those trade secrets.” Some companies require high-level executives to pay back their vested or unvested equity if they go to work for a competitor. Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group, said the proposed rule doesn’t directly address whether a clawback would be prohibited, but it does contain language saying agreements requiring a worker to pay damages if they compete against their employer “effect the same restriction.” “Does that mean forfeiting vested shares, or paying back funds would violate this rule? I definitely think it’s potentially on the table from the FTC’s perspective,” Baker said. In the meantime, companies should re-evaluate what type of employees are currently subject to non-competes. “You’re just setting yourself up for a better defense of your non-competes if you’re only using it with a population that requires those restrictions—don’t use it with everyone at the company. The employees who really should have non-compete restrictions are those who have the keys to the kingdom, or who know the secret sauce.” Weil litigation partner Eric Hochstadt said there’s no need to panic. The rule is still in its nascent stage, and the final version could look much different after the close of the 60-day public comment period. The proposal also offers a “safe harbor” for companies to terminate non-competes for 180 days after the rule becomes final. That means the earliest possible date for noncompliance would be in September of this year, though because the FTC will need time to consider comments it likely would be a few months later than that. “You don’t want to overreact and do something rushed,” he said. “This is something you can do with deliberate, careful guidance with counsel within the next few months.” Hochstadt said the FTC has finite resources, and will have to be selective about where it focuses its enforcement efforts. “The disparity in bargaining power is animating the majority of the FTC commissioners who have proposed this rule,” he said, making it all the more likely that regulators will target companies that require non-competes from low-wage workers. “It also remains to be seen what both the potential legal and legislative reactions in Congress to this will be,” he said.
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Companies would have until at least September to get in compliance.
  • Businesses should act now to limit non-competes to employees for whom they are essential.
  • FTC enforcement likely would focus on companies using non-competes with low-wage workers.

With the Federal Trade Commission poised to sharply curtail non-compete clauses, litigation experts say now is the time for companies to take stock of their employment agreements.

“You want to have a clear message when the FTC or anyone else comes calling and asks, ‘Why do you have these agreements?’” said John Barry, who heads Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ employment litigation practice and co-authored a recent client_briefing on the issue.

Barry said companies should audit their agreements to ensure they’re justifiable and reasonable in scope. Legitimate business reasons like protecting trade secrets or preserving customer goodwill can be a shield against antitrust scrutiny.

Adding another complication, the FTC’s rule proposes to ban any employment contract language that the FTC views as a “de facto” non-compete clause. Customer non-solicitation agreements, non-disclosure agreements and equity forfeiture provisions could all be interpreted to function as such.

“There’s a threshold question about this proposed rule as to whether it would apply to incentive compensation arrangements that contain non-competes,” Barry said. “There’s a possibility that non-competes in connection with equity might still be OK. That’s what we who advise businesses are trying to figure out; are forfeiture for non-competition provisions at risk? If that ability to incentivize talent to come to companies goes away, that’s going to be every problematic for companies, particularly the startups.”

Prohibitions on non-compete agreements already are familiar territory to Silicon Valley tech companies, as California already deems them unenforceable. Their disallowance is part of the reason why the Northern District of California is home to the largest docket of trade secret cases in the country.

For those outside of California, non-competes are a handy tool to protect against trade secret and intellectual property theft.

“If these rules are passed, which is a big if, the companies will certainly have to rely on and follow the California approach,” Barry said, “which is to make sure they’ve identified their trade secrets so if someone does go to work for another company and starts producing a similar product, they’ll be in a better place to enforce and bring an action to try to protect those trade secrets.”

Some companies require high-level executives to pay back their vested or unvested equity if they go to work for a competitor.

Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group, said the proposed rule doesn’t directly address whether a clawback would be prohibited, but it does contain language saying agreements requiring a worker to pay damages if they compete against their employer “effect the same restriction.”

“Does that mean forfeiting vested shares, or paying back funds would violate this rule? I definitely think it’s potentially on the table from the FTC’s perspective,” Baker said.

In the meantime, companies should re-evaluate what type of employees are currently subject to non-competes.

“You’re just setting yourself up for a better defense of your non-competes if you’re only using it with a population that requires those restrictions—don’t use it with everyone at the company. The employees who really should have non-compete restrictions are those who have the keys to the kingdom, or who know the secret sauce.”

Weil litigation partner Eric Hochstadt said there’s no need to panic.

The rule is still in its nascent stage, and the final version could look much different after the close of the 60-day public comment period. The proposal also offers a “safe harbor” for companies to terminate non-competes for 180 days after the rule becomes final.

That means the earliest possible date for noncompliance would be in September of this year, though because the FTC will need time to consider comments it likely would be a few months later than that.

“You don’t want to overreact and do something rushed,” he said. “This is something you can do with deliberate, careful guidance with counsel within the next few months.”

Hochstadt said the FTC has finite resources, and will have to be selective about where it focuses its enforcement efforts.

“The disparity in bargaining power is animating the majority of the FTC commissioners who have proposed this rule,” he said, making it all the more likely that regulators will target companies that require non-competes from low-wage workers.

“It also remains to be seen what both the potential legal and legislative reactions in Congress to this will be,” he said.

article.title: Laid-Off In-House Lawyers Still Finding Jobs, But Could Face Stiffer Competition
article.description: January 13, 2023 at 10:00 AM 4 minute read Recruiting Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house…
article.text: January 13, 2023 at 10:00 AM 4 minute read Recruiting Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs pummeling the tech industry. And while there are still jobs aplenty for those seeking reemployment, legal recruiters warn that the tide could be turning. “We haven’t seen a lot of in-house lawyers desperately looking for jobs,” said Sean Burke, founding partner at legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. However, he added, there’s been a marked increase in applications from law firm lawyers looking to go in-house, leading him to suspect that layoffs have mostly affected the other side. Twitter was an outlier among tech giants when it lost the bulk of its 150-person legal department last year, but Burke noted that most attorneys left willingly after Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the social media company, installed himself as CEO and demanded employees either work “long hours at high intensity” or walk. “The Twitter attorneys I’ve spoken with left by choice, and they are all very confident in their choice,” Burke said. “They took the money and ran.” But some were also part of a mass layoff that slashed more than 50% of Twitter’s workforce. Ashley Roybal-Reid started as a product counsel at Twitter in February 2022, and by November she was out of a job. In an interview, Roybal-Reid said she received an email announcing “the rumors were true” that Twitter was planning a mass layoff. The following Monday, staff would find out if they were among those cut. “I was trying to wrap up some work that [Thursday] night and my access got cut so I stopped working,” she said. Roybal-Reid said she expected to face some difficulty in trying to land a new job at the end of the year. But after posting about her loss on LinkedIn, she was flooded with messages from colleagues and friends, some of whom she hadn’t spoken with for years. “I was obviously a little bit discouraged. I really liked my job at Twitter and the people I worked with, but fairly quickly I got a sense there was hope out there,” she said. Newly inspired, Roybal-Reid spent the next few weeks on her job search. “I treated it like a 40-hour-a-week job,” she said. This week, Roybal-Reid made another announcement on LinkedIn: she had joined the in-house legal team at Mozilla. Now, she’s the one offering to help her laid-off colleagues find work. “I suspect there are more job seekers than jobs right now, but there are jobs. It’s just a question of finding them,” she said. “It takes a little more legwork. Capitalizing on your network as best you can is probably the No. 1 thing.” John Gilmore, founder and managing partner of the legal recruiting firm BarkerGilmore, said job seekers are having to rely more on their networks and companies are becoming more selective in hiring. “There are still a number of opportunities out there, but companies are being highly selective and they’re moving a bit slower than they ever have to make the hires, so it’s become a bit more of a challenge,” he said. “People are definitely having success in finding new positions, but it’s taking more networking.” Gilmore said using social media to announce you’re looking for a job is a smart move. “I would take advantage of all of that for sure, even reaching out to outside counsel you worked with or law school grads and colleagues,” he said. “Really sit down and exhaust your network.” Burke of Whistler Partners said he expects layoffs to ramp up at outside law firms, which will make competition for in-house jobs more fierce. Lawyers who are already laid off will have a better shot at finding another in-house job now than in a few months. “Somewhere in the near future there’s a dotted line, and if you get laid off after that dotted line, it’s a lot harder because there’s way more competition and not enough jobs,” he said. While that hasn’t happened yet, Burke said things appear to be trending in that direction. “We’re going to see more and more pressure on in-house jobs, and there’s going to be more attorneys from firms looking for them,” he said.
article.html:
January 13, 2023 at 10:00 AM

4 minute read

Recruiting

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.
  • Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions.



In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs pummeling the tech industry. And while there are still jobs aplenty for those seeking reemployment, legal recruiters warn that the tide could be turning.

“We haven’t seen a lot of in-house lawyers desperately looking for jobs,” said Sean Burke, founding partner at legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. However, he added, there’s been a marked increase in applications from law firm lawyers looking to go in-house, leading him to suspect that layoffs have mostly affected the other side.

Twitter was an outlier among tech giants when it lost the bulk of its 150-person legal department last year, but Burke noted that most attorneys left willingly after Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the social media company, installed himself as CEO and demanded employees either work “long hours at high intensity” or walk.

“The Twitter attorneys I’ve spoken with left by choice, and they are all very confident in their choice,” Burke said. “They took the money and ran.”

But some were also part of a mass layoff that slashed more than 50% of Twitter’s workforce.

Ashley Roybal-Reid started as a product counsel at Twitter in February 2022, and by November she was out of a job.

In an interview, Roybal-Reid said she received an email announcing “the rumors were true” that Twitter was planning a mass layoff. The following Monday, staff would find out if they were among those cut. “I was trying to wrap up some work that [Thursday] night and my access got cut so I stopped working,” she said.

Roybal-Reid said she expected to face some difficulty in trying to land a new job at the end of the year. But after posting about her loss on LinkedIn, she was flooded with messages from colleagues and friends, some of whom she hadn’t spoken with for years.

“I was obviously a little bit discouraged. I really liked my job at Twitter and the people I worked with, but fairly quickly I got a sense there was hope out there,” she said. Newly inspired, Roybal-Reid spent the next few weeks on her job search. “I treated it like a 40-hour-a-week job,” she said.

This week, Roybal-Reid made another announcement on LinkedIn: she had joined the in-house legal team at Mozilla. Now, she’s the one offering to help her laid-off colleagues find work.

“I suspect there are more job seekers than jobs right now, but there are jobs. It’s just a question of finding them,” she said. “It takes a little more legwork. Capitalizing on your network as best you can is probably the No. 1 thing.”

John Gilmore, founder and managing partner of the legal recruiting firm BarkerGilmore, said job seekers are having to rely more on their networks and companies are becoming more selective in hiring.

“There are still a number of opportunities out there, but companies are being highly selective and they’re moving a bit slower than they ever have to make the hires, so it’s become a bit more of a challenge,” he said. “People are definitely having success in finding new positions, but it’s taking more networking.”

Gilmore said using social media to announce you’re looking for a job is a smart move. “I would take advantage of all of that for sure, even reaching out to outside counsel you worked with or law school grads and colleagues,” he said. “Really sit down and exhaust your network.”

Burke of Whistler Partners said he expects layoffs to ramp up at outside law firms, which will make competition for in-house jobs more fierce. Lawyers who are already laid off will have a better shot at finding another in-house job now than in a few months.

“Somewhere in the near future there’s a dotted line, and if you get laid off after that dotted line, it’s a lot harder because there’s way more competition and not enough jobs,” he said.

While that hasn’t happened yet, Burke said things appear to be trending in that direction. “We’re going to see more and more pressure on in-house jobs, and there’s going to be more attorneys from firms looking for them,” he said.

article.title: As Companies' Fears of Data-Breach Litigation Soar, Legal Terrain Rife With Uncertainty
article.description: Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to…
article.text: Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims. The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies. But any comfort the ruling, which involved the Fair Credit Reporting Act, brought to attorneys defending data breaches began to fade last year when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled in one such case that the future risk of identity theft is a sufficiently concrete injury. That case, Clemens v. ExecuPharm, involved a known gang of hackers publishing personal data stolen in a ransomware attack on the dark web. The court based its decision on the specific facts of that breach, and what it means for future cases is unclear, Jennifer Romano, a litigation partner for Crowell & Moring in Los Angeles, said in a report issued by her firm this week. Weighing in favor of standing was the fact that it was a cyberattack from a very sophisticated organization. “What other data breach class actions will satisfy the injury requirement under TransUnion? Will it always depend on the facts? This makes it incredibly difficult for parties to assess the risks and potential exposure, which is particularly problematic when the amount of statutory damages could bankrupt a company,” Romano said in the report. Another litigation forecast, this one from Baker McKenzie, included the results of a survey of 600 senior litigation attorneys at large companies on four continents. The attorneys are expecting an action-packed year; just 17% of respondents said they expect the number of disputes this year to decline from 2022. Asked to identify disputes that present a risk to their organizations, 62% of respondents cited cybersecurity/data, putting it at the top of the list. No. 2 was environment, social and governance, at 58%. After that, no dispute type garnered more than 37%. The report noted that cyberattacks are becoming more common, with attackers’ tactics becoming more sinister. Ransomware attacks saw a 13% jump from 2022. The attacks increasingly use “double extortion,” in which cybercriminals not only encrypt files but take a copy and threaten to release them if ransom is not paid, and “triple extortion,” which involves ransom payments from victims’ clients or suppliers whose data was compromised. Scott Giordano, general counsel at data privacy software company Spirion, said the high court’s ruling in TransUnion doesn’t change the dynamic for companies dealing with the aftermath of data breaches, as they will still need to calculate the extent of the harm done. “You’re still going to hire an economist and a data scientist, and have those folks go through the data and find what the potential is for harm,” he said. Giordano said companies should try to reduce their exposure by knowing the type of data they have and paring it down. “First, have a very crisp idea of what sensitive personal information you have inside your information ecosystem, and once you have that, determine what you need and what you can do away with,” he said. “It’s historically been a problem that companies in America collect way more data than they need, thinking they’re going use it down the road. But too often it’s the bad actors who end up using it.” He noted that data encryption can provide a safe harbor for companies under privacy statutes. “Encrypt, encrypt, encrypt,” Giordano said. “If the data is encrypted, in many if not most cases, the statute doesn’t apply. And if the bad guys can’t use it, then it’s harder to articulate the damages you could have.” In an email, Crowell’s Romano said that if companies do suffer a breach, they should gather as much evidence as possible on the incident, and hire experienced forensic teams to investigate. “What happened? When? What information was accessed? What information was exfiltrated? What can you know with certainty? What cannot be determined? Why? These will be key facts in the case, including in opposing class member standing under TransUnion,” Romano said. “Preserving and marshalling the evidence relating to the incident will be central to show that plaintiff has not satisfied that burden.”
article.html:
Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims.

The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies.

But any comfort the ruling, which involved the Fair Credit Reporting Act, brought to attorneys defending data breaches began to fade last year when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled in one such case that the future risk of identity theft is a sufficiently concrete injury.

That case, Clemens v. ExecuPharm, involved a known gang of hackers publishing personal data stolen in a ransomware attack on the dark web.

The court based its decision on the specific facts of that breach, and what it means for future cases is unclear, Jennifer Romano, a litigation partner for Crowell & Moring in Los Angeles, said in a report issued by her firm this week. Weighing in favor of standing was the fact that it was a cyberattack from a very sophisticated organization.

“What other data breach class actions will satisfy the injury requirement under TransUnion? Will it always depend on the facts? This makes it incredibly difficult for parties to assess the risks and potential exposure, which is particularly problematic when the amount of statutory damages could bankrupt a company,” Romano said in the report.

Another litigation forecast, this one from Baker McKenzie, included the results of a survey of 600 senior litigation attorneys at large companies on four continents. The attorneys are expecting an action-packed year; just 17% of respondents said they expect the number of disputes this year to decline from 2022.

Asked to identify disputes that present a risk to their organizations, 62% of respondents cited cybersecurity/data, putting it at the top of the list. No. 2 was environment, social and governance, at 58%. After that, no dispute type garnered more than 37%.

The report noted that cyberattacks are becoming more common, with attackers’ tactics becoming more sinister. Ransomware attacks saw a 13% jump from 2022. The attacks increasingly use “double extortion,” in which cybercriminals not only encrypt files but take a copy and threaten to release them if ransom is not paid, and “triple extortion,” which involves ransom payments from victims’ clients or suppliers whose data was compromised.

Scott Giordano, general counsel at data privacy software company Spirion, said the high court’s ruling in TransUnion doesn’t change the dynamic for companies dealing with the aftermath of data breaches, as they will still need to calculate the extent of the harm done.

“You’re still going to hire an economist and a data scientist, and have those folks go through the data and find what the potential is for harm,” he said.

Giordano said companies should try to reduce their exposure by knowing the type of data they have and paring it down.

“First, have a very crisp idea of what sensitive personal information you have inside your information ecosystem, and once you have that, determine what you need and what you can do away with,” he said.

“It’s historically been a problem that companies in America collect way more data than they need, thinking they’re going use it down the road. But too often it’s the bad actors who end up using it.”

He noted that data encryption can provide a safe harbor for companies under privacy statutes. “Encrypt, encrypt, encrypt,” Giordano said. “If the data is encrypted, in many if not most cases, the statute doesn’t apply. And if the bad guys can’t use it, then it’s harder to articulate the damages you could have.”

In an email, Crowell’s Romano said that if companies do suffer a breach, they should gather as much evidence as possible on the incident, and hire experienced forensic teams to investigate.

“What happened? When? What information was accessed? What information was exfiltrated? What can you know with certainty? What cannot be determined? Why? These will be key facts in the case, including in opposing class member standing under TransUnion,” Romano said. “Preserving and marshalling the evidence relating to the incident will be central to show that plaintiff has not satisfied that burden.”

article.title: Barrage of New Laws, Regulations Coming in 2023
article.description: Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS "It's going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. January 11, 2023 at 03:13 PM Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to…
article.text: Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS "It's going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. January 11, 2023 at 03:13 PM Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Amendments to California's consumer-friendly privacy statute are kicking in.An SEC proposed rule would require public companies to disclose material cyber incidents within four days.A U.S. Department of Labor proposed rule would classify more workers as employers rather than contractors. A host of new laws, regulations and reporting requirements are taking effect in 2023 that will keep tech companies on their toes. State laws on pay transparency and data privacy are kicking in, and new Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure rules on climate change and cybersecurity also likely will be in the offing. The Department of Labor also is pushing a rule change that will affect the gig economy. Here is a rundown: Climate Change Disclosures Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a rule requiring publicly traded companies to disclose climate change risks. The rule faces strong pushback as Republicans, having retaken control of the House of Representatives, have vowed to probe the SEC’s interest in climate change and other governance issues. “It’s going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. Rosen said the rule will likely become final this year despite potential roadblocks, though some of its more contentious provisions may be watered down. “It will not be a total surprise if the final rules are somewhat pared down from the initial proposals,” Rosen said. Michael Littenberg, a partner at Ropes & Gray who advises companies on environmental, social and corporate governance matters, said that while the rule will inevitably face legal challenges, companies will still be expected to comply. He added that it’s unclear whether the final rule will cover indirect emissions that occur in a company’s supply chain, known as “scope 3,” which comprise the bulk of emissions for which tech companies are responsible and can be produced by business travel, commutes and purchased goods and services. Littenberg said such emissions can be hard to quantify. Companies often rely on third-party data sources to calculate those emissions. “If scope 3 disclosures are mandatory for purposes of the rule, that raises the question of what is the liability for that data?” he said. Cybersecurity-Incident Disclosures Another SEC-proposed rule would require publicly traded companies to report “material” cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining an event has occurred, a tight timeframe that observers say poses some risk. “You’re telling the world you’ve had an incident. If you were wrong or made misleading statements those are some of the risks and pitfalls that could come along with those types of reporting obligations,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance. “It is now public and you cannot unring the bell.” RECOMMENDED FOR YO Whether it’s a failure to disclose or making a false statements, Baker said, “these types of disclosures are going to then be one more thing that plaintiffs and regulators will grab hold of.” Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said it likely will be difficult for companies to determine whether an incident qualifies as disclosable. “Since the materiality of the incident is the determining factor, that puts a lot of pressure on companies—in a situation that is often very dynamic—to assess and make that determination,” said Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo, who served as regional trial counsel for the SEC. “It calls for companies to do a lot of prep work ahead of time to make that assessment if an incident comes up. It’s a matter of both making sure that information about an incident circulates to the right people on a timely basis and also making sure that they’re getting the kind of information they need.” The requirement that companies disclose their risk management practices and cybersecurity response also could leave them vulnerable to from bad actors, who could access that public information “You could give would-be attackers a road map about how to get around those risk management practices,” Longo said. Privacy A litany of state privacy laws will become operative this year, starting with amendments to the California Consumer Privacy Act embodied in the California Privacy Rights Act, a ballot initiative voters passed in 2020. The CPRA amendments took effect on Jan. 1 of this year, and enforcement is scheduled to start July 1. California’s amendments gives the CCPA more teeth, and more rigor. It also clarifies the scope of what it covers. Companies that “share” data for the purposes of targeted advertising rather than sell it will be covered by the law. The CPRA also sunsets the CCPA’s exception for employee personal information and business-to-business data. Katie Pimentel, assistant general counsel and head of global privacy at Yahoo, said the amendments also introduce the new, European-imported requirement that companies conduct regular data protection risk assessments. During that process, companies must weigh the privacy and security risks to consumers against the benefits of processing their personal data. Pimentel said California’s law isn’t completely clear on the standard for risk assessments, though it could be clarified in the future. “It all comes down to what the consumer would expect. Is it clear to the consumer what you’re doing? There’s nuance in there that I think will really start to be broken down in the industry and regulatory landscape. Consumer expectation looks pretty clear, but when you start to break it down it looks really messy.” Compliance presents a huge cost to smaller companies that gather less-specific data on consumers. “Most shops are not going to be able to handle it in-house; they’ll have to outsource it,” Pimentel said. An additional headache for in-house is the annual cybersecurity audit. Pimentel said organizations will no longer be able to rely on current contracts as a liability shield if data is misused by a third-party vendor. Instead of conducting a full audit, smaller companies might just send forms to their vendors, asking them to certify that they won’t sell or otherwise abuse consumer information. “The shops that are larger and more inclined to get an attorney general’s attention are probably going to have to engage in actual audits, which are so expensive to do,” Pimentel said. It remains to be seen whether a form will suffice. “We’ll have to see what the enforcement looks like in 12-24 months,” Pimentel said. That’s when we’ll really start to see if there are clarifying amendments coming out.” As more states add to the patchwork of privacy laws, it may make sense for companies to adopt a common, consumer-friendly approach. “While a standardized approach for the entire nation may increase the volume of requests from people who do not have codified data privacy rights in their state yet, this approach helps future-proof operations once new data privacy laws are passed across the nation,” said Merry Marwig, a consultant with privacy platform DataGrail. Privacy Laws As a result of a pay transparency law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in late 2022, California requires companies with 15 or more employees to publicly post pay ranges in job listings. Companies with 100 or more employees will also have to file annual wage reports with the California Civil Rights Department, formerly known as the Department of Fair Employment and Housing. Similar transparency laws have been enacted in Colorado, Washington and New York City. In addition, New York state is poised to enact a law requiring compensation ranges in job. California’s law the only one to require employers to share pay range information with existing employees upon request. Additionally, employers with five or more employees must offer five days of unpaid bereavement leave within three months of losing a family member under a law Newsom signed in September of last year. California also expanded its California Family Rights Act, adding a “designated person” to the list of people an employee can take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave to care for, provided they’ve worked for their employer a least a year. The designated person can be a blood relative or anyone with whom the employee has the equivalent of a family relationship, but the law limits an employee to one designated person each year. The new law also allows employees to use time under the California paid sick leave law to take paid time off to care for a designated person. Gig Workers In the ongoing battle over the distinction between employees and independent contractors, the U.S. Department of Labor in October issued a proposed employee classification rule under the Fair Labor Standards Act. It would rescind a Trump administration rule that made it easier for employers to classify workers as a contractor by focusing primarily on profit and loss as well as control. Timothy Taylor, an employment and litigation partner at Holland & Knight, says the Biden labor department is moving in a “more employee-friendly direction,” though it isn’t nearly as stringent as California’s ABC test. Under that test, workers can only be classified as an independent contractor if all three of these conditions are met: they are in control of their work, they are performing a job that is beyond what the business usually does, and they are engaged in an independent trade, occupation or business of the same type that the hiring business is engaged in. “The proposed rule is less friendly to independent contractors than the Trump rule but it is not scorched-earth devastating like the California rule,” Taylor said. “The proposed rule shift things two or three notches toward the employee side of the pendulum, but it’s not Armageddon.” But the new rule makes classification a bit more ambiguous, Taylor said, adding, “It injects a level of uncertainty and a level of enforcement discretion for the Department of Labor and a level of opportunity for enterprising plaintiff lawyers,” he said.

Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch




ANALYSIS


"It's going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer.

January 11, 2023 at 03:13 PM


Risk and Compliance

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • Amendments to California's consumer-friendly privacy statute are kicking in.
  • An SEC proposed rule would require public companies to disclose material cyber incidents within four days.
  • A U.S. Department of Labor proposed rule would classify more workers as employers rather than contractors.

A host of new laws, regulations and reporting requirements are taking effect in 2023 that will keep tech companies on their toes.

State laws on pay transparency and data privacy are kicking in, and new Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure rules on climate change and cybersecurity also likely will be in the offing. The Department of Labor also is pushing a rule change that will affect the gig economy.

Here is a rundown:

Climate Change Disclosures

Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a rule requiring publicly traded companies to disclose climate change risks.

The rule faces strong pushback as Republicans, having retaken control of the House of Representatives, have vowed to probe the SEC’s interest in climate change and other governance issues. “It’s going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer.

Rosen said the rule will likely become final this year despite potential roadblocks, though some of its more contentious provisions may be watered down. “It will not be a total surprise if the final rules are somewhat pared down from the initial proposals,” Rosen said.

Michael Littenberg, a partner at Ropes & Gray who advises companies on environmental, social and corporate governance matters, said that while the rule will inevitably face legal challenges, companies will still be expected to comply.

He added that it’s unclear whether the final rule will cover indirect emissions that occur in a company’s supply chain, known as “scope 3,” which comprise the bulk of emissions for which tech companies are responsible and can be produced by business travel, commutes and purchased goods and services.

Littenberg said such emissions can be hard to quantify. Companies often rely on third-party data sources to calculate those emissions. “If scope 3 disclosures are mandatory for purposes of the rule, that raises the question of what is the liability for that data?” he said.

Cybersecurity-Incident Disclosures

Another SEC-proposed rule would require publicly traded companies to report “material” cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining an event has occurred, a tight timeframe that observers say poses some risk.

“You’re telling the world you’ve had an incident. If you were wrong or made misleading statements those are some of the risks and pitfalls that could come along with those types of reporting obligations,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance. “It is now public and you cannot unring the bell.”

RECOMMENDED FOR YO


Whether it’s a failure to disclose or making a false statements, Baker said, “these types of disclosures are going to then be one more thing that plaintiffs and regulators will grab hold of.”

Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said it likely will be difficult for companies to determine whether an incident qualifies as disclosable.

“Since the materiality of the incident is the determining factor, that puts a lot of pressure on companies—in a situation that is often very dynamic—to assess and make that determination,” said Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo, who served as regional trial counsel for the SEC.

“It calls for companies to do a lot of prep work ahead of time to make that assessment if an incident comes up. It’s a matter of both making sure that information about an incident circulates to the right people on a timely basis and also making sure that they’re getting the kind of information they need.”

The requirement that companies disclose their risk management practices and cybersecurity response also could leave them vulnerable to from bad actors, who could access that public information

“You could give would-be attackers a road map about how to get around those risk management practices,” Longo said.

Privacy

A litany of state privacy laws will become operative this year, starting with amendments to the California Consumer Privacy Act embodied in the California Privacy Rights Act, a ballot initiative voters passed in 2020. The CPRA amendments took effect on Jan. 1 of this year, and enforcement is scheduled to start July 1.

California’s amendments gives the CCPA more teeth, and more rigor. It also clarifies the scope of what it covers. Companies that “share” data for the purposes of targeted advertising rather than sell it will be covered by the law.

The CPRA also sunsets the CCPA’s exception for employee personal information and business-to-business data.

Katie Pimentel, assistant general counsel and head of global privacy at Yahoo, said the amendments also introduce the new, European-imported requirement that companies conduct regular data protection risk assessments. During that process, companies must weigh the privacy and security risks to consumers against the benefits of processing their personal data.

Pimentel said California’s law isn’t completely clear on the standard for risk assessments, though it could be clarified in the future.

“It all comes down to what the consumer would expect. Is it clear to the consumer what you’re doing? There’s nuance in there that I think will really start to be broken down in the industry and regulatory landscape. Consumer expectation looks pretty clear, but when you start to break it down it looks really messy.”

Compliance presents a huge cost to smaller companies that gather less-specific data on consumers. “Most shops are not going to be able to handle it in-house; they’ll have to outsource it,” Pimentel said.

An additional headache for in-house is the annual cybersecurity audit. Pimentel said organizations will no longer be able to rely on current contracts as a liability shield if data is misused by a third-party vendor.

Instead of conducting a full audit, smaller companies might just send forms to their vendors, asking them to certify that they won’t sell or otherwise abuse consumer information.

“The shops that are larger and more inclined to get an attorney general’s attention are probably going to have to engage in actual audits, which are so expensive to do,” Pimentel said.

It remains to be seen whether a form will suffice. “We’ll have to see what the enforcement looks like in 12-24 months,” Pimentel said. That’s when we’ll really start to see if there are clarifying amendments coming out.”

As more states add to the patchwork of privacy laws, it may make sense for companies to adopt a common, consumer-friendly approach.

“While a standardized approach for the entire nation may increase the volume of requests from people who do not have codified data privacy rights in their state yet, this approach helps future-proof operations once new data privacy laws are passed across the nation,” said Merry Marwig, a consultant with privacy platform DataGrail.

Privacy Laws

As a result of a pay transparency law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in late 2022, California requires companies with 15 or more employees to publicly post pay ranges in job listings. Companies with 100 or more employees will also have to file annual wage reports with the California Civil Rights Department, formerly known as the Department of Fair Employment and Housing.

Similar transparency laws have been enacted in Colorado, Washington and New York City. In addition, New York state is poised to enact a law requiring compensation ranges in job. California’s law the only one to require employers to share pay range information with existing employees upon request.

Additionally, employers with five or more employees must offer five days of unpaid bereavement leave within three months of losing a family member under a law Newsom signed in September of last year.

California also expanded its California Family Rights Act, adding a “designated person” to the list of people an employee can take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave to care for, provided they’ve worked for their employer a least a year.

The designated person can be a blood relative or anyone with whom the employee has the equivalent of a family relationship, but the law limits an employee to one designated person each year. The new law also allows employees to use time under the California paid sick leave law to take paid time off to care for a designated person.

Gig Workers

In the ongoing battle over the distinction between employees and independent contractors, the U.S. Department of Labor in October issued a proposed employee classification rule under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

It would rescind a Trump administration rule that made it easier for employers to classify workers as a contractor by focusing primarily on profit and loss as well as control.

Timothy Taylor, an employment and litigation partner at Holland & Knight, says the Biden labor department is moving in a “more employee-friendly direction,” though it isn’t nearly as stringent as California’s ABC test.

Under that test, workers can only be classified as an independent contractor if all three of these conditions are met: they are in control of their work, they are performing a job that is beyond what the business usually does, and they are engaged in an independent trade, occupation or business of the same type that the hiring business is engaged in.

“The proposed rule is less friendly to independent contractors than the Trump rule but it is not scorched-earth devastating like the California rule,” Taylor said. “The proposed rule shift things two or three notches toward the employee side of the pendulum, but it’s not Armageddon.”

But the new rule makes classification a bit more ambiguous, Taylor said, adding, “It injects a level of uncertainty and a level of enforcement discretion for the Department of Labor and a level of opportunity for enterprising plaintiff lawyers,” he said.

article.title: 'There Are Headaches Galore': 3 Risk Areas That Will Reign in 2023
article.description: Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS “2023 will be a momentous competition law year," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman. January 11, 2023 at 04:08 PM 6 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know The…
article.text: Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS “2023 will be a momentous competition law year," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman. January 11, 2023 at 04:08 PM 6 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come.The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies.The Biden administration stepped up antitrust enforcement in 2022 and likely will escalate those efforts this year. General counsel are entering 2023 facing a raft of global uncertainty, regulatory risks, and legal battles with major implications for the digital economy. Lawmakers, regulators and the courts have all ramped up pressure on the tech industry and show no sign of letting up this year. How companies deal with climate change, compete for business, and collect and protect user data will be top risk areas in 2023. Data Privacy and Protection The consequences for neglecting to protect consumers’ private information are increasing in severity, and enforcement is intensifying. “General counsel can only expect enforcement activity to increase and accelerate in number,” said Todd Ruback, former chief privacy officer and general counsel for ad-blocker and privacy browser Ghostery. He said companies can expect to see more enforcement actions as states continue to adopt their own privacy laws. Companies can also anticipate a rise in class actions over wrongful data collection and third-party tracking. “It’s your obligation to know what third parties are on your website, and that’s where privacy is hard because businesses move fast and are always looking for ways to use data,” Ruback said. “There are headaches galore.” The Federal Trade Commission is also wading in on privacy. Its eye-watering $520 million penalty against Fortnite developer Epic Games for collecting data on children and duping them into making in-game purchases shows the commission is serious about enforcing data protection and privacy laws, said George Washington University Law School professor and former FTC chairman William Kovacic. “These are the largest fines that the FTC has gotten. For most general counsel that’s a significant consideration. What’s evident in just the Epic experience is the commission is making stronger and stronger demands for effective remedies and the price for violations is going up.” General counsel also will be bracing for final approval of new Securities and Exchange Commission cyberattack disclosure rules that would give public companies only four days to disclose a material incident. “Accuracy within the time frame is the risk. If you’ve suffered an incident, your focus is on your business and on identifying potentially compromised information,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance. “Four days will go by in a flash, so to have these reporting obligations going out to the public adds a wrinkle to how you respond to this quickly and correctly.” It can be difficult for general counsels to make sure they’re in the know about privacy vulnerabilities given the pace of business, Ruback said. “Too often the general counsel is looked at as a roadblock and brought in at the 11th hour,” he said. “But the companies that are going to thrive in this new hyper-regulated world we are moving toward in the U.S. are the ones that align their general counsel with the business early and often, so he or she is sitting with the product team and software development folks and providing that sage legal advice that ‘we need to take privacy and data protection into consideration with our products.’” Climate Change Companies also are bracing for final approval of new SEC rules requiring public companies to disclose climate-related risks that could affect their business operations. This is a touchy subject for tech companies, said Will Masters, an ESG and sustainable investments consultant at Arup, as the bulk of their emissions are graded as “scope 3,” which are not produced by the company itself but are derived from intangibles like purchased goods and services, business travel and employee commutes. “Tech companies’ scope 3 emissions are massive,” he said. “And there is no way they can actually prove their scope 3 offsets.” The shift to mandatory disclosures can pose new risks for companies that previously made them voluntarily, Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said, as shareholder suits seize on differences between old and new filings. “For companies already making climate disclosures this may impose a requirement to make disclosures in a new way, which can trigger disclosure lawsuits,” Longo said. “Even where you voluntary make disclosures on a topic, there’s a potential basis for liability. Whether the rule passes as proposed or not, the SEC and shareholder plaintiffs will focus on disclosures about climate risk as an area to try to bring more enforcement cases.” Matthew Gabin, chief legal officer at Arbol, a parametric insurance company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, agreed climate-related disclosures are receiving closer and closer scrutiny. “This area is getting serious attention from regulators and getting increasing attention every year—If companies are leaving out disclosures they should be making or being or overstating what they’re doing in their efforts to be climate conscious,” he said. Gabin said another climate challenge for companies is the risks from severe whether. While those risks might have been an abstraction 10 years ago, they’re starting to have tangible effects. When it gets too hot and Phoenix shuts down its airport, for instance, online retailers suffer from shipping delays and supply chain pressures mount across industries. “The first thing business should do is get a cross-functional team in place for assessing risks and responding to them. Lawyers are trained to think critically and draw distinctions. That mode of thinking lends itself toward climate risk response assessment and response,” he said. For tech companies, climate change can affect the reliability of data centers, as extreme weather events like wildfire, drought and severe storms threaten to overwhelm the electrical grid, causing outages and other disruptions to data transmission. “As weather events become more severe and frequent and chaotic, the companies that have resiliency built into their operations will have a competitive advantage,” Master said. “Investors and credit agencies want to see that you’ve identified the risks and how you’re mitigating them.” Antitrust The Federal Trade Commission will also be bringing more enforcement cases around suspected anti-competitive behavior, legal observers say, adding to the uncertainty around which M&A deals might pass regulatory muster. Kovacic said this will be a big year for antitrust enforcement as FTC chair Lina Khan looks to restrain tech giants from gobbling up innovative upstarts. One big case to watch is the FTC’s lawsuit challenging Meta’s $400 million acquisition of virtual reality startup Within. The FTC’s move to block the Within deal is Khan’s first major assault on big tech and is backed by nearly two dozen state attorneys general. “If they win it will be a very big deal and it will add great credibility to their enforcement program. They may look at other major tech companies and say, ‘We’re coming after you too,’” Kovacic said. Another ambitious case is the FTC’s lawsuit to block Microsoft from acquiring video-game maker Activision Blizzard, which could cause companies to pull back on mergers for the time being. Kovacic predicted that Biden’s FTC and Justice Department each will bring a monopolization case against big tech this year. “Given all the expectations they’ve set, it’s inevitable that both the DOJ or FTC will each bring a case alleging improper behavior by major tech companies,” he said. “2023 will be a momentous competition law year.”
article.html:
Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch




ANALYSIS

“2023 will be a momentous competition law year," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman.

January 11, 2023 at 04:08 PM

6 minute read

Risk and Compliance

Maria Dinzeo




What You Need to Know

  • The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come.
  • The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies.
  • The Biden administration stepped up antitrust enforcement in 2022 and likely will escalate those efforts this year.

General counsel are entering 2023 facing a raft of global uncertainty, regulatory risks, and legal battles with major implications for the digital economy.

Lawmakers, regulators and the courts have all ramped up pressure on the tech industry and show no sign of letting up this year. How companies deal with climate change, compete for business, and collect and protect user data will be top risk areas in 2023.

Data Privacy and Protection
