The consequences for neglecting to protect consumers’ private information are increasing in severity, and enforcement is intensifying. “General counsel can only expect enforcement activity to increase and accelerate in number,” said Todd Ruback, former chief privacy officer and general counsel for ad-blocker and privacy browser Ghostery. He said companies can expect to see more enforcement actions as states continue to adopt their own privacy laws. Companies can also anticipate a rise in class actions over wrongful data collection and third-party tracking. “It’s your obligation to know what third parties are on your website, and that’s where privacy is hard because businesses move fast and are always looking for ways to use data,” Ruback said. “There are headaches galore.” The Federal Trade Commission is also wading in on privacy. Its eye-watering $520 million penalty against Fortnite developer Epic Games for collecting data on children and duping them into making in-game purchases shows the commission is serious about enforcing data protection and privacy laws, said George Washington University Law School professor and former FTC chairman William Kovacic. “These are the largest fines that the FTC has gotten. For most general counsel that’s a significant consideration. What’s evident in just the Epic experience is the commission is making stronger and stronger demands for effective remedies and the price for violations is going up.”

General counsel also will be bracing for final approval of new Securities and Exchange Commission cyberattack disclosure rules that would give public companies only four days to disclose a material incident.

“Accuracy within the time frame is the risk. If you’ve suffered an incident, your focus is on your business and on identifying potentially compromised information,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance.

“Four days will go by in a flash, so to have these reporting obligations going out to the public adds a wrinkle to how you respond to this quickly and correctly.”

It can be difficult for general counsels to make sure they’re in the know about privacy vulnerabilities given the pace of business, Ruback said.

“Too often the general counsel is looked at as a roadblock and brought in at the 11th hour,” he said. “But the companies that are going to thrive in this new hyper-regulated world we are moving toward in the U.S. are the ones that align their general counsel with the business early and often, so he or she is sitting with the product team and software development folks and providing that sage legal advice that ‘we need to take privacy and data protection into consideration with our products.’”

Climate Change

Companies also are bracing for final approval of new SEC rules requiring public companies to disclose climate-related risks that could affect their business operations.

This is a touchy subject for tech companies, said Will Masters, an ESG and sustainable investments consultant at Arup, as the bulk of their emissions are graded as “scope 3,” which are not produced by the company itself but are derived from intangibles like purchased goods and services, business travel and employee commutes.

“Tech companies’ scope 3 emissions are massive,” he said. “And there is no way they can actually prove their scope 3 offsets.”

The shift to mandatory disclosures can pose new risks for companies that previously made them voluntarily, Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said, as shareholder suits seize on differences between old and new filings.

“For companies already making climate disclosures this may impose a requirement to make disclosures in a new way, which can trigger disclosure lawsuits,” Longo said. “Even where you voluntary make disclosures on a topic, there’s a potential basis for liability. Whether the rule passes as proposed or not, the SEC and shareholder plaintiffs will focus on disclosures about climate risk as an area to try to bring more enforcement cases.”

Matthew Gabin, chief legal officer at Arbol, a parametric insurance company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, agreed climate-related disclosures are receiving closer and closer scrutiny.

“This area is getting serious attention from regulators and getting increasing attention every year—If companies are leaving out disclosures they should be making or being or overstating what they’re doing in their efforts to be climate conscious,” he said.

Gabin said another climate challenge for companies is the risks from severe whether. While those risks might have been an abstraction 10 years ago, they’re starting to have tangible effects. When it gets too hot and Phoenix shuts down its airport, for instance, online retailers suffer from shipping delays and supply chain pressures mount across industries.

“The first thing business should do is get a cross-functional team in place for assessing risks and responding to them. Lawyers are trained to think critically and draw distinctions. That mode of thinking lends itself toward climate risk response assessment and response,” he said.

For tech companies, climate change can affect the reliability of data centers, as extreme weather events like wildfire, drought and severe storms threaten to overwhelm the electrical grid, causing outages and other disruptions to data transmission.

“As weather events become more severe and frequent and chaotic, the companies that have resiliency built into their operations will have a competitive advantage,” Master said. “Investors and credit agencies want to see that you’ve identified the risks and how you’re mitigating them.”

Antitrust

The Federal Trade Commission will also be bringing more enforcement cases around suspected anti-competitive behavior, legal observers say, adding to the uncertainty around which M&A deals might pass regulatory muster.

Kovacic said this will be a big year for antitrust enforcement as FTC chair Lina Khan looks to restrain tech giants from gobbling up innovative upstarts. One big case to watch is the FTC’s lawsuit challenging Meta’s $400 million acquisition of virtual reality startup Within. The FTC’s move to block the Within deal is Khan’s first major assault on big tech and is backed by nearly two dozen state attorneys general.

“If they win it will be a very big deal and it will add great credibility to their enforcement program. They may look at other major tech companies and say, ‘We’re coming after you too,’” Kovacic said.

Another ambitious case is the FTC’s lawsuit to block Microsoft from acquiring video-game maker Activision Blizzard, which could cause companies to pull back on mergers for the time being.

Kovacic predicted that Biden’s FTC and Justice Department each will bring a monopolization case against big tech this year.

“Given all the expectations they’ve set, it’s inevitable that both the DOJ or FTC will each bring a case alleging improper behavior by major tech companies,” he said. “2023 will be a momentous competition law year.”

article.title: Elon Musk Fires Twitter Deputy GC James Baker Over Possible Role in Squelching Hunter Biden Story
article.description: "In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Elon Musk tweeted. What You Need to Know Elon Musk fired Twitter Deputy General Counsel James…
article.text: "In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Elon Musk tweeted. What You Need to Know Elon Musk fired Twitter Deputy General Counsel James Baker.Musk said Baker might have helped squelch a 2020 article about President Joe Biden's son Hunter.The dismissal followed disclosure of internal Twitter communications by Substack newsletter publisher Matt Taibbi. December 06, 2022 Elon Musk fired another member of Twitter’s legal top brass, confirming in a tweet on Tuesday that Deputy General Counsel James Baker was “exited from the company” because of his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter. “In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Musk wrote. The brouhaha involves a 2020 New York Post article that raised questions about the propriety of Hunter Biden’s business dealings in Ukraine. Musk has been critical of Twitter’s decision to block the article on Twitter, saying last spring that it was “incredibly inappropriate.” The article was sourced from files discovered on Biden’s laptop after he left it at a computer repair shop and never retrieved it. The owner of the shop turned over the laptop to the FBI, but not before copying the hard drive and giving it to former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani’s lawyer, Robert Costello, according to the Post’s article. Giuliani later gave a copy to the Post. Musk’s tweet Tuesday came in response to Twitter posts by Matt Taibbi, who publishes the Substack newsletter TK News, that cited emails and other internal documents shedding light on the company’s decision to limit dissemination of certain information before the 2020 presidential election, including the New York Post report. Also on Twitter, Taibbi posted a column by George Washington University School of Law professor Jonathan Turley asserting that Baker had been part of an effort to smother coverage that raised questions about Hunter Biden’s conduct. The disclosures are being widely described by conservative media as the “Twitter files.” The trove of documents posted by Taibbi included email discussions among Twitter executives, including former Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde and former trust and safety chief Yoel Roth about banning the New York Post’s article from the platform under its “hacked materials” policy. “The policy basis is hacked materials—though, as discussed, this is an emerging situation where the facts remain unclear,” Roth wrote. “Can we truthfully claim that this is part of the policy?” former global communications head Brandon Borrman asked. Baker responded in the chain, “I support the conclusion that we need more facts to assess whether the materials were hacked. At this stage however, it is reasonable for us to assume that they may have been and that caution is warranted. “There are some facts that indicate that the materials may have been hacked, while there are others indicating that the computer was either abandoned and/or the owner consented to allow the repair shop to access it for at least some purposes. We simply need more information,” Baker added. Musk on Tuesday said he communicated with Baker about his possible role in censoring information but found his characterization of what occurred “unconvincing.” Baker, a former FBI general counsel and former CNN legal analyst, had been with Twitter as deputy general counsel and vice president of legal since 2020. He is the latest victim of Musk’s housecleaning at Twitter’s legal department since he completed the $44 billion purchase of the San Francisco-based social media giant on Oct. 27. Immediately on taking the helm, Musk dismissed Gadde and General Counsel Sean Edgett, as well as CEO Parag Agrawal and Chief Financial Officer Ned Segal. Taibbi also tweeted Tuesday afternoon that Baker had reviewed the first batch of “Twitter files” documents without Musk’s knowledge, a move Taibbi said contributed to the firing. “The news that Baker was reviewing the ‘Twitter files’ surprised everyone involved, to say the least. New Twitter chief Elon Musk acted quickly to ‘exit’ Baker Tuesday,” Taibbi said. Another Taibbi tweet suggested Baker was responsible for delaying their release. “On Friday, the first installment of the Twitter files was published here. We expected to publish more over the weekend. Many wondered why there was a delay,” Taibbi said. “We can now tell you part of the reason why. On Tuesday, Twitter Deputy General Counsel (and former FBI General Counsel) Jim Baker was fired. Among the reasons? Vetting the first batch of ‘Twitter Files’—without knowledge of new management,” Taibbi said. Baker did not respond to a request for comment from Law.com.
article.html:
"In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Elon Musk tweeted.

What You Need to Know

  • Elon Musk fired Twitter Deputy General Counsel James Baker.
  • Musk said Baker might have helped squelch a 2020 article about President Joe Biden's son Hunter.
  • The dismissal followed disclosure of internal Twitter communications by Substack newsletter publisher Matt Taibbi.

December 06, 2022

Elon Musk fired another member of Twitter’s legal top brass, confirming in a tweet on Tuesday that Deputy General Counsel James Baker was “exited from the company” because of his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter.

“In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Musk wrote.

The brouhaha involves a 2020 New York Post article that raised questions about the propriety of Hunter Biden’s business dealings in Ukraine. Musk has been critical of Twitter’s decision to block the article on Twitter, saying last spring that it was “incredibly inappropriate.”

The article was sourced from files discovered on Biden’s laptop after he left it at a computer repair shop and never retrieved it. The owner of the shop turned over the laptop to the FBI, but not before copying the hard drive and giving it to former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani’s lawyer, Robert Costello, according to the Post’s article. Giuliani later gave a copy to the Post.

Musk’s tweet Tuesday came in response to Twitter posts by Matt Taibbi, who publishes the Substack newsletter TK News, that cited emails and other internal documents shedding light on the company’s decision to limit dissemination of certain information before the 2020 presidential election, including the New York Post report.

Also on Twitter, Taibbi posted a column by George Washington University School of Law professor Jonathan Turley asserting that Baker had been part of an effort to smother coverage that raised questions about Hunter Biden’s conduct. The disclosures are being widely described by conservative media as the “Twitter files.”

The trove of documents posted by Taibbi included email discussions among Twitter executives, including former Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde and former trust and safety chief Yoel Roth about banning the New York Post’s article from the platform under its “hacked materials” policy.

“The policy basis is hacked materials—though, as discussed, this is an emerging situation where the facts remain unclear,” Roth wrote.

“Can we truthfully claim that this is part of the policy?” former global communications head Brandon Borrman asked.

Baker responded in the chain, “I support the conclusion that we need more facts to assess whether the materials were hacked. At this stage however, it is reasonable for us to assume that they may have been and that caution is warranted.

“There are some facts that indicate that the materials may have been hacked, while there are others indicating that the computer was either abandoned and/or the owner consented to allow the repair shop to access it for at least some purposes. We simply need more information,” Baker added.

Musk on Tuesday said he communicated with Baker about his possible role in censoring information but found his characterization of what occurred “unconvincing.”

Baker, a former FBI general counsel and former CNN legal analyst, had been with Twitter as deputy general counsel and vice president of legal since 2020.

He is the latest victim of Musk’s housecleaning at Twitter’s legal department since he completed the $44 billion purchase of the San Francisco-based social media giant on Oct. 27. Immediately on taking the helm, Musk dismissed Gadde and General Counsel Sean Edgett, as well as CEO Parag Agrawal and Chief Financial Officer Ned Segal.

Taibbi also tweeted Tuesday afternoon that Baker had reviewed the first batch of “Twitter files” documents without Musk’s knowledge, a move Taibbi said contributed to the firing.

“The news that Baker was reviewing the ‘Twitter files’ surprised everyone involved, to say the least. New Twitter chief Elon Musk acted quickly to ‘exit’ Baker Tuesday,” Taibbi said. Another Taibbi tweet suggested Baker was responsible for delaying their release.

“On Friday, the first installment of the Twitter files was published here. We expected to publish more over the weekend. Many wondered why there was a delay,” Taibbi said.

“We can now tell you part of the reason why. On Tuesday, Twitter Deputy General Counsel (and former FBI General Counsel) Jim Baker was fired. Among the reasons? Vetting the first batch of ‘Twitter Files’—without knowledge of new management,” Taibbi said.

Baker did not respond to a request for comment from Law.com.

article.title: AARP In-House Veteran Tapped as 3E's GC
article.description: What You Need to Know Audrey Jean was AARP's chief privacy officer and earlier led data compliance at Bloomberg.Her new employer helps clients with environmental, health and safety compliance. 3E, a data and software company that helps companies…
article.text: What You Need to Know Audrey Jean was AARP's chief privacy officer and earlier led data compliance at Bloomberg.Her new employer helps clients with environmental, health and safety compliance. 3E, a data and software company that helps companies handle hazardous materials and comply with environmental health and safety regulations, tapped in-house privacy veteran Audrey Jean as its general counsel. “Happy to share that I’m starting a new position as General Counsel at 3E. Very excited to join this team!” Jean said in announcing her new position Monday on LinkedIn. Jean has developed extensive expertise in data privacy compliance, coming off a nearly four-year stint at AARP. As senior vice president and chief privacy officer, she helped the Washington, D.C.-based organization protect the data of its 38 million members when it shifted its operations to the virtual realm during the pandemic. “What I appreciate so much about privacy is that you’re doing technical, challenging, and interesting work, but fundamentally, you’re helping protect people,” she told Modern Counsel in an interview earlier this year. She also led data compliance efforts at media giant Bloomberg, including ensuring that it complied with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Her background makes her well-suited to lead the legal department at 3E, which counts top pharmaceutical and global chemical manufacturers such as Bayer, Dow and SC Johnson among the clients it advises on workplace and product safety, risk management and supply chain regulatory compliance. The company did not respond to a request for comment on its new hire, but noted in a press release earlier this year that it plans to expand its environmental, health, safety, and sustainability footprint worldwide. Earlier this year, Verisk Analytics sold the Carlsbad, California-based company to investment firms New Mountain and Endicott for up to $950 million in cash.
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • Audrey Jean was AARP's chief privacy officer and earlier led data compliance at Bloomberg.
  • Her new employer helps clients with environmental, health and safety compliance.

3E, a data and software company that helps companies handle hazardous materials and comply with environmental health and safety regulations, tapped in-house privacy veteran Audrey Jean as its general counsel.

“Happy to share that I’m starting a new position as General Counsel at 3E. Very excited to join this team!” Jean said in announcing her new position Monday on LinkedIn.

Jean has developed extensive expertise in data privacy compliance, coming off a nearly four-year stint at AARP. As senior vice president and chief privacy officer, she helped the Washington, D.C.-based organization protect the data of its 38 million members when it shifted its operations to the virtual realm during the pandemic.

“What I appreciate so much about privacy is that you’re doing technical, challenging, and interesting work, but fundamentally, you’re helping protect people,” she told Modern Counsel in an interview earlier this year.

She also led data compliance efforts at media giant Bloomberg, including ensuring that it complied with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation.

Her background makes her well-suited to lead the legal department at 3E, which counts top pharmaceutical and global chemical manufacturers such as Bayer, Dow and SC Johnson among the clients it advises on workplace and product safety, risk management and supply chain regulatory compliance.

The company did not respond to a request for comment on its new hire, but noted in a press release earlier this year that it plans to expand its environmental, health, safety, and sustainability footprint worldwide.

Earlier this year, Verisk Analytics sold the Carlsbad, California-based company to investment firms New Mountain and Endicott for up to $950 million in cash.

article.title: AT&T to Pay $6.25M to Settle SEC Charges It Leaked Internal Data to Analysts
article.description: What You Need to Know It was the largest-ever SEC settlement of alleged Regional FD violations.While agreeing to the penalty, the telecom giant did not admit or deny the allegations.Under the deal, three executives also will pay $25,000 each. AT&T…
article.text: What You Need to Know It was the largest-ever SEC settlement of alleged Regional FD violations.While agreeing to the penalty, the telecom giant did not admit or deny the allegations.Under the deal, three executives also will pay $25,000 each. AT&T will pay $6.25 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges that three of its executives in 2016 leaked internal smartphone sales data to Wall Street analysts to avoid falling short of revenue forecasts. It was the largest-ever penalty a case alleging a violation of the agency’s fair-disclosure rule, which bars selective sharing of "material nonpublic information” to market professionals and shareholders. The SEC said AT&T sought to avoid investor disappointment—and a drop in stock price— by getting analysts to lower their revenue forecasts to a number the company could beat when it announced its results to the public on April 26, 2016. AT&T learned in March 2016 that its smartphone sales were lower than expected and that it would likely fail to meet analysts’ revenue estimates for that quarter, according to a complaint the regulator filed in New York federal court last year. According to the SEC, the agency says three investor-relations executives made private calls to analysts at roughly 20 firms, where they gave them details about smartphone sales and their impact on internal revenue metrics. The three executives—Christopher Womack, Michael Black and Kent Evans—also will pay $25,000 each. “The actions allegedly taken by AT&T executives to avoid falling short of analysts’ projections are precisely the type of conduct Regulation FD was designed to prevent,” Gurbir Grewal, director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement, said in a statement Monday. A company spokesperson said neither AT&T nor its executives admitted or denied any wrongdoing. “We are committed to following all applicable laws and pleased to have resolution with the SEC,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • It was the largest-ever SEC settlement of alleged Regional FD violations.
  • While agreeing to the penalty, the telecom giant did not admit or deny the allegations.
  • Under the deal, three executives also will pay $25,000 each.

AT&T will pay $6.25 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges that three of its executives in 2016 leaked internal smartphone sales data to Wall Street analysts to avoid falling short of revenue forecasts.

It was the largest-ever penalty a case alleging a violation of the agency’s fair-disclosure rule, which bars selective sharing of "material nonpublic information” to market professionals and shareholders.

The SEC said AT&T sought to avoid investor disappointment—and a drop in stock price— by getting analysts to lower their revenue forecasts to a number the company could beat when it announced its results to the public on April 26, 2016.

AT&T learned in March 2016 that its smartphone sales were lower than expected and that it would likely fail to meet analysts’ revenue estimates for that quarter, according to a complaint the regulator filed in New York federal court last year.

According to the SEC, the agency says three investor-relations executives made private calls to analysts at roughly 20 firms, where they gave them details about smartphone sales and their impact on internal revenue metrics.

The three executives—Christopher Womack, Michael Black and Kent Evans—also will pay $25,000 each.

“The actions allegedly taken by AT&T executives to avoid falling short of analysts’ projections are precisely the type of conduct Regulation FD was designed to prevent,” Gurbir Grewal, director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement, said in a statement Monday.

A company spokesperson said neither AT&T nor its executives admitted or denied any wrongdoing. “We are committed to following all applicable laws and pleased to have resolution with the SEC,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.”

article.title: Ratings Giant Pays $2.5 Million to Settle SEC Conflict-of-Interest Charges
article.description: The regulator alleges that S&P Global commercial employees injected sales and marketing considerations into the agency's evaluation of a 2017 mortgage-backed securities transaction. Credit ratings giant S&P Global on Monday agreed to pay the U.S.…
article.text: The regulator alleges that S&P Global commercial employees injected sales and marketing considerations into the agency's evaluation of a 2017 mortgage-backed securities transaction. Credit ratings giant S&P Global on Monday agreed to pay the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission $2.5 million to settle charges that it violated the regulator’s rules against conflicts of interest. The SEC found that over five days in August 2017, S&P commercial employees, who are responsible for maintaining relationships with the companies that hire S&P to rate their debt, tried several times to influence colleagues who were determining the rating for a company’s jumbo residential mortgage-backed securities. The regulator says that while correspondence went through S&P’s compliance department, some emails commercial employees sent to the S&P analytical team contained statements conveying sales and marketing considerations. In a statement, the SEC said it found that “as a result of the content, urgent nature, high volume, and compressed timing of the communications, the S&P commercial employees became participants in the rating process during a time when they were influenced by sales and marketing considerations.” SEC rules prohibit ratings agencies from allowing sales and marketing considerations to influence credit ratings. New York-based S&P self-reported its employees’ conduct to the SEC, cooperated with the regulator’s investigation, and took steps to bolster its conflicts-of-interest policies. S&P did not admit or deny the charges but agreed to the entry of a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and other compliance measures on top of the $2.5 million penalty. While it declined to comment specifically on the settlement, S&P said in a statement that it “takes compliance with regulatory obligations very seriously and is committed to the integrity of its ratings process and high-quality independent credit ratings,” and that it is “pleased to have concluded this matter.” This is the SEC’s second enforcement action against a credit rating agency this year. In June, it alleged that Egan-Jones Rating Co. and its CEO, Sean Egan, were influenced by a client’s marketing activities while determining its credit rating, creating a conflict of interest. The firm settled the charges for $1.7 million, without an admission of any wrongdoing, and Egan agreed to pay $300,000.
article.html:
The regulator alleges that S&P Global commercial employees injected sales and marketing considerations into the agency's evaluation of a 2017 mortgage-backed securities transaction.


Credit ratings giant S&P Global on Monday agreed to pay the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission $2.5 million to settle charges that it violated the regulator’s rules against conflicts of interest.

The SEC found that over five days in August 2017, S&P commercial employees, who are responsible for maintaining relationships with the companies that hire S&P to rate their debt, tried several times to influence colleagues who were determining the rating for a company’s jumbo residential mortgage-backed securities.

The regulator says that while correspondence went through S&P’s compliance department, some emails commercial employees sent to the S&P analytical team contained statements conveying sales and marketing considerations.

In a statement, the SEC said it found that “as a result of the content, urgent nature, high volume, and compressed timing of the communications, the S&P commercial employees became participants in the rating process during a time when they were influenced by sales and marketing considerations.”

SEC rules prohibit ratings agencies from allowing sales and marketing considerations to influence credit ratings.

New York-based S&P self-reported its employees’ conduct to the SEC, cooperated with the regulator’s investigation, and took steps to bolster its conflicts-of-interest policies.

S&P did not admit or deny the charges but agreed to the entry of a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and other compliance measures on top of the $2.5 million penalty.

While it declined to comment specifically on the settlement, S&P said in a statement that it “takes compliance with regulatory obligations very seriously and is committed to the integrity of its ratings process and high-quality independent credit ratings,” and that it is “pleased to have concluded this matter.”

This is the SEC’s second enforcement action against a credit rating agency this year. In June, it alleged that Egan-Jones Rating Co. and its CEO, Sean Egan, were influenced by a client’s marketing activities while determining its credit rating, creating a conflict of interest.

The firm settled the charges for $1.7 million, without an admission of any wrongdoing, and Egan agreed to pay $300,000.

article.title: 'There Are Many, Many Pitfalls': How In-House Counsel Can Help Navigate Layoff Minefield
article.description: What You Need to Know In-house legal teams teams need to be involved from the get-go.In addition to mitigating risk, they need to ensure affected workers are treated humanely.That includes ensuring company communications are open and honest, not BS.…
article.text: What You Need to Know In-house legal teams teams need to be involved from the get-go.In addition to mitigating risk, they need to ensure affected workers are treated humanely.That includes ensuring company communications are open and honest, not BS. The tidal wave of layoffs sweeping through the tech industry is putting legal departments to the test, as in-house counsel seek to mitigate risk and ensure their companies carry out the cuts as humanely as possible. Following years of feverish hiring, tech companies are retrenching. Just in November, 196 companies cut more than 51,000 tech workers, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job losses in the industry. Foster Sayers, general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, said legal chiefs have an important role to play in helping companies implement layoffs thoughtfully while avoiding running afoul of labor laws. Twitter’s recent mass job cuts provide a glaring example of what to avoid. The company is facing at least three class actions alleging the social media giant violated the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, which requires companies to provide at least 60 days’ notice before cutting at least 50 full-time employees at a single location. Twitter also is facing allegations that it is shorting employees on severance. On top of that, it has faced widespread criticism for locking some employees out of their email before telling them they’d lost their jobs. Sayers said in-house counsel should try to make the best of a bad situation for laid-off employees by ensuring they tailor separation agreements to ensure employees don’t feel cheated. He noted that a friend who was laid off from Twitter revoked his separation agreement because it did not account for the equity that had been part of his compensation. “He felt that he was very clearly promised one outcome, but the severance package offered was not what was promised,” Sayers said. “I’m sure it was drafted from some boilerplate language that outside counsel had. In-house needs to be ready to rise to the occasion and rapidly develop some competency around separation agreements. You have to take the time to own your separation agreement and not just rely on outside counsel.” Sayers said in-house counsel can head off cybersecurity issues by ensuring that separation agreements obligate employees to return their equipment, as well as their logins and credentials. “People just don’t do this, and it’s a huge oversight. Cybersecurity is such a going concern and companies can’t afford to be neglectful,” he said. He added: “Make sure you have a seat at the table, so when your chief technology officer is talking to your head of DevOps and other parts of the business, you can say, ‘Look, this is what we need to be prepared to manage as we off-board employees.’ If you’re not actually at the table, you’re not going to be as effective in getting out in front of these issues.” Des Lafleur, a business attorney and lecturer at the UC Berkeley School of Law who consults with companies on minimizing risk, said cybersecurity is something companies should be thinking about well before employees depart the company. “If you’re worrying about it once the person is departing, you haven’t done enough in the beginning,” she said. While in-house attorneys are adept at managing legal risk, experts say they also should be equipped to handle the emotional weight of a mass layoff. “A corporate layoff is one of those most complicated and challenging activities an executive would ever undertake, and there’s no training at Harvard Business School to do this,” said Jason Winmill, managing partner of the legal department consulting firm Argopoint. “There are many many pitfalls. If there is going to be layoffs, the legal department needs to be involved early, and often, well before any public announcements.” Lafleur said companies should be honest with employees about the reasoning behind layoffs and not brush off their concerns with vague and noncommittal statements. “What a company needs to do is be respectful of people—setting expectations and being clear and transparent,” she said. “Don’t just blame the economy or the market, be specific because poorly handled layoffs can kill a company, even worse than just letting it bleed cash.” Winmill echoed that point. “A corporation is a complicated, interlaced web of relationships, and talking to individuals via a layoff is very disruptive to that, not just to the people impacted but to the entire web,” he said. “While in-house counsel should be advising on legal compliance, that’s only one dimension of the value they can bring. In-house lawyers are often some of the most skilled written communicators in a company. Any corporate communications on the subject of layoffs need to be open and honest, and provide a clear, rational explanation for the layoffs. In-house counsel are trained skeptics and are good reviewers for credibility and for tone.” Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said company leaders should remember that there are human beings behind the numbers. “Anytime you’re having any sort of reduction in force, it’s absolutely imperative for HR and the business to be consulting with legal counsel on how to ensure that a layoff or a closure is done in compliance with the applicable laws,” he said. “That’s just the floor of how to handle this stuff. Then there is a broader question of humanity; understanding these re actual human beings you’re dealing with. You need to make sure you’re treating people with dignity and with respect. They’re not just cogs in a wheel.”
article.html:
What You Need to Know

  • In-house legal teams teams need to be involved from the get-go.
  • In addition to mitigating risk, they need to ensure affected workers are treated humanely.
  • That includes ensuring company communications are open and honest, not BS.

The tidal wave of layoffs sweeping through the tech industry is putting legal departments to the test, as in-house counsel seek to mitigate risk and ensure their companies carry out the cuts as humanely as possible.

Following years of feverish hiring, tech companies are retrenching. Just in November, 196 companies cut more than 51,000 tech workers, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job losses in the industry.

Foster Sayers, general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, said legal chiefs have an important role to play in helping companies implement layoffs thoughtfully while avoiding running afoul of labor laws.

Twitter’s recent mass job cuts provide a glaring example of what to avoid. The company is facing at least three class actions alleging the social media giant violated the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, which requires companies to provide at least 60 days’ notice before cutting at least 50 full-time employees at a single location.

Twitter also is facing allegations that it is shorting employees on severance. On top of that, it has faced widespread criticism for locking some employees out of their email  before telling them they’d lost their jobs.

Sayers said in-house counsel should try to make the best of a bad situation for laid-off employees by ensuring they tailor separation agreements to ensure employees don’t feel cheated. He noted that a friend who was laid off from Twitter revoked his separation agreement because it did not account for the equity that had been part of his compensation.

“He felt that he was very clearly promised one outcome, but the severance package offered was not what was promised,” Sayers said. “I’m sure it was drafted from some boilerplate language that outside counsel had. In-house needs to be ready to rise to the occasion and rapidly develop some competency around separation agreements. You have to take the time to own your separation agreement and not just rely on outside counsel.”

Sayers said in-house counsel can head off cybersecurity issues by ensuring that separation agreements obligate employees to return their equipment, as well as their logins and credentials.

“People just don’t do this, and it’s a huge oversight. Cybersecurity is such a going concern and companies can’t afford to be neglectful,” he said.

He added: “Make sure you have a seat at the table, so when your chief technology officer is talking to your head of DevOps and other parts of the business, you can say, ‘Look, this is what we need to be prepared to manage as we off-board employees.’ If you’re not actually at the table, you’re not going to be as effective in getting out in front of these issues.”

Des Lafleur, a business attorney and lecturer at the UC Berkeley School of Law who consults with companies on minimizing risk, said cybersecurity is something companies should be thinking about well before employees depart the company.

“If you’re worrying about it once the person is departing, you haven’t done enough in the beginning,” she said.

While in-house attorneys are adept at managing legal risk, experts say they also should be equipped to handle the emotional weight of a mass layoff.

“A corporate layoff is one of those most complicated and challenging activities an executive would ever undertake, and there’s no training at Harvard Business School to do this,” said Jason Winmill, managing partner of the legal department consulting firm Argopoint.

“There are many many pitfalls. If there is going to be layoffs, the legal department needs to be involved early, and often, well before any public announcements.”

Lafleur said companies should be honest with employees about the reasoning behind layoffs and not brush off their concerns with vague and noncommittal statements.

“What a company needs to do is be respectful of people—setting expectations and being clear and transparent,” she said. “Don’t just blame the economy or the market, be specific because poorly handled layoffs can kill a company, even worse than just letting it bleed cash.”

Winmill echoed that point.

“A corporation is a complicated, interlaced web of relationships, and talking to individuals via a layoff is very disruptive to that, not just to the people impacted but to the entire web,” he said.

“While in-house counsel should be advising on legal compliance, that’s only one dimension of the value they can bring. In-house lawyers are often some of the most skilled written communicators in a company. Any corporate communications on the subject of layoffs need to be open and honest, and provide a clear, rational explanation for the layoffs. In-house counsel are trained skeptics and are good reviewers for credibility and for tone.”

Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said company leaders should remember that there are human beings behind the numbers.

“Anytime you’re having any sort of reduction in force, it’s absolutely imperative for HR and the business to be consulting with legal counsel on how to ensure that a layoff or a closure is done in compliance with the applicable laws,” he said.

“That’s just the floor of how to handle this stuff. Then there is a broader question of humanity; understanding these re actual human beings you’re dealing with. You need to make sure you’re treating people with dignity and with respect. They’re not just cogs in a wheel.”

article.title: Senior Attorney at Swiss Re Takes Legal Reins of Climate-Risk Startup
article.description: Matthew Gabin says he wants to help Arbol "reinvent the way the world manages climate risk." November 22, 2022 at 12:16 PM 2 minute read News Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Arbol has hired Matthew Gabin as chief legal officer and deputy chief…
article.text: Matthew Gabin says he wants to help Arbol "reinvent the way the world manages climate risk." November 22, 2022 at 12:16 PM 2 minute read News Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Arbol has hired Matthew Gabin as chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer.Gabin has extensive experience in insurance products that help companies manage climate risks.Gabin joins Arbol from Swiss Re, where he was a divisional general counsel. Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer. Gabin is a veteran in-house lawyer with expertise in insurance-linked securities, where investors speculate on events like hurricanes or earthquakes, and contracts involving weather risk transfer, where policyholders are compensated for losses stemming from extreme weather. He also has experience in parametric insurance and reinsurance, which offers policyholders a set amount of compensation for trigger events like environmental disasters. At Zurich-based reinsurance group Swiss Re, Gabin was general counsel for its weather risk and commodity trading businesses. He also advised insurers, investment firms and corporates at global white shoe law firm Mayer Brown. Prior to that, he spent nearly 10 years at Allianz Risk Transfer, providing legal and operational advice on alternative risk transfer, a non-traditional insurance product that allows companies to purchase coverage and transfer risk without using commercial insurance. “We are excited to welcome a colleague who has such relevant experience advising some of the world’s leading reinsurers on parametric risk transfer, weather risk and other areas so close to our core business,” Arbol founder and CEO Sid Jha said in a statement. Jha said Gabin’s specialized experience will be critical to the New York City-based company as it broadens its reach into new markets and verticals. In addition to building out Arbol’s legal and compliance teams, Gabin will help oversee the company’s operations and global expansion. According to its website, Arbol uses climate data, blockchain and an AI-powered pricing platform to help its clients “achieve financial climate resilience” through customized insurance to mitigate climate risk. It boasts a rapid settlements and quick payouts based on predetermined data triggers. “Parametric insurance is an indispensable tool for boosting resilience and closing the protection gap, and I’m thrilled to join a team that is driving innovation in the space,” Gabin said in a statement. “Arbol has achieved a lot in a short period of time and is positioning itself as a leader in parametric insurance and climate risk solutions for businesses globally. I look forward to putting my skills to work to help Arbol reinvent the way the world manages climate risk.”
article.html:
Matthew Gabin says he wants to help Arbol "reinvent the way the world manages climate risk."

November 22, 2022 at 12:16 PM

2 minute read

News

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • Arbol has hired Matthew Gabin as chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer.
  • Gabin has extensive experience in insurance products that help companies manage climate risks.
  • Gabin joins Arbol from Swiss Re, where he was a divisional general counsel.

Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer.

Gabin is a veteran in-house lawyer with expertise in insurance-linked securities, where investors speculate on events like hurricanes or earthquakes, and contracts involving weather risk transfer, where policyholders are compensated for losses stemming from extreme weather.

He also has experience in parametric insurance and reinsurance, which offers policyholders a set amount of compensation for trigger events like environmental disasters.

At Zurich-based reinsurance group Swiss Re, Gabin was general counsel for its weather risk and commodity trading businesses. He also advised insurers, investment firms and corporates at global white shoe law firm Mayer Brown.

Prior to that, he spent nearly 10 years at Allianz Risk Transfer, providing legal and operational advice on alternative risk transfer, a non-traditional insurance product that allows companies to purchase coverage and transfer risk without using commercial insurance.

“We are excited to welcome a colleague who has such relevant experience advising some of the world’s leading reinsurers on parametric risk transfer, weather risk and other areas so close to our core business,” Arbol founder and CEO Sid Jha said in a statement.

Jha said Gabin’s specialized experience will be critical to the New York City-based company as it broadens its reach into new markets and verticals. In addition to building out Arbol’s legal and compliance teams, Gabin will help oversee the company’s operations and global expansion.

According to its website, Arbol uses climate data, blockchain and an AI-powered pricing platform to help its clients “achieve financial climate resilience” through customized insurance to mitigate climate risk. It boasts a rapid settlements and quick payouts based on predetermined data triggers.

“Parametric insurance is an indispensable tool for boosting resilience and closing the protection gap, and I’m thrilled to join a team that is driving innovation in the space,” Gabin said in a statement.

“Arbol has achieved a lot in a short period of time and is positioning itself as a leader in parametric insurance and climate risk solutions for businesses globally. I look forward to putting my skills to work to help Arbol reinvent the way the world manages climate risk.”

article.title: 'Surprised, Angry, Dismayed': Legal Departments Vow to Fight Law Firms' Rate-Hike Plans
article.description: ANALYSIS “This feels more like law firms throwing spaghetti up against a wall and seeing what sticks," said Jason Winmill, managing partner of Argopoint. November 28, 2022 at 05:29 AM 7 minute read Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Law firms want to…
article.text: ANALYSIS “This feels more like law firms throwing spaghetti up against a wall and seeing what sticks," said Jason Winmill, managing partner of Argopoint. November 28, 2022 at 05:29 AM 7 minute read Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Law firms want to raise rates an average of 7% to 8% in 2023, according to the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group.A consultant said strategies differ dramatically from firm to firm, from no increase to a 45% hike.Legal departments say they're in a financial squeeze and can't absorb big increases. The in-house legal community is expressing outrage that law firms will be pressing for aggressive rate hikes in 2023, even though they know that legal departments are under extraordinary pressure as the economic outlook sours. “Law firms are claiming to raise rates due to inflation, but anyone who’s ever taken an economics class knows that the real reason they’re raising rates is because they think no one will notice under the guise of inflation,” said Stephanie Corey, a former legal-ops leader at HP and VMware who now leads the consulting firm UpLevel Ops. “That being said, legal departments who are budget-conscious—which are the majority, I believe—can’t shoulder this increase. Many of our clients are being asked to cut anywhere from 5-20% of their budgets, so the math just doesn’t work out.” Jason Winmill, managing partner of the legal department consulting firm Argopoint, said leading law firms are unleashing 2023 rate plans that are all over the map, ranging from no increase to hikes of 45%. “This feels more like law firms throwing spaghetti up against a wall and seeing what sticks. This is a corporate legal roller derby, and I’m predicting there’s going to be a lot of crashes, wipeouts and disabled vehicles on the other side of this,” he said. Winmill added: “How will in-house counsel respond? I have an idea: It’s not going to be good. In-house counsel is feeling surprised, angry, dismayed and perplexed as to how they’re going to make this work. The million-dollar question is: Can in-house counsel bring law firms to their senses, but not their knees. Outside counsel’s opening salvo isn’t going to make this easy.” Law.com reported this month that law firm leaders recently told the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group they plan to rate rates in 2023 an average of 7% to 8% before discounting—an effort aimed at overcoming inflation and other challenges, including the slowdown in M&A work. Average billing rates so far this year have climbed 5.9%, according to the group’s nine-month survey report published last week. “We’re seeing higher planned rate increases at this point than we’ve ever seen, and we’ve been tracking this for 15 years,” Owen Burman, senior consultant for the group, said in an interview. ‘Clients Will Vote With Their Feet’ Legal departments have a reputation for grousing about law firm rate hikes but then usually paying them. But legal department leaders and in-house consultants say this year marks a turning point. In an interview with Law.com this fall, Michael Wu, the chief legal officer of Bath & Body Works, said U.S. law firms are paying first-year associates at levels that are indefensible—and doing so on the backs of their law firm clients. “I think I share the view of many general counsel that we don’t want to pay for the training that these junior lawyers are receiving, particularly a fresh graduate making over $200,000 a year. We don’t believe those types of salaries and billable rates are sustainable,” he said. Wu added: “To continue to increase [associate] salaries and then try to pass it on, that’s just not defensible, given all the challenges businesses are facing in this environment.” Many legal chiefs and consultants plan to combat rising outside counsel costs by bringing more work in-house or shifting more work to alternative legal service providers, which advocates say can handle some matters better and more cheaply than law firms. But legal chiefs and consultants say legal departments will be pushing back against the rate increases head-on by playing law firms against each other. “I think in-house legal teams have more leverage than they realize,” said Stephen Mar, general counsel of software startup Odeko, noting that the vast majority of legal work can be done by a variety of firms. “Cost conversations are tough, but they’re also opportunities for forward-thinking firms to deepen relationships with their clients,” he said. “For example, there’s one law firm partner who has been extremely flexible with write-offs, alternative-fee arrangements and other billing-related issues. Because of that history of flexibility (and good work!), I often end up selecting them for projects over peer firms.” Legal departments should get out in front of rate negotiations by calculating the average increase for each of their law firms in recent years and identifying firms with outside-the-norm hikes, said Frederick Paulmann, founder of The Counsel Management Group, which uses analytics to help legal departments manage their budgets. Armed with those comparisons, a legal department can go to a client and say, “We appreciate the work you do, but you’re seeking to raise rates twice as steeply as the other four peer firms we work with. Help us understand what’s behind that, and how can we sharpen the pencil and make this more sustainable?” Another area for legal departments to scrutinize is year-end bonuses for associates and whether they are in step with current economic circumstances, Paulmann said. “Is it sound financial management, or a frothy arms race on the law firm side? If firms are assuming they can afford these bonuses by simply passing on these costs to clients, that is often not a sound assumption.” For certain highly specialized areas where few attorneys have the needed expertise, law firms genuinely do have the upper hand on rates, Paulmann said. “The real challenge for law firms comes when they think they are highly irreplaceable, but in fact they are not. And clients will vote with their feet when necessary.” “It’s Hard to Say to a Friend, ‘We’re Going to Fire You’” The bad news for legal departments is that to rein in outside counsel rate increases they will need to demonstrate far better negotiating skills with their outside law firms than they have in the past. A report from Wolters Kluwer issued in October found that many many legal departments do a pitiful job negotiating outside counsel rates—with companies in the financial and banking industries being the big exception. In fact, report author Nathan Cemenska said many legal departments “do not even attempt to exercise any central control, but decentralize rate negotiations out to in-house counsel, many of whom lack the skills, gumption, desire and/or temperament to take an arm’s-length tone in rate negotiations—with results that are all too predictable.” You’d think legal department leaders, as attorneys, would be savvy negotiators, but personal relationships often get in the way, said Ken Callander, a former head of legal ops at Uber who’s now the managing principal of Value Strategies, which helps legal departments improve their outside counsel relationships. “If you’ve worked with a partner for a long time, and you’ve gotten to really know them well, you’ve probably met socially and you’ve gotten to be good friends,” he said. “It’s hard to say to a friend, ‘We’re going to fire you.’” But some legal departments will face mandates from their CEOs that they cannot accept rate increases. In a year like 2021, when deal work was booming and law firms were flooded with work, law firms could afford to hold their ground, even if it meant losing a client that paid it millions of dollars a year, Callander said. “Just a year’s time has really turned things around,” he said. “Last year, the firms had leverage. This year, it’s the other way around.”
article.html:
ANALYSIS

“This feels more like law firms throwing spaghetti up against a wall and seeing what sticks," said Jason Winmill, managing partner of Argopoint.

November 28, 2022 at 05:29 AM

7 minute read

Maria Dinzeo

What You Need to Know

  • Law firms want to raise rates an average of 7% to 8% in 2023, according to the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group.
  • A consultant said strategies differ dramatically from firm to firm, from no increase to a 45% hike.
  • Legal departments say they're in a financial squeeze and can't absorb big increases.

The in-house legal community is expressing outrage that law firms will be pressing for aggressive rate hikes in 2023, even though they know that legal departments are under extraordinary pressure as the economic outlook sours. “Law firms are claiming to raise rates due to inflation, but anyone who’s ever taken an economics class knows that the real reason they’re raising rates is because they think no one will notice under the guise of inflation,” said Stephanie Corey, a former legal-ops leader at HP and VMware who now leads the consulting firm UpLevel Ops. “That being said, legal departments who are budget-conscious—which are the majority, I believe—can’t shoulder this increase. Many of our clients are being asked to cut anywhere from 5-20% of their budgets, so the math just doesn’t work out.” Jason Winmill, managing partner of the legal department consulting firm Argopoint, said leading law firms are unleashing 2023 rate plans that are all over the map, ranging from no increase to hikes of 45%. “This feels more like law firms throwing spaghetti up against a wall and seeing what sticks. This is a corporate legal roller derby, and I’m predicting there’s going to be a lot of crashes, wipeouts and disabled vehicles on the other side of this,” he said. Winmill added: “How will in-house counsel respond? I have an idea: It’s not going to be good. In-house counsel is feeling surprised, angry, dismayed and perplexed as to how they’re going to make this work. The million-dollar question is: Can in-house counsel bring law firms to their senses, but not their knees. Outside counsel’s opening salvo isn’t going to make this easy.” Law.com reported this month that law firm leaders recently told the Wells Fargo Legal Specialty Group they plan to rate rates in 2023 an average of 7% to 8% before discounting—an effort aimed at overcoming inflation and other challenges, including the slowdown in M&A work. Average billing rates so far this year have climbed 5.9%, according to the group’s nine-month survey report published last week.

“We’re seeing higher planned rate increases at this point than we’ve ever seen, and we’ve been tracking this for 15 years,” Owen Burman, senior consultant for the group, said in an interview.

‘Clients Will Vote With Their Feet’

Legal departments have a reputation for grousing about law firm rate hikes but then usually paying them. But legal department leaders and in-house consultants say this year marks a turning point.

In an interview with Law.com this fall, Michael Wu, the chief legal officer of Bath & Body Works, said U.S. law firms are paying first-year associates at levels that are indefensible—and doing so on the backs of their law firm clients.

“I think I share the view of many general counsel that we don’t want to pay for the training that these junior lawyers are receiving, particularly a fresh graduate making over $200,000 a year. We don’t believe those types of salaries and billable rates are sustainable,” he said.

Wu added: “To continue to increase [associate] salaries and then try to pass it on, that’s just not defensible, given all the challenges businesses are facing in this environment.”

Many legal chiefs and consultants plan to combat rising outside counsel costs by bringing more work in-house or shifting more work to alternative legal service providers, which advocates say can handle some matters better and more cheaply than law firms.

But legal chiefs and consultants say legal departments will be pushing back against the rate increases head-on by playing law firms against each other.

“I think in-house legal teams have more leverage than they realize,” said Stephen Mar, general counsel of software startup Odeko, noting that the vast majority of legal work can be done by a variety of firms.

“Cost conversations are tough, but they’re also opportunities for forward-thinking firms to deepen relationships with their clients,” he said.

“For example, there’s one law firm partner who has been extremely flexible with write-offs, alternative-fee arrangements and other billing-related issues. Because of that history of flexibility (and good work!), I often end up selecting them for projects over peer firms.”

Legal departments should get out in front of rate negotiations by calculating the average increase for each of their law firms in recent years and identifying firms with outside-the-norm hikes, said Frederick Paulmann, founder of The Counsel Management Group, which uses analytics to help legal departments manage their budgets.

Armed with those comparisons, a legal department can go to a client and say, “We appreciate the work you do, but you’re seeking to raise rates twice as steeply as the other four peer firms we work with. Help us understand what’s behind that, and how can we sharpen the pencil and make this more sustainable?”

Another area for legal departments to scrutinize is year-end bonuses for associates and whether they are in step with current economic circumstances, Paulmann said.

“Is it sound financial management, or a frothy arms race on the law firm side? If firms are assuming they can afford these bonuses by simply passing on these costs to clients, that is often not a sound assumption.”

For certain highly specialized areas where few attorneys have the needed expertise, law firms genuinely do have the upper hand on rates, Paulmann said.

“The real challenge for law firms comes when they think they are highly irreplaceable, but in fact they are not. And clients will vote with their feet when necessary.”

“It’s Hard to Say to a Friend, ‘We’re Going to Fire You’”

The bad news for legal departments is that to rein in outside counsel rate increases they will need to demonstrate far better negotiating skills with their outside law firms than they have in the past.

A report from Wolters Kluwer issued in October found that many many legal departments do a pitiful job negotiating outside counsel rates—with companies in the financial and banking industries being the big exception.

In fact, report author Nathan Cemenska said many legal departments “do not even attempt to exercise any central control, but decentralize rate negotiations out to in-house counsel, many of whom lack the skills, gumption, desire and/or temperament to take an arm’s-length tone in rate negotiations—with results that are all too predictable.”

You’d think legal department leaders, as attorneys, would be savvy negotiators, but personal relationships often get in the way, said Ken Callander, a former head of legal ops at Uber who’s now the managing principal of Value Strategies, which helps legal departments improve their outside counsel relationships.

“If you’ve worked with a partner for a long time, and you’ve gotten to really know them well, you’ve probably met socially and you’ve gotten to be good friends,” he said. “It’s hard to say to a friend, ‘We’re going to fire you.’”

But some legal departments will face mandates from their CEOs that they cannot accept rate increases. In a year like 2021, when deal work was booming and law firms were flooded with work, law firms could afford to hold their ground, even if it meant losing a client that paid it millions of dollars a year, Callander said.

“Just a year’s time has really turned things around,” he said. “Last year, the firms had leverage. This year, it’s the other way around.”

article.title: Paul Pelosi hospitalized after violent assault by home intruder
article.description: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Paul Pelosi, real estate investor and husband of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, was violently assaulted in his San Francisco home in what appeared to be a targeted home invasion early Friday morning. The attack happened in the…
article.text: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Paul Pelosi, real estate investor and husband of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, was violently assaulted in his San Francisco home in what appeared to be a targeted home invasion early Friday morning. The attack happened in the Pelosi’s home on Broadway Street in the tony neighborhood of Pacific Heights. At a press conference Friday, San Francisco Police Chief Bill Scott identified the assailant as 42-year-old David Depape. He declined to answer questions about how Depape was able to get into the home. Scott said the attack happened at roughly 2:30 a.m. Friday. When officers arrived at the home, they found Depape and Mr. Pelosi in the midst of a struggle. "Our officers observed and Mr. Pelosi both holding a hammer. The suspect pulled the hammer away from Mr. Pelosi and violently assaulted him with it. Our officers immediately tackled the suspect, disarmed him, took him into custody, requested emergency backup and rendered medical aid." The Associated Press has reported that Pelosi, 82, suffered blunt force trauma to his head and body. According to the AP, Depape shouted “Where is Nancy, where is Nancy?” during the attack. Scott said both the suspect and Pelosi were taken to the hospital for treatment. "The motive for this attack is still being determined," he said, adding that Depape will be booked on charges of attempted homicide, assault with deadly weapon, elder abuse, burglary and "several other additional felonies." "This is an active investigation currently being led by the SFPD's special investigation's division," Scott said. The Capitol Police said in a statement that Speaker Pelosi was in Washington with her protective detail at the time of the break-in. While “the motivation for the attack is still under investigation,” Capitol Police said it is assisting the FBI and the San Francisco Police Department with its investigation. In an evening press conference Friday, Scott said the attack was not intentional but could not give more information. He also clarified that a neighbor called 911, not Paul Pelosi as previously reported. Scott said the department could offer no new information, and referred inquiries about Pelosi's condition to a statement released by Pelosi's spokesperson Drew Hammill, which offered scant details. “Early this morning, an assailant broke into the Pelosi residence in San Francisco and violently assaulted Mr. Pelosi. The assailant is in custody and the motivation for the attack is under investigation. SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Paul Pelosi, real estate investor and husband of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, was violently assaulted in his San Francisco home in what appeared to be a targeted home invasion early Friday morning.

The attack happened in the Pelosi’s home on Broadway Street in the tony neighborhood of Pacific Heights.

At a press conference Friday, San Francisco Police Chief Bill Scott identified the assailant as 42-year-old David Depape. He declined to answer questions about how Depape was able to get into the home.

Scott said the attack happened at roughly 2:30 a.m. Friday. When officers arrived at the home, they found Depape and Mr. Pelosi in the midst of a struggle. "Our officers observed and Mr. Pelosi both holding a hammer. The suspect pulled the hammer away from Mr. Pelosi and violently assaulted him with it. Our officers immediately tackled the suspect, disarmed him, took him into custody, requested emergency backup and rendered medical aid."

The Associated Press has reported that Pelosi, 82, suffered blunt force trauma to his head and body. According to the AP, Depape shouted “Where is Nancy, where is Nancy?” during the attack.

Scott said both the suspect and Pelosi were taken to the hospital for treatment. "The motive for this attack is still being determined," he said, adding that Depape will be booked on charges of attempted homicide, assault with deadly weapon, elder abuse, burglary and "several other additional felonies."

"This is an active investigation currently being led by the SFPD's special investigation's division," Scott said.

The Capitol Police said in a statement that Speaker Pelosi was in Washington with her protective detail at the time of the break-in. While “the motivation for the attack is still under investigation,” Capitol Police said it is assisting the FBI and the San Francisco Police Department with its investigation.

In an evening press conference Friday, Scott said the attack was not intentional but could not give more information. He also clarified that a neighbor called 911, not Paul Pelosi as previously reported.

Scott said the department could offer no new information, and referred inquiries about Pelosi's condition to a statement released by Pelosi's spokesperson Drew Hammill, which offered scant details. “Early this morning, an assailant broke into the Pelosi residence in San Francisco and violently assaulted Mr. Pelosi. The assailant is in custody and the motivation for the attack is under investigation. Mr. Pelosi was taken to the hospital, where he is receiving excellent medical care and is expected to make a full recovery. The Speaker was not in San Francisco at the time.

“The Speaker and her family are grateful to the first responders and medical professionals involved, and request privacy at this time."

article.title: McKinsey & Company remains on hook in class action over opioid crisis
article.description: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Global consulting firm McKinsey & Company must face multidistrict litigation seeking to hold it accountable for its part in fueling a nationwide opioid crisis with aggressive marketing strategies, after a federal judge found it…
article.text: SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Global consulting firm McKinsey & Company must face multidistrict litigation seeking to hold it accountable for its part in fueling a nationwide opioid crisis with aggressive marketing strategies, after a federal judge found it cannot use jurisdictional grounds to escape liability. McKinsey is accused of devising strategies for its client, Oxycontin maker Purdue Pharma, that boosted sales of high-dose pills with deceptive messaging to doctors that downplayed the risks of addiction. The plaintiffs are private citizens, city governments, Native American tribes, school districts, and children with neonatal abstinence syndrome from opioid exposure in the womb. They are from 19 states: Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Hawai’i, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wisconsin, and the cases have been consolidated into a multidistrict litigation. The plaintiffs argued that McKinsey consultants conducted extensive research that helped Purdue carry out a targeted marketing plan to increase sales. “McKinsey’s documents contain email after email describing its consultants riding along with Purdue’s sales team visiting doctors, including in Tennessee, Maryland, Indiana, Louisiana, and other states where McKinsey claims it did not work. For example, Purdue arranged to have a McKinsey consultant spend a day working with a sales representative in Tennessee,” a recent court filing says. “Don’t think McKinsey didn’t know the consequences of its field research and doctor targeting. McKinsey analyzed those, too, developing a method for Purdue to identify abuse and diversion hot spots — but without ever acting to address them. McKinsey knew exactly the places it was targeting and where the harms of its work impacted communities.” U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer, who is overseeing the sprawling case, sided with the plaintiffs in a ruling Thursday. “Plaintiffs have established that McKinsey committed intentional acts directed toward the subject states,” he wrote. “McKinsey performed numerous acts directed at the subject states. These acts included creating granular analyses of market attractiveness of the subject states, creating target lists of prescribers in the subject states, working alongside Purdue sales representatives in the subject states, and working with Purdue to implement sales strategies in the subject states.” In its bid to fend off negligence, fraud, public nuisance, and state consumer protection claims, McKinsey claimed it never manufactured, distributed or sold prescription painkillers in any of these states, nor has it ever interacted with any of the plaintiffs, “much less made any representations to them about opioids.” Accordingly, “McKinsey is not subject to expansive nationwide personal jurisdiction in the same way that other defendants in other opioid-related litigation may be," the company said. In rejecting that argument, Breyer wrote, “McKinsey effectively contends that it can help Purdue develop and manage strategies to increase opioid sales in the subject states, but that it cannot be subject to jurisdiction when those strategies result in increased opioid sales that cause harm in the subject states.” The judge determined the plaintiffs showed more than random negligence. “To the contrary, plaintiffs plausibly allege that McKinsey’s actions significantly contributed to the wide-ranging harms that have affected the subject states,” he wrote. "McKinsey is more akin to an advertising agency that advised a manufacturer on how to sell boilers to residents of specific states, despite knowing that the boilers carried a significant risk of exploding. There is no random or attenuated chain of contacts here. Plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that McKinsey intentionally and purposefully directed contacts at the subject states for several years.” He also found the plaintiffs had adequately asserted that McKinsey's methods to increase opioid sales caused foreseeable harm because their consultants delivered presentations to Purdue that mentioned prescribers' concerns about opioid abuse, and even worked with Purdue to “counter emotional messages from mothers with teenagers that overdosed in [sic] OxyContin.” Breyer’s ruling allows the litigation to move forward, though McKinsey will likely try to get it dismissed on the merits. Attorneys for the parties did not respond to requests for comment by press time. The decision comes just as the firm announced it had reached an agreement to settle lawsuits brought by school districts and local governments. The details of the agreement have not been made public, but the parties expect to have an update for Breyer at a hearing in December. McKinsey also admitted no wrongdoing as part of a nearly $600 million settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia and five territories last year. Follow @MariaDinzeo

The plaintiffs argued that McKinsey consultants conducted extensive research that helped Purdue carry out a targeted marketing plan to increase sales.

“McKinsey’s documents contain email after email describing its consultants riding along with Purdue’s sales team visiting doctors, including in Tennessee, Maryland, Indiana, Louisiana, and other states where McKinsey claims it did not work. For example, Purdue arranged to have a McKinsey consultant spend a day working with a sales representative in Tennessee,” a recent court filing says. “Don’t think McKinsey didn’t know the consequences of its field research and doctor targeting. McKinsey analyzed those, too, developing a method for Purdue to identify abuse and diversion hot spots — but without ever acting to address them. These acts included creating granular analyses of market attractiveness of the subject states, creating target lists of prescribers in the subject states, working alongside Purdue sales representatives in the subject states, and working with Purdue to implement sales strategies in the subject states.”

In its bid to fend off negligence, fraud, public nuisance, and state consumer protection claims, McKinsey claimed it never manufactured, distributed or sold prescription painkillers in any of these states, nor has it ever interacted with any of the plaintiffs, “much less made any representations to them about opioids.”
